axes.part: Tracy Fullerton's formal elements, drama, and interface

code: row (M mechanics · D dynamics · F feelings) + part number (1 players … 10 interface) + place in the cell, e.g. F6·1

patterns.name: Role Fulfillment
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of performing your role in the group well; it is frustrating if the group still loses.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Roles must be distinct, matter for the group's success, and be performable in ways players can see and recognise. Team results should depend on each role's contribution.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Roles that exist only as labels, with all players doing the same things and contributing the same way.
patterns.knobs: how different the roles are; how much the group result depends on each; how visible each player's contribution is

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Roles can require players to stay true to the game world, and that world-faithfulness can in turn shape what a role is, so each feeds the other.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: A role may demand behavior that fits the game's theme, and the theme can in turn help define the role, so they reinforce each other.

patterns.name: Minimalized Social Weight
patterns.what_it_is: The game barely gets in the way of people talking to each other during play.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must demand little attention and have natural pauses, with little bookkeeping and no long waits. Players should be able to stop and resume freely.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game described as casual or social that still demands constant attention or long upkeep, so conversation suffers.
patterns.knobs: how much attention the game demands; how easy it is to interrupt; how much upkeep it needs

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: When a game barely intrudes on the social setting around it, it can blend into everyday places and activities instead of standing apart from them.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Because the game doesn't pull attention away from people nearby, it fits easily into many different social situations and groups.

conflicts_with.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

conflicts_with.name: Cutscenes
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes are made to draw attention to the story presentation, which runs against keeping social aspects of play small.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: If players can talk and interact while doing chores, the chores feel lighter and less burdensome.

conflicts_with.name: Mimetic Interfaces
conflicts_with.why: These interfaces draw attention to the player because they involve visible physical performance, which works against keeping social pressure low.

patterns.name: Guilting
patterns.what_it_is: The game makes the player act by making them feel pangs of conscience.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need real connections with other players (teams, guilds, reciprocity) and a situation where their action or inaction visibly hurts or helps someone. Social dilemmas or requests for help create it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pop-up message saying 'your friends need you' with no real person affected and no connection, so nobody feels anything.
patterns.knobs: strength of social bonds; how visible others' needs or losses are; reciprocity rules

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Because guilt can be sent or received, players can take on roles such as the one who pressures others or the one who is pressured.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Players can become adept at making others feel guilty, or at dodging and resisting that feeling, which counts as a social skill.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Feeling guilt is unpleasant, so being pressured, or just seeing that it might happen, makes players feel uneasy and strained.

conflicts_with.name: Togetherness
conflicts_with.why: Guilting splits players into those blamed and those not blamed, which works against everyone feeling united.

patterns.name: Own Agenda
patterns.what_it_is: Algorithm-controlled characters appear to pursue goals of their own.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Agents need actions towards their own goals, plus visible emotional reactions to progress, success and failure, supported by memory and context-sensitive responses. The impression must survive repeat play without obvious scripted patterns.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character with a stated goal who behaves the same whatever happens and never shows any reaction to progress or setbacks.
patterns.knobs: how many agents have goals; how rich their emotional expression and memory are; how varied their reactions are

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: When agents show feelings about their goals, it can look like they are playing a role, though players may struggle to tell character actions from the agent's programmed acting.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Agents who display emotions tied to their goals and actions make the characters feel coherent with the game's world and theme.

can_cause.name: AI Players
can_cause.why: To act like a player, the AI needs its own goal, such as winning or playing as well as possible.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: The pattern changes how these agents play their characters by making them show more clearly that they have and pursue goals.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Players interact with companions more deeply, so it makes sense to prioritize showing their own agenda before that of other characters.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Agents playing non-player characters can be made to express that those characters have goals they are working toward.

conflicts_with.name: Scripted Information Sequences
conflicts_with.why: In games meant for replay, scripted sequences get seen repeatedly and become noticeable patterns, which undermines the impression that agents act from their own goals.

patterns.name: Togetherness
patterns.what_it_is: The feeling that you are playing with others, not alone.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must share a space or a goal over time and have chances for shared experience, such as joint success, shared failure, or moments to socialise. Group symbols and a sense of team identity help.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A team label or a multiplayer lobby where players act separately and never rely on or notice each other.
patterns.knobs: team size and stability; how much players depend on each other; room for social downtime

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: Feeling like one group makes outside reasons for splitting up matter less, so players come to treat each other as fellow participants rather than as the people behind the avatars.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: When togetherness makes players interact more, they are likely to settle into different roles within the group.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Feeling part of a group lets players be valued for their involvement, which gives social regard without requiring gameplay success.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: If players' sessions barely overlap, they have little chance to feel they are playing with each other.

conflicts_with.name: Guilting
conflicts_with.why: Guilting splits players into those blamed and those not blamed, which works against everyone feeling united.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Players who are removed have to sit out, so the group does not finish the session together.

conflicts_with.name: Ragequitting
conflicts_with.why: Feeling close to other players makes someone hesitate to quit since it hurts them, and an actual rage quit breaks that closeness.

conflicts_with.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
conflicts_with.why: When players start and stop at different times, they are rarely in the game together, which makes feeling united hard.

patterns.name: Team Accomplishments
patterns.what_it_is: The satisfaction of achieving something together with a group.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The task must truly need several players' contributions and be hard enough that success feels earned. Credit for the result must feel shared rather than attributed to one star.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A group completes the goal, but one player could have done it alone, so nobody feels it was joint.
patterns.knobs: how much each task depends on all members; difficulty; how success is shown to the group

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: When a group achieves something together, everyone involved can get recognition and good feelings from each other, so a shared success becomes a social payoff.

patterns.name: Actor Detachment
patterns.what_it_is: The player does not attribute other people's in-game behavior to their real personality.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Gameplay should depend on in-game skill rather than outside traits, with anonymity or minimal personal information and a welcoming theme and presentation. Players must have little reason or means to judge each other by who they are.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Usernames are hidden but voice chat or profiles still reveal identity, or the game rewards real-world traits, so people are still judged outside the game.
patterns.knobs: how much player identity is revealed; whether AI or anonymous play is used; how much outside skill matters

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: When players' outside identities matter less than how they play, more kinds of people can join comfortably, so the game fits a wider range of social situations.

conflicts_with.name: Chat Channels
conflicts_with.why: Chatting lets players reveal personal details beyond gameplay, undoing the hiding of identities that mediated play would otherwise give.

conflicts_with.name: Communication Channels
conflicts_with.why: Talking to each other lets players share, on purpose or by accident, more about themselves than the game itself requires.

conflicts_with.name: Friend Lists
conflicts_with.why: Choosing to play with friends means existing opinions about those people, good or bad, affect how the game is played.

conflicts_with.name: Player Physical Prowess
conflicts_with.why: Needing bodily ability lets who a person physically is decide how they do, so outside traits leak into the game.

conflicts_with.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
conflicts_with.why: When things done outside the game change its outcome, players' real-life circumstances shape play instead of only in-game actions.

conflicts_with.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Knowing things from outside the game gives some players an edge, so their background affects results more than their play.

conflicts_with.name: Social Roles
conflicts_with.why: Taking on social roles during play makes interaction between players important, which makes it harder to keep people's identities out of it.

patterns.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
patterns.what_it_is: Enjoyment from handling chaos and difficult situations together.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs chaotic, overwhelming situations that a group faces jointly, with enough pressure that coordination matters yet manageable enough to leave a sense of getting through. Shared goals or teams help.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Chaos where each player is overwhelmed alone, or chaos so total that success is impossible and play is just frustrating.
patterns.knobs: how chaotic and pressured the challenges are; how much players depend on each other

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: When a group fails to cope with the chaos, players may blame one another, so shared struggle can turn into feeling guilty or accusing teammates.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: If the group manages to get through the messy, overwhelming situation together, the success feels like something the whole team achieved.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Struggling through chaos side by side makes players feel they are doing something as a group, which builds a sense of being together.

patterns.name: Sense of Self
patterns.what_it_is: A computer-controlled character reacts fittingly to events and to its own state.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The agent must react consistently to threats and to its own state, and remember earlier events. A single obvious failure breaks the impression.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character that has health and a name but ignores danger or forgets what just happened to it.
patterns.knobs: how many situations it reacts to; how long it remembers; how consistent reactions are

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: When an agent consistently cares about its own situation, that concern is itself a kind of emotional attachment, one directed at the agent itself.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: Because the agent visibly looks after its own situation, it comes across as pursuing goals of its own rather than just following the game's script.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Agents that react sensibly to their own condition and surroundings behave in ways that fit the game world, which often helps keep the theme coherent.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: You add this pattern into an agent's algorithms, so that its reactions to events and its own state make it seem to care about itself.

patterns.name: Freedom of Choice
patterns.what_it_is: The player has several actions available, and each feels meaningful.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Provide options with visibly different and relevant effects, and let players see or believe their choices matter. Avoid a dominant best option.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several options exist, but one is clearly best or all give the same result, so choosing changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: number of meaningful options; how different their outcomes are; how visible the effects are

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Goals
can_cause.why: When players in a multiplayer game each pick their own goals, they end up chasing different things, so their objectives differ from one another.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Having many options and seeing how they lead to a goal helps players judge how likely they are to succeed, though unclear options can confuse them.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Offering more choices makes players feel they can shape the outcome more than they really can, even if actual impact is small.

can_cause.name: Framed Freedom
can_cause.why: Choice is a prerequisite for this pattern, though it may fail to deliver it when players feel pressured to pick among the options.

can_cause.name: Misfortune Mitigation
can_cause.why: Choosing the order in which to perform actions that depend on chance lets players soften bad luck, as in Bloodbowl.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Being able to choose lets players plan their actions, which often gives them a sense of acting purposefully on the game.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: When choices give players differing abilities, each session can play out differently, which gives them reason to play the game again.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When every available choice carries some downside alongside its benefit, players face uncomfortable decisions, including ones involving other players.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Having real options to choose between pushes players to think ahead about which actions to take, both during and around play.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Choice invites players to plan ahead before and after a game, for example by studying replays or full views of a finished session.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: With several actions to pick from, players must weigh them moment to moment during play, which calls for tactical thinking.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When all options come with some negative effect, picking one means giving up something else, so players must trade one thing for another.

can_cause.name: Units
can_cause.why: Controlling several units lets a player make more decisions than controlling a single avatar, so more units means more choices.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: If the available actions need different skills or allow different strategies, choosing among them makes each play experience differ.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Letting players choose among actions or goals is what creates the dilemma, even if having to choose at all can feel like a downside.

can_cause.name: Player-Created Characters
can_cause.why: When players can decide freely how characters are built or grow, those characters become the product of the players' own decisions.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Planning only makes sense if players can pick among options for how things grow, so having real choices makes it possible.

changes.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
changes.why: Choice lets players decide how their abstract construct grows, so development follows their own plans.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars give players choices from a specific point in the world, but if the avatar acts on its own, that freedom shrinks.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Players can pick which skills or powers to develop, so character growth reflects their preferences.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Players can create characters themselves or choose between roles, shaping the character they play.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Having several items to choose between gives players meaningful decisions about what to equip.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: Having lots of options is a reason to add lengthy actions, which trim the choices available while an action is underway.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Choices about how to explore a story matter because players don't know what comes, though once explored the choices lose meaning.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Players may choose among several random results or the order of chance-dependent actions, shaping how luck affects them.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Players can choose which skills to develop.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Choosing where to spawn is one of the variations that widen player options.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: Letting players pick which ability they get changes how the ability is gained and lets them plan ahead.

changes.name: Role Fulfillment
changes.why: Letting players choose or create their characters lets them pick roles they can fulfill, making success easier and more enjoyable.

changes.name: Time Limited Game Instances
changes.why: Letting players pick the length themselves before starting gives them a say over the time cap while the session stays bounded.

changes.name: Varying Turn Orders
changes.why: Players are allowed to change the order through their own actions, such as placing tokens, rather than it being decided by a fixed rule.

conflicts_with.name: Action Caps
conflicts_with.why: Unless the cap is used to grant extra actions, restricting how many things you may do reduces how free your choices are.

conflicts_with.name: Cutscenes
conflicts_with.why: In cutscenes, players or other agents are made to act as scripted, which limits what players can choose to do.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: While waiting, players cannot act, so they lose the ability to choose what they do.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
conflicts_with.why: Enforcing actions limits or removes what players can pick, particularly when control is taken away outright.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Weaving choices into chores makes them feel less like pointless work, softening the upkeep.

conflicts_with.name: Facilitating Rewards
conflicts_with.why: If players weren't allowed to pick what they get better at, the reward gives them power without real choice, working against their freedom.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Skilled players find only a few actions interesting, so many options lose their meaning.

conflicts_with.name: Helplessness
conflicts_with.why: Having meaningful choices makes players feel they can influence outcomes, which works against feeling powerless.

conflicts_with.name: Illusion of Open Space
conflicts_with.why: It may reveal that the freedom players assumed they had is not real.

conflicts_with.name: Invisible Walls
conflicts_with.why: They can expose that players lack the freedom of movement they first assumed.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: When combined with turn-taking or fixed story, other players' needs or directions restrict individual choice.

conflicts_with.name: No Direct Player Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players set up their characters but then cannot act during play, so no choices exist in the gameplay.

conflicts_with.name: No-Ops
conflicts_with.why: Forced skipping of actions removes options, typically as a penalty.

conflicts_with.name: Player-Created Characters
conflicts_with.why: Making many character choices up front can work against smooth learning.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Once a story branch is explored, the outcome is known, so choices there become meaningless.

conflicts_with.name: Repetitive Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Even with options, the same choices recur, so at a larger scale no real choice remains.

conflicts_with.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: The playable space gets smaller as play proceeds, which limits what players can do.

conflicts_with.name: Turn-Based Games
conflicts_with.why: Waiting for other players' turns in multiplayer removes choice during that time, though it is accepted as fair.

conflicts_with.name: Zero-Player Games
conflicts_with.why: All choices are made before the game begins and none after, so it conflicts in one sense but not another.

patterns.name: Gameplay Mastery
patterns.what_it_is: The ability to perform actions and reach goals in the game with confidence.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Skill must matter: outcomes depend on player choices and execution more than luck, with consistent rules, readable feedback and challenge that is reachable but keeps pushing. There must be room to improve over repeated play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game where results are mostly random or one dominant strategy wins, so 'getting better' is not real, or levelling up that does the work for the player.
patterns.knobs: balance of skill vs luck; difficulty and learning curve; depth and complexity of the rules

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When others can see that you are skilled, that visible competence can help you feel separate from the character you are playing.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Getting good at a game shows players that their own actions and decisions really shape what happens, giving them a sense of control.

can_cause.name: Predictable Winner
can_cause.why: When one player has clearly mastered the game, that player will usually beat the others, so the result becomes easy to foresee.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Players keep coming back for more sessions because they want to reach mastery, which takes repeated play.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: In cooperative games with different roles, being skilled lets a player perform their role well and do what the role requires.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Other people can notice and admire your skill, so showing mastery earns you recognition from them.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: In cooperative games with distinct roles, mastery lets players actually fill those roles, which gives the group its social structure.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: As players master their roles in cooperative play, they fulfill social roles, and that is how the team grows together.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: When players feel they have mastered something, they see that the time and effort they put into practicing paid off.

changes.name: Middlegame
changes.why: Players who know when to shift phases or rush the end change how the middle part of a game plays out.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Skilled players are less likely to fail, so their uncertainty about whether they will succeed is reduced.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: When player skill grows large, the character's own abilities matter less, and this has to be considered when designing such games.

conflicts_with.name: Algorithmic Agents
conflicts_with.why: Mastering a game means seeing characters as mechanical functions, which makes it hard to feel emotionally drawn to those agents.

conflicts_with.name: Auto-Aim
conflicts_with.why: When the game handles part of the aiming, players no longer need to develop skill at it, so there is less ability to master.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: When the game levels out differences, a skilled player gets less sense of being better than others.

conflicts_with.name: Card Building
conflicts_with.why: The page lists this as conflicting without giving a reason.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: As players learn to manipulate the game's systems, challenges become easy and may reduce to repetition, so tougher ones are needed.

conflicts_with.name: Character Development
conflicts_with.why: When characters grow stronger by themselves, the game helps the player, which reduces how much personal skill matters.

conflicts_with.name: Difficulty Levels
conflicts_with.why: If players choose easy levels just to finish or dominate, they skip the growth that real mastery needs.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players who fully understand the game and can no longer improve know exactly how much influence they have, so there is nothing left to exaggerate.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Skilled players find only a few actions interesting, so many options lose their meaning.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: Luck limits how far skill determines results, so it weakens the effect of mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: When players are not evenly matched, strong mastery makes it hard to build mechanics that keep the game balanced.

conflicts_with.name: Player Augmentations
conflicts_with.why: The game helping the player makes challenges easier, which lessens the importance of the player's own skill.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Strong mastery can make it hard to create mechanics that keep players on equal footing.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
conflicts_with.why: Great player mastery can make the character part unimportant and make it hard to keep the game balanced.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Paying lets one player get the same progress that another earns through skill, which undermines the value of mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance limits what player skill can achieve, so it works against mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Vision Modes
conflicts_with.why: Game-provided help with seeing makes challenges easier, so players need less of their own skill.

patterns.name: Casual Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: The game is easy to start, pause, and finish without spoiling the experience for oneself or others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Short or pausable sessions, a gentle learning curve, low stress and little punishment or dependence on other players' behaviour.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game is marketed as casual, but it demands long sessions, has harsh failure or punishes quitting midway.
patterns.knobs: session length; ease of pausing; difficulty ramp; amount of penalty and time pressure

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because players can start or stop whenever they like, they get to decide when and how long to play.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Easy-to-leave sessions plus building or puzzle activities let players treat play as relaxed, aimless tinkering.

conflicts_with.name: Betrayal
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal can make players depend on one another, which suits poorly with relaxed play that doesn't demand worry about others.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Casual play must be easy to take up, and demanding challenge works directly against that.

conflicts_with.name: Handicap Achievements
conflicts_with.why: Such achievements usually push players into harder play, which clashes with the easygoing nature of casual games.

conflicts_with.name: Social Dilemmas
conflicts_with.why: Casual games avoid situations that pit players against each other, and dilemmas create exactly that kind of social strain.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Casual play should be easy to stop and start without stress, but tension makes players feel unable to walk away.

patterns.name: Player Agency
patterns.what_it_is: The player can change the course of the game through their actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Choices must have visible, lasting consequences, and several options must be viable rather than one obvious best. The game must respond clearly to what the player did.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game offers many buttons and options, but the result is the same whatever the player picks, or the game plays itself.
patterns.knobs: number and meaningfulness of choices; how strongly and visibly actions change the state

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: When players use their ability to steer the game on purpose, their effort visibly changes the game state, so that effort feels worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Feeling that one's actions matter in the game is closely tied to perceiving influence over what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: Waiting removes the player's ability to act and influence the game, turning them into onlookers.

conflicts_with.name: Facilitating Rewards
conflicts_with.why: When the improvement is handed out rather than chosen by players, being stronger doesn't give them real control over their development, undermining agency.

conflicts_with.name: Helplessness
conflicts_with.why: Helplessness stops players from affecting how the game turns out, which directly takes away their agency.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: Players may feel a result was just luck rather than their own doing, which weakens their sense of control.

conflicts_with.name: Lucky Guess Solutions
conflicts_with.why: If players feel a guess did not come from their own intent, the success feels hollow and undermines their sense of control.

conflicts_with.name: No Direct Player Influence
conflicts_with.why: Without direct input during play, the game always acts to some degree on its own, which reduces players' sense of control.

conflicts_with.name: No-Ops
conflicts_with.why: Making players pass removes their ability to act on the game, so they have less control over what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Player Augmentations
conflicts_with.why: If players do not feel the enhanced abilities are under their control, the augmentations fail to give them real influence.

conflicts_with.name: Repetitive Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When there are no real choices to make, or no time to consider them, repeated play leaves players little influence.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Game States
conflicts_with.why: If players are trying to win but can no longer do so, their actions stop mattering to the goal they are pursuing.

conflicts_with.name: Zero-Player Games
conflicts_with.why: The game runs without players acting at all, so there is nothing for them to influence.

conflicts_with.name: Game Time Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: When one player's time manipulation is applied in a multiplayer game, it typically takes away the other players' ability to make meaningful choices that affect the game.

patterns.name: Lull Periods
patterns.what_it_is: Stretches of the game when players do not need to rush their actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have stretches with no urgent threats, such as gaps between waves, and not force fast actions. Players need to know it is safe for the break to feel relaxing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A break is announced but threats keep coming or timers keep running, so no relaxation occurs.
patterns.knobs: length of breaks; how often they come; whether threats are fully absent

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: With no pressure to react fast, players can wander around and fiddle with things casually, so the calm stretch becomes a time for aimless tinkering.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When nothing urgent demands a response, players have spare time and attention to think ahead and plan their next moves.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Quiet stretches with little gameplay let players chat and socialize without having to act in the game, which builds closeness.

changes.name: Waves
changes.why: Calm gaps placed between successive attack waves give players a break, as seen when intense enemy rushes are separated by quiet moments.

conflicts_with.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Constant focus is required, so quiet periods where nothing demands attention cannot coexist with this kind of play.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Tension requires players to feel pressured, while calm periods are defined by the absence of stress, so the two work against each other.

patterns.name: Gamer Mode
patterns.what_it_is: The player sees the game as a system of rules and looks for winning tricks in it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs to make effort feel worthwhile and the player absorbed, with clear goals and feedback so they willingly commit and treat play as serious. The page is a stub, so this is inferred from the patterns it lists.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Labelling a mode or menu option 'gamer' or 'hardcore' without any change in challenge, stakes or engagement.
patterns.knobs: how much effort the game demands and how clearly that effort is rewarded

patterns.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
patterns.what_it_is: The game helps estimate how likely a planned action is to succeed or fail.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must have consequences players can predict, and the game must give enough information or experience to let them estimate the odds. The estimate can be a little wrong but must be usable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Odds are shown as a number that has no link to what really happens, so players can't judge anything from it.
patterns.knobs: how much information on odds is shown; how much hidden randomness there is

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players believe they can read their odds, they may read them too optimistically and feel more in control than they really are.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Feeling that success is possible but not guaranteed makes players invested in each attempt, which builds suspense about how it will turn out.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Knowing the odds of several different actions gives players real options, so the choice between ways of trying and reasons for acting becomes meaningful.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: Since the game shifts help and penalties to players, they cannot reliably calculate their own odds of success.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Feeling empowered by knowing your odds is fragile, since challenges can feel so hard that success seems impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Enemies whose abilities or odds are hidden make it hard for players to tell how likely they are to win.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: This pattern makes players overestimate their odds, so what they believe no longer matches their true chance.

conflicts_with.name: Fudged Results
conflicts_with.why: Secretly altering outcomes means the odds players think they face are not the real ones.

conflicts_with.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
conflicts_with.why: Sudden overwhelming events can wipe out whatever sense of their odds players had built up.

patterns.name: Framed Freedom
patterns.what_it_is: Choice feels rich but does not overwhelm with too many options or the need to prioritize.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Offer a small, clearly presented set of actions with limited resources, and open goals without forcing or timing them. Players must feel agency, not obligation or overload.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A menu lists lots of options, but a timer or forced objective pushes one path, so the freedom is only felt on the surface.
patterns.knobs: number of distinct action types; how strongly goals and time pressure are imposed

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Because the options on offer are kept few and clear, players aren't swamped, yet they still pick among them and see their choices matter.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: With pressure from choices lowered, players can set modest goals and tinker at ease, which makes relaxed, aimless-feeling activity a natural fit.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Framed freedom often works by giving players only limited resources to work with, so deciding how to use and spend them becomes a central activity.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Framed freedom is meant to let players set goals without much pressure, so anything that brings tense, high-stakes feelings works against that calm.

patterns.name: Tension
patterns.what_it_is: Worry about the outcome when you cannot fully control it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must care about the result and not control it fully, with real stakes for losing. Uncertainty has to be real and not too easy to see through.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Dramatic music and a countdown, but failure costs nothing and the outcome is certain.
patterns.knobs: size of stakes; amount of randomness or hidden information; closeness of outcomes

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Strong feelings from tense play can carry over from the game into real life, especially when real rewards or statuses are attached to the outcome.

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Some players actually enjoy the stress of tense play, so for them the discomfort becomes a pleasure in itself.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Feeling suspense about possible failure, and still feeling it while the failure slowly unfolds, sets up the enjoyment of watching it happen.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Being under stress makes it harder to perform precise actions like aiming.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Feeling tense makes careful planning harder to carry out.

conflicts_with.name: Casual Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Casual play should be easy to stop and start without stress, but tension makes players feel unable to walk away.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: Idle players tend to feel less tension, though it can arise if they expect something bad to happen.

conflicts_with.name: Framed Freedom
conflicts_with.why: Framed freedom is meant to let players set goals without much pressure, so anything that brings tense, high-stakes feelings works against that calm.

conflicts_with.name: Game Pauses
conflicts_with.why: Stopping the action lets players disengage, which can dissipate the tension that continuous play builds up.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: When entities cannot be hurt, there is little at stake, so the feeling of danger fades.

conflicts_with.name: Narration Structures
conflicts_with.why: A story can lack tension itself, or block players who want to interact with the game system, which reduces tension.

conflicts_with.name: No-Ops
conflicts_with.why: Too many idle moves wear down suspense, even though some forced or voluntary waiting can build it.

conflicts_with.name: Pottering
conflicts_with.why: Constant tension keeps players stressed about their activities, which works against the relaxed, self-directed nature of pottering.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: A certain winner drains the tension about who will win, though tension might still exist over who comes second.

conflicts_with.name: Private Game Spaces
conflicts_with.why: Without direct interference from others, play feels less pressured, so games with private spaces are less likely to be tense.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: Tension depends on not knowing what comes next, and experiencing the same situations again makes it weaker.

conflicts_with.name: Safe Havens
conflicts_with.why: Safe places let players relax, which reduces stress, so they can undercut the pressure a game builds.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: Once you can undo a dangerous moment by reloading, you experience it without the emotional strain it was meant to cause.

conflicts_with.name: Turn Taking
conflicts_with.why: On your turn you can plan without interruption, which can lower or remove tension.

conflicts_with.name: Lull Periods
conflicts_with.why: Tension requires players to feel pressured, while calm periods are defined by the absence of stress, so the two work against each other.

patterns.name: Challenging Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: The player feels the game is testing their skills to the limit.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The difficulty must match the player's skill, failure must be possible but recoverable, and success must be seen as the player's own doing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies simply have inflated numbers, or the game is difficult through opaque rules or luck, so players feel cheated rather than challenged.
patterns.knobs: enemy strength; margin for error; difficulty levels or adaptive difficulty; pace of the ramp

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When hard challenges meet real-time pressure, play turns chaotic, and players who keep going through the mess enjoy the mayhem and feel skilled.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Handling tough challenges, whether judged against your own past results or what others find hard, signals that your skills are actually improving.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: To stay challenging over time, tasks must keep getting harder, which naturally produces ever bigger goals and wrap-ups as the game advances.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: When tasks are hard, players can't be sure they will pull them off, so the result of their own effort stays in doubt.

can_cause.name: Ragequitting
can_cause.why: Hard challenges make failure likely, and repeated failing, especially when teammates fail to cooperate, can make players angrily quit.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Even when players lose at a hard challenge, the way they fail can be entertaining, so losing isn't always unpleasant.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because difficult tasks carry a real risk of failing, players feel nervous strain while attempting them.

changes.name: Endgame Quests
changes.why: Adding difficulty to final quests makes them feel more important within the game.

changes.name: Finale Levels
changes.why: Making last levels especially hard, often with boss fights, raises their significance.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Real-time movement that must account for acceleration, momentum, and turn radius is made harder.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Skill gaps between competitors can make the game too hard for some, while stronger opponents offer rising challenge.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Differences in skill make the game too hard for some and too easy for others, upsetting fairness.

changes.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
changes.why: Speeding up the pace at which actions must be performed makes them harder.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Single-player campaigns can be reused with different challenging goals, such as time limits, to keep them demanding.

conflicts_with.name: Casual Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Casual play must be easy to take up, and demanding challenge works directly against that.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: Feeling empowered by knowing your odds is fragile, since challenges can feel so hard that success seems impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players feel they have no chance, the hard challenge undermines their sense of being influential.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: As players learn to manipulate the game's systems, challenges become easy and may reduce to repetition, so tougher ones are needed.

conflicts_with.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
conflicts_with.why: Taking away map aids or outlines, as in realism mode, makes finding things harder, so the aids work against challenge.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Repeating easy tasks once mastered counters the idea of challenge, though grinding can also be turned into one.

conflicts_with.name: Improved Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Stronger characters can make tasks easy, so too much improvement erases the challenge.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Uneven skill among competitors can make the game too hard for some and too easy for others.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Hard challenges make it difficult for varied groups to play together unless challenges are optional or balanced by handicaps.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: When players come and go, the difficulty may no longer fit the remaining group, making it hard to keep the game demanding.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: In games that never end, players grow more skilled and more powerful, which can make the challenge too easy unless difficulty rises too.

patterns.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
patterns.what_it_is: The player feels they affect the outcome, whether or not they really do.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give players many visible options and strong-feeling feedback for their actions, such as buffs, tools and abilities, while keeping the real outcome only loosely tied to them. It has to stay hidden: if players figure out the trick, or fully master the game, the feeling collapses.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A flashy upgrade or button that plainly does nothing, which players spot quickly and then feel cheated rather than powerful.
patterns.knobs: how strong and how numerous the visible player controls are, compared with their real effect on the outcome

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When players feel their choices matter, they are encouraged to think ahead and plan, though limited foresight and planning ability in the game restrict this.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Feeling that their actions shape the game makes players believe their effort counts, so what they do seems important.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: Players feel they affect results, such as by starting a random process, even though they are really only watching the outcome unfold.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Players who overrate or misjudge how much their skill matters become unsure whether their performance will be enough.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Even if players' real impact is small, making their actions feel important gives them the impression that they steer the game.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If players feel their choices matter, they keep believing that learning more will help them, so they are willing to replay.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: When a game is so complex that beginners do not know the consequences of their actions, the perception of influence lets them feel they can still affect it.

changes.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
changes.why: The perception can make players believe they have more room to improve than they actually do.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: It makes players unsure about their own performance, which can hide a predictable winner and keep play feeling meaningful.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Having more choices makes players feel they shape the outcome more.

conflicts_with.name: Ability Losses
conflicts_with.why: Losing abilities shrinks what players can do, which tends to weaken their feeling that they have great influence over the game.

conflicts_with.name: Algorithmic Agents
conflicts_with.why: When players create agents beforehand and the game then runs without their input, they can't feel more influential than they truly are; shared control with agents also muddles agency.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: If players can see that balancing is what tipped the result, they no longer feel their own actions made the difference.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: If players feel they have no chance, the hard challenge undermines their sense of being influential.

conflicts_with.name: Cutscenes
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes remove player agency, which makes it hard to also make players feel their influence is larger than it is.

conflicts_with.name: Decreased Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Weakened abilities tend to be felt as penalties, which makes it hard for players to believe their influence on the game is bigger than it is.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: This pattern makes players overestimate their odds, so what they believe no longer matches their true chance.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: Those who just arrived or soon leave cannot have shaped the game much, so feeling very influential is hard.

conflicts_with.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
conflicts_with.why: If players can spot cases where the system rather than they themselves decided the result, the false sense of control can collapse instead of growing.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Opponents can offset players' gains and, when more difficult than expected, work against the feeling of influence.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
conflicts_with.why: Having actions forced, especially during cutscenes, makes it hard for players to feel they have more control than they do.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: A game master who uses powerful events too freely overrides players' actions and works against their sense of influence.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Players who fully understand the game and can no longer improve know exactly how much influence they have, so there is nothing left to exaggerate.

conflicts_with.name: Helplessness
conflicts_with.why: Being unable to act undermines the sense of influence, although dependence in multiplayer games can sometimes still produce it.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptible Actions
conflicts_with.why: Actions that can be interrupted add uncertainty that makes any displayed success chance inaccurate, which can lower the perceived influence.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: Social dynamics where players decide who wins can leave a single player with little influence, particularly when in the lead.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Other players can reduce a person's influence through balancing, shared penalties, alliances and voting, which weakens the perception.

conflicts_with.name: No-Ops
conflicts_with.why: Forced moments of doing nothing make it hard to maintain a global sense of influence.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Consistent Narration
conflicts_with.why: When separate game instances do not affect the larger story, players' sense of power over the narrative is limited.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: If outsiders easily change the game state, players have a harder time feeling that their own choices were what mattered.

conflicts_with.name: Player Augmentations
conflicts_with.why: Aids that perform actions for players can make them lose the sense of their own agency, depending on how they see it.

conflicts_with.name: Player Kicking
conflicts_with.why: Players who can be removed by others may lose their sense of influence, even though kicking others feels powerful.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: A set story limits possible actions and event order, which restricts how much influence players feel they have.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: When the winner is clear, players can see their influence is small, though the exaggerated perception can mask this.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: If players do not feel lucky, chance counters the effect, and players who know the statistics will not hold the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Scripted Information Sequences
conflicts_with.why: If players notice that information follows a script, they realize events are predetermined and feel less influential.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Players may suffer penalties they did not cause and could not avoid, which clearly shows how little control they have.

conflicts_with.name: Skills
conflicts_with.why: Skills often state success likelihood, and deterministic skill tests leave less room for misjudging influence.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Knowledge
conflicts_with.why: Players who know the statistics or hidden systems can see through the hidden help or randomness and lose the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Surprise Attacks
conflicts_with.why: Events that cannot be anticipated cannot be influenced by players, which destroys the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Time Pressure
conflicts_with.why: Little time to consider options limits planning, which works against feeling that choices have an effect.

conflicts_with.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
conflicts_with.why: These events develop beyond players' control, so even if players trigger them they cannot affect how they unfold.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: Since players cannot truly win, a global sense of influence is hard to keep, so designers rely on local influence.

conflicts_with.name: Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Suffering a penalty can shatter players' belief that they have great control over what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Players know a game does not promise they will keep playing to the finish, which undermines feeling overly powerful.

conflicts_with.name: Zero-Player Games
conflicts_with.why: With no choices during play, players have little to feel influential about unless the set-up phase is designed to give that feeling.

patterns.name: Luck
patterns.what_it_is: The feeling that random events are not fully random and tend to work out in the player's favor.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Random outcomes with visible uncertainty, plus ways for players to feel they may influence them, such as choosing when to roll or risking something. The outcome reveal needs to be noticeable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Random results occur but are hidden or happen without the player's involvement, so they never feel lucky.
patterns.knobs: how random the outcomes are; how visible the roll is; how much the player can bet or choose

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Feeling lucky makes players believe their own actions or wishes steered a random result, so they overrate how much control they had.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Having an unusually large run of good fortune stands out from normal play, so it gets noticed as a remarkable occurrence.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: When players sense luck is on their side, they may feel their choices matter, though they may also dismiss results as just luck.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Hoping for luck while the outcome is still unknown keeps players on edge, especially when results arrive later and they can't be sure.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: When results come from chance, players can feel fortunate or unfortunate without actually steering anything in the game.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Chances
conflicts_with.why: With retries, a good result needs less luck, and others' bad luck is less likely to benefit you.

conflicts_with.name: Fixed Distributions
conflicts_with.why: When players succeed at using the known mix to predict or soften outcomes, results feel earned rather than lucky, which weakens the feeling of luck.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: When success comes from chance, players have less control, so there is little reason to think getting better would matter.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Luck limits how far skill determines results, so it weakens the effect of mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Goal Achievements
conflicts_with.why: If chance can stand in for skill, such as a random enemy attack being hit by accident, the achievement stops proving mastery and drifts toward grinding.

conflicts_with.name: Misfortune Mitigation
conflicts_with.why: Opponents' mitigation can counter a player's luck and spoil the feeling of being fortunate.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: Players may feel a result was just luck rather than their own doing, which weakens their sense of control.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: If players already know what will happen, there is nothing left to feel lucky about.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Knowledge
conflicts_with.why: Knowing the odds or what will happen reduces the room for outcomes to feel like fortune.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: When luck rather than effort decides outcomes, players can't feel that their hard work paid off.

patterns.name: Solution Uncertainty
patterns.what_it_is: The player does not know whether a solution to the task exists, which creates uncertainty.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The challenge must be complex or information-poor enough that players cannot tell the answer at once, and the answer must not be easily learned from earlier plays. Players must believe a solution may exist.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A puzzle with an obvious answer or one that can be brute-forced by trying every option, or a puzzle whose solution is copied from a guide.
patterns.knobs: amount of hidden information; size of the option space; how much feedback hints at the answer

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: When players must work out what to do and many options exist, they can get stuck thinking too long about which action is right.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because the difficulty lies in working out what to do, players face a mental challenge that takes effort to overcome.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: Uncertainty about solutions makes players think about how to manipulate the game state, rather than just directly changing it, which supports this kind of play.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: When the main task is figuring out which actions reach the goal, play naturally becomes solving a puzzle.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: Players who cannot work out what is coming or what the solution is cannot foresee an attack, so they become easy targets.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Not knowing the right course of action pushes players to think ahead and plan their moves.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: If players don't know whether or how a goal can be reached, the result of the game stays open.

can_cause.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
can_cause.why: Since it is hard to know who has found or will find the best solution, the winner can stay unclear until play is over.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: Challenges built on finding a solution lose their improvement value once the solution is known, unless something else is added.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Knowledge
conflicts_with.why: If players bring knowledge from earlier games, the solution may become obvious, which removes the uncertainty the game relies on.

patterns.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
patterns.what_it_is: Enjoyment when things are going badly but the player keeps fighting.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Real-time pressure, more demands than the player can comfortably handle, and difficulty rising with skill, while keeping success still possible. Failure must seem close but not certain.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The screen is busy with enemies and effects, but the game is easy or pausable, so there is no pressure to cope.
patterns.knobs: density and simultaneity of threats; difficulty ramp rate; time pressure

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Because players must perform at their very best just to stay in the fight, they come away feeling skilled, and the pattern arguably produces that real skill.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: The enjoyment is the pleasant side of an outcome that stays undecided, since players are constantly on the edge of failing yet still fighting.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: The fun comes from handling hard challenges in chaotic, stressful conditions, so how well players cope is inherently in question.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When players do finally fail, the situation was already chaotic or extremely hard, so the collapse itself becomes entertaining.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment is the same enjoyment of chaotic, hard situations, just made to happen for a group rather than one person.

patterns.name: Time Pressure
patterns.what_it_is: The game creates a feeling that you must act and reach goals quickly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A real deadline or a race against others, committed goals, and a time budget that is tight for the players' skill level. Players must be able to sense the clock through indicators or alarms.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A visible timer that is so loose, or so lightly penalised, that nobody feels hurried or changes how they act.
patterns.knobs: time budget relative to task difficulty; severity of failure; how visible the clock is

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: Having little time to plan means players may freeze up while trying to decide, so the hurry itself can cause the very stalling it seems to prevent.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Worrying about finishing before time runs out makes players nervous about possibly failing, and that worry is felt as tension.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: How much time is allowed has to suit how complex the game is, since a limit that rushes a beginner may not trouble an expert.

conflicts_with.name: Analysis Paralysis
conflicts_with.why: Limited time to plan usually stops players from overthinking, yet it can also push them into freezing, so the effect goes both ways.

conflicts_with.name: Pottering
conflicts_with.why: Having to act quickly causes stress and removes the freedom to take one's time, which pottering depends on.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Little time to consider options limits planning, which works against feeling that choices have an effect.

patterns.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: You can play almost any time and in most places with little preparation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must need little setup or equipment, work without a fixed place or simultaneous players (for example asynchronous play), and allow short interruptible sessions.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A mobile app that needs a constant connection, a long session or a quiet setting, so it still can't be played at most times and places.
patterns.knobs: required equipment and connection; whether play is asynchronous; session length

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because a game can be played almost anywhere and anytime, it is easier to start, which lowers the barrier needed for casual play.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Playing in many everyday contexts makes it hard to prevent the game from having effects on things outside the game itself.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: Since play happens in varied surroundings, outside things unavoidably feed into the game, so such input tends to appear even if unplanned.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: When play can happen anywhere, it can blend into other everyday activities, which is what makes gameplay pervasive.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: A game that can be played in most places and times can be fitted to whatever social situation players are in.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Playing in public places makes it likely that bystanders watch, even if they do not realize a game is happening.

can_cause.name: Tiered Participation
can_cause.why: If only some of a game's interactions can be done anywhere, players taking part that way end up at a different level of involvement.

conflicts_with.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: Since play needs the facilitator to be present, the game cannot be played anywhere and anytime.

conflicts_with.name: Game Boards
conflicts_with.why: A physical board forces players to be near it to play, which works against gameplay that can happen anywhere.

conflicts_with.name: Game Element Trading
conflicts_with.why: Making trading central requires either players everywhere or electronic exchange of elements, which is hard to combine with play available anywhere.

conflicts_with.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
conflicts_with.why: Players need less than a whole game to play, but they must still have their own pieces, or carry spare ones for others to borrow.

conflicts_with.name: Memorabilia
conflicts_with.why: Physical keepsakes must be handed to players, so needing them in hand works against letting people play anywhere and anytime.

conflicts_with.name: Seamful Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The pattern relies on dead spots, so a game designed to work everywhere has no gaps to exploit, making the two hard to combine.

conflicts_with.name: Algorithmic Agents
conflicts_with.why: Agents are usually run by computer code, so needing a computer limits play to places and settings where computers are available.

patterns.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: The boundary is blurred, so it is unclear whether events belong to the game or to real life.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Game information must be hidden within ordinary media and activities, with several channels and imperfect information, plus puppetmasters who react to players. Players need to be able to mistake it for non-game content.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game is marketed as 'alternate reality' but is clearly labeled and runs in one app, so nobody is ever unsure.
patterns.knobs: how well game content is disguised; number of media used; how much staff react live

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: Because performers and ordinary people are mixed into the game and rules on player actions are loose, outsiders may end up assisting players without meaning to.

can_cause.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
can_cause.why: Game events can be tied to particular physical locations, so many such games end up played partly in actual places rather than only on screens.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Games use public media and everyday settings, so bystanders can watch what happens, even without realizing they are watching a game.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When players can't tell whether something belongs to the game, that doubt adds an extra layer of unease on top of the normal challenge.

patterns.name: Replayability
patterns.what_it_is: How many new challenges, lessons, and experiences the game offers when played again.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each playthrough needs different challenges or room to improve, through randomness, many routes, or goals that differ. Outcomes must stay uncertain and mastery must not run out quickly.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Randomness that changes only surface details, so every run plays out as the same solved sequence.
patterns.knobs: amount of variation between plays (randomness, content size); depth of mastery available

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When players can imagine several different ways to approach the game next time, they start thinking ahead about how they might play differently.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Replaying invites players to consider alternative ways of playing, which leads them to plan their approach deliberately before and during later sessions.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Replayable games tend to give different experiences from one session to the next, so play does not feel identical each time.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: In games meant to be replayed, an agent's apparent agenda is strengthened in later plays by variation such as differing fates for the agents.

conflicts_with.name: Algorithmic Agents
conflicts_with.why: If players fully understand computer opponents that never vary in their destiny, there is nothing new left to discover on replay.

conflicts_with.name: Memorizing
conflicts_with.why: If remembered information can directly solve a puzzle, later playthroughs become trivial because the answers are already known.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: When a game is replayed and the story reused, players can predict it and lose surprises.

conflicts_with.name: Puzzle Solving
conflicts_with.why: If the same puzzles appear every session, players already know the answers, so there is little reason to play again.

conflicts_with.name: Quizzes
conflicts_with.why: Once a player has learned a question's correct answer, there is nothing left to figure out about it, so playing the same quiz again is less interesting.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Knowledge
conflicts_with.why: If players come to know everything about how to play well, replaying has no purpose because nothing remains to learn.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Tension depends on not knowing what comes next, and experiencing the same situations again makes it weaker.

conflicts_with.name: Unknown Goals
conflicts_with.why: Once players have played, the goals they didn't know about become known, so the mystery is absent in later sessions.

conflicts_with.name: Scripted Information Sequences
conflicts_with.why: Seeing the same sequence repeat across playthroughs reveals its artificial nature, weakening the illusion that characters act independently.

patterns.name: Value of Effort
patterns.what_it_is: The feeling that the effort put into the game is worth something.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need real agency, visible feedback that links their actions to outcomes, and some permanence of results, such as persistent worlds, self-set goals or measurable improvement. Effort that gets overwritten or ignored kills it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Reward screens and numbers pop up regardless of what the player did, so effort and outcome are unrelated.
patterns.knobs: how permanent results are; clarity of feedback on actions; proportion of outcome that depends on player choices

can_cause.name: Gamer Mode
can_cause.why: If effort feels too valuable in a game meant for another purpose, such as teaching, players may fixate on playing well and ignore that purpose.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When effort matters, each action counts for more, so players feel pressure to succeed with it.

conflicts_with.name: Backtracking Levels
conflicts_with.why: Without an extra reward at the far point, walking all the way back feels like effort that earns nothing, weakening the sense that effort pays off.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: If leaders are penalized and trailing players helped, hard work counts for less in the final standing.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: Help given to newcomers can make the hard work of those already playing seem to count for less.

conflicts_with.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
conflicts_with.why: Adapting the challenge to the player can cast doubt on whether effort led to success, though skillful use may avoid it.

conflicts_with.name: Fudged Results
conflicts_with.why: If results can often be overridden, players' skill and effort matter less, so fudges must be rare or limited.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: If players realize their repeated actions barely affect progress, the sense that effort is worthwhile is undercut.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptible Actions
conflicts_with.why: If an action can be interrupted and fail, the effort already put into it may be wasted, undermining the sense that work pays off.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: If players get something from their play even when they can't win, they have less reason to quit or unbalance the game by kingmaking.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Newcomers can get benefits that others worked for, such as rewards, or lack them, which makes earlier effort feel less valuable.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: When luck rather than effort decides outcomes, players can't feel that their hard work paid off.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Late joiners, undone effects or less effective story influence can make some players' work count for less.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: When outsiders do things easily for players, the players feel their own work counts for less.

conflicts_with.name: Player Augmentations
conflicts_with.why: Because help reduces how much player skill and work determine results, their effort seems to matter less.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Players lose all value of what they invested when forced out before finishing, which damages their feeling that effort pays off.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
conflicts_with.why: If player mastery outweighs character growth, the effort spent on building the character feels less valuable, and vice versa.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: When the winner is obvious, trailing players feel their effort no longer matters.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: When others can simply buy what you worked for, your achievements feel less worthwhile.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: When chance heavily affects outcomes or can flip success into failure, players feel their effort matters less.

conflicts_with.name: Repetitive Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Repetition can leave players feeling their work achieves little, though it can also make them feel proud of having endured it.

conflicts_with.name: Setback Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Losing progress already earned can make players feel their earlier work was wasted, which undermines the sense that effort pays off.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Game States
conflicts_with.why: If winning is impossible, nothing a player does can pay off toward victory, so their effort feels wasted.

patterns.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
patterns.what_it_is: As the game goes on, the stages that get completed become more and more significant.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Later achievements must be bigger in stakes, rarity, and effect than earlier ones, supported by gating, rising difficulty, or goal hierarchies, and checked in playtests. Late moments need to feel meaningfully more important, not just harder.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Later goals are just the same task with bigger numbers, so finishing them feels no more significant than the first one.
patterns.knobs: how much importance or reward grows per stage; spacing and gating of milestones

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: The page only lists this relation in its consequences, saying closures that grow in importance typically bring tension, without explaining what in play causes it.

changes.name: Encouraged Return Visits
changes.why: Closures that grow stronger with play time reinforce the other tricks used to bring players back.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Gameplay closures can be lined up with story closures, letting this pattern shape how the narrative is structured.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: Boss monsters and finale levels show how rising closures can alter goals of beating obstacles by making the later ones bigger payoffs.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Gameplay closures can be matched to planned story beats, so the pattern can shape how those fixed stories unfold.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Because the game never ends, it is hard to keep making closures steadily more intense, so the two rarely combine.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: With no way to win, there is no building toward ever-larger closures, so the two generally can't be combined.

patterns.name: Hovering Closures
patterns.what_it_is: An upcoming event that the player can clearly see in advance.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to see a specific upcoming outcome and have reason to care, and it needs time to loom (a timer, a delay, a visible progress). The outcome must remain uncertain or influenceable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An outcome shown in the interface that is unavoidable, trivial, or too hidden to notice, so nobody feels any suspense.
patterns.knobs: how visible the pending outcome is; how long the delay is; how much stands to be gained or lost

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When players can clearly see an outcome approaching, good or bad, they feel anticipation and strain while waiting for it to resolve.

conflicts_with.name: Complex Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Too many requirements, or ones shown unclearly, keep players from feeling any goal is nearly reached.

patterns.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
