patterns.what_it_is: Enjoyment from losing or making a mistake in a loud and dramatic way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Failure must be dramatic, visible and slow enough to watch, and the game must be hard enough for mistakes to snowball. Players must be willing to take the stakes lightly.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A plain game over screen or quiet elimination, or failure that is punishing and silent so nobody laughs or retells it.
patterns.knobs: difficulty level; how much mistakes cascade; how visible failures are; how fast failure unfolds

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: A spectacular failure is comical or remarkable, so it turns into an unusual moment that stands out from ordinary play.

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Because these failures are unusual and memorable, players want to retell them to others, making them good material for stories about a particular play session.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Going through misfortune together and enjoying it creates a bond among players who shared the mishap.

conflicts_with.name: Ragequitting
conflicts_with.why: A player who enjoys failing in dramatic ways is not frustrated by it, and rage quitting needs that frustration, so the two experiences can't coexist.

patterns.name: Ragequitting
patterns.what_it_is: A player abandons the session out of anger, without thinking how it affects others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It emerges when frustration rises beyond tolerance, often from repeated failure, unfair treatment or betrayal. Designers mainly limit it through fairness, mitigation of its effects and easy exits.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A quit penalty exists, but players leave calmly and not out of anger, so it is plain quitting.
patterns.knobs: frustration level and difficulty; quit penalties; how well the game absorbs a departure

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: Designers can attach an award to staying through a whole session, so a stretch where people often walk out gets an incentive to remain.

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: When a rage-quitter leaves because of anger over what happened in play, the practical result is that they give up on that game.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: A player who storms out leaves their team short-handed, and the team may also be where the player aims their frustration, such as through own goals.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: In sports-style games, an NPC that gives up when its mood sours shows its state in a believable way.

conflicts_with.name: Achievements
conflicts_with.why: Achievements may be tied to a game ending early or to staying through, so a player leaving a match can clash with earning one.

conflicts_with.name: Communication Channels
conflicts_with.why: The sense of togetherness that talking creates can work against players angrily leaving, so the two pull in opposite directions.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: Easy joining and leaving softens the damage of a quitter but clashes with designs wanting everyone to commit to finishing the whole session together.

conflicts_with.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
conflicts_with.why: A player who enjoys failing in dramatic ways is not frustrated by it, and rage quitting needs that frustration, so the two experiences can't coexist.

conflicts_with.name: Togetherness
conflicts_with.why: Feeling close to other players makes someone hesitate to quit since it hurts them, and an actual rage quit breaks that closeness.

patterns.name: Thematic Consistency
patterns.what_it_is: Characters, items, and their behavior fit together with the theme of the world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters, objects, rules and behavior must all follow the same set of expectations, and features that break the theme must be avoided or explained. Rules should plausibly follow from the fiction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The art matches a theme, but rules and behavior contradict it, so the setting is only decoration.
patterns.knobs: how strictly rules follow the fiction; level of detail in setting; how many off-theme features are allowed

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: When a game follows a theme players already know, they can guess what actions, events and especially penalties will do, so outcomes feel foreseeable.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: A theme can suggest roles as goals, and players who follow the theme by playing their role in character keep the game consistent, so each supports the other.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Items in a set nearly always share a theme with each other, and that shared theme is part of what defines them as a set.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: If a game fits a theme the player already knows, they arrive with expectations about how it works and what to do, giving them a head start.

can_cause.name: Feelies
can_cause.why: A player aid becomes a feelie when its design matches the game's theme, so thematic fit is part of what makes it count.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: A story prepared in advance has to fit the game's theme, so keeping the theme consistent is what lets the story elements feel like they belong.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: When players are encouraged to stay true to the game's theme while roleplaying, they more readily adopt roles for their characters.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Theme affects how agents should look and act, requiring believable behavior while they remain interactive.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: The theme can require alarms and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Computer-run agents can easily be forced to behave as the theme requires, though capturing human nuance takes extra effort.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: The theme can require avatars and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: The theme can require boss monsters and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: Clues that fit the theme let players draw on their knowledge of the genre, but clues made as non-diegetic features do not fit.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: The theme can require companions and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Clues that fit the theme let players use their knowledge of the genre, which shapes how the detective structure works.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: The theme can require enemies and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: The theme can require environmental effects and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: The theme can require items and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Many themes imply large game worlds with believable density and contents, which shapes how worlds are built.

changes.name: Landmarks
changes.why: The theme can require landmarks and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Theme shapes how players perceive each level, along with what has previously happened in it and how it will develop.

changes.name: Loot
changes.why: What can be found as loot must comply with the theme to keep consistency.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Thematic consistency is seen as a basic requirement for quality narration, so it affects how narration is designed in general.

changes.name: Traces
changes.why: The theme can require traces and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: The theme can require units and limits how they are realized.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: To stay believable in the setting, a character's growth should show up in the game world, such as in how its avatar looks.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: The fiction can explain and restrict who may get or use tools.

conflicts_with.name: Alien Space Bats
conflicts_with.why: If the effects of the fantastical element aren't carried through to the story, world, and gameplay, the setting stops feeling coherent and the theme breaks.

conflicts_with.name: Chat Channels
conflicts_with.why: Players control what they write, so they can say things that clash with the game's theme and designers cannot guarantee a fitting tone.

conflicts_with.name: Easter Eggs
conflicts_with.why: Hidden surprises often carry out-of-world, humorous material that doesn't fit the game's setting, so players who find them see the theme broken.

conflicts_with.name: Emotes
conflicts_with.why: Since players can write anything into a freeform emote, they may add content that clashes with the game's intended theme.

conflicts_with.name: Events Timed to the Real World
conflicts_with.why: In a game set in an invented world, bringing in real-world holidays can feel out of place, such as fantasy citizens celebrating Valentine's Day.

conflicts_with.name: Extra-Game Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Consequences outside the game are not part of the game's theme, so informing players of them clashes with the setting.

conflicts_with.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
conflicts_with.why: Widgets are non-diegetic additions in the world, so the game's theme can't be fully kept intact.

conflicts_with.name: Ghosts
conflicts_with.why: Few game themes include immaterial agents whose actions cannot be influenced, so adding ghosts can clash with the setting a game is built around.

conflicts_with.name: Grind Achievements
conflicts_with.why: Achievements built on collecting spawned items are problematic when the items appear from nowhere.

conflicts_with.name: Illusion of Open Space
conflicts_with.why: If players discover the illusion, such as hitting a barrier, the theme's promise of open space is broken, even though the in-world fiction may hold up.

conflicts_with.name: Inaccessible Areas
conflicts_with.why: If the reason an area can't be entered doesn't fit the game's setting, such as an invisible wall, the theme feels broken.

conflicts_with.name: Instances
conflicts_with.why: When an instance is recreated many times, players notice its enemies and rewards are just game mechanics, which breaks the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Inventories
conflicts_with.why: Inventories can show items differently from the game world or allow unrealistically large loads, and pausing screens make this worse.

conflicts_with.name: Invisible Walls
conflicts_with.why: Hitting a barrier that cannot be seen or explained breaks the believability of the world, unless it is given an in-world reason.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Immunity that the game's fictional world doesn't explain, such as protecting story characters, feels out of place in that world.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: New avatars, characters or units appearing mid-game can break the setting unless the fiction explains their arrival.

conflicts_with.name: Lives
conflicts_with.why: Real characters don't have several lives, and returning after death through spawning also feels unrealistic, which can clash with the theme.

conflicts_with.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
conflicts_with.why: Splitting players into instances and the difficulty of continually producing enough story for a huge lasting world make it hard to keep the theme coherent.

conflicts_with.name: Minigames
conflicts_with.why: If they do not share the main game's theme, as with easter eggs, they break consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Mules
conflicts_with.why: A Mule must cover tasks like dialogue, which is hard to automate convincingly, and player-made Mules leave consistency up to the players.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Players joining and leaving, or speaking out of character, can break the game's setting.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Consistent Narration
conflicts_with.why: Repeating story content makes characters act as if earlier events never occurred, which clashes with the theme the world is supposed to hold.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: When out-of-world talk happens inside the game world, it breaks the theme by introducing elements that don't fit it.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Features
conflicts_with.why: Out-of-world elements don't match the game's theme or setting, which challenges how well everything fits together thematically.

conflicts_with.name: Penalties
conflicts_with.why: A penalty that ignores the game's story or world, like killing a character yet restarting them earlier, breaks the sense of fit.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Without a never-ending story, a world that goes on forever struggles to keep its theme consistent, especially when it has small scripted pieces.

conflicts_with.name: Private Game Spaces
conflicts_with.why: Private spaces can clash with the story, since rivals leaving each other's holdings untouched can seem illogical in the setting.

conflicts_with.name: Props
conflicts_with.why: When a prop looks the same as or very similar to other game items, it blurs what is functional and breaks the theme.

conflicts_with.name: Quests
conflicts_with.why: Quests openly spell out mechanical rewards and requirements, which can expose awkward spots where the game's theme doesn't hold together.

conflicts_with.name: Regenerating Resources
conflicts_with.why: Some resources refilling by themselves may not fit the game's story or setting, which can make the world feel less believable.

conflicts_with.name: Rewards
conflicts_with.why: A reward design may not fit the game's fiction, so it can break the theme when theme matters.

conflicts_with.name: Roleplaying
conflicts_with.why: Too much player freedom, or stepping out of character, can break the setting's theme.

conflicts_with.name: Safe Havens
conflicts_with.why: A safe zone may seem unexplained in the setting, so it needs an in-world reason to fit the theme.

conflicts_with.name: Scores
conflicts_with.why: Points are difficult to justify within a game's theme, so they easily clash with it.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: Players improvise descriptions and story, and the rules can't dictate how, so fit with the theme can't be guaranteed.

conflicts_with.name: Spawn Points
conflicts_with.why: Real life has no place where things simply appear, so spawn points need an explanation like magic or teleportation to fit the setting.

conflicts_with.name: Spawning
conflicts_with.why: Few game settings have a believable reason for things to simply appear, so spawning is hard to fit into the story.

conflicts_with.name: Ability Losses
conflicts_with.why: Blocking actions can keep a story consistent, but for roleplayers it breaks the sense of the world by stopping things they would expect to do.

conflicts_with.name: Clues
conflicts_with.why: Clues containing information from outside the game, like how controls work, break the consistency of the game world's theme.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: Outsiders and their actions have no natural place in the game world, so unexplained appearances can break the setting's believability.

conflicts_with.name: Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: Since players control how their characters behave, they may act in ways that don't fit the game's theme unless someone supervises or their actions are limited.

conflicts_with.name: Power-Ups
conflicts_with.why: Their immaterial, vanish-on-touch nature feels out of place next to ordinary items and landmarks, which can clash with the game's theme.

conflicts_with.name: Storytelling
conflicts_with.why: Storytellers with creative control may add unfitting objects or events, or make characters act out of character, spoiling the fiction's coherence.

conflicts_with.name: Warp Zones
conflicts_with.why: Warp zones can break the theme by pointing to unreachable areas, or by skipping the time that such travel should take.

patterns.name: Diegetic Consistency
patterns.what_it_is: Nothing appears on screen that doesn't exist in the game world itself.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Everything shown must belong to the game world, so interface elements, scores and hints must be kept out or disguised as part of it. Repeated actions such as retries must also make sense in the world.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A world that looks real but shows floating score counters and tooltips all over the screen.
patterns.knobs: how much non-world interface is shown; how it is styled

can_cause.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
can_cause.why: If the game world never shows anything outside its fiction, players don't get a signal that it's a game, and that is nearly required for games blending into real life.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: A consistent fiction gives players a reason not to break it, and playing the part well in turn keeps that consistency going, so each feeds the other.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Anything outside the fiction, like interface overlays, also breaks the theme, so a purely in-world presentation must exist before the theme can hold throughout.

can_cause.name: Feelies
can_cause.why: A player aid is only a feelie when it is made to fit the game world in its own medium, such as a map styled like part of the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Whether the world is shown only through its own elements changes how players perceive it, as everything present in it seems part of the fiction.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Whether a level shows only fiction-appropriate elements changes how players perceive it.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: These games try to build complete, plausible physical settings, so staying in the fiction is usually more important to them than to other games.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemy appearances and behaviors, such as fleeing when hurt, can be explained by the game world's logic.

conflicts_with.name: Cameras
conflicts_with.why: A camera is an incorporeal thing that gives views no character in the game world has or could have, which clashes with in-world consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Chat Channels
conflicts_with.why: Text boxes or overlays sit outside the game world, and mixing player and character channels can also break the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Check Points
conflicts_with.why: Check points are typically geospatial widgets, objects that exist for game purposes rather than belonging naturally to the game world, so they clash with a consistent fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Communication Channels
conflicts_with.why: Players can use the open channel to speak out of character, which breaks the believability of the game's fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
conflicts_with.why: Elements that stand out strongly may be perceived as not belonging to the world, even if they technically do.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: Players joining and leaving at will require the fiction to explain why controlled figures suddenly vanish or reappear.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: When someone quits mid-game, the fiction must explain the sudden disappearance of what they controlled, which is hard.

conflicts_with.name: Emotes
conflicts_with.why: Truly freeform emotes let players put anything they like into the game world, which can break what fits inside the game's fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Enactment
conflicts_with.why: If everyone is expected to act in-world but not all do, the fiction breaks, and players' free choices may bring in non-diegetic elements.

conflicts_with.name: Entitled Players
conflicts_with.why: Such players may use their abilities in ways that disrupt the fiction for the rest.

conflicts_with.name: Extra-Game Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Telling players about consequences outside the game brings in things that don't belong to the game's own world, which breaks its internal consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Extra-Game Input
conflicts_with.why: Dropping outside input straight into the game as content can clash with the game's story world unless that world resembles where the input came from.

conflicts_with.name: Game Pauses
conflicts_with.why: Pausing often sends players to interface screens outside the fiction, which reminds them they are operating a game.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Showing numbers like lives or scores in any form can push players to see other elements as game systems instead of in-world things.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Overviews
conflicts_with.why: Summaries of the game's state encourage players to view elements through the lens of the system rather than the setting.

conflicts_with.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
conflicts_with.why: Widgets are not actually part of the game world yet appear in it, so the world can't stay fully consistent.

conflicts_with.name: Ghosts
conflicts_with.why: Few game settings include see-through beings that nobody can touch or affect, so a ghost often does not fit what the story world allows.

conflicts_with.name: God Fingers
conflicts_with.why: A free, world-external pointer to manipulate things isn't part of the fiction, unlike a figure the player controls inside it.

conflicts_with.name: HUD Interfaces
conflicts_with.why: Information overlaid on the display isn't part of the world, and may clash with some themes.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptibility
conflicts_with.why: If play can be interrupted, the fiction must account for characters suddenly stopping or disappearing.

conflicts_with.name: Lives
conflicts_with.why: A counter of lives is a system element shown to players, which shifts how they perceive other game elements.

conflicts_with.name: Meta-Postures
conflicts_with.why: Gestures used to signal out-of-game messages are not part of the fiction, though they are less noticeable than speech.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: With several people involved, someone is more likely to quit or introduce non-diegetic elements, which threatens the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: Talk about the game itself, outside the fiction, interrupts the shared sense of being in the world.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Features
conflicts_with.why: Having elements that aren't part of the world directly contradicts a world made only of its own elements.

conflicts_with.name: Phasing
conflicts_with.why: Players see different versions of the world, so those comparing their experiences find the world doesn't add up.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Keeping player knowledge in line with the character's is often easiest with elements from outside the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Power-Ups
conflicts_with.why: They clearly affect gameplay, which makes them look like game-system devices instead of things belonging to the world.

conflicts_with.name: Reflective Communication
conflicts_with.why: It is a form of out-of-fiction talk, so wanting both it and a fully consistent world makes design harder.

conflicts_with.name: Reward Widgets
conflicts_with.why: These widgets float in the game world yet are not truly part of it, so they break the sense that everything shown belongs to the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Roleplaying
conflicts_with.why: Because players are free to choose, they might add non-diegetic elements, which undermines the shared fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Scores
conflicts_with.why: Showing scores makes players see the game as a system, which can change how they perceive everything else.

conflicts_with.name: Seamful Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Visible seams in the game's presentation can force explanations for characters or units appearing and vanishing.

conflicts_with.name: Secondary Interface Screens
conflicts_with.why: These screens often hold non-diegetic features and take players away from the world itself.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: No dedicated person is handling the presentation, so keeping to the fiction can't be guaranteed.

conflicts_with.name: Setback Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Having to redo sequences of actions repeatedly often makes no sense within the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Storytelling
conflicts_with.why: Players' freedom to tell their own story can introduce non-diegetic elements that break the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Tooltips
conflicts_with.why: Pop-up text is not part of the game world, so showing it can break the feeling that everything seen belongs inside that world.

conflicts_with.name: Warp Zones
conflicts_with.why: If a zone itself, or the areas it leads to, aren't part of the world, using it reveals the fiction as constructed.

conflicts_with.name: Alarms
conflicts_with.why: Letting only special avatars or units raise alarms keeps the story on track but may make no sense within the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Explaining why enemies can't be met early or why they appear can strain the game world's logic.

conflicts_with.name: Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Invisible walls used to bound an open world are not part of the fiction, so they can break the world's believability.

conflicts_with.name: Props
conflicts_with.why: A prop that looks like a usable object but does nothing, or draws interest and then can't be used, exposes an inconsistency in the world.

conflicts_with.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Changing the world during play without a sensible in-story reason can make the world feel illogical and break its internal consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Territories
conflicts_with.why: Showing ownership usually means drawing a colored overlay on the world, which is not something that exists inside the game world's fiction.

patterns.name: Game Instance Stories
patterns.what_it_is: Stories based on the events of one particular game that was played.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Games need chances for remarkable, varied events, and ways to record or share them, such as replays. Exceptional or failure moments help.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A replay or save feature exists, but games unfold the same each time, so nothing worth telling comes out.
patterns.knobs: variance of events; ability to record and share; frequency of dramatic moments

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: A story about a particular play session lives on after the session ends and affects things outside the game, so telling it counts as such a consequence.

can_cause.name: Memorabilia
can_cause.why: A retold story keeps a memory of what happened in a session, working as a keepsake made of narrative instead of a physical object.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Players who build a story together through play share an experience that binds them as a group.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: When session stories circulate among players, listeners can pick up strategy from what happened, so the stories change what players know about playing well.

patterns.name: Easter Eggs
patterns.what_it_is: Hidden surprises unrelated to the game's story and world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The secret must be hidden well enough to feel like a discovery but findable through exploration or hints, and it must be fun or funny when found. Players also need a reason to suspect secrets exist.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hidden thing that is trivially visible, or so obscure and dull that nobody finds it or cares when they do.
patterns.knobs: how many there are; how hidden they are; how strongly clues point to them

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Players who know hidden surprises exist have a reason to poke around every corner of the world, so looking for them becomes a motivation to explore.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Players race to find the hidden items before others do, which creates a side contest about discovery that sits outside the main game.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Finding a hidden surprise isn't required to progress, so once players know one exists, tracking it down becomes a goal they can choose to chase.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Since hidden surprises may be missed on one playthrough, players have a reason to start again and search more thoroughly.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Because the surprises sit in places harder to find than other hidden spots, searching for them demands more effort and so adds difficulty to the optional hunt.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Hiding surprises in the world gives its places and objects extra secrets, changing what the world holds beyond its ordinary content.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Hidden surprises often carry out-of-world, humorous material that doesn't fit the game's setting, so players who find them see the theme broken.

patterns.name: Environmental Storytelling
patterns.what_it_is: The story is revealed as the player walks around and explores a place.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The world must hold readable traces of past events in props, items and layout, placed where players pass, and players need freedom and a reason to look and interpret.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Decor that is only decor, or story info tucked in a place nobody sees and tells them nothing about what happened.
patterns.knobs: density and placement of story clues; how obvious they are; how much is optional

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Objects and effects left in the world can hint at what happened, so players can use them to piece together events or find resources.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: The story sits in the world rather than a forced cutscene, so players decide whether to notice or engage with it.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Players may skip the environmental story, so working out what happened becomes something they choose to pursue, not a requirement.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers fix the story ahead of time and embed it in the level, so the planned narrative is told through the surroundings.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Players often see only fragments of what happened, so they must reason or guess to reconstruct the events.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: The narrative is delivered as players move through and explore the world, so the environment itself becomes the storyteller.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Marks and remnants of earlier events in the surroundings show that something happened there before the player arrived.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The same elements that make up the world also carry the story, so storytelling shapes how the whole world is experienced.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Story elements are built from the same design pieces as levels, so they affect how each level looks and what it conveys.

changes.name: Resource Locations
changes.why: Story elements can be placed at resource spots to give players a reason to look at them, and can hint where resources are.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: Routes between places can be dull, but players focus on them while traveling, so putting story elements there makes them more interesting.

patterns.name: Emotional Attachment
patterns.what_it_is: Game characters show noticeable feelings toward phenomena and creatures of the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters need reactions that fit events and relationships and visible consequences of what happens to them, so players believe they care.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character who says it is sad or fond in a line of text but acts exactly the same afterwards.
patterns.knobs: how many events characters react to; strength and visibility of reactions; how long memory of events lasts

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When agents show feelings about things tied to their goals, players can see that those agents are pursuing aims of their own.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Agents whose emotions fit the game world's events keep the setting believable, so the story and world feel coherent rather than broken.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: When agents show emotional attachment to things, that display becomes part of the story being told.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: Computer-controlled players are one kind of algorithmic agent whose design changes depending on whether they are given ways to show they care about events.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Giving agents emotional reactions changes how they appear, letting them show they care about what happens in the game world.

changes.name: Storytelling
changes.why: Agents' fitting emotional reactions help stories stay consistent with their theme instead of breaking it.

patterns.name: Big Dumb Objects
patterns.what_it_is: Huge man-made objects hinting at powerful creators.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The object must be seen from far away and feel vastly larger than the player, with hints about its makers. It should be a notable landmark players move toward or can't reach.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A big model is in the background but is not noticeable, has no hints of origin, and is just scenery.
patterns.knobs: size and visibility; place in the world; how much is hinted about its makers; reachable or not

can_cause.name: Alien Space Bats
can_cause.why: When a huge unexplained structure is placed in a world otherwise modeled on reality, it becomes an out-of-place element that doesn't fit the setting.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Because the objects are so huge and mysterious, characters inside the game world would notice them, so they stand out as notable features.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: Such an obvious object can't just appear unexplained, so it should carry story hints through the surroundings, or it clashes with the world's logic.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: If players can see the giant object from afar but can't get to it, it becomes a visible place they know they can't enter.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: Since the objects are visible from far away and easy to recognize, players can use them as reference points to orient themselves.

can_cause.name: Line of Sight
can_cause.why: Their enormous size lets players see them from long distances, giving a clear view of a recognizable target.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because they're so noticeable, they have to fit into the designed story ahead of time rather than being added as unexplained scenery.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Designers often include them because they reinforce the game's chosen theme and atmosphere, such as wonder or otherworldliness.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Large mysterious objects tempt players to travel to them just to look into them, creating a destination goal.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Designers must decide where on the game board the object sits, so it shapes how that board looks and is laid out.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Being visible from far away and easy to recognize, the objects give players something to steer by when finding their way.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The object can be placed in the world as a feature, or be so large that the entire world is the object itself.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Designers choose where within a level such an object goes, and its scale affects how that level looks and feels.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: Placing the object so it can be seen while travelling makes otherwise dull movement between places more interesting to look at.

patterns.name: Memory of Important Events
patterns.what_it_is: Game characters remember important past events and show that they do.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design needs a way to detect and record significant events, and then characters must refer to them later in speech or behavior at fitting moments. The recall has to be specific to what the player did.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Characters say a generic scripted line that sounds like remembering but is identical whatever the player did.
patterns.knobs: how many event types are tracked; how long they are kept; how visibly characters react

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When characters recall past events and respond to them, they seem to pursue goals shaped by their own history rather than just reacting to the moment.

can_cause.name: Sense of Self
can_cause.why: A character that recalls what happened to it during play seems to have a continuous personal identity, as if it were a someone with a past.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Giving agents recollection of past events makes them seem more socially believable, as they can show they recall and react emotionally to what happened.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Algorithmic agents are changed by this pattern because they need extra event-tracking and recall logic, which in turn is also how the pattern gets implemented.

changes.name: Awareness of Surroundings
changes.why: Agents that remember events can show they know what has happened in their environment, which widens how aware of their world they appear.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: The pattern is applied to non-player characters acting as agents, so those characters seem to recall and respond to earlier play events.

patterns.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: After playing, a person understands real-life phenomena differently.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game system must model the real phenomenon faithfully, or tie game state to the real world (location, real activity), and players must be willing to draw the connection.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game has a real-world theme painted on top, but the rules don't model it, so players learn nothing new about it.
patterns.knobs: how closely the model matches reality; how strongly game state is tied to real-life data or places

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Changing how players see real-world things is the very effect the designer is after, and that shift carries beyond the game into players' lives.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Linking game state to real-world phenomena binds play to each player's own surroundings and social setting, making it harder to adapt the game to different social situations.

patterns.name: Critical Gameplay Design
patterns.what_it_is: Game rules are built to make the player think and doubt something.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game's own rules and dynamics must model something in the real world so that players feel its structure and see it differently. The critique must come from play, not from text or the story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The theme or story talks about a real issue, but the rules play like an ordinary game and the issue is not felt.
patterns.knobs: how closely the rules mirror the real phenomenon; how strong the feedback loops and social dilemmas are

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: The pattern aims to get players to think critically about real-world phenomena, so when it works, players end up seeing those phenomena differently.

patterns.name: Clickability
patterns.what_it_is: A responsive reaction to clicking that is pleasing in itself.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Instant, noticeable audio-visual feedback for every click, and a chance to repeat actions in a rhythm.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Things are clickable, but the response is delayed or flat, so clicking feels like filling in a form.
patterns.knobs: feedback speed and strength; how often one can repeat; effects on combos and timing

can_cause.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Repeated clicking with quick, noticeable responses lets players fall into a steady beat of actions, which they then try to keep going.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: When clicking is the fun part, the player's pointer or focus point must do the clicking, which changes how players relate to that focus point.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Items that react noticeably when clicked, like switches, pick-ups, and reward widgets, become more appealing to interact with once players notice them.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: When important parts of the environment are easy to click, exploring them is trivial, so players need to learn less before they can master the game.

changes.name: God Fingers
changes.why: A pointer that can click anywhere in the world or interface is the best tool for delivering clickable fun across everything on screen.

changes.name: Pottering
changes.why: Enjoyable clicking helps casual aimless play feel less like a chore, though it is not enough alone to sustain that kind of play.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Clicking that is fun in itself makes repetitive actions feel enjoyable, which works against the feeling of grinding through tedious tasks.

patterns.name: Cooperation
patterns.what_it_is: Players act together, sharing information and resources toward a common goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need shared goals or rewards, and tasks that really are easier or only possible together. They also need to be able to communicate and swap information or resources.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are put on a team and share a score, but each can win alone without caring what the others do.
patterns.knobs: how shared the goals and rewards are; how often joint actions are required; communication limits

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When players are busy working together on shared tasks, they pay less attention to who the others are in real life and more to their in-game roles.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Having to coordinate with others adds more things to track and decide, and this grows even more when players also compete.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Players may help someone who gets little back right now, trusting that the favor will be returned to them later.

can_cause.name: Ragequitting
can_cause.why: If teamwork breaks down and joint efforts fail, frustrated players may storm out of the game.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: When players need to work together, they tend to settle into different parts or jobs within the group.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Working jointly with others rewards players who communicate, negotiate and read others well, so they show these abilities to do better.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Coordinating with partners, or even just deciding whether to team up at all, pushes players to think ahead.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: When players must work toward shared benefit and do so at different times, the result is collaboration without simultaneous or observed action.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: Since no single entity can do everything, participants must work together, which makes each of them rely on others' specialized roles.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Relying on other players' actions leaves your result partly in their hands, which makes it tense.

changes.name: Competence Areas
changes.why: When players work together, specialties can turn into more formal roles, and cooperating becomes more efficient when players specialize.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Cooperation is the most natural fit for games with several players, shaping how they relate, though it can also be used outside them.

conflicts_with.name: Betrayal
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal undermines the reliance players place on each other and lessens how much cooperation is felt, even while it adds tension.

conflicts_with.name: Internal Conflicts
conflicts_with.why: Strong disagreements within the group can be so disruptive that working together becomes impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Preventing Goals
conflicts_with.why: Aims that stop others from achieving things clash with joint effort at a basic level, though teams can oppose each other.

conflicts_with.name: PvP
conflicts_with.why: Players fighting each other are at odds with working together, though both can coexist when teams compete.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Cooperation is easier to get with all players working together, but friendly fire, mistrust and sabotage can limit it in teams.

patterns.name: Agents
patterns.what_it_is: Game creatures and objects that seem to have goals of their own.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Elements need visible abilities and actions that look purposeful and respond to circumstances, not fixed predictable motions. Players need to see them change the world in ways that suggest an aim.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game element wears a creature's face but moves on a fixed track, and players quickly see it as an obstacle, not an agent.
patterns.knobs: how adaptive and varied their actions are; how visible their goals are

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Agents that oppose or help the player through conflict or cooperation create the difficulty the player must deal with, so they generate challenge.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Agents can be companions or teammates who work alongside the player, giving players partners to coordinate with.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Because agents are seen as having intentions about the future, they can take part in favor-trading where repayment comes later.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: Human players act through agents such as avatars and characters, so having agents with human controllers produces games with several players.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Agents are the story's anchors and conflict sources, so a game's story structure has to be designed together with them.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Agents can be authored as fixed parts of a pre-written story, so designers shape the agents themselves to fit that plot.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Players often simplify agents into mental models of things that move and act in reliable ways, so their effects become foreseeable.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Players must keep guessing what agents will do next, which pushes them to think ahead and plan.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Agents give players characters to care about and are usually where conflict comes from, which stories need.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When agents are used as opponents, players feel forces working against them, which creates tension.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Game elements that act on their own become enemies when they try to hinder the player or when players have goals regarding them.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: Killing only registers when players can tie the removal to some actor who caused it, so an identifiable agent is central.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Roleplaying means taking on the goals and behavior of agents, so having agents in the game is what gives players something to roleplay.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: A team can be formed simply by having several agents who all pursue the same mutual goal.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: By using agents for conflict or cooperation, designers can raise or shape the challenge players face.

changes.name: Herd
changes.why: Agents among those being herded move on their own, which makes herding goals harder.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Giving NPCs the ability to act on their own in the world changes them from passive figures into participants.

changes.name: Spectators
changes.why: Spectators who see game elements that look capable of thought and self-directed action tend to treat them as having intentions.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Inhabitants such as enemies and non-player characters populate a world and make it feel occupied and active.

conflicts_with.name: Moveable Tiles
conflicts_with.why: Tiles are elements that don't move by their own will, while agents act on goals, so the two fit poorly together.

patterns.name: Social Roles
patterns.what_it_is: Roles that people receive or take toward one another because of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be several players with different abilities or tasks, a way to communicate, and enough gameplay differences that people fall into distinct positions. Anonymity and cut communication weaken it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Named roles listed in the game that players never actually take on, because everyone does the same things and has the same standing.
patterns.knobs: how different player abilities are; how strong group structures are; how much players can communicate

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Some roles give their holders little to do in play, so those players sit idle unless the role's importance is deliberately kept frequent.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Players want to talk about the roles and related topics outside the game fiction, which raises how much out-of-game chatter happens.

can_cause.name: Role Selection
can_cause.why: When players are free to choose which social role they take, that choice is itself a form of picking a role.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Many roles demand social ability to play well, and negotiating who gets which role also takes those skills.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Roles give players a structure and encouragement to interact, and that shared interaction builds a feeling of being together.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Freedom to pick different roles lets players experience the game in different ways, which makes play more varied.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Social roles can be applied on top of cooperation that already exists in a game, altering how it plays out.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Taking on social roles during play makes interaction between players important, which makes it harder to keep people's identities out of it.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: With players judged only on their play and not on who they are, it becomes hard for lasting social roles to form.

conflicts_with.name: Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Social roles are harder to establish when players don't know who others are, since roles depend on recognized identities; gameplay-based roles can work around this.

conflicts_with.name: Possibility of Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Even the option to stay anonymous works against social roles, making them less present or harder to adopt.

patterns.name: Betrayal
patterns.what_it_is: A character breaks an explicit or unspoken agreement with another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must depend on each other through promises or alliances, with imperfect information and a real gain from betraying. Anonymous actions or traitor roles intensify it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game has a 'traitor' label or alliance rules, but betraying brings no benefit or is impossible, so everyone just cooperates.
patterns.knobs: gain from betraying versus cooperating; how hidden actions are; use of traitor roles

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Adding a traitor, like the bio-terrorist in Pandemic's expansion, forces players to work against a hidden threat as well as the game, making success harder.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: A broken promise is an unusual, standout moment in a game, so betrayal naturally produces events that break the normal flow of play.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Without hidden actions, a betrayal is exposed once and cannot be repeated or undone, so it happens only one time.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Because a player might secretly plan to break an agreement, others cannot be sure how that player will act.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers can deliberately write betrayal into a game's planned storyline as a theme, building it into the story's built-in turning points.

can_cause.name: PvP
can_cause.why: Even when players mostly cooperate, they must consider that others might turn on them, which adds a player-against-player element.

can_cause.name: Ragequitting
can_cause.why: Being betrayed stirs strong negative emotion, and a player who feels wronged enough may simply storm out of the game.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: Betrayal can require taking on a particular role, such as traitor, so pulling it off successfully feels like playing that part well.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Setting up a betrayal often takes time, as with traitors, so players must act in character and keep up a pretense.

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: Planning to betray means hiding your real intention from the others, which makes that plan a private goal.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Where betrayal isn't already based on a conflict between group and personal gain, it tends to create that tension itself.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Unless every player must do it, choosing to betray means stepping into a distinct position among the group, such as the traitor.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing betrayal is possible makes players anxious and anticipating, as they try to work out what others truly intend.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: When someone may secretly work against the group, players must handle both cooperating and hindering, which complicates decisions.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Even in joint actions, such as attacks in Illuminati, a partner might betray the others, though in a milder form.

changes.name: Committed Goals
changes.why: Betrayal feels stronger when it concerns a goal the player was bound to, rather than one they could freely skip.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Possible betrayal makes cooperative play more challenging and complex, but also weakens how much players can truly rely on each other.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Placing players in factions and then having traitors within them heightens how betrayed others feel.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: Shared goals make betrayal sting more when a player secretly works against them, as traitors do.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Betrayal is a classic theme that produces twists like role reversals and surprises within a game's story.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Computer or facilitator-run characters can be the ones who betray players or the ones betrayed by them.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Having betrayal possible in a party makes tension and anticipation greater, while lessening how much the party feels like a united group.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Possible betrayal within teams adds tension and anticipation but reduces how united and trusting the team can be.

conflicts_with.name: Casual Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal can make players depend on one another, which suits poorly with relaxed play that doesn't demand worry about others.

conflicts_with.name: Cooperation
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal undermines the reliance players place on each other and lessens how much cooperation is felt, even while it adds tension.

conflicts_with.name: Parties
conflicts_with.why: The possibility of betrayal reduces how much a party feels like a trusting group, even if it adds anticipation.

conflicts_with.name: Teams
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal threatens the trust teammates need, lessening the sense of a team even while it increases tension.

patterns.name: Player Unpredictability
patterns.what_it_is: While it is unknown how others will act, the game's course cannot be foreseen exactly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be several real opponents with meaningful choices, and information that is hidden or imperfect so their moves cannot be easily deduced. No single dominant strategy should exist.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Opponents are present but all follow the same obvious best line, so their moves are easy to predict.
patterns.knobs: number of opponents; how much information is hidden; how many viable strategies exist

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Being hard for opponents to read is itself worth practicing, so in games with deception or secret aims, getting good at hiding your intentions is a path to mastery.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When you can't tell what others will do, you have to weigh the risks and rewards of the options you can see, which pushes you to plan.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: Because you can't know what others will choose, you can't see far ahead or plan perfectly, so how the game ends stays open.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: If a player's moves can't be easily predicted, others can't tell when they are faking, so bluffing becomes possible.

changes.name: Analysis Paralysis
changes.why: Trying to plan around opponents whose moves are hard to guess can be so difficult that players get stuck deliberating.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: When you can't assume what teammates will do, working together becomes harder.

conflicts_with.name: Endgame
conflicts_with.why: Final phases often settle into locked positions, often from depleted resources, so players become easier to predict.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: When it's clear who is ahead, what that player will do next becomes obvious, removing the uncertainty.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Knowledge
conflicts_with.why: A player who understands the game's strategies can more easily guess what others will do, making them less unpredictable.

conflicts_with.name: Trial and Error Solutions
conflicts_with.why: If solutions can simply be tested one after another, outcomes become foreseeable, which works against unpredictability.

patterns.name: Social Skills
patterns.what_it_is: Success in the game depends on the players' ability to communicate and persuade.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Outcomes must depend on how players deal with each other, through bluffing, trading, negotiation or alliances, and the interaction must not be fully mediated away by rules.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with a negotiation phase where the best move is always the same calculated trade, so charm or bluffing never changes anything.
patterns.knobs: how many social actions affect outcomes; how open communication is; how much information is hidden

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Since success depends on how you come across to others, being persuasive and socially savvy becomes a skill you can get truly good at and show off.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Players can enjoy being seen as socially adept for its own sake, so showing these skills earns appreciation apart from any in-game effect.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When your results depend on how others react to you, players feel pressure about whether they will be believed, trusted or accepted.

patterns.name: Delayed Reciprocity
patterns.what_it_is: You help others now, expecting the favor to be returned later.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to help one another at a cost to themselves, without a guaranteed immediate payback, and meet again later so that returning is possible. Trust and the chance of betrayal must be real.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A gift button that gives help to anyone for free, so there is no cost, no trust and nothing to repay.
patterns.knobs: cost of helping; how likely and how soon players meet again; whether repayment is enforced

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Since the game doesn't guarantee a favor will be returned, the helped player can simply never pay back, which makes breaking trust possible.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Because helping creates a sense of owing, the helper can pressure the receiver into repaying, turning the bond into a social dilemma of guilt.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Players who gave help wait for a payoff that hasn't arrived yet, leaving the exchange open and unresolved until the favor comes back.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Helping now with nothing immediate in return works like putting resources in, hoping for a later payoff, especially when players commit to shared goals.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: The waiting player expects a later benefit from the one they helped, so the eventual returned favor acts as a delayed reward.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Helping costs the giver something while repaying costs the receiver, so players must choose between self-interest and honoring the exchange, as when guilt is used.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Between giving help and getting something back there is a time gap and a chance of betrayal, so the players involved feel uneasy.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players must trust that a partner will return a favor later, adding risk to cooperative choices.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: You return to find out whether others repaid your help, or because you feel you now owe them help in turn.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, depending clearly on other players can paradoxically give players a sense that their own actions matter.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Rewards
conflicts_with.why: If the reward is already split among everyone by design, individual helpful acts need no repayment, so situations of owing a favor happen less often.

conflicts_with.name: Teams
conflicts_with.why: When team success rests on common goals, members help each other as a matter of course, which makes room for favors owed later smaller.

patterns.name: Beat the Leader
patterns.what_it_is: Several players team up against whoever is leading the session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to see who is ahead and must have ways to hurt or hinder that player together. Hidden scores kill the effect; open scores and interference actions support it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The leader is shown on a scoreboard, but players have no way to affect each other, so nobody can target them.
patterns.knobs: visibility of scores; how much players can interfere with each other; hidden or open goals

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: When players gang up on whoever seems ahead, they pull the leader back toward the others, which evens out how well everyone is doing.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Because the pacts against a leader are temporary and a leader can shift, a player may drop an ally and break the agreement.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: Players may act weaker than they are to avoid being targeted, or falsely label someone else as the leader to redirect the group.

can_cause.name: Mutual Goals
can_cause.why: Everyone who is not ahead shares the same aim of bringing down the perceived leader, so their interests briefly line up.

can_cause.name: Negative Feedback Loops
can_cause.why: Being ahead draws the others' joint resistance, and that resistance is controlled by players, so leading makes further success harder.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Players pushing down the apparent front-runner tend to keep everyone's standing close, if the leader was identified correctly.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Each player must choose between spending effort against the leader for everyone's benefit or pursuing their own gain and hoping others do the work.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: In games where individual players compete, the leader is a single player and the others can join forces against them.

changes.name: Tied Results
changes.why: Collective action against the leader tends to bring scores closer together, making a tie between players more likely.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: In team competitions the leader can be a whole team, so the other teams can unite against it.

conflicts_with.name: End State Scoring
conflicts_with.why: If points are only counted at the end, players cannot tell who is ahead during play, so they have no clear target.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Goals
conflicts_with.why: Hidden objectives keep players from knowing how close others are to winning, which makes naming a leader hard or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Scoring Mechanisms
conflicts_with.why: When scoring is hidden, players cannot judge who is in front, so they lack the basis for ganging up on anyone.

patterns.name: Functional Roles
patterns.what_it_is: Different kinds of actions are assigned to different participants.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give entities different abilities and make tasks too many for one to cover, so cooperation and division of labor is necessary. Limited gear slots or exclusive abilities force specialization.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Class names exist, but everyone can do everything equally well, so the roles are just labels.
patterns.knobs: how different abilities are between roles; how much one entity can cover alone; number of slots

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When roles demand different skill levels, beginners can pick an easier role and take part without carrying the hardest responsibilities, such as playing a medic or engineer.

can_cause.name: Role Selection
can_cause.why: Once actions are split among roles, players naturally have to choose which role to take, so choosing becomes a normal part of play.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Besides the gameplay duties they carry, functional roles also hint at how players behave toward one another within the group.

can_cause.name: Tiered Participation
can_cause.why: When some roles ask for far more involvement in play than others, players end up engaged at different levels depending on their role.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, differing roles and role changes can set group members against each other and create rivalry.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: In multiplayer play, players can take on different sub-challenges, so swapping roles between games gives a new experience.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players in a multiplayer game each take a different functional role, they end up doing different things and interacting differently, which adds variety, though only modestly.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Dividing responsibilities among players lets each try different roles for varied experiences, though limited role slots can cause rivalry between them.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Because roles are usually divided among players, they give a reason for a group to exist so every needed function is covered.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Teams can enforce cooperation among role holders, and varying expertise needs within a team let novices ease in through simpler roles.

patterns.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
patterns.what_it_is: The player can still improve their own skills in this game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Outcomes must depend on skill with room above average play, plus feedback that shows how well players did. Changing rules or rising challenge keeps the headroom open.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game claims depth, but outcomes are mostly luck or skill caps quickly, so practice yields nothing.
patterns.knobs: skill ceiling; amount of performance feedback; how outcome depends on skill versus luck

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: When a game leaves room to get better, it shows players they can reach a higher level of skill than they currently have.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If players can improve between sessions, by sharpening their actions or learning strategy, they have a reason to play again.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: In team games, room for improvement shows that the team can grow and perform better together over time.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Seeing that better play is possible tells players that their effort to improve can actually pay off.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Puzzles that stay the same between sessions leave little room for players to get better, so this potential suffers.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: When success comes from chance, players have less control, so there is little reason to think getting better would matter.

conflicts_with.name: No Direct Player Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players cannot meaningfully affect the game at all, there is no skill to develop and nothing to improve.

conflicts_with.name: Puzzle Solving
conflicts_with.why: Once a puzzle's answer is found, nothing more remains to learn from it, so no further improvement is possible.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Heavy randomness weakens player control, so players doubt that improving their play is possible or worthwhile.

conflicts_with.name: Solution Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Challenges built on finding a solution lose their improvement value once the solution is known, unless something else is added.

conflicts_with.name: Trial and Error Solutions
conflicts_with.why: Luck or simply trying every option can reveal the answer, so skill is not needed and there is nothing to improve.

patterns.name: Symbiotic Player Relations
patterns.what_it_is: One player's success or failure affects the other player in the same way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players' outcomes must be genuinely linked (shared goals, shared enemies, or helpful actions that benefit others), so helping is in their own interest. Helping must also be possible through actual actions.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are put on a 'team' by name, but their results are independent and nothing one does changes another's outcome.
patterns.knobs: how much one player's results spread to others; shared versus individual rewards; availability of helping actions

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: When players aren't sure why they act, they may help others without any reward for themselves, and shared fortunes make such helping fit naturally.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When staying in the partnership is optional rather than required, a player can drop or exploit partners, and well-timed defections can be powerful.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Because one player's gains or losses carry over to others, players have reason to work together toward outcomes that help everyone involved.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Benefits needn't reach everyone immediately, since players can expect that help they give now will be returned to them later.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Players who expect a favor to be repaid, or who coordinate with each other, can pressure partners who haven't contributed.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: When the shared fate is expressed in terms of the game's fiction, sticking by one's partners feels like faithfulness to them.

patterns.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
patterns.what_it_is: The starts and ends of different players' game sessions do not line up in time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must let people join, leave, quit or be eliminated at different moments, and the server or facilitator must keep play going for those who remain. Without free entry and exit, everyone ends up starting and finishing together.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A lobby with a join button that in practice always waits for a full group and ends for everyone at once, so sessions stay aligned.
patterns.knobs: how freely players may join or leave mid-game; how elimination and surrender are handled

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Players may need to wait for others to finish their sessions before their own can start.

conflicts_with.name: Togetherness
conflicts_with.why: When players start and stop at different times, they are rarely in the game together, which makes feeling united hard.

patterns.name: Early Leaving Players
patterns.what_it_is: Players abandon the session before the end, though the game didn't force them to.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Leaving becomes likely when games run long, feel lost or depend heavily on others; the design must decide how the game copes when someone departs.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rule saying what happens when someone leaves, in a game short or engaging enough that nobody ever does.
patterns.knobs: game length; how hopeless a losing position feels; what the game does with a departed player's position

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: When a player quits, they effectively vanish from the match just as an eliminated player would, so the same problems and fixes apply.

can_cause.name: Kingmaker
can_cause.why: A departing player may use their final moves to decide who wins, handing victory to someone of their choosing.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When some players drop out partway, participants no longer share the same progress or timing through the game, so sessions drift apart.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: For people to drop out, the game must cope with someone quitting before the session finishes.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Players often know who is ahead in the final phase, so quitting there matters more and the endgame must handle it more often.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Players who see the game as unwinnable tend to quit, a problem designers should plan for.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Teammates depend on one another, so one person leaving hurts the others more than in games where everyone plays alone.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: In team-versus-team play, losing a member weakens their side and the reliance on each other makes departures more damaging.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: When someone quits mid-game, the fiction must explain the sudden disappearance of what they controlled, which is hard.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptibility
conflicts_with.why: Games that can be paused or interrupted give people fewer reasons to quit for good, so they work against players leaving early.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
conflicts_with.why: Letting players adjust how long a game runs fits their available time, reducing the need to leave early.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
conflicts_with.why: Letting players tailor sessions to their schedule removes a common reason for quitting partway.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
conflicts_with.why: Letting players adapt play sessions to the time they have lessens the motivation to leave before the end.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: When someone leaves, the remaining players' standing can become uneven, disrupting the fairness the game was built around.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: A planned story can break when a participant disappears, since the facilitator or system counted on that player's role.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Losing a member leaves one team weaker than another, upsetting the even match the game aimed for.

patterns.name: First Player Advantages
patterns.what_it_is: The benefit of taking actions before everyone else.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs turn-based play where moving first matters and starting positions are equal. The size of the edge depends on how much a single move can change the game, and balancing needs its own fix such as rotating order.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are labelled first, but moving first changes nothing, so no advantage exists.
patterns.knobs: how much one early move is worth; whether compensation (turn rotation, bonuses for later players) is added

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: Because someone has to move first, players begin in unequal positions, so the opening advantage itself becomes a built-in difference between players' starting situations.

changes.name: Startgame
changes.why: The advantage of moving first shows up mostly in the opening phase of play, so it shapes how the early game unfolds.

conflicts_with.name: Back-to-Back Game Sessions
conflicts_with.why: Moving first gives an edge that makes a single session lopsided, and repeating with swapped roles is meant to cancel it out, so the pattern works against that advantage.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: An edge for whoever starts first makes players unequal in their chances, which undermines the goal of fair, balanced competition.

patterns.name: Team Balance
patterns.what_it_is: Competing teams have about equal chances of success and victory.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Team makeup and rules must offset advantages, with some correction for teams that fall behind. Features that snowball or cause lopsided numbers must be controlled.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Teams have equal member counts, but skill spread, roles, or snowballing make one side win most of the time.
patterns.knobs: team composition rules; handicap strength; strength of catch-up effects

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: When teams are evenly matched, each player can estimate their odds of winning from how many teams are competing, since no side holds a hidden edge.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Balance changes how teams are built and adjusted so that no team starts with a clearly better chance of succeeding.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Team-versus-team play becomes more interesting for everyone when the competing sides have roughly equal chances.

conflicts_with.name: AI Players
conflicts_with.why: Swapping AI in and out during play can leave teams uneven, unless the game is purely cooperative.

conflicts_with.name: Death Consequences
conflicts_with.why: How dead avatars return to play can favor one team over another, upsetting fairness between teams.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: Gaining or losing members can leave one team stronger than another, which is hard to correct.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: Losing a member leaves one team weaker than another, upsetting the even match the game aimed for.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: If one side keeps immunity for long, it dominates and the teams stop being evenly matched.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
