conflicts_with.why: A newcomer can make one team stronger or weaker than the other, because they differ from existing members.

conflicts_with.name: New Abilities
conflicts_with.why: As different teams develop abilities at different rates, one side can end up stronger than another.

conflicts_with.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
conflicts_with.why: Teams with entities that have unique abilities are hard to make even, though giving every team the same differentiated set resolves the problem.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: When teams exist, losing members unevenly can leave one team much weaker than another.

conflicts_with.name: Player Killing
conflicts_with.why: Penalties for being killed fall on individual players but still shift the strength of their teams, which can tilt a team-versus-team match.

conflicts_with.name: Positive Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: Snowballing lets one side pull far ahead of the other, which undermines keeping teams evenly matched.

conflicts_with.name: Privileged Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Special abilities held by players on one team can make teams unequal, unless the other teams have matching abilities.

conflicts_with.name: Team Development
conflicts_with.why: Growing teams can be designed toward balance, but even small differences in how they grow can widen the gap instead.

conflicts_with.name: Teams
conflicts_with.why: Giving certain members special powers in a team-versus-team game can make the sides unequal, causing problems with fairness.

patterns.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
patterns.what_it_is: Players talk to each other as real people, not as characters of the world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need channels and reasons to talk outside the fiction, such as shared information, social settings or non-diegetic UI. Designers who want less of it must give diegetic substitutes or remove the triggers.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Chat that exists but nobody uses to talk about anything outside the story, or a chat that is framed as in-world speech while players still use it for out-of-game coordination.
patterns.knobs: how much out-of-fiction communication is allowed or provided with channels; how much non-diegetic information the game exposes

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: When out-of-world talk happens inside the game world itself, it brings in elements that don't belong to that world, creating non-diegetic features.

changes.name: Social Roles
changes.why: Talking outside the fiction gives players a way to negotiate and keep up their roles more easily.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: By definition, in-world talk refers to nothing outside the game world, so speaking about outside matters directly breaks it; designers mostly separate or minimize one.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Talk about the game itself, outside the fiction, interrupts the shared sense of being in the world.

conflicts_with.name: Meta-Postures
conflicts_with.why: Having gestures available can lead players to exchange more out-of-game information overall, which undermines the aim of keeping that communication low.

conflicts_with.name: Prompting Techniques
conflicts_with.why: Prompting gives players other ways to pass information, so they have less need to step outside the fiction to speak.

conflicts_with.name: Substitute Actions
conflicts_with.why: Players can express information through stand-in actions instead of speaking as themselves, so out-of-world talk is avoided.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: When out-of-world talk happens inside the game world, it breaks the theme by introducing elements that don't fit it.

patterns.name: Asymmetric Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Players' game experiences are built differently, or do not repeat earlier sessions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must have really different actions or goals, and those differences must matter to how they decide and play. The differences need enough balance that no side is plainly better, and variety should not run out in one session.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players get different names, pictures or flavour text, but the same actions and goals, so everyone plays the same game.
patterns.knobs: how many aspects differ (abilities, goals, information, roles, start); how far apart they are

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because different games or players offer different kinds of play, one session won't use up every type of gameplay, so people have reasons to play again.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players get different actions and goals, or those change between sessions, what people actually do in the game differs, producing variety.

patterns.name: Backseat Gamers
patterns.what_it_is: Non-playing people influence the session with advice and opinions that players hear.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Spectators must be able to see the game and talk to players, and players must care about their input. Drop-in play lets people move between watching and playing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: There is a spectator mode, but spectators cannot communicate or players ignore them, so no one is influenced.
patterns.knobs: spectator visibility; communication allowed; drop-in/drop-out possibility

can_cause.name: Tiered Participation
can_cause.why: Onlookers who don't hold the controls still shape the game through advice, so people take part at different levels of involvement.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Non-players who weigh in on the action feel part of the shared experience instead of being left out, which bonds them with those playing.

conflicts_with.name: PvP
conflicts_with.why: Outside help can feel like cheating and break the players' shared agreement, which matters most when opponents face each other directly.

patterns.name: Reflective Communication
patterns.what_it_is: Players discuss their actions with each other and think about the game together.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must depend on each other and have reasons to share knowledge, take each other's view and agree on methods. The game should give space and time for discussion and reward working it out together.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A chat channel or team mode exists, but no one has to talk to succeed, so nobody discusses or reflects.
patterns.knobs: how much team success depends on shared understanding; time and channels available for discussion

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: In games with negotiation, players may share only part of what they think, hiding some of it to mislead others, which turns open reflection into bluffing.

can_cause.name: Non-Consistent Narration
can_cause.why: When players step out to talk openly about their situation, the story being told stops matching itself, so narration becomes inconsistent.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: In roleplaying games, reflecting between the real people rather than between their characters means they are talking outside the game world.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Recognizing and managing the need for other players leads people to take on the group roles a game offers.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Any game with several players can see this kind of talk, though it may hurt a player's interests unless cooperation is needed or wanted.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Players who roleplay can reflect as their characters would, so the reflecting happens in-world, with others answering in character too.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: Players mixing in-world talk with reflective talk must keep switching between the two, and slips in that switching can break the world's consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: It is a form of out-of-fiction talk, so wanting both it and a fully consistent world makes design harder.

patterns.name: Kingmaker
patterns.what_it_is: A player cannot win themselves but decides which of the others wins.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It arises when positions are clear and a hopeless player still has influence over others, as with early elimination or a predictable winner. A designer avoids it by keeping outcomes uncertain, hiding information, or giving losing players reasons to keep playing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A player is called a kingmaker but their choice has no real effect on who wins, so nothing happens.
patterns.knobs: how early outcomes become clear; how much hidden information there is; how much a trailing player can still affect others

can_cause.name: Predictable Winner
can_cause.why: When players are nearly settled in the endgame, few can still win, so a kingmaker's choice narrows the field and makes the likely winner easy to spot.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Game States
can_cause.why: A player who can't win themselves may still decide who does, and their choices can leave another player with no way to win.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Kingmaking mostly shows up late in a game, when standings are mostly fixed, so it shapes how the final stretch of play unfolds.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: By keeping the outcome open, balancing avoids situations where a losing player decides who wins.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Social dynamics where players decide who wins can leave a single player with little influence, particularly when in the lead.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: A kingmaker can decide the outcome for others arbitrarily, so players no longer have equal standing in determining the result.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance makes it harder to know in advance who is ahead, so it is less clear that anyone is stuck as a kingmaker.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Hidden information can keep players from realizing a kingmaking situation exists, so they don't act on it.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
conflicts_with.why: When the result stays open, it is less likely that one player is clearly out of the running yet able to pick the winner.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If players get something from their play even when they can't win, they have less reason to quit or unbalance the game by kingmaking.

patterns.name: Perspective Taking
patterns.what_it_is: The player tries to see events through another player's or fictional character's eyes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs roles or characters that players must understand to act well, such as role-playing or a game master voicing characters. Rewarding choices that fit another's view makes it more likely.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A role-play label or character sheet that players never need to consider when deciding, so everyone just acts as themselves.
patterns.knobs: how much the game rewards acting from another's view; how detailed the characters or roles are

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Showing the individuals affected as characters lets players imagine their view and feel more involved in the dilemma.

patterns.name: Races
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of finishing under pressure, often ahead of others or before a deadline.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need a shared target with limited time or competitors, and progress should be visible. Excluding goals and a clear end condition create the pressure.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A finish line or score target exists, but with no rival or time pressure players just proceed at leisure.
patterns.knobs: time limit; number of rivals; target distance; visibility of others' progress

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: When a time limit or running out of resources ends the race, play becomes about lasting and constantly handling the present moment rather than reaching a final state.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: Only one competitor can be first, so winning the race means the others cannot also win it.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Your standing in a race depends on how far along other agents are, so their progress directly changes your position.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because players are hurrying toward a goal, certain places in the world, like pick-ups or shortcuts, become especially valuable to reach.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Races can be attached to a game's other aims, so that many games use them as a smaller pressure-adding goal.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Working toward a goal while others or the clock threaten to beat you puts players under pressure to succeed.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: In turn-based games, several players can finish on the same turn, which gives them an equal result.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Even without a clock, a race forces players to finish before an opponent does, which acts as an implicit deadline.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Racing games commonly slow the leader or boost those behind, such as with a speed cap, to keep competitors close.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Racers can be handicapped by head starts or movement limits, so a race is a setting where the handicap can be applied.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: Everyone taking part tries to reach the end or finish before the others, so each participant has the same objective.

can_cause.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
can_cause.why: Being first to reach a finish ends the game and names the winner, so a race is one way to build this pattern.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: The hurry to finish first can change how players find their way, since they must pick routes that are fastest.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A literal race can lead designers to shape the layout of the world around a course.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: When several players share the same goal, a race turns their play into a competition.

patterns.name: Meta Games
patterns.what_it_is: Games built on the results and consequences of other games.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Results must carry over and be comparable between games, through scores, rankings or tournament structure. Players need a reason to care about this layer.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A leaderboard or achievement list that is displayed but changes no decisions and which nobody pursues or compares.
patterns.knobs: what carries between games; how results are compared or rewarded

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Players can do things like buying and trading cards that never happen inside the underlying game yet still belong to the game built on top of it.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because a meta game is built on other games' results, what happens in a single game carries over and affects the game layered above it.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Any meta game that needs several rounds of the underlying game gives players a reason to come back and play it again.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a game links separate play sessions, a player may need to wait for others' sessions to finish first.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: A larger overarching game made of short rounds gives players repeated points where they can step in or out.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: A self-run layer of games built from timed instances lets players choose how many or which timed games to play, setting the total length.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: Player involvement is moved to creating agents, setting up the starting state, or choosing when to play, rather than acting during play.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Optional goals can sit in a meta game layer, and players can also create their own meta game by adding such goals to a game.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: The wider game of being a good player in Go or Golf has its own numbers, such as handicaps, acting as scores.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Meta games make differences in skill visible, so it's easier to see who the experts are.

changes.name: Spectators
changes.why: People watching one game can take part in another game that uses what they saw, giving watching a purpose.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Layering a game on top of one that can't be won gives players goals and a reason to push further than they otherwise would.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Organizing play around the game, such as in tournaments, adds structure on top of it.

patterns.name: Game World Exploration
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: learn how the game world is laid out or find a needed place or item in it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must not see the whole world at once, and they must have real choices about where to go. Something worth finding, such as secrets, resources or shortcuts, must be spread across the unknown areas.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A big map where everything is already shown or marked, or where the path is a single corridor, so 'exploring' is just walking.
patterns.knobs: how much of the world is hidden; how much is hidden and where rewards are placed; how much help (maps, clues) is given

can_cause.name: Easter Eggs
can_cause.why: Hidden extras exist regardless of exploration goals, but sending players to search the world makes them far more likely to actually stumble onto them.

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: Finding or charting places means players must plan routes and find their way around the world to get there.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Unless an overview shows explored areas, players have to remember the layout of places they have already seen.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Some quests send players out to search unknown parts of the world, so exploring can bring about quest-based play.

can_cause.name: Startgame
can_cause.why: Exploration usually dominates the opening of a game, so it often ends up defining what that early phase feels like.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Worlds players can't see all at once invite them to go looking around, especially when they know hidden items exist but not where, so exploring shapes how the world is experienced.

conflicts_with.name: Mini-maps
conflicts_with.why: If a mini-map shows places the player hasn't been to, it hands over what they were supposed to discover.

conflicts_with.name: Quests
conflicts_with.why: Quests that give known locations to visit remove the need to look around, so players may skip exploring.

patterns.name: Stealth
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to move and act so that you are not detected.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Enemies or opponents must detect and punish being seen, and the player must have cover, routes and the time to move carefully. Waiting or slow movement must be a real option.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A stealth label on a game where enemies barely notice you or where running through everything works just as well, so hiding is pointless.
patterns.knobs: enemy sight range and awareness; penalty for detection; amount of cover; noise from movement

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Staying hidden while moving is not a one-off task but an ongoing aim that players must keep up the whole time they travel.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Some sneaking actions would damage a player's standing or reputation if seen, so players try to avoid being observed doing them.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Sneaking past watchful opponents, or sneaking up on them, gives designers a ready basis for missions that players are sent on.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Slow pace and pauses let players think ahead, and how perception works, especially sight lines, gives them things to plan around.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Because sneaking moves slowly with pauses, players can use what they know of the area, like alarm positions, to map out a route.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: Players may want to stay unseen so they can strike opponents who aren't expecting it.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Plans made in advance often break down when something unexpected appears, such as a guard, so players must adjust their approach on the spot.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Being spotted brings clear penalties, so players feel pressure the whole time they try to stay unnoticed.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Sneaking goals can become more demanding when combined with herding goals.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Sneaking past threats without being noticed requires careful, well-timed movement, which makes success depend on the player's motor control.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: Stealth pitted against Guard or Reconnaissance creates goals where one side succeeding means the other fails.

can_cause.name: Rescue
can_cause.why: Players can reach the captive by sneaking past guards instead of fighting them, avoiding confrontation altogether.

can_cause.name: Scouting
can_cause.why: Scouting happens when a player's goal of staying unnoticed is combined with a goal of gathering information about threats.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Stealth makes moving risky, so players must slow down or be careful, since fast or large movements may give them away.

patterns.name: Reconnaissance
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of going around areas of the world and noticing what has changed in them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must not know where things are and must be able to find out by spending time or effort. The information must change, so old knowledge goes stale and checking again is worth it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A scouting action exists, but everything is already visible or never changes, so nobody bothers to use it.
patterns.knobs: how much of the world is hidden; how fast information goes stale; cost and range of observing

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Watching and gathering information must go on over a period of time, so the goal is sustained rather than instant.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Scouting is a narrower kind of information-gathering, aimed at learning where enemies are or whether they exist when that is uncertain.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Since the places are already known, players must remember how things looked before so they can notice what has changed.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Scouting tasks can be placed in scripted scenes or levels to introduce players to threats, though the enemies met don't move the story forward.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: When hidden agents are trying to avoid being spotted, scouting works to stop them from staying undetected.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Players must plan patrols without knowing the situation, and must plan how to avoid being spotted by others' scouting.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Information gained by scouting forces players to rethink what to do next in response to what they found.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: Pairing Reconnaissance with Stealth creates goals where being detected or avoiding detection by one side prevents the other side's goal from succeeding.

can_cause.name: Scouting
can_cause.why: Scouting happens when a player's goal of gathering information is combined with a goal of staying unnoticed while doing it.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Scouting goals shape stealth goals because anyone trying to avoid detection is being searched for, which makes scouting a counter to their hiding.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Overviews
conflicts_with.why: Overviews can reveal too much information, making scouting for it less necessary.

conflicts_with.name: God Views
conflicts_with.why: With an unrestricted view, scouting becomes trivial because players can simply look wherever they like, unless information is hidden from them.

patterns.name: Pottering
patterns.what_it_is: Fiddling with game resources for the sake of the activity, not for a goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need open-ended activities with no pressure, such as safe spaces, no hard deadlines, sorting or building tools, and freedom to set their own goals. Anything that threatens or interferes with their work must be limited.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A sandbox or farm exists, but constant threats, timers or mandatory objectives push players along, so nobody tinkers aimlessly.
patterns.knobs: amount of pressure and threat; how many self-directed activities are offered; how safe the space is

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since nothing forces what to do or when, players decide for themselves which activities to carry out, so pottering naturally hands them choices.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because players freely do lots of whatever small actions they enjoy, they end up repeating the same kinds of actions over and over.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players slowly shape the game toward goals they set or half-notice themselves, so the work they put in quietly becomes meaningful to them.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: Since pottering phases aren't very time-critical, they suit the growth phase where players slowly extend what they have.

changes.name: Exploitation
changes.why: Exploiting what one has built is typically not urgent, so players can approach it in a leisurely, self-directed way.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Pottering usually means players tinkering with game elements or small parts of the world itself, changing it bit by bit.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Whatever players do while pottering affects how resources get used and handled in the game, even when the world doesn't change.

conflicts_with.name: Committed Goals
conflicts_with.why: Pottering relies on handling resources without pressure from rewards or penalties, while committed goals depend on exactly that kind of pressure.

conflicts_with.name: Narration Structures
conflicts_with.why: Idle tinkering by design produces nothing noteworthy, so it gives the story no events to build on.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Constant tension keeps players stressed about their activities, which works against the relaxed, self-directed nature of pottering.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limits
conflicts_with.why: Deadlines force players to hurry or follow the game's schedule, undermining the freedom to act whenever they wish.

conflicts_with.name: Time Pressure
conflicts_with.why: Having to act quickly causes stress and removes the freedom to take one's time, which pottering depends on.

patterns.name: Speedruns
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to finish the game or part of it as fast as possible.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a real-time structure, a trustworthy time measure and a way to compare or share results, ideally with replays. Routes should be learnable and improvable so there is room to get faster.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A built-in timer shown on screen that nobody tracks or compares, with no record, so there is no reason to try again faster.
patterns.knobs: time limit or par times; whether records are stored and shared; how many shortcuts exist

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Players run speedruns mostly to show off their skill, so a notable run becomes something they can retell afterward as a story of that play session.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Beating a faster time requires getting better at the game, and runs are usually done to display that skill, so the player's mastery grows and shows.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: When a speedrun is measured against earlier player times, those stored performances serve as recorded data about how players have done.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: A time target can be added on top of an existing objective, as in Cogs, where finishing fast earns extra stars beyond simply completing the puzzle.

can_cause.name: Handicap Achievements
can_cause.why: Designers can attach an explicit time requirement to an achievement, so finishing within that limit becomes a harder rewarded challenge, as with the Left 4 Dead 2 example.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Speedruns sit on top of the normal game, giving players a competition about time, either against their own records or others' times.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Fast or interesting runs are the sort of thing players want to tell others about afterward, so they produce material for stories.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When a speedrun covers a whole game, its time sets a minimum length, helping establish how short a session can be.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Since a speedrun means doing something better than before, it is a challenge players choose to take on after completing the main goal.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Players race against a clock, either competing with their own or others' times or trying to finish a section within a set duration.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because players want to better their own results, they go back and replay the same game or section several times.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Trying to meet a time limit puts the player under pressure to perform, which very likely makes play feel tense.

can_cause.name: Time Limited Game Instances
can_cause.why: When a speedrun covers a whole game, that play session has a time boundary tied to finishing within the target duration.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: A speedrun needs a time boundary attached to some other goal, whether the designer sets it or it comes from earlier performances.

can_cause.name: Time Pressure
can_cause.why: Because the player is trying to beat a time limit, they must hurry and feel the clock pushing on their choices.

can_cause.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
can_cause.why: Recorded fast runs let other players see and compare against someone else's performance within their own game, so one session informs another.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Fast completions gain worth when shown to others, since viewers can see the skill and work behind them.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Players can try to clear a level as fast as possible, so a time goal changes how an existing level is played, as in Portal.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Speedruns need a real-time game, because counting turns or moves in other games turns the challenge into puzzle solving rather than racing the clock.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: These ask players to ignore everything except the most efficient play, so the story is disregarded.

patterns.name: Player-Defined Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal where players themselves create or customize goals and subgoals in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs open systems, readable information such as scores and state, and room for varied approaches. Players must feel free to set aims beyond the official ones.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game has a 'custom goal' menu that nobody uses, because the game offers no way to track or measure progress toward it.
patterns.knobs: how open the sandbox is; how visible scores and progress are; whether goals can be formally set up

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: Since players invent their own goals, they can revise them mid-game, unless the game uses a rule system that forces goals to be tied to the game state.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Goals players make up for themselves tend to be short-lived, since they are dropped or replaced once the player loses interest or achieves them.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Players can attach their own prizes or punishments outside the game's rules to goals they set, so what happens reaches beyond the game itself.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because players can pick or invent goals, they get to decide which aims to pursue instead of being limited to a fixed set.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: A goal players come up with themselves is not demanded by the game, so pursuing it is a matter of personal choice.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: When a player sets a goal in reaction to what other players are trying to achieve, that goal can become about stopping them.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: Several players can agree to share a goal they defined themselves, though when game rules force such goals into being, the players must negotiate.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: If the game helps detect a player's own goals, it can automatically apply penalties on failure; players can also invent penalties outside the rules.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: If the game helps detect a player's own goals, it can automatically give rewards on success; players can also invent rewards outside the rules.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Players can set their own winning conditions in a game that has none, giving closure and structure to what would otherwise feel like one endless experience.

conflicts_with.name: Goal Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Showing designer-made goals pulls players' attention toward them, which competes with players inventing and following objectives of their own.

patterns.name: Goal-Driven Personal Development
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: after finishing earlier goals, the character sets new ones for themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goals must be measurable from game state and link into chains, so finishing one opens the next, with a way for the agent to pick from them. For computer agents this needs detailed encoded conditions and benefits.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character whose 'new goals' are scripted text or a changed title, while behaviour and choices stay the same.
patterns.knobs: how many chained goals; how much choice among next goals; how closely goals depend on past outcomes

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: Because an agent picks fresh goals after finishing old ones, it ends up pursuing its own changing purposes over time rather than only what the game hands it.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Agents that choose new goals based on how earlier ones turned out act like believable characters, which helps the game world feel coherent.

can_cause.name: Open Destiny
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled characters that pursue their own goals can end up in different places, giving them destinies that vary between playthroughs.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Computer characters pursuing their own growth can end up in different places, which varies the story across playthroughs.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Giving agents goals that build on one another, with new ones picked once old ones close, makes their behavior and growth change over the course of play.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Computer-controlled agents can use finer-grained quests with explicit benefits and requirements, so they too choose follow-up goals and develop differently each game.

patterns.name: Construction/Scoring Phase Shift
patterns.what_it_is: Players stop growing stronger and begin collecting victory points.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Building up an engine must pay off, but score-taking must eventually be worth more than more building. Players need to be able to judge when to switch, and the game must end in a way that makes the switch matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: There are build actions and scoring actions, but scoring is best from the start or building is always best, so no switch is ever needed.
patterns.knobs: how quickly building pays back; scoring value; game length or end trigger

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Players who spot when the switch from building up to collecting points happens, or trigger it when it helps them, show skill at playing the game well.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because play splits into a building stage and a point-gathering stage, the game always has at least two phases with different player goals.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: The shift to point-gathering works as a kind of endgame, so it influences when that final stage of play is considered to begin.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: The building phase corresponds to expansion, so when players shift to scoring, their expansion activity is changed or stopped.

changes.name: Exploitation
changes.why: The scoring phase corresponds to exploitation, so the timing of the shift decides when players start cashing in on what they built.

changes.name: Gameplay Engines
changes.why: The shift marks the point where building engines stops being worthwhile and maximizing points becomes more important.

changes.name: Middlegame
changes.why: Since the shift acts as a kind of endgame start, it determines where the middlegame stops and the endgame takes over.

changes.name: Positive Feedback Loops
changes.why: The shift sets the moment when growing your strengths for compounding gains stops paying off and points matter more.

patterns.name: Playing to Lose
patterns.what_it_is: The player deliberately loses with their character because it is more interesting.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Failure must be allowed to be interesting, and players need room to roleplay and to shape their characters' fate. Rules should not wipe out a character too early, and the group should value dramatic loss.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players say they will lose on purpose, but they still try to win, or losing simply ends the game with no story value.
patterns.knobs: how harsh the penalty for losing is; how much roleplay freedom players have; protection against early removal

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Players give up comfort, their character's fortunes, and some of their own play so that others get better drama, which makes losing a shared effort.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Others notice and value a player's skillful losing, and the player is seen as serving everyone's fun rather than only their own position.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Players usually steer their characters toward ruin on purpose, because watching a dramatic, memorable downfall is the fun they are after.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Losing on purpose lets players choose a negative arc for their character, so how the character fails becomes the way it changes.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: The focus shifts to how characters lose rather than whether they win, so they act sensibly from their own view yet head toward bad outcomes.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: It doesn't oppose roleplaying: players have characters choose reasonably given what they know, even though the player knows the choice will likely go badly.

changes.name: Storytelling
changes.why: Players use deliberate failure to shape a particular kind of story, putting drama and narrative ahead of improving their own standing in the game.

conflicts_with.name: Early Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Early elimination makes it hard for players to want to deliberately lose, since being out is already a drawback.

patterns.name: Extermination
patterns.what_it_is: A stage of play where the main task is to destroy, most often other players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Elimination goals and combat must be available, with the strongest combat units or tools held back until late. Games must be long enough to contain distinct phases, and elimination must really be possible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Attacking is allowed from turn one and nobody can be eliminated, so no distinct late stage of destruction ever forms.
patterns.knobs: when strong combat units unlock; whether and how players can be eliminated

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: Because the push to eliminate rivals makes a good final stretch of a game, designers often place an Extermination phase at the end.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: When players can actually be knocked out, a phase focused on elimination creates bigger, more final wrap-ups of parts of the game as play moves forward.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Focusing everyone on wiping out opponents makes it more likely that someone actually gets removed from the game, provided the rules allow removal at all.

can_cause.name: PvP
can_cause.why: When the main aim is eliminating other players, those players end up fighting each other directly, so player-versus-player play grows stronger.

conflicts_with.name: Early Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Ending the game with an extermination phase pushes knockouts toward the end of the game instance, so players are not removed early.

patterns.name: Stimulated Planning
patterns.what_it_is: The game's design pushes players to think through their actions ahead of time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Results of actions must be predictable enough for plans to be trusted, and there must be goals that need several steps. The option space should be large enough to need planning but not so large that it is hopeless.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that lets you plan but where randomness or a single obvious move makes any plan pointless.
patterns.knobs: predictability of outcomes; number of steps to goals; number of options per turn

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Planning takes thinking time, and in multiplayer turn-based games one player's long planning leaves the others waiting with nothing to do.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: When players lack enough information to plan well, they can try things out to learn what actions do.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Planning can happen between play sessions, such as thinking about character development or building decks, outside the game itself.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When players can't see enough to plan, they set themselves goals of finding out what they need to know.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Being able to plan efficiently shows how well a player understands and handles the game.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: To reach a big end state, players break it into smaller goals that together lead there.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: In real-time games, feeling the need to plan quickly can be enough to create tension.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Other encouragement to plan makes players more or less likely to actually use the strategic knowledge they have.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Enemies disturb what players are doing, making careful planning harder or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: Constant time pressure limits how much players can plan ahead, which undermines designs that encourage careful planning.

patterns.name: Varied Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Gameplay changes within one game or from game to game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Choices have to lead to meaningfully different situations, supported by changing rules, random elements or generated worlds, and by feedback that discourages repeating one approach. Differences must affect how play develops, not just surface details.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Many options or levels that all play the same, so players settle into one routine within minutes.
patterns.knobs: amount of randomness; number of distinct viable goals or strategies; how often rules or content change

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: When play keeps shifting, players must keep adapting to new situations, so the game becomes harder on top of how hard each individual activity is.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Because players keep facing shifting contexts, mastering such a game is affected, usually becoming harder.

conflicts_with.name: Camping
conflicts_with.why: Since waiting in one spot can be a winning tactic, players have less reason to try different things.

conflicts_with.name: Entrenching Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When the game state can change less and less, players are unlikely to gain new kinds of actions, so variety in play tends to shrink.

conflicts_with.name: No-Ops
conflicts_with.why: Doing nothing too often becomes repetitive like any overused activity, leaving play less varied.

conflicts_with.name: Symmetric Goals
conflicts_with.why: Playing another role with the same goal as before feels much the same, so replays offer less variety than with differing goals.

conflicts_with.name: Symmetric Resource Distribution
conflicts_with.why: Symmetry removes variety, so when everyone has the same resources there is less difference between players and sessions.

patterns.name: Tactical Planning
patterns.what_it_is: Planning based on what is known about the current state of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need several meaningful options whose value depends on the current situation, plus enough time and information to weigh them. Costs or trade-offs must make the choice matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: One option is always clearly best, or there is too little time or information to compare, so choosing is just habit.
patterns.knobs: number of options; how much outcomes depend on local state; time to decide; amount of hidden information

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because planning to improve your odds feels effective, players may come to believe their own choices shape outcomes more than they truly do.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Planning only makes sense when players have several possible actions to pick between, so offering tactical planning implies those options exist.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: When results depend on how well players plan, getting better at planning gives them a route to mastering the game.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Since planning is meant to raise your chances of succeeding, players cannot be sure their plan will work out as hoped.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: If players in a multiplayer game can plan their moves, others cannot know in advance what they will choose.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: When success hinges on how well players use their available choices, their own planning skill becomes part of the overall skill needed.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: The chance to plan in order to improve your odds of success encourages players to think ahead and actually do so.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players who see their planning bring good results can feel that the thought they invested in the game was worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When players must plan tactics without seeing everything, they need to find out missing facts, which creates information goals.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Having to plan within a time limit or in real time pushes players to decide faster, while tension can also make planning harder.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Adding tactical planning to a real-time game makes the overall gameplay harder, since players must plan within a limited amount of time.

patterns.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
patterns.what_it_is: Success depends on hand and eye skill rather than calculation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must run in real time with quick, low-lag feedback, and outcomes must depend on how precisely the player acts. The challenge should fit what players can learn to do.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Actions that look like they need aiming or timing, but an assist makes them succeed whatever the player does.
patterns.knobs: required speed and precision; size of the target or timing window; lag

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because players use their bodies with fine control over results, they may feel their own skill shaped the outcome more than it really did, as with dice throwing.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Dexterous actions usually take place over a stretch of time rather than in an instant, since the player has to keep performing them.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Getting good at physically performing the actions is often the central thing players improve at, making dexterity the core of mastery.

can_cause.name: Mimetic Interfaces
can_cause.why: Actions judged by how the player physically performs them often use controls that imitate the real movement, so the two commonly appear together.

can_cause.name: Physical Enactment
can_cause.why: Since success depends on the player's actual bodily performance, the player is physically acting out the task, and the two often go together.

can_cause.name: Player Physical Prowess
can_cause.why: When results depend on motor ability in real-time play, being physically skilled becomes what separates stronger players from weaker ones.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Players' own motor skill gives an easy way to blend their abilities with the character's, so outcomes depend on both.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Being real time alone is not enough; the pattern adds actions that must be done while the game keeps changing, shaping how these games play.

patterns.name: Strategic Planning
patterns.what_it_is: Planning based only on knowing the rules and what other players can do.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs learnable general structures and real strategic choices, plus replays so players can try and refine strategies. Outcomes should be predictable enough to reward a plan.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several listed strategies that all lead to the same result, so choosing a plan changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: number of viable strategies; predictability of results; how much replay is encouraged

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Because players can plan ahead using general knowledge of the game, they end up doing that planning outside actual moves, such as thinking or discussing between turns.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When a game lets players prepare using general structures and rules, it gives them reason and room to make plans, so planning becomes a prompted activity.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players notice how their strategies work or can be adjusted, so the thinking they put into planning feels like it paid off.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: Where planning is the only activity, players set up the system beforehand, often by building agents, and then the game runs itself according to that plan.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with replayability, games that encourage planning make it more certain that varied play is present.

changes.name: Replayability
changes.why: Players can think about how to improve their play and try different strategies, which gives them reasons to play again.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Since future events cannot be calculated, long-term planning gets harder, though known odds still allow planning at a higher level.

patterns.name: Downtime
patterns.what_it_is: Time when a player has to wait during a game session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It comes from rules that block actions, such as turn order, penalties or slow players. It stays bearable when there is something to watch or plan.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pause screen of a second or two that nobody notices as waiting.
patterns.knobs: length of enforced waits; how often they occur; what players can do during them

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: Being forced to wait can itself be dealt to a player as harm, a cost they suffer apart from any health loss.

can_cause.name: Individual Penalties
can_cause.why: Waiting can be imposed on one particular player as a punishment, such as after that player's avatar dies.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: Since a player cannot act at all while waiting, it is an extreme version of a quiet stretch in play.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Making players sit idle works as a cost for failure, for example as part of what happens when a character dies.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Unable to act, the waiting player loses their agency and can only watch the game continue, becoming a temporary onlooker.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: While idle, players often use the time to think ahead and plan their next moves, even when others' planning caused the wait.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Waiting players can watch play unfold and expect something bad to happen, which builds tension, though idleness otherwise tends to weaken it.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: A critical hit can leave the target unable to act for a while, adding a delay on top of losing health.

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: In roleplaying games, giving characters idle time alongside uncertain knowledge leaves room for them to chat and swap rumors.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Reloading downtime leaves players exposed for a while, so they must plan when it is safe to fire.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Having to reload when ammo runs out brings idle moments, so players must pick a good time to reload.

changes.name: Closure Points
changes.why: Idle time lets players just take in the result of what they did rather than starting new actions, making endings clearer.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Waiting can be part of what a character's death costs the player, such as sitting out until a new round.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: By watching the game while idle, players can better anticipate what will happen next.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Waiting happens when players are eliminated or when late arrivals must be brought up to date.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: The facilitator may deliberately force waiting, such as after dying, yet computer facilitators can also be used to avoid such waits.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: While waiting, players cannot act, so they lose the ability to choose what they do.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Letting players join late spares others from waiting for everyone to be present before play begins.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: Waiting removes the player's ability to act and influence the game, turning them into onlookers.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: Because play continues continuously, players must act or at least pay attention, leaving less room for idleness.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Idle players tend to feel less tension, though it can arise if they expect something bad to happen.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limits
conflicts_with.why: A deadline pushes players to plan and act instead of idling, since once time is up they can no longer act.

patterns.name: Player-Planned Development
patterns.what_it_is: The player can plan in advance how the game's stats and objects will develop.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be several development paths with different long-term payoffs, and enough time and information for players to plan. The consequences have to carry forward.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A skill tree where every path ends up with the same power, so planning changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: number of branches; how different their payoffs are; how costly it is to change plans

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Because players choose how their elements grow, they can steer growth toward particular skill specialties and focus on being good at specific things.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Working toward a planned development gives players an ongoing target that they keep pursuing over a long stretch of play instead of finishing quickly.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: To reach the development they planned, players may have their controlled elements act in required ways, whether or not those actions are otherwise desirable.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Making plans for growth can lead players to believe they steer outcomes more than they really do.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Planning ahead can happen entirely outside actual play, such as thinking through or discussing a development path away from the game itself.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Different parts of a plan can compete with each other, or clash with what is best right now or for winning, so players must trade off.

can_cause.name: Open Destiny
can_cause.why: Being able to plan how their elements grow supports the feeling that the future of those elements is not fixed and can go many ways.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: Since players decide how their elements should develop, they end up setting their own objectives rather than only following ones given by the game.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When growth can be mapped out in advance, players are encouraged to think ahead and lay out steps toward it.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Listed as combining with Persistent Game Worlds to create Investments, but the page gives no explanation.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players choose how their character grows, so the progress reflects their own plans and effort.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Letting players plan development lets them alter how the story structure unfolds, rather than just following it.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Planned development is typically given so players can control how their own characters grow.

changes.name: Player Created Game Elements
changes.why: Planned development is typically introduced so players can control how things they created in the game grow.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: Special abilities can become targets players aim for, and they can also steer which direction the planned growth takes.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Players may adjust how they act in character so it makes sense in the story with the development they planned.

changes.name: Team Development
changes.why: When planned growth applies to members of a team, it changes how the team as a whole grows.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
conflicts_with.why: Forced behavior can override players' own plans for their characters, unless the constraint comes from those plans.

conflicts_with.name: Narration Structures
conflicts_with.why: A story fixed before play works against letting players plan how things develop.

patterns.name: Encouraged Return Visits
patterns.what_it_is: Game design that makes players want to come back to the same places and activities.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must be persistent and able to be left and re-entered, with timers, regenerating resources or growing rewards that make coming back worthwhile.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A daily login prompt or reminder with a trivial reward that players claim and ignore.
patterns.knobs: length of timers; regeneration rate; size and growth of rewards for repeated visits

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Many of the same reasons that pull players back to a game also push them to repeat similar activities over and over, which is what grinding is.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Pushing players to come back at certain times, together with ongoing goals, makes scheduling your play part of the challenge.

changes.name: Continuous Goals
changes.why: When actions can be interrupted, return visits make never-ending goals more challenging, since leaving the game carries risk.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: The pattern assumes you can join and leave often, and it gives you reasons to rejoin the game repeatedly.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: These games want a certain number of players present at all times, so they commonly use ways to bring players back.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: These games want enough players around at all times, so they commonly use features that make players return.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Such worlds continue between sessions, so return incentives like regenerating resources and delayed effects naturally build on them.

patterns.name: Game World Navigation
patterns.what_it_is: Finding a way from one place in the game world to another when the route is not obvious.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Need a world with several possible routes and no obvious best one, so wrong turns are possible, and a destination worth reaching. Navigation aids must not give the answer away.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A level with a single path, or a minimap and waypoint line that always shows where to go, so there is nothing to work out.
patterns.knobs: how many routes and branches; how strong the navigation aids are (map, markers, landmarks)

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: When aids make finding the way easy, moving around becomes a relaxed activity that asks little of the player.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: When aids are scarce or misleading, working out where to go becomes a real test of the player's ability.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Navigating only makes sense when players can pick among several routes; with one forced path there would be nothing to figure out.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: While finding their way, players can stumble upon places they haven't seen, so navigating can lead to exploring.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: In text games where going one way and back doesn't return you to the start, working out the routes becomes a puzzle.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Navigation is the act of working out how to reach a destination, which is how players accomplish goals of getting somewhere.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Physical navigation is what you get when ordinary game-world wayfinding is carried out in real physical space rather than a fictional one.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Overviews
conflicts_with.why: Overviews can reveal too much, lessening the challenge of finding your own way.

conflicts_with.name: God Views
conflicts_with.why: A view that lets players look around the world freely, ignoring in-game objects, makes finding the way trivial.

conflicts_with.name: Mini-maps
conflicts_with.why: Showing position and direction on a small map takes away the uncertainty that navigation depends on, so the challenge can vanish.

conflicts_with.name: Privileged Movement
conflicts_with.why: Abilities like flight can reveal the surroundings and open up movement, which can undercut the difficulty of finding the way.

patterns.name: Grinding
patterns.what_it_is: Repeating simple actions many times to get resources or complete a goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a need for resources or progress that can only be met by repeating a simple, low-challenge action many times, with rewards that don't advance the player too much. Players must choose or feel pushed to repeat it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A repeating task that is quick and varied enough that players don't feel repetition, or one the player never needs to do.
patterns.knobs: amount needed; drop rates; how repetitive and easy the action is

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because grinding is made of trivial, repeated actions, players can do it with little attention or skill, which suits relaxed, low-demand play.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players don't notice their repeated actions barely move their progress, they keep believing the effort matters more than it does.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Players usually experience grinding as labor, so the repeated chores become tedious extra work added to the game.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Grinding offers harmless small things to do without pushing progress, which is welcome for players who just like puttering around.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Doing the same simple action over and over is exactly what makes the play feel repetitive.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Grinding needs something given back for the repeated effort, though these rewards are kept from advancing players' overall position.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: In games that can never be won, grinding supplies activities for players to keep doing without ever reaching an end.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Repetitive play can challenge players to find ways to put in as much time as possible.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: In worlds meant not to change over time, grinding gives players things to do that don't alter the world's state.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Repeating easy tasks once mastered counters the idea of challenge, though grinding can also be turned into one.

conflicts_with.name: Clickability
conflicts_with.why: Clicking that is fun in itself makes repetitive actions feel enjoyable, which works against the feeling of grinding through tedious tasks.

conflicts_with.name: Ephemeral Goals
conflicts_with.why: Constantly changing goals keep play from settling into repetitive routines, so they can help avoid grinding.

conflicts_with.name: Mules
conflicts_with.why: Mules are AI players built to perform grinding in place of people, so players no longer have to do it.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: Others who carry out game-influencing actions on players' behalf lessen how much grinding players must do.

conflicts_with.name: Testing Achievements
conflicts_with.why: Encouraging players to try other parts of the game gives them a break from grinding.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limits
conflicts_with.why: Limits such as automatic collection before a deadline make the repeated tasks optional rather than required.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If players realize their repeated actions barely affect progress, the sense that effort is worthwhile is undercut.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Returns
conflicts_with.why: Repeated trips over known ground feel like grinding, and a fast way back removes that repetition, so the two pull in opposite directions.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Travel
conflicts_with.why: Skipping repeated trips through already known areas removes a repetitive chore, so jumping counters the grind of long, linear travel.

patterns.name: Player Killing
patterns.what_it_is: Players are removed from active play by the deliberate actions of others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to harm each other, and the harm must be traceable to a real agent. Penalties for dying and rewards for killing have to make it a real choice.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players can technically shoot each other, but death costs nothing and the victim returns at once, so it is just noise.
patterns.knobs: cost of dying; reward for killing; who can attack whom and where

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because players know others can remove them from play, they feel uneasy; the unease grows or shrinks with how harsh the death costs and kill payoffs are.

can_cause.name: Friendly Fire
can_cause.why: Friendly Fire needs players able to kill other players; combined with shared teams, those kills can land on teammates.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: When other human players are able to carry out lethal actions, players clearly see the source as an agent, so killing fits naturally.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Whether players may kill members of their own party is an open design question, and loot disputes could push players toward it.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Team members may be able to kill one another through friendly fire, and the penalties for being killed also shift the balance between teams.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Immune players cannot be killed by others, so attacking them becomes difficult or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Killing can eliminate players or bring death consequences, which are misfortunes that disturb equal chances.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Penalties for being killed fall on individual players but still shift the strength of their teams, which can tilt a team-versus-team match.

conflicts_with.name: TvT
conflicts_with.why: In team-versus-team play, kills and their penalties can tilt the contest toward one side and upset fairness between teams.

patterns.name: Memorizing
patterns.what_it_is: It benefits the player to remember facts about the game or its state.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Information must be shown briefly or only once, and later decisions must depend on recalling it. It must not be easy to look up again, and there must be enough variation that memory beyond one session helps.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with facts to remember, but the interface always shows them again or they never affect any decision.
patterns.knobs: how long information stays visible; how much has to be remembered; whether it can be looked up again

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When some of what must be remembered isn't known yet, players set out to find it first, so seeking information becomes a goal supporting memorization.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Remembering rules and facts well is a skill that separates players who have mastered the game from those who haven't.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Because memory is a skill that can fail, players can't be sure they will recall things correctly, which makes outcomes uncertain.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: When remembering boosts something also driven by a character's powers or abilities, players use it anyway, blending their own skill with the character's.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Removing tokens in a game with open information forces players to hold the game state in their heads, as in blindfold chess, making it harder.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Remembering what has already been drawn or used lets players figure out plausible future plans.

changes.name: Action Programming
changes.why: Making players hold a planned action sequence and its effects on the game state in mind while planning makes programming harder.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: Players must remember the rules so the game runs smoothly, or else play stops while someone checks them.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Indicators
conflicts_with.why: If the game displays the details, players needn't remember them, which reduces or removes the memory challenge.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Overviews
conflicts_with.why: When the state is shown to players, there is less need to remember it themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: If remembered information can directly solve a puzzle, later playthroughs become trivial because the answers are already known.

patterns.name: Experimenting
patterns.what_it_is: Trial actions to learn the rules and game state or to practice skills.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Failure must be cheap and actions reversible, and the game must have something worth finding out (hidden information, complex systems, enemy weaknesses) with predictable cause and effect. Heavy penalties or too much randomness make players stop trying things.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A sandbox with lots of options, but one mistake is punished harshly or results are so random that nothing can be learned.
patterns.knobs: cost of failure and reversibility of actions; how much randomness hides cause and effect

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Trying things out reveals strategic knowledge that isn't obvious, and as players keep learning from their trials they gradually get better at the game.

can_cause.name: Illusionary Rewards
can_cause.why: Test actions usually don't advance any actual goal, so the player feels they are accomplishing something without it counting toward winning.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Some games hide how their world behaves, so players must experiment to work out what unknown items or effects do.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When a trial can have heavy or costly outcomes, the player feels pressure about whether it's worth risking.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Using non-renewable resources while experimenting makes players commit more to careful planning.

changes.name: Casual Gameplay
changes.why: How expensive it is to try things affects how relaxed play feels; cheap experiments keep play casual.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Costly experiments make the game harder, while cheap ones ease it, so the cost of trying shapes difficulty.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Trying actions out lets players uncover the strategic knowledge that is available to be learned in the game.

conflicts_with.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
conflicts_with.why: Widgets that highlight important objects take away the need for players to explore and look around on their own.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: If actions can't be undone, trying things out becomes risky, so players avoid it.

conflicts_with.name: Point of Interest Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Pointing out important entities for the player removes the need to search and explore for them.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Experimenting needs consistent outcomes to learn from, and chance results make it harder to draw conclusions from trials.

conflicts_with.name: Vision Modes
conflicts_with.why: Modes that reveal important objects spare players from exploring to find them.

patterns.name: Save-Load Cycles
patterns.what_it_is: The player saves and loads again and again until the game reaches the state they want.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs easy, fast saving and loading and challenges where a bad result can be undone by reloading. Restricting save timing or slots reduces how often it happens.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A save system that is so slow or restricted that players never use it to retry, so no cycles of save, try, and reload actually occur.
patterns.knobs: how fast and how often saving is allowed; how many slots; ironman-style limits

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Saving and loading are things you do outside the game's actual challenges, so each one makes the player wait a little.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: If something goes wrong, you can load an earlier state and try again, so a failure doesn't have to stand.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because you can stop and resume from stored states, you decide when you play and when you stop.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Reloading after a bad outcome and replaying with what you learned lets you shape the outcome to look better than it really was.

can_cause.name: Game Pauses
can_cause.why: Saving lets you stop a real-time game and come back later, giving it pauses it wouldn't otherwise have.

can_cause.name: Game Time Manipulation
can_cause.why: Loading rewinds the game to an earlier moment, and you do it through menu actions rather than through anything done in play.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Since you can store the state and quit, you can break off play whenever life interrupts and pick it up again.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Players can decide for themselves where one session ends and the next begins, because saving lets them split play at will.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Loading lets you replay the same stretch of a game instance more than once, even without starting the whole game over.

can_cause.name: Save Scumming
can_cause.why: If you lean heavily on saving and reloading to get exactly the result you want, it turns into a habit of constant retrying.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: The breaks between sessions give you time to think ahead about what you will do next.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Single-player games let players undo harmful outcomes by reloading, which removes the fear of trying things.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Saving lets you pause a game that keeps running continuously, so it gains stopping points that turn-based games already have between turns.

conflicts_with.name: Death Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Players can reload a saved game after dying, undoing the cost and making the consequences hard to enforce.

conflicts_with.name: Difficulty Levels
conflicts_with.why: Repeatedly saving and reloading lets players dodge consequences, which undermines the difficulty the level was meant to enforce.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: If players can save and reload, they can return to an earlier state, so events cannot be totally permanent.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Players must agree on when to reload an earlier state, which makes loading awkward.

conflicts_with.name: Penalties
conflicts_with.why: In single-player games, players can reload an earlier save to undo a penalty, making it avoidable.

conflicts_with.name: Permadeath
conflicts_with.why: Saving and reloading at will lets players reverse deaths, so the character's loss is never truly permanent.

conflicts_with.name: Scores
conflicts_with.why: A score no longer shows how well you played in one continuous run if you can rewind and retry parts of it.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: What you do in play no longer matches the order of events in the story world, because reloading jumps you backward.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Once you can undo a dangerous moment by reloading, you experience it without the emotional strain it was meant to cause.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limited Game Instances
conflicts_with.why: With saves, a time limit loses its point from a planning view, since you can restore the state and try again.

patterns.name: Bluffing
