patterns.what_it_is: A player gives false information to influence others' decisions in their own favor.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Hidden information and unpredictable players are needed, plus ways to send misleading signals and a payoff for being believed. Face-to-face play adds skill, but any communication channel works.
patterns.just_a_label_when: All information is public or actions reveal intentions, so a bluff cannot work, or a bluff costs and gains nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much is hidden; signals available; payoff and cost of being caught

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Some players are better at deceiving than others, so being skilled at bluffing becomes a way to show mastery and gain an edge.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Skill at bluffing influences which roles players take in the group, for example whether someone manages to dominate the others.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Players differ in how convincingly they bluff, so social ability directly shapes how the game turns out.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Bluffs make results uncertain, so players feel on edge, most of all the one who is bluffing.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Hiding planned betrayals and negotiating convincingly requires bluffing, so deceiving others lets the betrayal be set up and enjoyed.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Succeeding at deceiving others relies on how convincingly the player carries out the social act, so the result is uncertain.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Deceiving or misleading others about your intentions makes it hard for them to deduce what you will do next.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: When players bluff while communicating, others can't tell whether what they hear is true, so their information becomes doubtful.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: Players can set off false alarms, which makes warnings something that might be a trick rather than reliable information.

changes.name: Bidding
changes.why: Players can pretend to bid on something they don't actually want, so a bid doesn't reliably show real interest.

changes.name: Surrendering
changes.why: A player who bluffs skillfully makes opponents more likely to give up, since they believe the bluffer's position is stronger.

patterns.name: Collecting
patterns.what_it_is: The player gathers items or elements, aiming to complete a needed set.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Collectable items must be spread out so that gathering them takes effort, and the gathering must serve some goal or reward.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Items lie everywhere and are picked up automatically, with no choice or effort and no use.
patterns.knobs: item scarcity and spread; effort per item; what collections give

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Gathering items is a common bottom-level goal that feeds into a higher goal in the hierarchy.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Requiring players to gather resources that are easy to find but needed in large amounts creates repeated, trivial work.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: Gathering game elements in different amounts invites players to decide on their own targets, such as how many or which ones to get.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Collectable resources are not always available and show up at spawn points or generators, so you must come back to find new ones.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Growth is often driven by collecting things like experience points, which are gathered up until a progress goal is reached.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Players collect items to take ownership of them and to complete collection goals.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Players may have to gather resources from locations or generators in the game world.

patterns.name: Flip-Flop Events
patterns.what_it_is: The last turn of one round and the first of the next go to the same player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The turn order must change between rounds, and players need actions (like claiming first-player spot) that let them end one round and start the next. Without such player-driven control it happens only by accident.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Turn order shifts on paper, but nobody can steer it, so the back-to-back turn is a random side effect nobody plans for.
patterns.knobs: how turn order is reassigned; how much players can influence who goes first next round

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Moving two turns back to back lets a player chain actions together with no opponent interrupting, which is a special kind of combo that is hard to arrange.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Because lining up back-to-back turns takes careful planning, a player who manages it repeatedly shows they understand the game well.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: The pattern bends the normal alternation of turns, since a player can act twice consecutively when the order is reshuffled between rounds.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: If double turns happen by chance or luck rather than by player choice, some players gain a strong advantage unfairly, upsetting the fairness between them.

patterns.name: Analysis Paralysis
patterns.what_it_is: The game stalls while someone takes too long weighing the consequences of possible moves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Appears when many options have predictable consequences and a player's turn blocks others, especially with high stakes in the middle or end of a game. It arises from player behavior rather than a direct rule, so designers can only make it likelier or rarer.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game has many options on paper but one is clearly best, so nobody deliberates and no stalls occur.
patterns.knobs: number of options per turn; predictability of results; turn time limit

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a player in a turn-based game thinks too long over a move, everyone else has to wait for them.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: In turn-based play, players waiting on someone who cannot decide may push that person to hurry, making them feel bad for holding things up.

conflicts_with.name: Action Caps
conflicts_with.why: Caps push players to plan carefully, which can cause overthinking in multiplayer turn-based games, though a small enough cap keeps the choices few.

conflicts_with.name: Private Game Spaces
conflicts_with.why: With fewer causal links between players, competition is less likely to cause overthinking, so the pattern tends to reduce this problem.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: Little time to plan means players can't get stuck over-thinking their options, so real time works against this problem.

conflicts_with.name: Time Pressure
conflicts_with.why: Limited time to plan usually stops players from overthinking, yet it can also push them into freezing, so the effect goes both ways.

patterns.name: Camping
patterns.what_it_is: A player stays in one spot of the world for a long time, waiting for something to appear.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Waiting must be cheap, and a spot must give a lasting edge (range, cover, a spawn or resource point). Powerful ranged tools and hard-to-reach spots help it appear, while safe zones and alternative routes limit it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A nice-looking vantage spot exists, but it is easy to flank or the target never comes there, so no one stays.
patterns.knobs: strength and range of weapons; how defensible spots are; spawn or resource frequency; number of flanking routes

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: If players can already see the whole game state clearly, the waiting stops feeling like expectation and becomes just idle time with nothing to do.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Camping works best with knowledge of good spots, so players are pushed to think ahead about where and how to set up.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Campers wait for events they expect but cannot time exactly, and that uncertain waiting builds suspense.

changes.name: Collecting
changes.why: Camping to collect depends on how often items appear at spawn points, so players wait there for the next one.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Players wait with powerful long-range weapons in hard-to-reach places and fight only when opponents come into view.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: When guarding needs no movement, staying put and waiting is exactly what camping involves.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Stealth goals call for the same patient, still waiting that camping uses, so the two fit together easily.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: Some games make teams camp at spawn points in order to change who owns an area.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Enemies disturb players who try to stay in one place, making camping harder or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Flanking Routes
conflicts_with.why: Routes around a camper's position let opponents attack from other directions, making camping pointless.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: If others cannot disrupt campers, especially those at spawn points, the campers dominate and the game becomes lopsided.

conflicts_with.name: Safe Havens
conflicts_with.why: Protected spots attract campers, yet that same protection discourages anyone from camping near them.

conflicts_with.name: Varied Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Since waiting in one spot can be a winning tactic, players have less reason to try different things.

patterns.name: Team Strategy Identification
patterns.what_it_is: A team finds and picks a shared strategy, often based on a mix of strengths.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need complementary abilities or synergies to find, a reason to work together (common threat or goal), and room to talk. The game must not hand them one obvious best plan.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Roles are clearly labelled and the optimal team plan is spelled out, so there is nothing to discover.
patterns.knobs: how varied and hidden synergies are; how different the roles are; communication options

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: When players work out a shared plan successfully, the people who took part in finding it feel socially appreciated and rewarded by each other.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because players know that a joint strategy might be found, they are pushed to think ahead, as long as some of them notice that possibility.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: A strategy that players successfully figure out together can be seen as something the group achieved as a whole, not just one person.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Working out how to coordinate actions usually leads players to find, or deliberately set up, combinations where their moves reinforce each other.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Both coming up with the plan and then carrying it out as part of the group can make players feel united.

patterns.name: Gameplay Engines
patterns.what_it_is: A structure the player builds so that it works for them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need to be able to build components that feed each other so output grows (positive feedback, combos), with several possible builds to choose from. There must be a payoff, such as a scoring phase, that makes the engine worth the investment.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Upgrades that are just flat bonuses and do not interact or compound, so there is no engine to build, only a list of purchases.
patterns.knobs: how strongly parts reinforce each other; cost and speed of building; when and how scoring starts

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: An engine is itself a thing players build and own in the game, so it counts as one kind of player-made construct.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: Once built, a strong engine produces most of its payoff in the phase where players harvest results, making that phase defined by engine efficiency.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Players spend effort and resources building an engine up front, accepting a cost now in return for greater benefit later.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: When an engine is running smoothly, players may only need to maintain or watch it, so little active decision-making happens.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Making an efficient engine requires understanding how the game's pieces fit and reinforce each other, which players must know to build well.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Because an engine is assembled gradually from many parts, players must plan ahead so the pieces end up working together.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Building an engine is a means to an end, since it helps players progress toward winning rather than being the final aim.

can_cause.name: Construction/Scoring Phase Shift
can_cause.why: When players can build engines that boost their later actions, there is a natural moment to stop building and start cashing in on them.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: Engines act as a supporting goal in games relying on expansion phases, since building them helps players grow their position.

changes.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
changes.why: Letting players build engines gives them extra goals to pursue while the winner remains undecided until play ends.

patterns.name: Altruistic Actions
patterns.what_it_is: Actions that benefit someone else rather than the player themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Helping others must cost the helper something or carry no obvious reward, with no shared payoff that makes it simply self-interest. Players must have a reason (social or hoped reciprocity) to do it anyway.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'gift' action exists but pays the giver as much or more, so players just do it for profit.
patterns.knobs: cost to the helper; whether payoffs are shared; whether gifts can be returned

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When helping costs the giver something and nothing comes back, the giver is likely to feel let down, which is the sense of betrayal.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Helping others without direct payoff can draw them into working together, expecting that the favor will be repaid later.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Because the helper gains nothing right away, the gesture works on the hope that the receiver will return the favor at some later time.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: In persistent or drop-in worlds, both the giver and the receiver of help feel pressure to come back and keep the exchange going.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Receiving help that you did not pay for can make the receiver feel they owe something in return.

can_cause.name: Individual Rewards
can_cause.why: Since the action does not benefit the actor, it can simply reward one other player rather than the whole group.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: Individual voluntary helpful acts by separate players, when viewed together over time, add up to a collaboration.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Unselfish actions suit these games because players visit each other's own spaces and need harmless things to do there.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: Because unselfish actions are not hostile, they fit what visitors can safely do inside another player's own space.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Unselfish actions can be used in teams, but how rewards and penalties are set up decides whether they make sense.

changes.name: Visits
changes.why: Helping is a non-aggressive thing for neighbors to do when they drop by another player's space.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Penalties
conflicts_with.why: When teammates suffer together, helping a teammate also helps yourself, so the action stops being truly unselfish.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Rewards
conflicts_with.why: When the whole team gains together, helping a teammate is tied to your own gain, which undermines the unselfish quality of the act.

patterns.name: Expansion
patterns.what_it_is: A stage where the main aim is to increase the share of the game world you control.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a world big enough to grow into, a way to own territory (occupation or building), and costs or unlocks that pace how fast growth happens. Goals that reward gaining ownership push players into it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A map with claimable spots, but claiming gives no benefit or is capped so tightly that nobody spends a phase of play on growing.
patterns.knobs: map size and terrain; cost and unlock requirements for claiming or building

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Growing your hold on the world usually means claiming areas and building things, and that naturally pushes players to develop their in-game assets and holdings.

can_cause.name: Middlegame
can_cause.why: When players don't know the map at the start, they must explore first, so spreading out into the world falls in the middle of the game.

can_cause.name: Startgame
can_cause.why: When players already know the map, they can skip exploring and begin claiming territory immediately, so expansion makes up the opening of the match.

patterns.name: Repetitive Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: The player repeats the same actions or choices over and over.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game's loop must offer few action types and the best choice must stay the same across rounds. Whether it feels like practice or tedium depends on the skill growth and rewards around it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with many menus or content on offer, but the same few actions win every time, so variety exists only on paper.
patterns.knobs: variety of actions needed; how long one action type is demanded; how fast the best play changes

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Doing the same thing over and over can make players feel they earned something just by sticking with it, even though it can also make the effort feel pointless.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Repeating the same actions gives players practice that helps them master the game, but once mastered, little novelty remains to keep them interested.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Even with options, the same choices recur, so at a larger scale no real choice remains.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: When there are no real choices to make, or no time to consider them, repeated play leaves players little influence.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Repetition can leave players feeling their work achieves little, though it can also make them feel proud of having endured it.

patterns.name: Feigned Die Rolls
patterns.what_it_is: The game master rolls dice for show, and the result does not affect how the game goes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs a human game master, hidden rolls, and players who cannot check results (screens, secret rolls). The game master must be willing to override outcomes to shape the story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game master rolls openly in front of everyone or follows the dice anyway, so the roll is not feigned at all.
patterns.knobs: how many rolls are hidden; how often the game master ignores or overrides the dice

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: By announcing whatever result suits the moment, the game master can make players believe their rolls and choices mattered more than they truly did.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Since the roll is hidden and doesn't affect the game state, the game master is free to pick any outcome and report it as the dice's verdict.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: The game master can claim the hidden roll came out well or badly, so players feel fortune favoring or abandoning them.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: The game master pretends to let dice decide while secretly choosing the outcome, a deception that tabletop groups accept as part of running a game.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: By announcing a dangerous or near-miss outcome from the hidden roll, the game master can make players feel the stakes are real and uncertain.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Players can't see the rolled number or know whether a roll mattered, so they cannot be sure how their action was really resolved.

changes.name: Dice
changes.why: The game master uses the act of rolling as a show, so dice appear to decide outcomes while actually having no effect on them.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: It gives the game master an extra tool for steering a session, letting them decide results in secret rather than leaving them to chance.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The game master can develop the story the way they or the players want, rather than letting random die results dictate how events unfold.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: A bad roll could derail a planned plot, so faking the roll lets the game master keep the intended story from breaking.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: A game master can secretly fake a roll when a skill test would produce an outcome that harms the story, such as killing a player.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Game masters can secretly adjust their own and players' abilities by pretending dice decided the outcome.

patterns.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
patterns.what_it_is: Players help each other at different times and need not see each other's actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Game state must persist between sessions, and one player's action must give a real benefit to another who acts later. Players need enough trust, so keep the number of steps and the timing of rewards reasonable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game has a shared goal or gifts, but each player's progress would be the same without anyone else, so nobody is really working together.
patterns.knobs: how many steps needed to benefit; whether rewards come together or separately; time limits

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because collaborating without being present together is harder than collaborating live, it adds difficulty and layers to the game.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: When the joint effort takes several steps or can be done again, players must come back repeatedly to continue it.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: Players end up with different roles either because their abilities differ or because the moment they act defines what part they play.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Since players depend on others who may not act, they can pressure or make each other feel bad for not doing their part.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: Players needn't watch or interact with each other to collaborate, so they can contribute without being identified, though this isn't guaranteed.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Relying on others whose actions you can't see forces players to choose between trusting and contributing or protecting their own interests.

patterns.name: Back-to-Back Game Sessions
patterns.what_it_is: Right after one session, players play again with roles swapped.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must actually play again with roles swapped, so sessions need to be short enough and scores easy to compare across rounds. Lobbies help when players are remote.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The rules suggest playing twice with swapped sides, but nobody does or no one adds up the results, so imbalance stays.
patterns.knobs: session length; whether scores carry across sessions; how roles rotate

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because everyone takes each side in turn, an advantage one player enjoyed in one session is matched by a disadvantage in the next, evening out results.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Linking several sessions together with swapped roles creates a larger game around the individual sessions, where players compare how they did across the whole set.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Switching roles means a player experiences the game from a different position each time, so the sessions feel different, especially when starting conditions are uneven.

changes.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
changes.why: When sides begin with unequal setups, replaying with roles exchanged lets each player hold every side, so the unevenness stops deciding who is better.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Tournament opponents often play multiple games against each other and alternate who goes first, which adds a fairness layer on top of the existing competition.

conflicts_with.name: First Player Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Moving first gives an edge that makes a single session lopsided, and repeating with swapped roles is meant to cancel it out, so the pattern works against that advantage.

patterns.name: Speedending
patterns.what_it_is: A player sure of the lead tries to end the game as fast as possible.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to estimate who is ahead, and must have actions that bring the end closer, such as emptying a shared supply. The winner must be decided after play ends, not by an instant win.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game-end condition that is nominally reachable but that nobody can judge or trigger in time, so players play on and the ending is never rushed.
patterns.knobs: how clear the score standings are; what triggers the end; how fast end triggers can be depleted

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: When a leading player pushes the game to finish early, it succeeds in closing the game for one or several players.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skilled players show they can tell when the moment has come to stop building up and start finishing the game, or to react to others doing so.

can_cause.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
can_cause.why: null

changes.name: Construction/Scoring Phase Shift
changes.why: Recognizing the time to hurry the ending means switching focus from building up toward scoring, and those watching a rival do this must switch too.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Rushing the finish heavily changes any existing closing phase of the game, since players start working toward the end instead of long-term goals.

conflicts_with.name: Investments
conflicts_with.why: Players focused on ending quickly, or on scoring while others end it, avoid spending effort on things that only pay off later.

patterns.name: Middlegame
patterns.what_it_is: All stages of the game between the beginning and the end.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs recognizable phases, so the middle must have its own goals and kinds of action, such as expanding or building, different from the opening and the end. Rules like balancing effects can be tied to it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game whose phases are named in the manual but play feels the same throughout, with no real shift in goals or actions.
patterns.knobs: how long the middle lasts; what shifts in goals and rules separate it from other phases

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: Because the middle phase is intricate, players facing many options can get stuck overthinking, so planning there sometimes stalls into endless deliberation.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: The intricate choices of a middle phase give players plenty to weigh, which encourages them to think ahead and work out plans.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: As in other phases, playing through the middle lets players learn what works strategically, and the phase rewards applying that learning.

patterns.name: Save Scumming
patterns.what_it_is: The player keeps reloading a save and replaying a hard spot until they get lucky.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It shows up when saving is unlimited and cheap, retrying costs almost nothing, and outcomes are random or hidden. To prevent it, limit slots or saving, or make failure persistent.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that technically has a save limit but lets players copy or back up files, so reloading still costs nothing and the limit changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how many save slots; where saving is allowed; how costly reloading is

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Once players lean on reloading to beat challenges, they end up doing tedious repeated work outside the intended play that exists only to get past obstacles.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Saving and loading are things players do outside the game's own world, so using them repeatedly to beat challenges turns those actions into a strategy.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Reloading again and again until things go well becomes repetitive effort for a small gain, which amounts to grinding.

conflicts_with.name: Difficulty Levels
conflicts_with.why: Reloading saves to undo bad outcomes defeats the intended challenge of the chosen level, so designers may adjust levels once it is detected.

conflicts_with.name: Permadeath
conflicts_with.why: If players can reload an earlier state whenever they like, they can undo any death, which empties permanent death of meaning.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Caps
conflicts_with.why: A cap on how many save files a player may have limits reloading, so the cap works against this behavior.

conflicts_with.name: Save Files
conflicts_with.why: Limiting players to a single save file works against save scumming, since they cannot keep many fallback states to reload.

patterns.name: Unpredictable Behavior
patterns.what_it_is: Characters are capable of unexpected actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Agents need real variation, through randomness, complex rules or human control, while still staying within sensible limits. Players should not be able to learn and exploit a fixed script.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Agents that follow a fixed script with a bit of random flavour that never changes what they do.
patterns.knobs: amount of randomness in agent decisions; complexity of agent rules

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When an agent acts in ways players can't foresee, it looks as if the agent is pursuing goals of its own.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Agents that seem to have their own motives make the game world feel more believable and coherent, which indirectly supports its theme.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: If players can't guess what agents will do next, they also can't be sure how situations involving those agents will end.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: When an AI or system player acts unpredictably, its performance becomes uncertain, creating the pattern instead of just adjusting it.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Non-human players that act in ways that can't be easily worked out give other players something they cannot anticipate.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: The pattern changes how any agent acts by making what it does next harder to anticipate.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Computer-controlled agents can be made unpredictable by adding randomness, sufficiently complex rules, or deliberately vague responses.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Non-player characters can be made unpredictable by having a game master decide their actions instead of fixed rules.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Agents that act unpredictably make it harder for players to figure out what will happen next.

patterns.name: Scouting
patterns.what_it_is: Moving through the world to learn about dangers while staying unseen.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs partial visibility of the world, a real chance of being detected, and a payoff for information such as threats or ambushes. Hiding places and routes make the activity richer.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Exploring the map with no enemies or no detection risk, so scouting is just walking around and nothing is learned or threatened.
patterns.knobs: detection range and chance; how much of the map is hidden; how many hiding places

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: Once you have safely learned where enemies are without being noticed, you can strike when they aren't expecting it, provided attacking is possible in the game.

patterns.name: Cycle Deck Engines
patterns.what_it_is: Cards that let you draw new cards, so the player runs through nearly the whole deck.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs deck building, cards that draw further cards, and a deck small or thin enough that cycling through it is possible. Costs and limits must keep the loop strong but not endless.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A few draw-a-card effects that are lost in a big deck and never let a player cycle it.
patterns.knobs: how many cards give extra draws; deck size; limits on plays per turn

can_cause.name: Gameplay Engines
can_cause.why: Cards that let you draw more cards snowball, so each extra card adds more benefit than the last, which makes the deck behave like a self-feeding engine.

patterns.name: Strategic Knowledge
patterns.what_it_is: Knowing the rules, possible actions, and value of moves apart from any specific situation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have stable rules and structures that carry across sessions, and hidden or deep parts worth learning. Playing must give feedback that shows what works.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that changes so much each time, or is so shallow, that nothing learned in one session helps in the next.
patterns.knobs: how much stays the same between sessions; amount of hidden rules; how much depth rewards learning

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: When players understand how the game consistently works, they can judge more accurately how likely their planned actions are to succeed.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Because the knowledge holds across sessions, players can step outside play to learn it, memorize it, and share it with others.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: If players can apply what they know about the game's constant aspects to their actual moves, they become skilled and in control of play.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Knowing the risk and reward structures makes players more aware of costs and payoffs, so they feel torn between tempting choices.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Since the knowledge stays valid from one session to the next, players can extract it and commit it to memory for later use.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: Such games only run if someone understands and carries out the rules, so knowing how the game works is a prerequisite.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing the game's constants lets players think ahead and plan, both before and during play.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing the game's constants lets players think ahead and plan, both before and during play.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Hidden rules give useful strategic knowledge, so players want to discover them, which makes finding such rules an information goal.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Players build up understanding between sessions to play better, though knowing everything perfectly would make further play pointless.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Knowing which areas matter most helps players decide where to concentrate their efforts to gain control.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: If the odds and payoffs are open or can be worked out, players can use that knowledge to bet wisely.

changes.name: Bidding
changes.why: If the values at stake are clear or can be deduced, players can apply their knowledge to bid sensibly.

changes.name: Camping
changes.why: Knowing the best spots to place oneself helps players camp effectively.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Knowing how environmental effects work lets players turn the surroundings to their advantage in a fight.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: When teammates share what they know about the game, they communicate in ways that reflect on the game itself.

changes.name: Deck Building
changes.why: Players use what they know about the game to assemble decks that are more likely to produce combos or working engines.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Knowing the world's layout and features helps players move through it well, for instance when winning races.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Understanding the value of different rewards and risks influences which goals players choose to prioritize.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: Knowing the best positions helps players defend or watch over something effectively.

changes.name: Optional Goals
changes.why: Understanding the risks and rewards involved shapes whether players choose to pursue an optional goal.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: The more a player knows about the game, the better their chances of executing well, which reduces uncertainty about their performance.

changes.name: Selectable Set of Goals
changes.why: Understanding the risks and rewards involved shapes which goal a player picks from the available options.

changes.name: Solution Uncertainty
changes.why: With several valid solutions, knowledge helps players work out which ones are possible or likely, though a single solution becomes pointless once known.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Knowing how obstacles and other world elements can be used helps players stay hidden and succeed.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players who know the statistics or hidden systems can see through the hidden help or randomness and lose the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: Knowing the odds or what will happen reduces the room for outcomes to feel like fortune.

conflicts_with.name: Player Unpredictability
conflicts_with.why: A player who understands the game's strategies can more easily guess what others will do, making them less unpredictable.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: If players come to know everything about how to play well, replaying has no purpose because nothing remains to learn.

conflicts_with.name: Solution Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: If players bring knowledge from earlier games, the solution may become obvious, which removes the uncertainty the game relies on.

patterns.name: Predictable Consequences
patterns.what_it_is: You can estimate in advance how the game will change after actions or events.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Rules must be deterministic and clear enough to read, and the game must show state and effects. Little hidden information or randomness should sit between an action and its result.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Rules are written down, but dice, hidden effects or opaque systems make outcomes impossible to foresee, so players cannot plan.
patterns.knobs: amount of randomness and hidden information; clarity of feedback and previews

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: When players can foresee outcomes well, they may plan so far ahead and so long that they stall the game for everyone else.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because each single action is understandable, players can chain many of them into long logical sequences, which makes the game as a whole deep and intricate.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: If players can see what their actions will do, they can work out how likely a plan is to work, and see what that likelihood is.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Knowing how actions change the game state is itself a skill, so players who learn these consequences well become better at the game.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Being able to foresee future states lets players notice an ending or goal approaching before it actually arrives.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: When players know what each choice will lead to, they must weigh those known outcomes against each other, which makes picking an action a struggle.

can_cause.name: Kingmaker
can_cause.why: Foreseeing outcomes shows a player who will win, so a player who cannot win themselves may decide which rival gets the victory.

can_cause.name: Predictable Winner
can_cause.why: Since players can see where the game is heading, they may judge that one player is practically certain to win from the current course of play.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: A player who sees they are about to win only in the short run may rush to finish the game before the long-term picture changes.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When effects of actions are easy to understand, players are encouraged to think about future moves and work out sequences ahead of time.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Understanding what actions lead to lets players make better-informed risk and reward choices, building up knowledge of what works strategically.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Players can only plan long-term strategies if they can reasonably foresee how their actions will change the game, which this pattern gives them.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Testing is only worthwhile if outcomes are consistent, and it works best when players can't see far ahead on their own.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: Because outcomes follow predictable statistical patterns over many rounds, players can estimate odds when deciding what to wager.

changes.name: Closure Points
changes.why: Foreseeing where the game is going lets players notice approaching endings, which shapes how those ending points feel when they arrive.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Damage and similar penalties are normally expected in size and type, since surprising ones could make players feel the game broke an implicit promise and quit.

changes.name: Delayed Effects
changes.why: Actions whose results arrive later are easier to evaluate and so more appealing to try when players can foresee what they will cause.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: Players are only willing to invest if they can anticipate roughly what they might gain, so investments need a foreseeable range of results.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Unexpected penalties may drive players away from a game, so penalties are typically kept foreseeable to respect what players assume about the experience.

conflicts_with.name: Anonymous Actions
conflicts_with.why: Since players struggle to link actions to people and their strategies, they can't foresee what will follow, so outcomes become less predictable.

conflicts_with.name: Complex Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When a game is complex, players struggle to know what their actions will cause, so outcomes are less predictable.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Failures
conflicts_with.why: Since a random extra-bad result can strike any attempt, players cannot be sure what an action will lead to, making consequences less predictable.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Hits
conflicts_with.why: Because a critical hit can unexpectedly add extra harm, players cannot be sure what an attack will do, which undermines predictability.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Misses
conflicts_with.why: Since a rare disastrous result can strike even a sound action, players can't count on their choices leading to the outcomes they expect.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Results
conflicts_with.why: Chance plays a bigger role and the rare results have effects ordinary ones cannot produce, so players cannot reliably foresee what an action will do.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Successes
conflicts_with.why: Since a critical success is a lucky, exceptional outcome, it makes it less likely that players can foresee exactly what an action will result in.

conflicts_with.name: Delayed Effects
conflicts_with.why: A very long wait may leave the situation changed by the time the effect lands, so players can no longer foresee what it will do.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: When effects are delayed to keep events permanent, players cannot easily see in advance what their actions will lead to.

conflicts_with.name: Open-Ended Die Rolls
conflicts_with.why: Because extra dice can keep adding to the total, you cannot know the range of outcomes beforehand, so results are harder to foresee.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance in results makes outcomes less certain in the short term, reducing how well players can foresee what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Trumps
conflicts_with.why: Adding trump cards to trick-taking games makes it harder to guess what other players will play.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Hidden or missing information about relevant parts of the game state makes it harder for players to foresee what their actions do.

conflicts_with.name: Unpredictable Behavior
conflicts_with.why: Agents that act unpredictably make it harder for players to figure out what will happen next.

conflicts_with.name: Variable Accuracy
conflicts_with.why: Making attacks hit with varying precision means players cannot be sure of an attack's result, weakening foresight in combat.

conflicts_with.name: Exceptional Events
conflicts_with.why: Exceptional events are unusual and unexpected by nature, so having them in a game means players can't always foresee what will follow their actions.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: If players already know what will happen, there is nothing left to feel lucky about.

patterns.name: Player Balance
patterns.what_it_is: Game design that gives everyone equal chances of success or victory.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Starting positions, resources and abilities must be near-equal, or any asymmetry must be offset by something else. Designers must watch for feedback loops that let an early lead decide everything, and test with real play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The sides look symmetrical on paper, but one option or position wins nearly every time in practice.
patterns.knobs: how equal starting resources and abilities are; strength of catch-up or anti-snowball rules

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: When players start with roughly equal odds, they can reasonably estimate how likely they are to succeed or win.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Balance does not stop skill from mattering; it makes contests last longer and demands more from players to show they are better.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: When opponents have different levels of mastery, balancing them is the main way to keep a contest between players fair.

conflicts_with.name: AI Players
conflicts_with.why: AI can skip physical interfaces and may join or leave mid-game, which can make the sides unequal.

conflicts_with.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
conflicts_with.why: Development gives some players more power than others, and over time this gap makes it hard to keep players evenly matched.

conflicts_with.name: Abstract Player Constructs
conflicts_with.why: Giving different constructs different starting strengths, as in Europa Universalis and Victoria, makes players unequal and so disrupts balance between them.

conflicts_with.name: Asymmetric Goals
conflicts_with.why: Because goals differ, some players may get easier or more rewarding objectives, making it harder to keep everyone's chances fair.

conflicts_with.name: Asymmetric Resource Distribution
conflicts_with.why: Unequal resources give some players more possibilities to compete than others.

conflicts_with.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
conflicts_with.why: When players start with different possibilities, it is hard to keep their chances equal unless the designer adds balancing measures or tests heavily.

conflicts_with.name: Camping
conflicts_with.why: If others cannot disrupt campers, especially those at spawn points, the campers dominate and the game becomes lopsided.

conflicts_with.name: Character Development
conflicts_with.why: Characters that have grown unevenly give players unequal strength, so those who played more or earlier gain an edge over latecomers.

conflicts_with.name: Characters
conflicts_with.why: Differences in character abilities, especially unequal ones from the start, can make some players stronger than others.

conflicts_with.name: Combos
conflicts_with.why: Combos often bring fast-growing or sudden jumps in power, so players who master them can gain large advantages and upset fairness.

conflicts_with.name: Crafting
conflicts_with.why: If crafting effort does not match item value, those who craft heavily can gain an unfair edge over other players.

conflicts_with.name: Death Consequences
conflicts_with.why: How a dead avatar is placed back into the world can tilt fairness between individual players.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: When someone leaves, the remaining players' standing can become uneven, disrupting the fairness the game was built around.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Enemies with special abilities or extra information can feel unfair and upset players' sense of balance.

conflicts_with.name: Entitled Players
conflicts_with.why: Special abilities given to some players can tilt the playing field, making their position stronger than that of the others.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Turns
conflicts_with.why: Because one player acts twice before opponents respond, they gain an advantage that can tip the game in their favor and upset fairness.

conflicts_with.name: First Player Advantages
conflicts_with.why: An edge for whoever starts first makes players unequal in their chances, which undermines the goal of fair, balanced competition.

conflicts_with.name: Flip-Flop Events
conflicts_with.why: If double turns happen by chance or luck rather than by player choice, some players gain a strong advantage unfairly, upsetting the fairness between them.

conflicts_with.name: Game Element Insertion
conflicts_with.why: Inserting player characters for players who arrive late can make the game unfair for the ones already playing.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Strong mastery can make it hard to create mechanics that keep players on equal footing.

conflicts_with.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
conflicts_with.why: Differences in the combos players can build from their own elements can leave some players stronger, undermining even footing between them.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Long-lasting or unequal immunity gives some players a lasting edge over others, upsetting fairness between them.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: A kingmaker can decide the outcome for others arbitrarily, so players no longer have equal standing in determining the result.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Newcomers may have more or fewer resources and abilities than existing players, which makes players unequal.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Advantages that build up over time, late joiners, skill and tool differences, and cheating make balance hard to keep.

conflicts_with.name: New Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Giving some players abilities that others lack can tilt the game in their favor, making the contest uneven.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: Letting outsiders change the game state too easily can tilt the game in favor of players who have helpers available.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Crafting and character growth accumulate over time in a persistent world, which can ruin fairness between players.

conflicts_with.name: Player Augmentations
conflicts_with.why: How fair the game feels depends on who receives the help and how much, so uneven assistance can upset balance between players.

conflicts_with.name: Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: Characters of late-arriving players can be inserted into the game, giving them different conditions from the others.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Removing a player completely is the most definite misfortune and ends their chance of success.

conflicts_with.name: Player Killing
conflicts_with.why: Killing can eliminate players or bring death consequences, which are misfortunes that disturb equal chances.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
conflicts_with.why: Mixed player and character skill makes mastery differences stack up with ability differences.

conflicts_with.name: Positive Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: Gains that make further gains more likely let a leader pull ahead and widen differences.

conflicts_with.name: Power-Ups
conflicts_with.why: They reward some players without compensating others, though random, circumstance-weighted effects can help balance.

conflicts_with.name: Privileged Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Giving some players special abilities creates imbalances in what players can do, though it can also be used to compensate.

conflicts_with.name: Privileged Movement
conflicts_with.why: Special movement abilities for some players create imbalances in their abilities.

conflicts_with.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Generated worlds can spread strategic locations, tools or weapons unevenly across players.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Buying advantages from outside the game can easily destroy equal chances.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance can counter snowballing, but the dice themselves can give some players luckier outcomes and disturb balance.

conflicts_with.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Changing the world can spread tools, weapons or locations unevenly, though it can also be used to balance.

conflicts_with.name: Skills
conflicts_with.why: When skills are distributed unevenly among players, their chances end up unequal.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Locations
conflicts_with.why: Uneven access to key places gives some players advantages over others.

conflicts_with.name: Tiered Participation
conflicts_with.why: Players in higher tiers can have more power than others.

conflicts_with.name: Tools
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of tools among players leads to imbalances.

conflicts_with.name: Vehicles
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of vehicles among players leads to imbalances.

conflicts_with.name: Weapons
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of weapons among players leads to imbalances.

conflicts_with.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
conflicts_with.why: Since differentiated entities need unique abilities, players end up with unlike things, which is hard to square with equal footing unless everyone gets the same set.

patterns.name: Social Adaptability
patterns.what_it_is: The game easily adjusts to different groups of people and circumstances.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design must offer real options such as pausing, drop-in/out, adjustable length or location, and players or a facilitator must have the power to use them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rulebook line saying you may adapt the game to your group, while the rules give no practical way to pause, shorten or change anything.
patterns.knobs: how easily play can be paused or joined; how adjustable session length is; who may change the rules

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When a game bends to fit the social setting, players get to decide when and how they play it, which is exactly choosing freely.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Because players can shape when and how the game fits their situation, they gain real control over their play experience.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: When players use the game's flexibility to suit their own preferences, that shared control strengthens their feeling of being a group.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Hard challenges make it difficult for varied groups to play together unless challenges are optional or balanced by handicaps.

conflicts_with.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Linking game state to real-world phenomena binds play to each player's own surroundings and social setting, making it harder to adapt the game to different social situations.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: Facilitators enforce rules, so players cannot easily bend them, for example to adapt to circumstances or let novices retake moves.

conflicts_with.name: Mediated Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Since mediation makes interruptions harder to support, it works against letting a game fit players' varying social situations.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Changing rules is problematic for the same reason, as players must agree on which rules to use.

conflicts_with.name: Player Physical Prowess
conflicts_with.why: Players differ in physical ability and in willingness to improve it, which makes it harder for the game to fit varied groups.

patterns.name: Fudged Results
patterns.what_it_is: The game bypasses its own calculation rules or makes hidden exceptions to them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Someone must be able to override results, either secretly by a facilitator or via a scarce player resource, and it must be rare so effort still matters. Hidden use requires outcomes not being fully open.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The rulebook mentions bending outcomes, but dice are rolled openly and rules are enforced, so nobody ever fudges anything.
patterns.knobs: how often overrides are allowed; whether they are secret or a limited player resource

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players can bend outcomes themselves, they feel their choices steer events more than the underlying rules actually allow.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: A player-triggered fudge is a gift that makes play easier, so earning or holding that ability works as a reward that helps them.

can_cause.name: Misfortune Mitigation
can_cause.why: Players who can fudge can soften a bad outcome that has hit them, cushioning the damage of unlucky events.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: A token or card that lets its holder ignore an adverse effect gives that player a special power others lack.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: The ability to fudge can be handed back to players as a prize, such as fate points that are replenished for good play.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Adjusting outcomes lets the group get the play experience it wants instead of whatever the mechanical rules would have produced.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Fudging gives the people mediating or running a game a tool for that facilitating job.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: A fudge overrides the normal rules and can reverse results, so it acts as an event stronger than ordinary play, even when players trigger it.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Fudging can bend what opponents do or how their actions affect players, changing how dangerous they actually are.

changes.name: Game Termination Penalties
changes.why: A fudge can step in to prevent a game-ending loss, softening it or cancelling it depending on how often it is used.

changes.name: Life Penalties
changes.why: Fudging is often used to avoid losing lives, so it reduces or removes those penalties depending on its frequency.

changes.name: Player Elimination
changes.why: Facilitators or players can fudge to keep someone from being knocked out, which weakens or cancels elimination.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Overriding or secretly altering rolls and chance outcomes skews the randomness so results no longer follow the raw odds.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: Secretly altering outcomes means the odds players think they face are not the real ones.

conflicts_with.name: Game Termination Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Fudging exists to dodge game-ending outcomes, so used often it cancels the penalty's effect.

conflicts_with.name: Life Penalties
conflicts_with.why: If fudges frequently prevent life loss, the penalty stops meaning anything.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Frequent rescues from elimination mean being eliminated no longer reliably happens.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If results can often be overridden, players' skill and effort matter less, so fudges must be rare or limited.

patterns.name: Competence Areas
patterns.what_it_is: Heroes and other entities have specializations that can be developed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Entities must have uneven abilities that matter for real tasks, and a reason to divide work or to choose a niche. Choices should be meaningful and not obviously one-sided, so no single specialty is always best.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Classes or units have different names and icons, but their numbers and options are so alike that any of them can do any job.
patterns.knobs: how different the abilities are; whether specialties are fixed at start or chosen and changed during play

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: When specialties can be acquired while playing, players get a concrete aim: work toward becoming good at a particular kind of action.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skilled players show mastery by being good at their own specialty, and choosing which specialty to pursue can itself be a way to master the game.

can_cause.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
can_cause.why: When entities are each good at different things, they differ in kind rather than in raw power, so none simply outclasses the others.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: If players choose which specialties to develop, each playthrough can go differently depending on the choices made.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Different unit or character types are good at different things, which gives players a larger set of possible actions.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: Roles need entities that are good at different things, so giving each a distinct area of competence creates the specialization.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, developing a particular skill area ties a player's social role directly to that gameplay ability.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Specialties shape which abilities an entity has or is good at, since being a specialist means excelling at particular types of action.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: With specialized abilities, these constructs matter differently in play, because each is suited to particular tasks.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Specialties make characters matter in different ways, because each is functionally suited to certain tasks.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Specialties make different unit types matter in different ways, since each handles certain tasks better than the others.

conflicts_with.name: Ability Losses
conflicts_with.why: Losing abilities can wipe out areas where a player was skilled, while other players may become the only competent ones left.

patterns.name: Game Element Trading
patterns.what_it_is: Players exchange, in real life, the items that make up the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must own different tradable items that keep value beyond one session, and be able to meet or exchange them. Item rarity and sources shape demand.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Items are labelled tradable, but all are equal or worthless, so nobody wants to swap.
patterns.knobs: rarity of items; how they are obtained; how easy trading is

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: Once players are used to handing game elements to one another, wagering those same elements on outcomes becomes a natural next step.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: The actual swap of items can happen outside the game itself, such as players arranging exchanges on their own rather than through game mechanics.

can_cause.name: Memorabilia
can_cause.why: When a traded element is very rare or especially important to play at the moment it changes hands, it can become a keepsake.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Because players want particular elements, trading creates a separate challenge of building up a desired set of items beyond playing individual matches.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Players can carry out the exchange of elements through an in-game trading feature, so the swap happens inside the game.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Players who put time into a game may sell rare items, areas or characters to others for real currency, creating real-world market effects.

changes.name: Collecting
changes.why: Moving elements between players changes how easy it is to complete a collection, since pieces can be acquired from or lost to others.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: Because trading hands control of elements to other players, it changes how easily someone can reach goals of owning particular things.

conflicts_with.name: Player Created Game Elements
conflicts_with.why: If players produce too many of a type of element, its value drops very low and the trading market can collapse.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Making trading central requires either players everywhere or electronic exchange of elements, which is hard to combine with play available anywhere.

patterns.name: Positive Feedback Loops
patterns.what_it_is: An effect reinforces itself: each next such effect is stronger than the previous one.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Rewards must make the next success easier or larger, with no strong caps or counter-effects. Designers must check how quickly the effect grows, or the leader runs away.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bonus is given for winning, but it is so small or so capped that early leads fade and nothing compounds.
patterns.knobs: growth rate of the reward; strength of caps or counter-loops; how much advantage carries over

can_cause.name: Critical Gameplay Design
can_cause.why: Designers may deliberately include these loops when they want the game to have particular system-wide behaviors, so the loop is a tool for shaping those properties.

can_cause.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
can_cause.why: When the loop feeds on the challenges players face, success brings harder challenges, so the game keeps getting tougher as players do well.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Engines
can_cause.why: Players can build setups where each reward makes the next gain easier, and the loop is what lets such an engine grow itself.

can_cause.name: Predictable Winner
can_cause.why: Whoever pulls ahead keeps widening the gap, so the eventual victor becomes easy to guess long before the game ends.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Self-reinforcing growth makes effects bigger as play goes on, so later closures outweigh earlier ones.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Combined with investments, they make successes and failures grow, so what you have committed feels more at risk.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players can set up loops that build on compounding gains, so earlier effort snowballs into bigger results.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Rewards from loops often come as resources, so the loop strongly shapes how resources are gained and accumulate in a game.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Rewards can also take the form of access to units, so the loop changes how quickly players can obtain and grow their forces.

conflicts_with.name: Negative Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: The two work in opposite directions, so they can't both be applied to the same aspect of the game state, though they may govern different parts.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Gains that make further gains more likely let a leader pull ahead and widen differences.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Caps
conflicts_with.why: A cap on resources that fuel the player's actions stops the gains from compounding, so the loop cannot keep growing.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Snowballing lets one side pull far ahead of the other, which undermines keeping teams evenly matched.

patterns.name: Helplessness
patterns.what_it_is: Situations in which the player cannot change anything themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to see the game going on while having no useful input, and the state needs a clear end (a timer, a rescue by others, or the situation resolving). Without a way out or a clear duration it just feels broken.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A brief animation or stun where the player can still steer, act, or skip ahead, so nothing about their choices is actually removed.
patterns.knobs: how long the state lasts; what ends it (timer, rescue, none)

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: A helpless player can't act, so they must wait while the game continues, though other players may still be playing.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Being stripped of the ability to act is unpleasant, so designers can use it as a punishment for failing or taking damage.

can_cause.name: Rescue
can_cause.why: When one player is stuck and can't help themselves, others get a goal of freeing them, which creates rescue situations.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: A stuck player can become the victim while teammates step into the role of helpers who save them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Helplessness acts like a huge event players can't control, so they nervously wait to see whether help arrives or doom comes.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Taking away all of a player's ability to influence outcomes is a drastic, overwhelming event that quickly raises players' tension.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: A stranded or incapacitated player can only be freed by someone else, who helps in the hope of being rescued in turn later.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, being clearly dependent on others can still leave players with an inflated feeling of their own influence.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Putting a player in a stuck state where they need aid lets them appeal to others, who then feel bad if they ignore it.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Making some players unable to act while others must help is a riskier way to get the group working through trouble together.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, being able to free other players from a helpless state is a power that only some participants hold.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: A player may choose a long, powerful action that leaves them unable to defend themselves until it finishes, making helplessness a price they accept.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Being unable to act undermines the sense of influence, although dependence in multiplayer games can sometimes still produce it.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Having meaningful choices makes players feel they can influence outcomes, which works against feeling powerless.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: Helplessness stops players from affecting how the game turns out, which directly takes away their agency.

patterns.name: Entrenching Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: As the game goes on, the situation becomes harder and harder to change.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must be irreversible and combine so that earlier choices lock in later ones; resource loss helps. Reversibility must be mostly avoided.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Irreversible-looking moves that are easy to undo or have so little effect that the state remains open to the end.
patterns.knobs: how irreversible actions are; how strongly effects accumulate; resource depletion rate

can_cause.name: Critical Gameplay Design
can_cause.why: Because the game's overall course is shaped by how it locks in, designers get a built-in structure that makes the game's outcome follow the system's behavior.

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: As changes pile up and the state loosens less, players end up in a late phase where they mostly defend what they hold.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Early on, players compete to claim open space or territory before it gets locked in, which makes a middle phase of growing and grabbing.

can_cause.name: Middlegame
can_cause.why: Competition over claiming room to grow tends to fill the middle of play, once early choices have started to fix the state in place.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Since play reliably follows the same shape of opening up and then settling, the game offers a ready-made story arc, though it needs characters or factions to feel intentional.

conflicts_with.name: Varied Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When the game state can change less and less, players are unlikely to gain new kinds of actions, so variety in play tends to shrink.

patterns.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
patterns.what_it_is: Players can move and change game elements outside of the rules.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Components must be physical or open to hand manipulation, with no automated enforcement, and the group must tolerate rule bending. A human or self-run setup is needed rather than a strict program.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The rulebook says players may adjust things, but software or a strict facilitator blocks any rule-breaking move.
patterns.knobs: how much the facilitator or software enforces rules; how easily components can be altered

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since players may move pieces whatever way they like, they can decide to bend or ignore the rules, so they choose how the game is played.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Because players can touch and alter game elements directly, they can quietly nudge outcomes, which lets them shape results in small ways while still playing.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Players being able to handle elements freely means they can add new pieces or elements to the game while it is going on.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Players can change the starting setup or the current state of the game to even out differences in strength between them.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Since players can reshape the game by changing elements and rules as they wish, the game can fit whatever the group wants it to be.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: Mechanical and computer facilitators do not naturally let players move game elements freely; this needs deliberate design.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: A game master may overrule what players did with elements, forcing them to retract their moves, which cuts against players' free manipulation.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: With so much power over elements in players' hands, it is hard to make an event that players cannot simply undo or change.

conflicts_with.name: No Direct Player Influence
conflicts_with.why: Free manipulation gives players direct hands-on influence, so a game where they have none is hard to combine with it.

conflicts_with.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
conflicts_with.why: Players holding this much power over elements makes it hard for a game to include events that overwhelm everything else.

patterns.name: Negative Feedback Loops
patterns.what_it_is: Rules that bring some game measure back toward a preset value.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must measure a part of the state, such as relative position, and apply a counter-effect strong enough to matter but not so strong that effort is pointless. It usually needs playtesting.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A catch-up bonus so small that leaders still win, or so large that it flips results no matter how people play.
patterns.knobs: how strong the correction is; what is measured; how soon it triggers

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the loop pushes a measured value back toward a target, players who pull ahead get held back and those behind get help, evening out the game.

can_cause.name: Critical Gameplay Design
can_cause.why: A loop that keeps undoing player attempts to shift the balance can make a point about how futile it is to try to disrupt a situation.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
can_cause.why: The loop checks how players are doing and changes the game in response, so challenge is nudged toward a set level as play proceeds.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Since the loop works against whoever leads, differences between players' standings stay small and no one gets too far ahead of the others.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: When the loop acts on team standings, it holds back the leading team, which keeps the teams close in strength.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with geometric progression, they reduce the value of repeating the same efforts, nudging players toward varied goals.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: In networks where players compete, the loop shifts power away from the strongest, helping keep the rival parties' strengths in balance.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Because position in a race can't be directly swapped, the loop alters things like speed so trailing racers catch up and leaders slow.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Resources decide which actions players can take, so the loop adjusts who gets access to them and thereby steers the measured game state.

changes.name: Varying Turn Orders
changes.why: The loop can let the lowest-scoring player act first next turn, so the order of play itself helps weaker players recover.

conflicts_with.name: Positive Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: The two work in opposite directions, so they can't both be applied to the same aspect of the game state, though they may govern different parts.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Since leaders are pushed back and are harder to identify, runaway leads are unlikely, which undermines an early, obvious winner.

patterns.name: Ninja Looting
patterns.what_it_is: Taking loot that the player has no right to.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Loot must be physically takeable by anyone nearby and ownership must not be enforced. The reward must be worth taking, and other players must be near enough to do it.
