patterns.just_a_label_when: Loot labeled as shared or ownable that is in fact automatically assigned, so nobody can take anything from others.
patterns.knobs: who can pick up loot and when; how long loot stays unprotected

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Once a player grabs loot they weren't entitled to, or is accused of it, they become known as a 'ninja looter', a role among other players.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: When a teammate grabs loot others see as improper, the group itself falls into disagreement and tension among its own members.

patterns.name: Investments
patterns.what_it_is: A player gives up resources for a time for gain later, not knowing how it will turn out.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resources must be spent with the payoff delayed and uncertain, and the payoff must be worth the wait. Players need enough knowledge to weigh the risk.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Spending resources that return immediately or with certainty, so it is just a purchase.
patterns.knobs: cost; delay before payoff; size and certainty of the return

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Players willingly put a resource at stake hoping for a later reward, which ties them to making that payoff happen.

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: Resources are spent now and the payoff arrives later, so the return is delayed from the commitment.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Players can pay to obtain new game elements, such as buying players in a sports league, so acquiring them by purchase is a way of drafting.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Putting resources in now to get a payoff later is a specific delayed effect, so you must return to collect the payoff.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Players keep putting effort or resources in over time before getting the effect, which occupies their options and drains resources while it continues.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Choosing how and when to invest gives players decisions about development, such as planned character growth.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Earlier investments pay off by making a character stronger, so receiving that payoff completes a goal of gaining competence.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Spending on skills and attributes brings no immediate reward but makes the character stronger later, so the cost pays off as better abilities.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Resources are tied up for a time so that a bigger payoff arrives later, such as Tetris giving more points for clearing several rows together.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Spending now for a later payoff requires players to plan which investments to make.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Resources you have committed could be lost, so you worry about their outcome.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Controlling a territory can be linked with investments, which give a reason to pursue ownership of it.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: When investing is mixed with capturing, players weigh options to find the choice that gives the best payoff.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Investing is a choice with costs and possible payoffs, so players must plan whether and when to commit resources to capture something.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: In turn-based games, spending resources can be the means for capturing, rather than only moving pieces.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Spending resources to add new cards to your draw pile lets you steer, indirectly, what your future hands will contain.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Investments commit Resources for a time without immediate results, so players must decide how to spend them with an uncertain future ahead.

conflicts_with.name: Speedending
conflicts_with.why: Players focused on ending quickly, or on scoring while others end it, avoid spending effort on things that only pay off later.

patterns.name: Trading
patterns.what_it_is: Players exchange resources with each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must hold different things of different value to them, be allowed to exchange them, and have a way to find and talk to each other. Needs must differ enough that swaps benefit both sides.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A trade menu in a game where everyone has the same needs and goods, so nobody ever gains from using it.
patterns.knobs: how unequal the holdings are; which items can be traded; trade limits or fees

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Control can be acquired indirectly by exchanging resources with other players instead of conquering the place.

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: Trading lets players coordinate, for example by refusing deals with the leader, once they agree someone is in front.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Trades whose effects arrive later let a player take what they want and then fail to hold up their side.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: Trading is a form of negotiation, which gives players a channel and a reason to mislead each other.

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: A trade needs both sides to act, so each player's action depends on the other's without necessarily involving cooperation.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Exchanges combined with delayed effects make results uncertain, as players cannot see right away how a trade pays off.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Exchanging goods requires both sides to agree and collaborate, even when it's unclear who benefits more.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: A trade that favors one side lets the worse-off player accept it now, expecting the other to compensate in a later deal.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: When players can swap goods with others, those other players become a place from which resources are obtained.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Trading can be rewarding in itself, and other rewards can make it more appealing.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Trading lets negotiators help others, but a dominator can pose as a negotiator to exploit it.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Players who are good with people may gain better deals when trading, so social skills are likely displayed in it.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Players can acquire ammo by exchanging with others or buying it, which is another way to restock.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Players can obtain armor by exchanging with others or with the game, which is one common way to gain protection.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Exchanging items is a possible action for avatars, though it is more often given to characters.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: Exchanging items with other players gives a route to ownership that avoids or softens conflict.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Players can swap items with other players or characters, turning acquisition into a trade-off against other items or resources.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Having several players enables swapping, often outside the formal rules.

changes.name: Optional Goals
changes.why: Trading is rarely required, so it nearly always offers players a goal they may take on or skip, even if winning is hard without it.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Players can exchange resources among themselves when the resources can be transferred.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Players can obtain weapons by exchanging them with others.

patterns.name: Exploitation
patterns.what_it_is: A game stage where the main aim is to use what you already have as efficiently as possible.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need owned resources, locations and abilities to optimize, plus enough system depth that efficient setups (gameplay engines) beat sloppy ones. Unlock timing and costs decide when this stage starts.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Resources are available, but there is only one obvious best use, so there is nothing to optimize and no phase of optimizing.
patterns.knobs: resource yield and number of resource sources; when optimizing abilities become available

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Because players are busy making what they already own work better, their holdings become more refined and developed over time.

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: When the exploiting is aimed at raising a score rather than building up, it tends to take place at the close of a game.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: Once players feel they have squeezed all they can from their resources, they only need to watch things run, so action slows down.

can_cause.name: Middlegame
can_cause.why: Improving and maximizing what you already hold is usually what players do in the central stretch of a game, after growing and before finishing.

patterns.name: Resource Management
patterns.what_it_is: Allocating and spending available supplies wisely.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resources must be limited, useful for several competing ends, and spending must have consequences later. Players need enough information to plan their use.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Resources are shown on screen but are so plentiful or so single-purpose that no real choices arise.
patterns.knobs: scarcity; number of competing uses; income versus spending rate

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Adding resources also adds actions, so players must juggle many pieces and decisions.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide how to use, store or convert resources, including choosing to do nothing with them.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Deciding how to spend and keep resources during play is a planning skill players can improve.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Many kinds of resources or individual items to handle, combined with complex gameplay, create a lot of repeated handling work.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Sorting and arranging resources can be satisfying in itself, giving players an activity to do for its own sake even without changing the world.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Managing resources offers many choices about what to produce, save and invest, all of which require planning.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Spending, saving and allocating resources means each use competes with other possible uses, so players weigh them.

patterns.name: Complete Resource Depletion
patterns.what_it_is: Some resource in the game is gone entirely, temporarily or permanently.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resources must be finite or consumed faster than they are replenished, and something must actually use them up, whether players or the system. The running out must change what is possible afterwards.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A resource is labelled scarce, but it replenishes so fast or is so plentiful that it never actually hits zero.
patterns.knobs: starting stock; regeneration rate; consumption rate

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: Once a particular resource is gone, the conditions of play change, and that shift can mark the start of a game's final phase.

can_cause.name: Entrenching Gameplay
can_cause.why: Running out of a resource changes what players can do in the game, which can lock the situation into a fixed pattern.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: When running out of a resource signals that the game is over, players can deliberately drain it to finish the game sooner.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: With a resource gone, certain actions become impossible, so players can't compete against each other effectively and the outcome ends up level.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: The pattern determines whether a given kind of resource is available to players at all, either for a limited time or for good.

patterns.name: Resource Competition
patterns.what_it_is: Players compete for limited resources.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resources must be scarce, shared and valuable, so one player's gain is another's loss. Players need to be able to interfere with or beat each other to it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Each player has a private supply of the same resource, so they never actually compete.
patterns.knobs: total supply versus demand; how much is shared; how easily players can block each other

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: When several players want the same resource, they must take each other into account in how they act.

conflicts_with.name: Regenerating Resources
conflicts_with.why: If supplies keep refilling with time, players have less reason to fight over a scarce amount, so competition for them weakens.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Caps
conflicts_with.why: With each player able to hold only so much, there is less reason to fight over resources, so competition weakens.

patterns.name: Puzzle Solving
patterns.what_it_is: Tasks that are solved mainly by thinking.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The challenge must be solvable by deduction or experiment, with clear information, fitting difficulty and no pressure that replaces thinking. Brute-force trial should be costly or impossible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A puzzle is presented, but it can be solved by trying every option or by luck, so no reasoning is needed.
patterns.knobs: difficulty; amount of information given; number of attempts; time pressure

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Solving puzzles creates no pressure to act before you are ready, so players can take it slowly and play in a relaxed way.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Designers can precisely tune how many steps and pieces a puzzle involves, so they can make it demanding enough to stretch players.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because designers control how many elements and events a puzzle contains, they can pile on enough parts to make the play intricate.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: When a puzzle is solved by rearranging things in the game world, players are really trying to get the pieces into the right setup through movement.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Since a manipulation puzzle can be cracked by trying every combination, players may end up grinding through tedious repeated actions instead of thinking.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Getting good at working out puzzles is itself a skill players can build up and take pride in.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: When not everything needed is visible at once, players have to remember what they saw earlier to reason toward the answer.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: Puzzles that you solve by manipulating the game environment pit players against the game's own challenges rather than other people.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: The difficulty lies in working out the right combination of actions, not in carrying them out, so thinking ahead is what the puzzle asks for.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: The planning needed to find the right sequence of moves is short-range and concrete, matching tactical thinking.

can_cause.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
can_cause.why: When it's unclear where the game lives, hunting for and judging information is natural; clues can be scattered widely and groups can solve them online.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Finding the right action means trying candidates, which works well when the player can undo each attempt.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Working on a puzzle involves finding out how to solve it, so the activity is driven by wanting that knowledge.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When each short level is solved as a puzzle, every level works like its own small game within the larger sequence.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Puzzle games with small self-contained levels give very short complete experiences, so the minimum session length can be very low.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: Clues can be scattered over wide areas and many players can pool their efforts, so puzzles typically form the main activity.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Multiple solutions to a puzzle can add replay value when they lead to different developments of the story.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Puzzles need no time pressure or opponents, so they fit games played alone more than multiplayer ones.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Puzzles tend to appear in turn-based play because there is no pressure to act quickly, leaving time to think.

changes.name: Zero-Player Games
changes.why: In these games players have to plan ahead what their agents will do, which amounts to solving a puzzle.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: If the same puzzles appear every session, players already know the answers, so there is little reason to play again.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: Once a puzzle's answer is found, nothing more remains to learn from it, so no further improvement is possible.

patterns.name: Complex Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: It is hard to plan actions or understand what they will lead to.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be enough components, rules and options that interact, so that deciding or foreseeing outcomes is truly hard. The complexity must be in decisions, not just in bookkeeping.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Lots of tokens, stats and menus, but one option is clearly best, so there is little to decide.
patterns.knobs: number of components, rules and available actions; how much they interact; how much information is shown

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: When there are many actions and interacting parts to weigh, picking a good move becomes hard, so players feel tested.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: If players must handle lots of separate game pieces to play, they spend effort on tedious manipulation instead of meaningful choices.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Because outcomes are hard to foresee in a tangled system, players try things out to learn what happens.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: Complexity shows up in the middle of a game, once the board is rich, and can be used to create such phases.

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Complex games can be hard enough that players fail or mess up, and the failure itself becomes fun.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Learning to cope with all the parts, such as using every combo skillfully, is itself a way of getting good at the game.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Many requirements that must be met together keep several goals almost within reach at once, though too many or unclear ones stop feeling close.

can_cause.name: Middlegame
can_cause.why: Complexity grows after early moves have built up a rich state but before the struggles are settled, so it marks that phase.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: If a complex game isn't very challenging, players can simply tinker around in it, as with building in Minecraft.

can_cause.name: Solution Uncertainty
can_cause.why: With so many possibilities and interacting rules, players can't easily tell which course of action will work.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since the game has so many parts, each playthrough may have players focus on and use different pieces.

can_cause.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
can_cause.why: Even when everything is visible, the calculations can be too heavy to do during play, so the winner stays unclear until the end.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Many kinds of resources or individual items to handle, combined with resource management, create a lot of repeated handling work.

changes.name: Analysis Paralysis
changes.why: A moderate amount of complexity can make players overthink, but piling on more can lower this effect.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Some complexity encourages players to plan ahead, but too much reduces how much planning they do.

conflicts_with.name: Hovering Closures
conflicts_with.why: Too many requirements, or ones shown unclearly, keep players from feeling any goal is nearly reached.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: When a game is complex, players struggle to know what their actions will cause, so outcomes are less predictable.

patterns.name: Performance Uncertainty
patterns.what_it_is: The outcome depends on how skillfully the player performs the action themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Outcomes must depend on skill in a physical, mental or social task that varies from player to player and moment to moment. Success must not be guaranteed by simply knowing a procedure.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An action that looks skill-based but has a fixed outcome whatever the player does, or one so easy that everyone succeeds every time.
patterns.knobs: how demanding the skill task is; how much the result depends on performance versus system; tolerance for error

can_cause.name: Context Dependent Reactions
can_cause.why: Because results hinge on how someone performs, that performance can shift with the current game situation, opponents, or onlookers, so reactions vary by context.

can_cause.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
can_cause.why: When success depends on skill, players can usually get better, and against other players a stronger opponent always leaves a higher level to aim for.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Not knowing whether your own execution will succeed makes each action feel risky, which builds tension.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: If results depend on how well players carry out actions, nobody can be sure how things will end, so outcomes stay open.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: Players can act less skilled than they are, so opponents wrongly judge them and pick poor actions or strategies.

can_cause.name: Physical Enactment
can_cause.why: Because players must carry out the actions themselves, they may not manage it well, so doubt about their own performance appears, as with other enactment.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Failures
conflicts_with.why: Critical failures come from chance rather than how well the player did, so they undercut outcomes depending on the player's own performance.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Hits
conflicts_with.why: Critical hits add more chance to combat, which works against games where the outcome depends mainly on how skilled the player is.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Misses
conflicts_with.why: Dramatic misses that come from chance emphasize bad luck over the player's skill, reducing the role of performance.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Results
conflicts_with.why: These rare results add more chance to the outcome, so what happens depends less on how well the player performs and more on luck.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Successes
conflicts_with.why: Critical successes usually add extra randomness to deciding how an action turns out, which works against the player's ability to judge how well they will perform.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: If performance is uncertain, it is harder for the winner to be known beforehand, since anyone's execution may vary.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance decides outcomes, which lessens how much the player's own performance influences results.

conflicts_with.name: Trial and Error Solutions
conflicts_with.why: If possible answers can simply be tried mechanically, success no longer depends on how well players perform, so performance uncertainty vanishes.

patterns.name: Trade-Offs
patterns.what_it_is: The player chooses among several options and weighs what can be given up for what.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Options must have genuinely different, comparable costs and benefits, with no choice that is better in every way. Players must understand the consequences well enough to weigh them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A choice between options where one is clearly best, so the 'decision' is obvious and players never hesitate.
patterns.knobs: relative size of the gains and costs of each option; how well the effects are shown to the player

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because choosing one option means accepting a downside or giving up a rival option, strengths and weaknesses end up offsetting each other.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Understanding how the options compare lets players choose better, so learning the trade-off itself becomes a skill they can improve.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Having to weigh options against each other makes players think ahead about which choice will serve them best.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing how the competing consequences stack up helps players pick wiser options, so that knowledge becomes valuable.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: When each choice carries a cost and a gain, players must work out short-term moves by comparing what they give up and get.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Facing choices where something good or bad is at stake makes players uneasy about whether they picked correctly.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Adding choices with competing costs and benefits makes challenges more complex, because players must work out the best option.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Trade-offs bring different kinds of risks into sneaking challenges, so players weigh safety against progress.

patterns.name: PvE
patterns.what_it_is: The game itself, not other players, creates the challenges for the player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs system-controlled opponents or hazards with enough behaviour to be a real challenge. Players need reasons to team up against them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies exist but are passive or trivial, so there is no real challenge from the system.
patterns.knobs: enemy strength and number; AI behaviour; difficulty scaling

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: When the game itself supplies the opposition, players share the same opponents and have a reason to work together instead of against one another.

can_cause.name: Symbiotic Player Relations
can_cause.why: Shared opponents let players put their own disputes on hold and rely on each other, since everyone benefits from beating the common challenge first.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Having the game system push back against what players want is a basic way to create challenge, and challenge produces tension.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Setting players against the game system rather than each other makes them a united group facing the same chaotic challenges.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Facing a common threat from the game itself pushes players to side together, giving them a shared aim to accomplish.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: Fighting threats from the game itself gives players a shared reason to find common strategies, since they all face the same opposition.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Adding challenges from the game to a multiplayer game lets players team up even when the design doesn't require it, and shapes how they relate.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: The two kinds of challenge can coexist, and most games lean toward one; mixing some game-made opposition into a player-versus-player game shifts its balance.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: With no other players present, the challenge must come from the game's design, so game-made opposition is a basic way to give a solo game challenge.

patterns.name: Internal Rivalry
patterns.what_it_is: The opponent or competitor is in the same social group as you.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must belong to a shared group while having goals that conflict, and the rules should keep the conflict from ending in outright elimination. The group's norms or limited actions keep it ongoing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Teammates labelled rivals but with fully aligned goals, so no one ever works against another.
patterns.knobs: how strongly individual and group goals diverge; what actions are allowed against rivals

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because rivals share a social network, players must weigh how others react to their moves, so reaching a goal involves more considerations than a plain fight.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Rivals inside a group are a kind of enemy, but their conflict is held in check by the group's social norms.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Learning about rivals' plans lets players compete without fighting, so information gathering becomes a likely goal when rivalry exists.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Rivals often want the same items, such as loot, so claiming and holding those items becomes a goal that avoids direct combat.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Rivalry between members of the same group readily grows into wider conflicts inside that group.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Where players can fight each other, rivalry can end with one participant being knocked out of the game.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: When combat between players is allowed, rivals may attack and kill each other's characters.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: A scripted story can set up, develop and resolve a rivalry, so the narrative itself can control the rivalry.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Social consequences differ with how and where a player pursues a goal, so rivalry offers different ways to play and gives a change from other conflicts.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Handling conflicts inside a group of non-player characters requires players to think through social situations to resolve them.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Rivalry inside a group that otherwise feels loyal or shares goals or enemies makes members weigh competition against cooperation.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Rivalry within a group, combined with roleplaying, makes players more likely to adopt social roles for their characters.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Competing with teammates can help one's own aims but may hurt social standing, so players balance the two.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Rivalries inside a faction are part of a character's social position.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Gaining companions can be a reward for resolving a rivalry, since other characters share the social network.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Rivalry among members for advancement adds challenge and changes how a faction's internal dynamics play out.

changes.name: Loyalty
changes.why: Rivals inside a faction make the player choose sides or support, putting pressure on the loyalty they owe the group.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Rivalry can be built into a scripted story but can also arise on its own in other kinds of storytelling.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: Rivalry typically supplies goals of overcoming a rival or obstacle within the group.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Rivalry played out in character creates social roles and pushes players toward less direct ways of solving problems.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Competition among members makes teamwork harder, though it normally doesn't break the team up.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: An NPC competing with the player within the same group gives that NPC a special social status.

conflicts_with.name: Friendly Fire
conflicts_with.why: Friendly fire can spark rivalry, but because violence can quickly settle the dispute, it also makes it hard to keep a rivalry going long term.

patterns.name: PvP
patterns.what_it_is: Players, as individual people, directly compete against each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need opposed goals, ways to affect one another and roughly matched skill. Matchmaking or balancing tools help sustain it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Many players share a space, but they cannot hurt or compete with each other, so it is parallel solo play.
patterns.knobs: how much players can harm each other; matchmaking; balance and handicap tools

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because players are set directly against one another, the contest itself makes things feel tense, beyond whatever tension the specific actions already create.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Player-versus-player games are where preemptive balancing aims to keep players evenly matched so large gaps never open.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: When cheating is allowed in player-versus-player play, players can pose as other players or roles to deceive their opponents.

can_cause.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
can_cause.why: Facing other players whose performance decides the outcome lets nearly everyone keep improving, as in Chess and Go.

can_cause.name: TvT
can_cause.why: Taking player-versus-player competition and grouping the players into teams turns it into team-versus-team play.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: The idea began in these online games, where players fighting each other was distinguished from fighting the game world, and it can be added as an option.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Playing against one another needs several people, so it fits multiplayer games as a way to shape how those players relate to each other.

changes.name: PvE
changes.why: The two can sit in the same game, and a game mostly about fighting players can still include some challenges against the game environment.

conflicts_with.name: Backseat Gamers
conflicts_with.why: Outside help can feel like cheating and break the players' shared agreement, which matters most when opponents face each other directly.

conflicts_with.name: Cooperation
conflicts_with.why: Players fighting each other are at odds with working together, though both can coexist when teams compete.

conflicts_with.name: Single-Player Games
conflicts_with.why: Fighting other players needs opponents, so it obviously suits games with several people rather than ones played alone.

patterns.name: Social Dilemmas
patterns.what_it_is: A choice between benefiting yourself and benefiting another player or your group.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Selfish choices must truly pay in the short term while hurting the group, and players must be unsure what the others will do. They also need other human participants who can be trusted or betrayed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A shared-pool choice where cooperating is plainly best for everyone, or where the selfish option gives no real advantage, so there is nothing to agonize over.
patterns.knobs: size of individual vs. shared payoff; how hidden or delayed others' choices are; group size

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: When someone resolves a dilemma without gaining more than others, it can look like a selfless act, even if they really just did nothing.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Betrayal happens when a player takes a personal reward over a shared one, dumps penalties on others, or fails to repay an earlier favor.

can_cause.name: Critical Gameplay Design
can_cause.why: Because dilemmas exist in real life too, playing one can make players notice similar situations outside the game and reflect on them.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can freely decide whether to act selfishly or for the group's benefit, though their feelings toward affected players may sway them.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Players' relationships with those hurt by a selfish move can make them feel guilty about taking it.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Selfish moves may anger other players, so the one facing the dilemma feels pulled between personal gain and the group's goodwill.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: When a dilemma shows characters' choices instead of players', those choices can become key moments in a fixed storyline.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Facing animosity from possible selfish choices pushes the player to settle on an explicit role among the others.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Selfish acts risk upsetting others and trust is uncertain, so players feel pressure over what to do and what others will do.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: A dilemma forces a choice that can sharply change the character, and may or may not be part of a scripted story.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Bargaining over how to handle a conflict between personal and group interest can lead players to agree to work together.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Dilemmas change how players relate to each other, since other people fill the groups in which the choices are made.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Dilemmas that show characters' choices can become important events in how the story is told.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Competing interests among members can create choices where group and individual benefit clash, changing how the faction operates.

changes.name: Loyalty
changes.why: Situations where showing loyalty competes with other beneficial actions change how hard it is to remain faithful.

conflicts_with.name: Casual Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Casual games avoid situations that pit players against each other, and dilemmas create exactly that kind of social strain.

patterns.name: Uncertainty of Information
patterns.what_it_is: The player is unsure whether the information they have can be trusted.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Some relevant information must be hidden, noisy or possibly false, and players must need that information to decide. It should not be so extreme that decisions become pure guesses.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Hidden information that does not matter for any decision, or that players can easily look up elsewhere.
patterns.knobs: how much is hidden; how reliable the information is; available sources of clarification

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: When players can't be sure what is going on, nobody can tell who did something, which gives actions the cover they need to stay anonymous.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: Because players can't know who is trustworthy or what others secretly plan, it becomes possible to turn on someone without being noticed in advance.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Not being sure of what you know gives players a reason to set themselves the goal of finding out more.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When players don't know what the world holds, they are encouraged to go look around to reduce that doubt.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: If players can't be sure what others know or intend, they can't predict each other's moves, so behavior becomes harder to foresee.

can_cause.name: Secret Resources
can_cause.why: Doubt about what others know or hold makes it possible to keep resources hidden from opponents without them finding out.

can_cause.name: Solution Uncertainty
can_cause.why: When players can't rely on what they know, they can't be sure which choice is the right one, so solving the challenge stays open.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Not knowing whether your information is trustworthy keeps players worried about outcomes, which raises the overall sense of tension.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: Bluffing only works if some of the game state is hidden from others, since there must be something unknown to lie about.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: Not knowing where enemies are gives players a reason to search, and fog of war can be the cause of that uncertainty.

changes.name: Delayed Effects
changes.why: With uncertain information, players can't be sure how actions will play out later, which adds doubt to effects that arrive after a delay.

changes.name: Interferable Goals
changes.why: Uncertainty makes it more likely that others get in the way of a goal, or makes players worry more that they will.

changes.name: Outcome Indicators
changes.why: Indicators normally reveal results, but they can themselves be made unreliable or unclear so they add doubt instead of removing it.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: When players can't trust what they know, they can't foresee well what their actions will cause, so consequences become less predictable.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Not being sure of the situation pushes players to think ahead and plan to cope with the different possibilities.

conflicts_with.name: Game State Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Giving players extra information about the state removes some of what they would otherwise be unsure about.

conflicts_with.name: Goal Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Goal indicators give players information about their objectives, and that openness removes the not-knowing that uncertainty of information depends on.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: Hidden information can keep players from realizing a kingmaking situation exists, so they don't act on it.

conflicts_with.name: Outcome Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Indicators exist to tell players what an outcome was, so the more clearly they do that, the less is left unknown to the player.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Hidden or missing information about relevant parts of the game state makes it harder for players to foresee what their actions do.

conflicts_with.name: Progress Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Displays give players more information about the game state, which reduces the uncertainty that pattern depends on.

conflicts_with.name: Public Player Statistics
conflicts_with.why: Public stats openly reveal what players have done, so there is typically nothing left unknown about that information.

patterns.name: Internal Conflicts
patterns.what_it_is: Desired actions get in each other's way: progress in one costs you in another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The goals must be of similar appeal, with consequences players can foresee or learn, so that choosing one really costs another. Choices should be hard to take back.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several goals offered where one is plainly the best or all can be done anyway, so there is nothing to agonise over.
patterns.knobs: how many incompatible options; how equal their appeal; how reversible the choice is

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: When group members hold goals that clash with each other, they end up competing within their own group, and that rivalry can in turn spark more internal conflict.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Tough choices in a fixed story can lock in what happens next, and a set plot can also let players guess where each choice leads.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because several options are worth taking and each rules out others, players can come back and try a different path, such as another ending.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: A group facing several goals it cannot all reach must settle on one and work out together which plan will actually let it succeed.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Since taking one goal or action makes the others harder or impossible, players must give something up to get something else.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: With multiple choices that deserve consideration, players can pursue different options, so no two plays need feel the same.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Facing a conflict within the character can force a choice that radically changes them, making that choice a defining moment.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Conflicts among the player's own choices make predictable consequences a necessity to plan around.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can be given clashing goals, and how they settle the clash can reveal who they are.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: A whole faction may need to pick one goal from several, or its members may hold goals that clash with each other.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Having multiple possible goals means players must think not just about how to reach an aim but about which aim to pick.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Groups of players can face internal conflict over which goal to choose, or over a member's action others consider inappropriate.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: They bound the freedom so that at least one action or goal gets selected.

conflicts_with.name: Cooperation
conflicts_with.why: Strong disagreements within the group can be so disruptive that working together becomes impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Teams
conflicts_with.why: Conflicting goals among members can cause rivalry and a breakdown of the group, working against the unity a team needs.

patterns.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Any minute of inattention can cost the player dearly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Several things must be able to hurt a player at any time, such as real-time events, multiple threats or continuous goals, with a real penalty for lapses. Lull periods must be kept rare.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A timer or enemies are on screen, but nothing bad happens when the player looks away, so they can safely ignore it.
patterns.knobs: how many things need watching; penalty for inattention; real-time pace; time limits

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When players slip up and lose focus, the resulting mishaps and their consequences can turn into chaotic, fun failures that players enjoy.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because a lapse can cost players at any moment, they feel constantly on edge and have to keep their focus on play.

conflicts_with.name: Game Pauses
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

conflicts_with.name: Lull Periods
conflicts_with.why: Constant focus is required, so quiet periods where nothing demands attention cannot coexist with this kind of play.

conflicts_with.name: Minimalized Social Weight
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

patterns.name: Lucky Guess Solutions
patterns.what_it_is: A player can guess the correct answer to a problem by chance.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The puzzle or choice must have several options that can simply be tried with quick feedback. Few options and cheap retries make guessing likely.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A puzzle looks like it could be guessed but the choices are so many or penalties so harsh that guessing never works.
patterns.knobs: number of options; cost of a wrong try; how quickly feedback comes

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: When a guess happens to hit the right answer, the player succeeds through chance rather than skill, so the game gives them a taste of good fortune.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Because players may rely on guessing, nobody can be sure whether a given attempt will succeed, which makes outcomes hard to predict.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: A correct guess can feel like the player's own choice paid off, giving a sense of control over events.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: When players lean on guessing instead of reasoning, others cannot tell what they will pick, so their behavior becomes harder to foresee.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: How a puzzle is built can let players skip the reasoning and stumble onto the answer, changing how solving it plays out.

changes.name: Solution Uncertainty
changes.why: How unclear the right answer is shapes whether players resort to guessing, so letting guesses succeed changes how uncertain the solution feels.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: If players feel a guess did not come from their own intent, the success feels hollow and undermines their sense of control.

patterns.name: Surprise Attacks
patterns.what_it_is: Attacks that the target did not expect.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Combat must exist alongside hidden information (fog, stealth, hiding spots, traps), and attackers need a real way to approach unseen. Defenders must be able to be caught unprepared, with a cost for being caught.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies pop out of nowhere on a script, or the player is warned so clearly that it is just an ordinary fight with a jump-scare sound.
patterns.knobs: how much each side can see; how many hiding or flanking routes exist; damage bonus for striking unseen

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: A surprise attack you plan against someone who trusts you as an ally, like striking a partner at a convenient moment, is a clear case of betrayal.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: If a player cannot spot an attack coming in advance, it works as plain harm to them, since nothing could be done to avoid it.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Setting up an ambush takes forethought, and so does arranging your defenses so a possible ambush hurts less, so both sides end up planning.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players feel tense both when an unexpected attack actually lands and when they merely expect one might come.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: A cutscene can show a surprise attack by not letting players react, forcing them to appear surprised.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Unexpected attacks add a different kind of event to fights, changing how combat plays out and adding extra worries for players.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Events that cannot be anticipated cannot be influenced by players, which destroys the perception.

patterns.name: Trial and Error Solutions
patterns.what_it_is: The solution is found by simply trying all the possible options.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The set of possible solutions must be small and visible, and trying a wrong one must be cheap enough that testing is possible. The solution should be found only by testing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A puzzle with so many options, or such heavy penalties for a wrong try, that testing is unrealistic, or whose answer is obvious.
patterns.knobs: number of candidate solutions; cost of a wrong attempt; whether the answer changes between plays

can_cause.name: Lucky Guess Solutions
can_cause.why: When players can try visible options one after another, they may stumble onto the right answer by chance instead of through skill or understanding.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: If players test options in a haphazard order, they can't predict whether or when they'll hit the right one, so their result stays uncertain.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Players who test the available solutions without a system choose in ways that are hard for others to foresee, making their behavior unpredictable.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Being able to test the known candidate solutions directly makes a puzzle easier to crack, since players can experiment instead of working it out purely by thought.

changes.name: Solution Uncertainty
changes.why: Having a limited, visible set of options to try shrinks how unsure players are about the answer, though some doubt about which one is right remains.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: Luck or simply trying every option can reveal the answer, so skill is not needed and there is nothing to improve.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: If possible answers can simply be tried mechanically, success no longer depends on how well players perform, so performance uncertainty vanishes.

conflicts_with.name: Player Unpredictability
conflicts_with.why: If solutions can simply be tested one after another, outcomes become foreseeable, which works against unpredictability.

patterns.name: Area Control
patterns.what_it_is: Power over a zone: who can move through it and which actions are available there.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Areas must differ in value, be contestable by several players, and give real benefits (resources, abilities) to the holder. Taking and holding must require effort and be possible to challenge.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Areas are marked as owned, but all areas are equal or no one can contest them, so ownership means nothing.
patterns.knobs: how many areas; how valuable each is; how hard they are to take and hold

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Holding an area is never finished, since you must keep it for as long as others might take it, so the goal keeps running.

can_cause.name: Entrenching Gameplay
can_cause.why: If control of an area can't be challenged, the holder just digs in and the game settles into a static position.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Making control the focus of play pushes players to claim more and more places, creating a phase of growth.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Control works as a form of ownership, so players pursue goals of getting areas, especially when territories or check points mark clear targets.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: When control can change hands later, players must defend what they hold to avoid losing it.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Keeping an area is a goal that opponents can disrupt by attacking or entering it, so holding it is never safe.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Controlling a place can restrict where opponents may go, so their movement is limited by who holds the area.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: When someone else already holds an area, wanting it for yourself sets up an obstacle you must beat.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Losing control of a place takes away its abilities and resources, and designers can add extra punishments to encourage defending.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When several players want to reach the same area, getting there first becomes a competition.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: With many areas to hold, a player must keep checking on them all to know what is happening.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Controlled areas give benefits like resources and special abilities, and designers can add bonuses for conquering them.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: With many areas worth controlling, players choose which ones to go after, and that choice is itself a goal selection.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: If control requires staying alone in an area for a time, hiding can be a successful way to achieve it.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing how valuable each controllable area is gives players an informed edge when choosing where to fight.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Taking an area often serves a larger aim, such as positioning pieces to set up combos.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Since not every area can be controlled, players weigh which ones are worth the effort against the others.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: To control an area you first have to get to it, which gives players a goal of travelling there.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Holding an area that grants special abilities makes those abilities privileged when they are not offered in many places.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Because controlling a place can grant its location-bound abilities, those abilities become scarce or temporary depending on who holds the area.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Building a base can directly give a player control of the area around it.

changes.name: Combos
changes.why: Controlling areas lets players position their pieces better, which helps set up combinations of actions.

changes.name: Controllers
changes.why: Controlling an area can give access to controllers, which are location-bound abilities found in particular spots.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Control is a type of ownership that shapes a game world by making some parts of it more valuable than others.

changes.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
changes.why: Holding the place gives access to abilities tied to it, so these become scarce, privileged, or temporary depending on ownership.

changes.name: Resource Locations
changes.why: Controlling an area gives access to the resource spots in it, which is a main reason to want it.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Holding areas that are too large to watch from one position is one reason players take on scouting goals.

patterns.name: Pervasive Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: A game that coexists with everyday activities or blends into them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Gameplay must be able to happen alongside ordinary activities, through real-life actions that affect the game state, ubiquitous access and safe spots or drop-in and drop-out. It must not demand dedicated places or equipment.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A mobile game that is said to be played anywhere but needs focused attention and a dedicated session, so it never blends with other activities.
patterns.knobs: which real-life activities count; how often and when the game asks for attention; how interruptible it is

can_cause.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because pervasive games can sit alongside everyday activities, they can hide or blend into them, which is what lets a game pass as part of real life.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: Pervasive games run amid ordinary life, so outside happenings are likely to influence play, which makes the game's timing follow real-world events.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: Since other activities occur alongside play and the designer cannot fully control the setting, outside influences on the game tend to creep in, whether planned or not.

can_cause.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
can_cause.why: Pervasive games often happen at least partly in public, everyday places, so those real places naturally become where play takes place.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Because play happens in public settings, people nearby who aren't playing can see what is going on and end up watching.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can do non-game activities while playing, adding things they can choose to do alongside the game.

can_cause.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
can_cause.why: Together with extra-game input, play that blends into the everyday world is the typical way to let real-life activities affect the game.

changes.name: Robotic Players
changes.why: Automated players must handle the game and also behave sensibly toward the other activities overlapping with play, which raises what is demanded of them.

patterns.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
patterns.what_it_is: Each person decides how long to play, and this does not spoil the session for others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to leave and return without breaking progress for themselves or others, through pauses, saves, turn breaks or drop-in play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pause or save feature that exists but penalizes leaving, or is unusable in multiplayer, so players must stay until the end.
patterns.knobs: how easy it is to pause or leave; how much progress is lost by stopping

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because players choose when to stop, they can play in short bursts whenever it suits them, which is how casual play works.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: When players need to agree on or discuss how long a session lasts, that talk happens outside the game's rules itself.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: Letting players decide session length gives a base for also letting them shape how long a whole game instance runs.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Control over play session length is the starting point that makes it possible to also negotiate the larger game sessions.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Deciding for yourself how long to play gives players real control over their own experience of the game.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since players can play parts of the whole game whenever and wherever they like, play can fit into any moment of life.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When each player picks their own session length, players no longer need to be playing at the same times as each other.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: Letting players adapt play sessions to the time they have lessens the motivation to leave before the end.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: One player leaving can unbalance or spoil the game for the others who remain.

patterns.name: Arenas
patterns.what_it_is: Open places in the game world where fights happen on their own or by design.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Open spaces must be bounded and contain attractions such as resources or objectives, with other terrain types around them for contrast. Players must be drawn there by what it offers.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An open area is labeled an arena but has nothing to want, so players avoid it and fight elsewhere.
patterns.knobs: size and openness of the area; what draws players in; how many entrances

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Since holding an arena gives access to key spots, players compete to dominate it and keep opponents out.

can_cause.name: Sniper Locations
can_cause.why: Thinking about the spots next to an arena naturally leads designers to place sniper positions overlooking it.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Controlling an arena opens access to check points and other parts of the world, so players treat it as valuable ground.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Arenas draw players into the same open spaces, so fighting concentrates there rather than spreading across the whole world.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Arenas are made by having open, bounded areas within a board, shaping where on the board play happens.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A world gets arenas by including open but constrained areas, which become noticeable battlegrounds beside other kinds of space.

changes.name: Herd
changes.why: Because arenas are so open, whatever is being driven along has many more directions to stray, making guiding it harder.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Designers add open, enclosed areas to a level so that fighting gathers there and the level has distinct zones.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Arenas draw players into one place, so they actually meet in a large game world.

changes.name: Team Combos
changes.why: In team-based multiplayer, arenas give teammates a shared space where they can coordinate attacks or defenses together.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: With teams, an arena is a place where members can organize joint offense or defense against the other side.

patterns.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
patterns.what_it_is: Real-life knowledge about the game's subject helps the player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Game decisions must depend on facts that exist outside the game, and the game must not hand those facts to everyone. Players must also differ in how much they know.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Trivia sits in the game's theme or flavor text, but anyone can do equally well without knowing it.
patterns.knobs: how much outcomes depend on outside facts; how much of that information the game supplies itself

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: When a player's outside knowledge gives them a clear, visible edge, they can show off their skill, and others can easily see and recognize it.

changes.name: Bluffing
changes.why: If you know a lot about the other players and what they can do, they have a harder time fooling you with a bluff.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Knowing things from outside the game gives some players an edge, so their background affects results more than their play.

patterns.name: Seamful Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Knowing where sensors and connections work gives the player an advantage.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs location-sensing technology with real, learnable coverage gaps, and gameplay where being out of coverage helps, such as hiding. It does not work where coverage is everywhere.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Dead spots that exist but offer no advantage, or that players cannot find out about, so they are just glitches.
patterns.knobs: where and how large coverage gaps are; how much being unsensed helps players

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players start noticing where the invisible technology coverage begins and ends, so the physical places around them look different once they learn those hidden boundaries.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Coverage boundaries are usually hidden, so learning where they are is a skill that players build up over time and that gives them an edge.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Even a game that wouldn't otherwise be playable everywhere can become so, because dropping out of coverage is itself turned into something players can do in play.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Gaps in the technology's coverage can be exploited by players, who move into those gaps to avoid being detected.

changes.name: Player-Location Proximity
changes.why: Because location sensing doesn't work everywhere, gaps in coverage change how a player's position counts, turning dead spots into places with their own gameplay meaning.

changes.name: Player-Player Proximity
changes.why: The game can treat the technology's uneven accuracy at detecting where players are as part of the proximity rule rather than hiding it.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Visible seams in the game's presentation can force explanations for characters or units appearing and vanishing.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The pattern relies on dead spots, so a game designed to work everywhere has no gaps to exploit, making the two hard to combine.

patterns.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
patterns.what_it_is: A player can influence how long they play without spoiling the game for others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must give a meaningful experience at both short and long lengths, with natural stopping points and ways to extend or shorten play. Other players must not be harmed by the choice.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game claiming flexible length while the content or progression needs a fixed time, so short sessions feel incomplete.
patterns.knobs: minimum and maximum session length; points where play can end

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players can pick how long a game lasts, they can fit it into short or irregular free moments, which is a key ingredient of casual play.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Because the length is up for negotiation, players have to talk with each other outside the game's rules to agree on how long to play.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Letting players decide how much time a game takes gives them real control over their own play experience.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Flexible session length lets the game fit different groups and their time constraints, so it adapts to the social situation.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Adjustable session length is one needed ingredient for playing anywhere and anytime, since players can fit games into whatever time is available.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When each player can shape how long they play, their sessions are likely to start and end at different times.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: When players agree on a maximum amount of time or when play happens, that limit also caps how long the whole game can run.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: Letting players tailor sessions to their schedule removes a common reason for quitting partway.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: One player leaving can unbalance or spoil the game for the others who remain.

patterns.name: Tournaments
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to win a series of matches arranged as a competition.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Matches must be linked by a bracket or standings so that earlier results shape later play, and there must be enough players and a schedule to run it. Players need a reason to care about the overall result.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A list of unconnected games with a 'tournament' label, where results never feed into a ranking or later matches.
patterns.knobs: format (elimination vs. round-robin); number of rounds; length of each match

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: A tournament's end clears away its ongoing state and replaces it with another, marking a clear closure.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Games made only of fighting are organized into tournaments, with later opponents getting harder so progress is visible.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Entering and leaving are tied to the start and end of each event, which avoids mid-game disruption to fairness.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Prizes of money or valuable items for winning or placing high are real-world rewards, and entry fees can be real costs.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Each individual game's result is a lower goal, and winning the whole tournament is the higher goal above them.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Rounds knock out participants, so later closures involve fewer players and are more important than early ones.

can_cause.name: Illusionary Rewards
can_cause.why: When earlier rounds have already settled the overall result, a prize in a later round no longer changes anything and becomes meaningless.

can_cause.name: Late Arriving Players
can_cause.why: Keeping each round's result separate from the overall standing lets newcomers start fair in a round and catch up in the total.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Individual game results feed into an overall competition, so the tournament is a game built from the outcomes of other games.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: A big field of opponents gets split into several smaller contests, each with fewer rivals, so one large goal becomes many small ones.

can_cause.name: Polyathlons
can_cause.why: A tournament can be built from rounds of different game types, which makes it a multi-skill contest rather than repeats of one game.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: A tournament has the same game played again and again across rounds, so players keep facing the same kind of play.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: A tournament's result comes from playing a game several times, so repeated play is built into the competition.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: Players can organize a tournament around a game and run it themselves, though judges are often added for disputes.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Events with many matches mean participants not in a given game, plus interested outsiders, watch the individual games and the whole competition.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Rising stakes across rounds provide fresh challenges, which helps tension survive repeated play.

can_cause.name: Tiebreakers
can_cause.why: Extra games or game portions can be played again until the tie is broken, which resolves it.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: Wagering is quick and distinct from other play, so it makes a convenient activity to build a tournament around.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: They let players see each other's skills, offering a stage for showing mastery.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Organizing players into contests lets even solo games be played against others.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Matching players against others so that obvious differences in their chances are small keeps contests fairer.

patterns.name: Endgame
patterns.what_it_is: A final stage that happens in every play of this game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Earlier play must lead to a state with a distinct character, such as fewer options, high stakes or elimination, and the game needs a regular way of finishing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A phase labelled endgame in the rules that plays like the middle game, with the game just stopping.
patterns.knobs: what ends the game; how play narrows toward the end; how strongly earlier choices matter at the end

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: Because the final phase makes every earlier choice matter, players may study their options so long that they stall the game.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Starting the last phase, finishing it, and naming a winner are all big turning points, so any game with an endgame has such closures.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Since all earlier effort comes to a head in this phase, players are pushed to think ahead carefully to get the best outcome.

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: When players can see they cannot win in the final phase, they may choose to give up rather than play on.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: The final phase makes visible how earlier actions shaped the result, so players feel their past work counted.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Having a distinct final phase lets players build knowledge specific to it, such as what to do when the game is closing out.

conflicts_with.name: Player Unpredictability
conflicts_with.why: Final phases often settle into locked positions, often from depleted resources, so players become easier to predict.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: A game that can never be won has no end, so it normally cannot have a final phase.

patterns.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
patterns.what_it_is: Before the game starts, it is hard to say reliably how it will end.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be real sources of variance, such as chance, deep strategy or unpredictable players, and no dominant strategy or runaway leader. Skill should still matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with random elements that rarely change who wins, so the result is clear well in advance.
patterns.knobs: amount of randomness; balance between players; strategic depth

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: Betting only makes sense, or stays interesting, when nobody can be sure how the game will end, so players have something to wager on.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: When players can't know how things will end, a good result feels like fortune, so uncertainty alone is often enough.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If the result isn't known beforehand, each session can end differently, which gives players a reason to come back and play again.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Not knowing who will win keeps players on edge about whether their efforts will pay off, creating a basic sense of suspense.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Uncertainty lowers the chance that skilled players win every time, though their expertise still gives them an edge.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: When the result stays open, it is less likely that one player is clearly out of the running yet able to pick the winner.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Making the result uncertain is the main way to prevent anyone from being the obvious winner.

patterns.name: Surrendering
patterns.what_it_is: A player stops the game, admitting defeat.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a visible losing position and a cheap way to quit, and the rest of the session should survive someone leaving. How readable the standings are decides how early people give up.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'concede' button exists but nobody ever uses it, or using it ruins the game for everyone else so it is effectively unavailable.
patterns.knobs: how clearly standings show who is losing; how easy it is to quit; what happens to the others afterwards

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: A player who gives up is out of the game before its intended end, so the surrender itself is an early exit.

can_cause.name: Early Leaving Players
can_cause.why: Someone who concedes stops playing while others carry on, so they become a player who departs before the session finishes.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: The player removes themselves by choice rather than being knocked out by opponents, which is a self-inflicted form of elimination.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When one player gives up but play can go on for the rest, participants no longer start and finish the session together.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: In competitive play, leaving can simply be treated as giving up, so exits fit into the game naturally.

changes.name: Last Man Standing
changes.why: Conceding gives players an extra way to drop out besides being beaten, though it is rarely a pleasant one, so designers seldom encourage it.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: A whole team can collectively decide it is beaten and give up to another team.

conflicts_with.name: End State Scoring
conflicts_with.why: When it is hard to tell who is winning, players are less likely to decide they are beaten and quit.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Goals
conflicts_with.why: Because the winner is unclear, players keep believing they still have a chance, so they are less tempted to give up.

patterns.name: Early Elimination
patterns.what_it_is: A player is knocked out long before the session ends for everyone else.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to lose out long before the game ends, and no role is kept for them, so they wait a long time. The effect grows with game length and a lack of short rounds.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An elimination rule that exists but only triggers in the last minutes, so nobody sits out for long.
