patterns.knobs: how easy and how early elimination is; game length; what eliminated players can still do

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: A player knocked out long before the game finishes has to sit idle, unable to take part like everyone else, for however long the game still runs.

can_cause.name: Kingmaker
can_cause.why: If eliminated players are given neutral enemies to control as something to do, they might end up deciding who wins among those still playing.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Players who are out can be turned into onlookers, watching the remaining game, which happens naturally in face-to-face play and can be supported with special views.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knocking players out early changes suspense in much the same way as ordinary elimination in multiplayer games does, though the effect is stronger.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: In game worlds where characters die often or at random, removing players early fits the setting and so can be justified.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Games with eliminate goals or player destruction must decide whether knocking players out early is wanted.

changes.name: Player Elimination
changes.why: Early elimination is a more extreme form of player elimination, where players are removed much sooner relative to when the game ends.

conflicts_with.name: Extermination
conflicts_with.why: Ending the game with an extermination phase pushes knockouts toward the end of the game instance, so players are not removed early.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Giving players temporary protection at the start stops them from being knocked out early in the game.

conflicts_with.name: Playing to Lose
conflicts_with.why: Early elimination makes it hard for players to want to deliberately lose, since being out is already a drawback.

patterns.name: Predictable Winner
patterns.what_it_is: During the session, players can see who will almost certainly win.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It emerges when snowballing mechanics, big skill gaps, readable scores and kingmaking exist without comeback tools. Designers mostly work to prevent it with uncertainty or catch-up mechanisms.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A leaderboard shows someone ahead, but comebacks or hidden scoring keep the result open, so nobody treats the winner as settled.
patterns.knobs: strength of positive vs negative feedback; hidden information; randomness; catch-up mechanisms

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: When everyone can see who is ahead, the other players tend to change their tactics to gang up on that front-runner.

can_cause.name: Kingmaker
can_cause.why: Players who feel they have no hope left may use their remaining moves to decide which rival wins instead of trying to win.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: The player who is clearly going to win wants the game over quickly, so they try to finish it early.

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: Players who see the outcome as settled and feel their effort is pointless may simply quit, especially if the game gives no graceful way out.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Game States
can_cause.why: Once one winner is truly certain, every other player is left in a position where they can no longer win.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: With a winner already obvious, the closing stage of a game loses its interest because nothing is left to be decided.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: In competitive games, players may think the winner is already clear, especially when scores are public.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: Holding leaders back and helping others makes it hard to tell early who will win.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: When the winner is clear, players can see their influence is small, though the exaggerated perception can mask this.

conflicts_with.name: Increasing Rewards
conflicts_with.why: Growing rewards can keep a likely winner from being obvious, but only when it is still uncertain who will actually earn those rewards.

conflicts_with.name: Negative Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: Since leaders are pushed back and are harder to identify, runaway leads are unlikely, which undermines an early, obvious winner.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: If performance is uncertain, it is harder for the winner to be known beforehand, since anyone's execution may vary.

conflicts_with.name: Player Unpredictability
conflicts_with.why: When it's clear who is ahead, what that player will do next becomes obvious, removing the uncertainty.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Chance events blur who is ahead, though players who understand statistics may still predict results when many random events occur.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Goals
conflicts_with.why: Hidden objectives make players unsure what others are aiming for, so the likely winner is unclear.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Scoring Mechanisms
conflicts_with.why: Hiding how points are counted stops players from working out who is leading, so a winner can't be foreseen.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: A certain winner drains the tension about who will win, though tension might still exist over who comes second.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
conflicts_with.why: Making the result uncertain is the main way to prevent anyone from being the obvious winner.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: If nobody can win in the first place, there is no one to predict as winner, unless players compare scores against each other.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: When the winner is obvious, trailing players feel their effort no longer matters.

conflicts_with.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
conflicts_with.why: If everyone can already see who will win, the winner is clearly not being decided after play finishes.

patterns.name: Unwinnable Game States
patterns.what_it_is: States from which no actions can lead to a win anymore.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules need irreversible actions, dominant strategies or kingmaking that can lock a player (or everyone) out of any route to victory, and the player must be able to notice or suspect this. Hidden scoring or a late-revealed winner can mask it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that merely feels hard or a player who is far behind but still has a clear comeback path; nothing is actually closed off.
patterns.knobs: how reversible actions are; strength of catch-up mechanisms; how visible the score is

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: When a player sees or believes no route to victory remains, continuing feels pointless, so they give up the match instead of playing on.

can_cause.name: Early Leaving Players
can_cause.why: When a player believes they can no longer win, they see no reason to continue and are more tempted to walk away.

changes.name: Save Files
changes.why: A saved game captured in a hopeless state becomes pointless to load for someone trying to win, since nothing they do can succeed.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: If players are trying to win but can no longer do so, their actions stop mattering to the goal they are pursuing.

conflicts_with.name: Secret Scoring Mechanisms
conflicts_with.why: Players trailing on visible scores can still hope that hidden points or others' unknown totals will let them catch up, so they feel less beaten.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If winning is impossible, nothing a player does can pay off toward victory, so their effort feels wasted.

conflicts_with.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
conflicts_with.why: Since the winner is only decided once play is over, players can't be sure they've lost beforehand, so the hopeless feeling is avoided.

patterns.name: Roleplaying
patterns.what_it_is: Players take on the goals and behavior of fictional characters.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give players an agent-like character or faction with goals of its own, real freedom in how to pursue them, and some internal tension or hidden aims. Add a world with enough texture that staying in role has something to respond to.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hero with a name and a portrait whose goals are just the player's own score, so nobody ever acts as the character would.
patterns.knobs: how much character goals are set by the game versus chosen by the player; how much freedom there is in pursuing them

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: In multiplayer roleplaying, players interact as their characters, so what one character does can affect how other characters in the fiction treat them.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: When players act out their character, this can show how much they care about what happens to that character in the game world.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Roleplaying usually leads players to speak or act as their character would, though a player may merely state actions without acting them out.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Characters being played need a setting that offers them chances and obstacles, so roleplaying always takes place in some game world and fills in its details.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Players roleplaying together may step out of character to talk as themselves, and they can disagree about how much of that is acceptable.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Because roleplaying is a kind of performance, players can feel unsure about how well they are doing it.

can_cause.name: Perspective Taking
can_cause.why: Roleplaying pushes players to consider the character's in-world viewpoint beyond game mechanics, making them more likely to see things as that character does.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: Players feel fulfilled when they manage to play in line with their character's wants and personality, whether or not the character succeeds.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Characters usually hold roles in their world, so players acting as them tend to behave according to those roles.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Players need skill to act out someone's social behavior convincingly, and also to support others' roleplaying without taking over scenes.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Acting out characters in the fiction helps keep play in line with the setting's theme.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Roleplaying means controlling game elements as if they had their own goals, which is what makes them agents.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Roleplaying encourages players to notice their character's actions and separates player from character, making those actions read as defining the character.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: When players try to meet their character's goals, succeeding or failing at them can itself change the character.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: In multiplayer roleplay, players must cooperate to keep the fictional world believable, whether or not their characters would.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can act in character in many ways beyond core gameplay, which gives them additional things to choose.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Convincingly playing a character who did not perform some hidden action is a skill that shows mastery.

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: When players stay in character, they can share rumors as their characters, especially when they have free time to talk.

can_cause.name: Live Action Roleplaying
can_cause.why: The pattern is built on direct, unmediated roleplaying, with the added step that the playing is acted out physically instead of just described.

can_cause.name: Player Characters
can_cause.why: Players controlling characters and sharing their goals with them is a form of roleplaying, which is how player characters arise.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: When players describe what their characters do, that description is itself telling a story, so roleplaying produces storytelling.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: In a lasting world, players must think about long-term effects of their actions, and their roleplaying can in turn change that world.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Roleplaying can happen with no other players, such as steering a country as history did or playing a character as decided at its creation.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Roleplaying makes players act toward a character's goals instead of their own, shaping how the agent is played.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Players acting out their characters can develop them in ways the rules would miss.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Historically, many of these games have been roleplaying games, so playing characters is a common form of action in them.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Because players are free to choose, they might add non-diegetic elements, which undermines the shared fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
conflicts_with.why: If the character design isn't consistently reflected in gameplay, the enforced behavior clashes with how players want to play the role.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Too much player freedom, or stepping out of character, can break the setting's theme.

patterns.name: Character Defining Actions
patterns.what_it_is: The actions chosen during play determine what kind of character one becomes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters need abilities that change or get interpreted according to the player's choices, and the game or its group must register and remember those choices.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Character traits are chosen from a menu at the start, and nothing the player does later changes them.
patterns.knobs: how strongly actions feed back into stats, relations or story; how many distinct paths exist

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Because every action a character performs shapes how players see them, using characters at all brings in this pattern, even without any system tracking.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Actions that shift a character's alignment or destiny can be notable enough to count as exceptional events, unlike routine ones such as raising a skill.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: When actions drive character development, players see their character grow more capable, which supports goals centered on becoming more competent.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: Since these actions are hard to undo and shape the character and its relations, they're interesting enough to be worth recording as statistics.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Actions that define a character only feel defining if they can't easily be undone, so they typically produce permanent consequences.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: A chain of defining actions traces how a character develops and how relations with NPCs change, forming a story even when none was planned.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: If players are free to choose how their character develops, they can set a direction and steer toward it through their actions.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: When players aim to fulfil a character's role, their defining actions let them feel they are living up to that role.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Because defining actions are hard to reverse, many trigger major, lasting events, especially when combined with predetermined story structures.

changes.name: Character Alignments
changes.why: Actions that push an alignment to change count as defining the character, so the alignment shifts as a result of what the player does.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: The pattern changes characters either through the game system or through the players' shared view of who the character is.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Defining actions can alter relations with companions, since how the player treats them and behaves around them shapes the character.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: When a character's fate is undecided, the actions that determine which destiny comes true are the ones that define the character.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: The pattern is most typically applied to player characters, since players see the resulting changes as stemming from their own actions.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: How a player treats NPCs, individually or as members of a group, shapes who the player's character becomes and what is open to them.

conflicts_with.name: Cutscenes
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes take control away from players and may show the character acting against how players see them, undermining the sense that their own actions define the character.

conflicts_with.name: Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: If defining actions shape a player character in ways the player dislikes, it can break their emotional engrossment, since players feel they own that character's interpretation.

patterns.name: Open Destiny
patterns.what_it_is: Characters' stories turn out differently from game to game because of what happens.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters or factions need tracked state that actually changes in response to events, and endings must differ enough to be noticeable. There must be few enough distinct outcomes, each reachable by different play, for players to see the difference.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several endings that are only a cosmetic text change on top of the same arc, or a branching that always converges to the same fate.
patterns.knobs: how many distinct endings; which characters or factions have a tracked arc; how much play affects each arc

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Players may set themselves the aim of seeing every possible ending, which turns the full list of destinies into something to gather.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Because endings differ, players can build an outer game around reaching all of them, which can be tracked with achievements.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Players can choose to aim for particular outcomes, such as making a country unify, which become extra targets they may pursue or skip.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When agents' fates can differ between playthroughs, their agenda feels stronger in later games because outcomes are not fixed.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: When players know what destiny their own character might have, they can steer play toward the arc they want.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If players know other destinies exist, they have a reason to play again and try to get a different story arc.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: When the destinies are clearly different from one another, each one becomes a goal the player can pick and work toward.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Events in the world leave lasting marks on the characters living there, so the world feels like it responds coherently.

can_cause.name: Playing to Lose
can_cause.why: Because a character's fate isn't fixed, players can choose how it goes wrong, and so losing becomes something they are free to aim for.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with a limited set of actions, letting players decide where the game goes gives them choices that lead to varied play.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Letting computer-controlled characters have varying fates helps keep up the impression that they have intentions of their own.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Any character, not only the player's, can be given a story arc that changes with what happened in play.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Players interact most with companions and feel attached, so spending effort on their varied endings is worthwhile.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Groups, not just individuals, can end up with different fates depending on what happened during the session.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: It is one way of building a game's storytelling, letting the arc that emerges differ from game to game.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Giving non-player characters their own possible endings multiplies how many overall outcomes a game can have.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Player characters are the most common place for it, since their story can unfold differently depending on how the player acted.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Designers can write several set endings into the planned story and pick among them based on play.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Different players get different experiences, giving them something to talk about with one another.

conflicts_with.name: Scenes
conflicts_with.why: Scenes let designers give players local influence over events without letting the overall story arc vary, so they serve as a way to avoid this pattern.

patterns.name: Diegetic Communication
patterns.what_it_is: Players communicate as people do in the game world, without leaving their roles.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must give players a reason and a way to speak in character, and avoid options that pull them out of it. Separate channels for out-of-game talk help.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A fantasy setting where players chat about scores and tactics in ordinary terms the whole time.
patterns.knobs: which channels exist; how strongly in-character talk is encouraged

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: When players talk only as people inside the game world, nothing from outside intrudes, so the world stays believable and coherent.

can_cause.name: Live Action Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Live action roleplay depends on players speaking to each other in-world, so staying in-world in conversation is a core part of how that style is played.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Speaking in ways that suit the game world keeps the talk matching the game's theme, so the mood and setting feel unified.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: In-world communication shapes how players talk, since they must speak through their characters, who are the ones doing the talking in the fiction.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Speaking in-world is widely seen as improving roleplaying, because players keep acting as their characters rather than stepping out to talk as themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: By definition, in-world talk refers to nothing outside the game world, so speaking about outside matters directly breaks it; designers mostly separate or minimize one.

conflicts_with.name: Reflective Communication
conflicts_with.why: Players mixing in-world talk with reflective talk must keep switching between the two, and slips in that switching can break the world's consistency.

patterns.name: Exceptional Events
patterns.what_it_is: Rare events that are remembered because they are so unlikely or affect the game so strongly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Include rare, high-impact or surprising outcomes (critical results, betrayals, spectacular failures) that cannot be undone at once. Hidden information and randomness help, but the events must really change the game state, not just flash by.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rare-sounding event that happens often, or one that changes nothing and is quickly reversed, so nobody remembers it.
patterns.knobs: how rare the event is; how large and how permanent its effect on the game state

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Because a memorable, unusual moment sticks in players' minds, they tend to retell it later, and that retelling becomes the seed of a story about that particular play session.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Exceptional events are unusual and unexpected by nature, so having them in a game means players can't always foresee what will follow their actions.

patterns.name: Enactment
patterns.what_it_is: The player personally does and says what their character does and says.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs characters, a setting that invites in-character action and an audience of other players; rules should reward or at least allow performance.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players pick a character name and class but speak and act as themselves.
patterns.knobs: how much the rules reward in-character play; presence of a facilitator or audience; warm-up support

can_cause.name: Context Dependent Reactions
can_cause.why: Because players act out things themselves, each performance varies with the surrounding situation, so the game can respond differently depending on where and how the action happens.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: When players speak and act as their characters, the performance itself keeps what happens in line with the game world's own logic.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: Having personally performed what a character does, players tend to identify with that character more and grow fond of them.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Any part of a performance that doesn't change the game's state still has real effects outside the game's rules, such as how others react.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Acting out a character well is a skill, so improving at it counts as getting better at playing the game.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Since players perform actions themselves, each attempt can come out slightly different, so how well it goes is never fully certain.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: A player's own performance can sway other players or the game master, so the player's real skill adds to what the character can accomplish.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: When players successfully carry out the actions their character is supposed to do, they feel they have truly lived up to that role.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Others watching a performance can appreciate it, so players can earn praise and approval from their fellow participants.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Performing draws attention to the player, which suits and encourages someone who enjoys taking the exhibitionist, show-off role in a group.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Performances that involve interacting with other people usually call on the player's ability to deal well with others.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: When players act out what their characters do, the resulting events form a story, so acting it out produces storytelling.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If everyone is expected to act in-world but not all do, the fiction breaks, and players' free choices may bring in non-diegetic elements.

patterns.name: Multiplayer Games
patterns.what_it_is: Games in which more than one player takes part.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must give each player a real role with consequences for the others, through competition, cooperation or communication. Players need ways to find and join each other.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that supports several players but where they play in parallel with no effect on one another.
patterns.knobs: number of players; competitive or cooperative; how much they affect each other

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Skilled human opponents are an easy source of challenge in competitive play, since you can simply face someone who is good at the game.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Teams and groups let each player specialize and build up a particular strength for their character over time.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Having other players around, plus social interaction and social skills, lets players help each other now and trust they will be repaid later.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: When players compete directly against one another, the other players become opponents to be beaten, especially when losing means being knocked out.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Players who share a game tend to coordinate, brag, negotiate and trade outside the formal rules, even if designers never planned for it.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because players interact socially around the game, what happens between them can carry on beyond the game itself without designers needing to plan it.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Playing with others lets people choose how to organize themselves socially, form groups and identify with them.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Other players allow kinds of skill that solo games lack, such as negotiating, roleplaying and storytelling with the group.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Since you cannot be sure what other players will do, their actual moves can feel like chance when they are revealed.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Only with several players can the game contain participants whose choices are truly unforeseeable, so multiple players are required for this unpredictability.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: With several players and their differing specialties, people naturally settle into recognizable roles within the group.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Playing with others makes abilities like negotiating and reading people useful or necessary, though other patterns may be needed to guarantee it.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must plan short-term moves while allowing for what the others might do next.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: A tie needs someone to be equal with, so having several players in the same game normally makes ties possible.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Sharing the activity gives players a common focus, especially when they laugh at failures together or chat during quiet moments.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Even when players are not cooperating, having others to deal with opens up swapping items, knowledge or favors.

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Players in the same party can build their own norms, and other players simply change their attitudes toward those who break them.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: With several competitors, players see the leader as a common target and join forces against them, which levels results.

can_cause.name: Bidding
can_cause.why: Bidding needs several potential bidders, so a game with multiple players naturally offers it as a shared activity.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Having several people in one game, especially with roleplaying, creates the setting in which players must work together to keep the fiction going.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: With several players, someone may be removed from play or must wait for their turn, leaving them idle.

can_cause.name: Early Leaving Players
can_cause.why: With several people involved, any one of them might leave for outside reasons, so such games naturally face players quitting midway.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Players compete over tools, which makes the other players into targets to be removed.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players are clearly dependent on others, as with helplessness or delayed reciprocity, they can come to feel more influential than they are.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: Having multiple players allows responsibilities to be divided among them, and access to different devices can force specialization.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Several players are needed so that someone is available to hold and swap game elements with.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: With several human players and social interaction, rivalries form among them, and in guilds they may be hard to avoid.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: With several players competing and limited lives, opponents can be knocked out one at a time until one is left.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Loyalty can exist between players as mutual ties, mapped onto in-game representations, when alliances or guilds are present.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: The pattern needs several players sharing the chaotic experience, so the game must be multiplayer and players must feel they play together.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: With several players pursuing their own short-term goals, others can easily choose to block them.

can_cause.name: Private Game Spaces
can_cause.why: Multiplayer games can give each player a space that is temporary (time limits, distance) or permanent through restricted actions.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: In games with several players, some players can have abilities that others lack, so differences between players arise.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Combined with distinct roles, playing with others lets people try different sub-challenges across sessions, giving each game a different feel.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games with sanctioned cheating, players pretend not to be doing certain actions, much like the pretending in betrayal.

can_cause.name: Single-Player Games
can_cause.why: A game built for several people can end up played by just one person, for example against computer opponents, so it works as a single-player game.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: In games with several players, a player may try to carry out forbidden actions without others noticing, when cheating is allowed.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Groups such as alliances, guilds or parties need to coordinate and cooperate, which calls for shared planning.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: When several players take part in a race, all of them strive to finish first, so their goals are identical.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: A shared accomplishment needs several people acting together, so a game with multiple players is required before the group can feel it succeeded as one.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Multiplayer games with players holding distinct abilities or skills create situations where combos need several people acting together.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: Having several players is the basic requirement, since there must be others to coordinate with and a reason to look for shared strategies.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: With real players there is the chance of cheating, and players must consider what others might do outside the rules.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Having several players is a precondition here: only with more than one person can their session timings differ, though this alone doesn't cause it.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with functional roles, having several players with different roles adds to the variety of play.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Skilled opponents are an easy way to make a game challenging, particularly in competitions.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Teams and groups let players develop specialties and team skills, and social abilities add new things to master.

changes.name: Helplessness
changes.why: When a player is stuck, others can rescue them, which changes how helplessness plays out.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: The more players there are, the harder it is to keep a fixed story and still let each player's actions shape the outcome.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Playing with others adds social layers to acting in character, but players may also step out of the game's theme.

changes.name: Spectators
changes.why: The shared experiences, group effects and drama of several players make a game more interesting to watch.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Players tend to swap what they know about good strategies before, during and after sessions.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: How hard it is to plan depends on how many actions other players take and how predictable they are.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: In multiplayer games run through a medium, the same world can be shown differently to different players via phasing, so the world's presentation varies per player.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Human-controlled members add team accomplishment and togetherness, and make party size and loot division harder to manage.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: In multiplayer games, different players can independently have the same quests, which saves development effort but causes inconsistent narration.

conflicts_with.name: Cooperation
conflicts_with.why: Cooperation is easier to get with all players working together, but friendly fire, mistrust and sabotage can limit it in teams.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Chances
conflicts_with.why: Other players keep acting, so a retry may become impossible, making the pattern hard to offer without special powers.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: When combined with turn-taking or fixed story, other players' needs or directions restrict individual choice.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptibility
conflicts_with.why: Others may not want to wait around, so one person's interruption can cause idle time for fellow players.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
conflicts_with.why: One player leaving can unbalance or spoil the game for the others who remain.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
conflicts_with.why: One player leaving can unbalance or spoil the game for the others who remain.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Advantages that build up over time, late joiners, skill and tool differences, and cheating make balance hard to keep.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: With more players, it gets harder to let everyone affect a fixed story, and some players' effort matters less.

conflicts_with.name: Save Points
conflicts_with.why: It is hard to agree on a good moment to save unless all players are cooperating.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: Players must agree on when to reload an earlier state, which makes loading awkward.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Changing rules is problematic for the same reason, as players must agree on which rules to use.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players joining and leaving, or speaking out of character, can break the game's setting.

conflicts_with.name: Turn-Based Games
conflicts_with.why: Waiting for others to plan and act forces downtime and can lead to over-long deliberation.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Late joiners, undone effects or less effective story influence can make some players' work count for less.

conflicts_with.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
conflicts_with.why: With several players developing at different paces, their strengths can drift apart, which upsets fairness between them.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Uneven skill among competitors can make the game too hard for some and too easy for others.

conflicts_with.name: Character Development
conflicts_with.why: Because some players progress further than others, growth can leave participants with unequal characters, hurting fairness among them.

conflicts_with.name: Crafting
conflicts_with.why: In shared games, crafting can disrupt the economy and balance between players if making items is not weighed against their value.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: With several people involved, someone is more likely to quit or introduce non-diegetic elements, which threatens the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
conflicts_with.why: In multiplayer games, the fiction of the game world can be broken when people appear and disappear.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Other players can reduce a person's influence through balancing, shared penalties, alliances and voting, which weakens the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: When players are not evenly matched, strong mastery makes it hard to build mechanics that keep the game balanced.

conflicts_with.name: Tools
conflicts_with.why: Tools can give holders a clear edge over those without them, which creates unequal standing between players.

conflicts_with.name: Weapons
conflicts_with.why: Weapons delivered by vehicles can upset fairness between players, because vehicles also improve movement and may add armor.

patterns.name: Teams
patterns.what_it_is: Agents or game elements acting toward one shared goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Members must share rewards and penalties so their interests align. Some actions should benefit or depend on teammates.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players wear the same colour but are scored individually, so teams have no effect on decisions.
patterns.knobs: team size; which rewards and penalties are shared; friendly-fire rules

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: When the game stores facts about a team beyond just who belongs to it, such as traits or scores, the team becomes its own tracked construct.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Because team members share goals, they must work together, for example by splitting up to hold more area or passing items among themselves.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: When a team fails to reach its goals, members can feel bad about letting their teammates down.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Working together can give players a sense of social reward whether or not the team actually reaches its goals.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Playing as part of a team leads players to take on social roles within the group.

can_cause.name: Symbiotic Player Relations
can_cause.why: Members depend on each other to reach shared goals, so players' fortunes become linked, which matters most in multiplayer and online games.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Pursuing goals as a group creates a feeling of being together, whether or not the team ends up succeeding.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Team members can be undermined by a traitor, which complicates cooperation within the group.

can_cause.name: Friendly Fire
can_cause.why: Friendly Fire needs players grouped into teams so there are allies to hit; with player killing, that makes accidents on teammates possible.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Teammates may disagree when one does something others find inappropriate, creating friction inside the group.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Team members who can earn personal rewards by racing ahead of each other end up rivals within the team.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Placing players in teams makes them feel they are handling the overwhelming situation together as a group.

can_cause.name: Shared Resources
can_cause.why: Team members who jointly hold things like lives or retries have a supply that all of them access, which makes it shared.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Having teams in a multiplayer game makes social skills very likely to appear, though not always to affect gameplay.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Putting players on a team gives them shared goals, so whatever they achieve is felt as a group success.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Teams provide the coordinated group whose joint, well-timed actions form a team combo, especially when members are differentiated.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: Development needs a team to exist, so in any game with teams, the changes happening to those teams are what make up this pattern.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: Teams supply shared goals and a group structure, and an opposing team provides an external threat, both motivating players to agree on strategies.

can_cause.name: TvT
can_cause.why: Once players are grouped into teams and those groups are set against one another, you have team-versus-team play.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Putting agents on a team makes them work toward common goals, and reserves can let some rest.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Teams require the avatars to cooperate, and to a lesser extent coordinate, with each other.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Teams make characters cooperate and coordinate, and character development can improve the whole team.

changes.name: Instances
changes.why: Teams can be required to be formed before players are allowed to enter a game instance.

changes.name: Last Man Standing
changes.why: Applying teams to last-man-standing play pits team against team instead of individual against individual.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Teams influence large online games strongly because they tie players' fortunes together and bring on many social patterns.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Teams matter most with several players, because they create dependency between players and lots of social interaction.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Putting teams into player-versus-player play turns it into team-versus-team contests.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Teams push players to act out their roles in character rather than only chase their characters' goals.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Team play can pit personal gain against group benefit, for example through individual rewards or the risk of hitting teammates.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Players must think ahead about how best to cooperate and coordinate with teammates.

changes.name: Trick Taking
changes.why: With teams in trick-taking games, such as Contract Bridge, partners naturally collect tricks and points together.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Lobbies can help team members meet and sort out how to play together in a mediated game.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: In team games, physical actions can be shared among members, with reserves letting players or coaches choose who performs what.

changes.name: Player Physical Prowess
changes.why: The page only mentions teams as the setting where reserves allow resting during physically exhausting play, not a direct modulating reason.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can serve on a team, as when a player's character fights alongside many computer-controlled creeps.

conflicts_with.name: Betrayal
conflicts_with.why: Betrayal threatens the trust teammates need, lessening the sense of a team even while it increases tension.

conflicts_with.name: Delayed Reciprocity
conflicts_with.why: When team success rests on common goals, members help each other as a matter of course, which makes room for favors owed later smaller.

conflicts_with.name: Internal Conflicts
conflicts_with.why: Conflicting goals among members can cause rivalry and a breakdown of the group, working against the unity a team needs.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Giving certain members special powers in a team-versus-team game can make the sides unequal, causing problems with fairness.

conflicts_with.name: Spawning
conflicts_with.why: As long as team members can spawn again, the team cannot be eliminated.

patterns.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
patterns.what_it_is: A program, machine, or person who keeps records and manages the game's participants.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The facilitator must truly take over the work, such as hidden information, bookkeeping or fair judging, so that players need not do it. It must be reliable and trusted.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A computer or person nominally in charge, while the players still do all the tracking and rule checks themselves.
patterns.knobs: which tasks are handed over; who or what acts as facilitator

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: A neutral facilitator can be trusted to record what players accomplish, so it keeps track of achievements across separate game sessions.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Facilitators control enemies and non-player characters, and designers can make these look like independent agents even though the facilitator runs them.

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: Because the facilitator handles the interface and game state, players can act without others seeing who did it.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Planned player actions must be stored until they are resolved, and a facilitator is typically what holds them.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Seeing the whole game state, the facilitator can measure player progress and apply effects to even things out, including when players join.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: By managing information and unfolding the planned story, the facilitator can make betrayals and other intended story effects happen.

can_cause.name: Cameras
can_cause.why: The facilitator often renders what players see, including the viewpoint a camera gives in third-person or god-view presentations.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: By tracking how well players are doing, the facilitator can adjust difficulty so the game stays demanding enough.

can_cause.name: Chat Channels
can_cause.why: When players cannot talk directly or must be limited, the facilitator supplies the channels through which they can message each other.

can_cause.name: Communication Channels
can_cause.why: The facilitator can carry messages between players, so it supplies the channels for games where players lack direct contact or have limited communication.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since the facilitator updates the state and applies the rules, players need not handle complicated states or know every rule themselves.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: The facilitator can present story material, including through cutscenes, as part of unfolding the narrative structure.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Computer facilitators can keep the game world believable when the content itself is designed that way.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Facilitators are instrumental in showing players the standout elements of the game world, such as non-player characters.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: A facilitator can force players to wait, for example after dying, and computer facilitators can also shorten waits by doing heavy calculations.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: The facilitator keeps game components and resources going when players change, adjusting balance or switching AI players on and off.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
can_cause.why: Because it monitors player progress through full knowledge of the state, the facilitator can raise or lower difficulty as play proceeds.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Facilitators commonly run opponents in conflicts and combat, especially when a game has only one player.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: As an impartial non-player, the facilitator can compel agents and players to act in set ways, such as limiting when actions are allowed.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: Human facilitators can schedule happenings to coincide with real-world time, which a fixed automated system does less easily.

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Human facilitators can change the rules as play goes on, which fixed rule enforcement would not allow.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: A facilitator that introduces or adjusts rules and content changes the game state in ways the game itself did not predetermine.

can_cause.name: First-Person Views
can_cause.why: The facilitator holds the full state, so it can render or describe what a character perceives from their own position.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Human facilitators can bend outcomes quietly, since they control resolution of actions and are not bound to apply results mechanically.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Humans can invent new elements and decide when they appear, while servers carry out the actual insertion into play.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Since it sees the whole game state, the facilitator can show players particular pieces of information they could not otherwise get.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Having the full state in hand, the facilitator can offer players a general summary of the situation they could not otherwise assemble.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: The facilitator presents the game world to players, whether by rendering it on screen or describing it aloud.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: As a trusted non-player, the facilitator can reliably record and keep statistics about play.

can_cause.name: God Views
can_cause.why: The facilitator, holding the whole state, can produce an overhead perspective that shows more than any one character would perceive.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Mechanical and computer facilitators can objectively enforce that things which have happened cannot be undone.

can_cause.name: Late Arriving Players
can_cause.why: The facilitator manages changes in player numbers, so someone joining after the start can be fitted in with suitable balancing.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: A facilitator controls when players may act, so it can impose quiet stretches in which they are held back.

can_cause.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
can_cause.why: Such games need constant updates and huge states tracked, a load that computers, sometimes aided by people, take from players.

can_cause.name: Mediated Gameplay
can_cause.why: The facilitator sits between players and the game, deciding what information they get and so shaping how they experience it.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: By looking after components and resources, the facilitator lets a larger game continue across instances even as players come and go.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: Facilitators run the characters players do not control, such as monsters and townsfolk, and present them in the world.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: By taking over bookkeeping and rules knowledge, the facilitator spares players effort, which counts as help from outside the players.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game Worlds
can_cause.why: The facilitator stores information about the world instance so it continues to exist between play sessions.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Watching how players are progressing, the facilitator can apply effects that keep their standing even.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: When the facilitator makes things harder for players, such as by controlling enemies in combat, it creates play against the game.

can_cause.name: Real-Time Games
can_cause.why: The facilitator tracks when updates are due as time passes, so players do not need to.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Because the facilitator controls the game state and its content, it can support changing the layout or makeup of the world.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: By easing setup and takedown and by adding or tweaking content, the facilitator makes playing again easier and more varied.

can_cause.name: Replays
can_cause.why: Since the facilitator generates the views of the game, those same views can be reused to show earlier play again.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: When people serve as facilitators, holding that important position can give them a satisfying role.

can_cause.name: Save-Load Cycles
can_cause.why: The facilitator can store the game state and restore it later, supporting play spread across several sessions.

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: The facilitator can keep track of hidden objectives so that individual players do not see each other's aims.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: The facilitator can deliver the story to players, improvising it if human or presenting it through scenes if computerized.

can_cause.name: Synchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Especially in games played over networks, a facilitator may be needed to keep everyone's play coordinated in time.

can_cause.name: Temporal Consistency
can_cause.why: Computer facilitators can keep time-related matters coherent in the world only as far as their rules manage to.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Although merely having them does not cause it, facilitators are often essential to building suspense.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Computer facilitators can keep the world fitting its theme only as well as their rules can express.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: The facilitator often creates the camera-based rendering of the world seen from outside a character.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: The facilitator keeps track of when each update is due and stores planned actions until the tick comes.

can_cause.name: Turn Taking
can_cause.why: The facilitator can stop players from acting out of turn, making sure the turn order is followed as designed.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: With control of the game state, the facilitator can easily make overwhelmingly strong events occur.

can_cause.name: Unknown Goals
can_cause.why: The facilitator can hold information about goals that players do not know and keep them concealed.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Since the facilitator holds the state and actions, players need not be present at the same time.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: With no players present, someone or something must run the game, so a facilitator is required.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: Being a neutral third party, the facilitator can safely hold the stakes that players wager.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Facilitators control enemies and resolve fights, and computers can do heavy combat calculations without making players wait.

changes.name: Game Element Insertion
changes.why: Facilitators check that new elements are introduced properly, with humans deciding what and when and servers carrying it out.

changes.name: Handicap Systems
changes.why: Trustworthy records kept by the facilitator provide the statistics that inform how handicaps are set.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: Because the facilitator applies rules and tracks information, players need to remember less of it themselves.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The facilitator keeps track of how the story develops and adapts it when something unforeseen happens.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: The facilitator follows the planned story and makes sure it unfolds as intended.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: As an impartial party, the facilitator can generate random results fairly, provided it does so openly.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: In roleplaying games the facilitator describes the world, plays the non-player cast and resolves what characters do.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Facilitators typically run the opposition, such as enemies and non-player characters, that a lone player faces.

changes.name: Speedruns
changes.why: Being a trusted keeper of records, the facilitator can track completion times across game instances.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: At the start of each turn, round or phase the facilitator performs the needed updates and can stop out-of-turn actions.

changes.name: Player-Artifact Proximity
changes.why: Facilitators, like sensors, can measure how far players are from artifacts to decide whether the proximity condition has been met.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: The facilitator may deliberately force waiting, such as after dying, yet computer facilitators can also be used to avoid such waits.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: The page treats removing excise as a facilitator job, yet it never explains how the two conflict.

conflicts_with.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: Mechanical and computer facilitators do not naturally let players move game elements freely; this needs deliberate design.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: If the facilitator generates random results out of sight, players may suspect cheating instead of chance.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: Having a dedicated facilitator is by definition hard to combine with players running the game themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Facilitators enforce rules, so players cannot easily bend them, for example to adapt to circumstances or let novices retake moves.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Since play needs the facilitator to be present, the game cannot be played anywhere and anytime.

patterns.name: Game Masters
patterns.what_it_is: People who run the game world and the players' interaction with it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give one participant the authority to run the world, adjudicate and improvise, backed by tools such as scenarios and rules. Players must accept their rulings.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A GM role is named, but it only reads out fixed text and cannot adapt anything, so it is a narrator.
patterns.knobs: how much authority and freedom the GM has; tools provided; whether the role rotates

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: A game master can grant brand-new abilities or alter existing ones whenever they judge the situation needs it.

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: A game master can negotiate with players to take abilities away, which helps keep the players evenly matched.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: A game master plays the characters and units that players do not control, such as opponents.

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: Players can secretly write down what they do, and the game master later acts it out so nobody can tell who caused it.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the game master can adjust how likely players are to succeed, they can even out differences between players.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: The game master's control over gameplay lets them tune difficulty so the whole group stays properly challenged.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: A game master can interpret, add, or change rules and adapt socially, so play can be richer than other facilitators allow.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: The game master has full creative control over building and maintaining the game world, so they do most of its construction.

can_cause.name: Context Dependent Reactions
can_cause.why: Since the game master's actions can be tailored to each specific session and situation, the game can react to exactly what is happening.

can_cause.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
can_cause.why: A game master is one kind of facilitator, a person or program devoted to running the game rather than just playing it.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: By controlling agents and portraying the world, the game master keeps details fitting the game world even when improvising.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: A game master can tweak details of the game world so they stand out, making things easier or harder for players.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
can_cause.why: The game master can change difficulty on the fly, for example by altering world details, to match how the players are doing.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Game masters interact with players by acting out characters and events themselves, which creates opportunities for enactment.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: When the game master controls non-player agents, those agents do exactly what the game master decides, which is human-whim for people.

can_cause.name: Entitled Players
can_cause.why: A game master is a player who holds abilities to affect the game's structure, so they are a standard case of entitled players.

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Because the game master controls the rules, they can change them as play goes on, so the rule set keeps developing.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: The game master can add abilities or follow players' unexpected ideas, making players feel their choices matter more than they do.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: A game master takes bookkeeping chores onto themselves, sparing players, but a human doing this has to carry the workload.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: When a game master changes rules or content, it is allowed but not governed by the game's rules, so it comes from outside them.

can_cause.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
can_cause.why: A game master can let players freely rearrange game elements, though they can also cancel those changes afterward.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: The game master has such broad power over how play unfolds that they can choose to trigger big events whenever they like.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Because the game master decides outcomes, they can quietly bend a result, such as a die roll, to protect the story or a player.

can_cause.name: Game Time Manipulation
can_cause.why: A game master can retcon what happened or let players redo actions, effectively rewinding or changing game time.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Game masters often portray and describe the game world to the players, especially when it differs a lot from reality.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: A game master can declare any event permanent, but can also overturn it later by changing their ruling.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: The game master controls outcomes, so they can make players feel lucky by letting them succeed.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: The game master controls when players act, so they can share quiet stretches equally among everyone.

can_cause.name: Memory of Important Events
can_cause.why: A human game master can remember what happened earlier and let it shape later events.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: The game master takes over administrative work like tracking character details, acting as help that is not another player.

can_cause.name: Open Destiny
can_cause.why: A human game master can enact characters flexibly, so the story's outcome stays open rather than fixed.

can_cause.name: Optional Rules
can_cause.why: Since the game master has authority over the rules, they and the players can agree to add optional ones.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game Worlds
can_cause.why: The game master builds and maintains the game world over time, so it keeps existing between sessions.

can_cause.name: Perspective Taking
can_cause.why: Acting out non-player characters and judging how players see situations means the game master must think from others' viewpoints.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: The game master role gives the player in it a lot of power to shape what happens.

can_cause.name: Player Augmentations
can_cause.why: A game master supplies information and guidance, or even steers a player's character, which extends what the player can do.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: By adjusting chances and negotiating ability losses, the game master can keep players on an even footing.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: A game master can avoid knocking players out by fudging, but can also remove players whenever they wish.

can_cause.name: Player Kicking
can_cause.why: Holding great power over the game, the game master can remove a player from it on their own decision.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Players get a say in how their characters develop because the game master can accommodate their plans in the story.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: The game master can change explicit rules to reflect players' plans and descriptions, so real player skill counts alongside the character's.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: The game master is a player with far more power than the others, such as shaping rules and the world.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: Being a game master is a role players can step into and feel they are living up to.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Game masters play out non-player characters, giving chances for in-character speaking and acting.

can_cause.name: Scenes
can_cause.why: Game masters can create new scenes and rework existing ones as play develops.

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: A game master can hold hidden aims of their own to challenge players and nudge play toward certain outcomes.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: A game master can respond to the group's mood and wishes, though the players do not directly control that flexibility.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Being the game master is a distinct role a player takes on, separate from the other players' roles.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: The game master commonly tells or improvises the story to players as part of running the game.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: Since the game master can drop any planned plot at any moment, they can spring unexpected attacks on players.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: The game master can build tension by adding short-lived goals or by changing the story unexpectedly.

can_cause.name: Turn Taking
can_cause.why: The game master controls when players may act, so they can enforce an orderly sequence of turns.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: With so much control over play, the game master can bring in huge events when they want, such as to move the story along.

can_cause.name: Unpredictable Behavior
can_cause.why: A human game master playing agents can act in complex, surprising ways that fixed rules would not produce.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Because the game master can alter rules during play, the rules in effect can differ from one moment to another.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: A game master can narrate or describe scenes to players, and can adapt them fully to the game state and the players.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: A game master can take over or add roles when the number of players changes, keeping the group's game intact.

can_cause.name: Late Arriving Players
can_cause.why: A human game master can adjust rules or write a newcomer's character into the story, making late joining easy.

can_cause.name: Mediated Gameplay
can_cause.why: A human game master holds the game state and delivers the world to players, so play reaches them through that person.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: If enemies don't seem to act on their own, players can blame the Game Master for deaths, making those deaths feel like killing.

can_cause.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
can_cause.why: A game master can judge players' real-world activities by qualitative standards and adjust how they map to game changes on the fly.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: A game master can enforce believable agent behavior and moderate players' improvisation so it stays in line with the theme.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: The game master can allow entirely new abilities or change existing ones as they see fit.

changes.name: Adventures
changes.why: If players' actions make a prepared adventure stop working, the game master can modify it.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: Games set in the real world have unpredictable events, so a game master adjusts the game to fit them.

changes.name: Campaigns
changes.why: A game master can revise a campaign when players' actions mean it no longer works as originally written.

changes.name: Character Defining Actions
changes.why: A game master can negotiate with players so that what they do is understood as defining their character.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: The game master supplies pre-made characters and can take control of players' characters.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: The game master plays companion characters when needed to keep the game fitting its theme.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: The game master supplies the information players use to judge their odds, so they strongly affect how clear those odds are.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: The game master controls opponents and can use pre-made characters as enemies.

changes.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
changes.why: A game master can permit players to freely handle game elements, yet cancel whatever they did afterwards.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: A game master teaches and explains rules and world facts, so players need to memorize less.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Where the role can rotate among players, game masters provide a facilitator in games that have several players.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The game master is often responsible for the story structure and can change or drop it at any time.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: The game master enacts non-player characters, deciding what they say and do.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: The game master can take control of player characters, for example to keep them consistent or cover for absent players.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: A game master can modify prepared story structures, or tell them, to fit what the players actually do.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: A game master can change existing scenes as well as create new ones to suit the situation.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: A rotating game master role gives a dedicated facilitator to games the players otherwise run themselves.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Game masters are uncommon here because humans are too costly and a computer one blends into the system, though some games have one.

changes.name: Thematic Consistency
changes.why: The game master can steer non-player characters and even override players' actions to keep everything fitting the game's setting.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: The game master controls units serving as the players' opponents.

changes.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
changes.why: The page lists this relation but never explains why it holds, so no reason can be given.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Human staff can handle troublesome player interactions and gather information that guides how the rules should change.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: A game master who uses powerful events too freely overrides players' actions and works against their sense of influence.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: A game master can remove upkeep from players, though doing so means the game master takes on that work themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: The game master can make any event permanent, yet can also undo it by changing their ruling.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: A game master can prevent eliminations by fudging results, but can also kick players out whenever they please.

conflicts_with.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: A game master may overrule what players did with elements, forcing them to retract their moves, which cuts against players' free manipulation.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: Dice can kill characters when neither the game master nor players want it, working against the master's control.

patterns.name: Single-Player Games
patterns.what_it_is: Only one player can take part in each game session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Without other people to push back, the game must supply its own opposition through puzzles, scripted enemies or time pressure. It also needs a clear decision on whether the game can be won at all.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A multiplayer-style game that is simply played alone, with no automated opposition or puzzle to replace the missing opponents, so nothing resists the player.
patterns.knobs: strength and behaviour of automated opposition; whether the game can be won; time limits

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: With nobody else involved in the game's state, a lone player can act with less social consequence, which makes it feel detached from their real self.

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: With only one player receiving information, the designer doesn't need to coordinate several people gathering clues together, which makes mystery-style play easier to build.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: Since no other player takes part in or can influence the session, the player can act without anyone knowing who they are or what they did.

can_cause.name: Private Game Spaces
can_cause.why: Because nobody else can change what happens in the game, the player's play area belongs to them alone.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players needn't coordinate a start time with anyone, and with pauses or turns they choose when to play, which is one condition for playing anywhere and anytime.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: With computer-controlled agents as opponents, a lone player can still have combat despite lacking human rivals.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Adding extra players to a one-player game makes it behave like a multiplayer game, so entry and exit becomes a design concern.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: With no opponents to punish mistakes, harmful results can be undone through reversibility or reloading, so trying things is easy.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players alone usually decide when they play, and designs often unlock options gradually, so they can pick when to engage and which new actions to use.
