can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: A solo game becomes multiplayer when something such as a tournament or shared score information connects its players.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: With no other players, removing resource needs and threats through sanctioned cheating doesn't harm balance, so players can potter freely.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: In single-player games, rewards can include gaining the ability to manipulate game time.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: One player controlling several units that can combine abilities forms a team without needing other human players.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: A plot is simpler to write when the player controls one character and the designer needn't handle complications arising from several players interacting.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: In single-player games, rewards can be accompanied by story scenes that give them extra attention.

changes.name: Thematic Consistency
changes.why: The game controls everything except the player's actions, so keeping the theme is easier, though players can still break it by ignoring goals.

conflicts_with.name: PvP
conflicts_with.why: Fighting other players needs opponents, so it obviously suits games with several people rather than ones played alone.

conflicts_with.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
conflicts_with.why: Deciding a winner afterwards only makes sense when several players could win, so it doesn't fit a game with one player.

patterns.name: Companions
patterns.what_it_is: Game-controlled characters that follow the player and help them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A companion needs a real role: abilities or goals that cover what the player's own character lacks, and behaviour reliable enough that the player can count on it. If they follow and talk but never change what the player can do, nothing happens.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character trails behind the player and chats, but can't be hurt, doesn't act, and the player's outcomes are the same without it.
patterns.knobs: how strong and independent the companion is; how many can be had; whether they can be lost or turn traitor

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Companions are game-controlled characters that notice what the player does, so they naturally behave as believable agents who react to the player.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because a companion shares the burden of overcoming problems, play becomes easier and less demanding, which suits relaxed, casual players.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: A companion may secretly be a traitor and turn against the player, becoming a hostile opponent after having seemed a friend.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Players control or outrank their companions, so they feel far more powerful and important than the other inhabitants of the game world.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: Companions can be given abilities the player's character lacks, letting them cover jobs in the group that the player's character doesn't fill.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: By helping the player in play, companions make challenges easier, especially when tied to a mechanism that adjusts difficulty automatically.

can_cause.name: Helpers
can_cause.why: Companions are designed so their goals line up with the player's, which makes them characters that actively assist the player's progress.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Players can obtain a companion by paying resources for it, so the companion is something spent on in hope of future benefit.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Since companions follow and work with the player, designers must decide how faithful they are to the player and the player to them.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A companion's own skills let the player's group do things it couldn't before, effectively giving the player extra abilities through the companion.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: Companions are often characters run by the game rather than a person, so they carry all the design concerns of such characters.

can_cause.name: Parties
can_cause.why: Companions join the player's group as supporting members, forming part of the party that travels and acts together.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because companions stay close to the player's character, they are a natural focal point for scripted story events in main plots or sidequests.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Companions can hold special powers that the player gains access to through them, such as perks granted when a companion joins.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: When players must choose among a limited number of companions, or can lose them to death, companions become something to manage like a scarce resource.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: A companion can be given to the player as a prize for finishing a quest.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Companions who can be lost, or who might betray the player, create worry about what will happen to them.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: The theme can call for companions and shape their form, so those that suit the setting help keep the world consistent.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: How a player behaves toward companions, and in their presence, is a kind of action that shows and shapes the character's nature.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Players can build companion characters, like the grogs and companions in Ars Magica, so building produces them.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Companions that follow and aid the player, when run by algorithms, give the player a dependable partner to work with.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: A single player can be given computer-controlled companions, which stand in for teammates in a team.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Companions that follow an avatar, but are simpler than full AI players, blur the line between controlling one avatar and many units.

changes.name: Helplessness
changes.why: Companions could in principle rescue players from helpless situations, although the page notes designers rarely use them for that.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Allies who accompany a player character, sometimes controllable by the player, add to what the character has and can do.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Allies who accompany a character form part of its social ties and can prompt its development.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: NPCs given goals that support the player become allies who travel with and help them.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Non-player characters can be made into enemies or companions, so players can end up choosing one over the other.

patterns.name: AI Players
patterns.what_it_is: Software characters that play roughly like humans and take their place.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The AI must play by the same rules as humans, with a visible aim of winning, and work in the available modes (teams, drop-in). Skill level should be adjustable to fit the people it replaces.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bot occupies a seat but plays passively or randomly, so it cannot substitute for a real player.
patterns.knobs: AI skill level; when AI can join or replace players; how predictable it is

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: Since a computer-run player can stand in for a person, the game can be played without a human fully taking on every role, though social contact disappears too.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: An AI player is itself a computer-controlled character that acts in the game on its own, so using one means the game contains agents.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because an AI can fill in for a person who is away, players don't all need to be playing at the same moment.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: When someone leaves mid-game, an AI can take over their slot, so players can come and go without ruining the session.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: AI players can be made to always obey players' suggestions or orders, though the page says this is largely redundant since they already strictly follow their rules.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When players write or program their own AI players, they are adding new elements into the game that then act within it.

can_cause.name: Game System Player
can_cause.why: If an AI is simple enough and players know how its algorithm works, it behaves more like part of the game's system than like a real opponent.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Since an AI can play in your place, you can step away from a game and it can keep going without you.

can_cause.name: Late Arriving Players
can_cause.why: An AI can occupy a slot until a person shows up, so those who join after the start can still enter a game already running.

can_cause.name: Mules
can_cause.why: Players can start AI players, even ones they programmed, to take their place and do repetitive grinding work while they are away.

can_cause.name: Parties
can_cause.why: AI players can be designed to be members of groups, working together with others inside them.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Graceful Surrender
can_cause.why: When a human quits, an AI can take over their position, so leaving doesn't destroy the game for everyone else.

can_cause.name: Robotic Players
can_cause.why: When an AI controls a physical robot, the result is a robot that takes part in the game as a player.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Offering several kinds of AI players, each playing differently, gives people different styles of play to experience.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: If every player in a game is replaced by an AI, nobody plays directly and the game runs by itself.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Building can be used to define how units or AI players behave, as in P-Robots and Crobots, where players only shape the robots' conduct.

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: When players can program AI players, the code counts as part of the rules, so changing it changes the rule set.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When a game runs itself without a human facilitator, the work of operating computer-controlled participants falls on the players and becomes upkeep.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: AI players can fill in for someone who leaves, letting people close their session when they wish without disturbing others.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: AI opponents can be set at different strengths, which, along with difficulty levels, gives players challenges to master.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When players must build the AI that plays instead of playing themselves, the contest becomes about creating those programs, which is a game on top of the game.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: A computer-controlled participant can stand in as another player, so a game can feel multiplayer even when only one human plays.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled players only create this uncertainty when their behavior is unpredictable; otherwise they merely change it. This case is covered under Unpredictable Behavior.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled players can do the killing, but players are less likely to see them as real actors with intent than human opponents.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled opponents can supply the pattern as long as they behave in ways that players cannot easily predict.

can_cause.name: Single-Player Games
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled participants can fill every other seat in a game made for several people, so a single person can play it alone.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: AI players let a multiplayer game be played alone or with more participants than there are people available.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Players' ability to learn or deduce how the AI behaves changes how unsure they are about their own execution; unpredictable AI creates such uncertainty.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: In games run by the players themselves, an AI means people must carry out its instructions by hand, which adds tedious extra work.

changes.name: Solution Uncertainty
changes.why: AI players think differently from people, so they change how hard it is for players to work out what to do.

changes.name: Team Strategy Identification
changes.why: Working out a shared team plan normally needs negotiation, which is hard for AI, so players can instead just give it orders to follow.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: AI players can fill empty spots so teams have equal size, and they must be able to cooperate within a team.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Computer players can fill missing slots so opposing teams are the same size.

conflicts_with.name: Mimetic Interfaces
conflicts_with.why: A computer player doesn't use the physical interface, so when people must act with their bodies, the AI clearly isn't competing under the same conditions.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: AI can skip physical interfaces and may join or leave mid-game, which can make the sides unequal.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Swapping AI in and out during play can leave teams uneven, unless the game is purely cooperative.

patterns.name: Parties
patterns.what_it_is: Groups of characters acting together toward a common goal within the world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters must need each other, for example through complementary roles, and the group must have a size limit or composition choices. The relationships among them must give real reasons for cooperating.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A group of characters that follow the player around but are interchangeable and contribute nothing, so the party is just a count.
patterns.knobs: party size and maximum; how roles are distributed; how many characters each player controls

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When members plan how to work together, one of them can break the trust of the group, which may end the party or stop it forming.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Planning how characters should work together in a party naturally leads members to combine their efforts toward shared goals.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Because members plan around working together, they can help each other now with the expectation of being helped back later.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Members of a party can compete with each other, either spontaneously or because a storyline deliberately introduces tension within the group.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Planning how characters work together can lead members to feel bound to the group and to each other.

can_cause.name: Parallel Lives
can_cause.why: When every character in a party matters equally and a single player controls them all, their separate stories run side by side.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Planning how characters work together leads members to settle into particular roles within the group.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: In multiplayer parties, players must reach agreement on plans of action, so they need to be able to communicate and persuade each other.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Planning how characters work together lets members coordinate their abilities so that combined actions achieve more than separate ones.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: A party can be a team, but it is not required to be one, since it need not have explicit gameplay goals.

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Groups of players can set their own norms, so members' actions change how teammates treat them.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Encouraging or enforcing parties groups players together, making them feel they tackle the messy challenges as one unit.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Groups acting together must coordinate, and coordination requires planning.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Grouping players into a party gives them a common purpose, so what they achieve is felt as shared.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: Parties give players a structured group with shared goals, which encourages them to settle on common strategies or helps cooperative players find each other.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Playing actively alongside one another in a group is one direct way for a shared sense of belonging to form.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: With limited resources to hand out, players must choose which member gets what, since each choice leaves others without.

changes.name: Loot
changes.why: In multiplayer parties, dividing found treasure can cause disputes, so games add rules for how the loot is split among members.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Placing player characters in a party puts them in a group where they need to cooperate.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Small groups support coordination and cooperation, in both player-versus-player and player-versus-environment play.

conflicts_with.name: Betrayal
conflicts_with.why: The possibility of betrayal reduces how much a party feels like a trusting group, even if it adds anticipation.

patterns.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
patterns.what_it_is: The game is built so players can join and leave during a session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must keep working when the player count changes: it needs a way to rebalance, hand over or park a leaver's pieces, and bring a returner back without wasting others' effort.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A menu that says you may join or leave at any time, yet a leaver breaks the game or a newcomer is hopelessly behind and cannot take part.
patterns.knobs: how and when players may join or leave; what happens to their assets; how newcomers are caught up or balanced

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since people can come and go freely, they no longer have to be playing at the same moment as everyone else.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When a person joins or leaves, the game may have to add or remove things like characters to match.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Players can use leaving and rejoining to mark their own pauses, so the game can be stopped and resumed without trouble.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Because each person can enter and exit independently, nobody has to fit their play to when others start or stop.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Because each person can enter and exit independently, nobody has to fit their play to when others start or stop.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Players decide where the breaks fall by leaving and returning, so play can bend around their other social situations.

can_cause.name: Tiered Participation
can_cause.why: Onlookers who watch over a player's shoulder can step in to play and step back out again whenever they like.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Joining and leaving freely lets people play anywhere and anytime, even though latecomers have little effect on how the whole game turns out.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Players can enter and exit on their own schedules, so their time in the game need not overlap much or at all.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Where game instances last long enough, delayed effects and favors owed make coming back for later sessions worth considering.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can end their session while others carry on unaffected, giving them freedom over when to stop playing.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: When a player leaves, a computer-controlled agent can take their place so the game's presentation continues undisturbed.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Letting players come and go is the pattern's usual home, since people rarely can all start and stop together.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: In cooperative groups, shared goals mean newcomers and leavers can be balanced without upsetting those who stay.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: With huge numbers of players spread around the world, it is impractical to get everyone to play and stop simultaneously.

changes.name: Pervasive Gameplay
changes.why: Players can ease in and out of the game to avoid awkward encounters with people around them.

changes.name: Predictable Winner
changes.why: When it looks clear who will win, players can leave gracefully instead of continuing an interaction they no longer want.

changes.name: Ragequitting
changes.why: Because the game already copes with people departing, an angry quit barely affects what other players experience.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Letting extra players join a solo game raises the same issues as in a multiplayer game.

changes.name: Split-Screen Views
changes.why: When the number of players shifts, designers must decide whether and how the divided screen should adjust.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Teams losing or gaining members mid-game can throw off the fairness between sides.

changes.name: Backseat Gamers
changes.why: When people can freely join or leave play, they can switch between giving advice from the sidelines and actually playing.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When players come and go, the difficulty may no longer fit the remaining group, making it hard to keep the game demanding.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players joining and leaving at will require the fiction to explain why controlled figures suddenly vanish or reappear.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Those who just arrived or soon leave cannot have shaped the game much, so feeling very influential is hard.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: In multiplayer games, the fiction of the game world can be broken when people appear and disappear.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Gaining or losing members can leave one team stronger than another, which is hard to correct.

conflicts_with.name: Togetherness
conflicts_with.why: If players' sessions barely overlap, they have little chance to feel they are playing with each other.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Help given to newcomers can make the hard work of those already playing seem to count for less.

conflicts_with.name: Ragequitting
conflicts_with.why: Easy joining and leaving softens the damage of a quitter but clashes with designs wanting everyone to commit to finishing the whole session together.

patterns.name: Factions
patterns.what_it_is: Groups in the game world united by which deeds they reward and forbid.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Set clear criteria to join, stay and advance, and make group membership change what members can do or must do. Gatekeepers, quests or requirements make joining meaningful, and group rules must be enforced.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A faction label or banner that has no effect on abilities, access, goals or how others treat the player.
patterns.knobs: requirements to join and stay; how many factions one can belong to and what membership grants

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Factions have rules about acceptable behavior, so breaking them or advancing inside the group brings reactions from members, making player actions matter socially in the story world.

can_cause.name: Characteristics
can_cause.why: Which faction a character belongs to becomes a lasting trait of that character, describing who they are in the game.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Membership can mean the player keeps loyalty to the group as a goal they chose, provided belonging gives them some benefits.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Staying in good standing within a faction takes ongoing social upkeep, so players must keep working at it rather than finish once.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Hostile factions give the player many opponents at once, so conflict does not end after beating one foe.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Faction consequences push players either to follow the group's limited allowed actions and timing, or to risk breaking them.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Joining a faction can give access to training, so becoming a member serves as a step toward learning skills.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Membership can unlock knowledge held by the group, so joining often helps the player reach an information-gathering goal.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Factions can sell or provide special tools to members, so joining often supports a goal of obtaining items.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Rising within a faction needs specific tasks that stack into quests, forming layered goals tied to the unfolding story.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Because members have different interests and rules to follow, tensions can arise inside a faction, especially in multiplayer groups the designer cannot fully control.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Competing for advancement inside a faction sets members against each other, adding challenge, and can even arise from game events.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Being in a faction implies the member owes allegiance to it, either as a given goal or one the player commits to.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Factions can reward members with training or purchasable tools that give the player abilities they did not have before.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: With rivals inside the player's own faction, the player must find non-combat ways to beat obstacles and complete overcome goals.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: For a faction to feel distinct, members who act against its norms need to be punished, such as by being cast out.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: Joining a faction or being expelled from one permanently alters the player's standing and how the world treats them.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: When players can choose which factions to join, the different goals and rewards each offers let them plan how their character grows.

can_cause.name: Predefined Goals
can_cause.why: Loyalty to the faction can be a goal set by the game itself, expected from members as part of belonging.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Factions are often central to a scripted storyline, appearing in main quests and shaping how the plot and their internal rivalries unfold.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Faction membership and advancement typically depend on completing specific tasks, which naturally take the form of quests.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Since getting in means achieving a goal, membership usually comes with payoffs like training, tools, companions or favors.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Competing interests inside a faction, especially in multiplayer, can put players in choices where group and personal benefit clash.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Joining a faction is usually a stepping stone toward bigger aims like gaining information, skill or items, rather than the end goal.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, factions give players a natural reason to group together and act as teams.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Faction membership can open access to buying and selling special tools, and factions can affect prices set by NPCs.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Letting players move up through ranks of a group gives each promotion more weight than the previous one.

can_cause.name: Shared Rewards
can_cause.why: Effects applying to a whole faction hit all of its members alike, so the faction's reward is shared by every member.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Depending on how much the game is diegetic, a faction's members may be the players' characters as well as NPCs, shaping who is in the group.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Belonging to a faction can let players recruit allies as a reward for joining.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Because a hostile faction has many members, defeating one enemy does not finish the conflict, changing how elimination goals play out.

changes.name: Improved Abilities
changes.why: Factions can offer training or purchasable tools as membership rewards, making the player's existing abilities stronger.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Factions can control which quests NPCs offer and supply tasks linked to advancement, shaping what quests are available.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Faction membership can give access to special tools for purchase, and joining may require owning certain tools.

changes.name: Trading
changes.why: Factions held by NPCs can change what prices players pay and what they can buy, affecting trade.

changes.name: Loyalty
changes.why: The structure and goals of a faction affect what loyalty to it demands and where it can be tested in the world.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Factions give players goals to join and allow designers to plan loyalty or rivalry among members.

patterns.name: Late Arriving Players
patterns.what_it_is: The game lets you join at any moment without waiting for someone else's start.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The system must be able to insert a new player into a running game, with spawning, a fair starting state, and some answer to the balance problems newcomers cause. It needs players to actually arrive at different times.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A join button exists but latecomers start so far behind or ahead that they cannot take part in a meaningful way.
patterns.knobs: how late one can join; what starting resources a newcomer gets; whether bots fill empty slots

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: Newcomers rarely begin in the same state as players already in the game, so letting them join late means everyone starts from different footing.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can decide for themselves when to begin a session instead of waiting for everyone else to arrive.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When a late player joins and brings a new avatar, character or unit, the game must add fresh elements into the ongoing play.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Making room for a newcomer by kicking out a human player removes that person from the game, which counts as eliminating them.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Since players enter at different moments, their play sessions no longer start or line up together.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: For people to drop in, the game must be able to bring in someone after the session has already started.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: People who join after play began may do so to aid those already playing, so their arrival itself is the help.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Players take turns at different times, so the game would have to be started by synchronizing everyone unless late arrival is supported.

changes.name: Game Termination Penalties
changes.why: Depending on how easy it is to rejoin a running game, late arrival can soften or cancel the penalty for leaving.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: With very many players coming and going at all hours, such games basically need people to be able to join whenever.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Players start at different times, but whether this is true late arrival depends on how much they can actually help each other.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: The pattern only matters when several players are involved, since a single player has nobody to join or wait for.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Players may want to join a group after it forms or miss the session's start, so late joining lets them still take part.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Since the world keeps running, players must be able to come and go at will rather than start together.

changes.name: Possibility of Anonymity
changes.why: Not needing everyone present at the start makes it easier for strangers to join without being known.

changes.name: Startgame
changes.why: Because players can join after play has begun, the opening phase of the game is typically affected.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: On teams, teammates are more likely to be left waiting for someone, so supporting late joiners matters more.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: In team-versus-team play, people on both sides would otherwise wait for absent members, which makes late arrival more important.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: Letting players join late spares others from waiting for everyone to be present before play begins.

conflicts_with.name: Game Termination Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Easy rejoining turns the removal into a temporary penalty, so it no longer ends the player's participation.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Newcomers may have more or fewer resources and abilities than existing players, which makes players unequal.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Extra characters brought by newcomers strain a fixed story unless a game master can work them in.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: A newcomer can make one team stronger or weaker than the other, because they differ from existing members.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: New avatars, characters or units appearing mid-game can break the setting unless the fiction explains their arrival.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Newcomers can get benefits that others worked for, such as rewards, or lack them, which makes earlier effort feel less valuable.

conflicts_with.name: Game Element Insertion
conflicts_with.why: Adding a newcomer's character into an ongoing multiplayer game can upset how even the match is.

conflicts_with.name: Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: Bringing in a newcomer's character mid-game is hard to do fairly, since the character holds the game values players care most about.

patterns.name: Spectators
patterns.what_it_is: People who watch the players' actions but do not affect the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Public information must be available to outsiders in a form they can follow, such as a view of the game or replays. Players eliminated early also need a way to keep watching.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Watching is allowed in theory, but the information shown is unreadable, hidden or too fast to follow, so spectators learn nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much information spectators see; delay of the view; whether they can talk to players

can_cause.name: Backseat Gamers
can_cause.why: When onlookers know a game is underway and try to steer it with advice or orders, they act as backseat gamers instead of quiet watchers.

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: People who aren't playing can still take part by wagering on how the watched game ends, which gives them a stake in it.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: Watchers who can talk to players, knowingly or not, may pass along information or hints that help the players, especially when players signal them through extra-game actions.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Watching without being able to act is a role a person can hold within a game, distinct from the roles of those playing.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: By seeing which actions work in different situations, onlookers learn how to play well, even when nobody is actually playing, as in games with no players.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing others are watching makes players feel pressure about how well they perform, which adds nervousness to their play.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Having onlookers lets players display their skill, especially in hard feats, and earn recognition from those watching.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: Newcomers can watch the ongoing game first, which helps them grasp the situation before they join in.

changes.name: Mules
changes.why: Watching how automated stand-in characters are doing helps players decide whether to take over or leave them running on their own.

changes.name: No Direct Player Influence
changes.why: Such games can still be meaningful when people watch the events unfold, even if nobody steers them during play.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Casting real onlookers as in-game characters gives those characters more agency and unpredictability than computer-controlled ones.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Observers can push players to do better, but being watched can also make them anxious about whether they will succeed.

changes.name: Zero-Player Games
changes.why: A game with no one acting still has value when people watch it run, and they can learn from what works.

changes.name: Extra-Game Actions
changes.why: Since players know others may be watching, this changes how they use outside actions, and onlookers can also offer help.

patterns.name: Handles
patterns.what_it_is: Nicknames by which players and their achievements are recognized.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Names or symbols need to be tied to records or accounts and shown where others see them (scores, chat, over avatars). Decide how they are chosen and moderated.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A name field that is never shown or saved anywhere, or auto-generated names everyone ignores.
patterns.knobs: length and format; free vs preset choice; where they are displayed

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When players get to pick or invent their own handle, they get a small but real choice over how they appear to others.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Showing a handle next to an avatar tells everyone which player controls which avatar, so the handle works as a status display.

can_cause.name: High Score Lists
can_cause.why: Players type their handle beside a score, so a ranked list of results can be tied to specific people and compared.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: A name that identifies a player's character to others, shown through an interface, adds an abstract quality that works as a minimal character.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: Players appear under a chosen name rather than a real one, so others can't tell who they actually are.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: When players are not present together, a handle is the main way to tell who is who and who did what.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Handles shown over or beside avatars make clear which player each avatar belongs to.

changes.name: Chat Channels
changes.why: In chat, handles let participants see who is speaking and recognize each other.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Distinct handles let teammates tell each other apart and predict what each will do, which helps them work together.

changes.name: Crosshairs
changes.why: A handle can be displayed in the crosshair when it is aimed at an avatar or enemy, naming the target.

changes.name: Emotes
changes.why: Placing the handle at the front of an emote gives these actions a common format so they are easy to recognize.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: Handles let players see and recognize one another while gathering before a match.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: When players only interact through a system, handles are what tell participants apart, which would otherwise be hard.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Handles give players ways to identify each other, find friends, and keep records, supporting play among many people.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Handles let party members tell one another apart and anticipate what each will do, helping them coordinate.

changes.name: Public Player Statistics
changes.why: Stats are stored and displayed under each player's handle, so others can look up and compare performance.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Handles can be displayed along with the team a player belongs to, set by the game or by player agreement.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Names and other identifying labels can expose who someone is, so they need to be restricted in what they allow.

patterns.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
patterns.what_it_is: Players begin the session with different capabilities.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Differences at the start must affect early choices and the likely course of play. Balance through playtesting, rotating roles or handicaps, and decide whether they are fixed, random or player-made.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Starts differ only in cosmetics or trivial amounts, so after a few turns no one can tell who began where.
patterns.knobs: how large the start differences are; fixed, random or player-chosen; compensation for weaker starts

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Gameplay
can_cause.why: Giving players different starting positions is the main way to make them play differently from one another, so unequal starts are chiefly used to produce asymmetric play.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: A deliberately uneven start can act as a handicap, where one side gets a built-in disadvantage or compensation to even out differences.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If starts are randomized or chosen by players, each session begins differently, giving people a reason to play again and see new outcomes.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Real situations with several actors are rarely equal, so unequal starts make a game's fictional world feel believable and fit its theme.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because players begin with different setups each time, the games that follow unfold in different ways rather than repeating the same pattern.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Giving players uneven starting positions, such as historically weaker or stronger countries, makes some starts more difficult than others.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Unequal starting conditions such as uneven resources or goals add asymmetry to the worlds and scenarios players act within.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: The pattern only matters with several players, since only then can one player's start differ from another's.

changes.name: Startgame
changes.why: Since the differences exist at the beginning of play, they directly shape how the opening phase of a game plays out.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: When players start with different possibilities, it is hard to keep their chances equal unless the designer adds balancing measures or tests heavily.

conflicts_with.name: Characters
conflicts_with.why: Characters that differ from the start may not be equally powerful, which can upset fairness between players.

patterns.name: TvT
patterns.what_it_is: Games where teams compete against each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Fixed teams with shared goals and a scoring rule that compares teams, plus attention to team balance and to players leaving or joining. Teams must be able to affect each other.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players wear team colours but score and win individually, so team membership changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: team size; balancing methods; how team results are scored

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Everyone, even opponents on other teams, shares the same game session, so the sense of being together reaches across team lines as well as within a team.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: In team-versus-team games, balancing effects are used to keep the competing teams evenly matched.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: When cheating is allowed in team-versus-team play, players can pose as members of other teams or roles to deceive the opposition.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Team balance only has meaning when teams compete against each other, and that competition is where the pattern gets applied.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Pitting teams against each other changes how a team plays, since its members now share the goal of beating rival teams.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Lobbies can help opposing teams get acquainted and agree on how a mediated match is played.

conflicts_with.name: Player Killing
conflicts_with.why: In team-versus-team play, kills and their penalties can tilt the contest toward one side and upset fairness between teams.

patterns.name: Team Development
patterns.what_it_is: Teams change over time because of the game's progress and the players' growing skills.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be real improvement options that cost resources and change what the team can do. Improvements should be visible and should shape later play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The team has a level or rank that goes up, but it changes nothing in what the team can do.
patterns.knobs: cost and speed of improvement; what can be improved; caps on growth

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: When the team is a game-defined entity rather than real players, improving the team directly means that entity grows over time.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: As a team grows, its individual members can end up specializing, so each becomes the one who is good at particular things.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: If a team persists across several game sessions, whatever it gains or loses in one session carries into later ones outside the match itself.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Improving a team costs something now, such as training or resources, in exchange for a stronger team later, so it works like putting money in.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When teams last between sessions, getting the team as strong as possible becomes its own goal, a game layered around the actual matches.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Because growing a team takes limited things to spend, players must decide where to put them, which means handling resources.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: When real players make up the team and grow together, they share that progress, which can create a sense of belonging to the group.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: How much or how fast teams can develop depends on their relative position, and it lets them adapt to opponents' strategies.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Team growth can be designed to keep sides equal, but it is fragile since small differences can instead widen the gap.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Team development affects player-versus-player play, since it can even out the strengths of players within a team or make existing differences larger.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Development changes what a team is like over time, so it alters how the team itself behaves and what it is capable of.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Team development affects team-versus-team play, because it can narrow the gap between teams but can also widen imbalances that already exist.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Growing teams can be designed toward balance, but even small differences in how they grow can widen the gap instead.

patterns.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
patterns.what_it_is: Games where hundreds or thousands of players live and communicate in one world at the same time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A server infrastructure, support for joining and leaving at any time, and communication tools. Enough players need to be online and reasons to return so social play appears.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A big shared world exists but players hardly meet or affect each other, so it is solo play in a crowd.
patterns.knobs: player capacity per world; how much players interact; how often content is updated

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Such games need frequent patches for bugs, real-world timed events, and balance problems caused by player behavior, so their rules inevitably keep changing over time.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: With so many players talking and dealing both in and out of the game, trading for advantages is hard to prevent, though a design can openly embrace it.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Because so many different activities are available to a huge crowd of players, distinct roles tend to emerge among them naturally.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Social interaction and long-term time investment each make effort matter, and together they reinforce each other, so effort counts for more than in games with only one.

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: Online worlds shift into a distinct final phase once characters hit the top level, with competition, gear collecting and special quests.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Having very many players means designers must weigh the usual multiplayer options, such as letting people join late or leave without synchronized sessions.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Splitting players into instances and the difficulty of continually producing enough story for a huge lasting world make it hard to keep the theme coherent.

conflicts_with.name: Main Quests
conflicts_with.why: Online worlds must welcome players who join late and keep opposing factions apart, who don't share quests, so one shared overarching quest fits poorly.

patterns.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
patterns.what_it_is: The game uses data from other players' sessions, but everyone plays separately.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Servers must carry other players' results, such as scores, ghosts or gifts, into each person's game in a visible way. Players need to notice and react to this input.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A leaderboard exists but sits in a menu and never changes how anyone plays.
patterns.knobs: what data is shared between players; how visible it is; how much players can help each other

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: Since players only lightly affect each other and needn't know or talk to one another, they stay emotionally distant from the other people shaping their game.

can_cause.name: Mediated Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because these games rely on servers to carry information between players' separate game instances, play is passed through a technical intermediary rather than happening directly.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: One player's game instance changes another's, which creates interaction about the game itself, beyond what happens inside a single play session.

changes.name: Casual Gameplay
changes.why: Players get some social interaction through others' influence without needing to know or coordinate with them, so relaxed play isn't spoiled.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Adding information from other players' sessions turns an otherwise isolated game into one where other people's play affects yours.

patterns.name: Zero-Player Games
patterns.what_it_is: People make no direct decisions during play; the game runs by itself.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must run by themselves, with any player influence confined to setup, programming or rule creation, and be rich enough for interesting outcomes to emerge. Observers need a way to watch and compare.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game where a player presses a button now and then but the outcome never depends on it, billed as a zero-player game with no real setup choices either.
patterns.knobs: how much freedom the setup phase gives; complexity of rules; how agents are programmed; observation options

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: When players write the programs that act for them, the program's rules fully dictate what the agents do once play starts.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: If people run the game's updates themselves instead of a game master or computer, the game's inner play is just mechanical bookkeeping, with the real game moved elsewhere.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Since nothing can be done during a session, players find their fun around it, such as watching, solving puzzles or building setups.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Player skill goes into programming, preparing starting states or writing rules, and the game then carries those out without further input.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Players who design agents that then play on their own need to know how the game works, and can learn by watching others' agents.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: With no choices during play, players have little to feel influential about unless the set-up phase is designed to give that feeling.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: All choices are made before the game begins and none after, so it conflicts in one sense but not another.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: The game runs without players acting at all, so there is nothing for them to influence.

patterns.name: Public Player Statistics
patterns.what_it_is: Information about players that is easily available to everyone else.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Stats must be visible to others, tied to a persistent identity and connected to meaningful performance. Who can see them must be decided.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Stats are kept but hidden, anonymous or irrelevant, so nobody sees or cares about them.
patterns.knobs: what is tracked; who can see it; how long it persists

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: When your stats are visible to others, your skill shows up outside the game itself, so how well you play can shape how people see you.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Because everyone can see the numbers, players start competing to have better statistics than others, which becomes a separate game layered on top.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Players can look at others' stats to pick opponents of similar skill, so matches end up fairer.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Since stats update as players progress, outsiders can follow along and watch what players do even when watching wasn't otherwise possible.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Displaying results like high scores lets others see how well someone played, giving the effort extra worth.

changes.name: Achievements
changes.why: Achievements can serve as public stats when others are able to view them, so their meaning changes once they are shown to others.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: Lobbies are a good place to show information about other players, so people can judge who they are about to play with.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Public stats let players display how skilled they are at the game for others to see.

changes.name: Goal Achievements
changes.why: Goal achievements are tied directly to a player's progress, so making them public makes for a natural way to show how far someone has got.

changes.name: Value of Effort
changes.why: When your performance is visible and you must stand behind it, the work you put in matters more and gives you status.

changes.name: Gameplay Statistics
changes.why: Making players' records visible to everyone changes who can see them, letting players compare themselves with others.

conflicts_with.name: Possibility of Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Stats that follow a player across multiple game sessions can reveal who they are, undermining their ability to stay hidden.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Public stats openly reveal what players have done, so there is typically nothing left unknown about that information.

patterns.name: Non-Player Help
patterns.what_it_is: The game expects people who are not playing to help the players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Outsiders must know they can help, and the help must be restricted by limited actions, power and cooldowns so it does not skew balance or devalue players' own effort. Information from helpers can be unreliable to keep it risky.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A help feature that nobody outside the game is told about, or that gives such weak or restricted help that it never changes any outcome.
patterns.knobs: how strong helpers' actions are; how often they can help; how helpers are informed and admitted

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: Outsiders assist players without gaining anything in return, so the help they give is by nature a selfless act.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: When an outsider helps a player, the two end up working together toward the player's goal, even briefly.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Broadcasting
can_cause.why: Potential helpers must first learn that they can help, so players or the game send out calls to people beyond the game.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: The help comes from people who are not playing, so their contributions enter the game from outside its normal participants.

can_cause.name: Public Player Statistics
can_cause.why: Asking for outside help signals that a player is struggling or doing well, which makes aspects of their performance visible to others.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: A human facilitator who counts as outside help can narrate and present the story in a lively way for players.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Advice from outsiders, like a friend's phone-in answer, may be wrong, so players cannot be sure how far to trust it.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Outside help lets players affect each other's separate private spaces, where a helping act can be its own reward.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: Even non-players can assist with chores in the space, and the owner still keeps essentially full control.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If outsiders easily change the game state, players have a harder time feeling that their own choices were what mattered.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Outside assistance can take over repetitive or uninteresting actions so players don't have to do them.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Others who carry out game-influencing actions on players' behalf lessen how much grinding players must do.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Letting outsiders change the game state too easily can tilt the game in favor of players who have helpers available.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Outsiders and their actions have no natural place in the game world, so unexplained appearances can break the setting's believability.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: When outsiders do things easily for players, the players feel their own work counts for less.

patterns.name: Entitled Players
patterns.what_it_is: Players get the right to change how the game goes and are responsible for everyone's experience.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Some players must get real powers over how the game runs, such as creating content or removing players, along with a role that expects them to use these for others' benefit.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A title or badge for certain players that gives them no abilities to shape the game.
patterns.knobs: which powers are granted; who gets the role; limits on how powers are used

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because these players can reshape how the game works, not just its state, they may feel their say over the game is bigger than it really is.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Entitled players are often given the power to add content to the game world, so they end up authoring new things others encounter.

can_cause.name: Player Kicking
can_cause.why: Removing other players from a session is one kind of power that can be handed to entitled players, as a way of managing the game.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Making someone an entitled player simply means choosing which special powers over the game's workings to give them, which others lack.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: When entitled players use their powers generously, they can adjust the game to suit the group, helping it fit different people.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Holding abilities to mediate or facilitate play gives these players a recognized part among the group, separate from just competing in the game.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Entitled players can often narrate or invent events, even if only by creating content, so they take on a story-telling part.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Players allowed to alter the game itself can tune it so that working together becomes more enjoyable.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Entitled players are most often found in games where players work together, and their facilitating role fits and supports that shared effort.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: Sharing out facilitation powers to players means the game master does not have to do all of the upkeep work alone.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: Less powerful entitled players can be used alongside a game master to take over some of the chores.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: The pattern is about choosing special abilities to give certain players among several, so it only makes sense when more than one person plays.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Since there is no winning to protect, extra powers for some players rarely cause unfairness, so the pattern is mostly used in such games.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Such players may use their abilities in ways that disrupt the fiction for the rest.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Special abilities given to some players can tilt the playing field, making their position stronger than that of the others.

patterns.name: Tiered Participation
patterns.what_it_is: The game offers different ways to take part, differing in time and kind of actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each tier must have a real, distinct role and requirements, and tiers must stay meaningfully connected to the same game. Players should be able to choose or move between tiers.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tiers are only labels for how much someone plays, with no different game roles.
patterns.knobs: number of tiers; time and activity required per tier; ease of moving between tiers

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Players in lightly involved tiers may sit idle between actions, and designers accept this on purpose because those players don't want to be active as often as others.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Offering several ways to join in, with different time and activity demands, lets a game fit people whose availability and interest differ.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: When each tier asks for different involvement and actions, players naturally end up with distinct parts to play within the group.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Players in higher tiers can have more power than others.

patterns.name: Synchronous Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: All players' game sessions run at the same time and overlap.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs ways to get everyone present together and a pace that suits shared time, with breaks handled. Communication and waiting rules matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are online together but each plays alone and never has to react to anyone else's timing.
patterns.knobs: turn or real-time structure; how long sessions last; how breaks and late joiners are handled

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Because everyone must play at once, the group has to wait for latecomers at the start, and anyone who pauses makes all the others sit idle.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: When several people are playing during the same stretch of time, the game is by nature a multiplayer one, and more overlap means more multiplayer.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Having everyone present and playing at the same moment is a direct way to give players the feeling of doing something together.

conflicts_with.name: Turn Taking
conflicts_with.why: If a turn leaves the other players with nothing to do, they are not really playing at the same time, which clashes with simultaneous play.

patterns.name: Possibility of Anonymity
patterns.what_it_is: The player can choose not to reveal who they are.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must give players a way to hide their identity and must not leak it elsewhere, e.g. through cross-session statistics or friend lists. Communication has to go through masks such as handles or avatars.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A nickname field exists, but real names, linked accounts or public stats still reveal who the player is, so hiding changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much identity is shown; whether names, profiles and stats are linked across sessions

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When you can hide who you are, other players can more easily treat you as just a game participant rather than a known person.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide for themselves whether to show their real identity or conceal it, and that option to pick either one is itself a choice.

can_cause.name: Player Anonymity
can_cause.why: The pattern gives players the power to decide whether they will be anonymous, so when they use it, they end up unidentified.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Players may pretend to be someone else so they can stay anonymous when socially interacting, which is a form of roleplaying.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: If anonymity is wanted, designers need not help players identify each other.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Forcing anonymity removes the player's option to choose whether to be anonymous, which is the core of that other pattern.

conflicts_with.name: Friend Lists
conflicts_with.why: A list is about knowing who others are, so it works against letting players stay anonymous.

conflicts_with.name: Public Player Statistics
conflicts_with.why: Stats that follow a player across multiple game sessions can reveal who they are, undermining their ability to stay hidden.

conflicts_with.name: Social Roles
conflicts_with.why: Even the option to stay anonymous works against social roles, making them less present or harder to adopt.

patterns.name: Coaches
patterns.what_it_is: People who lead a team and give its members advice.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The coach must have actual levers (training, tactics, reserves) that change team outcomes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A coach title exists, but the coach can't affect anything the team does.
patterns.knobs: scope of the coach's powers; how team development is controlled

can_cause.name: Entitled Players
can_cause.why: A coach is a person with special standing over a team, so holding that role means being a player with extra entitlements.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Guiding and instructing teammates without playing yourself is a distinct position within a team, so being a coach is a social role.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Instructing and guiding team members, and deciding how to direct them, requires dealing well with people, so coaching calls on social skills.

changes.name: Reserves
changes.why: Coaches decide how the spare team members are used, so their choices shape how reserves come into play.

changes.name: Team Development
changes.why: Coaches choose which direction a team's growth and training takes, so they shape how the team develops.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: A coach is a special team member who helps with management and training instead of doing the regular actions.

patterns.name: Friend Lists
patterns.what_it_is: The game keeps a list of players who matter to each person so they are easier to find.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Provide ways to add, confirm and find friends, and tie services such as chat, invites and gifts to the list. Needs server infrastructure to track players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A list screen exists, but it connects to no matching, chat or gifts, so it is just a contact book.
patterns.knobs: how friends are found and confirmed; what features are limited to friends; friendship levels

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because players know how their friends play, they can pick the kind of session they want by choosing who to join.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Players can shape the social side of a game to their taste by choosing which known friends to play with.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Friends already share past play, so a list makes it easier to team up with them again and feel together.

changes.name: Chat Channels
changes.why: The list narrows general chat so a player can talk only with chosen friends instead of everyone.

changes.name: Communication Channels
changes.why: The list limits a general communication service so a player reaches only their friends.

changes.name: Free Gift Inventories
changes.why: Neighbor-style friends in the list are the ones a player can give things to from their gift inventory.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: The list lets players quickly set up a game with their friends in a lobby rather than with strangers.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Players here need help from others to progress, so lists (often filled by invites) let them gain that help.

changes.name: Meta Servers
changes.why: The list needs supporting infrastructure, which meta servers supply so friends can be found and tracked.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: The list helps players find friends and info on them, so they can join the same match or start a new one.

changes.name: Public Player Statistics
changes.why: The list makes it simpler to look up information on one's friends among all the players' public stats.

changes.name: Visits
changes.why: Neighbor-style friends in the list allow players to visit each other's play areas, which they otherwise could not do.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Choosing to play with friends means existing opinions about those people, good or bad, affect how the game is played.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Keeping lists of known players lets people recognize each other, which defeats hiding identities, so they should be avoided.

conflicts_with.name: Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: A list works by naming known players, which goes against keeping players anonymous.

conflicts_with.name: Possibility of Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: A list is about knowing who others are, so it works against letting players stay anonymous.

patterns.name: Game System Player
patterns.what_it_is: A passive participant controlled by the system under simple rules, with no visible will.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give it simple fixed rules players can understand and perform, with enough power to actually threaten them. Its actions should be easy to carry out in self-run games.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A dummy opponent exists but can't affect the outcome, so it is just scenery.
patterns.knobs: how complex its rules are; how strong its actions are; how much randomness it uses

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Because the system-run opponent threatens everyone at once, the human players share a common foe and have reason to team up against it.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: A player run by the game itself acts against the human players and can beat them, so it naturally becomes an opponent they must face.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Since its actions must be simple to carry out and easy to choose, it often gets special moves that ordinary players don't have.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: The system player is passive and rule-bound, so the players' challenge comes from the game itself rather than from other human players.

can_cause.name: Symbiotic Player Relations
can_cause.why: Having the same system-run enemy in common ties the human players' fortunes together, so helping each other serves each one's own interest.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When the game system itself acts as a participant in a self-run game, players must carry out its work for it, creating upkeep.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: A system-run player with unpredictable behavior brings in uncertainty of its own, rather than just adjusting existing uncertainty.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Opponents run by the game itself add this uncertainty when their behavior is unpredictable, since the pattern needs unpredictable other players.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: With no separate game runner, players must carry out the system player's moves themselves, so its rules need to be simple and easy to perform.

patterns.name: Player Anonymity
patterns.what_it_is: Other players do not know who exactly is playing.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must remove or block identity cues such as names, voice and friend links, and enforce this consistently. Designers must decide whether anonymity is optional or forced.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are called 'anonymous' but use persistent handles, or can easily be recognised from chat or friend lists.
patterns.knobs: whether anonymity is forced or optional; which identity cues are hidden; whether communication is allowed

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When nobody can link a player's real-life traits to what happens in the game, others feel more separated from the person behind the actions.

conflicts_with.name: Friend Lists
conflicts_with.why: A list works by naming known players, which goes against keeping players anonymous.

conflicts_with.name: Social Roles
conflicts_with.why: Social roles are harder to establish when players don't know who others are, since roles depend on recognized identities; gameplay-based roles can work around this.

patterns.name: Reserves
patterns.what_it_is: Team members who wait outside the game because not everyone can play at once.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The active-slot limit must be lower than the team size, and swapping must be allowed with some cost or timing. Members must differ in skill or stamina so choosing who plays matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Bench players exist, but all members are identical and swaps never happen, so the bench changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: number of active slots versus team size; swap rules, timing and cost

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: A player whose character sits on the bench isn't taking part in the action, so being held in reserve means stretches of waiting with nothing to do.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: While waiting on the sidelines, players can think ahead, and choosing which characters to bench or bring in is itself a planning decision.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Because only some team members can be active, reserves let a team swap which agents are in play instead of using the same ones throughout.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Reserves let players change which characters are on the active team, so the lineup can be adjusted rather than staying fixed.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: When physical exhaustion makes players' results unpredictable, rotating tired members out for rested ones evens out how well the team performs.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: If playing means physically acting things out, members tire, so reserves let them rest while others take over their role.

changes.name: Player Physical Prowess
changes.why: Games that demand bodily effort wear players down, and having substitutes lets them recover while the team keeps going at full tempo.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Reserves change a team by letting it hold more members than can be active, so it can handle uneven sizes and rotate people in and out.

patterns.name: Invites
patterns.what_it_is: Actions by which a player calls new people into the game, sometimes earning a reward for it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a way to reach people outside it (online link, share feature) and must let newcomers join a running game or world. A reward or social reason for inviting helps players actually use it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An invite button exists but newcomers cannot join anyway, or nobody has a reason to press it, so no one ever arrives.
patterns.knobs: what the inviter gets as reward; how many invites are allowed; how easily invitees can join

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Sending an invite happens partly outside the game world, such as contacting someone who isn't playing, so it counts as an action beyond normal in-game play.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: When players invite people to get assistance, they are asking someone who isn't currently playing to join and lend a hand.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: A game can pay players for successful recruiting, and an invite can itself be a gift waiting for the person being invited.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Bringing in more players helps games that depend on working together, since extra teammates improve how well a group can cooperate.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: Invites only work if a game lets newcomers join an ongoing session, so games using them must already allow players to come and go.

changes.name: Friend Lists
changes.why: Invited people are often added automatically to the inviter's list of friends, so sending invites grows those lists.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
