changes.why: Invites bring people in after a session has begun, so the game must already be able to accept those latecomers.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Invites suit games with very many players, because recruiting more people fits a large online population.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Invites make most sense in these large-population games, where recruiting more people adds to the crowd of others sharing the world.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Players may invite people to fill out their team or to strengthen the opposing one, changing team balance and how challenging play feels.

patterns.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
patterns.what_it_is: The system itself hides from players who the other players are.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must remove or limit names, friend lists and open chat, so players really cannot tell who others are or contact them outside gameplay.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Anonymous-looking nicknames that are still consistent and linkable, and open chat that lets players reveal who they are.
patterns.knobs: what identity info is hidden; which communication channels exist; whether exceptions for known friends are allowed

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When players can't tell who others are, they judge each other only by what they do in the game, which separates the person from their in-game actions.

can_cause.name: Player Anonymity
can_cause.why: Because the system hides who players are, nobody can know the real identity of anyone else, so anonymity arises as a direct result.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Players lack knowledge of who others are, so they can't be sure about the people they cooperate or compete with.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Since partners can't know who they are working with, cooperating involves added uncertainty about the other participants.

changes.name: High Score Lists
changes.why: The page only notes that anonymity could apply to high score lists, without explaining why.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Hiding identities makes most sense when several people play together, where the design restricts what information flows between them.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Players facing a choice between self-interest and the group must decide without knowing who the others are, adding uncertainty to the dilemma.

conflicts_with.name: Chat Channels
conflicts_with.why: Because free text can reveal outside-the-game details about players, it is hard to keep them truly anonymous.

conflicts_with.name: Communication Channels
conflicts_with.why: Players tend to reveal personal details in conversation, and can also set up outside channels, which makes forced anonymity hard to maintain.

conflicts_with.name: Extra-Game Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Anonymity is used to prevent harm from players oversharing with strangers, so real-world consequences of play become much less likely, which clashes with them occurring.

conflicts_with.name: Friend Lists
conflicts_with.why: Keeping lists of known players lets people recognize each other, which defeats hiding identities, so they should be avoided.

conflicts_with.name: Handles
conflicts_with.why: Names and other identifying labels can expose who someone is, so they need to be restricted in what they allow.

conflicts_with.name: Possibility of Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Forcing anonymity removes the player's option to choose whether to be anonymous, which is the core of that other pattern.

conflicts_with.name: Social Roles
conflicts_with.why: With players judged only on their play and not on who they are, it becomes hard for lasting social roles to form.

patterns.name: Robotic Players
patterns.what_it_is: Real robots that take part in the game on equal terms with players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The robot needs sensors, movement and an AI that can really act in the physical play space and follow the game's rules, as a human participant would. The game must be built so that physical actions by the robot count in the game state and other players can respond to them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A robot sits on the table or moves along a fixed script while a person or a program secretly makes all the decisions, so it takes no real part in play and nothing depends on it.
patterns.knobs: how much the robot can sense and do; how skilled its AI is; how much the robot's physical actions affect the game state

can_cause.name: Physical Enactment
can_cause.why: When a program controls a physical robot, the robot's body can act out things in the real world, so the machine player performs physical actions itself.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: A robot given a program as its brain can move its body through real space, so the machine player itself travels around the play area.

patterns.name: Initiative
patterns.what_it_is: The ability of agents to act on their own, not only in response to events.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Agents must be able to start actions that are not simply triggered by something the player did, and these actions must affect play. Players need to notice that the agent chose to act.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Agents that only react to player actions or follow a script that looks spontaneous, so they never start anything.
patterns.knobs: how often agents act on their own; what range of actions they can start

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Characters who act on their own help capture believable human behavior, supporting the theme.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Agents that act on their own rather than only reacting feel more tied to the world and less predictable.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: When NPCs act on their own, they seem more like agents, though it can make outcomes less predictable.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Autonomous units can act on their own, such as attacking enemies they find after moving to a location.

patterns.name: Traverse
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to move a game element from one point in the world to another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear start and end point with a route that holds obstacles, choices or opposition, so the journey is not trivial. Progress should be readable to the player, for example through checkpoints.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A destination marker reached by simply holding a key down, with nothing to cross or avoid.
patterns.knobs: distance; obstacles along the way; number of checkpoints

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: Navigation tasks can demand that you reach a particular place, so the goal of getting somewhere is what the task actually asks of you.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Since reaching a destination can be a goal, moving between places can carry a story along as players progress through it.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Finishing a traversal guarantees the player has ended up in a new environment, which gives a fixed story a clear step forward.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Several traversal goals chained together, or intermediate points along a route, show players how far along they are.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Many quests simply ask players to go to specific points in the world, sometimes within a time limit.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Designers often set a destination goal so that several competitors rush toward it, and the competition emerges when multiple agents pursue the same traversal goal.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Moving through a space with limited resources requires thinking ahead about the route.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When reaching a destination has several possible routes, the player chooses among them, so a set of selectable goals for a traverse task gives real choice.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Exploring is a form of traveling combined with learning, so having goals to cross the world contributes to it.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Stealth is formed by joining the aim of hiding with the aim of getting somewhere; moving across the game space is its other necessary part.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Trying to shoot while also trying to get somewhere is harder than doing just one of the two.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Traversal goals are often used to make sure players visit certain parts of the world.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Traversal goals make sure players pass through certain parts of a level.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Scouting goals can be set by having players follow specific routes so they notice differences in the world.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: Enemies that fill the route players must cross can block the way and make crossing harder.

patterns.name: Quests
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of completing a task for which a reward is given.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each needs a clear task, a visible reward and a way to be offered and completed. Rewards must be worth the effort and tied to the world.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A quest log exists, but tasks are trivial, rewards meaningless or the requirements unclear, so players ignore it.
patterns.knobs: number and type of quests; reward size; how they are offered; difficulty

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Because quests steer what a player's agent does and become, they can grow the player's in-game construct whether or not a reward is given.

can_cause.name: Adventures
can_cause.why: A single quest or a handful of them can serve as the backbone around which a larger adventure is built.

can_cause.name: Campaigns
can_cause.why: Several quests strung together can form the core of a campaign.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Quests tie into the game's story and direct how agents act, so working through them can change a character over time, regardless of rewards.

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Finishing a quest, or failing it for good, marks a clear moment where that piece of play ends.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Quests are planned in advance, including how they begin and finish, so they are temporary goals that exist only until resolved.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Quests can be nested as subgoals under bigger ones, and they work as building blocks for goal structures linked to the story.

can_cause.name: Goal-Driven Personal Development
can_cause.why: Quests link story structure to how agents behave, shaping where they end up by giving them goals to pursue.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Since players can see their progress and know exactly what completion needs, the approaching end of the quest stays in view.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: A quest can reward the player by letting them show faithfulness, for example to a faction or companion.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers must plan why a task exists and what completing it changes, so quests amount to pre-written story structure.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Quests that tell players exactly where to go push them to simply travel to destinations instead of searching around.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Finishing a quest pays out rewards or moves the story ahead, and even failure can matter if it visibly shows what the effort changed.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Randomly generated quests change what players are asked to do, so each new game has different tasks.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Randomizing quests makes the tasks players take on different from one play to the next.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Quests link the story with how agents behave, so they help define what those agents do and where they are headed.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Gaining a companion can be a fitting reward for a quest, and companions can have quests of their own.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Quests often unlock closed-off areas while active or as a reward when completed.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Quest-giving characters tied to factions can set groups against each other within the game.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: Quests can create or steer the paths agents take, shaping their otherwise open fates.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Quests may be needed in such worlds to carry predetermined story, though their stated rewards also make the mechanics obvious there.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: Quests are a very typical way of handing players a goal that becomes available at some point and may later expire.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: Games built around quests often send players to far-apart places, so the travel between them tends to be skipped through instant jumps.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Exploration
conflicts_with.why: Quests that give known locations to visit remove the need to look around, so players may skip exploring.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Quests openly spell out mechanical rewards and requirements, which can expose awkward spots where the game's theme doesn't hold together.

patterns.name: Clues
patterns.what_it_is: Items or information that hint to the player how to achieve a goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must carry real information about goals, appear at the right moment, and match the game's setting.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Hints exist but are too vague, too late or say what the player already knows.
patterns.knobs: how explicit they are; when and how often they appear; whether they adapt to player struggle

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Hints that tell players what to do make a game less demanding, so players can progress without getting stuck, which gives a relaxed, easy-going experience.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
can_cause.why: A game can hand out extra hints once a player has failed a task several times, so help scales with how the player is struggling.

can_cause.name: Illusionary Rewards
can_cause.why: A clue only informs the player and changes nothing in the game state, so it feels helpful without actually giving any concrete benefit.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: Clues that explain controls or mechanics, or sit in the interface, come from outside the game world, so they become features the characters could not perceive.

can_cause.name: Rabbit Hole Invitations
can_cause.why: Some clues hint not at how to act in the game but at how to begin playing it, which makes them a special kind of clue.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: A clue can push players toward actions that don't help their own goals but serve the story, so it misleads them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Hints about what players may meet ahead, such as dangers, make them anticipate threats and feel uneasy about what comes next.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Clues written as facts and events of the game world fit its setting, letting players use their understanding of that world to read them.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When a story is predetermined, clues make players want to work out what will happen next, which creates information-seeking goals.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: In story-driven games, story progress depends on getting certain clues, so obtaining them becomes an ownership goal without needing conflict.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Clues placed in the game give players pieces of the story to find, so they can form the story, provided they fit the game's theme.

changes.name: Achilles' Heels
changes.why: Clues can help players find out about a boss's weakness, making discovering that information a goal in a story.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Clues are introduced to tune difficulty, easing the challenge or letting players focus on the core of it.

changes.name: Easter Eggs
changes.why: Clues can lure players into finding hidden extras that are not needed to complete or win the game.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Traces and warnings can hint at where enemies are located, so players can anticipate them.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Clues can sit on the board or hint at where enemies and traps are on it.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Encouraging feedback about an area or object can push players to keep exploring it further.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Clues tied to movement, like signs and direction markers, help players find their way through the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Clues can be placed in or point to places in the game world, shaping what players notice and where they go.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Encouragement clues signal that a low-level subgoal has been completed, showing progress toward higher goals.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Clues can be located in levels or hint at what is in them, guiding players through the level.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Clues about movement, such as warnings of upcoming curves, tell players how to move.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Hints about what to do make puzzles easier for players to work out.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Clues such as helper hints or map markers show players how to complete or where to find quests.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Clues leading to secret areas can reveal resources that indirectly help players reach their goals.

changes.name: Secret Areas
changes.why: Clues can lure players toward hidden places they would otherwise not find.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Traces and explicit warnings let players figure out where traps are or that danger lies ahead.

changes.name: Unknown Goals
changes.why: Clues leading to hidden extras can be seen as hints toward goals the player has not yet been told about.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: When players find clues, they get hints that something may happen, which strengthens the pattern, as long as the clues fit the game's theme.

changes.name: Scripted Information Sequences
changes.why: Hiding useful hints inside the sequence gives players a gameplay reason to watch it, even though their attention cannot be forced.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Features
conflicts_with.why: Clues delivered through interface elements from outside the game world break the consistency of its setting.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Clues containing information from outside the game, like how controls work, break the consistency of the game world's theme.

patterns.name: Gain Ownership
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: become the owner of a certain game element.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Make ownership of items, pieces or areas matter, giving benefits, points or progress, and make it contestable. Without contest or reward it is just a pickup.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players can own things, but ownership gives no benefit and nobody can take it, so there is no pursuit.
patterns.knobs: value of owned elements; how contestable they are; how many can be owned

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: Ownership of an object or area can be made the stake of a wager, either chosen by players or required by the system.

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Taking ownership of items one by one can end up completing a collection the player was building.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: When the contested object or area can be hidden, its current owners may try to hide it so ownership cannot pass to others.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: Players who want to acquire elements are often motivated to pursue arrangement goals, since succeeding at one usually lets them capture pieces.

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Having to first obtain the item before carrying it adds a preliminary step that makes the delivery goal harder.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Winning ownership of new objects or areas typically makes a player's holdings grow.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When owning an object or area reveals new content, such as texts in a book, it helps complete goals about learning things.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: Holding the special position that defines this goal normally requires first winning control of it, so ownership goals form its basis.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Ownership goals can be used to build story structure, and in turn story elements can supply information and motivation for those goals.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Ownership goals give designers a ready way to build quests, and obtaining the sought object can finish the quest.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Succeeding at sneaking past guards can be the way, or the only way, to obtain something without fighting its owners.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Contesting something another player holds creates opposition and uncertainty, which makes players feel strain.

changes.name: Resource Management
changes.why: Ownership goals tied to resources, such as taking resource locations, directly or indirectly shape how players handle their resources.

patterns.name: Optional Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal that need not be completed to win or finish the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The goals must be visible and worth pursuing for their own sake, and the game must not require them to win. Tracking them with a reward or penalty gives them more weight.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A listed side goal with no reward or interest, so nobody ever goes for it, or one that is secretly required to progress.
patterns.knobs: how many optional goals; whether the game tracks them; what reward or penalty they carry

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: A goal built into the game's own structure can be turned into a tracked achievement, so a skippable objective becomes a recognized extra target.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players must decide which extra goals to chase, and the goals themselves can be hard, so the choosing and the doing both add difficulty.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because these goals aren't required, players decide for themselves whether and which ones to pursue, which is why designers add them.

can_cause.name: Goal Achievements
can_cause.why: An optional goal can be linked to an achievement that rewards finishing it, giving players a meta-game nudge to attempt it.

can_cause.name: Handicap Achievements
can_cause.why: Optional goals can be set up as a harder way of doing something, and the achievement marks that players chose the tougher route.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: If players leave some optional goals unfinished, they may start another playthrough to complete more or all of them.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: With several skippable goals available, players pick which ones to go after, so together they form a menu of goals to choose from.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Some skippable goals help players with the main goals, such as collecting extras that make required progress easier.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Because players choose to take the goal on rather than being forced, the commitment is theirs once a penalty attaches.

can_cause.name: Grind Achievements
can_cause.why: Many small, non-mandatory goals can be tallied up, and finishing enough of them awards the grind achievement.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When a game offers goals that aren't required, players can make a game out of completing them.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: Making a short-lived goal optional means players don't have to complete it when it appears, though they might interrupt other plans to try.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Giving members a range of skippable goals shows what the group wants, needs and intends, adding detail to who they are.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Skippable goals can fill in a sparse goal structure, adding more branches without making them required.

patterns.name: Eliminate
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: remove certain elements from the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be targets that can be removed and ways for players to remove them, and the goal must matter to winning or progress so players pursue it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Targets that are listed as removable but cannot be hurt in practice, or removing them gains nothing.
patterns.knobs: how many targets; how hard they are to remove; what removal gives

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Trying to remove game elements often leads players to seize them instead of destroying them, so going after targets can turn into capturing.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: When players aim to remove each other's pieces or characters, they end up fighting, which creates combat.

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: If goals involve removing players or their pieces, some participants can be knocked out well before the match ends.

can_cause.name: Extermination
can_cause.why: When removing targets is the main activity for a stretch of play, that stretch becomes a phase of wiping out opponents.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Removing opponents is a way of beating them, so goals of removal naturally produce goals about defeating opposition.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Those who are targeted risk suffering a loss or setback if the removal goal is achieved against them.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: When the targets are players themselves, successfully removing them means they are out of the game.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Targets of removal want to avoid it, so they develop their own aims of stopping the others from succeeding.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A removal goal can be handed to players as a task to complete, giving them a clear mission.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: When generators keep supplying the things players must eliminate, the amount left to remove depends on how fast they are produced, so the goal's size changes during play.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Game elements aiming to destroy the player's pieces make them hostile, or players avoiding being destroyed marks them as enemies.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Removing opposing forces from a territory can be the way a player comes to control that territory.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: The pattern needs players to be able to remove each other from play, so an elimination ability together with shared goals makes it work.

can_cause.name: Team Elimination
can_cause.why: If every member of a team has a goal of being removed, completing all of those goals removes the entire team.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Being targeted for removal changes how players steer their characters.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can be assigned goals to remove game elements players care about, which makes them enemies and targets.

changes.name: Survive
changes.why: Removing the threats that endanger the element is another active route to success, instead of passively waiting out the danger.

changes.name: Team Elimination
changes.why: Designing the individual removal goals for each member encourages team wipe-out, as long as those members can actually be removed.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Targets that cannot be harmed make a removal goal impossible to achieve.

patterns.name: Gain Information
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: act so as to obtain information and draw conclusions from it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Hide information that matters for decisions, and give actions to uncover it. The knowledge must change what players do.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players can discover facts, but the facts are irrelevant or already obvious, so searching has no use.
patterns.knobs: how much is hidden; cost and means of uncovering it; how useful the information is

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: When some agent in the game wants to stop others from learning something, hiding that information becomes its own goal, a counter to the seeking goal.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Learning where an item is located can be a first step toward getting it, so finding information leads into goals of acquiring things.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Non-player characters can ask players to find out something for them, which turns an information-seeking goal into a quest.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: When the information being sought is useful for something else the player is doing, finding it serves that other aim and becomes a supporting goal.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: When players lack knowledge about rules or state, they try actions to find out, especially if information is imperfect.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Exploration is partly about learning about the world, so combining information-seeking with travel produces it.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Discovering facts, phrases or action sequences is the heart of a puzzle, so any goal of finding information drives it.

can_cause.name: Rescue
can_cause.why: Players may need to discover where the captive is held before they can free them, and finding them can be part of the reward.

changes.name: Player-Artifact Proximity
changes.why: In games where players move physically, an information goal can require being near a specific object before the knowledge is obtained.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: Rescuing someone can serve an information goal, since those saved may carry knowledge players didn't expect, or the rescue may need information first.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Players may need to learn about weaknesses before they can beat an enemy, which changes how the encounter goes.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: If players aren't told where the goal is or what lies between, they must find out first, adding discovery to the task.

patterns.name: Gain Competence
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: learn to perform a certain skill in the game at the required level.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Offer abilities players can obtain through items, levels or upgrades, with real gameplay effects and a choice of paths. Players need a reason to want more power.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Upgrades exist but only give tiny or cosmetic bonuses, so nobody pursues them.
patterns.knobs: number and size of upgrades; cost to obtain; how many paths to choose

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Becoming stronger or learning a skill is often needed to beat a boss or get past a barrier, so a story can turn that aim into a quest.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: When the aim is to improve skills, players practice by trying variations of actions and learning how they turn out.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can choose which skills to build up, which feeds into freedom of choice about their own development.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Acquiring a tool can make a player more skilled, which gives a reason to want ownership of the tool.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Improving in a skill or area leads to unlocking actions connected to it, like leveling up in a skill.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: The simplest form of planned growth is players deciding how to get better at things, which builds on competence-gaining goals.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Improving skill can be a race when it gives the winner a temporary edge, provided the goal is exclusive or shared by all.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Working toward competence gives players a sense of power because their abilities get better, shaping how those abilities develop.

changes.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
changes.why: Development can happen without competence goals, but when players adopt them, their growth gets a direction and purpose.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Character growth can occur without these goals, but players who adopt them steer it and look forward to what comes next.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Competence goals are about wanting new or better skills, so they shape which skills players try to develop.

changes.name: Symmetric Goals
changes.why: When several players or agents share the same aim of becoming stronger, it becomes a symmetric goal, producing Red Queen Dilemmas or races.

patterns.name: Evade
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: avoid being caught and avoid being hit.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a clear threat with a penalty if it hits, and the player must have means of avoiding it, such as movement, and a real chance of failing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A danger so slow or easy to dodge that it can be ignored, or a hit that costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: speed and accuracy of threats; the player's mobility; penalty for being hit

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Dodging never reaches a finished state by itself; the danger keeps coming, so players must keep avoiding it for as long as it threatens them.

can_cause.name: Maneuvering
can_cause.why: When dodging happens live in real time, players need to steer their position skillfully to stay out of harm's way.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Evasion tasks can be packaged as quests, and chaining such quests together can build up a story structure.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: When the danger comes from other agents' actions, evading means stopping those actions from succeeding against you.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: In turn-based games there is no reflex pressure, so working out a safe move by thinking is the skill that evasion calls for.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Avoiding a threat can be turned into a formal task given to the player, which makes it a quest.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Staying unharmed helps players reach other aims such as traversing an area or delivering something, so evasion backs those goals up.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because failing to dodge brings a clear penalty, players who are trying to evade feel pressure and unease.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Fleeing and chasing pair up, and giving the pursuing side special movement makes escaping difficult.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Combined with Overcome, evading forces players to decide at each point whether to play defensively or offensively.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Targets that are trying to dodge keep moving, which makes them harder to line up and hit.

changes.name: Deliver
changes.why: Avoiding danger on the way supports the delivery goal, since the carrier must get through safely to hand something over.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Dodging the attacks of those trying to kill you makes their elimination goal harder to complete.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: Either evading or overcoming can solve a problem, so the existence of one reduces the need for the other.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Avoiding hazards helps players get across an area, so evasion supports the crossing goal.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Having to avoid collisions or attacks makes you steer carefully, since mistakes bring penalties and good timing keeps you safe.

patterns.name: Survive
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to keep your game elements from being destroyed or removed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a real threat (enemies, hazards, draining resources) and a real loss when the thing dies. Players must be able to act to prevent that loss.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The thing to protect cannot realistically die, or dying costs nothing, so 'survive' is only a label on the screen.
patterns.knobs: threat strength and frequency; how fast resources drain; how many lives or how much health

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Staying alive is not a one-time achievement; you have to keep your element alive for as long as play goes on.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Surviving means stopping something from happening, and it especially works this way when another participant is actively trying to eliminate your element.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: When the thing to keep alive is a non-player character, protecting it can be handed to players as a task that fits into the story.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: With no winning condition, play simply continues until the survival goal fails, so the game can only be lost, never won.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Adding a survival goal to the target of an elimination goal gives the pursued side a purpose of resisting, so each goal works against the other.

changes.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
changes.why: Needing to stay alive on top of many simultaneous challenges makes play more overwhelming, which makes a chaotic, barely-coping experience more likely.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: If the thing being guarded can die, then failing to protect it ends the guarding goal, which gives it real stakes.

changes.name: Herd
changes.why: When the herded targets can die, players must keep them alive as well as steering them, which adds a way to fail.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Giving rivals a survival goal means killing a rival can no longer serve as an easy way to settle the rivalry.

patterns.name: Ephemeral Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: it appears and disappears mid-game, and you can fail it through no fault of your own.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goals must appear and expire during play on their own terms, with failure possible beyond the player's actions, and be worth chasing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Temporary goals that stay available long enough that everyone completes them eventually, so timing never matters.
patterns.knobs: how often goals appear; how long they last; how they are triggered, random or state-based

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: Goals that are hard to pull off, like stopping a rival carrier, can be rewarded with special achievements that recognize the skill needed to beat them.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: Ephemeral goals that are mandatory work like sub-goals of a larger goal, so the larger goal's requirements shift as these small goals come and go.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: When a goal can be dropped or lapses at an uncertain moment, the opportunity it creates is short-lived, though how long it lasts isn't fixed.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Because ephemeral goals add local detail unrelated to the main objective, players may misread them as meaningful clues in the story.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: They add small, local details to the game world that don't serve the main goal, making the fictional setting feel more believable and coherent.

can_cause.name: Unknown Goals
can_cause.why: Players usually can't know in advance that such a goal exists or what it will be, since it appears only mid-play.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since goals keep being added and removed during play, what players are working toward keeps changing, and random triggering makes each session differ.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Short-lived goals appearing during a session give players optional things to choose to pursue or ignore.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Short-lived goals given to players in multiplayer games let other players easily take up the simple, short-term aim of stopping them.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: When randomness generates temporary goals anew each game, the objectives players pursue differ every time they play.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: Goals designed in advance can be handed to players selectively, by chance or on a fixed cycle, so they show up only at certain moments.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Goals that pop up and vanish can break the expected story flow and spoil plans unless they fit the story or are clearly signposted.

changes.name: Selectable Set of Goals
changes.why: Making some options in the set available only at certain times keeps the choices changing during play.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: A game with no final victory can be built entirely from goals that come and go, so there is always something to pursue.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Constantly changing goals keep play from settling into repetitive routines, so they can help avoid grinding.

patterns.name: Preventing Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of stopping some other goal from being completed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The target goal must be one that can be interfered with, and the blocking agent needs real means, information and time to act. Opposing goals must conflict directly.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies exist with a blocking role, but they are too weak, too passive or unable to reach the target, so nothing is ever prevented.
patterns.knobs: strength and number of blockers; the information they have; time limits

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Goals
can_cause.why: The one defending against a goal and the one pursuing it want opposite things, so their goals differ in nature rather than mirroring each other.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Concealing only matters when someone seeks the hidden thing, and successful hiding is what blocks those seekers from reaching their aim.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Since someone keeps trying to block the target, the blocking goal stays active until the target can no longer possibly be completed.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Whoever works against your goals, especially a computer-controlled character, tends to be perceived by players as an opponent or enemy.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: If one side succeeds, the other must fail, so both goals cannot be reached together.

can_cause.name: Incompatible Goals
can_cause.why: The preventer's aim and the target's aim cannot both be achieved, which makes them clash by design.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Opposing forces to a group make it natural to give players or agents a side they feel bound to.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Characters whose aim is to block the player act as the opposing force that the player must fight.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Whether they hold the goal being blocked or the blocking goal, players are likely to start seeing these characters as enemies.

changes.name: Survive
changes.why: Survival involves active threats and passive ones like starvation, so designers of blocking goals must balance those two forces.

conflicts_with.name: Cooperation
conflicts_with.why: Aims that stop others from achieving things clash with joint effort at a basic level, though teams can oppose each other.

patterns.name: Continuous Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: keep part of the game state within set limits.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Something must threaten the held state so that it needs attention, and failing must have a consequence. The player must be able to tell how well they are doing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game says keep something above a level, but nothing pushes it down or failing costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: how long it must be held; how tight the limits are; how strongly the state is pushed away

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since the goal must be kept up while players do other things, they must keep switching focus to check on it, which makes play demanding.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Because the goal has to stay satisfied over time, it is never fully finished and the possible ending keeps hanging over the player.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players must keep holding the goal state while a looming end or time demand weighs on them, which builds tension.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Players aware that a goal must be sustained start thinking about duration, so the goal can lead them to consider time limits.

can_cause.name: Time Pressure
can_cause.why: Holding a state over time means players are always under pressure to keep it up, which adds time pressure to play.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: If failing to maintain the goal state ends the game for the player, the game can be built so that it only gets lost, never won.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Goals that never finish, paired with reasons to return, make timing your play a challenge.

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: A companion needs to share ongoing aims with the player so it keeps staying alongside and helping throughout the game.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Ongoing shared aims let players negotiate how to deal with dilemmas over them, and teamwork can emerge from that bargaining.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Rewards can be made larger or better the longer players have kept the goal up, so lasting success pays off more.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Linking a dilemma to a sustained goal means players can't settle it once and for all but have to keep managing it over a longer stretch of play.

patterns.name: Mutual Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal in which the same task faces two or more participants.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must truly succeed or fail together, with shared rewards or penalties. Added individual incentives decide whether the shared goal stays shared.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A team label or common objective in the text while outcomes and rewards stay individual, so players just pursue their own aims.
patterns.knobs: how much is shared versus individual; how big the shared reward is

can_cause.name: Symbiotic Player Relations
can_cause.why: When players share a goal and its rewards, each one's success helps the others, so they end up depending on one another.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: A goal held jointly is by nature the same goal for everyone sharing it, so every holder is aiming at the identical target.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Because the goal belongs to the whole group, reaching it counts as something the team achieved together rather than any single player.

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: A companion needs aims it shares with the player so that helping the player also advances its own purposes.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: When players share an objective and also share the reward, they have good reason to pursue it jointly.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When everyone is working toward the same aims, players feel they are facing the chaos together instead of separately.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: A shared aim combined with rivalry among the members makes players choose between helping the common goal and beating each other.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Agents who share the same goal need to work toward it together, which is what makes them a team.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Within a faction, what some members want logically becomes wanted by the whole group, so shared goals shape the faction's overall aims.

changes.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
changes.why: With shared goals present, players who enjoy things going badly can end up enjoying the disaster together instead of only individually.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Sharing goals changes how players see penalties, compared with suffering a penalty when nobody else does.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Sharing goals changes how players value rewards, compared with receiving one when nobody else gets anything.

changes.name: Shared Resources
changes.why: When players already hold resources in common and are then given a common goal, it affects how they treat those resources.

conflicts_with.name: Incompatible Goals
conflicts_with.why: A set of goals can't both exclude each other and be shared by everyone, so the two kinds can't describe the same goals.

patterns.name: Achievements
patterns.what_it_is: Goals whose completion is remembered beyond a single play session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs persistent storage across sessions, goals that point at varied or unusual play, and visibility to others if they are to carry social value. Goals should require effort or experimentation rather than happen on their own.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Badges pop up for things everybody does anyway, with no persistence or visibility, so they change nobody's play.
patterns.knobs: how many achievements; how hard they are; how visible and what they ask players to try

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Players can be asked to do an action or goal several times, or gather sets of other achievements, so achievements naturally form collections.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Achievements are recorded outside any single play session, so earning one leaves a lasting effect beyond the match where it happened.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Achievements are optional targets, so players decide for themselves whether to chase them, which gives them a choice beyond the main goals.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Hard achievements, such as those needing skillful play, show how good a player is; in single-player games they may be the only way to display it.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: Achievements are kept as records of what a player did, stored between game sessions, so they work as a type of saved play statistic.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Separate achievements can exist for individual goals plus one for finishing the whole set, as with the quest-area and region achievements in World of Warcraft.

can_cause.name: High Score Lists
can_cause.why: When achievements carry numbers, such as a completion percentage or summed point values, they can be ranked and compared like a score table.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Players can set their own aims around achievements, like earning every one or sets of them, creating a game layered on top of the main game.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Achievements give players extra targets they may pursue but need not, such as trying other play styles or completing tasks beyond the main objective.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: When achievements are tied to required goals arranged in tiers, earning them shows players how far through the game they have gotten.

can_cause.name: Public Player Statistics
can_cause.why: Achievements are stored outside the player's own computer and can be viewed online, so others can see what a player has accomplished.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Because earning achievements can bring social standing, players may compete to get them before other players do.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Achievements for optional goals, alternative play styles, or every possible ending give players reasons to play the game again.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Each achievement is given for something the player did, and in-game items may also come with it, so it acts as a reward.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: Others can see the achievements a player has earned, so getting them can win recognition and status from the community.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: Achievements start out unearned and become available to the player once the required action or goal is done, including a goal of unlocking them all.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Achievements reward effort like repeated actions or hard play, and broadcasting them lets others notice that effort and give social standing.

changes.name: Campaigns
changes.why: Achievements can be given for finishing campaigns, such as completing all of them on the hardest difficulty, which shapes how players approach them.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: In games where characters' fates can vary, an achievement for each possible ending gives players a reason to replay to see them all.

changes.name: Sidegrades
changes.why: If achievements give in-game effects, sidegrades are fitting since they change options without upsetting the balance between players.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: A game with no way to win lacks clear aims, but achievements supply goals for players to pursue, though only optional ones.

conflicts_with.name: Ragequitting
conflicts_with.why: Achievements may be tied to a game ending early or to staying through, so a player leaving a match can clash with earning one.

patterns.name: Overcome
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of defeating an opposing force.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be an opponent with a way to resist or act against the player, and clear rules for what counts as defeating it. The opposing force needs agency or a story that makes it feel like a force.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An enemy that is on the goal list but is passive and cannot resist, so defeating it is just a chore, or a victory that is announced without any real opposition.
patterns.knobs: what opponents are to be defeated; how many; how defeat is defined and how strong they are

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: When you are trying to defeat an opposing force, the natural way to show that struggle is as a fight, so combat tends to appear.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: The opponent can try to defeat you too, so your goal and theirs cannot both be met; one side's win is the other's loss.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Beating an opponent often hands over control of things they held, so the winner ends up owning what was taken.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Winning against opposition usually depends on skill, so players are motivated to practice and get better at the game.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Stories are often written to give players a reason to want to defeat the opposing force, supplying motive and theme.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: After a defeat is completed, the loser may be removed from the game as a consequence of being overcome.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: Because the opposing side can also try to defeat you, both sides end up chasing the same kind of goal against each other.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: An opponent who acts on their own and can resist you makes the outcome uncertain, which creates nervous excitement.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Combined with Evade, pursuing offensive goals forces players to decide when to attack instead of defending.

changes.name: Deliver
changes.why: Agents in the game can try to defeat whoever is carrying something to its destination, which makes delivering harder.

patterns.name: Goal Hierarchies
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: goals are linked so that completing or failing some affects others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goals must really depend on each other, so finishing lower goals is needed for, or helps, higher ones. The relationships should be visible to players so they can plan around them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A list of tasks that can all be done in any order with no effect on one another, just presented as a tree.
patterns.knobs: number of levels; how strict the dependencies are; whether lower goals are required or optional

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because goals are linked to each other, players must think about how the pieces connect and which route through them to take, which adds depth.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: When lower goals must be finished before higher ones, each completed layer ends a bigger chunk of play, so closure steps up as you advance.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: A hierarchy of goals can suggest or serve as a starting skeleton from which a story's sequence of events is built.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Seeing goals that depend on one another pushes players to think ahead and plan how to work through them.

changes.name: Companion Quests
changes.why: A companion's story can be too long for one quest or need pacing, so several smaller quests get linked together under a larger goal.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: The conflict with an enemy can be broken into many subgoals that players must complete in turn.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: The top of a hierarchy is a natural choice for a game's main goal, and the innermost goal is typically the main goal.

changes.name: Supporting Goals
changes.why: A goal becomes supporting once it relates to a higher goal, so being placed in a hierarchy turns it into one.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: A long journey can be split into a tree of smaller goals, as in the overall structure of many Mario games.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The structure of a story tends to shape layered goals, so the two can influence each other.

patterns.name: Herd
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: bring objects to a needed place not by moving them directly but by acting through others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The herded elements need their own movement and a limited set of ways for players to nudge them (pushing, luring, blocking), with a clear destination. The herded things must be able to go the wrong way so steering takes real effort.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Elements that just follow the player or a fixed path to the goal, so the player never has to handle their independent movement.
patterns.knobs: how stubborn or erratic the herded things are; how strong the player's influence is; distance to the goal

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: When the things you herd can wander apart, you end up having to gather scattered pieces and bring them back together, which feels like collecting.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Herding is easy to phrase as a concrete task, like guiding someone to a spot, so games commonly hand it to players as a quest.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Since the herded things must reach a destination, getting them there means crossing the game space, so a traversal goal comes along automatically.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Adding herding goals on top of sneaking makes the task more demanding than stealth alone.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Agents that the player tries to herd become enemies when they resist, since they are trying to avoid the player's aim.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Each successful herding into an area can be a lower goal, with finishing all herding being the higher goal (together with One-Way Travel).

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Steering your own piece gets harder when you must also track how several herded elements are moving at the same moment.

patterns.name: Secret Goals
patterns.what_it_is: A goal where a player has a task that the others do not know about.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give players private goals that matter for winning, and keep them hidden through cards or a facilitator. Other players must have a reason and a way to guess or probe.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Hidden goals that all players have identical or that do not affect how anyone plays, so there is nothing to guess or hide.
patterns.knobs: how many secret goals; how different they are between players; whether they must be fulfilled to win

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: Since knowing others' goals helps, players act misleadingly to hide their own aims, which is bluffing.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Hidden aims make players guess others' intentions while concealing theirs, adding extra layers of reasoning to the game.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Because rivals' goals are hidden yet useful to know, players set out to discover them as a goal of their own.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: When nobody knows what others are really trying to achieve, their moves become harder to anticipate.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Keeping your aim hidden means acting as a version of yourself without that goal, which is a form of acting.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Not knowing who is secretly closing in on a win keeps players uncertain and on edge.

changes.name: Internal Conflicts
changes.why: Hidden goals can create or deepen conflicts, since players or characters pull toward aims others don't know about.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: With several players, hidden goals are most useful, making it harder to spot who is winning and adding uncertainty.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Characters can carry hidden goals, which the player may then adopt as their own secret aims.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Character goals that stay hidden give players a stronger basis for more challenging acting of their role.

conflicts_with.name: Beat the Leader
conflicts_with.why: Hidden objectives keep players from knowing how close others are to winning, which makes naming a leader hard or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Hidden objectives make players unsure what others are aiming for, so the likely winner is unclear.

conflicts_with.name: Surrendering
conflicts_with.why: Because the winner is unclear, players keep believing they still have a chance, so they are less tempted to give up.

patterns.name: Guard
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: keep other players or elements away from certain zones or objects.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be something worth guarding and real opponents trying to get it, with ways for the guard to fail. The guard needs means to watch and block, either passive (traps, alarms) or active (combat).
patterns.just_a_label_when: An objective marked 'defend' that nobody ever attacks, or that cannot be lost.
patterns.knobs: what is guarded; how strong and how frequent the threats are; what means of defence are available

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Defending something means constantly watching the area, items, or opponents involved, so the player's attention is kept busy.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: A guard goal is never truly finished until there is no remaining chance of the protected thing being taken or entered.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: If many players or agents share one guard goal but only one may fulfil it at a time, they end up competing for that spot.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Guarding is about stopping others from capturing, rescuing, or sneaking, so it works as a goal of blocking opponents' aims.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: When the guarded area is too big to see all at once, players must go look around to find out what is happening.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When players can freely place the pieces they use for guarding, they must think ahead about where to put them.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Players may choose between actively defending and chasing other goals, weighing the risk and reward of each tactic.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: Guarding something against Capture, Rescue or Stealth makes the guarder's goal and the opposing goal impossible to both complete.

can_cause.name: Rescue
can_cause.why: Rescue arises when some agents are assigned to guard something and others are given the aim and means to free it.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Opponents set to watch for intruders make it more likely a sneaking player is caught, so the goal gets harder.

patterns.name: Supporting Goals
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to complete a task that mainly helps reach the game's other goals.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reward must really make the main goal easier, and the link must be visible to players. Whether the goal is required or optional decides if players weigh trade-offs.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A side goal whose reward has no effect on the main goal, so it only looks like it helps.
patterns.knobs: size of the help given to the main goal; whether the goal is required or optional; cost to complete

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: When a helper goal must be finished before the bigger goal can be completed, goals end up stacked in layers, with small ones feeding larger ones.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Required helper goals that lead toward a main goal show players how far along they are, since finishing each one marks a step closer.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: A helper goal's challenge can differ from its main goal's challenge, so players get to do different kinds of activities along the way.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Computer characters pursuing goals that help the player make the game gentler and keep casual play more firmly in place.

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: A companion needs goals aimed at assisting the player's objectives, which is what makes it act as a helper.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Computer characters whose aim is to help the player will assist rather than betray them.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Giving computer-controlled characters goals that help the player makes them coordinate with the player, producing team-combo-like results.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Players can attack the main goal head-on or use helper goals that might make it easier, which changes how hard the game is.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Helper goals placed around the world give players reasons to go look around and also lead to unexpected finds.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: Their rewards are meant to make a larger goal easier or more achievable, so they change how players approach it.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: They can give trailing players a chance to catch up, provided leaders don't find them easier and chasing them doesn't set trailers back further.

changes.name: Trade-Offs
changes.why: When helper goals are optional, players must choose between spending effort on them or going straight for the main goal.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Helper goals along a route split a long journey into smaller pieces and can sit at places like boosters or check points.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Giving NPCs aims that help the player makes them cooperative, leading to teamwork and simpler play.

conflicts_with.name: Red Herrings
conflicts_with.why: Something players take to be a helpful side goal may turn out to be a decoy, so the two can be confused.

patterns.name: Selectable Set of Goals
patterns.what_it_is: A goal where the player chooses which goals to pursue from a set.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Offer several goals that really differ in risk, reward, or path, and make choosing among them matter, for example by excluding others. The set may change during play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A list of goals where one is clearly best or all lead to the same result, so choosing is not a real decision.
patterns.knobs: how many goals are offered; whether the set changes; whether choices exclude each other

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: When players must pick among several goals, having so many options to weigh against each other can leave them stuck and unable to decide.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Letting a player who is behind decide which goals from the set count gives that player a way to catch up with rivals or NPCs.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: If goals differ in difficulty and players can tell which are harder, they can pick tougher ones to make the game more demanding for themselves.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Because the available goals are fixed in advance, players can only choose among them, which pushes their behavior toward those particular options.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players get to decide which goals to pursue, so they have real say over what they do, such as picking which quest location to travel to.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Having to choose between goals that all appeal to the player can pull them in different directions and make the decision feel hard.

can_cause.name: Open Destiny
can_cause.why: Choosing among goals gives players a sense of steering where their character ends up, as long as the options represent distinct destinies.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Since players can choose different goals each time, they have reason to play again, especially when picking one goal rules out others.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Picking some goals from the set means giving up others, so players must weigh what they gain against what they leave behind.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Different goal choices lead players into different play experiences, provided the choices actually change how the game unfolds.

changes.name: Excluding Goals
changes.why: Making the choice explicit shows players that picking one goal shuts out others, and it can include goals that don't exclude anything.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: A single required goal in the hierarchy can be swapped for a set of goals, letting players choose which one to work on.

changes.name: Grind Achievements
changes.why: Players need not be locked into one specific grind goal, because a set lets them choose among several to fulfil it.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: Even when a game has open destiny, being made to choose goals forces players to commit to decisions about what their character is aiming for.

changes.name: Polyathlons
changes.why: Players may be allowed to choose which events make up the polyathlon, so the selection itself shapes the competition.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Within a fixed story, goal choices let players make some decisions, giving them a feeling of influence over how things go.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: With several goals to choose from, players and spectators know roughly what outcomes are possible but can't foresee the exact result as precisely as with a single goal.

patterns.name: Excluding Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: choose one of several, because completing one closes off the others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define goals whose completion conditions really conflict, with clear rules for who or what wins when they clash (usually order of completion or a tiebreaker). Players need to be able to choose among them for the trade-off to matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several goals are listed as alternatives, but a player can achieve all of them anyway, so nothing is given up.
patterns.knobs: how many goals exclude each other; whether exclusion is between players or within one player's own choices

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Once one excluding goal is finished, you know which futures are now impossible, so the game can safely remove leftover elements and actions tied to the failed goals.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: When finishing a goal cuts off other goals, such as pruning branches of a goal tree, players must be shown goal information that changes as play proceeds.

can_cause.name: Incompatible Goals
can_cause.why: Completing one goal makes the others fail, so those goals cannot all be achieved together, which is one way goals become incompatible.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: Because finishing one goal knocks out the others, players effectively choose which goals to pursue and can only complete a subset of them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Since one player's success blocks another's, or one goal blocks your other goals, stakes rise and conflict between players and choices increases tension.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When a goal to build competence can only be won by one party, it becomes a race to get there first.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: When choosing one goal rules out another, players must replay to try the alternatives, especially when goals are selectable.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When achieving one goal rules out another, players must decide which is more valuable to them.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Finishing your side of an excluding group voids the enemy's goals against you, so the need to evade disappears too.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Working out which goals exclude each other can be a skill players learn, especially if the game does not explicitly tell them.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: In a tree-shaped hierarchy, completing one goal can cut off branches, removing the goals under them and reshaping what remains available.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Rewards
conflicts_with.why: Excluding goals tie one player's success to others' failure, which is at odds with rewards that all players share.

conflicts_with.name: Tied Results
conflicts_with.why: Since completing one goal voids the others, a shared or equal outcome cannot occur, making ties impossible.

patterns.name: Deliver
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: move a game item to a specified object or place.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The object and the destination must both be specific, the trip must have some difficulty or opposition, and the delivery must be recognized by the game. The way there should require real movement.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An item that appears at the destination or is handed over by a menu, so no trip is made.
patterns.knobs: distance; what opposes the trip; how many items must be delivered

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: If the thing being delivered must be launched or thrown toward its destination, players end up needing to aim and shoot it.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Completing a delivery is a clear player action, so story threads can be advanced or changed depending on whether it succeeded.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A delivery task gives a clear errand to hand out, so it forms a natural basis for quests.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: When enemies actively oppose the delivery by evading or overcoming them, players must sneak the item past them, which creates stealth goals.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Since the item has to get from one place to another, the player must cross the game space, so traversal becomes part of the goal.

can_cause.name: Herd
can_cause.why: Herding is delivering with a twist: the thing being brought moves by itself, and players can only influence it indirectly rather than carry it.

can_cause.name: Player-Location Proximity
can_cause.why: Delivering means carrying an item to a spot, and if the item's position matters, players must go there themselves, making their own location matter.

changes.name: Artifact-Location Proximity
changes.why: In games played in the real world, deliveries may need the game to track how close the item is to its destination.

patterns.name: Collections
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: complete a whole set of smaller goals.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear set with visible progress, items with effort or variety behind them, and a reward for completion.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A completion list is displayed, but finishing it yields nothing and the items are trivial to get.
patterns.knobs: set size; rarity of items; reward for completion

can_cause.name: Check Points
can_cause.why: A collection can be made of checkpoints, so passing each one tracks progress, which helps most in races where players aren't forced down a single route.

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Since a collection needs its parts gathered, wanting the whole collection naturally pushes players to go out and gather the required items.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: When a collection requires certain game items, players may also have to arrange or combine them correctly, which can create configuration goals.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: A collection is itself a goal made from other goals, so having one automatically stacks smaller goals beneath a larger one.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Bringing several items together or solving several story problems can drive the plot forward, so collections can carry a story's progression.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Gathering items such as parts for repairing or building something gives players a purpose to pursue, so collections help form or structure quests.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: When resource generators feed items that a collecting goal needs, how many items are available varies with how often they are produced, so the goal's requirements keep shifting.

can_cause.name: Grind Achievements
can_cause.why: A grind achievement can be built by requiring a set of many small goals to be completed, so a collection of them forms the grind.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Collections paired with testing achievements can push players to repeat actions to complete sets, producing grinding and grind achievements.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Gathering a full set of things, such as every achievement, gives players a goal that spans many games.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: When victory is calculated from sets of gathered resources, that combination effectively forms a points system.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Almost any game item can be the thing that is gathered, so a collection goal shapes why those items matter to players.

changes.name: Team Elimination
changes.why: A team wipe-out can be seen as a set of individual removal goals gathered together, so designing that set shapes how it plays.

patterns.name: Alignment
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: line up your pieces or elements in a row.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to move or place pieces, and opponents must be able to interfere, so completing the line takes planning. The line needs a clear payoff such as a capture or a win.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Lines form by chance with no player influence or no payoff, so there is nothing to aim for.
patterns.knobs: required line length; how pieces move or are placed; whether opponents can block

can_cause.name: Capture
