can_cause.why: In board games, once pieces line up, the alignment commonly triggers a capture, so lining things up is the step that lets you take pieces.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: Getting pieces into a line is just one specific way of arranging elements into a required layout, so it counts as a configuration goal.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: A line that is almost complete is easy to see, so players can tell they are close to finishing and feel pulled toward it.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Opponents or moving pieces can block or remove elements from a line, which makes it harder to finish and gives players a reason to stop others.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Each piece added makes the line look more complete, so players can read their progress straight from the board.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Working out how to move or place elements into the right positions, or remove ones in the way, is a puzzle players must figure out.

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Aiming means lining up two points, the shooter and the target, so the aligning goal is what the shooting action consists of.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: Alignment can serve as the starting goal that players compete over, with the hill being a state only one of them can hold.

changes.name: Game Element Insertion
changes.why: Since players must place elements to form a line, the alignment goal changes how and where adding new pieces matters.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Players must move elements into position, and alignment can even decide which paths pieces take, so it shapes how movement works.

patterns.name: King of the Hill
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: take a desirable position in the game and hold it while others try to take it away.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Several players must want the same hold-the-spot condition that only one can have, with holding rewarded over time. The holder needs some edge or pressure so the position matters and the others are pushed to contest it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A marked zone exists but holding it gives nothing, or nobody can contest it, so people ignore it.
patterns.knobs: time required to hold; how fast score builds; advantage or penalty for the holder

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Players not holding the hill share a common enemy in whoever holds it, so they team up against that player, which pulls the leader back.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: The goal is never finished once and for all; a player must keep holding the position, and play continues while control is contested.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: Whoever currently holds the hill becomes everyone else's target, so who is being pursued keeps changing as control passes between players.

can_cause.name: Incompatible Goals
can_cause.why: Only one player or side can satisfy the goal at a time, so one player's progress means everyone else's is blocked.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Since others can take over the position, a player holding it can be disrupted, and each player can stop the others from succeeding.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: Every participant is given the very same goal to chase, so no player has a different objective from the rest.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Constant competition and conflict over holding the hill, plus the shifting alliances against the holder, keep players on edge and uncertain of the outcome.

can_cause.name: Alignment
can_cause.why: A hill-style goal can be built by changing an alignment goal, so alignment can serve as the way that goal is played.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Holding the top position requires winning control of it first, so that goal is carried out through ownership.

patterns.name: Predefined Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal set by the developers in advance, before the game starts.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Requirements and outcomes must be fixed in advance and visible enough for players to plan. A reward or consequence has to be attached to completing them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal list is shown, but completing items gives nothing and changes no decisions, or players invent their own aims anyway.
patterns.knobs: how many goals; how they are ordered or nested; how much is revealed up front; reward size

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Because the goals are fixed ahead of time and often must be met to finish, players are pushed to steer toward particular game states.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Since the goals stay the same, players can practice reaching them quickly or again across several games, and that skill is what mastery looks like.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Because the designer settles in advance how each goal relates to the others, it is easy to arrange them into ranked layers.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: Since how goals relate is decided before play, the designer can easily offer players a preset group of goals to pick from.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Even when it is random which goal applies, knowing the set of possible goals is already knowledge about the game.

changes.name: Analysis Paralysis
changes.why: When players face many preset goals, or ones that are hard to tell apart, choosing among them can become so taxing that they stall.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: When several preset goals are on offer, players get to decide which one to chase, giving them real choice.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Having preset goals in a game can reliably make players compete against one another over reaching them.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Goals introduced mid-game that support the story are set in advance, so they don't give away plot early or disturb the order of events.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: When players can pick among several preset goals, they can plan how their position will grow toward the one they chose.

changes.name: Supporting Goals
changes.why: Supporting goals can be preset by the designer, so their link to other goals is fixed before play starts.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: They are the simplest way to link players' goals to the story.

patterns.name: Conceal
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: prevent other players from learning the information they need.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need a way to hide things (hiding places, hidden information, decoys) and an opponent who actually searches or benefits from knowing. Without both, hiding is pointless.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal says to hide, but everything is visible to everyone anyway, or nobody is looking.
patterns.knobs: how much information is hidden; how many hiding places or decoys are available; how well opponents can search

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Hiding is something a player keeps doing for as long as someone could be searching, so the goal never gets finished once and for all.

can_cause.name: Unknown Goals
can_cause.why: Opponents can't see what a player is hiding, so they may not even realize that player is working on a concealment goal.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: Hiding the cheat actions from others, since they aren't shown as normal gameplay, is a main way to make cheating allowed yet secret.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Stealth is formed by joining the aim of hiding with the aim of getting somewhere; hiding is one of its two necessary parts.

changes.name: Survive
changes.why: Staying out of sight is one way to stay alive, so players with a survival goal tend to adopt hiding as well.

patterns.name: Rescue
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of freeing someone who is guarded or cannot move on their own.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a held target, something that guards it, and means to overcome or avoid the guards. Rescuing must change the game state, such as progress or reward.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A captive mentioned in the story, but freeing it takes no effort or has no effect on play.
patterns.knobs: strength and number of guards; distance and obstacles to the target; reward for success

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a player's own character is the one needing rescue, that player may be stuck waiting and unable to act until someone frees them.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Rescue goals give a story something to hang on, and the plot can supply motivation and information for them, so they support each other.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Freeing someone means getting past the guards holding them, so rescue is defined through goals of beating or getting around those opponents.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Rescue goals are often used as fixed plot points in a game's story, such as a kidnapped character who must be freed.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Guards actively try to stop players from freeing the captive, so the rescue goal is defined by overcoming opposition working against it.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A captive in need of freeing is an easy, ready-made starting point for building a quest around.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: A Guard keeping a prisoner against Rescue means the guarder's goal and the rescuer's goal cannot both be completed.

can_cause.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Giving some players the goal of saving helpless teammates ties them together in a stressful, shared situation.

patterns.name: Committed Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: the player commits in advance to completing a task, as if by contract.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Taking the goal must be optional, with a real cost for failing or for giving up other goals.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'commitment' prompt that can be dropped at any time with no penalty.
patterns.knobs: penalty for failure; reward for success; whether goals exclude each other

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Helping others now at a cost to yourself is a commitment, and you only get paid back if they return the favor later.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: When failing a goal would hurt badly, characters or players are effectively pushed to act in ways that serve that goal.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Having several goals to pick from means choosing one gives up others, so the player is pulled between competing options.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Even a single committed goal makes players weigh taking it on versus ignoring it, and several exclusive goals make that choice sharper.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: A goal an opponent is locked into becomes an especially valuable thing to uncover when it is also kept secret, so players seek that information.

changes.name: Closure Points
changes.why: Since players chose the goal and face penalties, both succeeding and failing hit harder emotionally, making the ending moment feel stronger.

conflicts_with.name: Pottering
conflicts_with.why: Pottering relies on handling resources without pressure from rewards or penalties, while committed goals depend on exactly that kind of pressure.

patterns.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: the conditions of the goal itself change as the game goes on.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Changes must follow clear rules and be visible enough that players can replan, yet not so large that the goal feels like a different one.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal whose displayed numbers or wording shift but whose real task, cost and approach stay the same.
patterns.knobs: which goal parameter changes; how big and how frequent the changes are; what triggers them

can_cause.name: Unknown Goals
can_cause.why: When players don't know what a goal currently requires because it has shifted, the goal is effectively hidden from them, which pushes them to go find out what it is now.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Changing goal characteristics can add goals to a hierarchy or remove some from it, altering which goals players have to pursue.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: Even the overarching goal of a game can have parts that change, such as a story twist revealing a new objective.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: When a goal shifts, plans players made toward the old goal may no longer fit, so they have to rethink and replan their development.

patterns.name: Main Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal that shows the player which challenges to take on and gives motivation to play.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must state the overarching aim clearly and tie play actions to reaching it. Completing it should be how one wins or finishes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A stated goal exists but other activities are more rewarding, so players ignore it.
patterns.knobs: how many main goals; whether all are required; how clearly they are shown

can_cause.name: Mandatory Goals
can_cause.why: A main goal has to be reached to finish the game, so by its nature it is a goal players must complete.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Main goals often sit at the top of a goal hierarchy, or stand for the whole hierarchy, shaping how the smaller goals beneath them are arranged.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Story and main goals are two separate ways to motivate players, so a main goal can be shaped to support the story's progression.

changes.name: Polyathlons
changes.why: Each game inside a polyathlon has a clear main goal, and those individual outcomes are what decide the overall result.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: Because main goals tell players up front what to aim for, they are goals fixed by design, though details may be filled in later.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Each match in a tournament has its own clear main goal, so the results of those matches determine the tournament outcome.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Games that can't be completed can still give a main goal showing what to strive for, such as surviving longer, so players can judge success.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: A main goal normally lets the game be completed, while an unwinnable game by definition cannot be completed, so the two pull against each other.

patterns.name: Configuration
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: arrange game elements in a required order or layout.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The target arrangement must be clear, and there must be real obstacles to reaching it, such as opponents, hidden information, time or a puzzle. Progress toward it should be visible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An arrangement is named as the goal, but it is reached automatically by ordinary moves, so it asks for no planning.
patterns.knobs: size and complexity of the pattern; how many elements; how hard it is to place them

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Completing a successful arrangement typically rewards the player by letting them take some game elements, so achieving the goal shows up as capturing pieces.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Because the goal depends on where elements sit relative to each other, players can see an arrangement nearly finished, which creates a sense of being close to completion.

patterns.name: Sidequests
patterns.what_it_is: A goal made of tasks that can be skipped when completing the main story.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Side quests need their own goals and rewards that are worth the detour, and a main quest they can be skipped from without breaking it. Some should lead to different outcomes or exclude each other so that choosing between them matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A fetch-and-return errand marked as optional whose reward is trivial or duplicated by the main path, so skipping it costs nothing and doing it adds nothing.
patterns.knobs: how many side quests there are; how big their rewards are; how many exclude each other

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because sidequests are extras, players decide for themselves how much of the game world to explore beyond the main path.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Sidequests sit beside the main quests and can be skipped, so they give players goals they are free to take or leave.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Sidequests are often built into the game's fixed story, adding detail to it without being required to progress.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A sidequest is simply a quest that is not part of the main quest line, so each one is a quest.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: When sidequests exclude each other or there are too many to finish in one session, players have reasons to play again.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Sidequests give rewards and character growth like other quests, which helps players with the main game, so they work as supporting goals.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Sidequests give players free choice over which tasks to take on, and those choices can themselves define the character.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Sidequests can add depth to the story around companions, letting players learn more about them without being forced into it.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Sidequests can flesh out the story of factions, so players get more detail without having to join or side with them.

changes.name: Main Quests
changes.why: Sidequests only exist alongside main quests, which they complement with optional extra content.

patterns.name: Interferable Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: other players or the game itself can speed up, slow down or break its completion.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Other agents need actual actions that can hamper the goal, and a reason to use them. Players should be able to tell who might interfere.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal others could theoretically interfere with, but no action in the game lets them, so it is effectively safe.
patterns.knobs: what actions interfere; who can interfere; how visible the goal and threat are

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When a goal can be meddled with, even someone on your own side may choose to meddle with it, which amounts to betraying you.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Because others can affect a goal's progress, they can be given the aim of stopping it, so the interferable goal becomes the target of their own goal.

changes.name: Symmetric Goals
changes.why: Players who share the same goal can still be given ways to disturb one another's progress, so the goals stay equal while remaining interferable.

patterns.name: Repeat Combos
patterns.what_it_is: Combinations where the same action must be repeated a set number of times within a time limit.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The required count and time window must be tight enough to need effort or skill but reachable. The reward must be worth the effort, and progress should be visible so players feel the chain.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A combo counter that rewards nothing, or a window so generous that every ordinary play meets it without trying.
patterns.knobs: number of repeats; length of the time window; size of the reward

can_cause.name: Arithmetic Progression
can_cause.why: Finishing one combo usually starts the next, and each new one asks for a steadily larger count, so the targets grow in even steps.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: The pattern is a kind of combo: you chain the same action several times in a row to earn something extra.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Completing a combo typically kicks off another one, so there is always a fresh target waiting for the player.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: The goal only exists while the clock is running, so it vanishes if the player can't finish the repetitions in time.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Players only chase these combos if they can see how far along they are, so progress is nearly always displayed on screen.

can_cause.name: Goal Achievements
can_cause.why: Some games turn a repeat combo into a named achievement, as in Team Fortress 2 where timed repeated kills unlock special awards.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Hitting the required number of repeats within the time limit pays out a bonus, which is the whole point of the combo.

changes.name: Grinding
changes.why: Bonus rewards for repeating an action quickly make tedious repetition feel more worthwhile, so grinding becomes more interesting.

changes.name: Reward Widgets
changes.why: Collecting reward widgets is a common action to count, so gathering them in quick succession can earn the player extra rewards.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Chaining the same combo again and again is a hard feat, so a goal asking for it or an audience watching it pushes players to sharpen their skill.

patterns.name: Unknown Goals
patterns.what_it_is: A goal that is unknown to the player at first, and sometimes later too.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goals must be genuinely hidden from the player at first and revealed later through play or clues. Hints should exist so players know something is there.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Goals that are labelled hidden but are listed in the menu or manual, or that can be guessed from the start.
patterns.knobs: when and how goals get revealed; how many hints are given

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When players know a hidden goal exists but not its details, they are pushed to set themselves the task of finding out more about it.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Even if which goal applies is hidden, knowing the full list of possible goals is already useful knowledge.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: Hiding goals is often used on the smaller steps leading to a main objective, so those subgoals are discovered along the way.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: When new goals are revealed mid-game, players who planned ahead have to rethink and change their plans.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: Designers often conceal goals that were fixed in advance so players can't see the planned story structure too early.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Keeping goals hidden lets a scripted story unfold in order without giving away what comes next, so players' actions fit the narrative.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Players can be shown what they will win for finishing a goal while the way to achieve it stays hidden.

changes.name: Selectable Set of Goals
changes.why: When hidden goals get revealed later, players who chose among goals have to reconsider which ones they picked.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: Once players have played, the goals they didn't know about become known, so the mystery is absent in later sessions.

conflicts_with.name: Symmetric Goals
conflicts_with.why: Hidden goals are pointless if players can guess from others' behavior that they want the same thing, or if goals can't be detected.

patterns.name: Enclosure
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: surround game elements with an unbroken line or wall made of other elements.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Pieces need placement or movement rules that allow forming a closed boundary, and enclosing must earn something such as capture or ownership.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An enclosing shape that can be formed but gives no benefit, or the board makes closing it impossible.
patterns.knobs: size of the board; what can enclose and be enclosed; what enclosing yields

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Once you successfully wall in something, those enclosed pieces typically end up captured by the player who built the surrounding wall.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: Enclosure is a kind of Configuration, because pieces must be arranged in a particular surrounding layout to count as succeeding at it.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Closing off an area can hand the enclosing player control or ownership of what lies inside, as an alternative to simply removing it.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: Enclosure can serve as the starting goal that players compete over, with the hill being a state only one of them can hold.

changes.name: Game Element Insertion
changes.why: Since the aim is to surround things, it shapes where and how players place new pieces, which must be positioned to form the surrounding barrier.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Because surrounding is the goal, it affects how pieces are moved, as they are steered to close gaps in a wall or avoid being trapped.

patterns.name: Symmetric Goals
patterns.what_it_is: A goal where the sides have essentially the same tasks and the same rewards for them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: All sides must have the same objective with the same requirements and rewards, and the means to pursue it must be comparable. Differences in start or tools quietly break the symmetry.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Everyone has the same stated goal, but different starting powers or rewards make it effectively different goals.
patterns.knobs: sameness of objectives and rewards; how equal starting conditions are

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: When every player pursues the same goal, nobody starts with a different objective, so the game is evenly set up between players.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because everyone's aims look alike, players can easily read what opponents are after and use that understanding to plan their own moves.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: If all players share the aim of eliminating each other, together with the ability to do it, each is pursuing being the last survivor.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Giving everyone the same goal makes them chase it at once, which is the plain form of a race.

conflicts_with.name: Asymmetric Goals
conflicts_with.why: Goals cannot be both identical and different for the same set of goals, so the two patterns exclude each other, though a game may use each for separate goals.

conflicts_with.name: Unknown Goals
conflicts_with.why: Hidden goals are pointless if players can guess from others' behavior that they want the same thing, or if goals can't be detected.

conflicts_with.name: Varied Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Playing another role with the same goal as before feels much the same, so replays offer less variety than with differing goals.

patterns.name: Asymmetric Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: players have tasks of different kinds that cannot be swapped between them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each goal needs a different path and a different payoff, with abilities fitted to the goals, and some check that no goal is clearly easier. Cyclic strengths between goals can keep fairness while keeping the difference.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are handed different goal cards, but all goals reduce to the same thing, like 'collect the most points', so play looks identical.
patterns.knobs: how much goal requirements and rewards differ; whether goals are assigned or chosen; how well they are balanced against each other

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players pursue goals with different requirements, they have to act differently from one another, so what each person does during play ends up unlike the others.

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: If goals differ from the very start of a game, players begin with unequal objectives, so their starting situations are already not the same.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Different goals create varied play, and that variety gives players reasons to play again, unless a single session already shows them everything.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since players work toward unlike goals, each game plays out differently, giving more variety than when everyone chases the same thing.

changes.name: End State Scoring
changes.why: Players can have different requirements and rewards when final scores are counted, so the same end result is judged differently for each of them.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Because goals differ, some players may get easier or more rewarding objectives, making it harder to keep everyone's chances fair.

conflicts_with.name: Symmetric Goals
conflicts_with.why: Goals cannot be both identical and different for the same set of goals, so the two patterns exclude each other, though a game may use each for separate goals.

patterns.name: Endgame Quests
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: complete a task available only at the end of the game, with a reward suited to that stage.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Quests must be unlocked by reaching the end phase and be hard enough for experienced characters, with rewards that matter to players who have already maxed out.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Extra quests that are just earlier quests with bigger numbers, giving rewards nobody needs.
patterns.knobs: unlock condition; difficulty; reward type and value

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Once players hit the endgame or finish the main objectives, these quests give them extra things to pursue that they aren't required to do.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Endgame quests are simply quests built like any other, differing only in being offered at the late stage where they fit.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: Players only get access to these quests after reaching the endgame phase, so the content is opened up by that progress.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Since players may have maxed out normal growth, these quests can reward stronger armor that is unobtainable before the endgame.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: These quests give players things to do once the endgame has begun, so they can keep playing as long as they find them interesting.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: The quests are meant to fit after the main storyline is done, so they usually avoid tying into it and instead extend play beyond it.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Because normal development may be capped, these quests can hand out better tools that only players in the endgame can earn.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Since players may have maxed out normal growth, these quests can reward stronger weapons that can't be gained before the endgame.

patterns.name: Team Elimination
patterns.what_it_is: Removing all members of the opposing team from the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Teams must be able to lose all their members for good, with no endless respawning. Eliminating members must be possible and worth pursuing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Members come back immediately, so 'wiping the team' never ends anything.
patterns.knobs: how hard members are to eliminate; respawn rules; team size

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: When a team is wiped out, its members have no way to keep playing, so the loss ends the game for everyone on that side.

can_cause.name: Mutual Goals
can_cause.why: Since wiping out a team is a way to win, opposing teams can all share the aim of removing the others.

can_cause.name: Shared Penalties
can_cause.why: Every member of a team suffers the same loss when the whole team is eliminated, rather than just the one who fell.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Watching a whole team go down can sometimes be dramatic and fun in itself, even for those who lose.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: When every character on a team is wiped out, the players controlling them are eliminated too.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Allowing a team to be wiped out changes how multiplayer matches are won and lost, since groups can be knocked out together.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Making team wipe-out possible changes what being on a team means, because the group's survival now depends on all its members.

conflicts_with.name: Spawning
conflicts_with.why: If team members keep respawning, a team can never be completely wiped out.

patterns.name: Main Quests
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of completing a task whose completion wins the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: One overarching quest must organize the main story and places, with side quests supporting it. Its completion should be what wins or concludes the game.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A quest is labeled main but can be skipped without consequence, and players never need it.
patterns.knobs: length of the quest chain; how many places and characters it touches; whether finishing ends the game

can_cause.name: Main Goals
can_cause.why: The main quest is the overarching quest of the game, so finishing it is what counts as achieving the game's central objective.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: The main quest carries the game's fixed story, tying plot events to gameplay so players follow a planned narrative path.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A main quest is itself a quest, just the biggest one, built like other quests and framing the smaller ones around it.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Because the main quest drives where players go, important groups are usually written into it so players at least learn these groups exist.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The main quest pushes players through the world, so key places are typically tied to it and players end up seeing them.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: The main quest guides who players meet, so major characters are usually woven into it and players become aware of them.

conflicts_with.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
conflicts_with.why: Online worlds must welcome players who join late and keep opposing factions apart, who don't share quests, so one shared overarching quest fits poorly.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: Finishing the main quest is a way to win, so a game designed so that nobody can win clashes with having one.

patterns.name: Mandatory Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of a task that must be completed in order to move forward.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must make it truly required for completion, with the requirement known to players. Any bypass undermines it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal is marked required but a shortcut lets players finish without it.
patterns.knobs: how many goals are required; whether all or a subset must be done

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: A hierarchy can contain required goals, as it must when it includes the main goal, though it need not.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Required goals tied to parts of the story make sure players experience those parts and connect goal completion to the narration.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: When defeating the opposition is required, a story reason for it is implicitly present.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: A required goal can be preset, so the designer decides ahead of time which goals players must complete to finish the game.

patterns.name: Combat
patterns.what_it_is: Actions aimed at killing or defeating opponents.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Opponents with opposing goals, an action set with real tradeoffs, and meaningful stakes for winning or losing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Fighting animations play, but outcomes are decided by stats alone and nothing the player does matters.
patterns.knobs: damage and health; range of weapons and abilities; enemy strength; penalty for losing

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Fighting gives players a set of capabilities they can use to deal with conflicts that arise in the game.

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: When players choose to attack other players, especially by killing or eliminating them, others in the game world react to that aggression.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Enemies can cause trouble for the player during a fight, so the player must keep watching and responding closely.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: A fight needs an opposing force pushing back, so games with it tend to be harder than games without it.

can_cause.name: Destructible Objects
can_cause.why: Fighting typically ends with things being removed or broken, so objects in the game can be destroyed.

can_cause.name: Extermination
can_cause.why: Some games let fighting take a back seat early and then make it the main focus in a late phase of wiping out opponents.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When joining a fight or picking targets is optional, or when attacks can be done in different ways, players get to decide how to act.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Losing fights can knock a player out of the game, particularly in fighting games where defeat removes the loser.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: In games where players control avatars, fighting can lead to one player's avatar being killed by another.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: Fighting against opponents that the game controls is a straightforward way to make players face challenges from the game rather than from each other.

can_cause.name: PvP
can_cause.why: Fighting between players is the typical way player-versus-player conflict shows up, so combat is the usual route into this pattern.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Since enemies can hurt the player during a fight, the player feels pressure and uncertainty about the outcome.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When players can pick between fighting and other activities, or among several attacks, each option costs something, forcing them to weigh choices.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Fighting that depends on aiming, timing and moving while the world keeps changing makes the player's physical skill decide who wins.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Fights often split results so player ability decides whether you hit while character skills and weapons decide how much harm is done.

can_cause.name: Rescue
can_cause.why: Players can free the captive by fighting and defeating the guards who are holding them.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Wanting to hold territory is often the underlying reason players fight, so combat shapes who controls areas.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Bases usually cannot fight themselves but can be targets of attack, so combat shapes how they are threatened.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: How well a player fights can be rewarded with experience points, which drives how the character grows.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Fighting is common in these games, either against other players or computer enemies, and it is often optional.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Fighting can cause units to be lost, so combat shapes how many units a player keeps.

conflicts_with.name: Boss Monsters
conflicts_with.why: Immunities and weak points can make fighting an ineffective way to beat a boss, so other solutions may work better than fighting.

conflicts_with.name: Private Game Spaces
conflicts_with.why: Giving players a private space lets them stay safe from attacks unless they allow neighbors in, reducing fighting.

patterns.name: Movement
patterns.what_it_is: Action of moving game elements around the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a space and clear rules for how elements move through it. The terrain and goals should make where and how far one moves matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Things technically move, but in a space so empty or with goals so unrelated that position never matters.
patterns.knobs: speed or distance per move; terrain costs; restrictions on direction

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Moving is one of the most common abilities in games, and different movement powers are what set apart pieces or characters.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Getting your elements to the right place or next to a target is how you catch or take something, so moving makes capturing possible.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Harder movement, such as more directions, momentum, or turning limits, makes controlling your element difficult and so makes play more challenging.

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: You have to move elements through the world to reach items and gather them, so movement is a prerequisite for collecting.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Many movement options and complications like acceleration, fuel, or line of sight give players many factors to juggle, making play complex.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: When moving elements pushes other elements around, that pushing can build or arrange structures in the game world.

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Through traversing, players can carry something from one place to another, which is what delivering requires.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Movement with no choices or challenge, especially over familiar ground, feels like tedious busywork players would rather skip.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Being able to move lets players pick where to go and what to do, which is a basic way of giving them choices.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Players have to move around a world to discover its areas, so movement makes exploring possible.

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: Any intentional movement through a world requires players to find their way, so navigating comes along with moving.

can_cause.name: Herd
can_cause.why: Because moving lets players cover distance and get things across the world, it also lets them guide other elements somewhere.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Moving is what lets players compete to get somewhere first, so racing depends on it.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Moving elements is how players cross the game world from one place to another.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Moving things that players don't control, like tiles or obstacles, can force players to react by moving, for example to dodge damage.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Evasion is done by moving something out of harm's way, so being able to move is what makes dodging possible.

can_cause.name: Maneuvering
can_cause.why: Maneuvering is essentially just moving game elements, so ordinary movement becomes maneuvering once it happens in a live game.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: In turn-based play, moving a piece often needs thought first, especially with blocks, obstacles or warps in the way.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: When capturing depends on moving, players must plan where to go based on the positions currently in play.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Movement can make aiming easier, and accuracy systems may punish fast movement or demand that players stand still.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Movement is an ability given to avatars, affecting how they behave in the world.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: When moving is the way to capture, the movement rules shape how hard it is to perform a capture.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Movement is something enemies can be given, and it shapes how they act in the game.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Moving elements change the world's state as they go, and the world's design in turn shapes how elements can move.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Movement is an ability units can be given, and it affects how they behave in the game.

changes.name: Variable Accuracy
changes.why: Moving quickly can ruin the chance of succeeding with an aimed action, so how a player moves changes how accurate they are.

changes.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
changes.why: How players move decides whether they reach or miss ability spots, and with random movement landing on one becomes luck rather than skill.

conflicts_with.name: Scenes
conflicts_with.why: Scenes can make the movement actions of gameplay unnecessary, which takes away the very activity that movement is about.

patterns.name: Construction
patterns.what_it_is: The player adds or rearranges elements to create buildings or structures.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Building must have a material or cost, restrictions, and results that affect later play, such as defence, production or scoring. Players need real freedom in what and where to build.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players press a build button and a fixed object appears, with no choices and no effect on the game.
patterns.knobs: cost and materials; build limits; how much freedom in placement

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Things players build become game elements in the world, and building them gives those elements new capabilities they did not have before.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: When building is made safe from destruction through private spaces or permanent results, it becomes a relaxed, low-pressure way to play.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Building offers many possible arrangements, so players are likely to stumble on combinations of parts that produce combo effects.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: A heavy focus on building in part of a game, when it adds new game elements, makes that part of play a growth phase.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: A heavy focus on building, when it improves elements that already exist rather than adding new ones, makes that part of play a phase of squeezing more value from them.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When there are many possible ways to combine what and how to build, players get to pick among a wide range of options.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Engines
can_cause.why: Players can assemble working structures or mechanisms inside the game world through building, though designers more easily provide them as features of abstract player constructs.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Building takes effort and materials up front for later benefit, so each construction action works like putting something in to get something back.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: The story of a game can itself be the thing players build, as in roleplaying games where the narrative is added to during play.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: What players build stays in the world, so their construction actions can leave lasting marks on how the game world looks and works.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Building alone does not make elements player-created; it does so only when players also have real creative control or craftsmanship over what they make.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Games can restrict building to certain players or roles, such as the engineer class in Team Fortress, which limits how much construction happens.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Building cannot usually be done without limits, so the material used for it turns into a resource that players must have or manage.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Because players can build structures, they can easily end up making protected places for themselves within the game world.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Choice among many things to build, together with creative control and self-set goals, makes it quite likely that players will plan ahead.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: When the story is something built during play, players and game masters need to tell and add to it as the game goes on.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Building can bring new elements into the world with a diegetic explanation, so they appear without feeling out of place in the setting.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Building things can create unexpected emergent effects, and players must try combinations to discover them; it also rarely triggers competition.

can_cause.name: Framed Freedom
can_cause.why: Letting players build things of their own within limits on what they have access to gives them creative freedom inside a clear boundary.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: When building things can produce combos or emergent play, players can get good at exploiting those possibilities.

can_cause.name: Player-Created Characters
can_cause.why: Assembling a character from parts or options before play, such as personalization, directly gives players a hand in what the character becomes.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: Building things lets players think in terms of different quantities of elements, and with creative control they can set their own aims for what to build.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: When players also have creative control, building things gives them an activity worth doing for its own sake.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Building things can produce combos and engines, and knowing how to build them well is knowledge that carries between sessions.

can_cause.name: Tile-Laying
can_cause.why: The page says laying tiles is nearly always a way of constructing something, since the world or structure is built piece by piece through placement.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Building something lasting, which others can also see, shows players a visible result of their work.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players building persistent worlds naturally end up with different game worlds, and so different play, between game instances.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Building can be offered more abstractly, letting players make structures or functions in constructs like gameplay engines rather than in the physical world.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Letting players build bases changes how bases work in the game, since they become something players make rather than receive.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can be what players construct, which changes how they appear in the game, as with player-made characters in roleplaying games.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Building lets players change the game world, and in early online worlds the world itself was the product of player construction.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Allowing installations to be built by players changes how they function, since they appear where and when players choose.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: In early online worlds, committed players could expand the rules and world, and later ones let players buy and build houses.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: The page does not give a reason for this relation beyond saying the building material becomes a resource when it was not one already.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Because other players or enemies cannot destroy constructions in single-player play, building suits it, and results can still be shown to spectators.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can be the result of building, as in Age of Empires and Civilization, and this changes how they come into being.

changes.name: Zero-Player Games
changes.why: By programming how robots or AI behave, players can still influence gameplay in a game where they take no direct actions.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: What players build remains after they log off, which gives their effort lasting value and a reason to return.

patterns.name: New Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: Skills gained during the game that open up new actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The ability must allow an action that was not possible before and be introduced at a time that opens new options. The game must give uses for it, such as new challenges.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A new ability that is only a number increase or a reskin of an old action, or one with no situation that calls for it.
patterns.knobs: when abilities are given; how many; how different they are from existing ones

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Handing out abilities depending on who is behind in the rankings, or trading them against losses elsewhere, evens out the field between players.

can_cause.name: Card Building
can_cause.why: When cards are what grant the abilities, players get new options by assembling or constructing those cards.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Gaining abilities opens up new kinds of things a player or character can do, which become areas where they are skilled.

can_cause.name: Deck Building
can_cause.why: With cards as the source of abilities, choosing which cards go into a deck decides which abilities a player gets.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Fresh abilities can make it harder for players to judge how likely their actions are to work, at least for a while.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: A spot or condition in the world can be defined by the ability it hands out, so entering it gives that power.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Gaining abilities makes players feel more powerful, even when enemies gain matching abilities and nothing really shifts.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Wanting more abilities becomes a goal because they give players more control over what happens in the game.

can_cause.name: Increasing Rewards
can_cause.why: Spreading new abilities over a session means players keep receiving something better as they progress.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Some abilities hurt the player, like gaining the power to spread a disease, so receiving them works as a punishment.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: The designer can fix in advance which abilities arrive at which points, so they follow the planned story.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: A new ability is something others lack until they get it too, and limiting how many can obtain it keeps it exclusive.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Because abilities widen what players can do, getting them is normally felt as a prize for progress.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Since abilities give more influence over the game, players pursue getting them as a stepping stone toward larger aims.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: New abilities, such as extra weapons, let players act in different ways as time passes, so play does not stay the same.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Granting abilities the player did not have before is a typical way the construct develops.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Acquiring new abilities can result from choices tied to advancement, so the character is shaped by what the player chose.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Gaining a power the character lacked before widens what it can do, which counts as growth.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: When individual units gain different abilities, they become distinguishable from one another, and so turn into characters.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Handing players an action they couldn't perform before is a direct way to reward them with new capability.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Owning a tool can give the player a new ability, which is a reason to chase ownership of it.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Players can plan by choosing which new abilities to acquire, which is a simple way to direct how their elements grow.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: Giving team members abilities they did not have before, on characters or on an abstract team construct, is a way the team develops.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: Handing players a new ability and tying it to a time limit makes it the clearest case of a temporary ability.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Gaining a power is attractive, but if it costs another ability, players must decide whether the swap is worth it.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Giving players new things they can do mid-game changes the active rules gradually, which also eases them into complexity.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: New abilities add to the set of actions already available, changing what is on offer.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Abilities can be granted to a player's abstract entity rather than a single character, so it develops over time.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Ammunition is a resource, so new abilities can provide new variants of it rather than being delivered by it.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars are one of the things that receive abilities, changing which actions they can carry out.

changes.name: Character Levels
changes.why: Gaining a level is one way abilities arrive, and new abilities are often what a level up brings.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can receive abilities as they develop, and these are tied to the actions they can take.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: When abilities become available influences whether players spend a phase growing their position.

changes.name: Exploitation
changes.why: The moment abilities are unlocked affects when players are able to make use of what they have gathered.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: Abilities can be attached to the things players act through, either to specific ones or to players generally.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Having more abilities gives players more options to pick from, increasing their freedom in the game.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: When abilities arrive affects whether and when players explore the world, particularly if some places need those abilities.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: Spending effort on things like technology advances can pay off by giving players abilities.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Power-ups are items placed in the world that give abilities, often only briefly.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Abilities can be presented as personal skills that a character develops over the course of play.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can be given abilities, which makes each one more valuable and possibly more like a character.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: Gaining abilities adds to what players can do, which lifts their perceived chance of succeeding at those actions.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Giving some players abilities that others lack can tilt the game in their favor, making the contest uneven.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: As different teams develop abilities at different rates, one side can end up stronger than another.

conflicts_with.name: Units
conflicts_with.why: Giving an ability to individual units can make them stand out so much that they act more like characters than units.

patterns.name: Self-Facilitated Games
patterns.what_it_is: The players themselves enforce the rules and keep all the records.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Rules must be clear and simple enough for players to apply and check themselves, with tokens or turn order lessening what must be remembered. Players also need to be able to agree on disputes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that claims players run it but hides required calculations or rule enforcement in an app or referee, so players do none of the work.
patterns.knobs: how much bookkeeping players do; rule complexity; helper tokens

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Since players can freely change the game state, they can improvise a way to let someone join or leave midway, mostly when the game isn't fiercely competitive.

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Because players interpret and uphold the rules themselves, they can also change them as play goes on, especially when a human game master is present.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: With no one else handling setup and bookkeeping, players must do that work themselves, and it grows with many game elements or large worlds.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: Players control the game state, so they can let beginners undo basic mistakes and try again.

can_cause.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
can_cause.why: Since no outside facilitator enforces how pieces and state are handled, players are free to move and alter game elements as they wish.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players are able to change rules and the game state, and can set the game up in varied ways, so they choose how it is played.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: Players can swap any outcome for one they agree on themselves, since nothing outside the group enforces the original result.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Players can improvise advantages or penalties on the spot to even out skill differences in head-to-head play.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Running the game takes effort from the people who facilitate it, and that contributed work counts as an investment in the game.

can_cause.name: Minimalized Social Weight
can_cause.why: Because players run the game themselves, they can pause play or the bookkeeping at any moment to talk to each other.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Players hold control over how play runs, so they can bargain over how a game session is arranged and carried out.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Players' ability to adapt things socially lets them agree together on how a play session goes.

can_cause.name: Optional Rules
can_cause.why: Since the players run the game themselves, they can make up extra rules before starting, and even while playing, to fit their tastes.

can_cause.name: Player Kicking
can_cause.why: Since the group itself runs the game, it can throw out a player whose behavior the others find unacceptable.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: Players can bend or break rules when everyone agrees, to make the game more enjoyable for the whole group.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Because players can interrupt, reinterpret and change things, they gain the power to shape play, including the setup of the gameplay space.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Nobody else supplies descriptions or narrative, so the players, and any game master, must create the story themselves.

can_cause.name: Synchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players are present together, which makes it easier to talk, share the workload fairly, and watch each other for mistakes or cheating.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: Players themselves can describe effects or tell uninterrupted stories, which plays the role of a cutscene without a separate facilitator.

can_cause.name: Late Arriving Players
can_cause.why: Players run the rules themselves, so they can slightly change or add rules to bring in someone who arrives late.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Players can run and organize things themselves, so they easily invent their own games on top of existing ones, like wagering.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: Players who run the game themselves can pair it with timed game instances in a meta game, letting them choose the overall duration.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Players run the game themselves, so they can change the state or ignore rules to even out how things are going.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Players run the game themselves, so they can agree to change rules or game state whenever the teams feel uneven.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Early online worlds were set up and maintained by their own players, with trusted ones allowed to change the code.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Players deciding rules together can improvise handicaps to keep one-on-one competition balanced.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Players deciding rules together can improvise handicaps between teams to keep them evenly matched.

changes.name: Configurable Gameplay Areas
changes.why: When players run the game themselves, they are the ones who decide how the play area is set up, so this shapes how configurable it is.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: With no outside referee, players themselves must track whose turn it is, so clear signals matter since mistakes are hard to undo.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: Having a dedicated facilitator is by definition hard to combine with players running the game themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: No dedicated person is handling the presentation, so keeping to the fiction can't be guaranteed.

conflicts_with.name: Game Servers
conflicts_with.why: A server implements rules in code, which leaves little room for players to run the game themselves, so the two are hard to combine without extra simulation effort.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Players hold the power to ignore or change the story, which undermines its being fixed beforehand.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players improvise descriptions and story, and the rules can't dictate how, so fit with the theme can't be guaranteed.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limits
conflicts_with.why: Players control the pace and can bend things, so deadlines are harder to enforce.

conflicts_with.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
conflicts_with.why: Players can replace any outcome with their own decision, so an overwhelming event can be softened or ignored.

patterns.name: Aim & Shoot
patterns.what_it_is: The player aims at a target and shoots.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need a way to point at a target and an outcome that depends on accuracy, with some difficulty from movement, distance or limited ammunition. The target must be clearly visible and the control precise enough to feel fair.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Shots auto-hit or snap to targets, so aiming is just pressing a button.
patterns.knobs: aim difficulty (target speed, size, distance); ammo count; hit tolerance

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: When an in-world character performs the aiming and firing, that power counts as something the character can do, so the pattern becomes an Ability.

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: Because aiming is a skill players can point at anyone, they can easily turn it toward whoever is ahead and attack that player.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Aiming can be used to take hold of targets, such as grabbing visible enemies or even collecting information instead of objects.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Taking aim and firing at enemies is a common way to fight, with hits causing damage or removing the target.

can_cause.name: Destructible Objects
can_cause.why: Shooting gives players a way to hit and break objects in the world, so those objects can actually be destroyed.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Successful shots at visible enemies can damage them or remove them from play, which achieves the goal of getting rid of them.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Players see and picture themselves hitting or triggering what they point at, so their action feels more powerful than it really is.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Once there is more than one possible target, players must pick which one to aim at, giving them a real choice.

can_cause.name: Line of Sight
can_cause.why: Normal aiming needs a clear view between shooter and target, so the shot depends on that visibility existing.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Hitting a target usually takes skill, so players cannot be sure a shot will land, except where dice-style rules replace aiming skill.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: When a straight view is not enough, players must work out a trajectory, such as an arc or a bounce, to reach the target.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Shooting gives you opponents and threatens damage or lost lives, though the stress can in turn make aiming harder.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Hitting a target while everything else keeps moving requires precise hand-eye coordination, which is exactly the dexterous skill this pattern describes.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Aiming takes a moment of sustained effort before firing, so the shot is itself an action stretched over time.

changes.name: Achilles' Heels
changes.why: Enemies with a weak spot make aiming harder in some fights, since players have to hit that specific spot.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Using friendly fire with aimed shots makes fights more challenging, because a missed or careless shot can hurt allies.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Enemies that aim at the player give the player something to dodge, creating goals about avoiding shots.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Enemies shooting at the player make it harder to move skillfully, just as enemy maneuvering makes the player's own aim harder.

conflicts_with.name: God Views
conflicts_with.why: From a high overview it is too hard to line up the shooter and target accurately, so precise aiming does not work well.

patterns.name: Turn Taking
patterns.what_it_is: One player takes actions, then the turn passes to the next players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear order and clear conditions for when a turn starts and ends, enforced by the rules or system. Designers should also deal with the first player's advantage and with waiting time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Nominal turns that nobody enforces, so players act whenever they like.
patterns.knobs: turn order; what ends a turn; whether there are extra turns or time limits

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: When only one person acts at a time, everyone else waits, and the active player may take ages weighing choices while others sit idle.

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: Someone has to go first, so the player order itself gives players unequal positions from the very beginning of the game.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: If turn order lets you finish one round and start the next back to back, you get two turns in a row, which is a strong chain.

can_cause.name: First Player Advantages
can_cause.why: Because one player must act before the others, moving first can give them a lasting edge, especially in games where everything is visible.

can_cause.name: Interruptible Actions
can_cause.why: When an action takes several rounds to finish, other players get turns in between and can change the situation, disrupting it.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: Players' waiting leads to slow play, so they start pushing one another along themselves to keep the game moving without a dedicated referee.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Players whose turn hasn't come must wait and watch, so they effectively observe others play, possibly guessing hidden aims.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: While waiting, players can think ahead about their next move, and aiming for back-to-back turns also rewards planning in advance.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Turns can ease pressure for the active player, yet waiting, slow thinkers and possible interruptions can make everyone else more anxious.

can_cause.name: Trick Taking
can_cause.why: Each player plays one card or tile in turn inside the larger round, which is the basic structure of a trick.

can_cause.name: Turn-Based Games
can_cause.why: Letting only one player update the game at a time divides play into turns, so any game using it is turn-based.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, players must wait for others to finish their turns before getting their own.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: When players act one after another, a slow player can feel pressured by others waiting and sense they are holding everyone up.

changes.name: Bidding
changes.why: Bids can be placed one after another in sequence, or everyone can bid freely at once, so turns change how the bidding feels.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: Games with cards often have players play or take them one at a time, so turns shape how cards are used.

changes.name: Drafting
changes.why: Picking cards or pieces from a shared pool goes player by player, so turns decide who picks what and when.

changes.name: Game State Overviews
changes.why: Waiting players have idle time, which they can spend studying the state of the whole game.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Turns let each player separate planning, acting and watching results, and also create waiting time, organised negotiation and calmer social contact.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: How well players can foresee what happens depends on whether the order of turns is fixed or flexible, since that tells them who acts next.

changes.name: Role Selection
changes.why: Choosing roles or actions requires an order in which players choose, and that order is supplied by turns.

changes.name: Secret Goals
changes.why: Players idle during others' turns can watch their opponents and try to work out what hidden objectives they are pursuing.

changes.name: Tension
changes.why: Waiting while an outcome is pending or an interruption could come makes existing nervousness stronger, though your own turn can relieve it.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Games with tiles often have them placed or drawn one player at a time, so turns shape how tiles are used.

changes.name: Token Placement
changes.why: Placing tokens needs an order of who puts down a token when, which turn taking provides.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: Real-time play has the game moving on its own, which clashes with players waiting for their turn, except in tick-based combinations.

conflicts_with.name: Synchronous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: If a turn leaves the other players with nothing to do, they are not really playing at the same time, which clashes with simultaneous play.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: On your turn you can plan without interruption, which can lower or remove tension.

patterns.name: Combos
patterns.what_it_is: A set of actions that together achieve more than each does alone.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A specific order or configuration must give a bonus clearly beyond the parts, hard enough to need skill or planning but discoverable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A combo counter is shown, but the extra effect is tiny or comes from simply spamming one action.
patterns.knobs: bonus size; sequence complexity; timing window

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: A combo is a new ability formed by chaining other abilities together, so performing the right combination gives the player a capability none of the parts had alone.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because combos can be made as hard to perform as the designer likes, pulling them off becomes a difficult task that tests the player.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Having many possible combos, and having intricate ones to execute, gives players lots of options and requirements to keep track of, making play more complex.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: A combo is a particular arrangement of actions, so achieving that arrangement can become a goal the player works toward.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Combos are usually long sequences that must be carried out in the right timing, so they act as one drawn-out action rather than a single input.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Engines
can_cause.why: Gameplay engines are player-built setups meant to make combos possible, or so frequent that they happen continuously.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: The character may determine how well individual actions work, but arranging them so a combo happens is up to the player, mixing both kinds of skill.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Combos are often used to hand players special abilities, either as an extra reward or as a way to make characters different from one another.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Because a combo needs the right moment and situation, players must plan ahead to find or set up the conditions for it.

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Well-timed button presses chained together in real-time play create tight press-and-response loops, giving clicking-style enjoyment without needing any clickable object in the world.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Combos can be hidden or can emerge from building things, so players must try different action sequences to find them.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: When combos aren't explained by the game, players talk about them outside play, which is an extra-game action.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Pulling off combos in a hard or complex game takes skill, so doing so shows mastery.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Paired with progress indicators, a combo chain shows players how near they are to a payoff, making the coming result easy to see.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Learning which elements or moves chain together, including hidden or built ones, is lasting knowledge that players can reuse to play better.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Players who know how to arrange owned game elements so they combine well can plan that setup ahead based on their knowledge.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Letting individual units chain combos gives single-player games a stand-in for team combos, since the units act like a cooperating team.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Combos are very common in fighting, where chaining attacks changes what a fight yields compared with single strikes.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: Combos can accompany building, since putting pieces together in particular ways can trigger extra effects.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Combat combos often change how much damage is dealt, as chaining actions alters the result of the attacks.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Combos can allow movement that is normally impossible, such as a double jump or rocket jump extending how far you can go.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: The most obvious combo reward is changing the points players receive, so chains adjust how scoring adds up.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
