conflicts_with.why: Combos often bring fast-growing or sudden jumps in power, so players who master them can gain large advantages and upset fairness.

conflicts_with.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
conflicts_with.why: Not all elements work alike, so some combinations of them can be much stronger, and this can upset fairness between players.

patterns.name: Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: Actions a character or unit can take that change the state of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each agent needs a clearly defined set of actions that visibly change the game state, and the sets should differ between agents so that choosing who does what matters. Players must be able to see what an action does and why using it is worthwhile.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Elements have actions listed on paper, but the actions are the same for everyone or never matter, so nothing is actually done with them.
patterns.knobs: which actions each element gets; how many and how strong they are

can_cause.name: Action Programming
can_cause.why: Players often build programs by arranging abilities in sequence, though the finished program isn't something the game element itself does, so it doesn't count as an ability.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Once game elements can perform actions, players tend to see them as agents who act in the world.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Chaining basic abilities into a sequence gives players a higher-level action, either with extra effects or because the moves couldn't be done otherwise or as fast.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Giving players many different abilities to choose from makes the game harder to master and take in, producing complex gameplay.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because abilities let players change the game state, they may come to believe they affect outcomes more than they actually do.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Having abilities to change the game state means players can decide what to do among several possible actions.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Abilities change the game state without forcing players to face challenges, so players can simply fiddle around with them aimlessly.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: A character needs some abilities to act at all, and without actions there is nothing that could define the character.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Abilities give players ways to change the game state by acting through their avatars.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Abilities give players ways to change the game state by acting through their characters.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Abilities give players ways to change the game state by acting through their companions.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Abilities give players ways to change the game state by acting through their units.

patterns.name: Game Pauses
patterns.what_it_is: A deliberate halt to the flow of game time and events.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Game time must otherwise run on its own, and the pause must truly stop events, possibly with limits or saving. It must be available at useful moments.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pause button exists, but the game keeps running or it is blocked in tense moments, so it can't be used.
patterns.knobs: when pausing is allowed; maximum pause length; what remains active during it

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players can stop the action themselves, they can play in short, loose bursts without committing to a long uninterrupted session.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: While the game state stops updating, nothing is happening for the players, which is by definition a stretch of idle time.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: A player-triggered pause is an action taken outside the game's own rules that lets players control when they engage with it.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Being able to trigger a pause gives players the power to decide when they play, especially in single-player games.

can_cause.name: Game Time Manipulation
can_cause.why: Freezing the flow of events is a simple, limited way of bending how game time runs.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Stopping progress lets players step away mid-game, though it only works well if other players aren't forced to sit idle.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Because play can be halted on demand, players can agree on when sessions start, stop, and how long they last.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Players can stop the game to fit around other people or obligations, so the game bends to social circumstances.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: With events frozen, players can think calmly, for example by looking over game state overviews without any pressure.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Being able to freeze play lets people pick the game up and put it down anywhere, fitting it into everyday life.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: In a single-player game, pausing is a simple way to let someone step away and return.

changes.name: Framed Freedom
changes.why: Pausing relieves players of the stress of choosing between actions under pressure, making a limited set of options feel more comfortable.

changes.name: Game State Overviews
changes.why: Pauses give players time to study overviews of the game state in peace, without events moving on.

changes.name: Inventories
changes.why: Opening an inventory typically freezes everything except item handling, so a pause changes how inventories behave.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: These games keep progressing automatically, so a pause is needed to break that continuous flow.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: These games update automatically at regular intervals, so a pause is what lets players halt that progression.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Since such games have no natural end, pauses let players create their own places to stop.

conflicts_with.name: Always Vulnerable
conflicts_with.why: Being exposed while away cannot work alongside stopping the game, since a pause would freeze events and shield players from threats.

conflicts_with.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The page says the two are hard to combine but gives no reason why.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Pausing often sends players to interface screens outside the fiction, which reminds them they are operating a game.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Stopping the action lets players disengage, which can dissipate the tension that continuous play builds up.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limits
conflicts_with.why: Pausing lets players interrupt their experience of time pressure, though the limit still applies once play resumes.

patterns.name: Turn-Based Games
patterns.what_it_is: The game is split into clear parts where the player can think and choose an action.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must clearly mark when planning and acting are allowed and when not, with a clear end of turn. Decisions need to reward the time spent thinking.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game described as turn-based where actions are really continuous and the turns do not limit anything.
patterns.knobs: how long a turn lasts; actions per turn; whether turns are simultaneous or alternating

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Because play is split into clear turns, there are obvious stopping points, so everyone knows exactly where the game stands when they return.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Clear stopping points between turns give players natural places to agree on when to stop or continue, so session length can be discussed.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: When a shared time limit is put on the turns, play advances in fixed time steps, which makes the game tick-based.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, players wait while others take their turns.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Turns give players time to think through their many options, supporting the feeling that their choices matter.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: In games built on alternating moves, others must wait on each decision, so a player who stalls may feel bad and be pushed to hurry.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Taking turns gives players time to think about each move, which suits movement puzzles.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Turns give players voluntary time to plan, even in single-player games.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Clear turn boundaries let players act at different moments and do other things while waiting, which makes play across different times workable.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: With time between turns, players can think through captures carefully, so capturing relies more on thinking than on quick reflexes.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Taking turns gives players time to think, so fighting becomes about reasoning and planning instead of fast reactions.

changes.name: Game Pauses
changes.why: Turns create clear break points, so pausing is easy and players can tell exactly where to resume.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: Waiting time lets players plan ahead when consequences are predictable, though this can also make the acting player overthink.

changes.name: Synchronous Gameplay
changes.why: When players must wait for others to finish turns together, downtime appears, and it hits harder than in asynchronous play.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: One updates continuously with the clock while the other waits for players to move, so they are hard to combine, though some games manage it.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Waiting for other players' turns in multiplayer removes choice during that time, though it is accepted as fair.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Waiting for others to plan and act forces downtime and can lead to over-long deliberation.

patterns.name: Capture
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: remove a game element or bring it under your own control.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Clear rules for who can capture whom and by what action, plus a real consequence for the loser (lost unit, lost ability, retaliation).
patterns.just_a_label_when: Pieces are called 'captured' but nothing changes for either side; they come back at once or the loss costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: which pieces can capture or be captured; the capture method; whether captured pieces switch sides or leave play

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Capturing is tied to particular game elements, so each piece that can take others effectively carries its own capturing power as an ability.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Taking or removing opposing pieces is a common way for a game to give players fighting against each other.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Some captures need several pieces placed together, such as flanking a target from both sides, so combining positions produces the capture.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: If you are the target of capture, there must be a penalty and a way to move, so escaping capture is itself an evasion goal.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Capturing something can serve as a basic bottom-level goal whose completion contributes toward a higher goal in the hierarchy.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: When capturing a thing is the aim, others want to protect it, which gives them a goal of defending what could be taken.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Capturing is often how a player defeats an opposing element, so it commonly sits as a challenge to beat within the goal structure.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Being at risk of capture gives the targeted player a reason to avoid it, such as fleeing, which works against the capturer's aim.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Capturing something has a clear purpose that a story character can easily want, so it works as a quest with an in-world reason.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: When one side tries to capture and the other to evade, giving one side a movement edge makes the other's task hard.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Capture goals in real time require players to physically reach or catch things while the game keeps updating, which tests their coordination.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Elements that try to capture the player's pieces become enemies, or enemies arise from trying to avoid being captured.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: A Guard defending against Capture sets up goals where one side's success blocks the other's, so one completed goal rules out the other.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Taking an opponent's pieces together with a change of who controls them makes the capturing player the new owner.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Taking over enemy units through a change of control gives players the abilities those converted units have.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Capturing an item or unit and gaining control of it moves the special abilities attached to it over to the captor.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: When capturing is paired with bidding, movement or investment, players must reason out the best way to take pieces with the smallest cost.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Capturing through movement or investment gives players alternative ways to act, and picking among them depends on the current state.

changes.name: Deliver
changes.why: When items being carried to a place can be captured, those carrying them need to defend them, which changes how delivering plays out.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Because a mistake in positioning can lead to a piece being lost, careful steering and placement matter more.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: A capture can happen when guards fail at protecting something, which then gives players the chance to rescue it and restore the guarding.

patterns.name: Extended Actions
patterns.what_it_is: An action lasts so long that nothing else can be done during that time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The action must take long enough that doing it means giving up other actions, and it should carry risk, such as being interruptible or locking the player in. Effects can scale with duration or kick in after a threshold.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A short animation or brief delay that never stops the player from doing anything else, so no real trade-off exists.
patterns.knobs: duration required; whether it can be interrupted and how effects scale with time

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Stronger actions can demand more preparation and resources before they work, so power is paid for with commitment and the options end up evened out.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because an action must be kept up for a while instead of finishing instantly, it is harder to carry out than ordinary actions.

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: Since the action must run for some time before it pays off, anything you start has its result arrive later than the moment you began.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: If the required time is long enough, players probably cannot finish in one sitting and must come back in another session to see it completed.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: With several things to watch, the stretch before completion can be a quiet wait, and handling it well takes skill at shifting attention between them.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: When an action has a threshold before any effect, finishing it is a visible moment of completion, particularly when several players are doing it together.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When an action needs commitment up front or a stretch of uninterrupted time, players have to think ahead about when and how to start it.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Staying committed to an action that can be interrupted, or leaves you open to enemy attacks, makes players anxious about whether it will succeed.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Time spent on one lengthy action is time not spent on other things, so players must choose between that one and several ordinary actions.

can_cause.name: Variable Accuracy
can_cause.why: Holding an aim longer can make shots more precise, so the time invested in the action directly improves how accurate the result is.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Combined with interruptible actions, simply finishing a lengthy action becomes a goal that players must keep protecting until it completes.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Actions that grow in consequence through compounding progression make effort pay back more and more over time.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Making an ability require sustained performance changes how it is used, so lengthy actions can be seen as altering abilities.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Taking control of a place can require holding it continuously for a long time, as in capturing spawn points.

changes.name: Artifact-Location Proximity
changes.why: Games detecting real-world nearness may need the action to last a while so the technology can reliably confirm it.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: When several players must keep performing an action together, finishing it shows that they were all willing to cooperate.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: Building activities can be lengthy actions, needing many individual steps or resources that could have gone elsewhere.

changes.name: Controllers
changes.why: Controllers are game elements that supply lengthy actions which don't come from the player's own focus locus.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Crafting is a lengthy action tied to a focus locus, so making things takes sustained effort by that element.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Lengthy actions can limit choice when there seems to be too much, though they can also add ways of using actions.

changes.name: Player-Artifact Proximity
changes.why: Games detecting real-world nearness may need the action to last a while so the technology can reliably confirm it.

changes.name: Player-Avatar Proximity
changes.why: Games detecting real-world nearness may need the action to last a while so the technology can reliably confirm it.

changes.name: Player-Location Proximity
changes.why: Games detecting real-world nearness may need the action to last a while so the technology can reliably confirm it.

changes.name: Player-Player Proximity
changes.why: Games detecting real-world nearness may need the action to last a while so the technology can reliably confirm it.

patterns.name: Real-Time Games
patterns.what_it_is: Game time runs at the same pace as real time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game state must update continuously on its own, with something (a computer, a timer, physics) driving it. Events must demand reaction within a short span so waiting has a cost.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with a visible clock or animation, but the state only changes when a player acts, so waiting costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: speed of the game clock; how long players have to react; whether pauses are allowed

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Because the game keeps moving without waiting, players must steer and fire at targets that are also moving, so aiming becomes a core action.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since the game keeps running on its own, players must either time actions well or react quickly, so they cannot look away.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: The game must run along with the passing of time, so that real-world moments can line up with and trigger game events.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Because the game keeps flowing continuously, actions can stretch over a period of time instead of finishing in one step, though they can be interrupted.

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When the game keeps going and challenges players, they can fumble and fall behind, and the chaos of failing becomes fun, even with pauses available.

can_cause.name: No-Ops
can_cause.why: The game updates itself regardless of what players do, so choosing to do nothing is always possible and the world still moves on.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Since the game doesn't wait, players must respond within a limited window or the situation changes without them.

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Because actions happen live, players can time button presses and chain them into combos, producing feedback loops that make pressing buttons satisfying.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Real time is needed for these actions, since they only matter when the player must act while the rest of the game keeps changing.

can_cause.name: Maneuvering
can_cause.why: Because events keep happening without waiting for you, movement demands constant attention and good timing, which turns it into maneuvering.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: On their own they do not create tension, but fast planning or action demands in real time can.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Parts of asynchronous play can take on real-time traits, so the real-time quality changes how that kind of play feels.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: Capturing often depends on good timing against how the game updates, so real-time pace shapes how capture actions are done.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fights often hinge on correct timing, though in real-time strategy the fighting between units can resemble turn-based or tick-based combat.

changes.name: Synchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Players acting together at the same moment fits well with a game that runs continuously, so real time suits and shapes this kind of play.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Planning has to happen while the game keeps running, so players feel short on time and tension rises.

changes.name: Togetherness
changes.why: Moving play to real time can shift the shared feeling from talking with each other to interacting through physical, bodily action.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Real-time elements can be mixed in, such as physics playing out within a turn, so a turn-based game can partly run in real time.

conflicts_with.name: Analysis Paralysis
conflicts_with.why: Little time to plan means players can't get stuck over-thinking their options, so real time works against this problem.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: Because play continues continuously, players must act or at least pay attention, leaving less room for idleness.

conflicts_with.name: Stimulated Planning
conflicts_with.why: Constant time pressure limits how much players can plan ahead, which undermines designs that encourage careful planning.

conflicts_with.name: Token Placement
conflicts_with.why: Placing tokens depends on a fixed order of turns, which is hard to keep when everything runs continuously.

conflicts_with.name: Turn Taking
conflicts_with.why: Real-time play has the game moving on its own, which clashes with players waiting for their turn, except in tick-based combinations.

conflicts_with.name: Turn-Based Games
conflicts_with.why: One updates continuously with the clock while the other waits for players to move, so they are hard to combine, though some games manage it.

patterns.name: Secondary Interface Screens
patterns.what_it_is: Screens with actions and data that add to the game's main interface.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Move actions and information that do not fit the main view into dedicated screens, such as inventory or character sheet, and make them quickly reachable. They matter when they hold real decisions.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A menu screen that only repeats what the main interface already shows and offers no extra actions.
patterns.knobs: which actions and information go on separate screens; how many screens; whether the game pauses when open

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Clues can be handed to players on a separate screen, and from there switched on so they appear in the main view.

can_cause.name: Dialogues
can_cause.why: Conversations get their own screen, which is a typical case of a game element that needs a separate interface.

can_cause.name: Game Pauses
can_cause.why: Opening a side screen commonly stops the main action while the player reads or chooses, so the pause comes along with the screen.

can_cause.name: Inventories
can_cause.why: Item holdings are usually managed on a dedicated screen because they don't fit the main view, as in Diablo.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: These screens offer actions the game world doesn't show as real things, so features that exist only for the player appear.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Since the screens pause play and show extra information, players get time to think ahead before acting.

can_cause.name: Transferable Items
can_cause.why: Inventory screens let players move items around, which turns those game items into things that can be passed on.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Map screens in the interface can display parts of the world beyond what players can reach, suggesting a larger world.

changes.name: Action Programming
changes.why: Programming a character's actions is one of the things that can get its own dedicated screen.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: A character screen is where players change a character's traits or grant abilities, so it shapes how growth happens.

changes.name: Characteristics
changes.why: On a character screen players can change a character's characteristics, so the screen is how those values get altered.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Character handling takes place on a dedicated screen, which changes how players manage their characters.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: Clues can be given on a side screen and then switched on to be displayed in the main interface.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: A party screen offers actions for managing companions that travel with the player.

changes.name: Difficulty Levels
changes.why: Players can change difficulty from a screen outside the main play view.

changes.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
changes.why: A side screen lets players turn automatic difficulty adjustment on or off.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Inventory screens change how players interact with their gear, such as handling what they carry.

changes.name: Equipment Slots
changes.why: Inventory screens can be used specifically for placing gear into the slots a character has.

changes.name: Free Gift Inventories
changes.why: Inventory screens can serve as the place where players access gifts offered to them.

changes.name: Game Element Trading
changes.why: Inventory screens can be the place where players exchange game elements with others.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Secondary screens can change how players perceive the game world compared with what the main interface shows.

changes.name: Gameplay Statistics
changes.why: Statistics can have their own screen where players look at figures about their play.

changes.name: Handicap Systems
changes.why: Handicaps can be reached through a side screen where players adjust them.

changes.name: High Score Lists
changes.why: Score lists can be displayed on their own screen separate from the main play view.

changes.name: Improved Abilities
changes.why: Character screens are where players apply upgrades so that existing abilities get better.

changes.name: Interruptibility
changes.why: Because these screens pause play, players can stop whenever they like and come back later.

changes.name: Mules
changes.why: Handling mules can be done on a separate screen, as part of managing programmed actions.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: On a character screen players can give characters abilities they didn't have before.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: A party screen can provide actions concerning non-player characters who accompany the player.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Managing a group of characters can get its own screen with actions for the members.

changes.name: Player Created Game Elements
changes.why: Things players make can have their own screen for creating and handling them.

changes.name: Player Kicking
changes.why: Removing other players from a game can be offered through a separate screen.

changes.name: Player-Created Characters
changes.why: A party screen can give access to actions for characters the player created.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: Players decide how a character grows by making choices on a character screen.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: Side screens don't show other players the same world the main view does, so they suit private areas.

changes.name: Public Player Statistics
changes.why: Secondary screens change how players view the publicly shared numbers about players.

changes.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
changes.why: Buying advantages can be handled through its own screen rather than in the main view.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Quest information and handling can be placed on a dedicated screen.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: Travel between places can be chosen through a side screen, skipping the main view.

changes.name: Save Files
changes.why: Handling saved games is an out-of-game action that side screens commonly support.

changes.name: Save-Load Cycles
changes.why: By managing save files on a screen, they influence how often and when players save and load.

changes.name: Sidequests
changes.why: Optional quests are among the elements that may have their own screen, like main quests.

changes.name: Sockets
changes.why: Inventory screens can be applied to socket handling, such as fitting things into items.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Spawning is one of the elements that may get its own screen for player choices.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: These screens often hold non-diegetic features and take players away from the world itself.

patterns.name: Maneuvering
patterns.what_it_is: Controlling the movement of objects in real-time games.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Real-time movement with consequences for bad control, such as obstacles, enemies or timing. Speed and number of hazards decide the difficulty, and players need a good view of space.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players can steer, but nothing needs avoiding or reaching, so movement is empty.
patterns.knobs: speed; number of obstacles; control sensitivity; penalty for collisions

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Steering things in real time means you must keep watching the screen and respond at the right moment, so your attention is constantly occupied.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Guiding an element through a live game takes hand skill, and fast speeds or tricky views make that physical skill matter even more.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Like other kinds of movement, steering lets you decide where to go and how to get there, giving you many options.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When the aim is to reach a place before others, controlling your movement skillfully is what decides who wins the race.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Steering and positioning tasks test player skill, so players feel they affect results even with just one correct course of action.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Aiming often happens while you or your target is moving, so how well you steer affects how easy it is to hit.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: No explanation is given on this page for the link beyond its mention as affecting how worlds are experienced.

patterns.name: Deck Building
patterns.what_it_is: During a session, players add cards to their deck and then play with them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a varied supply of cards with different prices and effects, and the cards must go into a deck that is reshuffled so that choices show up later. Players should be able to combine cards in ways that matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players add cards, but they are all alike or so weak that the deck plays the same whatever is chosen.
patterns.knobs: card supply and variety; card prices; whether cards can be removed

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Many different card types whose effects combine in varied ways give players a lot to juggle and understand.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Players assemble their own deck piece by piece, so deck building lets them construct something during play.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Cards are added to a deck one at a time as players pick them, which works like drafting.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide for themselves which cards go into their deck, giving them real control over its contents.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Improving a deck becomes a goal for players, and reaching it makes them feel more capable.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Cards enter decks that they weren't part of before, though only weakly since they already served as resources earlier.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Handling many card types and their interacting effects well lets players demonstrate skill.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Newly acquired cards can make what a player is able to do stronger than before.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Acquired cards cost something now and pay off later, since they may help once drawn at the right time.

can_cause.name: Legacy Games
can_cause.why: Permanently altering or destroying physical cards makes lasting changes to the game, turning deck building into a legacy game.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: If decks can be changed between game sessions, players get an extra layer of play around the deck itself.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Cards added to the deck can give players actions or effects they didn't have before.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Reaching deck-improvement goals pushes players to think ahead about what to acquire and how it fits.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Working toward a better deck leads players to plan longer-term about which cards to collect.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: With a large enough pool of cards, players rarely end up with the same deck twice, so games differ.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Shaping the set of cards you use lets you develop your player's construct through card choices.

can_cause.name: Cooldown
can_cause.why: Newly acquired cards go to the discard pile and likely won't be drawn soon, so they sit unusable for a while.

can_cause.name: Cycle Deck Engines
can_cause.why: Because players pick which cards join their deck, they can gather draw-granting cards that let them keep pulling new cards continuously.

changes.name: Combos
changes.why: Players pick cards that work well together, which raises the odds of pulling off combinations.

changes.name: Decks
changes.why: Cards get added to decks one at a time during play, so a deck's makeup changes over the game.

changes.name: Discard Piles
changes.why: Newly acquired cards usually land in the discard pile, so they wait before they can be drawn.

changes.name: Gameplay Engines
changes.why: Players choose cards that fit together into self-reinforcing setups, so deck choices shape how engines form.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: What is in a player's deck decides what they are likely to hold when drawing.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: By picking which cards to own, players influence how likely certain draws are, shaping the luck they face.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Building a deck over time is one way to grow and shape a construct.

patterns.name: Focus Loci
patterns.what_it_is: World elements through which the player performs actions and decides how to use them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Give players clear elements through which their actions affect the world, and decide how many there are and whether control can switch between them. The actions offered must really be tied to these elements.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character model is on screen, but all commands act on the world globally, so the avatar is just decoration.
patterns.knobs: how many controllable entities; which actions each one provides; whether control can be switched

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: When a focus locus sits inside the game world, it acts as the in-world entity that carries out the player's actions, so it counts as an agent there.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each individual locus may need its own steady attention, so having several of them to run can overload the player with things to watch.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Since most loci act by being present somewhere in the world, where they stand determines which parts of the map a player holds.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Loci are how players reach into the world, and each type changes the world in different ways, shaping how it can be affected.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The kind of locus decides what the player can see and know, so some story forms, like detective plots, fit poorly with certain loci.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Controlling several loci lets one player direct a whole group, with detail depending on how many individual loci they manage.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Which locus the player acts through affects how a fixed story can be laid out and what the player experiences of it.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Having multiple loci lets one player command a whole team at fine detail, though they must keep switching attention between its members.

patterns.name: Player Created Game Elements
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements that players make themselves for use in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must offer creation tools and a way for the made elements to enter play and matter there. Designers must also handle effects on balance and on the economy.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players can make things, but they stay cosmetic or are never used in actual gameplay.
patterns.knobs: what players may create; how much freedom they have; how created items enter the game

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because players get to make game elements themselves, they gain real decisions about what to build, which gives them more choice over how they play.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Created elements are only meaningful if they can be brought into play, so making them naturally depends on a way to insert them into the game.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Items that players make can be handed over or swapped with other players, which gives trading something to exchange.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Through building or crafting actions, players put new items into the game world and feel that they made those items.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: When players design whole levels, such as in editors outside the main game, the created elements can grow from single items to complete playable areas.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Being able to make things gives players relaxed, aimless tinkering to do, provided the game does not add pressure like tension.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: When players build parts of the game, especially their own characters, they decide how they will play their role.

conflicts_with.name: Game Element Trading
conflicts_with.why: If players produce too many of a type of element, its value drops very low and the trading market can collapse.

patterns.name: Drafting
patterns.what_it_is: Players take turns choosing game elements from a shared set until the choices run out.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be real choices between elements of differing value, with a clear order of picking. The picks must carry on to later play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players take items one at a time but they are all the same or the choice is forced, so it is only a handout.
patterns.knobs: how many options per pick; order of picking; how many picks

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: Drafting means several players take part in picking from shared game elements, so picking becomes a joint activity that the whole group takes part in.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: If players can't choose what to take and nothing happens between picks, drafting is just routine handing-out of items, which adds dull busywork.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When players get to decide which element to take from several options, drafting gives them real control over what they end up with.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Players can pick abilities or elements suited to counter the other players' strategies, which evens out matchups.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: When forming teams is part of the game, players choosing members in turn can spread talent more evenly across teams.

changes.name: Collectible Card Games
changes.why: A separate drafting phase at the start is needed here as a way to split cards among players before they play.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: Drafting can be how players build their future draw stacks, for instance by buying cards one at a time during play.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Drafting is often how a player's hand gets assembled, whether in a draft phase or by picking cards one by one.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: It is one of the tools for evening out players of differing ability, so matches against each other stay balanced.

changes.name: Resource Competition
changes.why: When players draft from the same limited pool, each pick removes an option for others, so they compete over scarce elements.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: When the drafted elements are members of teams, drafting can help even out the strength of opposing teams.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Letting players pick from several random outcomes gives them choice while the options themselves remain random.

patterns.name: Extra-Game Actions
patterns.what_it_is: Acts prompted by the game that do not affect the current play.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs real value in preparing, documenting, negotiating or running things outside the game state, such as planning, saving, storytelling or creating content, and the rules or interface must support it. Players should gain something from them later.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A menu or notebook option that nobody has a reason to use because nothing in play benefits from it.
patterns.knobs: how much the game supports and rewards out-of-game preparation, sharing or record keeping

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: When game events push players to do things outside the game, especially alongside outside input, they may start seeing real-world things differently.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Such actions are a way to give a game result effects beyond the game itself, since they don't touch the running game state.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players get extra options beyond in-game moves, and these can be used without changing how the game itself unfolds.

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Telling the tale of how a session went is an action outside the game, letting players describe characters and themes as their own.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: When a game offers lots of these outside actions, players may end up repeating them tediously.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Players put effort into things like stories or characters that don't belong to one game instance or any game state change, yet matter to them.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Betting or minigames need actions that live outside the inner game, so those actions create a further game around it.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: When nothing can be done during play, players' only choices come from actions taken outside it, such as setting the game going.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Players can make elements outside of play itself, such as before a session starts or by making real-world props.

can_cause.name: Save-Load Cycles
can_cause.why: Saving and loading store or restore the whole game state instead of being play moves, so they are outside actions that let players repeat them.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: If the game offers no actions while running, the 'players' need outside actions to start it or make meaningful choices about it.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: Players can send signals to onlookers, which makes it more likely or better quality that those watchers will help.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: Actions outside the regular game interface, when kept hidden, give players cheating moves the game tolerates; this works together with concealing them.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: For teams lasting beyond one match, members can train between games, and that outside practice is a way the team improves.

changes.name: Spectators
changes.why: Actions outside normal play let designers control how likely watchers are to notice what players are doing, and can pass information to them.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: The two are defined as mutually exclusive, so an action that doesn't touch the ongoing game's state can't also count as upkeep.

patterns.name: Hotseating
patterns.what_it_is: Players take turns sitting at one interface and making their moves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a clear rule for when control changes hands, and the waiting players need something to do or to watch so the wait is tolerable. If secrecy matters, players must not see each other's turns.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several players nominally share a device but the game never enforces turns, so they just crowd around or one person plays.
patterns.knobs: what triggers a handover (turn end, death, level end); turn length or time limit

can_cause.name: Backseat Gamers
can_cause.why: When players aren't meant to see each other's moves, everyone waiting beside the active player ends up watching and offering unrequested advice.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Only one person can use the interface at a time, so everyone else has to sit idle until their turn comes.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Players waiting for their turn can watch the current player, so they take on an onlooker role toward each other.

can_cause.name: Turn Taking
can_cause.why: Since only one player can use the shared device at once, the game must have a rule for when control passes to the next player.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: Players share a single device and take turns, which lets several people play without any extra communication interface.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Passing a single interface around lets several people play together even when only one player's worth of screen and controls exists.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: These games already have turns, so adding shared-device play is a small change that lets extra players take part.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Death is a natural moment to hand play over to another player, adding waiting time to the one who died.

conflicts_with.name: Split-Screen Views
conflicts_with.why: Both solve the same problem of several players sharing one screen, so using them together is redundant and one makes the other unnecessary.

patterns.name: Crafting
patterns.what_it_is: Creating game items from other items or materials.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Crafting needs inputs worth gathering and recipes or choices whose products matter for play. It should cost something, like materials, time, skill or tools, and the result should be better than what could otherwise be had.
patterns.just_a_label_when: There is a crafting menu, but the same items are easier to find or buy, so nobody needs it.
patterns.knobs: recipe cost; crafting time; skill or tool requirements; how many recipes

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Crafting means building game items through actions, so each crafted item is the result of a construction process the player carries out.

can_cause.name: Converters
can_cause.why: Crafters take in materials and turn them into different or improved items, so the people doing it act as converters.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: If the steps that make crafting possible can only be done before play starts, those steps sit outside the game itself.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Crafting needs no risk or player skill, so it is easy to turn into dull repeated work for materials or items.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Crafting can modify items you already own, and one result of that is making them work better.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Crafting normally uses up resources, at minimum play time, so the player pays now to get an item later.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Modifying or creating items, especially tools needed for other crafting, can give players things they could not do before.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Because players make the items themselves, what appears in the world is content that players produced.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Crafting can be restricted so only characters with special abilities can do it, which makes those abilities matter.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing which items can be made and what they require is information players can use to plan their choices.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Letting characters make artifacts helps explain how a world's civilizations exist, supporting the setting, provided only fitting items can be made.

can_cause.name: Framed Freedom
can_cause.why: Making items from available materials is a close relative of building, so players create freely but only within the tools and resources they hold.

changes.name: Deterioration
changes.why: Crafting can be used to alter existing items, and a common purpose is to repair or counter their wear.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Crafting is how items come into being or get improved, so it shapes which items exist and how good they are.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Players making things adds content to the world and gives an in-world explanation for where items come from.

changes.name: Grinding
changes.why: Crafting gives extra meaning to gathering resources, which makes that repetitive collecting feel worthwhile.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Items made by players keep entering a lasting world, which can upset its economy if effort and item value are unbalanced.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Making items can be set up to give growth, so the act of crafting feeds into a character's advancement.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: In shared games, crafting can disrupt the economy and balance between players if making items is not weighed against their value.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: In lasting worlds, repeated or chain crafting can flood the economy with items unless the effort matches their worth.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: If crafting effort does not match item value, those who craft heavily can gain an unfair edge over other players.

patterns.name: Minigames
patterns.what_it_is: A small game inside another game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The small game needs its own distinct rules, and its outcome should feed back into the outer game. They should be short and different enough to bring variety.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reskinned menu choice or a brief interlude with no skill or choice that changes nothing in the outer game.
patterns.knobs: how many there are; how long each lasts; how their results affect the main game

can_cause.name: Coupled Games
can_cause.why: When a minigame's result is passed into the main game, the two games become linked, so the bigger game depends on what happened in the smaller one.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: If a minigame is optional and its result matters outside it, players choose to play it for the sake of something beyond the minigame itself.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: A minigame's outcome can count as finishing a particular goal in the larger game, so the small game becomes one step toward a bigger aim.

can_cause.name: Minimalized Social Weight
can_cause.why: Because play is split into many short minigames, there are frequent natural breaks where players can pause and talk with one another.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: When a minigame passes nothing to the main game, playing it is an extra aim players may take up purely by choice.

can_cause.name: Polyathlons
can_cause.why: A series of different minigames can be strung together so players compete across several different challenges within one overall contest.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Using minigames over and over, or letting players replay a favorite one repeatedly, means players end up doing the same activity again and again.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: The result of a minigame can feed back into the main game as a direct prize for doing well.

can_cause.name: Tournaments
can_cause.why: A minigame can serve as the single contest that players compete in, with the outer game organizing the competition around it.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since each minigame can play differently from the main game and from other minigames, players get a change of activity.

can_cause.name: Easter Eggs
can_cause.why: A small game can serve as the hidden surprise itself, such as a whole earlier game or a different arcade-style game tucked inside another.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: A goal can be packaged as a small self-contained game that only appears in certain situations, like the taxi missions.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Small self-contained games combined with information carried between them, as in tournaments, join up into a larger game.

changes.name: Hotseating
changes.why: When a minigame finishes, that moment is a natural point for one player to hand over the game to the next.

changes.name: Thematic Consistency
changes.why: Minigames let a game bring in new kinds of play and themes without feeling out of place, provided they match the main theme or being a minigame fits it.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If they do not share the main game's theme, as with easter eggs, they break consistency.

patterns.name: Action Programming
patterns.what_it_is: The player chooses actions in advance, and they are carried out later.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a gap between choosing and execution in which things can change, plus a limited set or budget of programmable actions. Players need enough consequence visibility to plan but not so much that outcomes are certain.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players 'program' actions but execution is immediate or nothing changes in between, so it is just ordinary choosing.
patterns.knobs: how many actions are programmed at once; which actions are available; time allowed to plan

can_cause.name: Algorithmic Agents
can_cause.why: Because players set triggers and rules for which actions happen, they effectively build units that act by themselves, like Mules or coded robots.

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: Actions are chosen first and carried out later, so a choice made early only shows its result after the sequence plays out.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Once players program what a unit does, the unit must follow those instructions during play instead of being freely controlled.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When programming happens outside the game itself, players may have to update the game state by hand, which adds tedious bookkeeping work.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: If programming is done before play starts, such as writing robot code, the programming itself becomes a separate game from the actual match.

can_cause.name: Mules
can_cause.why: Programming lets players build simple automated helpers whose behavior follows chosen triggers and rules, with no moment-to-moment control.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Players must commit to many steps in advance, so they cannot be sure the programmed sequence will actually work as intended.

can_cause.name: Player Unpredictability
can_cause.why: Since choices are hidden and made ahead of time, especially across many steps, opponents cannot easily guess what a player will do.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Mistakes in a programmed sequence cannot be fixed, so players watch them play out, which can be entertaining, as in RoboRally and Space Alert.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must think ahead about what to queue up and how it will play out, so planning is required to play.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Players can build the code that will carry out the gameplay, as in P-Robots and Crobots, where programming is their only influence.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Choosing actions ahead of time and then watching them play out leaves you unable to change them, and a time limit adds more pressure.

changes.name: No Direct Player Influence
changes.why: Programming ahead of time lets players have some indirect effect on a game where they cannot act directly, especially when feedback is missing or slow.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Programming fits turn-based play well, but can cause waiting if players overthink their programmed choices.

changes.name: Zero-Player Games
changes.why: Setting actions before play begins lets players influence a game that otherwise runs without them, giving them some indirect effect.

patterns.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
patterns.what_it_is: The action must be timed to a set rhythm.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear, perceivable rhythm must exist and failing to match it must have a cost. Timing windows need to be tuned so success is possible but demanding.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Beat visuals or music that play along, but timing is not checked, so any input works.
patterns.knobs: tempo; width of the timing window; penalty for missing the beat

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Hitting the right buttons in a set sequence and rhythm is itself a combo, and combos can be the reason players perform the rhythm actions.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each rhythm action is self-contained, so designers can tune its difficulty very precisely, which makes it easy to build demanding, layered play.

can_cause.name: Configuration
can_cause.why: Players aim to line up their actions with the timing pattern, so the rhythm becomes a goal of arranging things correctly in time.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: Players must keep performing actions and hold the rhythm steady over a stretch of time rather than doing a single act.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Because rhythm sequences are combos, learning to perform them well is one way players show skill in the game.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Players need to know which action comes next, and the indicators showing this keep a small upcoming goal always in view.

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: In some games the timed button presses are mapped onto the character's moves, so pressing in rhythm makes the character move.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: When a combo is the only way to defeat enemies, performing the rhythm actions becomes the means to beat them.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Since players must hit precise timing over and over, they cannot be sure they will execute every action correctly.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: The rhythm repeats in its tempo or in the kind of action, so players keep doing similar things again and again.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Missing the timed actions can mean death, so players perform them in order to stay alive, sometimes with a story reason.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Pressing the right inputs in time with a beat is a narrower kind of dexterity, so it counts as a form of this pattern.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: In real-time games players must act as events happen, and rhythm actions shape this by making the timing and steadiness of those acts matter.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Some traps are repeating events that players get past only by acting in rhythm, so the rhythm changes how the trap works.

patterns.name: Excise
patterns.what_it_is: Side actions that are required to play but add nothing to the game by themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It appears when the game state must be updated by hand (bookkeeping, tracking statistics, handling many units or characters) with nobody or nothing doing it automatically. To avoid it, automate the upkeep or fold it into real choices.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A task that merely looks like chores, such as a quick, enjoyable action that is actually a meaningful choice, so it is not true excise.
patterns.knobs: how much state players must maintain by hand; how much of it is automated

can_cause.name: No-Ops
can_cause.why: Doing required upkeep gives no real choices or progress, so it works like being forced to idle while the game waits.

conflicts_with.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
conflicts_with.why: When tokens are used to cap how much of a resource can be held, the limit reduces the upkeep work of handling them.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: The page treats removing excise as a facilitator job, yet it never explains how the two conflict.

conflicts_with.name: Extra-Game Actions
conflicts_with.why: The two are defined as mutually exclusive, so an action that doesn't touch the ongoing game's state can't also count as upkeep.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Weaving choices into chores makes them feel less like pointless work, softening the upkeep.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: A game master can remove upkeep from players, though doing so means the game master takes on that work themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Minimalized Social Weight
conflicts_with.why: If players can talk and interact while doing chores, the chores feel lighter and less burdensome.

conflicts_with.name: Mules
conflicts_with.why: Letting others do the repetitive tasks removes the tedious effort from the player.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Help
conflicts_with.why: Outside assistance can take over repetitive or uninteresting actions so players don't have to do them.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Buying a result lets players skip the repetitive effort of earning it, removing that grind.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Returns
conflicts_with.why: Fast ways back cut down the dull effort of traveling, easing movement chores.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Travel
conflicts_with.why: Skipping across the map removes the need to cross uneventful ground by hand, reducing movement chores.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Caps
conflicts_with.why: When tokens are used to track resources, limiting how much can be held restricts how much tracking is needed.

conflicts_with.name: Vehicles
conflicts_with.why: Having a vehicle replaces plain on-foot travel, taking away the dull effort of ordinary movement.

patterns.name: Collaborative Actions
patterns.what_it_is: An action happens only if several participants each do their own part.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The result must really need more than one agent, with outcomes depending on coordination and a way for them to coordinate.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'team' action that one player could do alone, or participants who simply do their own thing in parallel.
patterns.knobs: number of participants; timing precision needed; how rewards are shared

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: When players combine their actions, they can unlock things no single player could do alone, which effectively gives them new abilities.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Players may team up against whoever is leading, and this ganging up pulls the leader back toward the others.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Several players, avatars or units doing linked actions together works like a combo, just spread across more than one actor.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Needing others to act with you adds extra things to handle, namely negotiating, coordinating and timing, so play becomes more complicated.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Acting together is a way for players to cooperate, though not every collaborative action involves real cooperation.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Players often must talk and bargain outside the game's formal rules to line up their joint action.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skill at coordinating joint actions becomes something players can get better at, especially when teams compete against each other.

can_cause.name: Shared Penalties
can_cause.why: When a joint action carries a cost for everyone involved, all participants bear it together, which binds them to finishing what they started.

can_cause.name: Shared Rewards
can_cause.why: Giving everyone a payoff from a joint action encourages players to start collaborating in the first place.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When a joint action rewards some players and penalizes others, those involved face hard choices about whether to take part.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because joint actions need negotiation and good timing, players must think ahead and plan with others.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Successful joint actions show off what a group achieved together, particularly when they give players new abilities.

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: Several players adding to one shared outcome, such as placing cards or chips, leaves others unsure who contributed what.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When effects of joint actions are delayed, a partner can quietly undermine the shared effort, as with crisis resolution in Battlestar Galactica.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: When players act together toward a goal and failure hurts them all, the goal becomes something the group has committed to.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: When joint actions pay off only one player, the others go unrewarded for now and must trust that the favor will be returned later.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Although joint actions open up new possibilities, they limit what a player can freely choose because they must coordinate with others.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Joint actions can make teamwork more efficient than solo play, though teams aren't required since temporary alliances form while players act together.

patterns.name: Physical Navigation
patterns.what_it_is: The player finds their way through the game environment by actually moving through space.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs real-world goal locations, a way to confirm arrival, and obstacles that make the route matter. Designers must also decide whether speed and fitness should count.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are told to walk somewhere, but the goal could be completed from the sofa or the route never matters.
patterns.knobs: distance between goal locations; how arrival is verified; time pressure

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since onlookers can't easily tell why someone is walking around, moving through real places blends into everyday life, as long as the pace stays socially normal.

can_cause.name: Physical Enactment
can_cause.why: Players use their own bodies to travel and find their way, so the navigation is itself a bodily act performed for the game.

can_cause.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
can_cause.why: Walking and finding your way are things people do in real life, so doing them directly changes what happens in the game.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: Players who already know the area they must travel through can find their way better, giving them an edge.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Exploring changes when players use all their senses and are limited by their own bodies instead of controlling a fictional character.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Moving becomes bound by players' own physical abilities and uses their real senses, which alters how movement works in the game.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Racing changes because contestants are limited by their own bodies and senses, so how physically capable they are matters.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Sneaking works differently when players are limited by real bodies and can use all their senses to notice or avoid others.

patterns.name: No Direct Player Influence
patterns.what_it_is: Games where the player barely or never directly controls what happens.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must cut players off from changing the game state, while still giving them something to do around it, such as betting, building an agent beforehand, or setting up an initial state. Their involvement has to be real enough that they stay emotionally invested.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with only a few trivial buttons that look like input but make no difference to the result, and nothing else for players to engage with.
patterns.knobs: how much input players get, if any; whether they can prepare in advance or place bets

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since players only hand over instructions or agents that run without them, others need not be present, so play can happen at different times for each person.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: When players cannot steer during play, any agents in the game must follow behavior fixed beforehand rather than responding to live commands.

can_cause.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
can_cause.why: When players write algorithmic agents that then play on their own, each player owns a different, self-made piece of the game.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: With no live input from players, the game effectively runs itself once started, so it behaves like a game that needs no players.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Because players' choices only take effect after being set up, they find out later how well those choices actually worked.

changes.name: Player Unpredictability
changes.why: Since the effects of player decisions on the game state show up only later, what players will do stays hidden for longer.

conflicts_with.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: Free manipulation gives players direct hands-on influence, so a game where they have none is hard to combine with it.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Players set up their characters but then cannot act during play, so no choices exist in the gameplay.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: If players cannot meaningfully affect the game at all, there is no skill to develop and nothing to improve.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: Without direct input during play, the game always acts to some degree on its own, which reduces players' sense of control.

patterns.name: Live Action Roleplaying
patterns.what_it_is: A role-playing game where participants physically act out their heroes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must act in person, in character, with believable props and costumes, and communicate in-world. The design must handle gaps between what players know and what characters know.
patterns.just_a_label_when: People wear costumes but talk and act as themselves, so it is just a normal tabletop game in costume.
patterns.knobs: how much in-character play is demanded; how real the props are; rules for out-of-game talk

can_cause.name: First-Person Views
can_cause.why: Since players physically act out their characters, each player is the character and experiences the game world directly from that character's own viewpoint.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Players sometimes need to talk about things their characters couldn't, so out-of-game talk can appear unless the design gives them a way to do it without breaking the fiction.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: Both players and facilitators may have to roleplay so they fit the real world and the fictional story laid over it at once.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Since everything is physically acted out, protective gear used in play must be real or look convincingly like the genuine thing.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Players do their characters' actions themselves, so the characters exist through the players' own bodies and behavior rather than through description.

changes.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
changes.why: It matters whenever a player's senses differ from those of the character they are enacting, which can create mismatches in what each can perceive.

changes.name: Props
changes.why: Because play is physical, objects used in the game must be real or look like real versions of what they stand for.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Since actions are physically performed, tools in the game must be real or look like real ones to be used convincingly.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Because play is physically enacted, weapons must be real or resemble real ones, which shapes what designers have to build or supply.

changes.name: Diegetic Communication
changes.why: Live action play involves lots of face-to-face talk, and treating that talk as in-world is a main feature of how it is played.

conflicts_with.name: Third-Person Views
conflicts_with.why: Showing the world from a position no in-world observer occupies can't be provided even by facilitators when everyone physically acts out their characters.

patterns.name: Role Selection
patterns.what_it_is: The player chooses their abilities by picking one of a few ready-made roles.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The roles must differ in what they offer, so that choosing is a real decision with trade-offs. Rules must state who can choose what and when.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A choice among roles that are effectively identical or where one is clearly best, so selection does not matter.
patterns.knobs: number and difference of roles; whether roles are exclusive; when selection happens

can_cause.name: Action Programming
can_cause.why: When roles are picked in a separate planning step before anything is carried out, the picks work like a weak program of what will happen next.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Picking a role means taking one option from a shared or personal set, which is a particular way of drafting what you get to use.

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: If only one player can take a given role, everyone who wants it is chasing something that rules the others out.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide for themselves which role, and so which actions, they take from the small set of available ones.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: When players can pick up goals tied to the role they chose, acting on those goals lets them feel they are living up to that role.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Roles chosen in a planning phase can decide who acts first when the actions are carried out later, shaping the turn order.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Choosing from a limited set of actions each turn shapes what players can do in their turn, giving turns a role-picking structure.

patterns.name: Tick-Based Games
patterns.what_it_is: Real-time games with long pauses between updates, leaving time to think.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Ticks must be long enough to plan within and must cap actions per tick. Someone or something must enforce the schedule.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Updates happen so fast or so freely that players act continuously, so it is simply real-time.
patterns.knobs: tick length; actions allowed per tick; how unused actions are handled

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Players who want to do more than a tick allows must wait for the next one, though the tick's length caps how long that wait can be.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Because a tick leaves time to plan and act, players can leave and return between ticks without being punished.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: The game must advance in regular time steps, so that real-world moments can line up with and trigger game events.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When ticks are long enough to plan carefully, players have plenty of time to think through their moves, which can make their impact feel bigger than it is.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When a tick gives plenty of time to plan and act, players can pick for themselves when they want to play.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Players can stop playing mid-session without harm as long as they still have time to make their needed moves before the next tick arrives.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: Since the tick leaves generous time to plan and act, players can fit play around their own schedule and decide when to engage.

can_cause.name: No-Ops
can_cause.why: Each tick allows only a limited number of actions, so a player may also choose to do nothing and let that tick's chance pass.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
