changes.why: With private game spaces, players can take their turns at different times between ticks, making the game asynchronous.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Ticks work like a time limit on action points, since unused allowance is lost or capped when the tick passes.

changes.name: Downtime
changes.why: Ticks decide how long players must wait when they want more actions than allowed, with the tick length setting the maximum wait.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Turning such a game tick-based limits how much each player can do or forces rests, while still requiring them to return regularly.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Ticks make a real-time game apply its changes in synchronized batches that players can notice and plan around.

changes.name: Synchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Ticks make everyone's actions and events update together at set moments, so shared play stays synchronized yet leaves room for planning.

patterns.name: Bidding
patterns.what_it_is: Players offer resources in competition for the right to make a purchase or trade.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need bid resources that are scarce and also matter elsewhere, a clear rule for who wins and a reward worth competing for. Caps or limited budgets keep it a real trade-off.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Bids are called, but resources are plentiful, so everyone can always outbid at no cost and nothing is given up.
patterns.knobs: type and amount of bidding resource; whether the bid resource is spent or returned; what the reward is

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Bids can win rewards tied to holding territory, so competing bids become a way of deciding who controls an area.

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: Bidding means staking resources on an uncertain result, and the uncertainty mostly comes from not knowing how much others will bid.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Winning a bid lets a player take something from others, so bidding can serve as a way of seizing ownership.

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: Bidding needs several bidders taking part in one shared activity, even though they are rivals rather than teammates.

can_cause.name: Converters
can_cause.why: Players turn resources they hold into rewards by bidding, so the bidding act works as an exchange of one thing for another.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Bidding is optional, so as long as a player has enough resources to raise the bid, they choose whether to join in.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Bid costs vary, and resources spent on a bid cannot be used elsewhere, leaving players torn about how much to commit.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: In Bridge, the winning bidder gets to impose a goal on the game, so the auction decides which goal applies.

can_cause.name: Resource Competition
can_cause.why: Players compete over who wins the rewards on offer, and those rewards are usually resources, so bidding is a contest over resources.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Bidding is built around something that favorable outcomes hand out, so there are always rewards to bid for and distribute.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Because bidding is won by driving everyone else out of the contest, it lets a player take the role of a dominator.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: When players bid just to make rivals pay more, they must read and influence other people instead of valuing the prize.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must work out how much to bid and what else the resources are needed for, which calls for planning around costs and rivals.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Resources spent on a bid are unavailable for other uses, so players must weigh the bid against alternative spending.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: No one knows in advance how much the other players will bid, so who wins stays unclear until the bidding ends.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: An auction shows a currently leading result that rivals can still overturn, so players see a likely outcome that remains open.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Combined with capturing, deciding what to bid has no perfect answer, so players reason out the best option.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Bidding is won by driving out every other player who is unwilling or unable to bid, so it works like an elimination goal.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: The usual aim of a winning bid is to come away owning the reward that was bid on.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Bidding needs several bidders, so it adds a shared activity that players in a multiplayer game take part in together.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Bidding requires resources to bid with, and winning bids typically pay out resources, so it shapes how resources are spent and gained.

changes.name: Trick Taking
changes.why: In Bridge, the bidding stage comes first and sets up the trick taking that follows, so it modifies how that play works.

changes.name: Trumps
changes.why: In Bridge, the bidding determines trump for the play that follows, so it alters how the trump mechanic is used.

patterns.name: No-Ops
patterns.what_it_is: Player actions that change nothing in the game state.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Waiting must be a legal choice, or a forced effect, and the game state must keep changing while the player waits so that waiting has a point. Whether it is voluntary or forced determines whether it feels like a strategic choice or a punishment.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pass button that is never worth using because the situation never rewards waiting, or a forced skip so rare that it never affects anyone.
patterns.knobs: whether no-ops are voluntary or forced; how often and how long they last

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Waiting out a turn lets a player hold off until the game reaches a state where a more active move becomes worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: When every other available move hurts opponents, choosing to do nothing becomes the generous option that spares them.

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: Staying put and doing nothing is what lets a player sit in one spot, so being able to idle is needed for it.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a player does nothing, they have nothing to engage with, so idle stretches of play appear.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When passing is optional, players gain one more choice, such as waiting for others to act first.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: If the game carries on without input when players choose nothing, they can step away briefly to do something else.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: If doing nothing is the only thing a game allows, players cannot affect anything and just watch events unfold.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Making a player skip a turn or sit out is a way to punish them by taking away their chance to act.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Being made to stand by while enemies act, or waiting for a foe to show up or an aim to settle, builds suspense.

can_cause.name: Turnovers
can_cause.why: A rule can cut a player's turn short so the rest of it is spent doing nothing, which acts as a setback.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Holding still while waiting for the aim to steady or for a target to line up often helps a shot succeed.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: When all other moves harm fellow players, doing nothing can be the cooperative choice within these dilemmas.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Staying motionless between careful movements helps players avoid being detected and so reach their stealth goals.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Making players lose actions or applying that to enemies changes how hard fights are.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: If nothing happens until the end and keeping it going is trivial, the steps before completion amount to doing nothing.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: If a player misses the time limit, being forced to do nothing serves as the penalty that makes the limit matter.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Forced moments of doing nothing make it hard to maintain a global sense of influence.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Forced skipping of actions removes options, typically as a penalty.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: Making players pass removes their ability to act on the game, so they have less control over what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Too many idle moves wear down suspense, even though some forced or voluntary waiting can build it.

conflicts_with.name: Varied Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Doing nothing too often becomes repetitive like any overused activity, leaving play less varied.

patterns.name: Tile-Laying
patterns.what_it_is: Placing pieces where their position relative to those already laid matters.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Where a piece goes must matter for what follows, with relations to neighbors affecting play. Placement must vary between games.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tiles are laid down but position has no effect, so it is decoration.
patterns.knobs: placement rules; who places; how many tile types and how drawn

can_cause.name: Fog of War
can_cause.why: If tiles, cards or tokens are put down face-down during setup, players can't see what lies beneath them, which hides parts of the world.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When players put down tiles as they actually explore, discovering the map and building it become the same action, so exploring is directly tied to placement.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: If pieces that have been placed can be moved afterward, the world layout can change during play, and layouts already differ from one game to the next.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since players choose placements or chance decides them, each game ends up with a different layout, so play is likely to differ each time.

patterns.name: Varying Turn Orders
patterns.what_it_is: The order of turns changes during the game, by itself or by the players' choice.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Order must really change between rounds by rotation, score-based ranking or player choice, and the first slot must carry a real advantage or disadvantage for the variation to matter. Limit player-driven changes so they do not dominate.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rotating order in a game where acting first or last makes no difference, so the rotation changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how order is determined (rotation, score, bidding); how big the first-player advantage is; how many changes players may make

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the starting advantage of going first is taken away or reduced as the order changes, no player keeps the benefit, which evens out the game.

can_cause.name: Flip-Flop Events
can_cause.why: When the order reverses, whoever played last in one round can play first in the next, so that player acts twice in a row.

changes.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
changes.why: Changing who goes first means the edge that one starting position gives is lessened or removed, rather than staying with one player.

changes.name: First Player Advantages
changes.why: Letting the first player drop to last in a later round, as in Puerto Rico, spreads that advantage around instead of fixing it on one person.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: The sequence in which players act is no longer the same every round, so the basic turn structure itself is altered.

patterns.name: Interruptibility
patterns.what_it_is: The game's design lets one player step out for a while without spoiling the game for others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Stopping must not harm the player or others, which means saving state, pausing time, or having others covered by AI when someone leaves. It works only if the rest of the system also copes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pause or save option that still costs the player progress, or that wrecks the game for other players.
patterns.knobs: where and how often saves/pauses are allowed; what covers an absent player

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When one player steps away, the others may have to sit idle waiting, so letting people interrupt play can create waiting time for the rest.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since players can stop without penalty, they get to decide for themselves when to play and when not to.

can_cause.name: Minimalized Social Weight
can_cause.why: If skipping play carries no punishment, other people put little pressure on you to be present, so social obligation to the game stays low.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because play can be dropped and picked up freely, it can blend into everyday life instead of needing dedicated blocks of time.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Being able to pause without negative effects lets players fit the game around their real-life schedules and situations.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Players can choose when to play, so they must weigh playing now against saving it for a later moment.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: With no penalty for stopping and resuming, a game can be played in many places and moments, whenever the player happens to be free.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If play can be interrupted, the fiction must account for characters suddenly stopping or disappearing.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: Games that can be paused or interrupted give people fewer reasons to quit for good, so they work against players leaving early.

conflicts_with.name: Mediated Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: When play happens through a medium, other players may not see why someone stopped, making the interruption confusing.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Others may not want to wait around, so one person's interruption can cause idle time for fellow players.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: The world keeps changing even when you're away, so stepping out can still bring negative consequences.

patterns.name: Team Combos
patterns.what_it_is: Coordinated actions by several players trigger an extra effect they would not have alone.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The extra effect must be big enough to justify coordinating, and players need to be able to notice or learn how to trigger it. Roles that differ, or timing windows, make it truly require several people.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players acting near each other get a small bonus that they would almost as easily get alone, so no one coordinates.
patterns.knobs: size of the combo bonus; timing window; how many players and which abilities are required

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: A team combo is a joint action done right away as part of working together, not something negotiated beforehand or slowly paying off over time.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Team combos are simply combos in which the chained or combined effect comes from several players acting together instead of one player.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Team combos happen as an immediate expression of players cooperating, with everyone acting together to produce a shared effect.

can_cause.name: Goal Achievements
can_cause.why: Designers can attach specific goals or rewards to team combos, which nudges players to try pulling them off.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Because players must coordinate, they usually end up taking on different roles so each contributes something distinct to the combo.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When a team misses a combo at a crucial moment, the result can be a big, memorable mess that players find entertaining.

can_cause.name: Team Accomplishments
can_cause.why: Pulling off a team combo is a success the whole group shares, since no single player could take credit for it.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: If combos aren't explained or obvious, or there are many ways to combine abilities, players must work out which combinations work best.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Differing abilities or skill levels let teammates combine their strengths for effects.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Coordinated moves by several members become possible when a team contains differently skilled or placed members.

patterns.name: Interruptible Actions
patterns.what_it_is: An action can be broken off before it has fully taken effect.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must have a delay or build-up in which others can respond, and there must be a means to stop them. The window should be long enough to react to.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An action that has a wind-up animation but cannot actually be stopped, so the wind-up is just decoration.
patterns.knobs: length of the interruption window; what can interrupt; cost to the interrupted

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Letting a strong, slow action be stopped gives opponents a counter, such as blocking attacks or breaking combos, so powerful moves are kept in check.

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: Because an action can be stopped before it pays off, players have a way to hold back whoever is ahead.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: An interruptible action only exists while it is still underway; once it finishes or is stopped, it is gone.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Others can stop the action only during a short window, so goals tied to it are available just briefly.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Finishing the action is itself something a player wants, and since others can interrupt it, that goal can be disrupted.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players can't be sure the action will succeed because others may stop it, and that uncertainty, plus waiting while unable to act, raises tension.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Combined with extended actions, the risk of being interrupted makes completing the action a goal players must keep working to protect.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: If an unfinished action can be disrupted, players feel they must complete it quickly, which they perceive as a time limit.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Many actions are abilities, so letting them be interrupted also changes what the ability is worth and how reliably it works.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: Capturing can take effect after a delay, so other actions can cancel it before it completes.

changes.name: Combos
changes.why: Players can break a combo chain partway, so executing it depends on how well the opponent counters it.

changes.name: Encouraged Return Visits
changes.why: When an action's effects take long to arrive, players must weigh how long they can stay away before it is interrupted.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: An action that takes time to carry out can be stopped before it finishes, so the long duration becomes a vulnerability.

changes.name: Irreversible Events
changes.why: An action that would cause a permanent change gets a window in which agents can stop it before it happens.

changes.name: Scripted Information Sequences
changes.why: Even a sequence the game itself plays out can be cut off partway, so its progress is not guaranteed.

changes.name: Storytelling
changes.why: Depending on the game, others may cut into a story being told, turning it into something the players build together.

changes.name: Trading
changes.why: Several players can jump into a trade at the same moment and cut in, which can put participants under time pressure.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: When another player's action is interrupted during their own turn, it changes how turns normally work, sometimes needing special sequences.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: When opposition can break off ongoing actions, completing them becomes harder.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Making a trap's activation something that can be halted lets players stop it before its effect lands.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If an action can be interrupted and fail, the effort already put into it may be wasted, undermining the sense that work pays off.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Actions that can be interrupted add uncertainty that makes any displayed success chance inaccurate, which can lower the perceived influence.

patterns.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Players do not need to play at the same time; each joins when convenient.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Game state must be kept while players are away, with turns or ticks that do not stall others, and ways to show who else is in the game. Handle waiting with long timers, recordings, AI or gifts left for others.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game is called asynchronous but still needs everyone online at once, or the world freezes and nothing happens in absence.
patterns.knobs: turn or tick length; how long state persists; what substitutes absent players (AI, ghosts, gifts)

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When players must wait for others to finish their sessions before a shared game can continue, that waiting time becomes idle time for those who are done.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: If players aren't tied to a shared schedule, they can decide for themselves when to play.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Because the game doesn't need everyone present at once, a player can stop and resume without breaking anyone else's play.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: The idle time spent waiting for others gives players a chance to think ahead about what they will do next.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Pushing flexibility of when to play further means people can fit the game into any moment or place they happen to have.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: Players act at different times, so any teamwork they do together naturally happens without simultaneous presence or observation.

can_cause.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
can_cause.why: When players take turns apart from each other, each in their own private space with little contact, each still treats the game as their own while others quietly influence it.

patterns.name: Token Placement
patterns.what_it_is: Players choose future actions by placing their tokens on them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Action slots must be fewer than the demand for them, so placing a token blocks others, and each player needs only a few tokens. A clear turn order for placement is required.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Every action slot is unlimited or open to everyone, so placing a token is just a bookkeeping step that blocks nobody.
patterns.knobs: tokens per player; number and capacity of action slots; placement turn order

can_cause.name: Action Programming
can_cause.why: Players choose which actions they will do ahead of time by placing tokens, but can still pick how to carry them out later, so it's a loose version of programming.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: During placement, players decide freely where their few tokens go, choosing future actions from the available options.

can_cause.name: Resource Competition
can_cause.why: Since each action slot can be taken only a limited number of times, players end up fighting over the same scarce spots.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Both the tokens players hold and the action spots they can fill become things of value that players manage and spend.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must work out where to put their own tokens while also guessing where opponents will put theirs.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When several players want the same action spot, the contest over who gets it creates anxious, uncertain moments.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Because tokens and spots are few, players must give up some useful actions to claim the most necessary or efficient ones.

can_cause.name: Varying Turn Orders
can_cause.why: Some placement spots can change who goes first next, so where you place a token also affects the order of play.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Players spend points to place tokens that mark which actions will be done later, splitting play into planning and carrying out.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Competing for limited action spots only makes sense with several players, so the pattern mainly shapes games with more than one participant.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Placement turns both the tokens and the available actions into valued items, adding to how resources work in the game.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Placing a token can change who acts next, so the placement pattern feeds back into how turns are ordered.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Placement isn't a test of reactions, so it fits games where players act in turns rather than simultaneously in real time.

conflicts_with.name: Real-Time Games
conflicts_with.why: Placing tokens depends on a fixed order of turns, which is hard to keep when everything runs continuously.

patterns.name: Information Passing
patterns.what_it_is: One character gives another information that can affect how the game goes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The information must change what players know or can do (a new goal, a clue, a better choice), and delivered through a channel such as dialogue or eavesdropping. It must be reliable or deliberately unreliable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Characters talk but say only flavour text, so players learn nothing that affects their decisions.
patterns.knobs: how much and how useful the information is; how it is delivered; whether it can be false

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: When a character passes along information the player can see, that information can hint at what to do or where to look next.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: A passing event can be enough to finish a goal of learning something, because the player receives the information it carries.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Passing information between characters can set up conflict inside a group without any fighting, for example by making members of a faction oppose each other.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: It is a main way to hand out story information bit by bit to the player, so it drives how a scripted story unfolds.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Because the player just receives information, what is passed can be misleading, steering attention toward something that turns out unimportant.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: When information can be overheard, goals to learn it can require staying unnoticed while listening in.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Passed information might be a red herring, so the player cannot be sure whether what they learned is reliable or useful.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: This is a way to make players aware that skippable goals exist, often through characters who tell them about these.

changes.name: Dialogues
changes.why: What players learned in past exchanges alters what they are able to say in a later conversation.

changes.name: Optional Goals
changes.why: What characters pass on can give the player a new goal they may choose to pursue, changing how play proceeds.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: What characters pass on can set, complete or fail a fixed goal, directly steering the course of play.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: NPCs can deliver or elaborate on the story by passing information to players.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Sharing or passing on information lets rivals compete through scheming rather than combat, which suits rivalry-focused games.

patterns.name: Mules
patterns.what_it_is: Programs that take over monotonous, repetitive actions from the player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have repetitive tasks worth delegating, and the automation must be able to run them without the player. Limits on efficiency or risks keep it from replacing play entirely.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An auto-play button that does the task but is so weak or so restricted that players still do everything by hand.
patterns.knobs: which tasks can be automated; how efficient; what risks come with it

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When players get to build their own Mules, designing and tuning the best automated helper becomes a separate challenge layered on top of normal play.

can_cause.name: Player Augmentations
can_cause.why: A Mule is a program that stands in for the player and extends what they can get done, so it works as an added capability for them.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: Letting a program do the player's work is a kind of shortcut, and it counts as cheating that either the players or the designers have agreed to allow.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: A mule is a game element that looks human-directed, so it can look like an agent even though it is not.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: A Mule has to be able to steer the player's Avatar, so its presence changes how the Avatar gets controlled.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Mules are mostly used to repeat actions that raise a character's abilities, so they change how quickly and how much effort players spend improving.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Mules often draw on information stored in a Character to decide what to do, so they shape how Characters get used in play.

changes.name: Emotes
changes.why: Since a Mule stands in for the player, it must handle expected social interaction, and letting it use Emotes is one way to do that.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Letting others do the repetitive tasks removes the tedious effort from the player.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Mules are AI players built to perform grinding in place of people, so players no longer have to do it.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A Mule must cover tasks like dialogue, which is hard to automate convincingly, and player-made Mules leave consistency up to the players.

patterns.name: Physical Enactment
patterns.what_it_is: The player personally performs actions that then happen in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a way to read or judge the body action, and a clear choice of which actions are enacted and which are abstracted. The physical demand has to be what decides outcomes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A motion-controller game where a button press or tiny flick does the same job as the gesture, so the movement is just decoration.
patterns.knobs: which actions must be physically performed; how large and demanding the movement is; how strictly it is judged

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: In live action roleplaying, every participant physically acts out their character, so the game world stays consistent, but it breaks easily if any single player fails to take part.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Physical enactment is a more demanding kind of enactment, where players do the larger or more dexterous actions with their own bodies instead of just commanding them.

can_cause.name: Live Action Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Live action roleplaying is roleplaying where players actually perform their characters' actions and attitudes with their bodies, so enactment combined with roleplaying produces it.

can_cause.name: Mimetic Interfaces
can_cause.why: The interface comes from asking players to physically carry out actions, which sensors then measure, so the physical performance itself is the input.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: When outcomes come from bodily activity, they depend on how well players physically perform it.

patterns.name: Game Time Manipulation
patterns.what_it_is: Actions by which the player changes the flow of game time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have a state and timeline that can really be paused, sped up, slowed or rewound, and the ability must cost something or be limited. In multiplayer, decide whose time is affected so others keep their agency.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rewind or slow-motion button so cheap, or so rarely needed, that nobody changes decisions because of it, or a visual slowdown that changes nothing in the rules.
patterns.knobs: which time effects exist (stop, slow, fast, reverse); how often and at what cost they can be used

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Being able to rewind or undo what happened lets players change their outcomes, so they can pick differently and reshape how a game session plays out.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Time control is usually handed to just one player and not to other agents, so it works as a special power only that player holds.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: In single-player games, slowing the player down or speeding up enemies makes play harder as a penalty.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: In single-player games, gaining the power to control game time can be part of what a reward consists of.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Power-ups can be the means by which a player gains the ability to stop, slow, speed up, or reverse game time.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Time manipulation is mostly found in real-time games, where players can alter the speed or direction of continuously running events.

changes.name: Time Limited Game Instances
changes.why: Being able to manipulate time changes how much actual time players have within a game session that is meant to be limited.

changes.name: Time Limits
changes.why: If players can stop, slow, or reverse time, the pressure of a time-limited challenge shifts because the time available is effectively altered.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: When one player's time manipulation is applied in a multiplayer game, it typically takes away the other players' ability to make meaningful choices that affect the game.

patterns.name: Polyathlons
patterns.what_it_is: Goal of completing several challenges, each needing different skills.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each event must need a different skill and have a clear result that can be combined into a final score. The mix must make players be either generalists or specialists.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several events are listed, but they test the same skill, so it is really one game repeated.
patterns.knobs: number of events; how different their skills are; how they are weighted in the total

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Since each event demands different skills, players must either focus on certain skill areas or become well-rounded across several of them.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Switching between events that each play differently gives players a changing mix of activities instead of the same play throughout.

patterns.name: Trick Taking
patterns.what_it_is: Several players play cards, and one of them wins that round.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Cards need ranked values with rules for following suit, a winner-determination rule, and a clear scoring goal (most, fewest, exact). A turn order must exist.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players play cards in a round but the winner is picked at random or the result changes nothing in scoring.
patterns.knobs: goal (most, fewest or exact tricks); suit-following rules; trump use

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Because rule breaks and played cards come to light only later, players gain from remembering which cards already appeared in earlier tricks, so these games push them to memorize.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Winning a trick means beating the other players' cards in that round, so each trick is a small challenge the player tries to conquer.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: The values of the cards played decide who wins the trick, and the pattern can matter so much that card sets get designed around it.

changes.name: Discard Piles
changes.why: Won tricks can be set aside as their own pile, acting like a special discard pile that players can look back through later.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Several players must each contribute a card to the same trick, with one of them winning it, so the pattern shapes play among many people.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Tiles, like dominoes, can be played into a trick and ranked by value so that one player wins them all.

patterns.name: Quick Time Events
patterns.what_it_is: The game shows a sequence of button presses that must be performed instantly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must be real-time, with clear prompts, fair time windows and meaningful consequences for failure. They work best where normal controls do not cover the situation.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Prompts appear but have no penalty or can't be failed, so they are a cutscene with a button press.
patterns.knobs: sequence length; time window; penalty for failure

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: A quick time event often plays out as a scripted scene showing the game world, so the prompts ride along with a cinematic-style presentation.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Each prompt asks for a specific input right now, giving players a short-lived objective that disappears once they succeed or fail.

can_cause.name: Minigames
can_cause.why: A quick time event can be packaged as a small self-contained challenge of timed inputs, separate from the main gameplay actions.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The instructions telling players which inputs to press are shown as interface overlays rather than things inside the game world.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: Events with custom animations are built to kill the character in that exact situation, so players may feel the designers are deliberately out to get them.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Like cutscenes, these events can carry fixed story moments, since the sequence of actions and outcomes is set in advance by designers.

can_cause.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Players must press a series of inputs in order and on time, which creates a beat-like pattern of actions.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: The prompts can show up unexpectedly, and the surprise of having to react instantly makes players feel pressure.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: These events only work when the game runs continuously, since players must respond within a short time window, so they shape how such games play.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: They offer players a way to dodge a trap by reacting with the right input, instead of only steering away from it or leaving its range.

patterns.name: Startgame
patterns.what_it_is: The first stage in games that have clearly separated stages.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The opening needs few options and distinct goals from later phases, and starting conditions must be fair. A following phase must be clearly different so the structure is noticeable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A section called the opening that plays exactly like the rest of the game, so players never notice a phase.
patterns.knobs: how many actions are available at the start; how long the phase lasts; how much starting positions differ

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because everyone knows the opening phase exists and how it tends to go, players are nudged to think ahead and prepare plans for it.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Openings repeat in similar ways each game, so players can learn and build up knowledge of different ways to begin.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Since openings follow common patterns and don't hinge on one game's exact state, players can make broad plans rather than reacting move by move.

patterns.name: Card Building
patterns.what_it_is: Players themselves change the effects and properties of individual cards.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Modifications must be meaningful and cost something, with real choices between them, and cards must be reused so the investment pays off.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Cards have upgrade slots, but one upgrade is clearly best or the changes are too small to affect play.
patterns.knobs: how many modifications a card can take; their cost; whether changes are permanent

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Handling many possible changes to your cards gives players a lot to juggle, which makes the game harder to take in all at once.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Players assemble and shape their cards by choosing how each one gets modified, so they are building something out of their card pool.

can_cause.name: Deck Building
can_cause.why: When cards are gathered into decks, changing the individual cards effectively means the player is also shaping the deck, so both happen together.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide which cards to change and how, so they have real say in how their cards end up.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Players have the goal of making their cards better, which gives them something to work toward and grow at.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Handling the many modification options well is a skill, so players who manage it effectively show they have mastered the game.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Modifying a card can make what it already does stronger, so a card's owner gets better effects than before.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Players spend resources now to change cards, hoping the changes pay off later, though the payoff is not guaranteed.

can_cause.name: Legacy Games
can_cause.why: When changes to cards are permanent, they carry over between play sessions, so the game changes as it is played repeatedly.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Permanent card changes persist outside a single session, creating a larger game of managing cards across multiple plays.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Modifying a card can give it effects it did not have before, widening what the player can do with it.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Deciding how to change cards gives players reason to think ahead about what they want their cards to become.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Choices about which card modifications to pursue shape longer-term play, so players need to plan strategically.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since players can modify cards in different ways, each game or player can end up playing differently.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: The page lists this as conflicting without giving a reason.

patterns.name: Auto-Aim
patterns.what_it_is: The game partly aims for the player, making targeting easier.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The assist must really change hit results, such as pulling the crosshair or bending shots, in the situations where aiming is hard. Tune its strength against skill and fairness in multiplayer.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An aim assist option exists but is so weak it never changes a shot, or it only shows a marker without helping.
patterns.knobs: assist strength and radius; type (reticle pull, bullet bend, lock-on); where it is active

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the game helps with aiming, weaker players get closer to stronger ones, though in multiplayer that same help can also tilt fairness the other way.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Since the game does part of the aiming, players land more hits and feel that those successes came mostly from their own actions.

can_cause.name: Player Augmentations
can_cause.why: Aiming help is an extra capability the game gives the player on top of their own ability, making them more effective than unaided.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Success at hitting a target comes partly from the player's own aim and partly from the game's built-in assistance, so both contribute to the result.

can_cause.name: Point of Interest Indicators
can_cause.why: Lock-on style aiming puts a visible marker on enemies, which draws the player's attention to the things worth targeting.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: The assistance takes over some of the aiming work, so pointing at a target and firing becomes easier for the player.

changes.name: Crosshairs
changes.why: Some forms of the help pull the player's crosshairs toward enemies, or let a button press jump them from one enemy to another.

conflicts_with.name: Balancing Effects
conflicts_with.why: Aiming help can narrow the gap between players, but in multiplayer it can also favor whoever uses it, so it may support or undermine balance.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: When the game handles part of the aiming, players no longer need to develop skill at it, so there is less ability to master.

conflicts_with.name: Near Miss Indicators
conflicts_with.why: Assisted aim bends shots toward targets, so it can become impossible to notice a shot that nearly missed, leaving nothing for such indicators to show.

patterns.name: Awareness of Surroundings
patterns.what_it_is: Computer-controlled characters notice everything important around them and react.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Agents must sense the relevant objects, agents and events and respond differently depending on them. Context-dependent reactions and memory make it more believable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Agents look like they see, but they ignore pick-ups, other agents or events and follow a fixed script regardless.
patterns.knobs: what agents can perceive; sensing range; how rich their reactions and memory are

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: An agent that notices what is around it has one of the basic ingredients it needs to seem to pursue goals of its own.

can_cause.name: Sense of Self
can_cause.why: Noticing and responding to things nearby is one of the prerequisites for an agent to come across as a distinct individual.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: When characters respond sensibly to what is in the world, the game feels more coherent and fits its fictional setting better.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: The pattern shapes how computer-run agents behave by making them respond to what exists in the game world around them.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Computer-controlled foes are given responses to the player, items and other enemies nearby, so they act less blindly.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Computer-run characters react to things in the world, such as movement and closeness, which makes them seem more socially believable.

patterns.name: Killcams
patterns.what_it_is: Right after a kill, the player is shown a replay of it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must record the moments before a death and show them right away, with a clear camera choice and view style. The replay must show enough to explain how the death happened.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A replay plays but from a useless angle or too late, so the player learns nothing about what killed them.
patterns.knobs: when the replay triggers; how long it is; camera angle; full screen or small inset

can_cause.name: Cameras
can_cause.why: A killcam needs a camera placed to film the lead-up to the death, so the designer must decide how that viewpoint is set up.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: Because it takes over play to show a short pre-made-feeling clip of a death, a killcam works like a small cutscene.

can_cause.name: Point of Interest Indicators
can_cause.why: When the killcam follows the action from a moving outside view, it can mark key things on screen so the player knows where to look.

can_cause.name: Replays
can_cause.why: A killcam is built from a replay: it plays back the moments just before a death right after they happened.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: A killcam can show the kill from outside the character, such as following a bullet, giving a moving third-person perspective on the event.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Showing how a kill happened lets players learn what worked and exposes killers' tactics and locations, helping others compete.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Killcams are mostly used in fights, where they replay how a fight ended and expose details players could not see in the moment.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: They are most common in first-person games, where players often cannot tell how they died, so the replay shows what the view hid.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: The replay is triggered by kills or other important deaths, so it presents the moment one player or enemy kills another.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: By showing the victim how they died, a killcam can help balance player-versus-player matches so one side dominates less easily.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: Replaying the fatal shot reveals where a hidden shooter was, so victims learn the sniper's spot and can respond to it.

patterns.name: Misfortune Mitigation
patterns.what_it_is: The player can act to reduce their own risk of failure.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Bad luck must be possible and costly, and players need real options to reduce it, such as rerolls, known odds or a choice of action order. The options must cost something.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A mitigation option that is available but either always the obvious choice or so weak that it does not change outcomes.
patterns.knobs: how many rerolls or extra chances; how much they cost; how well the odds are known

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skillfully reducing the damage of bad outcomes, such as choosing a smart action order, becomes a skill players can get better at, as in Bloodbowl.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: When players can guard against bad results, they can better foresee what their actions will lead to instead of being at the mercy of chance.

changes.name: Luck
changes.why: Players may feel lucky when they dodge misfortune, but the feeling can vanish when one player's good luck is another player's bad outcome.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Mitigation gives players ways to counter or reduce the effect of random results, so chance has a weaker hold on the game.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: Opponents' mitigation can counter a player's luck and spoil the feeling of being fortunate.

patterns.name: Turnovers
patterns.what_it_is: A game event ends one player's turn and immediately passes the turn to another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must carry a real chance of failure, and failure must end the turn immediately and cost the player their remaining actions. Players need to see that risk before they act.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A failure that is called a turnover but the player keeps acting or loses nothing meaningful.
patterns.knobs: chance of failure per action; which failures end the turn

can_cause.name: Action Caps
can_cause.why: Because each risky action might fail and end your turn, doing enough of them almost guarantees a stop, so the number of actions is loosely limited.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Losing the rest of your turn is the price of a failed action, so a turnover works as a punishment for failing.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Since a failure can cut your turn short, players must think about which actions to attempt first, putting the important or riskier ones in a sensible order.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: A player keeps going until failing at something, so success decides how long a turn lasts.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Ending a turn as punishment for failing at certain actions gives a way to decide when the turn stops.

patterns.name: Bag Building
patterns.what_it_is: Players put tokens into a bag and later draw them back out.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must choose what goes into the bag and when to draw, with token types that really differ in value, so the contents change draw outcomes. Decide whether bags are personal or shared.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tokens go in a bag but all are the same or are drawn without choices before, so bag contents don't matter.
patterns.knobs: token types; when tokens are added and drawn; personal or shared bag

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Choosing which tokens to add to your bag is a commitment now that shapes what you may draw later, so each token acts like a stake in future turns.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Because you pull tokens from the bag without seeing them, you cannot know which one comes out, which brings uncertainty into play.

patterns.name: Workshopping
patterns.what_it_is: Techniques used before the game: building the world together or preparing for the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Sessions must have defined techniques to create characters, relationships and setting together, with enough time and facilitation for everyone to take part. The output must feed into play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A group discussion that produces nothing used in the game, or a handout read silently.
patterns.knobs: length; techniques used; how much is created collectively; facilitator involvement

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Preparing together beforehand helps players create and portray characters so that what they do stays believable within the game's fictional world.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Because players shape their characters during the workshop, those characters become elements the players themselves made rather than ones supplied by the designer.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Preparing together beforehand helps players create and portray characters so that they fit the game's intended theme and tone.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Workshop activities help players build up and play their characters, filling in details and relations that would otherwise be missing.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: The practice began in Nordic live action roleplaying, where techniques like Ball of Yarn and Slow take-off ease players into the game.

changes.name: Player-Created Characters
changes.why: Giving players creative control over their characters' initial details can turn those characters into ones the players themselves made.

changes.name: Role Fulfillment
changes.why: Working out characters beforehand helps players set or grasp goals tied to their roles, making the feeling of fulfilling a role more likely.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Workshops support players who must take on roles by easing the difficulty of portraying characters, usually early in a game.

changes.name: Substitute Actions
changes.why: Workshop techniques can make players aware of how to use substitute actions properly, which is one of the challenges they help with.

patterns.name: Password Save Files
patterns.what_it_is: A save that consists of a single password.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game state to save must be small enough to encode in a short code that players can write down and type in. The code must be generated from the state and accepted on entry.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A code that is just a level name anyone can guess, or one that does not actually restore the progress it claims to.
patterns.knobs: what state the password encodes; its length and format; when it is shown

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Because a password is just a short piece of text, players can easily copy it and hand it to others, so sharing progress becomes simple.

can_cause.name: Save Files
can_cause.why: A password stores a small amount of game state and needs only a way to type it in, so it is a lightweight kind of save.

patterns.name: Extra Turns
patterns.what_it_is: A player takes another turn right after their own turn.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Specify the trigger (a reward, a roll, a card) and whether the player controls when it happens. Because it can double a player's actions, it must be balanced against how strong a single turn is.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An 'extra turn' that has nothing meaningful left to do, or comes only when the game is already decided.
patterns.knobs: how often extra turns are granted; what triggers them and whether players choose when

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: When a player's action fails, getting another turn right away lets them try again, so the extra turn works as a second shot.

can_cause.name: Flip-Flop Events
can_cause.why: Normally turns alternate between players, so a player moving twice in a row interrupts that back-and-forth, though only mildly.

can_cause.name: Game Time Manipulation
can_cause.why: The player gets to do twice as many actions before anyone else moves, effectively stretching their share of game time.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Extra turns change the usual order of play by inserting additional turns for the player who just moved, instead of passing to the next.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Because one player acts twice before opponents respond, they gain an advantage that can tip the game in their favor and upset fairness.

patterns.name: Meta-Techniques
patterns.what_it_is: In role-playing, players tell each other something without passing it on to their characters.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must give players actual methods for signaling about rules or desired direction without speaking through characters, and players must be taught and use them. The method must suit the fiction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rule that says players may communicate out of character but gives no actual technique, so it is just ordinary talking.
patterns.knobs: which technique types are offered; how intrusive they are

can_cause.name: Communication Channels
can_cause.why: Meta-techniques give players a way to pass messages about rules or what they want from play, so they work as an extra channel alongside in-character talk.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: In live action roleplaying, meta-techniques change how in-character communication can happen, letting players share information without having their characters say it.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: Meta-techniques shape scenes by letting players signal without interrupting them, or by inserting extra scenes that carry information, and by signaling when scenes should end or start.

changes.name: Diegetic Communication
changes.why: Meta-techniques supply extra ways to signal out-of-world needs, so ordinary conversation can stay in-world without interruption.

patterns.name: Bag Management
patterns.what_it_is: Players can remove or swap tokens in the bag without playing them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Removing or replacing tokens must really shift the odds, with a cost or limit so it is a decision. Choose how many tokens and what kinds can be manipulated.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players may remove tokens, but the effect on later draws is negligible or the action is free and obvious.
patterns.knobs: how many tokens can be removed or replaced; cost of doing so; whether draws are blind

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Letting players pull tokens out of a bag, or swap them, gives them real decisions about what stays in the bag, rather than leaving it to a fixed process.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Putting tokens into or out of a bag shapes a temporary player construct that changes during play.

changes.name: Bag Building
changes.why: Bag Building is about adding tokens to a bag; Bag Management changes how that works by letting players also take out or swap tokens without playing them.

patterns.name: Substitute Actions
patterns.what_it_is: One action stands in for another, as if replacing it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The replacement action should keep as much meaning as the original, and players must be told and have a chance to practice it. Without a shared understanding it does not work.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A named stand-in action that nobody has been told about or that resembles nothing of the original, so people stop and explain what it means.
patterns.knobs: how closely the action resembles the original; how much briefing and practice is given

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because players act out a stand-in gesture rather than stopping to talk outside the fiction, the game world stays unbroken and believable.

can_cause.name: Meta-Techniques
can_cause.why: Replacing an unplayable action with an acceptable stand-in is itself a technique players use from outside the fiction to handle a problem, so it counts as one.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: They let players handle out-of-game communication without interrupting an ongoing scene, while the fiction stays consistent.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: Players keep physically performing their character's deeds, but the movement is a safe stand-in, like touching only arms and shoulders instead of acting out sex.

conflicts_with.name: Meta-Postures
conflicts_with.why: Both address the same design problem in different ways, so choosing one approach works against using the other.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: Players can express information through stand-in actions instead of speaking as themselves, so out-of-world talk is avoided.

patterns.name: Warming-Up Roleplay Exercises
patterns.what_it_is: Exercises before the game that help players get into their roles.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Exercises must target the specific roleplay skills the game demands, be short and low-pressure, and be done right before play with everyone participating. They should also teach any special rules used.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A generic icebreaker listed in the rulebook that people skip or that has nothing to do with the roles in the game.
patterns.knobs: length; type of exercise; amount of group interaction; relevance to the game's roleplay demands

can_cause.name: Workshopping
can_cause.why: Warm-up exercises are one kind of workshop technique, so running them before a game is itself a way of doing workshopping with the players.

changes.name: Enactment
changes.why: How a warm-up is designed depends on getting players ready to physically act out their characters, so enactment shapes what the exercises look like.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: Warm-ups are built to ease players into live-action play, such as by energizing them or reducing social shyness before the larp starts.

changes.name: Role Fulfillment
changes.why: Practicing beforehand makes players more likely to perform satisfyingly and lets them shape or adjust their roles to suit themselves better.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Warm-ups are designed around preparing people to play characters, helping those who feel unsure about their ability or unfamiliar with the rules.

changes.name: Substitute Actions
changes.why: Warm-ups can be used as a chance for players to practice using substitute actions before the real game begins.

patterns.name: Characters
patterns.what_it_is: A set of traits and properties that make up fictional people and creatures in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They need a persistent identity with data that changes and matters, which players can identify with or role-play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A named figure appears on screen, but there are no data or changes behind it, so it is just a skin.
patterns.knobs: depth of personal data; how much players can customise; how much the character changes during play

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: Characters are hidden game-state values standing in for diegetic people, so they are a kind of abstract construct belonging to the player.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Characters give an acting entity its traits, though they usually need an Avatar or Unit to be shown in the game world.

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: If characters already differ in traits before play begins, players start the game with unequal strengths or abilities.

can_cause.name: Coaches
can_cause.why: Hattrick is given as an example where the coach is itself a character, so that game's coaches come from this pattern.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Characters keep hidden traits of in-world people out of view yet still let them influence play, so the fiction stays believable.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Players or game masters act out their characters using voice and body, even when no visual avatar is present.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When a lot of character information must be stored and kept up to date by players, that bookkeeping becomes tedious extra work.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: When there is no concrete game world or avatar, the character is what the player's attention and control attach to.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Characters can be the ones bound to or receiving faithfulness, giving personal ties and a way to choose whom to stay true to.

can_cause.name: MacGuffins
can_cause.why: Characters can be the thing that the story or the players' pursuits revolve around, serving as the object driving events.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Characters populate stories with people whose relationships matter, giving richer narrative material, though gameplay traits and storytelling can exist separately.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: Designers can create characters with traits and then have the game system control them rather than any player.

can_cause.name: Perspective Taking
can_cause.why: Because characters give players someone to identify with, especially through roleplaying or telling stories, players come to see through that person's eyes.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Developing a character or equipping gear boosts what it can do, yet the player's own skill still affects how actions turn out.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designed characters are important focal points around which designers plan what happens, and they engage players emotionally.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: When players act out their characters well and see that as a goal, succeeding at it gives them a sense of fulfilling the role.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Characters give players someone to tell stories about, and their traits supply material for those tales.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Characters can be harmed or killed, so keeping them alive becomes a goal for players.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because characters can take damage, suffer penalties or die, players feel anxious about what might happen to them.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Any action by a character shapes how players interpret it, even if the game has no system for changing the character's statistics.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Development is by definition a change in a character, so having characters whose traits can change is what makes it possible.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Characters are things players commonly hide, and if they are vulnerable or have a weak spot, players take up concealing them.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Because conversation must come from someone inside the game world, players speaking through their characters naturally produces in-world communication.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Characters keep track of internal states, which lets complex personality-driven behavior be maintained over time.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Characters are things players can move away from danger, so they serve as the bodies that carry out evasion.

can_cause.name: Melodramatic Structures
can_cause.why: Switching which character the player controls lets the player see events from several viewpoints, so they end up knowing more than any one character does.

can_cause.name: Player Characters
can_cause.why: Player characters come into being when players are given control of characters in the game.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Characters are something players control and can plan the growth of, so they must exist for character-based planning to happen.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Characters are tied to accounts whose passwords can be handed over, so a whole character can be bought and sold for real money.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Characters carry goals and intentions that players can take on, and acting according to their personality and context is roleplaying.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: When characters have different abilities, a combo can require their joint actions, so one player cannot perform it alone.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: When players control different characters with orthogonally differing abilities yet must act as a team, they have to figure out how those differences fit together.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Characters that players shape through their own planned growth give lasting proof that the player's decisions and work mattered.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Having characters allows enemies to be more detailed and to be tied into social relationships with the player's character.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Characters are the abstract side of the world's inhabitants, and they link hidden values to concrete things in the world.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: The many numbers attached to a character allow rewards such as raised attributes and skills, new abilities, or gained items.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Characters hold the abstract information like attributes and skills, while avatars are their tangible presence, so the two usually affect each other.

changes.name: Loyalty
changes.why: The characters one is loyal to, and the bonds with them, change how strong and personal the loyalty feels.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Persistent characters give players lasting roles and specialties within the group.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: If players feel attached to their characters, the penalties those characters suffer are felt more strongly.

changes.name: Role Fulfillment
changes.why: Paired with freedom of choice, characters let players pick or build the role they play, making success easier and more satisfying.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Individually managed units can become more like characters, though mostly units are indistinguishable from each other.

conflicts_with.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
conflicts_with.why: Characters that differ from the start may not be equally powerful, which can upset fairness between players.

conflicts_with.name: Death Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Death consequences applied to important characters in a fixed story can threaten to destroy that story.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Differences in character abilities, especially unequal ones from the start, can make some players stronger than others.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: If important characters die through death consequences, the planned story can be broken.

patterns.name: Privileged Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: Abilities that let someone do what others cannot.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The ability must open genuinely different tactics or goals, and access must be defined and balanced. Skilled play should not easily make up for its absence.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A special power is named, but it is weak or easily imitated, so privileged and ordinary agents play the same way.
patterns.knobs: who gets the ability; its power; how often it can be used; how it is obtained

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: If some special actions are available from the first moment, players start the game with different capabilities, so their starting situations are unequal.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: When actions are limited to certain players or units, each one becomes the one to turn to for particular tasks, giving them their own area of expertise.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: A game can adjust which special abilities players receive and when, for example based on race positions, so those behind are helped and the gap narrows.

can_cause.name: Interruptible Actions
can_cause.why: Being allowed to stop an action midway is itself a power others lack, so it counts as one of these special abilities.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Because some players can do things others cannot, unsupervised gaps may widen over time, though a game can also adjust who gets what to even things out.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Special abilities distinguish story characters, and gaining a new one can mark a key story moment, so they help the designer lay out an intended plot.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Certain special abilities, like creating or manipulating resources or restoring health, can become a steady source of supply that keeps replenishing.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Being able to enter places that others cannot is one form of special movement, so access to a refuge can be such a privilege.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: When special abilities exist from the start, players know what they have and can plan their approach over the long run.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Abilities gained mid-game change what players or their rivals can do, forcing them to adapt their short-term plans to the new situation.

can_cause.name: Boss Monsters
can_cause.why: Giving an enemy abilities the player lacks changes how the fight plays, making it feel like a distinct boss encounter.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: A special ability that lets players ignore a blocking hazard makes having that ability the condition for passage.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: A boss with powers others lack makes players work out how to cope with them.

can_cause.name: Spawn Points
can_cause.why: Letting only certain avatars act as spawn locations gives those avatars a special power that others lack.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: When only certain characters hold particular abilities, a combo depending on them can only happen if those players act together.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with boss monsters, special abilities held by only some enemies make those encounters feel different.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Providing certain abilities only to certain game elements gives those elements special standing among others.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Special abilities are typical parts of a construct, and giving them out makes constructs differ from one another.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: Switching alarms on or off is an unusual power, and when a game offers it, it often strongly shapes how play goes.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Special abilities can be expressed through an avatar's skills, which lets the ability be adjusted further.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Abilities can be tied to a character so that losing the character means losing the ability, which helps set characters apart.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Giving players special fighting actions, such as combos, changes what they can do during a fight.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Companions may have their own special abilities, and gaining a companion can bring the player extra abilities connected to it.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Some players can take less damage or be immune to it, which changes how harm affects them compared with others.

changes.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
changes.why: Special sight abilities can make certain things in the game world stand out, helping the player notice them.

changes.name: Discard Piles
changes.why: A player may be allowed to look through or take from the discard pile when others normally could not.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: Special rights may let a player search the draw pile or choose cards from anywhere in it rather than only the top.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Special powers that only enemies have make them harder, and are one way to create bosses.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: Special immunity or reduced effects means hazards in the environment do not hurt the privileged player the way they hurt others.

changes.name: Fog of War
changes.why: Some units can see more of the map than others, because they are less limited by hidden areas.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Tying an ability to owning an item gives an in-world explanation and makes players want to obtain that item.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Being allowed to look at another player's cards is an information power that sets the holder apart.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Being able to restore health is a special action that changes how long a player can keep going.

changes.name: Irreversible Events
changes.why: Being able to undo something that would normally be permanent is a power that some players have and others do not.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: Some units may follow different visibility rules from others, so they can see things that others cannot.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Special abilities for some players can encourage or require roles and enable team combinations.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: Because certain abilities are special to some players, getting a new one is worth more or less depending on what others already have.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Computer-controlled characters may have abilities that players do not, which distinguishes them from the human side.

changes.name: Obstacles
