changes.why: Some players can ignore or pass obstacles that block others, which changes how those barriers affect them.

changes.name: Parallel Lives
changes.why: When some of the several lives have special abilities, they become worth different amounts to the player and affect balance.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Special immunity can lessen or cancel penalties for some players, and giving penalties to others can leave the rest with relative advantages.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Special abilities can make the characters that players control exceptional compared with others in the world.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: Players may deliberately work toward special abilities, and the existence of such abilities creates choices they must weigh in planning.

changes.name: Role Selection
changes.why: A role's actions are only special if other players cannot do them, and extra bonuses can reward those who choose roles.

changes.name: Secret Resources
changes.why: Knowing about hidden resources is an information advantage that some players hold and others do not.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: Some players get special powers to change the game state or rules, like handling the bank, sharing the facilitating work.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: The effect of special abilities depends on teams, since they can be mirrored between teams or divided among members.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Certain units can have different vision rules or carry abilities, and abilities can move between players along with units.

changes.name: Warp Zones
changes.why: Being the one able to activate a warp zone can be a special power granted to certain agents.

changes.name: Zone of Control
changes.why: Some units can ignore zones of control that restrict others, which changes how they move.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Whether a user has special abilities can decide who is allowed to use particular tools.

changes.name: Transferable Items
changes.why: Transfers can be restricted so only characters able to use or equip an item may receive it, as with class limits in Dragon Age II.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Giving some players special abilities creates imbalances in what players can do, though it can also be used to compensate.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Special abilities held by players on one team can make teams unequal, unless the other teams have matching abilities.

patterns.name: Avatars
patterns.what_it_is: Figures in the game world through which the player acts; their fate depends on the player's success.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: One entity must be the player's main way to act and be affected, and its fate must matter to the player. The more defined the avatar, the more it limits how players can role-play it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character model is shown, but its fate doesn't touch the player's progress, or the player really controls many units, so the 'avatar' is only a picture.
patterns.knobs: how much personality and detail the avatar has; how tightly its fate ties to player success; one or switching avatars

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Avatars are the main protagonists, and as long as players pursue goals through them, they act as human-controlled agents inside the game world.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Avatars can fight, and that fighting ability is what makes goals about capturing something or someone possible.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Fighting is a common ability given to an avatar, so players do battle by acting through that one entity.

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: When a player can only know what their one avatar can perceive, the world is revealed piece by piece, like a mystery to investigate.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: How well an avatar's actions succeed can depend on the player's own skill, which makes physical execution a bigger part of play.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: An avatar is an entity inside the game world, so giving players a point of focus through it never breaks the fiction.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Avatars can be damaged and fight, so they can be knocked out, and removing them becomes a goal, especially between players.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games where players try to eliminate each other, one player's avatar is an opponent that other players must fight.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Players' main way of affecting the game is through a single entity in the world, which becomes the place their attention and actions centre on.

can_cause.name: Fog of War
can_cause.why: Because an avatar only perceives some of the world, players only see part of the game state, leaving the rest hidden.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: An avatar enters the game when a player joins and stands for their actions, so joining adds a new element to the world.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Whatever an avatar can perceive decides what counts as discovered, so moving it around lets players find new parts of the world.

can_cause.name: Loyalty
can_cause.why: Story and character-related patterns like loyalty to someone or something can be applied when players have an avatar to carry them.

can_cause.name: Parallel Lives
can_cause.why: When players look after several diegetic persons as one group, and losing one hurts at once, it resembles a weak form of parallel lives.

can_cause.name: Permadeath
can_cause.why: When an avatar is eliminated, the game may simply end for that player, since their success is tied to it.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers can hold back areas until the avatar gains certain abilities, so story progress follows the order they planned.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: An avatar with a personality and goals invites players to act in character, though a heavily defined one narrows which roles fit.

can_cause.name: Spawn Points
can_cause.why: In multiplayer shooters, some avatars can be given the special ability to act as a place where other players enter the game.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Since an avatar's loss ends a life or the game, keeping it alive becomes a central aim in many games.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: As the main protagonists, avatars are often essential to making the game fit its theme, though the theme also limits what they can be.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Avatars are things players commonly hide, and if they are vulnerable or have a weak spot, players take up concealing them.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Avatars are what players move to dodge threats, so they supply the thing that does the evading.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Avatars are solid objects in the game world, so they can stand in each other's way and hinder movement.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: When players meet only through an in-game representation, others see the avatar rather than the person behind it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Avatars need a world to exist in, and things like obstacles and hazards affecting them shape how that world feels and is understood.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: Whether an avatar blocks sight or not changes how it relates to the world around it.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Avatars are the usual visible form of a character, and some character traits are shown only cosmetically through them.

conflicts_with.name: God Views
conflicts_with.why: When an avatar limits what a player perceives, an all-seeing overview becomes impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Units
conflicts_with.why: Controlling several elements at once removes the single point of focus that an avatar relies on.

patterns.name: Randomness
patterns.what_it_is: Events and effects in the game cannot be predicted exactly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Random outcomes must have known ranges and affect decisions that matter. The balance with player skill needs to be chosen deliberately.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Random rolls happen, but the results are trivial or always overridden by skill, so luck changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: size of the random range; which events use it; probability distribution

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: Random elements can be applied before play starts, such as randomly generated characters or trump suits, so players begin the game with different circumstances.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because chance results ignore skill and hit everyone alike, they weakly even out differences between players, and more so when outcomes add up gradually.

can_cause.name: Critical Failures
can_cause.why: Random outcomes applied to skill use can land on extreme bad results, producing critical failures.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: When combat results are decided by chance, some rolls can land on exceptionally strong outcomes, which become critical hits.

can_cause.name: Critical Misses
can_cause.why: When combat results are decided by chance, some rolls can land on exceptionally bad outcomes, which become critical misses.

can_cause.name: Critical Successes
can_cause.why: Random outcomes applied to skill use can land on extreme good results, producing critical successes.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players physically shake and roll dice or handle cards themselves, they may feel they steer the result and credit luck as something they control.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Random events that are very unlikely, or that strongly change how play goes, stand out to players as exceptional.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: When results vary unpredictably, players cannot easily work out the rules by trying things, yet they may have to try things anyway, like testing potions.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Random elements like dice and card hands produce unpredictable results, and some of them will feel favorable to the player.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Since players often know the odds, and cards once drawn leave the pool, they are encouraged to remember distributions and played cards to guess what comes next.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Everyone has the same chance to receive a random result, which gives a basic but shaky equality, since players feel cheated once an outcome is revealed.

can_cause.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Randomness can go beyond shuffling placements and generate whole game worlds, so dungeons and levels differ each time they are played.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Chance changes each game session, and what puzzles require, so playing again gives different experiences regardless of what the players do.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Chance can create extreme or impossible odds that still take time to play through, so players enjoy watching an attempt fail dramatically.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Because players often know the odds, they can learn the distributions and use that knowledge to make better risk and reward choices.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: If players feel they influence the outcome or care about it emotionally, for instance through betting, not knowing the result creates suspense.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Players usually know the chances of outcomes but not the actual result, so what they know about upcoming events is limited yet bounded.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: Since effects and events cannot be exactly predicted, players cannot be sure how things will turn out, which is the most basic consequence.

can_cause.name: Unpredictable Behavior
can_cause.why: Adding a little chance to computer-controlled players or agents makes their actions harder to anticipate, so players cannot easily deduce the rules behind them.

can_cause.name: Variable Accuracy
can_cause.why: Chance lets a game mimic how real aiming is imprecise, replacing detailed deterministic rules with a randomized result.

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: When the game system itself adds random actions, any action seen might be the system's rather than a player's, which blurs who did it.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: Chance can decide when an event begins, so players get brief occurrences that they could not plan or predict.

can_cause.name: Loot
can_cause.why: What a player gets is not known beforehand and is left to chance; without that uncertainty it would just be a plain, predictable resource.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: Random processes like cards, wheels or dice settle outcomes, so players only initiate them or bet and never decide the result.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Random placement of resources can accidentally make some spots more valuable than others.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Chance applied to enemies, goals, worlds, levels or quests makes game instances differ from each other.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Chance can decide when a rule starts or stops applying, as in Fluxx, where drawn cards alter the rules.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Randomness can decide how agents move, making their movement unpredictable.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: A little chance in computer-controlled agents makes their behavior less predictable, so players find it harder to deduce the underlying rules.

changes.name: Asymmetric Resource Distribution
changes.why: Randomly handing out resources gives players unequal holdings, which is one of the main reasons games use chance.

changes.name: Balancing Effects
changes.why: Chance can hide balancing by giving players overlapping random ranges for rewards or penalties depending on their position, as with randomly effective power-ups.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: Players who bet on random outcomes become emotionally invested in the result, which heightens tension.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Chance can set the starting skills and conditions of characters, modeling the variety found in the real world.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Adding random actions to collaborative efforts makes it easier to disguise who contributed what, keeping others' actions anonymous.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Chance can decide fights, including damage and aiming, and it can create extreme outcomes like critical hits and misses.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Chance stands in for the detailed variation in real-world harm, so damage amounts vary randomly instead of following fine-grained rules.

changes.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
changes.why: Random results limit what a human facilitator can steer, which only matters when facilitation is done by people.

changes.name: Delayed Effects
changes.why: Chance can determine when an effect starts and how long it lasts, so its timing varies.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: Even when an outcome is uncertain, known odds let players weigh a risk-and-reward choice that does not rest on their own skill.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: Chance can decide when temporary goals appear and how long they remain available.

changes.name: Free Gift Inventories
changes.why: Chance can decide which rewards players receive from free gifts.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: Dice results can constrain a game master's power over player characters, though they may fudge results when a random outcome would be unwanted.

changes.name: Game System Player
changes.why: A modest amount of chance in computer opponents makes their behavior less predictable.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Randomly placing or changing world elements makes each game session differ from the last.

changes.name: Generic Adversaries
changes.why: Chance can vary individual enemies while still keeping them recognizably alike.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Drawing from shuffled stacks or decks gives players randomized hands.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Random placement or appearance of elements makes each play of a level different, though it may cause balance problems.

changes.name: Moveable Tiles
changes.why: Chance can determine how tiles move or where they end up.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Chance can determine how far or where agents and tiles move.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Chance can determine whether and how severely a penalty strikes.

changes.name: Player-Created Characters
changes.why: Random elements can be built into how characters are generated, as in many roleplaying games.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: The effect of a picked-up power-up can be set by chance, which can also mask balancing.

changes.name: Predefined Goals
changes.why: Chance can change the specifics of goals, so what players aim for differs between sessions.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Randomly ordered events can combine into a story, and seeded stacks can place key events within certain regions while keeping exact timing random.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: Because future events cannot be calculated, players find it harder to foresee what their actions will lead to.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Randomly changing what a puzzle requires makes puzzle games worth replaying.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Chance can vary the details of quests so that they differ between sessions.

changes.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
changes.why: When worlds can change, chance can alter them so each game instance differs.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Chance can decide whether and what players receive as reward.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Skill use is often settled with random results, abstracting messy or risky actions into something manageable, and creating critical successes and failures.

changes.name: Tile-Laying
changes.why: Drawing tiles from a shuffled stack randomizes what players get to place.

changes.name: Trumps
changes.why: In card games with trumps, the trump suit can be chosen randomly before play starts.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Chance can decide the order in which players take turns, making it unpredictable.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Chance applied to enemy traits makes their difficulty uncertain, adds variety, and encourages players to gather information.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Outcomes that depend on chance limit foresight and counter predictable consequences, reducing how much planning helps.

conflicts_with.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
conflicts_with.why: If the facilitator generates random results out of sight, players may suspect cheating instead of chance.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players do not feel lucky, chance counters the effect, and players who know the statistics will not hold the perception.

conflicts_with.name: Experimenting
conflicts_with.why: Experimenting needs consistent outcomes to learn from, and chance results make it harder to draw conclusions from trials.

conflicts_with.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
conflicts_with.why: Heavy randomness weakens player control, so players doubt that improving their play is possible or worthwhile.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: Dice can kill characters when neither the game master nor players want it, working against the master's control.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Chance limits what player skill can achieve, so it works against mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: Chance makes it harder to know in advance who is ahead, so it is less clear that anyone is stuck as a kingmaker.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Chance decides outcomes, which lessens how much the player's own performance influences results.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Chance can counter snowballing, but the dice themselves can give some players luckier outcomes and disturb balance.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: If much of the design depends on chance, planned story elements can become irrelevant.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Chance events blur who is ahead, though players who understand statistics may still predict results when many random events occur.

conflicts_with.name: Strategic Planning
conflicts_with.why: Since future events cannot be calculated, long-term planning gets harder, though known odds still allow planning at a higher level.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: When chance heavily affects outcomes or can flip success into failure, players feel their effort matters less.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Chance in results makes outcomes less certain in the short term, reducing how well players can foresee what happens.

patterns.name: Algorithmic Agents
patterns.what_it_is: Animals, monsters, and other creatures whose behavior follows rules rather than player control.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must respond to the game state and produce actions that look purposeful and relate to the player's goals (hindering or helping). Behaviour needs enough variety to avoid being solved at once.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Entities repeat a fixed loop regardless of what the player does, so they behave like scenery.
patterns.knobs: complexity and aggressiveness of behaviour; how much it reacts to the player; how many agents

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Because agents run on rules, designers can make those rules react to how the player behaves, so a companion may leave or attack after the player changes conduct.

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: Algorithms are what give game entities their own behavior, so any entity driven by them is an agent that acts without a player deciding for it.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Designers can write agent rules to oppose the player and tune them, so the agents reliably supply difficulty to overcome.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Agent rules can range from simple to learning-based, and richer behavior gives players more to read and respond to.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Designers give algorithm-driven entities goals that oppose the player's, and they reliably act on them, producing opponents.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Since developers write the rules, every agent follows what the designer fixed in advance, giving consistent behavior compared with other similar agents.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When players can write agent algorithms during play, they add new acting entities into the game world themselves.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: An agent can temporarily stand in for a human player, so the game can carry on while that person is away.

can_cause.name: Memory of Important Events
can_cause.why: Program-controlled characters can have this only if their code notices which events matter, stores them, and brings them up and reacts at fitting moments.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: When players write the agent algorithms in a set-up phase, creating and testing those algorithms becomes a game of its own around the main play.

can_cause.name: Mules
can_cause.why: When players write their own algorithms, those can be used as helper tools to carry out tasks for them.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Story characters the player can interact with need rules governing what they do, so agents supply the NPCs a narrative depends on.

can_cause.name: No Direct Player Influence
can_cause.why: If players write the agents beforehand and then only watch, the running game proceeds without their direct input.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: Agents can be given rules that pursue goals apart from the player's, so they appear to want something themselves.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Algorithms players author become new content in the game, particularly agents tied to characters that would not otherwise exist.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because designers must author agents ahead of time, their behavior is part of the fixed story whenever a game has narration.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Rules set by designers mean agent responses follow fixed patterns, letting players foresee results at a general level of the game.

can_cause.name: Sense of Self
can_cause.why: Game-controlled agents must react to their environment to act at all, so nearly any game with them already includes some degree of this pattern.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Agent behavior sets how much short-term planning players must do and how hard it is, since they must deal with what agents do.

can_cause.name: AI Players
can_cause.why: An AI player is built by designing rule-based agents that take on the role a player would have.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled opponents give a single player someone to fight, so combat can exist without other human players.

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled agents can react constantly to what the player does, which lets them play the role of a companion following and assisting the player.

can_cause.name: Context Dependent Reactions
can_cause.why: Code can make agents react to situations, though designers must write rules covering every plausible case, which is workable for large numbers of characters.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: As companions, algorithm-driven characters help the player and won't betray or trick them unless designers make them do so.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: Software-driven agents can only show attachment if their algorithms generate in-world social consequences, alongside the presentation needed to display it.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Computer-run characters who develop over time and may end up in different places make each playthrough differ from the last.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Players who build their own programmed agents must plan ahead, and complex agents make opponents consider what the agent will do.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: When players get creative control to build agents, planning is all they do, since the agents carry out the plan afterward.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: A lone player can have a team by playing alongside companions that the game's algorithms control.

can_cause.name: Zero-Player Games
can_cause.why: Agents following set algorithms, like Sims or robots, run the game on their own so humans have no need to act.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Agent rules can sometimes take over a player's avatar, such as acting bored when no input arrives, then give control back.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Algorithms can run or influence a character, such as backup players stepping in or showing idle behavior when the player is absent.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Most agents act through a game world, so algorithm-driven agents are a common building block of what populates and happens in it.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: When players write the algorithms, they must understand the game system in general, which pushes them to plan ahead.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: By adjusting how agents behave, designers control how much short-term planning the game requires and how hard it is.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: The number and behavior of computer opponents can be tuned to adjust difficulty.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Having at least one computer-controlled member makes it easy to enforce the faction's rules and their social consequences.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: A program can drive NPC behavior so they act in the world without a human controlling them.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Computer-controlled entities can supply the conflict and combat that other human players would normally provide, so a lone player still has opposition.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: When the system controls units, their behavior comes from algorithms, making them work as enemies.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: When players create agents beforehand and the game then runs without their input, they can't feel more influential than they truly are; shared control with agents also muddles agency.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Agents are usually run by computer code, so needing a computer limits play to places and settings where computers are available.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Mastering a game means seeing characters as mechanical functions, which makes it hard to feel emotionally drawn to those agents.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: If players fully understand computer opponents that never vary in their destiny, there is nothing new left to discover on replay.

patterns.name: Improved Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: An ability the player already has starts working more effectively.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The improvement must noticeably change what actions achieve, be tied to progress or rewards, and be paced so it does not erase challenge. Players should be able to feel the difference.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A level-up that raises a stat so slightly or so evenly with enemy scaling that play feels exactly the same.
patterns.knobs: size of each improvement; how often and by what route it is gained; whether players choose

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: When another party hands out boosts, or when boosts are paired with weakened abilities, power gets evened out between players, so the boost works as a balancing tool.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Stronger abilities make a player's actions more potent, which carves out the things that player is especially good at doing.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: If boosts are handed out before play begins, they set how hard or easy the game starts out for the player.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: Places or conditions in the game world can be defined by the boosts they give, so being there changes how effective your actions are.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because boosted abilities let players change the game state more, they feel like they are shaping events even more than they really do.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Stronger abilities are a natural prize for success, and since they make later actions work better, they help players keep achieving things.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Getting a boost is typically the payoff for finishing goals about becoming more skilled, so improvement and the goal reinforce each other.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Stories often make the hero and their foes grow stronger, and that growth lets the plot reach bigger, later-stage conclusions as play advances.

can_cause.name: Increasing Rewards
can_cause.why: When a character or construct keeps growing stronger through improvement, the player keeps receiving ever-larger benefits as the game goes on.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Making abilities stronger is an intuitive thing to give players for achievements, since it directly makes their actions more effective.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Stronger abilities empower players to influence the game state more, which in turn generates smaller aims that help them toward bigger ones.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Making existing abilities stronger is a typical way the player's construct develops.

can_cause.name: Boss Monsters
can_cause.why: Giving a normal enemy upgraded abilities makes it notably tougher, which is one way to turn it into a boss.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Gaining better abilities can follow from choices the player makes, so what the character becomes depends on what they chose to do.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Raising attributes, skills or caps makes a character more capable, which is exactly what developing means in play.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Owning controllers, equipment, sets, tools or vehicles can make a player stronger, so wanting the boost motivates the ownership goal.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Players can plan by choosing to upgrade abilities they already have, which is one simple way growth is directed.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: A stronger version of an ability that skill alone cannot make up for becomes a privilege over those who lack it.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: Making what members can already do stronger, whether on characters or on an abstract team construct, is a way the team develops.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with character or construct development, better abilities give players more things to do as they progress.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: This pattern is about changing how well abilities work, so designers choose which abilities to boost, by how much, and when.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Boosts can apply to these via investments, tech unlocking, or upgrading, though new abilities fit them just as plausibly as improved ones.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Ammo alone does not boost abilities, but several varieties of it, like in Fallout, can offer different improvements.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars can become stronger through stat increases or by owning items, which explains the improvement within the game's theme.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Improvement can add more action points or make actions cost fewer of them, so players get more done each turn.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Applied to foes, boosts make the game harder to beat, while lavishly given to players they can make it too easy.

changes.name: Character Levels
changes.why: Growing stronger can come with advancing levels, and levels can also let players choose which abilities to boost.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can have their attributes, powers, or skills raised, which makes improvement easy to explain in the game's story.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting is among the most common types of action to benefit from stronger abilities.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: Until players get used to their new strength, the boost can make it hard for them to judge accurately how likely an action is to work.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Opponents can be strengthened too, using whichever mechanism fits what they are, such as avatars, characters, or units.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Joining or teaming up with a group can be the reason for a boost, especially when the character represents an organization.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: When players pick which abilities to improve, they get real choices about how their character or construct develops.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Moving around is a very common action to boost, as with speed increases in racing games.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: If boosts arrive mid-game, they shift how much success relies on the character's strength versus the player's own skill.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Power-ups can be shaped by the improvement they offer, and they may make abilities adapt to the situation during play.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Skills are a direct target, and improving them can be done by raising a number or by using them often.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can receive boosts through items, investments, tech unlocks, or upgrading, which fits their place in the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Stronger characters can make tasks easy, so too much improvement erases the challenge.

patterns.name: Skills
patterns.what_it_is: A measure of how likely a character is to succeed at a task; it grows with experience.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Skill values must visibly change the odds or the outcomes of actions, and different skills must matter in different situations. Players need some way to raise them and to see the effect.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A skill list on the character sheet whose values barely move the success chance, or a skill that nobody ever has reason to check or improve.
patterns.knobs: number of skills; how strongly a skill value shifts success odds; how fast skills grow

can_cause.name: Characteristics
can_cause.why: A skill is one kind of trait describing how well something can do an activity that training could improve, so it counts as a characteristic.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Because characters differ in what they're good at, players end up with distinct areas where their character is the stronger choice.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Games with very many skills, or extra details like specialties and familiarities, give players lots of rules and options to juggle.

can_cause.name: Crafting
can_cause.why: A large skill list often includes making things, so having the right skill is what lets a character craft.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Since a skill value shows how likely an action is to work, players can judge their odds before attempting it.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Raising a skill makes later actions with it more likely to work, so the increase itself helps the player progress.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Skills that can be raised give players a clear goal to work toward: becoming better at something over time.

can_cause.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
can_cause.why: Giving characters different skills makes them differ in what they can do, not just in how strong they are overall.

can_cause.name: Player-Created Characters
can_cause.why: When building their own character, players pick which skills it has and at what levels, usually by spending a budget of points.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: In real-time games, a character's skill level can change how hard an action is, while the player's own execution also matters, such as aiming.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: A skill can act as the gate that decides which characters are allowed to use a particular ability.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: When skills unlock special abilities, different characters play differently, and players can choose which skills to improve.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Using a skill successfully earns experience in it, so the actions performed decide which areas the character grows competent in.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: A critical hit can reduce the target's skills as one of its extra harmful effects.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Different players having different skills means a combo can require several people's skills together, which one player alone could not supply.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Skills set how competent a character is with abilities, so the same ability can work better or worse for different characters.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: A character's skill can make aiming easier or harder, so physical shooting accuracy depends partly on the character and partly on the player.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Different skill sets help tell player avatars apart from each other by what each one is good at.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Gaining or raising skills is a usual way characters grow during play.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Skills make characters differ from one another, and which skills a player chooses to improve says something about the character.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: When a game has fighting, skill levels usually influence how well characters do in it.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Skills can make allied helpers differ from one another, just as they do for player-controlled characters.

changes.name: Controllers
changes.why: Having a particular skill can be what permits a character to use a specific controller.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Skills can determine whether and how well a character is able to make items.

changes.name: Critical Failures
changes.why: Higher or lower skill levels typically shift the odds of an especially bad outcome occurring.

changes.name: Critical Hits
changes.why: A character's skill level usually changes how often an attack lands as an especially strong hit.

changes.name: Critical Misses
changes.why: Skill levels typically affect how likely an attack is to go disastrously wrong.

changes.name: Critical Results
changes.why: Skill levels usually shift the probability of extreme outcomes, so skills and critical results influence each other.

changes.name: Critical Successes
changes.why: Skill level typically changes the chance of a roll turning out exceptionally well.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Skills can be used to make enemies differ from each other, as they do for player-controlled entities.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Skills can change how much health a character recovers when healing, so they influence restoration.

changes.name: Mules
changes.why: Because skills make characters differ in competence, a character carrying things for others is less useful than a skilled one.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: Since skills express chances of success, they affect how well players can foresee the results of what they intend to do.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Having the right skill can be required to use certain tools, so skills decide who may use them.

changes.name: Variable Accuracy
changes.why: Better character or player skills can reduce the wobble or hit-area size, making shots more accurate.

changes.name: Character Levels
changes.why: Some games, such as the Elder Scrolls, decide when a level is reached by counting skill points gained, so skills drive the levelling.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Skills often state success likelihood, and deterministic skill tests leave less room for misjudging influence.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: When skills are distributed unevenly among players, their chances end up unequal.

patterns.name: Environmental Effects
patterns.what_it_is: In a certain part of the world, actions and events work differently than elsewhere.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each area needs a rule that alters actions, movement or events, and it should be noticeable and matter to choices of where to go.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Areas with a different look or label that behave exactly like all others.
patterns.knobs: which areas have effects; effect type and strength; whether permanent or temporary

can_cause.name: Alien Space Bats
can_cause.why: When an area's special effect has no visible, believable cause in the game's world, players may feel it arrives from nowhere, which is what these are.

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: A harmful or slowing area pushes players to avoid crossing it and funnel through the narrow gaps left beside it.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: An area's effect can be explained by something that happened earlier, so players read the world's history from how the place behaves.

can_cause.name: Installations
can_cause.why: Effects that make player actions easier act like helpful tools placed in the world, giving a boost to whoever uses them.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Because an effect applies only in a certain spot, the ability it grants or removes is tied to that place.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Areas such as liquid, ice or vegetation can make travel slower or harder to steer, restricting how freely pieces move through them.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: An area that only slows progress rather than killing still stands in the way, so players must pay a cost to cross it.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: An area can give or negate abilities for some game elements, so only certain ones can use or resist what it does.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Some areas make travel quicker or easier, and a game element can be allowed to cross where others cannot.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: Harmful areas threaten players with no opponent involved, so they face danger from the world itself rather than from other players.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: When players know in advance what an area does, its position becomes valuable to reach, hold or avoid.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Since effects are known ahead of time, players can map out routes and goals around them long before reaching them.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Areas that cost lives or health create a need to endure them, making staying alive a goal in itself.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must work out moment-to-moment how to dodge or exploit area effects, particularly against other players or enemies.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Many settings are dangerous to humans or their stand-ins, so hazardous areas make the game world feel true to its theme.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Different areas change what actions are possible or costly, so play feels different depending on where you are.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Each effect applies only in its own place, so the rules players follow change from one spot in the world to another.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: Hazards in the environment prevent travel, and players need a switch, immunity or special ability to get past them.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: A place needs to be free of harmful environmental effects to be safe, and players can be made immune to them to create a haven.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Effects spread across an area, such as a lake of acid, can work as traps covering all the types of hidden danger.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Each effect has to be weighed against which of the player's characters it touches, changing what those characters can do there.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Terrain can make moving cost more or fewer points, changing how far a player's limited budget stretches.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Areas can change how fighting and its harm work for those inside them.

changes.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
changes.why: Designers must decide whether an area's effect applies to objects that exist within the game world.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Effects change details of the board, making some spaces behave differently from others.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Effects alter what parts of the world do, though how each part links to the rest remains most important.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Effects change details of a level, so different stretches of it play differently.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: Areas can block or alter what can be seen, as vegetation or height differences can.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Dangerous areas can take away lives from those who enter them.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Players must avoid disadvantages or use advantages from effects, shaping how they steer and position themselves.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Areas can speed up, slow down, or entirely stop travel through them.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Places where power-ups show up can be seen as effects, since the area produces them.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: When effects relate to how well players perceive things, they influence goals about scouting and finding information.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: Helpful effects in a region give players a reason to fight to own that region.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Designers must decide which of the player's units an effect applies to, changing what those units can do inside it.

patterns.name: Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: Unpleasant consequences for the player's position, progress, or abilities.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The effect must actually worsen the player's position, progress or abilities, and it must follow from specific events. It needs to be large enough to be felt but fair enough that it does not break the experience.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A penalty so small or so easily undone that players ignore it, or one that is announced but changes nothing in the game state.
patterns.knobs: how severe; what triggers it; whether it can be recovered from

can_cause.name: Destructible Objects
can_cause.why: Penalties can work by removing or destroying items a player owns, which turns those items into things that can be destroyed.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: Penalties usually happen at a specific moment and then pass, so they behave as short-lived events in play.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Because penalties set players back, especially by removing abilities, players must learn to cope with setbacks to become skilled at the game.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Heavy punishments for attackers, like guards intervening, discourage aggression and give a weaker form of safety in an area.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Penalties like downtime can bench a player, for example making them watch others play, which turns them into a spectator.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing something bad may happen to you creates worry and suspense while you play.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: A cost tied to a chosen goal turns it into a commitment, since failing or forgoing other goals has a price.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Evading only matters if being hit or caught costs you something, so a penalty gives the dodge its purpose.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: With the risk of penalties, a betrayal succeeds only if the betrayer plays the role well enough to avoid being detected.

changes.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
changes.why: Attaching penalties to different tasks signals how important each is, so players know where to put their attention.

changes.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
changes.why: Penalties can alter a goal's requirements so that it becomes harder to fulfill.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: Penalties on short-lived goals draw players to focus on them, while still leaving the choice to prioritize other things.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Being killed needs some penalty to hurt, and killing nearly always brings one, whether to the victim directly or by rewarding the killer.

changes.name: Quick Time Events
changes.why: Penalties for failing these events push players to attempt the required actions, since they have little choice.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Penalties can reduce or otherwise negatively change what a player holds.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Penalties can be used to temper rewards, balancing out what players gain.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Penalties can lower a player's score as a negative change.

changes.name: Parallel Lives
changes.why: Losing one of several elements normally costs little, such as only the actions that piece gave, which keeps the loss from stopping play.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Suffering a penalty can shatter players' belief that they have great control over what happens.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: In single-player games, players can reload an earlier save to undo a penalty, making it avoidable.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A penalty that ignores the game's story or world, like killing a character yet restarting them earlier, breaks the sense of fit.

patterns.name: Balancing Effects
patterns.what_it_is: Rules that shrink the leader's lead so the contest doesn't end too early.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must really give help to those behind or cost to those ahead, at the right game phase. Too strong and players feel effort is wasted; too weak and the gap stays.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A catch-up rule exists but gives such a small bonus that a leader still always wins, or it is only mentioned in the manual.
patterns.knobs: strength of catch-up; when it applies (early, middle, late); preemptive or corrective

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: In single-player games, balancing effects set how hard the game feels, so they can keep play relaxed and easy, often by adjusting difficulty on the fly.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: In single-player games, balancing effects can raise or hold the difficulty at a demanding level, often by adjusting it dynamically as the player performs.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players don't notice the balancing at work, they feel their own choices decided the outcome, so hidden balancing makes their influence seem larger.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Keeping players close in standing means bigger goals stay open to everyone longer, so larger outcomes get settled later in the game.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because leaders get held back and trailing players helped, nobody is clearly winning, so uncertainty about the result lasts as long as possible.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: They shift fortunes between opposing players or teams, pulling a stronger side back or helping a weaker side so contests stay even.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Graceful Surrender
can_cause.why: These can offset the unevenness caused when someone leaves, helping the remaining players keep a fair game after the exit.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Rules that help the struggling side and hinder the leading side during play push teams back toward even footing.

changes.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
changes.why: Corrective balancing can make up for uneven starts, such as a first-move edge, by giving the disadvantaged side compensation later on.

changes.name: Beat the Leader
changes.why: This pattern covers players choosing to act against whoever is ahead, which is a player-driven version of the balancing the page describes.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Characters who are already skilled can be made to progress more slowly, which evens out results without players seeing it.

changes.name: Drafting Spreads
changes.why: Charging extra for picking items deeper in the spread offsets the advantage some players have from picking first.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: Players who join midway are behind, so the balancing must correct gaps after they arise instead of preventing them at the start.

changes.name: First Player Advantages
changes.why: Compensation such as turn order changes or replaying sessions can offset the edge that moving first gives.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: Because late joiners start behind, balancing has to correct imbalances once they exist rather than head them off.

changes.name: Middlegame
changes.why: Balancing is typically applied here because it would be premature at the start and would cheapen the finish at the end.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: Balancing can be done by giving new abilities to trailing players, or by making new ones additions to choose from rather than automatic upgrades.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Racing games commonly give boosts to those behind or limit those in front, so that the field stays close.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Placing weaker players at strategic locations and stronger players at poor ones corrects imbalances.

changes.name: Tied Results
changes.why: Since balancing pulls competitors toward equal standing, games where ties are possible tend to end with players level.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Setting the order of turns so that disadvantaged players get the most favorable positions corrects imbalance between them.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: These help equalize the field when opponents differ in skill, so the player-versus-player contest stays fair.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: These mechanisms help keep the competing teams evenly matched so neither side dominates.

conflicts_with.name: Auto-Aim
conflicts_with.why: Aiming help can narrow the gap between players, but in multiplayer it can also favor whoever uses it, so it may support or undermine balance.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: Since the game shifts help and penalties to players, they cannot reliably calculate their own odds of success.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players can see that balancing is what tipped the result, they no longer feel their own actions made the difference.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: When the game levels out differences, a skilled player gets less sense of being better than others.

conflicts_with.name: Kingmaker
conflicts_with.why: By keeping the outcome open, balancing avoids situations where a losing player decides who wins.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Holding leaders back and helping others makes it hard to tell early who will win.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If leaders are penalized and trailing players helped, hard work counts for less in the final standing.

patterns.name: Character Development
patterns.what_it_is: Over the course of the game, a character gains new skills and grows stronger.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Visible progress with clear triggers, improvements that actually change what the character can do, and some player choice in direction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Numbers go up but the experience of play stays the same, since challenges scale in step and no new options appear.
patterns.knobs: growth rate; sources of progress; size of each improvement; amount of player choice

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: A character is something the player controls, so any growth in it is a case of the player's in-game stand-in getting stronger or changing.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Gaining new or better abilities, especially ones only the player has, makes players feel their own choices matter more than they really do.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Changes like a character's looks shifting as it grows have no effect on rules, yet remind players of what they did and signal ability to others.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Players who have progressed far create gaps with latecomers, and that imbalance pushes players to buy and sell characters or items outside the game.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: When progress carries over between sessions and players can look at it, those saved changes work as a record of how they have played.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Because growth often comes from collecting points through repeated activities, players may repeat those tasks over and over just to advance.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: When players know growth is coming and can see how near the next step is, the effort they spend becomes something they feel invested in.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Growth is commonly handed out as payment for achievements, such as experience points earned from winning fights or finishing quests.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: Handing out new or improved abilities opens up options that were closed before, so the character's growth works as unlocking.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Seeing progress accumulate, and in persistent worlds having others notice it, makes players feel their time spent has lasting worth.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Players need not think about rules for a power until the character gains it, so the rules they deal with change as the character grows.

can_cause.name: Player-Created Characters
can_cause.why: When characters grow over time and players have freedom or creative control, the character gradually becomes something the player shaped, not only something prepared beforehand.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: When characters can grow in chosen ways, players get a richer thing to plan, so planning naturally rests on this growth.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: When a team is made of characters, each character getting better over time automatically means the team as a whole is changing.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Characters who grow and change over time are one of the ways to reproduce the nuance of believable human behavior.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: As a character grows and gains new or improved abilities, players have more options of what to do as the game proceeds.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: As a character grows, its visual form should reflect that, so how the avatar looks changes along with the character's progress.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Development is a change applied to the characters themselves, shaping what they can do and how strong they are.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Joining a faction or improving standing with one counts as growth, and that standing then shapes what the character may do toward its members.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Character growth can advance a game's story, and it can also produce story structures of its own as the character changes.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: Since growth typically enlarges what a character can do, it changes how much of the outcome depends on the player's own skill versus the character's.

changes.name: Resource Caps
changes.why: One way a character grows is by having its maximum limits raised, so development directly changes these ceilings.

changes.name: Secondary Interface Screens
changes.why: Tracking growth needs places to show it, so development calls for dedicated screens or extra parts of existing ones.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: A character's skills are one of the things that get raised through growth, making the character more likely to succeed at actions.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Because some players progress further than others, growth can leave participants with unequal characters, hurting fairness among them.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: In a world that keeps running, those who started earlier or played more have stronger characters, so latecomers are at a disadvantage.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Characters that have grown unevenly give players unequal strength, so those who played more or earlier gain an edge over latecomers.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: When characters grow stronger by themselves, the game helps the player, which reduces how much personal skill matters.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
conflicts_with.why: Strong character progression can prevent players from mastering the game, since improved stats carry results instead of the player's own skill.

patterns.name: Game Element Insertion
patterns.what_it_is: New game elements are added to a game already in progress.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define what can be inserted, when, and by whom, and let the new elements really change the situation. Who controls the insertion shapes pacing and surprise.
patterns.just_a_label_when: New things appear, but they are the same as before or too weak to matter, so nothing changes.
patterns.knobs: what is inserted; how often; who controls the insertion

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: When players are the ones adding new elements, they can place pieces so that they interact with or build on what is already in the game.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Managing the adding of elements takes upkeep effort from players, which adds tedious bookkeeping that isn't really the fun part of play.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: If an inserted element wasn't among the elements the game originally defined, bringing it in counts as input from outside the game.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When several different elements are available to insert, players get to pick which one to bring in.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Controlling the pace at which new elements arrive lets the game build toward larger goals and wrap-ups as play moves forward.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Inserting often costs resources and the chosen element might turn out well or badly, so each insertion is a bet players make.

can_cause.name: Legacy Games
can_cause.why: When an insertion is permanent, it carries over and alters later game sessions, which is how legacy-style games are built.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Because new elements keep arriving into the game, they work like resources that are replenished, and may even have to be used.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Since inserting elements uses up resources and involves risky choices, players must plan how to spend and allocate what they have.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Enemies can be added during play instead of existing from the start, which brings new opposition into the game.

can_cause.name: Framed Freedom
can_cause.why: Placing elements into the game world is a creative act that gives players a hand in shaping play while staying within what the game offers.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Bringing in a boss is a less common form of insertion, mostly tied to quests and set story structures.

changes.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
changes.why: Facilitators can control the timing of when elements are inserted, so insertion shapes what they do.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: New elements such as spawned enemies and loot keep being added to the world, changing what it contains.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: New elements added into a level change what it holds and give players surprises.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Adding elements, even improvised ones, gives progress and surprise to stories and keeps endless stories from getting repetitive.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Introducing characters into the game is less common than other insertions but can move a story forward and surprise players.

changes.name: Pick-Ups
changes.why: Pick-ups are found in large numbers in games, so they are frequently the things that get inserted.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Player characters can be added and removed to match which players are present, though this is less common than other insertions.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Power-ups are plentiful in games, so they are common items to be inserted, sometimes at random times and places.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Planned insertions of characters or monsters can serve fixed story structures, especially around quests.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Inserted elements are resources, and the way they come in can be adjusted by converters, generators, or regeneration.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units exist in large numbers, so they are a common thing to insert, such as armies in strategy games.

changes.name: Game Element Trading
changes.why: The game itself can supply new elements, for example as loot, giving players a source of items to trade.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Adding a newcomer's character into an ongoing multiplayer game can upset how even the match is.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Inserting player characters for players who arrive late can make the game unfair for the ones already playing.

conflicts_with.name: Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: Putting new player characters in because someone arrives late can cause balance problems among the players.

patterns.name: Evolving Rule Sets
patterns.what_it_is: New rules are added to the game as it goes on.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There has to be a channel to deliver new rules (patches, expansions, a game master, legacy-style carry-over) and the rule set must be large enough that changes alter what good play is. Players need to be told or able to find out what changed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A patch that only fixes bugs or adds cosmetic items, so the way anyone plays stays exactly the same.
patterns.knobs: how often rules change; how big each change is and what it touches (new abilities, removals, balance)

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: Designers change rules over time by taking away things players could do, which is one typical way of altering how a game plays.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: When some players or teams gain an edge, new rules can be added later to even things out again.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Rules keep piling up or players must learn how new rules mix with old ones, so the game becomes harder to grasp.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: A rule added that only lasts for a limited period becomes a short-lived happening within the game.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Because short-lived rule events can come with objectives attached, those objectives naturally exist only while the temporary rule is active.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: When a temporary rule is linked to something happening outside the game, such as a date, the event follows real-world timing.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: If rule changes come neither from the game itself nor from players, they arrive from an outside source like a facilitator or game master.

can_cause.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
can_cause.why: Each time rules change, players must sharpen their skills or knowledge to keep up, so there is always something more to learn.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Adding fresh capabilities is a common choice when designers decide what to change in the rules.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Game masters or players alter rules so the game behaves more like how they believe things work in the real world.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Whether play feels different depends on whether changes merely rebalance or instead radically alter play through gained or lost abilities.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Since rules change as time passes, the game necessarily has different rule sets at different moments.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: As rules keep changing, unexpected interactions between them accumulate, so combos can slip in even though designers try to counter them.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Designers keep changing a persistent game, so you must come back regularly to keep up or you fall behind others.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: When new rules appear during play, players unaware of them may feel results were bent, even though no one cheated.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: In persistent worlds, changing rules can renew the need to explore after players have already seen everything.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Rules get revised over time so strong ways of playing are reduced and weak ones lifted, evening out differences in power.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Rules that change over time can smooth out imbalances that appear, easing the fragility of balance built from differing roles or growth.

changes.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
changes.why: When different players hold different elements, unexpected combinations arise easily, so adjusting rules over time is especially useful.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Changing rules over time helps these games keep players balanced, supply new content, and give people reasons to come back.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Worlds that keep running must change rules while people are playing, which can annoy players who feel hurt by the changes.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Rule changes can be used to keep fairness between competing players.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Changing rules alters what counts as good strategy, so players must keep updating what they know to stay current.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Rule changes can be used to keep fairness between opposing teams.

patterns.name: Ability Losses
patterns.what_it_is: The player loses abilities they once had, for example as a punishment.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The loss must have a clear trigger (a failure, an enemy effect, running out of a resource) and noticeably shrink what the player can do. The player also needs to see how it can be undone or worked around, or it just feels arbitrary.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'loss' is announced but the player can still do everything useful, or it lasts so briefly that it is ignored.
patterns.knobs: which actions are lost; what triggers it; how long it lasts

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: When a strong ability that few others have is taken away on purpose, the gap between players shrinks, so the loss works as a deliberate equalizer.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Losing abilities can wipe out a whole area where a player was skilled, though only once every unit holding that ability is gone.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: Taking harm can do more than lower health; it can also strip away actions, so the harm shows up as lost abilities.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: If enough abilities vanish, a player may be left unable to act meaningfully, which leaves them idle until something is restored.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: Hazards in the game world, such as radiation or solar flares, can remove abilities from players or their pieces.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: When lost abilities can be recovered, players get a new aim of working to win those abilities back.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Taking away abilities is a straightforward way to punish players who fail at goals or make bad choices.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: If the lost abilities are never recovered and leave the player unable to act, that is the same as being permanently removed from play.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: If the loss is only temporary and leaves a player unable to act, it equals being knocked out for a while.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Some stories require characters to lose their abilities or gear at set moments, so the designer scripts the loss into the plot.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Blocking actions that would not fit the setting, like attacking shopkeepers or allies, keeps the game world coherent from a story viewpoint.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When gaining one ability costs another, players must weigh what they give up against what they get.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Cursed items or hidden hazards can strip abilities from players who run into them without knowing the cost.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: When story events take away abilities, players must adapt to having fewer actions, which changes how the game feels.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Taking abilities away changes the player's construct too, though this is rare and mostly makes sense for story reasons.

can_cause.name: Cooldown
can_cause.why: Using an action temporarily takes it away from the player, and that short-lived loss is what a cooldown amounts to.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: A critical hit can take the form of the target losing abilities, which is an effect on top of ordinary health loss.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: A haven can let hostiles enter but strip their ability to act harmfully there, so the area stays safe despite their presence.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Rules that change which abilities players have, such as removing them as a penalty, alter what a player can do.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Losses can hit a single player character, so that one avatar loses actions it used to have.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Having fewer actions available makes the game harder, which can help keep it demanding.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Losing abilities counts as negative growth for a character, and restrictions from joining a group can shape how a character develops.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: Fewer available actions make the game simpler to handle, lowering its complexity.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Dying can cost players their abilities, for instance when respawning without earlier gear or skills.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: When players' abilities can vanish, it becomes harder for them to judge accurately how likely they are to succeed.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Each lost ability removes an option, so players have a smaller set of actions to pick from.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Items such as cursed objects can cause the loss, and gear may be taken away along with the abilities it gave.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Taking abilities from players can hurt everyone equally as a penalty, or can even things out if it targets an advantage only some had.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: A loss of ability may only become real once every unit that had it is gone, so the unit count affects it.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
