changes.why: Losing abilities is one way a construct's development can go, changing what the construct can do.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Losing abilities is a penalty that changes a character's traits and can be a form of character development.

conflicts_with.name: Competence Areas
conflicts_with.why: Losing abilities can wipe out areas where a player was skilled, while other players may become the only competent ones left.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Losing abilities shrinks what players can do, which tends to weaken their feeling that they have great influence over the game.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Blocking actions can keep a story consistent, but for roleplayers it breaks the sense of the world by stopping things they would expect to do.

patterns.name: Game Servers
patterns.what_it_is: Computers or mechanisms on which each separate play of the game runs.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Implement the rules and let players join and leave instances reliably, handling non-player actions and state. Stability and scale shape what is possible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A server is mentioned, but the logic really runs on clients, so it adds no mediation or consistency.
patterns.knobs: players per server; persistence of the world; rule enforcement versus simulation

can_cause.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
can_cause.why: A server can do the facilitating work, handling large amounts of data and complex calculations and executing things like element insertion.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Many servers are in charge of holding and showing the game world to players, in addition to running the rules.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: Running the game requires the server to track what happens, so those numbers exist already and are easy to expose outside the game.

can_cause.name: Instances
can_cause.why: Keeping track of separate game sessions is practical mainly when a server exists, so servers make frequent use of instances.

can_cause.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
can_cause.why: A server can sit between solo and multiplayer play by hosting online games where players mostly play alone, as in FarmVille and Candy Crush Saga.

can_cause.name: Mediated Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players act through the server program, which holds the state and relays events, so play is inherently carried by a computer or machine.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: The main purpose of a server is to give players a shared place to connect to and play together online.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Some servers host worlds that must never be reset, so copying the server would make versions drift apart.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: If the server simulates the game components instead of enforcing rules in code, players can run the game themselves on it.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Because the server holds the game state and handles all updates itself, players do not need to be present at the same time.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Servers can often handle both the individual games and what links them, so the higher-level game runs there.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: A server can offer optional help that takes over some of the bookkeeping chores players of self-run games would otherwise do by hand.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: With extra effort, a server can simulate the game's components, making self-run play possible on it, though this is otherwise hard to combine.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: A server implements rules in code, which leaves little room for players to run the game themselves, so the two are hard to combine without extra simulation effort.

patterns.name: Spawning
patterns.what_it_is: The moment an avatar, unit, or other element appears in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must say what appears, when, where and with what advantages or penalties. It must fit the pace of the game, such as reviving players or refilling enemies and resources.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Elements that reappear instantly in the same state with no cost or delay, so removal and death carry no consequence.
patterns.knobs: what spawns; how often; delay before respawn; where it can happen; penalties on respawn

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: When respawning follows a death, players only notice what they lost once they are back in the world and see their weakened state.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Entering the world can make players wait and look around before acting, and a respawn after dying also costs lost play time.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Spawning is a way for the game itself to drop new elements into the world, such as enemies or items, without a visible source.

can_cause.name: Interruptibility
can_cause.why: Because players can be put back into the game easily, someone who stepped away can rejoin without the game being ruined.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: How often and when new resources appear sets how plentiful or scarce those resources feel to players.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: In persistent worlds, spawning can be timed to happen at regular intervals, which makes the game progress in steps like a clock.

can_cause.name: Spawn Points
can_cause.why: Spawning needs a place to happen, so the act of spawning in a game world makes use of spawn points.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Spawning sets up player characters at the start, when they enter new levels, or when they are revived after dying.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Choosing when new elements appear changes how much pressure players face and so how hard the game feels.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Spawning can bring back objects after players have destroyed them, so they are available again.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Spawning is how opponents get introduced during play, and both their frequency and type can be tuned.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: New items such as installations and vehicles can be placed into the world during play by spawning them.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Spawning adds elements into the world while it is running, changing what is in it over time.

changes.name: Grind Achievements
changes.why: Spawn timing decides how quickly targets reappear, which determines how easily players can repeat tasks to reach grind goals.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Newly spawned things can be said to come from places players cannot reach, though this raises the question of why players cannot go there too.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Spawning can place structures into the world during play.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: New players can be dropped into an ongoing game through spawning, so they do not need to wait for a restart.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Spawning places players or other elements when a level begins or when players move into a new one.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Players can be killed and still return through spawning, so killing others does not remove them from the match.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Spawning can be limited to when players are active so that new elements match player activity.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Players are often at a disadvantage just after appearing, so the way spawning is designed decides how fair the game feels.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Because killed players come back, the game can allow them to be killed without knocking them out for good.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: After major story events, spawning can place players in new locations or introduce new story elements to move the plot along.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Spawning is a way to bring resources into the world while the game is running.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Vehicles can be introduced into the world during play by spawning them.

conflicts_with.name: Steadily Decreasing Resources
conflicts_with.why: Spawning brings in some kind of resource, which works against a game where resources only run down, unless spawning itself spends a resource.

conflicts_with.name: Team Elimination
conflicts_with.why: If team members keep respawning, a team can never be completely wiped out.

conflicts_with.name: Teams
conflicts_with.why: As long as team members can spawn again, the team cannot be eliminated.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Few game settings have a believable reason for things to simply appear, so spawning is hard to fit into the story.

patterns.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: Abilities are available only in certain places in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Certain spots must give real, useful abilities that are not available elsewhere, and be limited or contestable. Movement rules should let players choose to reach them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Special spots exist but give weak bonuses or nobody needs them, so players walk past.
patterns.knobs: how strong the ability is; how many such places; who can control them

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When abilities sit in specific places, players can decide whether to travel there and whether to use what they find, giving them real options.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Because such places are few, only whoever reaches or holds them gets the ability, so it becomes a limited advantage.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: If the ability at a spot is vital or gives a big edge, that spot becomes worth fighting over and planning around.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: When a player must take an action to trigger a place's ability, it feels like a short-lived power they borrow rather than own.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Abilities that fire automatically when a player enters a spot hit them without choice, producing dramatic, outsized moments.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Places in the world can make particular abilities stronger or possible at all, changing what players can do depending on where they are.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: An avatar gains new or better powers while at specific spots, so its capabilities shift with where it stands.

changes.name: Improved Abilities
changes.why: Certain spots can strengthen something a character already does, making it better only while at that place.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: Reaching a particular spot can hand a player something they could not do elsewhere.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: A tile can itself stand for a place-bound ability, or be altered by other elements that supply such an ability.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units get new or better abilities by being at specific locations, so where you station them changes what they can do.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Much of a world's gameplay character comes from abilities that are tied to particular spots in it.

patterns.name: Destructible Objects
patterns.what_it_is: Items that can be broken or destroyed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must have a means and a reason to break the objects, and the breaking must change the game state, such as opening a path or giving loot. The object needs a visible durability.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Scenery that looks breakable but is not, or whose destruction changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: durability; what destroys it; whether it comes back

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Because objects can be broken, smashing them becomes a natural goal players are asked to complete, especially when destroying them also drops rewards.

can_cause.name: Parallel Lives
can_cause.why: When a player's lives are tied to several breakable objects that are all in danger at once, the player is juggling multiple lives in parallel.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: If a destroyed object doesn't come back through respawning, its absence stays in the world and permanently alters it.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Breaking an object is a believable in-story reason for it to vanish from play, so removing elements doesn't clash with the game's setting.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Breakable objects that hurt things nearby when destroyed, or set off falls, avalanches or floods, can be turned into traps.

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: When a destructible object is broken it can leave obstacles behind, which narrow the route and so create a choke point during play.

can_cause.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Pieces of the world that can be destroyed or taken away let the play area get smaller one clear unit at a time.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Destructible objects that can act as traps let players use the environment, and deciding how to use them takes planning.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor can be made breakable, for example through wear, so protective gear eventually becomes useless.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Nearly any item can be given the ability to be destroyed, which changes how players treat it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: When things in the world can be wrecked, players must handle the world differently, and in some games even terrain or buildings can be lost.

changes.name: Obstacles
changes.why: Making an obstacle breakable lets players decide between going around it or spending effort to destroy it.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: In tile-based games a tile can be destroyed, which removes pieces of the board as play goes on.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: A trap that can be destroyed can be disarmed to remove the threat, or exploited to turn it against enemies.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons can wear down and break through use, so players cannot rely on them forever.

changes.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
changes.why: When a solid item can be broken, its blocking effect is only temporary and it can serve as a trap.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: An installation can have starting health and be destroyed, which makes it something players can lose.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Letting vehicles be destroyed gives players without them a way to deal with their advantage.

patterns.name: Fog of War
patterns.what_it_is: Unexplored or unseen parts of the world are hidden from the player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Hide parts of the world and make player entities with limited sight ranges reveal them, so lacking information truly affects choices. Decide whether terrain and units are hidden separately and whether revealed areas re-hide.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A dark overlay exists, but the map and enemies are fully known or revealed at once, so it never limits decisions.
patterns.knobs: sight range of units; whether explored areas re-hide; separate fog for terrain versus units

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Because knowing the terrain and what it holds gives a tactical edge, hidden areas make players want to find out what lies in them.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Unseen parts of the map create a reason to send pieces out to uncover them, so exploring becomes a goal in itself.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: When the fog returns to areas nobody is watching, players have to keep watching them repeatedly to notice changes, which becomes an organized guarding activity.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: When the fog returns to areas nobody is watching, players have to keep watching them repeatedly to notice changes, which becomes an organized scouting activity.

can_cause.name: Secret Resources
can_cause.why: A game can choose to leave resource locations hidden, so players only learn where they are once they have discovered them, whether or not terrain or enemies are hidden.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Since players only see what their own pieces can perceive, they cannot be sure about the rest of the world and must act on partial knowledge.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Hidden areas mean players can't see everything at once, so they must recall what they saw earlier.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: When you can't see parts of the battlefield, enemies can approach or strike from places you aren't watching, so attacks catch you unprepared.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Hidden enemy information is most noticeable in fights, since players cannot see opponents fully and so can be caught off guard by surprise attacks.

changes.name: Game State Overviews
changes.why: Overviews of the game state show only what the player's pieces have perceived, so uncertainty is built into what the overview reports.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: With two fog layers, never-seen and currently-unseen, players are pushed to revisit the same areas repeatedly to spot what has changed.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Fog hides the parts of the world nobody is observing or has yet explored, so players perceive only a portion of it.

changes.name: God Fingers
changes.why: Players can move freely across the whole world with this ability, yet fog stops that freedom from revealing everything inside it.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: A god view could show everything, but fog limits it to what the player's pieces could perceive, giving imperfect information as a first-person view naturally does.

changes.name: Mini-maps
changes.why: The fog hides information on mini-maps in the same way it does in the main view of the game world.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Resource locations can be left out of what the player sees, so players must find them rather than being shown them from the start.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Players must account for unseen areas and unknown enemies when planning, which changes how they need to prepare their approach.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Players must account for unseen areas and unknown enemies when planning, which changes how they need to prepare their approach.

changes.name: Third-Person Views
changes.why: Fog gives a third-person view the limited knowledge that a first-person view gets automatically, so the player cannot see everything from above.

patterns.name: Installations
patterns.what_it_is: Large tools in the world that the player cannot move or carry away.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must give actions that are better or different from those available elsewhere, and be placed where players would want to go. Limits like cooldowns or cost keep them from dominating.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A large fixed object in the scenery that offers nothing that could not be done elsewhere, so no one needs to use it.
patterns.knobs: where they are placed; what they offer; cooldown or cost of use

can_cause.name: Armor
can_cause.why: Some installations are protective structures, like sandbags in Memoir '44 that shield units in a hex, so they work as armor fixed in place.

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: Because installations are big and fixed, they can block or narrow routes, forcing movement through limited spots.

can_cause.name: Controllers
can_cause.why: Installations can be the thing players operate to gain access to actions or resources, so they act as fixed controls.

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: An installation can need certain items to function, so players get goals of bringing those items, like ammunition for a weapon installation.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Their sheer size makes installations stand out in the game world, and this can be reinforced by tying map widgets to them.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Installations are said to suit expansion phases, since placing or taking them extends what a player can do and reach.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: Installations give players special actions and resources at their location, which makes them well suited to the phase of exploiting what you hold.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: They offer players useful actions and can reveal the map around them, which draws attention and activity to their location.

can_cause.name: Fog of War
can_cause.why: Like avatars and units, an installation can reveal the area around it, thereby clearing hidden parts of the map.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: Being large and visible, installations are easy to recognise in the world, especially when linked to geospatial widgets, so players use them to orient.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Since an installation cannot be carried, the actions it grants are only available to avatars who go to where it stands.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Their size and fixed position mean they can physically get in the way of players moving through the space.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: They are large and usually scarce, so the actions they provide are only available at certain places, sometimes limited by cooldowns.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: When an installation works as a controller that gives access to resources, its location becomes a place players go to obtain them.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Having a fixed installation with useful actions makes its spot valuable, so players plan around holding or using it.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Because installations make certain places valuable, players must think ahead about where to go, defend or place things.

can_cause.name: Tools
can_cause.why: Installations are tools too large or fixed to carry, giving players actions that are unavailable or less efficient elsewhere.

can_cause.name: Weapons
can_cause.why: Heavy weapons such as ballistas, turrets and mounted guns are too big to carry, so they sit in place as installations.

can_cause.name: Easter Eggs
can_cause.why: A hidden surprise can be concealed inside an object in the game world, and interacting with it in the right way triggers it.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Installations give avatars abilities that only work at their location, changing what the avatar can do there.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: An installation has its own presence on the board, which alters the space it sits in.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Installations have their own presence in the world they occupy, changing how that world plays.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: Installations can hand benefits to whoever controls an area, which supports goals of holding a location.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Installations have a spot and presence within a level, shaping how that level plays.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: Installations make the places where they stand more valuable, which raises the worth of the territory containing them.

patterns.name: Vehicles
patterns.what_it_is: Elements that let you move faster or differently than usual.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Vehicles must provide clearly different movement, speed, protection or weapons from walking, and be reachable at set places or buildable. The world must be shaped so the difference matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A model you sit in that moves like the avatar at the same speed and gives no new access or power.
patterns.knobs: speed; terrain access (air, water); armor and weapons; spawn locations and numbers

can_cause.name: Armor
can_cause.why: A slow vehicle can make up for its sluggishness by shielding whoever rides inside it from attacks.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: A vehicle can hurt other game elements just by crashing into them, even if it carries no gun.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Vehicles are usually much bigger than the characters using them, so they stand out visibly in the game world.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Getting a vehicle is a prize because it makes later travel, access and play easier.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Because vehicles bring speed, access and protection, players want to get hold of one and set that as a goal.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Vehicles often steer differently from normal movement, so players improve their skill by learning to control them.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Riding a vehicle can let a character move faster, or trade speed for something else useful like protection.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Weapons mounted on a vehicle give its user attacks that others without the vehicle cannot make.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Some vehicles let players cross things normally impassable, such as air, water or lava.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Players may compete to reach the spots where vehicles are found first, and vehicles change how fast racers get places.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: The places in the world where vehicles can be found become valuable spots players seek out.

can_cause.name: Spawn Points
can_cause.why: Vehicle locations can be where vehicles are created during play, and in some games vehicles themselves let players respawn.

can_cause.name: Tools
can_cause.why: A vehicle changes how players can move around, so it works as an instrument for getting things done.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Reaching new areas and handling the vehicle itself both give players different kinds of play to enjoy.

can_cause.name: Weapons
can_cause.why: A vehicle can carry guns, or count as a weapon itself because it injures things it runs into.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Players in vehicles can be denied entry to certain areas, which restricts their advantage.

can_cause.name: Installations
can_cause.why: A vehicle that is immobilized but still works as a tool or weapon can serve as an installation.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Obtaining a vehicle gives the character actions, like new ways to travel, that come from the vehicle.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Vehicle locations are named as valuable places to control in shooter games.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Vehicles carry avatars and change how they get around the game space.

changes.name: Conditional Passageways
changes.why: Needing a certain vehicle can be the condition for passing, and vehicle users may also be barred from passages to keep things balanced.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Vehicles change how pieces or characters can move across a board.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Vehicles change how players travel through large or hazardous worlds.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Vehicles change how players get through a level.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: When a vehicle is destroyed, the game can make that cost players a life.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Each vehicle steers differently, so real-time controls for moving around change when riding one.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: The basic purpose of vehicles is to give faster or different ways of moving than normal.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Vehicles change how quickly players get places, which affects who wins a race.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Faster or otherwise impossible movement makes it easier to complete goals about reaching a destination.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Vehicles carry units and change how they move around the game space.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: A vehicle with special movement can carry players into places that would otherwise be closed to them.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Having a vehicle replaces plain on-foot travel, taking away the dull effort of ordinary movement.

conflicts_with.name: Inaccessible Areas
conflicts_with.why: Vehicles usually travel more easily, possibly across other terrain, so they can undercut the reasons an area was made unreachable and clash with the theme.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of vehicles among players leads to imbalances.

patterns.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
patterns.what_it_is: Events that players cannot influence in any way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The event must really be beyond player action and have a visible effect on play. Players should know about it in advance if you want planning around it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An event shown as unstoppable that players can in fact prevent or ignore with little effort.
patterns.knobs: when and how often it occurs; how large its effect is; whether it is announced

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: A forced event can guarantee that a new companion joins the player at a set moment, since the player cannot prevent or alter it.

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: Because players cannot stop an event once it is running, a consequence set to land later is certain to arrive.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: A very powerful event can disable or remove players' ability to act, leaving them waiting.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: If a huge event is announced ahead of time, players can see it coming, though only when it is clearly advertised.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Story structure is built mainly from events the player cannot change, so the narrative proceeds in the designer's chosen order.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Fixed story beats are made from events players cannot alter, so the plot unfolds in the designer's chosen way.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: When players know an unstoppable event is coming, they can foresee what it will cause in the game.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: When an event takes control away, the player can only watch it happen, becoming a spectator instead of an actor.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: If players know unstoppable events are coming and what they do, they can plan ahead around them.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing when and how an unstoppable event occurs, such as with moveable tiles, is information players can use to their advantage.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: An event that players cannot prevent can guarantee an ambush happens, no matter what they do.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Since players cannot halt the event, it can be used to make a countdown reliably run out.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: Making a lengthy action unstoppable means players cannot interrupt it once it has begun.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Events that players cannot change typically narrow what they are able to decide.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Game worlds are naturally prone to being changed by events players cannot influence, like the sun rising and setting.

changes.name: Ghosts
changes.why: A ghost's recorded actions must be unstoppable, because interrupting one would probably invalidate all its later actions.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Such events can force players to move, which changes how they have to position themselves.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: When quick travel is not already triggered by something else, the travel action can be made unstoppable.

changes.name: Storytelling
changes.why: The presence of unstoppable story events strongly shapes how a story can be told in the game.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Games with turns often have bookkeeping steps after everyone has played that players cannot affect.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: Sudden overwhelming events can wipe out whatever sense of their odds players had built up.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: These events develop beyond players' control, so even if players trigger them they cannot affect how they unfold.

conflicts_with.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: Players holding this much power over elements makes it hard for a game to include events that overwhelm everything else.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: Players can replace any outcome with their own decision, so an overwhelming event can be softened or ignored.

patterns.name: Death Consequences
patterns.what_it_is: What changes in the game when a character dies.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The cost of dying must be big enough to make players avoid it yet small enough not to make them quit. Saving and reloading must be limited, or the penalty disappears.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Dying brings back the player on the spot with everything intact, so death is just a short animation.
patterns.knobs: what is lost on death; how far away and how fast respawn is

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Permadeath-style deaths remove the player entirely, so a death can end the whole game for that player.

can_cause.name: Game Termination Penalties
can_cause.why: When dying means permanent elimination, the player is punished by having the game end, which is the harshest penalty a death can carry.

can_cause.name: Loot
can_cause.why: A killed character's gear can be left in the world, giving whoever caused the death something to pick up.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Dying is packaged as a cost to the player, such as lost lives, gear, or points, so death consequences work as penalties.

can_cause.name: Spawning
can_cause.why: Since a dead avatar must return to the game world to keep playing, dying leads to the avatar being placed back in play.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: If dying makes players lose their gear, the abilities that gear gave them end at death rather than lasting the whole game.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing that dying carries a cost makes players more anxious about the dangers they face.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: When consequences attach to avatars, how and where they return to the world shapes balance and how much lost gear remains.

changes.name: Character Levels
changes.why: Dying may lower a character's level, which is a common way to penalize death even if hard to justify in the story.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Death consequences can be applied to characters, such as requiring new ones or taking away abilities, changing what dying means for them.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Dying can make players lose their gear, which explains lost abilities naturally and decides how much is left behind for others.

changes.name: Friendly Fire
changes.why: If a kill comes from a teammate, the usual reward for the killer may not be given, so the consequence changes.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Death consequences bundle the penalties that come from players killing one another, deciding what the victim loses and the killer gains.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: A kill can raise the killer's score, and a death can lower the victim's score, so scores shift with deaths.

changes.name: Hotseating
changes.why: A player's character dying can serve as the signal that ends their turn and hands the device to the next person.

conflicts_with.name: Characters
conflicts_with.why: Death consequences applied to important characters in a fixed story can threaten to destroy that story.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: How a dead avatar is placed back into the world can tilt fairness between individual players.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: If a key character in a scripted story can die, the planned plot can be broken.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: Players can reload a saved game after dying, undoing the cost and making the consequences hard to enforce.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: How dead avatars return to play can favor one team over another, upsetting fairness between teams.

patterns.name: Difficulty Levels
patterns.what_it_is: A setting where the player chooses how hard the game will be.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each level must change the play in a meaningful way, such as the enemies' numbers, skill or the player's resources. Players must be able to pick and change the level.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A menu with easy, normal and hard that only change a name or a small number, so the games feel the same.
patterns.knobs: what each level changes; how many levels; whether the level can be changed during play

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players can pick an easier setting, so someone wanting a relaxed session can lower the demands and play without much pressure.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players can pick a harder setting, so skilled players can raise the demands and get a tougher test.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide for themselves how hard the game will be, which gives them a real choice about the kind of experience they get.

can_cause.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
can_cause.why: After finishing a game on one level, players can replay on a harder one, though the top level marks a ceiling on improvement.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Players who raise the level as they get better follow a gradual learning path toward mastery of the game.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Levels let players or opponents adjust how hard play is for themselves, which works as a handicap, especially when each player can set their own.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Levels change how many challenges must be beaten and how likely failure is, so a session can be adjusted to what players want.

can_cause.name: Optional Rules
can_cause.why: Since players may depart from the standard setting by choice, the chosen difficulty acts as a rule they can opt into.

can_cause.name: Permadeath
can_cause.why: Making character death permanent can be offered as an extra, harder mode, as in the hardcore versions of some games.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Players get some say in what the game demands of them, so it can fit different people's needs, though only in a basic way.

can_cause.name: Handicap Achievements
can_cause.why: A game with several difficulty settings can give a separate achievement for finishing on each setting, so harder settings act as the handicap.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: Levels can change how skilled computer-controlled opponents are, so they play better or worse depending on the chosen setting.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Levels can change how capable the automated agents controlling enemies are, making them tougher or weaker to face.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Levels can make ammunition more or less plentiful, so players have more or less to work with.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Levels can scale the damage players take or deal, making fights more or less punishing.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Levels can change how many enemies appear, so the same game throws more or fewer opponents at players.

changes.name: Framed Freedom
changes.why: Players use difficulty settings to decide how much freedom they want when some freedom is already built into the game.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: In multiplayer games, players typically pick the difficulty in the lobby before play begins.

changes.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
changes.why: Restricting map and position displays, as in the realism mode of one shooter, makes team coordination harder and so raises difficulty.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Levels can change how much health players have or how easily they recover it, altering how much punishment they can take.

changes.name: Sanctioned Cheating
changes.why: A level can forbid some built-in cheats, such as an ironman mode that blocks console commands, to make the game harder.

changes.name: Secondary Interface Screens
changes.why: Difficulty is usually chosen on menu-style screens outside the main play view.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Levels can change how often enemies appear or reappear, which raises or lowers the pressure on players.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Levels can make healing items and other tools more or less common, which shifts how hard it is to survive.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: If players choose easy levels just to finish or dominate, they skip the growth that real mastery needs.

conflicts_with.name: Save Scumming
conflicts_with.why: Reloading saves to undo bad outcomes defeats the intended challenge of the chosen level, so designers may adjust levels once it is detected.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: Repeatedly saving and reloading lets players dodge consequences, which undermines the difficulty the level was meant to enforce.

patterns.name: Player-Created Characters
patterns.what_it_is: Characters whose creation the player was able to influence in some way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need real options, such as traits, equipment and skills, that change how the character plays. Designers must balance the freedom against the time and knowledge it demands.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A long creation screen with only cosmetic choices, so every character plays the same.
patterns.knobs: number and depth of options; randomness in creation; when in the game customization happens

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: Because each player spends time building their own character, participants begin the game with different strengths and setups rather than identical ones.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Since players think through how a character should act while making it, that character ends up behaving in the way its creator chose instead of the designers.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Shaping a character from the start makes players feel their choices will steer how the story unfolds, perhaps more than they truly do.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: Characters that players build are themselves pieces of the game made by players, whether they are controlled by the player or by the game.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: Choosing freely how to build a character lets players pick what kind of role they want, and then enjoy succeeding at pursuing that character's goals.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Players can also create characters that the game controls, such as companions, so the pattern is not limited to the character they play.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Equipment is one of the typical things players can alter when shaping their character.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: Letting newcomers build their own character allows them to make one that suits the characters already present in a multiplayer game.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Players who shape their character may feel they are influencing how the narrative develops, changing how the story seems to unfold.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Some games let players build characters that are not controlled by them, like companions in roleplaying games.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: The most natural use is letting players make the characters they will control during play.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Having made the character themselves, players are more likely to act in a way that fits it when roleplaying is part of the game.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Skills are one of the typical traits of a character that players are able to choose or change.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Stories written in advance by designers may not have roles that fit characters players invented, making the two hard to combine.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Making many character choices up front can work against smooth learning.

patterns.name: Temporal Consistency
patterns.what_it_is: The order of events in the game matches the order of events in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design must remove or limit saving, reloading and free retries, so events stay as played. Lives or pauses must not let players erase outcomes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The story claims events are final, but players can reload a save and redo any moment freely.
patterns.knobs: whether and when saves are allowed; number of retries; how events are permanent

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: Because play can't be rewound or discarded, events stay in one fixed order; a mystery needs that, though players' viewpoint must also be limited.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Since gameplay can't be thrown away, designers must build the planned story around events that really happened in order, though flashbacks can still be used.

conflicts_with.name: Contextualization
conflicts_with.why: In live-action roleplay, staging scenes from the future or past steps outside the single running timeline, so the order of events is broken.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Chances
conflicts_with.why: Redoing events breaks the sense that the story world moves forward in one consistent order.

conflicts_with.name: Instances
conflicts_with.why: Since instances can be re-entered by the same or different groups, the same events replay, which clashes with a believable flow of time.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Consistent Narration
conflicts_with.why: Replaying story events that already happened makes the narration contradict the timeline of the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Save Points
conflicts_with.why: Going back to a save and replaying parts of the game can clash with the story's timeline and what the player already knows.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: What you do in play no longer matches the order of events in the story world, because reloading jumps you backward.

conflicts_with.name: Scenes
conflicts_with.why: Scene-based structure lets designers deliberately jump between times, as when a game switches between modern and historical characters.

conflicts_with.name: Setback Penalties
conflicts_with.why: If the story acts as though every challenge was passed on the first try, the repeated attempts caused by setbacks contradict the narrated timeline.

patterns.name: Decreased Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: An event after which an ability works worse than before.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reduction must visibly change what the player can do and be tied to a cause the player understands. It should usually be limited in time or reversible, or it becomes a dead end.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A penalty so small that the odds of success barely move, or one that is always cured at once.
patterns.knobs: size of the reduction; how long it lasts; how it is cured

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: If an ability is weakened so far that success becomes impossible, the weakening has effectively turned into a complete loss of that ability.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Weakening some abilities, especially when paired with strengthened ones elsewhere or limited in time, evens out how well players can act against each other.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: When units or team members end up weakened by different amounts, each is left strong in some areas and weak in others, which sets them apart.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Players can pick how much weakening they begin with before play starts, which makes the game easier or harder to their taste.

can_cause.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
can_cause.why: The game can quietly apply weakening depending on how well a player is handling challenges, adjusting difficulty without announcing it.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: Specific places in the game world can weaken whoever enters them, so the surroundings themselves cause the reduced effectiveness.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: If lost strength can be recovered, being weakened gives players a reason to set the goal of getting back to their former level.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Starting some players with reduced abilities evens out skill gaps, and either players or a game facilitator can set this up.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Reduced abilities can show up as slower or restricted movement, for example in certain areas or when wearing heavy gear.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Weakening what a player can do works as a punishment, since later actions become less effective or less likely to work.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: When weakening hits players who did not expect it, such as through items or surroundings that look harmless, it works as a trap.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Lowering abilities alters the construct, though it is uncommon and usually motivated by narrative.

can_cause.name: Cooldown
can_cause.why: A used action is temporarily weakened in availability, so the cooldown can be seen as a time-limited reduction of what the player can do.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Ability strength can be turned down without removing it, so the player keeps the action but it works less well.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Different ammo types can bring a drawback, such as less damage, in return for a benefit such as better penetration.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor's protection can come at a cost, like slowing the wearer or reducing athletic skill.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Weakening players makes tasks harder, so the level of challenge can be tuned without making the game more complicated.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can be made weaker by events in the story or by what happens to them, changing how well they perform.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Weakening a character after death is a typical way to make dying matter.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: Sudden weakening that players did not see coming lowers their odds of success, so they can no longer reliably judge those odds.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Cursed equipment shows its harmful effect only once it is put on, weakening the user who equipped it.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Actions stay available, but weakened ones become less effective, so players are pushed away from choosing them.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: An item can carry a downside as well as an upside, or be a trap that weakens its holder.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Weakening players who are ahead, or giving others advantages, narrows the gap and shifts how well players can act against each other.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: When skills are numbers, they can easily be lowered by adjusting the value, for example when wearing heavy armor.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Individual units can be weakened by events, such as damage, so they differ in how well they perform.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Weakening abilities is one form of development that alters what a construct can do.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Weakened abilities tend to be felt as penalties, which makes it hard for players to believe their influence on the game is bigger than it is.

patterns.name: Irreversible Events
patterns.what_it_is: Events whose consequences cannot be undone in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: No other rule or action may push that part of the state back, and the game must be able to enforce this (system or facilitator). Players must also understand that it cannot be undone.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The event is called permanent but a later action, undo, reload or house rule quietly reverses it.
patterns.knobs: which events are made permanent; how often they happen; how clearly players are warned

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Once an irreversible event happens, some parts of the game state no longer matter for later play, so players can treat that part as finished.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Combined with loyalty, an irreversible event such as a betrayal makes someone a lasting foe, helping build a fixed story.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Events that can be undone and repeated feel ordinary, so making them permanent lets them feel special and rare.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: When a player must pick among several choices that can never be undone, the weight of choosing creates inner conflict.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: When permanent events alter a game world that can be reconfigured, those alterations stay and cannot be restored.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: A story can only move forward meaningfully if past events stay fixed, such as leaving a level for good or changing loyalties.

can_cause.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Permanent events remove parts of the world that cannot return, so the playable space keeps getting smaller as play goes on.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Since actions cannot be taken back, players are pushed to think ahead before committing to them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players know a choice may be permanent and others may press them to act quickly, which creates pressure.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players understand permanent results as clear progress or failure, and built things cannot be destroyed, so their work feels worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Entrenching Gameplay
can_cause.why: Actions that cannot be undone gradually narrow what is still possible, especially when their combined effects interact, pushing play toward a few local situations.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Because many player actions are abilities, making those actions permanent in effect changes how the abilities work and are used.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: An alarm can only be triggered once, or its effects stay even when triggered again, so it acts as a permanent event.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Territory gained, like settlements in Settlers of Catan, cannot be lost later, so control becomes permanent.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Development choices that cannot be undone make a character's growth a series of lasting commitments.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: If built things cannot be destroyed, players need not worry about losing them, which makes building more rewarding.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Permanent events can change a game world so that it can shrink or change in ways that cannot be restored.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Finishing one level and moving on without any way back makes the transition between levels permanent.

changes.name: Loyalty
changes.why: Combined with loyalty, events such as revealing a traitor change allegiances in a way that is hard to take back.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: Permanent character-defining events shape how a character's path develops during play.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: With no way to undo moves, mistakes in puzzles cannot be fixed, so solving them becomes harder.

changes.name: Sockets
changes.why: Upgrades are one way to affect sockets, and since upgrade choices are permanent, they shape what the socket holds.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Moving where spawning happens is a permanent change that advances the story in real-time games without needing levels.

changes.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
changes.why: Unstoppable events are a good starting point for making permanent changes, though other events can still counter their effects.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: If actions can't be undone, each choice has lasting consequences, which makes the choice matter.

changes.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
changes.why: When a reconfiguration is caused by something that cannot be undone, the world's changes become permanent and the pattern is felt more strongly.

changes.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
changes.why: Making each shrinking step permanent is what keeps the world getting smaller, so it strengthens the effect.

conflicts_with.name: Delayed Effects
conflicts_with.why: Delaying consequences can discourage players from reloading saves to undo events, but it makes outcomes harder to foresee.

conflicts_with.name: Equipment
conflicts_with.why: Soulbound gear cannot be traded once equipped, which stops players from buying game advantages.

conflicts_with.name: Experimenting
conflicts_with.why: If actions can't be undone, trying things out becomes risky, so players avoid it.

conflicts_with.name: Free Game Element Manipulation
conflicts_with.why: With so much power over elements in players' hands, it is hard to make an event that players cannot simply undo or change.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: The game master can make any event permanent, yet can also undo it by changing their ruling.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: When effects are delayed to keep events permanent, players cannot easily see in advance what their actions will lead to.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Making equipment soulbound prevents trading it, which closes off one way of buying advantages.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: If players can save and reload, they can return to an earlier state, so events cannot be totally permanent.

patterns.name: Line of Sight
patterns.what_it_is: One game element must be able to see another directly.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The world needs things that block sight and actions that depend on seeing, such as shooting, stealth or detection. The blockers must be placed so that position matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A sight rule is declared but the map has almost no blockers, so everything can always see everything.
patterns.knobs: how much cover or obstruction exists; sight range; which actions need sight

can_cause.name: Alignment
can_cause.why: Because seeing is a game element, designers can turn visibility itself into a goal, such as getting pieces into positions where they can or cannot see each other.

can_cause.name: Fog of War
can_cause.why: Observation ranges work like line-of-sight functions with a maximum distance, so what a piece can see sets what is revealed and what stays hidden.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: When aiming cannot rely on a clear view, players need to think of other ways to reach the target.

can_cause.name: Sniper Locations
can_cause.why: A spot only works for sniping if it gives a clear view over large play areas, so open sightlines create such locations.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Players must plan routes to avoid being seen by agents when attempting stealth goals.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Agents that perceive the world only act on what they can see, so sight decides what they can notice or interact with.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: You can only aim at what you can see, so sight availability decides whether a shot is possible at all.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: When sight rules exist, holding certain parts of the world matters more, since those spots determine who can see and act on what.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: An avatar acts only on what it can perceive, so sight determines which targets and things it can interact with.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Attacks often require seeing the target, so sight decides who can fight whom, though some indirect attacks can bypass this.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Sight-triggered detection by traps or waiting agents shapes evasion, since avoiding being seen becomes the way to escape.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: Sight limits make a controlled unit's viewpoint the place where attention gathers, changing which areas and things players focus on.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Navigation only becomes a challenge when you cannot always see where you are going, so how often sight is available sets the difficulty.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The world must contain things that can block sight, so the layout of the world determines who can see what.

changes.name: Landmarks
changes.why: Landmarks help players find their way mainly because they can be seen from far away, so sight availability governs their usefulness.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Level layouts with walls and obstacles decide which spots can see which others, shaping how the level plays.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Sight can enable movement, such as grappling hooks or portals that only work toward spots the player can see.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Scouting succeeds by seeing things, so planning around where one can be seen or must look becomes part of the task.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: A sniper spot is good because it gives a clear view of many places while other places lack that view.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Being sighted by agents or traps is how stealth fails, so players must plan around which positions are visible.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Traps can trigger when something enters their view, such as laser beams or trip wires that detect a passing player.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units act only on targets they can see, so sight decides which enemies or objects each unit can affect.

patterns.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
patterns.what_it_is: An action's result depends on both the player's own skill and the character's attributes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each action's result must include a real contribution from the player's execution and from the character's attributes. Neither part should be able to cancel the other.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The character has stats, but the player's input decides everything, or the reverse, so one part is only for show.
patterns.knobs: relative weight of player skill versus character stats in outcomes

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: When success depends on both player and character skill, becoming more capable empowers players, which motivates them to chase competence goals.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Players who lack personal skill can make up for it by playing longer to strengthen their character or gear, which encourages repetitive play.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Character stats help results look like those of a skilled hero even while the player is still learning, so the story stays believable.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Players do the aiming, while the sway of the aim depends on weapons, upgrades and skills, blending player and character influence.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: When there are only weapons and tools and no abstract character, the pattern is a way to shape how the avatar performs.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fights frequently use this mix, for example player skill deciding hits while character skills and weapons set harm.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: When the character part actively carries out actions, the result becomes a mix of player and system, which changes how uncertain performance is.

changes.name: Player Unpredictability
changes.why: Because character stats influence results, outcomes depend less on how the player behaves, so the player's behavior is typically less unpredictable.

conflicts_with.name: Character Development
conflicts_with.why: Strong character progression can prevent players from mastering the game, since improved stats carry results instead of the player's own skill.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Great player mastery can make the character part unimportant and make it hard to keep the game balanced.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Mixed player and character skill makes mastery differences stack up with ability differences.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: If player mastery outweighs character growth, the effort spent on building the character feels less valuable, and vice versa.

patterns.name: Privileged Movement
patterns.what_it_is: A way of moving that is available to some and unavailable to others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game world needs obstacles, restricted areas or travel costs that the special movement overcomes in a meaningful way. Its effect on goals like capture or evasion must be considered.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A unit has a flashy movement type, but the map offers no obstacles it bypasses, so it travels the same as everyone.
patterns.knobs: which units can do it; what obstacles it ignores; duration or cost

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Some ways of moving, like swinging or being fired from cannons, force the player to aim and shoot in order to travel.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: When only certain avatars or units can move in a special way, they become the ones best suited to particular parts of play.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Moving through the air lets a player look over the world from above, giving a broad view of what is going on.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A special way of moving can be handed to the player later as a new power, opening up things they could not do before.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Giving a new way of moving lets designers decide which blocked places open up when, so story parts unfold in a chosen order.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Being able to move in a way others cannot is simply one kind of special ability granted to some game elements.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Special movement that is temporary, or picked as part of setting up a character, makes different play sessions feel different.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Letting one side move better than the other makes the disadvantaged side's chase or escape hard.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Requiring a special way of moving to enter an area keeps hostile units and avatars from getting inside.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Special movement can be given to the player's avatar so it moves differently from other game elements.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: If the chaser has special movement, catching targets is easier, but if the target has it, escaping becomes easier and capture harder.

changes.name: Conditional Passageways
changes.why: Special movement can let a character use routes that normally only open under certain conditions, reaching places others cannot.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies can be given special movement, or lack it, which changes how threatening they are and where they can reach.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: Special movement can lessen or fully avoid the harmful results of hazards in the environment, such as damage or lost abilities.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Special movement helps the one fleeing get away more easily, but gives the pursuer an edge if they hold it instead.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Sometimes the only way to explore parts of the world is through the special movement, making it the key to discovery.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Flying gives an overview of the world that aids finding your way, yet it can make navigation too trivial.

changes.name: Herd
changes.why: Special movement can make driving targets to a place easier for the mover, but harder when the targets are the ones who have it.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: A special way of moving can let a character enter places that others cannot reach, such as the air.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: The pattern changes the ordinary rules of movement for chosen avatars or units, so they move differently from the rest.

changes.name: Obstacles
changes.why: Some special movement lets a character pass over or ignore things that would normally block others.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Special movement makes getting from one place to another easier for the mover, and unlike other goals this is never reversed by giving it to a target.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Particular units can be given a different way of moving, making them more valuable than the other units.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Navigation
conflicts_with.why: Abilities like flight can reveal the surroundings and open up movement, which can undercut the difficulty of finding the way.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Special movement abilities for some players create imbalances in their abilities.

patterns.name: Controllers
patterns.what_it_is: Stationary world objects that provide actions available nowhere else.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A player must have to go to the controller to use it, and using it must have a useful effect on the world or on their abilities. Their location should matter so that fights or travel form around them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A lever or console is in the world, but it can be used from anywhere or does nothing significant.
patterns.knobs: where they are placed; who can use them; what the effect is and its cost

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Because a controller's abilities only work at its fixed spot, players may need to hold the surrounding area to keep using it.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Some controllers are intangible spots where players can build or destroy things, such as material boxes that get assembled into bridges or bases.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Controllers give new abilities, which makes players feel their actions matter more, especially when using them completes quests.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Controllers hand players new abilities, widening what they can do, and this is clearest when using them completes quests.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Since the abilities of a controller can require holding its location, players may set a goal of taking possession of it.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Installations, a kind of controller, give players stronger versions of abilities they already have, such as mounted weapons with more firepower.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: The effects a controller triggers can be permanent, and story-driving controllers typically cause changes that cannot be undone.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Controllers cannot be moved, so whatever abilities they give are available only to someone standing at their position.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Controllers give actions not possible elsewhere, and from the player's view they work as abilities they did not have before.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers decide where and when players can use controllers, so activating them can push a fixed storyline forward.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Units or avatars standing near a controller get access to its abilities, which others elsewhere lack, so these are often privileged.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: A controller's abilities can only be reached at its spot and may need area control, so that spot becomes valuable to hold.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Controllers look like big machines or control panels, so they can change far-off parts of the world without feeling out of place.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Controller effects, like activating moveable tiles or advancing the story, can produce large, dramatic changes in the game.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Controllers paired with resource generators are a place-based way to keep supplying resources, making them renewable.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: A resource generator that players can harvest gives some control-like interaction, and this makes that generator a resource location.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: Giving players a control to operate alarms lets them turn them off wrongly, fake them, or stop them being raised.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Controllers can be restricted to certain avatars, and may be placed to affect areas beyond what avatars can usually reach.

changes.name: Conditional Passageways
changes.why: Switches commonly work by opening a passage that was blocked until the controller was activated.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: A switch can alter environmental effects when their area is fixed; otherwise installations, which grant abilities, are more likely to affect them.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Controllers are among the elements a designer can put on a board to populate it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Controllers can influence parts of the game world that units or avatars cannot normally reach, and they are fixed within it.

changes.name: HUD Interfaces
changes.why: Using an installation may change the player's interface, including the HUD, to better suit the actions it offers.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Activating a switch can finish a level, and controllers can affect parts of a level out of the usual reach.

changes.name: Moveable Tiles
changes.why: Both kinds of controllers can affect moveable tiles, though switches are better at starting and stopping them than steering their movement.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Activating a controller can count as completing a quest or goal, which is how designers use them to move players along.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: A switch can start quick travel when activated, letting players move across the world in a way they could not otherwise.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Controllers can be restricted to certain units, and they affect parts of the world beyond what units can usually reach.

patterns.name: Variable Accuracy
patterns.what_it_is: A mechanic that imitates how hitting a target is sometimes easier and sometimes harder.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Shots must actually miss based on understandable factors the player can influence, and the current accuracy should be shown to them. The effect must be big enough to alter how they position and fire.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A crosshair that wiggles for show while every shot still lands exactly where aimed.
patterns.knobs: spread size; penalty from moving or taking damage; time to aim; effect of skills and upgrades

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Once a shot may miss, landing hits takes more effort, and the extra actions and upgrades involved make fights harder to master.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players must juggle things that affect their aim, like skills, upgrades and aiming actions, which adds more factors to track.

can_cause.name: Incompatible Goals
can_cause.why: With stationary aiming, moving and aiming pull against each other, so players cannot do both well at once.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Stationary aiming only lets players aim while standing still and may block unaimed shots while moving, restricting how they can move.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Designers use less certain hits to weaken some weapons, especially sniper ones, so different weapons end up more evenly matched.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Real aiming is hard, so missing sometimes makes shooting feel more believable, provided the skills, upgrades and weapons that affect it suit the setting.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: A critical hit can make the target's aim less reliable, adding a penalty alongside the health it loses.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: The player aims, but how much the aim wanders depends on the character's weapons and skills, tightly fusing the two.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Shots may miss their target, so the basic act of aiming and firing becomes harder.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Because aiming and shooting get harder, fights as a whole become tougher to win.

changes.name: Crosshairs
changes.why: The aiming reticle changes to show current accuracy, such as by moving slightly or showing a hit area.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Movement often worsens aim, and stationary aiming goes further by requiring players to stand still to aim.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: Since long-range shots become less certain to hit, spots favored by snipers are less useful.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Accuracy changes how well each weapon performs, and sights or upgrades for it can alter how reliable it is.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Making attacks hit with varying precision means players cannot be sure of an attack's result, weakening foresight in combat.

patterns.name: Dice
patterns.what_it_is: Physical cubes that give a random outcome from a set range, most often equally likely.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The kind and number of dice must match what is being decided, and outcomes must actually affect the game. Players can then learn the odds and use them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Rolls that are ignored or overridden, so the result never matters.
patterns.knobs: type and number of dice; what the roll decides

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Because dice sit on the table and players watch them land, they draw attention as a spot to look at, especially when actions or the world are abstract.

can_cause.name: Game Boards
can_cause.why: Dice are not a relation that follows from boards; the page only notes that when a game has boards, dice become an out-of-world element alongside them.

can_cause.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
can_cause.why: Some games make the dice themselves the main pieces, with each player owning different dice, much like owning different cards.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: On a board or map game, dice are not part of the fictional world, so players handle something that exists only outside the game's setting.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Rolling dice picks one result from a fixed set of outcomes, so what happens next is left to chance rather than player choice.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
