can_cause.why: Players can learn how likely different results are for the dice in use, and use that understanding to make better decisions.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Rolling several dice lets players aim for matching combinations, so the dice results themselves can form scoring sets.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Dice are often rolled to decide how much harm an attack does, making the amount vary from one hit to the next.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Dice can set how far a piece moves, as in classic race games where the roll decides how many spaces you advance.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Dice can be rolled to check whether a character succeeds at a skill, so chance affects the outcome of the attempt.

patterns.name: Equipment
patterns.what_it_is: Items that a character can wear or hold in their hands.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Items must change what the character can do when equipped, and there must be several to choose from with trade-offs, so choosing matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Items that can be equipped but give only cosmetic changes or are strictly better than every alternative.
patterns.knobs: number of equippable items; strength of their bonuses; wear or limited uses

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: Cursed gear is equipped like any other item but weakens the wearer instead of helping them.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players pick which item to use, and since several are usually on offer, that selection is a real choice.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Because gear can give better or new abilities, players have a concrete reason to want to acquire it.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Players usually put on an item to get a boost over what they could already do.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Some gear, like cursed items, cannot be taken off again, or cannot be traded once used, so equipping becomes permanent.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Equipping an item can let a character do actions it could not do before.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: If only certain characters are allowed to use particular gear, those characters gain special powers others lack.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Armor, tools, weapons and items giving passive benefits are all equipment, which makes equipment a group of game items.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: Gear grants abilities only while held, and it can be used up, worn out, or lost, which makes those abilities temporary.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Equipped items can change how the player's on-screen character looks, especially when they are purely cosmetic.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Allies who travel with the player can be given gear too, which lets a designer decide who gets it.

changes.name: Inventories
changes.why: Since gear is chosen from what the player holds, equipping changes how the inventory is used.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Computer-controlled characters can be allowed to use gear, and restricting it to some of them grants special powers.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Player characters can use gear, and in games where they are made by players, choosing their gear is part of that creation.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: Soulbound gear cannot be traded once equipped, which stops players from buying game advantages.

conflicts_with.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
conflicts_with.why: Games wishing to avoid buyable advantages can make equipping permanent, so used gear cannot be traded on to other players.

patterns.name: Delayed Effects
patterns.what_it_is: The result of an action or event appears not at once but after some time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The gap must be long enough to be noticed and the effect must still matter when it lands. Whether players can see when it will happen decides if it brings planning or suspense.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A delay of a moment that players do not notice, or an effect that no longer matters when it arrives.
patterns.knobs: length of the delay; whether the timing is shown

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Making stronger actions take longer to finish lets a designer even out different options, since power is paid for with waiting time.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: After you trigger something, the outcome is already decided but not yet shown, so you are left in a state of waiting for it.

can_cause.name: Interruptible Actions
can_cause.why: While an action is still waiting to take effect, there is a window in which an opponent or the player can stop it.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Because results arrive later, they can still stand as permanent outcomes, even though players are also warned that the later consequences are hard to foresee.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: When players cannot tell how long the wait is, they can feel fortunate or unfortunate before the result is revealed.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: If the wait always lasts the same amount of time, players can remember it and use that knowledge when deciding what to do.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing how delays work in a game is itself a skill that players can learn and use to make better long-term decisions.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: With a fixed, remembered delay, players can arrange their short-term moves so that other actions line up with when the effect lands.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Waiting for an outcome to arrive creates suspense, particularly when players cannot see the details or must rely on others.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Players who know an effect is coming feel pressure to act before it lands, especially when the action can still be interrupted.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When a trade or joint action pays off later, there is time for one side to break the deal before it does.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: If players know when delayed effects will land, they can time their actions so effects coincide and reinforce each other, forming a combo.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: When results of actions don't appear immediately, players find it harder to know what their actions accomplished.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: Because the payoff for helping arrives later rather than at once, the helper must wait and trust the other player to follow through.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: If results take long enough to appear, you must leave for real-life reasons and then come back to see what happened.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When results arrive later, such as after development time, players must plan to make good use of the timing.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: A pause before a capture takes effect gives the other player a chance to respond, as is believed for an ancient Roman board game.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Joint actions are normally immediate, but they can be changed so the result arrives later after players have cooperated.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Making the destruction of objects take effect after a delay is one way to introduce waiting into a game.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Adding a wait to a dilemma between players can raise the tension, since they must hold out before seeing how others chose.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: A trap can work after a delay, which can give a victim time to avoid its effect.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: A very long wait may leave the situation changed by the time the effect lands, so players can no longer foresee what it will do.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: Delaying consequences can discourage players from reloading saves to undo events, but it makes outcomes harder to foresee.

patterns.name: Handicap Systems
patterns.what_it_is: Rules that make the game easier or harder for individual players to even out their chances.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The adjustments must change real quantities, such as resources, health, abilities or head starts, in proportion to the skill gap. Players must accept them, whether voluntary or enforced.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'difficulty' setting that only renames levels or tweaks a number too small to feel, so strong and weak players still have very unequal chances.
patterns.knobs: size of advantage or penalty; which attribute is changed; voluntary vs enforced

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Giving weaker players help or stronger players a burden evens out their odds, so every participant feels they have a fair shot at winning.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because players can pick how much help they get, they can choose an easygoing experience instead of a demanding one.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players who want a tougher experience can take on a disadvantage, which raises the difficulty and gives them a real test.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Help given to weaker players makes everyone believe they can win, even when their actual impact on the outcome is smaller than they think.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Handicap levels follow players from game to game, so they can link separate matches into one larger ongoing structure such as rankings in Go or Golf.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Since handicaps give mismatched players similar chances, a player can find many more opponents with whom a game is worth playing.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Giving advantages to the weaker or later-moving side compensates for starting differences, as when Go gives points to the non-first player.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: Handicap ratings in games like Go and Golf can be read as numbers measuring how good a player is.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Giving weaker teams a head start or stronger teams a penalty compensates for skill differences before or during play.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: A designer can tune how well computer-controlled players perform, which lets handicap shape the challenge they provide.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Handicap can change the gaming skill of automated agents, which makes them easier or harder to deal with.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: When a handicap changes which actions are available to a player, it narrows or widens their options compared with others.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Letting players start with more or less health, as in Tekken, gives one a handicap over another.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: Raising or lowering skill levels in a character's makeup is one way to apply a handicap.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: When players face each other, handicap evens out their different skills, which creates balance between them.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Giving some racers head starts or movement limits changes how a race plays out, so the handicap shapes the race itself.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Bonuses added to some players' scores give them an edge or a cushion, which changes how results are compared.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: When teams compete, handicap evens out the difference in strength between them, which creates balance between teams.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Handicaps even out skill differences among players, helping balance and challenge.

patterns.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
patterns.what_it_is: A character is forced to take certain actions so that their personality is kept or developed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must actually limit available actions or take control at set points, and the enforced behaviour must fit the character or story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character described as loyal or cowardly whom the player can still make do anything.
patterns.knobs: which actions are forbidden or forced; when control is taken; how strictly this applies

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Controlling what characters do, by forcing events to happen or blocking them, keeps the story following its planned course.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Making it impossible for agents to act against teammates keeps cooperative groups intact in team-based games.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: When agents are made to act as the game world expects, their actions stay in line with the setting's theme.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: When specific defining actions must happen, the game can force the character to perform them, for example through cutscenes.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: The character carries out the action itself on the player's behalf, tying the result to character traits as well as the player's setup.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: Making an AI always follow players' suggestions or commands shapes how it behaves, though its rules already bind it.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: The pattern can be applied to some agents more strictly than others, shaping how constrained each one is.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Though their rules already fix behavior, the pattern can add specific constraints beyond what other agents have.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Forcing key actions steers a character's growth so it goes in the direction the designer planned.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Forcing agents to behave as the world would expect keeps their actions fitting the setting.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Blocking actions such as characters killing each other stops rivalry setups from ending too soon.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: Giving characters their own agency means outcomes depend partly on the system's actions, not only on the player's skill.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Constrained choices can support roleplaying, but only when the character's design carries over consistently into play.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Having actions forced, especially during cutscenes, makes it hard for players to feel they have more control than they do.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Enforcing actions limits or removes what players can pick, particularly when control is taken away outright.

conflicts_with.name: Player-Planned Development
conflicts_with.why: Forced behavior can override players' own plans for their characters, unless the constraint comes from those plans.

conflicts_with.name: Roleplaying
conflicts_with.why: If the character design isn't consistently reflected in gameplay, the enforced behavior clashes with how players want to play the role.

patterns.name: Sanctioned Cheating
patterns.what_it_is: Cheating that the rules allow or that other players consider acceptable.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Offer specific rule-bending actions, decide who may use them and what happens if caught, and keep them out of the normal action menu. In multiplayer, detection risk and some hidden information make it matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cheat menu that nobody needs or that has no effect on goals, or a 'cheat' that other players are never able to notice or object to.
patterns.knobs: which cheats exist; who may use them; chance and penalty of being caught

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because the allowed actions are normally off-limits, using them makes players feel they have more sway over the game than ordinary play would give them.

can_cause.name: Invulnerabilities
can_cause.why: Sanctioned cheats often let players make themselves immune to harm, such as a god mode, so being unkillable becomes an officially allowed shortcut.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Cheating can mean acting as if you had special powers other players lack, so allowing it hands someone abilities outside the normal rules.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: The rules let players take on another player's identity, such as a disguised spy, in opposed play, which makes deceiving them part of the game.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: In single-player play, cheating can give new actions and remove resource limits, so players have more options.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Allowed cheating tends to benefit disadvantaged players more, since they gain more from it without risking larger losses if caught.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: In single-player games, cheating removes resource worries and threats, so players can potter without upsetting balance against other players.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, players pretend not to be doing certain actions, which works like betrayal's pretending and so counts as roleplaying.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: When cheating is allowed, players get a goal of doing out-of-game actions without other players seeing them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: If cheating is allowed, players must watch for others' hidden actions outside normal play.

changes.name: Difficulty Levels
changes.why: Difficulty settings can decide which allowed cheats are available, for example a strict ironman mode that permits none of them.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Allowed cheating affects fairness between players, and can even be used to even out balance, though others' cheats are hard to notice.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: When players compete directly, cheating must be disguised, so they pretend to do one thing while doing another, risking exposure and creating suspense.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: With no rivals to wrong, allowed cheating gives players freedom to set their own goals and shape how they want to play.

changes.name: Speedruns
changes.why: Runners set extra, narrow goals for themselves, so exploiting glitches that would otherwise look like cheating is usually accepted.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: In team contests, allowed cheating forces members to act one way while doing another, adds tension, and can be used to balance the teams.

patterns.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
patterns.what_it_is: A hero's deeds change how other characters in the world treat them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Characters or factions need defined norms and a system (a score or behaviour rules) that visibly changes how they treat the player after relevant actions. The reactions must carry real benefits or costs.
patterns.just_a_label_when: NPCs say different lines after a theft but treat the player exactly the same, so nothing in play changes.
patterns.knobs: which actions count; how strongly NPCs react; how visible and lasting the reputation is

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: When actions needed for ongoing goals carry social fallout, players must keep up good standing over time, so the goal never really finishes.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: If players can pick which faction or set of norms to belong to, they decide whose approval matters and act accordingly.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: Characters who belong to several factions can hold clashing norms, so members of the same group end up disagreeing when they meet.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Overlapping faction memberships bring different norms into collision inside a shared group, producing competition among its own members and forcing players to choose whom to back.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Choosing which faction or norms to follow lets players take on social aims they may pursue or ignore.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: Encoding social reactions into computer-controlled characters changes how they behave in play, which shows them acting on their own motives.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Breaking a group's norms, or skipping expected deeds, can be punished when others notice, so social consequences naturally carry a cost.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Following a group's norms can be rewarded, and breaking some norms can even earn benefits, such as joining a thieves' guild.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: When players choose which faction or norms to join, each choice brings its own social aims, giving them a menu of goals.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: When some acts are shown as socially unacceptable yet still possible, and characters visibly react to them, the world feels believable and coherent.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Actions can change how the player character relates to NPCs inside the game world, and that change in relationships helps define the character.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled agents need rules making player actions change how others in the world treat them, which is how their emotional reactions get produced.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When a player's action affects how others in the game world treat them, that social cost must be weighed against what the action gains, especially alongside internal rivalry.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Social consequences change how computer-controlled characters act during play, since their behavior is shaped by what players have done.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Social consequences can be tracked per character, so a character's deeds define them and affect how others regard them.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Companions in a player's party react to the player's deeds, which narrows which actions the player can freely take.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Norms are often shared across a faction, so the group's members respond to actions according to those common rules.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A world can define norms that most inhabitants share, so acts within it are judged by those standards.

changes.name: Helpers
changes.why: Helpers nearby will notice and react to the player's actions, which limits what the player can comfortably do.

changes.name: Internal Conflicts
changes.why: Characters in the same faction as the player can disagree with their actions, turning social reactions into conflict within the group.

changes.name: No-Ops
changes.why: Since others expect certain actions, doing nothing can also have consequences, such as a friendship fading when neglected.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: In games with companions, party members respond to what the player does, changing which actions are practical for the group.

changes.name: Internal Rivalry
changes.why: Because actions have in-world social consequences, ending a rivalry by eliminating a rival becomes a costly trade-off or risk rather than a free choice.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: NPCs carry a world's social rules, so harming people in places where it is unacceptable can make them or the authorities react.

patterns.name: Critical Hits
patterns.what_it_is: Strikes that deal noticeably more damage or give a special effect.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The chance must be low enough that it feels special but high enough to happen in normal play, and the extra effect must be clearly larger than an ordinary hit. It may depend on skill or weapon.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hit is called critical and a number pops up, but the damage is barely different from a normal hit.
patterns.knobs: chance of a critical; damage multiplier or extra effects; skill or weapon modifiers

can_cause.name: Critical Results
can_cause.why: A critical hit is one kind of unusually good or bad outcome, so it counts as a member of the broader family of critical results.

can_cause.name: Critical Successes
can_cause.why: Landing a critical hit is a special kind of success for the attacker, which makes it a specific form of critical success.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: If the chance of a critical hit is very small, seeing one becomes a rare, memorable moment in play.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Because a critical hit comes from a chance roll, the player who lands one feels fortunate, while the one on the receiving end does not.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: A critical hit can inflict harm the target could not otherwise suffer, going beyond extra damage to add special negative effects.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Critical hits change how fights feel by adding a chance of surprising outcomes, so battles are less repetitive and predictable.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: A critical hit changes how much harm an attack does, making some hits far stronger than the usual ones.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Misses
conflicts_with.why: They are opposites: a critical hit is an extraordinary good result, a critical miss an extraordinary bad one, though one side's miss can feel like the other's lucky break.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Critical hits add more chance to combat, which works against games where the outcome depends mainly on how skilled the player is.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Because a critical hit can unexpectedly add extra harm, players cannot be sure what an attack will do, which undermines predictability.

patterns.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
patterns.what_it_is: The game changes its difficulty by itself depending on how the player is doing.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must measure performance reliably and link it to parameters that really change the challenge, with changes gentle enough not to feel like cheating or to be easily gamed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A system that is switched on but whose adjustments are so small, or tied to a poor measure, that a good and a bad player face the same challenge.
patterns.knobs: what performance is measured; how strongly and how quickly difficulty reacts; whether it is visible or optional

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the system shifts challenge toward how well someone is doing, it nudges outcomes toward evenness, though not necessarily between players and the game itself.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: In single-player games the adjustment can be tuned to keep difficulty gentle and forgiving, so play stays relaxed.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: The same adjustment can instead be tuned to keep pushing back as players improve, so they stay tested.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players don't know the system is quietly helping or hindering them, they credit their own actions for results that the system actually shaped.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: When the system secretly and forcefully changes how game events turn out, the outcomes shown to players are not the true ones.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Adjusting challenge to how well someone is performing is a way of giving weaker players help, so it is a kind of handicap.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Offering automatic difficulty adjustment as something players may switch on lets them choose an easier game by using it.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: It helps cover for a departing player, so people can leave a session without harming the others' game.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: The game changes how hard things are based on how players are doing, narrowing gaps between opposed players' fortunes.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: The game adapts its challenge as play goes on, so a team that is ahead or behind gets pulled back toward parity.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: How strongly computer-controlled participants perform can be raised or lowered to match how well the human players are doing.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: How much harm is dealt or taken can be scaled up or down, making fights easier or harder according to player progress.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: The number and performance of opponents can be changed to fit players, as when their strength scales to match the players'.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Top speeds can be altered, such as letting trailing racers go faster so they can catch up.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Between competing players, the adjustment is used to make their chances more even, producing balance among them.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Against the game system, it aims to hold challenge at a chosen level, which players may set through difficulty settings.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: In team-versus-team play it is applied so that the competing sides end up evenly matched.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players can spot cases where the system rather than they themselves decided the result, the false sense of control can collapse instead of growing.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Adapting the challenge to the player can cast doubt on whether effort led to success, though skillful use may avoid it.

patterns.name: Sets
patterns.what_it_is: Groups of game elements that are worth more together than apart.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define clear combinations that give a win, score, or bonus bigger than the parts, and make the parts available with enough chance and trade to work toward. Progress toward completing sets should be visible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A set bonus so small, or pieces so easy to get, that players never go after the combination deliberately.
patterns.knobs: which combinations count; bonus size; how rarely pieces appear

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Because a set only pays off when all its parts are held, players are driven to hunt for and gather the missing pieces.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Using several items together for a bonus makes equipping or picking them up act as a chain of actions that combine into one payoff.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Each piece needed to finish a set becomes something the player wants to acquire, so every missing piece is a goal to obtain.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: When every item of a group is equipped together, the player gets stronger than the individual items would make them.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Goals that ask for a group of items but not every possible one leave the surplus collecting as a goal players may ignore.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Defining certain combinations of items as sets gives those items extra effects beyond what each one has alone.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: A hand can be judged by the sets it contains, so completing a hand made of sets can end the game or decide ranking.

patterns.name: Temporary Abilities
patterns.what_it_is: Abilities available only for a limited stretch of game time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The ability must be strong enough to change what players do and must truly expire. Players should face a choice about when to use it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'temporary' power lasts so long, or recurs so often, that it is effectively permanent.
patterns.knobs: duration or number of uses; power level; how often it can be gained

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: When a temporary ability runs out, the player no longer has it, and that disappearance is exactly what an ability loss is.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: A short-lived boost such as invulnerability can help late-arriving players keep pace with others without permanently changing the game's power balance.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Giving newcomers a brief strong ability lets them feel their actions matter a lot, even though they have only just joined.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Since the ability will vanish soon, players feel pressure to get the most out of it before it is gone.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because abilities come and go during play, players keep switching between having and lacking them, so the way the game plays changes.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Abilities that can only be used a limited number of times are used up like a resource tied to action.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Making some abilities temporary changes how abilities work, since players only have access to them at intermittent points in play.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: When players join at different moments, temporary abilities can give those arriving late a helpful boost.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Newly spawned players can receive a short-lived ability, such as brief invulnerability, to help them get started.

patterns.name: Geometric Progression
patterns.what_it_is: With each step of effort, the result is multiplied by the same factor.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear multiplier applied to a cost, reward or effect, with a ratio above or below 1 chosen on purpose. The numbers must be large enough that players notice the growth or decay and change how they invest.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A ratio so close to 1 or with such low starting values that the growth is invisible, so it plays like a flat linear increase.
patterns.knobs: the common ratio; the starting value; where in the game it is applied (costs, rewards, scores)

can_cause.name: Negative Feedback Loops
can_cause.why: When each extra effort multiplies the effect by less than one, gains shrink, so players are pushed to spread their effort around instead of piling onto one thing.

can_cause.name: Positive Feedback Loops
can_cause.why: When each extra effort multiplies the effect by more than one, the more you already have the faster you gain, so leads snowball.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When investing, the growth rule makes players think ahead, either saving up enough resources for a big payoff or avoiding spending where returns would shrink.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Rewards that grow as a chain gets longer let combos of different lengths succeed, with longer ones paying off more.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Growth that compounds, combined with reinforcing loops, makes later effects far larger than early ones, so later closures matter more.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Reward size can be compared against player effort that grows by multiplying steps, linking investment of effort to payout.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Together with investments, it means a failed investment wastes resources and weakens those still unspent.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Consequences that multiply over time make effort feed on itself, so earlier work keeps strengthening later results.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with negative feedback, it makes repeating similar efforts less rewarding, so players are pushed to pursue different goals.

changes.name: Collecting
changes.why: Because gains grow or shrink by a fixed factor, players must rethink whether to concentrate or spread out what they gather.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: The longer an action continues, the more powerful or rewarding it becomes, so sustained effort pays off more and more.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: The growth rule decides whether one large investment beats several small ones, shaping how players split their resources.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Penalty schemes can use a progression directly, so each further penalty grows or shrinks by a constant factor.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Progression schemes get applied to resources, usually through investments, so how much they yield depends on how many are committed.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Reward schemes can follow the progression directly, making each added effort give a proportionally larger or smaller payoff.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Since scores come from rewards and penalties, those can be calculated with the multiplying rule when points go up or down.

changes.name: Sets
changes.why: The progression can apply to how many elements are collected or equipped, so each extra item changes the set's value by a constant factor.

changes.name: Trading
changes.why: Whether gains snowball or shrink changes what players consider worth trading for and how they value what they hold.

changes.name: Vulnerabilities
changes.why: The progression can govern how a vulnerability works, so each further hit or exposure changes its effect by a fixed multiple.

conflicts_with.name: Arithmetic Progression
conflicts_with.why: The two translate effort into effect in different ways: arithmetic depends only on a single unit, while geometric makes the effect depend on the number of units.

patterns.name: Permadeath
patterns.what_it_is: A character's death is irreversible and they cannot be brought back.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Death must truly remove the character with no respawn, and loading an earlier state must not be possible, or it loses meaning. The game must be built around the loss so it feels like a real stake.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A death that is advertised as permanent but can be undone by loading a save or a free revive, so it costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: what can permanently die; whether there are extra chances; whether saves are allowed

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because one mistake can end a character for good, players must play carefully, which makes the game harder and more tense.

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: When a character dies for good, that clearly ends something, giving the player a definite point where a chapter of play is over.

can_cause.name: Death Consequences
can_cause.why: Permanent loss of an avatar or character is a form of consequence for dying, and a very harsh one.

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: Since a single death removes you for good, a player can be knocked out long before the game would otherwise finish.

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Because the character's death ends the play session, dying permanently means the game is finished for that player.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Once the character dies there is no undoing it, so the death is something that can never be reversed.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Losing your character for good takes you out of the game, so the player is removed from play.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Since sessions end at death, players spread their total playtime across many separate runs and so keep starting the game again.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: In multiplayer, players who died for good can watch the remaining play, which helps keep them around for the next round.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, a player whose character dies for good cannot act and must wait for the others.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Permanent death mostly matters for avatars, since those are what players control, and it makes their loss final rather than temporary.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can be made to die for good, which changes how much their loss costs, especially when the characters are player-controlled.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: With several players, permanent death knocks some out while others carry on, leaving the eliminated ones idle unless they leave or watch.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Permanent death matters most for characters players control, unlike replaceable units or minor non-player characters whose loss is usually unimportant.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Killing another player is final and its rewards stay, which can tempt attackers, yet eliminating people also spoils shared enjoyment, which can discourage it.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: If a character the story depends on can die for good, the planned plot may break, so it must be designed around who can die.

conflicts_with.name: Lives
conflicts_with.why: Lives mean players have more than one, whereas permadeath means a single death is final, so the two cannot both hold.

conflicts_with.name: Save Scumming
conflicts_with.why: If players can reload an earlier state whenever they like, they can undo any death, which empties permanent death of meaning.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: Saving and reloading at will lets players reverse deaths, so the character's loss is never truly permanent.

patterns.name: Vulnerabilities
patterns.what_it_is: Weak points that others can take advantage of.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Weaknesses must change damage or effects noticeably, differ between enemies or situations, and be discoverable or hideable so players adapt their choices. Counter options must exist.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A listed weakness with a negligible bonus, or one that applies to every enemy equally, so there is nothing to exploit.
patterns.knobs: damage multiplier; which entities have which weakness; how obvious the weakness is; availability of exploiting weapons

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: A weakness being hit can strip an entity of some of its abilities, so the vulnerability's effect is a lost capability rather than just lost health.

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: Being struck in a weak spot can leave an entity less capable, so the vulnerability's penalty shows up as reduced abilities.

can_cause.name: Destructible Objects
can_cause.why: Ordinary objects become breakable because they carry a weakness that lets them be destroyed, so a vulnerability is what makes them destructible.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: A weakness to something like sunlight makes the surroundings dangerous only to certain creatures, so the setting affects some characters but not others.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: Penalties or lost abilities from a weakness usually last only briefly, appearing as short events unless an ongoing environmental condition keeps renewing them.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When players know weaknesses exist but not which enemy has which, they set out to discover that information.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing which entities have which weaknesses is valuable information that players can use to plan how they play.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because different enemies are weak to different things, players switch weapons or powers, and hiding their own weaknesses creates different play goals.

can_cause.name: Achilles' Heels
can_cause.why: The pattern is built by punching one specific weakness into that otherwise complete immunity, so the weak spot is what lets damage through.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: When game pieces can be exploited by others, players want to hide some of them while showing or giving up others.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: When something can be harmed easily in certain places, players must protect those places, which sets up evasion goals.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Fighting enemies prompts players to probe for their weaknesses, which requires trying out different actions against them.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing which enemies are weak to which weapons or powers lets players prepare before a fight.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: When enemies are weak to certain weapons or powers, players must plan which to use, and combining the two requires more planning.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Ammunition can be built to trigger a specific weakness, like silver bullets against werewolves, so its value depends on the target.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: A player's own avatar can have weaknesses, so players must protect them and hide them from opponents who could exploit them.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Bosses can be given weaknesses, which changes how they are fought and what players must do to defeat them.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters can be made weak to certain attacks or conditions, changing how they fare in fights and in different places.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Since enemies take more harm from some attacks than others, fights revolve around choosing what to use against whom.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: A weakness changes how much harm an attack does, such as adding extra damage or multiplying it when the attack type matches.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies with weaknesses give players openings to exploit, and players may test enemies to find out what hurts them most.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Because weaknesses change how much damage lands, they indirectly change how quickly an entity's health runs down.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: When a weakness ties to environmental effects, such as sunlight harming vampires, it affects where an entity can safely go.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units can be weak to certain attacks, so they are strong or fragile depending on what they face.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons gain or lose usefulness depending on whether they can trigger an enemy's weakness, which pushes players to switch between them.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Complete immunity cannot coexist with a weakness to the same danger, except where one weak point exists to beat an otherwise immune foe.

patterns.name: Player-Player Proximity
patterns.what_it_is: Rules depend on how close players are to each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must define what counts as near, which effects follow and how they are detected. It must also plan for the social contact this brings.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are told to stay close, but nothing in the rules reacts to the distance.
patterns.knobs: distance threshold; what is triggered when entering, keeping or breaking proximity

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: When the play area isn't fenced off from everyday places, needing players to be near each other pulls the game into ordinary surroundings.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Since players must get close to one another, they have to walk or move around in the real world, so moving becomes part of playing.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: When technology detects how close players are to each other, stepping outside its coverage lets a player go unnoticed.

changes.name: Bluffing
changes.why: Being physically near others means face-to-face interaction, which changes how deception works because players can watch and read each other directly.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: Because closeness between players counts in the rules, a game master can learn part of the game state without being present themselves.

changes.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
changes.why: Places where players are standing near each other gain extra meaning in the game, so the real-world area becomes more valuable to play.

changes.name: Social Skills
changes.why: Close physical contact makes interaction between players unmediated and likely, so abilities like persuading and reading people matter more in play.

patterns.name: Unlocking
patterns.what_it_is: Gaining access to new abilities or game content.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Content must be truly withheld until a clear requirement is met, and players should know it exists. The unlocked item should be worth the effort.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An 'unlock' that gives something trivial or that was available all along, or a requirement so easy it is never felt.
patterns.knobs: what is gated; the unlock requirement; how visible the locked content is

can_cause.name: Access Rewards
can_cause.why: Gaining entry to content that was already set aside for you feels like a prize of its own, specifically a reward of access.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: When players know something is locked, they may repeat tasks over and over just to reach the point where it opens.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Seeing in advance what can be unlocked lets players choose a path and plan their character's growth toward those goals.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Getting hold of something that was preordained and waiting for you naturally feels like being given a reward for what you did.

can_cause.name: Sidegrades
can_cause.why: Some unlockable items are not stronger but more specialized, so unlocking them widens the player's options instead of raising power.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Because unlocking follows the actions that earned it, those actions feel worthwhile, unless the player simply paid to skip ahead.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Designers decide which abilities can be unlocked and tell players, which shapes how and when those abilities become available.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Reaching the endgame phase of a game can open up new gameplay content, so unlocking affects what the endgame offers.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: Unlocking is commonly used to control how and when these special abilities are brought into play.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Designers often use unlocking to control when players get access to vehicles during play.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Unlocking is often used to pace the arrival of weapons, and in some games it supplies specialized options rather than better ones.

patterns.name: Arithmetic Progression
patterns.what_it_is: Reward or risk grows in direct proportion to the effort invested.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each unit of effort must give the same increment, with no multipliers or thresholds. Players need to see the relation so they can plan.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The rule is called linear, but bonuses or thresholds are hidden in the numbers so the real curve is not linear.
patterns.knobs: amount of reward per unit of effort; minimum or maximum investment

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Because rewards can be claimed anytime without spoiling later investments, players can put in small amounts and try things out without facing a big risk.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since investing in small chunks doesn't force big risk-or-reward gambles, players can decide how much to commit and where to put it.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: The payoff grows by a simple, easy-to-remember fixed step per unit of effort, so players can work out in advance what they will get.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Reward size can be set against player effort in steady, equal steps, so each increment of effort yields a matching reward step.

changes.name: Betting
changes.why: Players find linear outcomes intuitive, so they are often used when players wager resources against each other, with winnings scaling directly to the stake.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: Time spent on an extended action can be the effort that is tied in a straight line to the effect it yields.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: The pattern sets how much return each unit invested brings, so it shapes how investments compare with other options in the game.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: The effect linked to effort can be negative, so a failed action's penalty can grow by an equal amount per unit of effort.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Spent resources are the most common effort, and the pattern ties each unit spent to a proportional effect.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Rewards can be scaled so each extra unit of effort adds the same fixed amount of payoff.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Scores can be the effect that rises by a constant step for each unit of effort put in.

changes.name: Sets
changes.why: The number of pieces collected in a set can serve as the effort that is linearly linked to its effect.

changes.name: Value of Effort
changes.why: The pattern fixes what each unit of effort is worth; the value may be modest but is known beforehand and so is safer.

changes.name: Vulnerabilities
changes.why: Vulnerabilities can be the effect changed by effort, rising or falling by an equal amount per unit.

conflicts_with.name: Geometric Progression
conflicts_with.why: The two translate effort into effect in different ways: arithmetic depends only on a single unit, while geometric makes the effect depend on the number of units.

patterns.name: Invulnerabilities
patterns.what_it_is: The ability to take no harm from attacks and other dangers.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decide which damage types are blocked, for whom, and whether the immunity is permanent or timed. It only matters if the dangers it blocks are otherwise real, and if some others lack it so it is a privilege.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An entity is labeled immune but the threats it ignores never occur, or everyone has it, so it changes no decisions.
patterns.knobs: which damage types are covered; who has it; how long it lasts

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: When players meet an immunity they didn't know about, they try different attacks and actions to learn what works against it.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Immunity only matters if others lack it, so whoever holds it has a special advantage that sets them apart from other entities.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: A surprising immunity becomes a problem to crack, as players must work out how to get around it.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players who run into an unknown immunity must plan how to counter it, or how to use their own to advantage.

can_cause.name: Achilles' Heels
can_cause.why: A weak point only matters when the target is otherwise untouchable, so a near-complete immunity is the base the design starts from.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: Being immune to a blocking hazard lets players ignore it, so immunity becomes the requirement for crossing.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Learning what an enemy cannot be hurt by is useful knowledge, so uncovering such immunities becomes something players aim for.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Giving characters immunity to harmful effects that others lack, often briefly after spawning, makes them safe wherever they are.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Player avatars can be made immune to certain dangers, changing what threatens them in the game world.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Bosses are more often given immunities than ordinary foes, and these are often complete ones.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters under player control or opposing players can be given protection against particular dangers, changing how they can safely act.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Immune entities change how fights go, since some attacks stop working, and fighting may become impossible altogether.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Immunity limits which kinds of harm can affect an entity, shrinking or removing the damage it takes.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Such objects could be given immunity, but they are usually already safe from everything except what is specifically meant to destroy them.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Giving opponents immunity to some dangers makes them harder to beat and makes the game more challenging.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Because immune entities take less or no damage, their health is protected from being reduced.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Immunity to collisions, falls, or environmental hazards means entities can move through places that would otherwise hurt them.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: Newly spawned avatars are unprepared and vulnerable, so brief immunity can protect them while they get their bearings.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units controlled by players or by their opponents can be given immunity to certain dangers.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Making players unable to be harmed makes killing harder or impossible to carry out.

conflicts_with.name: Damage
conflicts_with.why: Permanent protection reduces how often damage matters, though it need not remove damage entirely if other damage types remain.

conflicts_with.name: Early Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Giving players temporary protection at the start stops them from being knocked out early in the game.

conflicts_with.name: Eliminate
conflicts_with.why: Targets that cannot be harmed make a removal goal impossible to achieve.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Long-lasting or unequal immunity gives some players a lasting edge over others, upsetting fairness between them.

conflicts_with.name: Player Killing
conflicts_with.why: Immune players cannot be killed by others, so attacking them becomes difficult or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: If one side keeps immunity for long, it dominates and the teams stop being evenly matched.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: When entities cannot be hurt, there is little at stake, so the feeling of danger fades.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Immunity that the game's fictional world doesn't explain, such as protecting story characters, feels out of place in that world.

conflicts_with.name: Vulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Complete immunity cannot coexist with a weakness to the same danger, except where one weak point exists to beat an otherwise immune foe.

conflicts_with.name: Achilles' Heels
conflicts_with.why: The weak point exists to break a complete immunity, so it works against the very invulnerability that it is built on.

patterns.name: Player-Location Proximity
patterns.what_it_is: Rules depend on whether the player is physically near a place.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs reliable position detection or self-reporting, defined places, and gameplay that truly depends on arriving there. The cost of travel has to be reasonable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Places are listed as targets, but the player's actual position is never checked or never changes anything.
patterns.knobs: trigger distance; number and spacing of locations; how position is verified

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players must visit places they don't know, going there for the game can make them see those real spots differently.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: When the playable area is big enough, like city-wide games, players have reason to come back to the places that matter in the game.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: If the game never clearly marks where play happens, location-based rules blend into everyday surroundings and play spreads into normal life.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Since rules react to where players really stand, they must find their own way to those physical places.

can_cause.name: Player Physical Prowess
can_cause.why: Reaching places on foot means a player's fitness and movement ability affect success, which can make play unbalanced.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When time is limited or someone arriving first blocks others from the effect, players compete to get to the place fastest.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: Players who know the area well can reach places sooner, giving them an edge that may unbalance the game.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Unless there are very many spots, the places that players' positions are checked against become important points in the game.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Rules that reward being at certain places naturally give players goals of travelling from one place to another.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: In games tied to where players physically are, casual play works when distance doesn't force more movement than players wish.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: In games that use technology to sense where players are, moving out of the sensed zone lets players avoid being detected.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: Knowing where players are lets game masters trigger events depending on players' positions.

changes.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
changes.why: Because rules depend on players' real positions, the game always ends up played within physical real-world space.

patterns.name: Characteristics
patterns.what_it_is: Numbers and facts that describe an individual hero, item, or other creature in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Values must differ between entities and affect outcomes, and some of them must be changeable during play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Entities have stats, but all are identical or ignored by the rules.
patterns.knobs: which stats exist; their ranges; how they change

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: When different agents carry different Characteristics, each ends up better at some things than others, so distinct areas of strength appear among them.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Any growth in a player's characteristics counts as development of the player's abstract construct.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Growth is usually carried out by changing a character's characteristics, which directly alters what the character can do in the game.

can_cause.name: Team Development
can_cause.why: Changing the traits of members, on individual characters or on a team described as an abstract construct, is one way to make the team develop.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Characteristics can describe things like countries or civilizations, so they shape how these abstract constructs behave in play.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Characteristics can be attached to bases, so the data stored there changes how a base works.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characteristics are naturally part of characters, so the data on each character strongly shapes how that character functions in play.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Teams can carry their own Characteristics, so the data attached to a team affects how it performs and develops.

patterns.name: Cooldown
patterns.what_it_is: After use, an action is unavailable for some time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The wait must be long enough to hold back repeated use, and the player must have other useful things to do meanwhile. The remaining time should be visible or learnable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An ability has a cooldown so short that it can effectively be used continuously, or nothing else is worth doing while waiting.
patterns.knobs: length of the wait; which actions are covered; shared or global cooldown

can_cause.name: Action Caps
can_cause.why: Each ability can only be used once per cooldown window, so cooldowns put a ceiling on how often a single action can be performed.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because the strongest actions can't be repeated endlessly, players can't rely on one best move, which keeps options more evenly useful.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: If a player has nothing else to do while an action recharges, the waiting becomes idle time with no meaningful choices.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Using an action makes it unavailable for a while, which works as a cost for acting, similar to spending energy.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Players know roughly how long the wait lasts, so the moment an action returns is always a looming, anticipated event.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Since a used action is locked, players must think about when to spend it and what to do in the meantime.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: When a shared cooldown covers nearly every action, play moves in fixed time steps, much like a game that runs on ticks.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: While one action recharges, players are pushed to use other actions, so they end up mixing different moves.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Designers pick which abilities get a waiting period before reuse, so cooldown shapes how often each ability is available.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: In card games, used cards can be turned sideways to show they can't be played again until they recharge.

changes.name: Collectible Card Games
changes.why: Used cards are tapped to show they are unavailable until they refresh, typically at the start of the owner's next turn.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Installations are among the actions commonly given reuse delays, so they can't be triggered over and over.

changes.name: Non-Player Help
changes.why: Putting a wait on help from outside the player's own actions limits how much outside input the game receives.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: Powerful abilities are often given cooldowns so they can't be spammed, and shared cooldowns link them without breaking the theme.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Tools are commonly given reuse delays, so players can't use them continuously.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: A waiting period after use can limit how often a weapon fires, either instead of or together with ammunition.

patterns.name: Fixed Distributions
patterns.what_it_is: Guaranteed randomness: by known moments, a preset set of outcomes will have come up.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must draw from a limited pool without replacement (like a deck) or force a spread over a cycle, and let players know or track what has appeared. Visible history lets them predict what is left.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A shuffled deck that is reshuffled every draw or a random roll, so past results never constrain future ones.
patterns.knobs: cycle length or pool size; whether players can see what has already been drawn

can_cause.name: Misfortune Mitigation
can_cause.why: Knowing what has already come out of a guaranteed mix lets players judge what is left, so they can prepare for or soften bad outcomes.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Because the overall mix is guaranteed, players can use what has already appeared to predict better what is likely to come next.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: When players aren't openly shown the mix, learning what it contains is valuable insight that they can use to plan their moves.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: When outcomes follow a known fixed spread but are hidden, tracking which results have already occurred gives an advantage.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Guaranteeing the overall mix over a cycle narrows how wild the random results can get, making chance less extreme.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: When random results come from a known, fixed set of possibilities, players can better estimate what outcomes are likely.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: When players succeed at using the known mix to predict or soften outcomes, results feel earned rather than lucky, which weakens the feeling of luck.

patterns.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
patterns.what_it_is: Items that really exist inside the game world, which can be seen and picked up.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The items must take part in the game's physics or rules, blocking movement or sight or being moved and broken. Players must be able to interact with them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Objects that are drawn solid but can be walked through and do nothing.
patterns.knobs: which items are solid; whether they can be moved or destroyed

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Because items physically occupy the world, players can place and arrange them to build structures, which lets them make new spaces or defenses.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: If a solid item can be moved, it can hurt other things when it crashes into them.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: Players can stack or position solid items to reach spots they otherwise couldn't, or use them to wall off spots themselves.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Anything with a physical body in the world takes up space, so it blocks passage and becomes something to get around.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Needing to place or stack solid items to reach somewhere out of reach turns arranging them into a puzzle.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Players can use solid items to build barriers that shield a spot from others, creating a protected place.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Players usually expect objects in a game world to be physically present, so solid items fit the theme they already imagine.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Solid items can be set up to break or to hit things when they move, so they can catch others out.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Solid items stand in the avatar's way and change how it must move, and avatars can themselves be solid things that others deal with.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: The pattern works by giving ordinary game items a physical body in the world, which changes what they are and how they behave.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Solid items fill the world with things that block, stack, and react, so the world's layout and how it can be traversed change.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Placing or moving solid items can open up places that were unreachable, or can close places off.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: A solid item physically sits between viewer and target, so it can hide things from view.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Because solid items take up space, characters can't pass through them and must go around, over, or push them.

changes.name: Props
changes.why: Props become something players can bump into, stand on, or move rather than just look at, which changes how the world feels.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units must route around solid items and may themselves be solid, so they can block each other and need arranging.

conflicts_with.name: Power-Ups
conflicts_with.why: Power-ups vanish when an avatar touches them, so there's little point making them solid objects that players interact with physically.

patterns.name: Events Timed to the Real World
patterns.what_it_is: Game events are triggered when a certain moment in real time arrives.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must run in real time or ticks and know the real date or time, and the event must offer something worth showing up for, with players told in advance.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A holiday theme that is only a visual reskin with no different gameplay or rewards, so nobody schedules around it.
patterns.knobs: which real-world dates trigger events; event length; how far ahead players are told

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Because holidays and big sports events are well known and set far ahead, players easily remember when to log in, and outside sources remind them too.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: Since an in-game event begins and ends together with its real-world occasion, it naturally appears for a limited time and then disappears.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Shared real-world dates let many players gather at the same moment without needing to coordinate through the game itself.

changes.name: Temporal Consistency
changes.why: Game time has to be matched to how time passes in the real world, which changes how consistently the game treats time.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: In a game set in an invented world, bringing in real-world holidays can feel out of place, such as fantasy citizens celebrating Valentine's Day.

patterns.name: Friendly Fire
patterns.what_it_is: Attacks by members of the same team damage their own teammates.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Teams must exist, and damage rules must apply to allies, with real cost to hitting them. Players need to be in situations where stray hits are plausible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Friendly Fire is switched on, but damage to allies is trivial or ranges are so short that nobody ever worries about it.
patterns.knobs: damage dealt to allies; area-of-effect size; whether the option is on at each difficulty

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since shots might hit teammates, players must aim more carefully instead of firing freely, which makes combat harder.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Teammates who get hurt by each other's shots can turn on one another, and blame for failures can create friction inside the team.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: When an accidental hit on a teammate happens without sparking real conflict, players can find the mishap funny and enjoy the blunder.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: In games that imitate real weapons, hurting allies by mistake matches how real firearms behave, so the rules fit the setting.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Letting players switch friendly fire on or off changes how risky play is, making the game harder or easier than the usual norm.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Teammates can be hit, so players must take care about who is in the line of fire when shooting.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Combat rules reach allies as well as enemies, so fighting means watching out for friends instead of just attacking.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Allied companions that can be damaged or killed can become victims or even culprits of stray attacks.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Team members can now harm each other, so being on the same side no longer guarantees safety.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Harming teammates can be used to make cooperation within teams harder.

conflicts_with.name: Internal Rivalry
conflicts_with.why: Friendly fire can spark rivalry, but because violence can quickly settle the dispute, it also makes it hard to keep a rivalry going long term.

patterns.name: Optional Rules
patterns.what_it_is: Rules that players themselves decide whether to use.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rule set must have clearly separate modules that can be added without breaking the core game. Too many options add confusion and production cost, so a small set that is easy to explain works best.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An option that is listed in the rulebook but changes nothing in play, or is so entangled with the core rules that nobody can use it without breaking the game.
patterns.knobs: how many optional rules; when they can be chosen (before play, during play, by whom)

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each optional rule adds to what players must know and handle, so a game with many extras becomes more complicated to play.

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: If extra rules are brought in mid-game and cannot be taken away again, the rules keep growing and changing as play goes on.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Any added rule means more bookkeeping, and optional ones add the further chore of remembering which of them are currently switched on.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players get to decide at the rules level whether to adopt each extra rule, which gives them real control over how the game is played.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: When extra rules can be introduced during play and also dropped later, the rules in force differ from one moment to the next.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Making features such as assistance or friendly fire optional lets players pick them to shift difficulty, so the choice itself becomes a level.

changes.name: Thematic Consistency
changes.why: Tabletop roleplayers often add optional rules so the game feels truer to its setting, though whether that is really theme or realism is debatable.

changes.name: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
changes.why: Making the adjustment something players can switch on or off lets it work as a difficulty choice, and also avoids weakening the value of effort.

patterns.name: Switches
patterns.what_it_is: World elements that players use to trigger events or actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The activation must change something that matters (open a path, alter hazards, change rules), and players must be able to find the switch and guess roughly what it does. Position and state handling are the main choices.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A lever that only plays an animation, or whose effect was already available some other way.
patterns.knobs: number and placement of switches; what each does; whether reusable, timed, or one-shot

can_cause.name: Alarms
can_cause.why: Agents that notice something specific can trigger a switch automatically, so the switch becomes an alarm instead of something a player presses.

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Just having a switch visible in the world invites players to try interacting with it.

can_cause.name: Controllers
can_cause.why: A switch is a simple control that permits only a few actions, usually turning an effect on or off.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: A switch that visibly changes look with its state shows its status itself, so no separate on-screen indicator is required.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: A switch can be made to work only once or to refuse further changes, so its effect cannot be undone.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: What a switch sets off can leave lasting alterations to the game world that remain afterward.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Single-use switches tell designers exactly when a player did something, so they can advance the planned story with cutscenes, dialogue or new areas.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Once players know what a switch does, they can think ahead about when and whether to use it.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: If players spot a switch in a different state than before or than expected, it shows them something happened earlier.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: The chain of events a switch starts can grow into something very large and dramatic.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Flipping a switch can bring new rules into force, so the game plays by different rules afterward.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
