can_cause.why: A switch can remove a barrier or hazard, so players must find and activate it before the way opens.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: Switches make environmental effects appear or vanish, letting players change conditions in the world.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Placed at particular spots on a board, switches change what happens there and so shape how the board plays.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Placed at particular spots in the world, switches alter what is possible there and so shape the world.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Placed at points within a level, switches can change its layout or rules, or even end it.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: A switch can be what players activate to start fast travel between locations.

patterns.name: Upgrades
patterns.what_it_is: Changes to items that make them more effective.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Upgrades must measurably improve an ability of existing equipment and cost players something, like scarce materials or an irreversible choice, so selection matters. Slots and acquisition rules must be clear.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cosmetic or tiny numeric bump that no one can feel, or one upgrade so obviously best that every player takes it.
patterns.knobs: size of the boost; cost and scarcity; number of upgrade slots; whether installing is reversible

can_cause.name: Equipment
can_cause.why: Upgrades are themselves items that are fitted onto other gear, so they count as a kind of equipment, like gems, scopes or silencers.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide when and which improvements to apply, so having upgrades available gives them real say over how their gear develops.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: The basic purpose of an upgrade is to make an item or its user better at something, such as dealing more damage.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Installing an upgrade is often permanent, so once a player commits to one, that choice cannot be taken back.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Because applying an upgrade is often permanent, players must weigh the different upgrade options against each other and give up some in favor of others.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor is one of the most common kinds of gear that can be improved by fitting upgrades onto it.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Adding upgrades can be controlled by the game's crafting rules, while giving wholly new abilities to gear is treated as crafting rather than upgrading.

changes.name: Critical Hits
changes.why: Upgrades can change how likely critical hits are, as a special case of improving damage-related abilities.

changes.name: Critical Misses
changes.why: Upgrades can alter the chance of critical misses, as a special case of improving damage-related abilities.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Damage is a common ability for upgrades to improve, so adding one makes a weapon hurt more.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Upgrades are fitted onto other gear to make it more effective, changing how well that gear performs.

changes.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
changes.why: When a game has composite skills such as accuracy, upgrades tied to the relevant skill change how well the character performs it.

changes.name: Sockets
changes.why: Sockets hold upgrades, but upgrades can in turn affect the sockets, for example by adding more slots.

changes.name: Variable Accuracy
changes.why: Upgrades can improve how precisely attacks land, since accuracy is one of the abilities they commonly enhance.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons are a common type of gear that upgrades improve, such as with scopes or extended magazines.

patterns.name: Character Levels
patterns.what_it_is: Stages of a hero's growth; each new one grants and strengthens abilities.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Clear thresholds, a meaningful reward at each step, and a sensible number of levels, with content for those who reach the top.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A level number is displayed but nothing is unlocked or improved when it rises.
patterns.knobs: number of levels; points needed per level; what each level grants

can_cause.name: Characteristics
can_cause.why: A character's level is one of the traits that describe that character, so having levels automatically adds one more such trait to the character.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Each new level is a goal players work toward, and reaching it marks that their character has become more capable.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: Because the level is a number that goes up with progress, it works like a score showing how far a player has come.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: Reaching a new level can open up things that were unavailable before, such as new abilities or powers.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Level-ups can offer choices presented as the character's own decisions, such as which teacher to study under, which then shape who they become.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Levels give a structured way to measure advancement, so moving up a level is the visible form that a character's growth takes.

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: In online games, reaching the top character level moves players into a distinct final phase of play with its own activities.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Levels change what a character is like, since each step up represents the character developing and becoming different from before.

changes.name: Helpers
changes.why: A level increase can have the side effect of letting the player have more helpers, which is an uncommon reward.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: With many players, someone will eventually reach the top level, so designers must provide endgame content for them to keep playing.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: Levels can serve as the requirement for getting new abilities, so the level system controls when those abilities become available.

changes.name: Characteristics
changes.why: Reaching a new level can change Characteristics broadly in one step, rather than each type of data being adjusted individually.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Advancing in character level can raise skills, and in some games gaining skill points is what earns a new level.

patterns.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
patterns.what_it_is: Entities differ in kind of abilities rather than in number: not stronger, but different.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each entity must be able to do something others cannot do at all, not just do the same thing better. The differences need to matter in play so that players need the entities for their special function.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Units with different names, looks and stat numbers, but who all do the same kind of thing, so they are just reskins with different values.
patterns.knobs: how many entity types; how unique each ability is; how the sets are distributed among players

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: When pieces can do truly different things, each one matters in its own way, so players must weigh many distinct roles and the game becomes more intricate.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because each entity carries distinct importance, there are different ways to use them, so playing again can feel different from the last time.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: If you control pieces with different kinds of abilities, you need to think ahead about how to make the best use of each one.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Pieces that act in different ways, not just stronger or weaker, give more variety than the same number of pieces that only differ in degree.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Team members with different strengths and weaknesses cover each other, so whole teams end up with equal overall chances.

can_cause.name: Team Balance
can_cause.why: Differently specialized team members can be designed to offset each other, though this is fragile because small inequalities can tip the balance.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Making characters differ in non-overlapping ways means no one player can do the whole combo, so teammates must combine their contributions.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: When characters have clearly different abilities or powers but still need to function as a team, players must find ways to combine those differences.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: The pattern works on abilities by making them differ in kind, so one entity can do something others simply cannot.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters get different kinds of abilities, making each one valuable for something unique, and in team games each player may have their own.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies can be given different kinds of abilities rather than just different stats, as with monsters that spawn others or resurrect the dead.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: Players can control entities with different ability types, but this makes it hard to keep sides alike unless everyone gets the same set.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Teams may have entities with differing ability types, which can be kept fair only if each team receives the same set of them.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units in a game can each have different kinds of capabilities, so a player must use a varied army to get full value.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Since differentiated entities need unique abilities, players end up with unlike things, which is hard to square with equal footing unless everyone gets the same set.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: Teams with entities that have unique abilities are hard to make even, though giving every team the same differentiated set resolves the problem.

patterns.name: Player Augmentations
patterns.what_it_is: Support that helps the player perform game actions better.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The help must truly change the success of specific actions, and must be tuned against the game's challenge. Designers must decide who gets it, so that it neither trivialises play nor feels useless.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An assist option exists but is so weak, or so hidden, that results are the same with or without it.
patterns.knobs: strength of the help; which actions it affects; who receives it

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: Because the augmentation acts on the character the player controls, that character can end up doing things on its own or by rule rather than by the player's direct input.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players feel the help is boosting their ability to shape events, they can come to believe they influence the game more than they really do.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: When the game itself hands the boost to players, it works as a reward that makes later play easier.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: If players sense that the help increases their power to affect what happens, they feel more in control of the game's outcome.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Giving help to some players and not others, or in different amounts, can even out or tilt how evenly matched they are.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Since the help acts on the in-game character, success comes from a mix of what the player can do and what the character is assisted to do.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: The boost applies to the characters or units players control in the game, so it changes how those agents behave and perform.

changes.name: Speedruns
changes.why: Assistance makes it easier to finish a game very quickly, which helps runners, though some see that as cheating unless exploit-finding is the point.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Aids that perform actions for players can make them lose the sense of their own agency, depending on how they see it.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: The game helping the player makes challenges easier, which lessens the importance of the player's own skill.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: If players do not feel the enhanced abilities are under their control, the augmentations fail to give them real influence.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: How fair the game feels depends on who receives the help and how much, so uneven assistance can upset balance between players.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Because help reduces how much player skill and work determine results, their effort seems to matter less.

patterns.name: Player Kicking
patterns.what_it_is: A player is removed from the session by others' decision, not by the game's rules.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Someone must hold the power to kick, such as a moderator or a vote, with clear criteria and a defined length and scope. Without that, it will be unfair or ignored.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A kick button exists, but kicked players can rejoin immediately or nobody has the authority to use it.
patterns.knobs: who may kick; vote threshold; duration and scope of the ban

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: Because players can be removed for social misbehavior, not just for breaking the written rules, anyone may be forced out of a game sooner than the rules themselves would end their play.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players can vote to remove others, they get to choose who they play with, which can make them feel their actions carry more weight.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Removing someone is done outside the game's formal rules, as a social or administrative step about behavior rather than a move within gameplay.

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: A kicked player's session ends right away, so being removed has the same result for them as the game finishing.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Kicking takes a participant out of the game instance, so they can no longer play, just as if they had been eliminated.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: A player who gets kicked takes on the label of being banned, an unwelcome reputation among the other players.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Together with voting, it lets players remove those who don't follow how the majority wants to play, choosing their co-players.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: Kicking usually applies to a single game server, and can be limited to the current game or extended to bans of set length or permanent.

changes.name: Meta Servers
changes.why: A meta server can apply a ban across all play instead of one server, widening the reach of a kick.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Kicking fits best where several people play together, since removing a misbehaving player there is clearly different from an ordinary game ending in single-player games.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players who can be removed by others may lose their sense of influence, even though kicking others feels powerful.

patterns.name: Shared Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: A goal where the reward must be split among several players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A reward must go to a group, with a clear rule on how it is divided or room to negotiate. Individual rewards on the side weaken it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reward everyone gets in full anyway, so there is nothing to share or argue about.
patterns.knobs: who shares; how it is divided; reward size

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: When a reward is split by the system or by players, the weakest players can be given the best share, which evens out the differences between them.

can_cause.name: Mutual Goals
can_cause.why: When everyone in a group receives the same payoff, they all want the same outcome, so their aims line up.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: A shared reward is simply a reward, just one that must be divided among several players rather than going to one.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: If a reward cannot easily be cut into equal parts, players must argue over who gets what, which creates a dilemma among them.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: When a reward is hard to split evenly, some players step up to handle the dividing, which gives them a special role in the group.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Getting the same reward together binds players into a unit, so a common payoff can be the basis for forming a team.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Because the reward goes to several players at once, they feel they succeeded as a group and share something common.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: When a prize is split among players alongside a common aim, working together is how each of them gains.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: When benefits go to all members of a faction, belonging to the group pays off collectively.

conflicts_with.name: Altruistic Actions
conflicts_with.why: When the whole team gains together, helping a teammate is tied to your own gain, which undermines the unselfish quality of the act.

conflicts_with.name: Delayed Reciprocity
conflicts_with.why: If the reward is already split among everyone by design, individual helpful acts need no repayment, so situations of owing a favor happen less often.

conflicts_with.name: Excluding Goals
conflicts_with.why: Excluding goals tie one player's success to others' failure, which is at odds with rewards that all players share.

conflicts_with.name: Individual Rewards
conflicts_with.why: A given reward cannot go to everyone and to only one player at once, so the two kinds exclude each other.

conflicts_with.name: Tiebreakers
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker picks a single winner from tied players, so the tie that would have led to a shared reward no longer occurs.

patterns.name: Cosmetic Game Items
patterns.what_it_is: Items that differ from others only in appearance.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must change looks only, not abilities, and be visible to others, with enough variety or rarity that players want them. Players should be able to choose, show or collect them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An item is sold as cosmetic, but only one player sees it or it is not displayed anywhere.
patterns.knobs: number of variants; rarity or cost; how they are obtained; how visible they are

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because an item's looks don't change how play works, players value it mostly for reasons outside the game, such as showing off or trading it with others.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Decorative ornaments placed in the game world can take up space, so they may end up blocking movement even though they exist for looks.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Cosmetic items stay appealing to players across sessions, and with several players present they can be swapped among them.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Items can exist purely for looks without changing gameplay, so they are a type of game item.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Wearable items can be given different looks without changing what they do, so players can alter how their avatars appear.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: A cosmetic item takes an ordinary item and gives it a distinct appearance, or exists as an item that serves only that visual purpose.

changes.name: Achievements
changes.why: Achievements can award appearance-only items, which show off accomplishments and signal status without affecting gameplay.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Items that only change looks can be shown on the avatar, helping express differences between avatars.

patterns.name: Varying Rule Sets
patterns.what_it_is: The game's rules change over time, but within a preset collection.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Clear triggers must change the active rules during play, such as random cards, locations, switches or new abilities, and players must be told about the changes. The shifts must alter what good play looks like.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rule list that technically has conditional clauses which never trigger in practice, so play stays the same throughout.
patterns.knobs: how often rules change; trigger type (random, location, progress); how many rules can change at once

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Having to keep track of rules that shift during play gives players more to think about, which makes the overall gameplay more intricate.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: When the rules change in step with a story's growing confrontations, each stage can end in a bigger, more significant wrap-up.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since the rules in force keep changing, players face different situations over time instead of repeating the same play.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Rules that shift temporarily can grant abilities for a limited period.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: In games meant to be complex, introducing rules in stages lets players learn bit by bit, which keeps the complexity manageable.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Changing the rules can produce the escalating effects that stories use to stagger significance.

patterns.name: Moveable Tiles
patterns.what_it_is: World elements that move, but not of their own will.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The tiles need clear movement rules, such as what triggers them and where they stop, and the level must be built so their movement matters, for example by carrying, blocking or opening routes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tiles that move as decoration, on a path that never affects where players can go or what they can do.
patterns.knobs: movement pattern, speed and what triggers it

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: A moving tile can squeeze a piece or character against a wall or another object, hurting or removing it.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: A tile that is itself a barrier can cut off parts of the world, though its movement can also reopen them.

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: Since the tiles travel through the world, their very presence introduces motion, which can carry avatars or units along.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Depending on size and position, a moving tile can stand in the way and keep other game elements from passing.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: When player actions cause the tiles to move, the layout of the world changes because of what players do.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Together with damage, moving tiles can cause harm that players cannot stop, so players must time their actions around it.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Shooters or targets riding on tiles, or tiles blocking the line, force players to account for the tiles' motion when aiming.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Tiles can serve as alternate routes that let players reach areas that were otherwise cut off.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Moveable Tiles are ordinary tiles given the ability to move, so the pattern adds motion to what a tile can do.

conflicts_with.name: Agents
conflicts_with.why: Tiles are elements that don't move by their own will, while agents act on goals, so the two fit poorly together.

patterns.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
patterns.what_it_is: Players themselves agree on how long the whole session will last.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have an adjustable end condition and a point before play where players agree on it. The game must still work at different lengths.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A length setting that exists in the menu but is nearly always left at default, or one where a short setting breaks the game.
patterns.knobs: which limits players can set: time, turns or score target

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Because players have to talk and agree on how long the game will last, that discussion itself becomes an activity outside the game's rules.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Players can fit the game's length around their other plans, so the game works for people with different amounts of free time.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Since the length is agreed in advance, everyone stays for the full game and experiences all of it together, rather than drifting in and out.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: Letting players adjust how long a game runs fits their available time, reducing the need to leave early.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: A story with fixed events assumes a certain length of play, so if players shorten or stretch the game, the story may not fit unless it can scale.

patterns.name: Transferable Items
patterns.what_it_is: Items that can be passed from one character to another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be an action to give, drop or swap items, and a clear set of limits about which items and to whom. Items must have value to other players or characters to make transfers worthwhile.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An option to hand over items that is blocked for nearly everything useful, or covers items nobody wants.
patterns.knobs: which items can be transferred; to whom; what limits apply (binding, class restrictions)

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because items can change hands, players get to decide which things they end up carrying instead of being stuck with what they started with.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Since possession of an item can pass to someone else, getting hold of particular items becomes something players can aim for as a goal.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Being able to hand objects to teammates lets players support one another and back up joint play.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Because items carrying abilities can change hands, the special powers move from one player to another.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars can stand in for characters as parties to a transfer, though anything beyond trivial exchanges still needs them to have inventories.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters are the ones who give, receive or lose items, so being able to pass items around changes what they can possess.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Players can pass items to companions to equip them well or let them carry loads, as in Fallout and Dragon Age II.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Trading may be allowed with every kind of character except enemies, so enemies mark a limit on who can take part in transfers.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Designers choose which items can be handed over and by what actions, so transferability becomes a property layered on top of items.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Some restricted items can still be sold to non-player characters, so these characters remain valid recipients even when players cannot exchange them.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Items can be handed between player characters, as in Left 4 Dead, so the group is equipped as well as possible.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Transfers are mostly done through menus rather than in-world actions, so the same system works for resources as well as items.

changes.name: Self-Service Kiosks
changes.why: Locked items can often still be sold to kiosks, which take them out of the game so other players never get them.

patterns.name: Access Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: A reward that opens up content or actions that were unavailable before.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Some content must be actually locked at the start and opened by an achievement, and the opened content must be optional and worth wanting. The gate must be visible so players know what they are working toward.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The 'unlocked' area or action was available all along, or it is forced on the player so it is not an optional access at all.
patterns.knobs: what is gated; what unlocks it; how soon new access arrives

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: New content is offered rather than forced, so players decide whether to use it, which leaves them in charge of how they play.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Because access is granted in a set sequence, players meet challenges in that order and finish them one after another, producing larger closures along the way.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: Since players are offered new options instead of being made to use them, they have more say over what happens in the game.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Gating access controls what players reach and when, so story parts can be told in the order the designer planned.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Access Rewards are one kind of reward: getting entry to gameplay that was previously unavailable is itself what the player is given.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Receiving a reward, usually for finishing a goal, can unlock an area that was closed off, so the blocked state is only temporary.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Access Rewards affect how levels work, since earning access can make additional levels open for players to choose between.

patterns.name: Context Dependent Reactions
patterns.what_it_is: Game characters respond differently to events and items depending on the situation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Agents must react to relevant conditions such as place, history or who is present, and those reactions must be seen to differ. This needs enough authored content or logic, or a human playing the agent.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Characters seem to react but use the same canned response whatever happens.
patterns.knobs: how many context factors are checked; how many distinct responses are written; human or algorithmic control

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Real-world behavior is never identical each time, so varying responses by situation makes the game world feel more like a believable place.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When characters respond differently depending on circumstances, players are more likely to feel those characters are pursuing goals of their own.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because identical repeated actions feel unnatural, tailoring responses to the situation helps the game stay true to the feel of its theme.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Giving agents situation-based responses lets them be personalized and lets their reactions fit many different things in the game world.

changes.name: Awareness of Surroundings
changes.why: Agents that respond differently depending on circumstances come across as noticing what is around them.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: If guards only protect certain places or times, they need to respond sensibly when they meet other agents elsewhere.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Code-driven reactions may be the only practical way to give a large crowd of non-player characters this kind of varied responding.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Computer-controlled characters can react differently when sneaking matters, which marks off the sneaking parts of a game from the rest.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Having agents react to the current situation in their world makes them appear more alive and delays players reducing them to simple objects.

patterns.name: Critical Misses
patterns.what_it_is: Predefined random failures in combat that harm the attacker themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a small random chance that a failed attack has a real penalty, such as dropping the weapon or hitting the wrong target. It should be rare enough not to feel unfair.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A miss is called critical, but the result is exactly the same as an ordinary miss.
patterns.knobs: chance of it happening; how severe the penalty is; skill or weapon modifiers

can_cause.name: Critical Failures
can_cause.why: A critical miss is just a critical failure that happens specifically during fighting, so it is a combat-flavored version of that broader idea.

can_cause.name: Critical Results
can_cause.why: Because a critical miss is a kind of critical failure, and critical failures are one kind of extreme outcome, it also counts as a critical result.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: A critical miss is rare, so it stands out from ordinary play and can count as an exceptional event, unless it happens so often it stops being special.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: When a critical miss happens, the attacker typically suffers some disadvantage as a result, which is exactly what a penalty is.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Players don't want to botch an attack, but when an over-the-top disaster does happen, watching it unfold can be fun in itself.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Critical misses add rare, extra bad outcomes for the attacker on top of the normal results the combat rules would produce.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Hits
conflicts_with.why: They are opposites: a critical hit is an extraordinary good result, a critical miss an extraordinary bad one, though one side's miss can feel like the other's lucky break.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Dramatic misses that come from chance emphasize bad luck over the player's skill, reducing the role of performance.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Since a rare disastrous result can strike even a sound action, players can't count on their choices leading to the outcomes they expect.

patterns.name: Legacy Games
patterns.what_it_is: The results of one game permanently change the conditions of later games.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must specify lasting changes, such as new components or rules, that carry to later sessions, while a core of fixed rules keeps it the same game. Players must be able to track the changes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A campaign log or score is kept but nothing in the next session actually differs.
patterns.knobs: how big and how frequent the permanent changes are; how much of the rule set stays fixed

can_cause.name: Evolving Rule Sets
can_cause.why: When the permanent changes involve rules rather than just components, the game's rules shift from one session to the next, so the rule set evolves.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Because each session leaves the game different in content, players keep finding new things, which lets them explore the game's world over time.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Since outcomes carry over and shape later sessions, play stretches across multiple sessions, which makes the game a meta game by its very nature.

patterns.name: Anonymous Actions
patterns.what_it_is: Actions from which you cannot tell exactly which player performed them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must be pooled or hidden (shuffled cards, simultaneous play) so no one can trace the source, and the identity must matter to the outcome. Social channels must not leak who acted.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Actions are called anonymous but everyone can tell who did them from turn order or table talk.
patterns.knobs: how contributions are mixed; whether identities are revealed afterwards; what penalty exists for revealing yourself

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When the setup hides even which players are taking part, nobody can tell who is acting, so players feel separated from the actions themselves.

can_cause.name: Player Anonymity
can_cause.why: If actions can't be tied to a particular player, others can't link moves to people, so players stay unidentified in the game.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Playing a role convincingly while pretending you did not perform certain hidden actions is a skill that counts as mastery.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: When actions are anonymous, players must roleplay themselves convincingly to hide their identity, so roleplaying becomes necessary to succeed.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: When an effect comes from a particular game element, hiding the player who triggered it changes how that ability works by keeping its user unknown.

changes.name: Betrayal
changes.why: Because nobody can trace actions back to a player, a betrayer can act against others without being noticed and may even do so repeatedly.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Since players struggle to link actions to people and their strategies, they can't foresee what will follow, so outcomes become less predictable.

patterns.name: Development Time
patterns.what_it_is: A set amount of game time needed for an event to produce its main effect.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The time must be fixed and known and must be long enough to make players plan around it. Showing progress makes waiting readable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A timer so short or so skippable that players never have to wait or plan.
patterns.knobs: length of the time; whether it blocks other actions; whether progress is shown

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: Because an action only pays off after a set wait, its result arrives later, and the wait is fixed and known in advance.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: If you must wait for a started action to finish and nothing else is available to do, you simply sit idle.

can_cause.name: Extended Actions
can_cause.why: When you cannot start the same action again until the first one is done, that action effectively stretches over the whole waiting period.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Players can remember when several timed events will finish so they can line them up and use them together at the right moment.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Since the waiting period is a known, fixed amount, players can tell ahead of time when an action will take effect.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because results land in the future, players must think about what the game will look like then, not only what it looks like now.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing how long events take lets players track them and arrange combinations of events so they land together at well-chosen moments.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: When things take a known time to develop, players can time their actions so results arrive together, creating combos if they manage the timing.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Making the wait before something finishes long enough forces you to leave the game, and you must return later to see the result.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Together with progress indicators, visible build-up time lets players see how close something is to being finished.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Actions that take time to complete and can be interrupted feel like deadlines, because delay raises the risk that others will thwart them.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: The pattern is mostly applied to building-type actions, where making something takes a set amount of time before it is complete.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Crafting is a kind of construction, so making an item commonly takes a fixed wait before the result is available.

patterns.name: Possibility of Graceful Surrender
patterns.what_it_is: The player can give up or leave without spoiling the session for others.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Leaving must not break the game for the others. That means handling the leaver's resources, closing kingmaker loopholes, and rebalancing or substituting an AI for the departed player.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A quit button exists, but leaving ends the match, ruins it for others or counts as a punishable desertion, so players stay on or ragequit.
patterns.knobs: what happens to the leaver's pieces and resources; whether an AI takes over; penalty for leaving

can_cause.name: Early Leaving Players
can_cause.why: Offering a clean exit means players who feel they can't win can quit sooner instead of staying on, so people leaving early becomes normal.

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: Letting someone leave without hurting others is itself a way of giving up, so allowing graceful exit amounts to allowing surrender.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When players can drop out at different moments, each person's session ends at a different time, so participants' play is no longer aligned.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Giving players a clean way to concede lets them exit mid-game without ruining things for others.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Final standings become easy to read late in a game, so players are most tempted to quit then and the exit option matters most there.

changes.name: Last Man Standing
changes.why: Players who see they can't be the final survivor can bow out gracefully instead of dragging on in a contest they can't win.

changes.name: Predictable Winner
changes.why: When a likely winner is obvious, trailing players lose hope, and a graceful exit lets them leave without spoiling things for others.

patterns.name: Save Files
patterns.what_it_is: Files with data that can be used to restore the state of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Build real storage and loading of the full or partial state, and decide how saving is triggered and how many slots exist. Slot limits and where saving is allowed decide whether it supports pauses or invites abuse.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A save that only records progress through a password or level number, or loads into a state that immediately kills the player, so it does not truly restore the game.
patterns.knobs: number of slots; manual versus automatic saving; how much state is stored

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Knowing they can go back to a stored state, players feel safe trying risky actions they would normally avoid.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Making, loading and destroying saves are things players do outside the game's own rules, so having saves creates these actions.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Because saves exist, players can take part in extra activities around them, and trading game elements is one of these.

can_cause.name: Save Scumming
can_cause.why: Players can reload a stored state whenever an outcome displeases them, so they repeat it until it goes their way.

can_cause.name: Save-Load Cycles
can_cause.why: Since a stored state is always available to return to, players can fall into repeatedly saving and reloading.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: A save file normally isn't a gameplay resource, but it becomes one when a cap limits how many can be kept.

changes.name: Game Pauses
changes.why: Built-in pauses cover only short breaks; saves let players stop for days or months and still rebuild their game later.

conflicts_with.name: Save Scumming
conflicts_with.why: Limiting players to a single save file works against save scumming, since they cannot keep many fallback states to reload.

patterns.name: Save Points
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the world or between levels where the player can save the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Put saving at chosen locations or between levels, ideally in safe spots, and space them so retrying costs real effort. Decide whether saving is manual or automatic and how much state is stored.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Save points placed so densely, or saving allowed anywhere anyway, that they never limit anything or mark any progress.
patterns.knobs: distance between save points; manual versus automatic; how much state is saved

can_cause.name: Check Points
can_cause.why: A save point placed at a spot in the world can double as a check point, or turn an existing one into somewhere you can save.

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Players have to reach a save point, and arriving there feels like finishing a stretch of play, so it marks a natural ending.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: Because players can restart from a saved point after failing, they effectively get another try at what they just lost.

can_cause.name: Password Save Files
can_cause.why: If a save point only records that the player got there, a simple password can store that and nothing else.

can_cause.name: Save Files
can_cause.why: Saving at a save point means the game must store some or all of its state somewhere, which requires a save file.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Players must travel through the world or finish a level to reach a save point, so getting there becomes a movement goal.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Game States
can_cause.why: If a save point sits where death follows right after loading, players can be stuck in a state they can never get out of.

changes.name: Check Points
changes.why: Save points can be added onto existing check points, changing them from a simple progress marker into somewhere players can also store their game.

changes.name: Goal Hierarchies
changes.why: When tied to check points, save points guarantee that progress on particular parts of the goal structure is kept rather than lost.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Save points can sit inside a level or in the gaps between levels, so designers choose where in the level structure saving happens.

changes.name: Permadeath
changes.why: Saving lets players go back, which undermines permanent death, but dying can be made to send players back to the last save point.

changes.name: Safe Havens
changes.why: Save points tend to be put in safe places so that a loaded game does not drop players straight into danger.

changes.name: Save-Load Cycles
changes.why: Designers decide where saving is possible, so spacing save points far apart makes retrying costly and discourages repeated save and reload.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Since players must get to save points, these locations shape where they head and can add new destinations to reach.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: It is hard to agree on a good moment to save unless all players are cooperating.

conflicts_with.name: Scores
conflicts_with.why: Players can return to earlier states and retry to push their score higher, so the score no longer reflects a single uninterrupted run.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Going back to a save and replaying parts of the game can clash with the story's timeline and what the player already knows.

patterns.name: Zone of Control
patterns.what_it_is: A game element affects how the elements next to it can act.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Units must project effects onto neighboring spaces, such as forced stops, extra movement cost or attack penalties, strong enough to shape movement and positioning. Terrain and choke points should make it matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A highlighted area around units that has no effect on movement or combat.
patterns.knobs: radius; effect strength (stop, extra cost, free attacks); which units generate it; exceptions

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Because a unit's zone reaches past its own square, claiming ground gets easier, so zones can make pushing outward into new territory the main focus of a phase of play.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Enemy zones can force a unit to stop, pay extra movement cost, or risk attacks when passing through, which restricts how freely pieces can move.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing how to use zone of control effects efficiently, especially with choke points, is something players can plan around ahead of time.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Units that extend a zone of control limit and shape where others can safely move, so players must plan around those zones.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Since a zone gives a piece influence beyond the exact spot it occupies, it changes how much of the map a player effectively holds.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars can project a zone, though rarely, giving the character reach over neighboring spaces beyond its own physical location.

changes.name: Choke Points
changes.why: Zones make passing through narrow spots more costly or dangerous, so these spots become much more important to hold or avoid.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Zones usually give friendly units advantages or hostile units disadvantages in fights, such as making enemy retreats impossible or tackles available.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Entering or leaving an enemy zone can stop a unit, cost extra movement, or allow attacks, so zones shape where pieces can go.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units are the most common source of zones, which extend their influence to adjacent spaces and change how they and nearby enemies can act.

patterns.name: Player-Artifact Proximity
patterns.what_it_is: Rules depend on how physically close the player is to certain objects.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a way to measure or verify closeness, a defined distance threshold, and events that really depend on it. The artifacts must matter to gameplay.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A proximity condition is claimed, but players can complete the task from anywhere or the check is never enforced.
patterns.knobs: distance threshold; what is triggered on entering or leaving; how long players must stay near

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: When the game uses physical artifacts whose positions it detects, those artifacts can serve as the items players trade.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because play is tied to real-world locations, if that area stays open for everyday activities, the game ends up woven into ordinary life around other people.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Since a player must be near an artifact to affect it, they have to actually move their body toward it or to a set distance from it.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Artifacts can be items such as tools, so where an item physically sits becomes part of how it works in play.

changes.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
changes.why: Tying interactions to physical closeness links the play area to actual places in the real world.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: When a tool is an artifact requiring closeness, its physical location becomes a gameplay feature that changes how the tool is used.

patterns.name: Always Vulnerable
patterns.what_it_is: A player's resources may be at risk even when they are not playing.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game world must keep running and allow harm to offline players' assets, with real losses possible. There should be no pause or protection for absent players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game claims offline risk but offline assets are protected or losses are trivial, so absence costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much can be lost offline; how long protection lasts, if any

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: If you stop watching the game, you may be hurt by events you missed, so players must stay alert to what is going on.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: When players cannot be online all the time, they come back regularly to check on and protect what could be harmed in their absence.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because things can go wrong while you are away or inattentive, players feel ongoing worry about what might be happening to their stuff.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting is where being exposed while absent shows most clearly, since attacks can land on a player who is not there.

changes.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
changes.why: It pushes players to focus more on the things they care about, which sharpens the fun of games built around things going wrong.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: A player's key places or objects can be attacked during others' sessions, making players keep watch over them.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: Whatever players have put effort into can be threatened even while they are away, so the investment is never fully safe.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: In these persistent worlds, a player who logs off can keep their belongings from being removed only if the game does not make them exposed when they leave.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: In group play, others or a game master can fairly act for an absent member, and it feels odd to protect only the missing player's stuff.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: One version needs player-versus-player play, because other players' sessions are what let someone's assets be threatened while the owner is away.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Players' resources are not automatically removed or protected when they leave or take a break; they stay at risk.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: Such games keep advancing on a timer, so players who leave still face consequences instead of the game halting for them.

conflicts_with.name: Game Pauses
conflicts_with.why: Being exposed while away cannot work alongside stopping the game, since a pause would freeze events and shield players from threats.

patterns.name: Critical Failures
patterns.what_it_is: An especially severe outcome of random failure that an ordinary miss never produces.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The bad result must be clearly worse than an ordinary failure and happen rarely, from a defined random chance. It must have effects the player really feels.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A critical failure is announced, but its effect is the same as an ordinary failure.
patterns.knobs: chance of it happening; how bad the effect is; which actions are covered

can_cause.name: Critical Results
can_cause.why: A critical failure is one kind of critical result, since it is an unusually extreme outcome of an action, here a bad one.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Because these bad outcomes are rare and go beyond ordinary failing, a critical failure can turn into a standout moment in play.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: The harm from a critical failure is usually delivered as specific penalties on whoever suffered it, ones an ordinary failure would never impose.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Skills and critical failures shape each other: skills offer an easy way to build the formulas that decide how likely a critical failure is.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Successes
conflicts_with.why: They pull in opposite directions: one is a randomly extreme bad result and the other an extreme good result of the same kind of action.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Critical failures come from chance rather than how well the player did, so they undercut outcomes depending on the player's own performance.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Since a random extra-bad result can strike any attempt, players cannot be sure what an action will lead to, making consequences less predictable.

patterns.name: Reward Widgets
patterns.what_it_is: Rewards placed around the world even though, by the world's logic, they should not be there.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must appear in the play area, be clickable or collectable, and be worth the effort of collecting. A time limit or auto-collect rule sets how much attention they demand.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reward icon that pops up and gives nothing extra, or is collected automatically so that clicking is pointless.
patterns.knobs: how often widgets appear; time before they auto-collect; reward size

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Because players must click the floating rewards to collect them, the game gains more clicking actions, which is the main reason designers use this pattern.

can_cause.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
can_cause.why: Putting a reward into the world as a clickable object means the game now contains widgets that sit in the environment without belonging to it.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: If players have to keep clicking each reward to collect it, that repeated clicking can become a chore, though it stops being required when collection is automatic.

can_cause.name: Ninja Looting
can_cause.why: Since the rewards sit out in the shared game space, someone other than the intended recipient might grab them first.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Instead of simply changing a value or handing over an item, the reward now has to be seen and picked up from the environment, changing how it is received.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: These widgets float in the game world yet are not truly part of it, so they break the sense that everything shown belongs to the game world.

patterns.name: Setback Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A penalty forces the player to repeat past actions or go back over the same path.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Failure must send players back to redo something that cost real effort. It should not remove them from the game, and the size of the loss decides how sharply it hurts.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'setback' that costs almost nothing to redo, such as a respawn a few steps back.
patterns.knobs: how much progress is lost; how far back the player is sent

can_cause.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
can_cause.why: Having to redo completed actions makes the player's goal harder to reach, so the goal's difficulty shifts depending on how often and how badly the player fails.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Undoing progress is a cost imposed for failing, so a setback is simply one particular way of penalizing players without removing them.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players know a failure could throw away earlier progress, so they feel uneasy, and the bigger the possible loss, the stronger that feeling.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A setback's design depends on which levels or stages the player must go through again, so it shapes how much of that progress is repeated.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Setbacks often work by pushing players back or forcing them to travel routes again, so they directly change how far and where players move.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Having to redo sequences of actions repeatedly often makes no sense within the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If the story acts as though every challenge was passed on the first try, the repeated attempts caused by setbacks contradict the narrated timeline.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Losing progress already earned can make players feel their earlier work was wasted, which undermines the sense that effort pays off.

patterns.name: Critical Successes
patterns.what_it_is: An action succeeds by chance and gives a special effect that would otherwise be impossible.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A rare random roll must give a clear extra benefit beyond normal success. The chance may be tied to skill or tools, and the bonus must be felt.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A roll is called a critical success, but it gives nothing extra over a normal success.
patterns.knobs: chance of a critical; size of the bonus; skill or tool modifiers

can_cause.name: Critical Results
can_cause.why: A critical success is one of two kinds of critical result; the other kind is its opposite, the critical failure, so success is a member of that group.

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Because a critical success gives special extra benefits that ordinary successes lack, it can stand out as an unusual, exceptional moment during play.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Using a skill is an action that can end in a critical success, so having critical successes as a possible outcome changes how skill use plays out.

conflicts_with.name: Critical Failures
conflicts_with.why: They pull in opposite directions: one is a randomly extreme bad result and the other an extreme good result of the same kind of action.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: Critical successes usually add extra randomness to deciding how an action turns out, which works against the player's ability to judge how well they will perform.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Since a critical success is a lucky, exceptional outcome, it makes it less likely that players can foresee exactly what an action will result in.

patterns.name: Artifact-Location Proximity
patterns.what_it_is: Rules depend on how close a real object is to a real place, detected by sensors.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Sensing hardware has to be reliable and tied to a clear game condition, such as delivering an item, and the sensing range and the thing that counts as 'near' must be chosen on purpose. A short delay or a required action on entering or leaving helps cover for sensor errors.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Objects carry tags or the place has a sensor, but the game never checks them, or the same result could be got by pressing a button, so carrying the object to the place means nothing.
patterns.knobs: sensing technology and range; which objects trigger it; delay or extended action on entering or leaving

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because items must be brought to real places, players start noticing ordinary spots and surroundings differently, seeing them through the lens of the game's goals.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Since the game checks where an item sits, players must come back to the same sensing locations again to place, retrieve or move artifacts.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Gameplay depends on real objects and real places being sensed, so the game spills out into the physical world rather than staying on a screen.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Delivering items to a specific location means players must find their way through real space to reach it.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: Players must visit actual locations, so knowing the real surroundings well helps them reach the sensing spots more effectively.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because a place triggers game events when an artifact is near, some locations become more valuable than others to control or reach.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Players have to visit locations to meet the game's conditions, so they must travel between places, even without the game tracking their own position.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Using the pattern means physical game items are modified so a sensor placed at a location can detect them.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: Sensed artifact positions let game masters remotely steer and keep track of a pervasive game or LARP without being present.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: The items that get modified to be sensed are quite often tools, so their position at a place affects play.

patterns.name: Critical Results
patterns.what_it_is: An unusual random outcome of an action with an effect not available from an ordinary result.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The special outcomes must be unusual, come from the dice or random process, and do things ordinary results cannot. Their trigger must be clear so players understand what happened.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Rare outcomes are listed, but they only repeat what ordinary successes or failures already do.
patterns.knobs: trigger chance or dice condition; size of effects; which actions can produce them

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Because these outcomes are rare by definition, whenever one happens it stands out from ordinary results and becomes a notable, out-of-the-ordinary moment in play.

changes.name: Open-Ended Die Rolls
changes.why: Rare outcomes can be triggered by dice combinations, such as collecting enough dice with particular values, so they change how such rolls are read.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Rare special outcomes change how using a skill plays out, since the usual result can occasionally be replaced by something extraordinary.

conflicts_with.name: Performance Uncertainty
conflicts_with.why: These rare results add more chance to the outcome, so what happens depends less on how well the player performs and more on luck.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Chance plays a bigger role and the rare results have effects ordinary ones cannot produce, so players cannot reliably foresee what an action will do.

patterns.name: Stack Seeding
patterns.what_it_is: Chosen cards are placed in set parts of the deck beforehand to steer random draws.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs drawing stacks and a rule that places certain cards in certain positions, at setup or in play. The seeding must be strong enough to shape what happens, not just reshuffled away.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rule that places key cards but then shuffles the whole stack again, so the seeding has no effect on what is drawn.
patterns.knobs: which cards are placed; how deep in the stack; when seeding happens (setup or during play)

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Placing key cards in set parts of the stack makes them appear in a planned order, such as guardians showing up before the thunderstones that follow them.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Because designers decide roughly where certain cards sit in the stack, they know better when those cards will come up, so outcomes become less left to chance.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: Designers choose where particular cards go in the stack, so when those cards get drawn is controlled instead of purely random.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: The stack itself is rearranged or built in sections, so certain elements are guaranteed to land in particular parts of it.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Chance still shuffles things within sections, but placing key elements in set zones narrows how wild the draw order can be.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Tiles drawn from a stack can be positioned the same way as cards, so designers can control roughly when specific ones appear.

patterns.name: Individual Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A penalty that affects only one of the players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The penalty must hit only the player who earned it and be meaningful enough to affect their choices. How it interacts with shared rewards or teams should be clear.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A penalty so small or so easy to dodge that the player ignores it, or one that spreads to others anyway.
patterns.knobs: size and type of the penalty; what triggers it; who chooses the target

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: It is the plain, basic kind of penalty: a setback that lands on just one player instead of being spread across several.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When a penalty hits one player while rewards go to that player or to everyone, players face tension between personal and group interests.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: If failure costs only the person who suffers it, players may be less willing to commit to a goal they all share, compared with shared penalties.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: With only one player, any penalty necessarily lands on that player, so individual penalties are the only kind of penalty available.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Penalties aimed at one member can blur into the whole group, for example when a punished player's absence also weakens teammates.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Individual penalties are designed to avoid hurting other players directly, whereas shared penalties deliberately hit several players, so the two pull in opposite directions.

patterns.name: Trumps
patterns.what_it_is: In trick-taking card games, a suit that beats the cards of all other suits.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The trump suit must really override normal ranking and must be chosen in a way that matters, such as being fixed, random or bid. There must be a trick-taking game for it to modify.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A named trump suit that happens to rank the same as normal, or is so rare it almost never decides a trick.
patterns.knobs: fixed vs. changing trump; how trump is chosen (random or bid)

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: A trump suit adds an extra rule about which cards win, so players have more to weigh when choosing what to play, making the game more complex.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Only cards of the trump suit can override the normal winning order, so holding and playing one gives a player a power others lack.

changes.name: Trick Taking
changes.why: Trumps change the basic trick rule, where the highest card of the led suit wins, by letting a special suit beat every other suit.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Adding trump cards to trick-taking games makes it harder to guess what other players will play.

patterns.name: Player-Avatar Proximity
patterns.what_it_is: Rules take into account how close the player and their avatar are in reality.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must track both the real position of one side and the virtual position of the other, and base events on how they relate. Both positions have to matter to play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Both positions are tracked but the relation between them triggers nothing.
patterns.knobs: distance threshold; how long proximity must hold; what it triggers

can_cause.name: Orthogonal Differentiation
can_cause.why: Because players and avatars rarely get the same ways of moving, the two end up with different movement abilities that don't directly compare.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Both players and avatars can move around, so closeness between them means someone must physically travel to get near the other.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Players and avatars are unlikely to move in the same ways, so one side tends to get movement options the other lacks.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Having two distinct kinds of movement gives players different experiences to try, especially when character classes offer only one of those kinds.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: In hybrid spaces this proximity rule changes how avatars matter, since their virtual positions affect and are affected by where real players are.

changes.name: Hybrid Gameplay Spaces
changes.why: It is a spatial feature that can be used in these mixed spaces, changing how players are able to act within them.

patterns.name: Ambiguous Responses
patterns.what_it_is: Game-controlled characters reply in ways that can be understood in more than one way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Responses need to be truly open to several readings with no signal telling which is meant, so players have to judge meaning. This requires some uncertainty to remain over time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A line is vague in wording but the context makes its meaning obvious, so nobody is ever unsure.
patterns.knobs: how many responses are ambiguous; how much context clarifies them

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Ambiguous replies can set up misunderstandings, like those in comedies of errors, so designers can use them as building blocks in a fixed story plot.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When a reply could mean several things, players cannot be sure what was actually meant, and that doubt creates tension.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: An ambiguous reply adds doubt about what was actually communicated, so the information players receive becomes less certain.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: Vague agent behavior lets players read their own thoughts and feelings into it, so agents seem to have goals on first and later plays.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Computer-controlled characters can give ambiguous replies, either through tagged dialogue options or, as ELIZA does, by only ever giving vague replies without understanding the conversation.

changes.name: Information Passing
changes.why: Making replies ambiguous changes how information moves between characters, since what is passed on can be read in more than one way.

changes.name: Agents
changes.why: Unclear responses help rule-based agents seem less predictable, so players keep them as agents rather than simplifying them.

changes.name: Dialogues
changes.why: When a character answers vaguely, players cannot take the reply at face value and must guess its meaning, making the conversation harder.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Vague replies help an NPC seem to understand the player even when the system cannot truly parse what was said.

patterns.name: Open-Ended Die Rolls
patterns.what_it_is: Some rolled values require rolling the dice again until a final result forms.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Certain results must trigger further rolls that add to the total, so the range has no fixed ceiling. The trigger value, the dice it applies to and any cap decide how often the extreme results happen.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A re-roll rule so rarely triggered, or so capped, that results never go beyond what a normal roll could give.
patterns.knobs: which results trigger rerolls; which dice it applies to; whether there is a cap on repeats

can_cause.name: Exceptional Events
can_cause.why: Because top results keep triggering extra rolls, totals can climb far beyond the normal range, producing rare, standout outcomes.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When working out the final total takes real effort from chained rolls and adjustments, the calculating itself becomes a burdensome chore.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Since a lucky streak of top results can push a roll unusually high, players can hope for a fortunate outcome.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: If only player characters get the extra-roll rule, they gain a special advantage that other characters lack.

changes.name: Dice
changes.why: The rule changes how ordinary dice behave, since certain faces cause more dice to be rolled and the result has no fixed ceiling.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Skill checks can use the extra-roll rule, or a game can make it available only after a successful skill roll, favoring skilled characters.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Consequences
conflicts_with.why: Because extra dice can keep adding to the total, you cannot know the range of outcomes beforehand, so results are harder to foresee.

patterns.name: Sidegrades
patterns.what_it_is: Item improvements that help only in certain situations, not in general.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each option must give a gain in some situations and a loss in others, balanced so no option is best everywhere. Players need to be able to tell when each is useful.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'sidegrade' that is strictly better than the base item, or whose downside never matters, so it is just an upgrade.
patterns.knobs: size of gain versus loss; how specialized; how it is unlocked

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Because a sidegrade is strong only in certain situations, players can use it to place themselves in a niche where they perform especially well.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Sidegrades trade a gain for a loss instead of being plain improvements, so players must decide which option suits them rather than just taking the best one.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skilled players can get more out of a sidegrade by spotting the moments where its strengths apply and exploiting them.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Whatever their skill level, players can swap in different specialized options whenever they like, which lets them change how they play.

can_cause.name: Upgrades
can_cause.why: A sidegrade is a specialized upgrade that offsets a gain in one ability with a loss in another instead of simply making things better.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Like ordinary upgrades, fitting sidegrades can either be open to anyone anywhere or be limited by a crafting system that controls how they are installed.

conflicts_with.name: Increasing Rewards
conflicts_with.why: Increasing rewards rely on things getting more powerful, whereas sidegrades only offer variety without more power, so the two pull in opposite directions.

patterns.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
patterns.what_it_is: The character knows about the world exactly what the player knows.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The interface and information rules must give the player only what the character knows, and the reverse. Any gap has to be closed on purpose.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The game claims the player sees through the character's eyes, but the UI shows hidden facts the character couldn't know.
patterns.knobs: how much information the player has beyond the character's knowledge; what the interface reveals

changes.name: Hiding Places
changes.why: Whether players can judge their hiding quality as well as their character could shapes how hiding works; the Thief Light Gem gives players that sense.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: The closer the player's knowledge matches the character's, the more the character acts on what the player actually perceives and understands.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Keeping player knowledge in line with the character's is often easiest with elements from outside the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: God Views
conflicts_with.why: Players can see far more than any character in the world could, so it's hard to limit their awareness to what the character knows.

conflicts_with.name: Third-Person Views
conflicts_with.why: Players see more than their avatar can, and the avatar may sense things players can't, so what each knows no longer matches.

patterns.name: Repetition of Position Draws
patterns.what_it_is: If a position repeats during a game, the game ends in a draw.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rules must define what counts as the same position and how many repeats end the game, and someone or something must track the history. The draw must be a real result that players can aim for or avoid.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A rule that is written down but never checked or enforced, so endless loops continue.
