patterns.knobs: number of repeats that trigger the draw; what counts as identical state

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: When a position keeps recurring, the rule ends the game as a draw, so neither side wins, and a player who is behind can aim for that outcome.

changes.name: Repetitive Gameplay
changes.why: Players whose moves cancel out and loop the game back to the same state would otherwise go on forever, so the rule stops that loop by declaring a draw.

patterns.name: Coupled Games
patterns.what_it_is: Events in one game affect events in another, and they depend on each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a real data link, such as a score, item or result, that changes the state of the other game. Players need to notice and care about the effect.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Two games share a brand or login, but nothing that happens in one changes the other.
patterns.knobs: which direction the effect goes; what is passed between them; how strong it is

can_cause.name: Crossmedia Gameplay
can_cause.why: When two linked games are woven together tightly enough, players stop seeing separate games and feel they are having one experience spread across several media.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: What happens in one game feeds into the other as outside influence, so the receiving game takes input that comes from beyond its own play.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: A fixed story in both games forces one to pause until the other catches up, or lets players learn upcoming events by playing the other game.

patterns.name: Revoke Rules
patterns.what_it_is: In trick-taking games: what to do if a player broke the rules of play.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The rule must say when a violation is detected, who decides, and what penalty applies. The penalty must be big enough to discourage breaking the rule yet allow play to continue.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A penalty written but never applied because violations are rarely checked, so breaking the rule costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: size of the penalty; time allowed to challenge; who checks

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Breaking a card-play rule costs the offender something, usually points, so the revoke handling works as a punishment placed on the guilty player.

can_cause.name: Sanctioned Cheating
can_cause.why: Since the game carries on after a violation with a fixed consequence, breaking the rule becomes an allowed, priced choice, though the harsh cost and easy detection make it rarely worthwhile.

changes.name: Kingmaker
changes.why: When one player would otherwise be handed a sure win, deliberately triggering the revoke handling may be the only way to stop that outcome.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: The usual consequence of a revoke is a change to the offender's points, so the rules adjust how scores are reckoned.

changes.name: Trick Taking
changes.why: These rules are added to trick games so that illegal card plays within a trick can be dealt with without wrecking the game.

patterns.name: Units
patterns.what_it_is: Expendable pieces controlled by a player or the game, usually faceless and acting in groups.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be many similar controllable or opposing elements whose individual loss does not decide the game, with actions that matter at a group level. Counts and costs should make losing units meaningful as a resource.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A single unit renamed as a group, or many units so identical and disposable that no one cares about losing them.
patterns.knobs: number of units; their cost and strength; how much autonomy they have

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Because units can fight, they make goals about capturing enemy pieces possible.

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: With several controllable elements, players can have units act together in ways one piece alone could not.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Units usually carry actions that harm other units, so fighting between them is a natural result of having them.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Having many units with different abilities lets players chain their effects together, which a single piece could not do.

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: Units can accompany a player's avatar or character, with varying autonomy or direct control through that avatar.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Managing many units forces players to keep switching attention between them, which makes play harder to keep track of.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Building a well-matched set of units is itself a kind of construction, besides producing each unit individually.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: When units are in danger of being lost, players are constantly trying to keep them alive.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Units give players several points of action in the game world without breaking the fiction.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Units can be destroyed by damage, so other players can set goals of removing them.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: When the game system controls units, they typically serve as opposing forces driven by algorithms or game masters.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Controlling many units demands lots of input, which can become tedious busywork, especially in self-facilitated games.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Each unit is a separate point through which players can act on the game world.

can_cause.name: Fog of War
can_cause.why: Each unit can reveal the area around it, so having more units clears more hidden territory.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since a separate decision can be made for each unit, players have more options than with one avatar of the same abilities.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Units can be taken from neutral pools or from enemies, so winning control of them becomes a goal.

can_cause.name: Parallel Lives
can_cause.why: Units are many game elements played at once, each more expendable than an avatar.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Because losing some units can even be useful or needed, players manage them as a resource at a higher level than with avatars.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Units are things players acquire, construct, and spend to reach their goals.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Several units acting like a team encourage players to plan when and where to use them, especially uncommon types.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Players who risk penalties from losing units have an ongoing aim of keeping them alive.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Units fit a theme of many individuals or groups working together, though that theme also limits how they look and act.

can_cause.name: Tile-Laying
can_cause.why: In some games units are placed as tiles rather than moved one by one, which makes them resemble tokens.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When unit types differ in what they can do, players must choose between them.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Different unit types suit different stages of play and can counter each other, so what players do changes over time.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Increasing the number of units or improving them strengthens the player's construct, as in the Civilization series.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Varying how many enemy units appear is an easy way to calibrate how tough a fight is.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Units that each receive their own new abilities become differentiated individuals, so characters emerge from them.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Units are things players commonly hide, and if they are vulnerable or have a weak spot, players take up concealing them.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Units are movable pieces players can pull out of danger, so they act as the things that evade.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Units are highly mobile and, being physical items in the world, can block one another's movement.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing how to get the most from units with different abilities is knowledge players develop and reuse.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Individual units in a single-player game can be seen as a team, so combining them acts like a team combo.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Units that can perform combined actions let one player command a team in a single-player game.

changes.name: Ability Losses
changes.why: Units can make abilities into limited resources, so losing a unit means losing what it could do.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: Units able to build bases or installations may be required before a player can expand.

changes.name: Exploitation
changes.why: Units good at collecting resources encourage players to focus on harvesting.

changes.name: Extermination
changes.why: Once units with the strongest fighting abilities are available, play tends to shift toward wiping out opponents.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Exploring may be allowed only to units with special movement abilities.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Units give players several points to affect the world, and many units make it hard to view and navigate everything.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: A basic design choice is whether units block sight lines, and unit abilities can vary around sight.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Each unit's movement and actions can count as its own turn, creating turns inside a turn.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Units can be part of a construct and also a way to develop it, as with cities and units in Civilization.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Units are a concrete form characters take, as in games controlling several individuals.

conflicts_with.name: Avatars
conflicts_with.why: Controlling several elements at once removes the single point of focus that an avatar relies on.

conflicts_with.name: Detective Structures
conflicts_with.why: Controlling several units gives players multiple viewpoints at once, which goes against restricting information to a single character's perspective.

conflicts_with.name: New Abilities
conflicts_with.why: Giving an ability to individual units can make them stand out so much that they act more like characters than units.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Player Characters
conflicts_with.why: NPCs are individual people with variation that players don't control, whereas units treat inhabitants as an undifferentiated group, so the two clash.

patterns.name: Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements that players spend to perform actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resources must be required for actions and be limited enough that spending is a choice. They need visible quantities so players can plan with them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A counter named like a resource that no action needs and no loss reduces, so it has no use in play.
patterns.knobs: what actions cost; starting amounts; income and loss rates

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: When valuable resources sit in the game world, players are motivated to claim and hold the areas where those resources are found.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: When one resource can serve several purposes, players must weigh competing uses, which makes the game harder to master.

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: If an ability's power or availability depends on a resource, having less of it makes the ability weaker.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Actions that need particular resources leave players unable to act while they lack them, so they must wait.

can_cause.name: Helplessness
can_cause.why: Running short of resources removes the means to act, so players feel unable to affect what happens.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Tying an ability's strength to a resource means that holding more of it makes the ability more effective.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Obtaining a resource you didn't previously have can unlock an ability that was unavailable before.

can_cause.name: No-Use Bonus
can_cause.why: Placing resources on actions nobody picks gradually makes those neglected options attractive, balancing the choice between actions.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Resources can be what players compete to gather first, so the contest to get them turns into a race.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Because resources are limited and needed for actions, players usually have to plan how to gather and spend them.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Resources can be handed out to players for finishing quests or reaching goals, serving as the payoff.

can_cause.name: Sustenance Rewards
can_cause.why: Resource rewards work well as sustenance when players might run out, since the reward keeps them supplied.

can_cause.name: Tiebreakers
can_cause.why: In games with a main score, the resources players hold can serve as a secondary count that separates tied players.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When one resource can be spent on several different things, choosing one use means giving up the others.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Damage applied to resources or attributes the player owns shrinks them, which is how the penalty is built.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: Gathered resources can be counted up to decide victory, which turns that total into a points value.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Using up resources to perform abilities controls how often players can use them, and more resources can strengthen their effect.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Resources help define and show the status of the constructs that players control.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Resources such as ammunition or energy are consumed when shooting, which changes how the shooting works.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Resources help define a character and show its condition.

changes.name: Controllers
changes.why: Resources like energy that change how actions work can also change what the controllers do.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Tools manipulate resources, and that manipulation is what shapes how crafting works.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Resources placed in the world, and how players find them, help define what the world is like.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Resources such as energy are spent on moving, which changes how movement works.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Resources can be given as rewards for completing quests or goals.

changes.name: Secret Areas
changes.why: Resources can be hidden inside secret areas, which affects how they are found.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Tying a tool's use to spending resources adds a cost that forces trade-offs.

patterns.name: Time Limits
patterns.what_it_is: Time allowed for an action, a goal, a game mode, or the whole game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The timer must be tied to a real consequence (failure, loss, elimination) and be short enough relative to the task that players must skip or trade off something. It must also be visible or otherwise noticed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A generous timer that nearly everyone beats with room to spare, or one with no penalty when it runs out.
patterns.knobs: how much time is given; what happens at zero; how time can be gained or lost

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players can see the clock counting down, they must keep glancing at it while playing, which pulls their attention and makes the game demand more focus.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: A time cap makes players unable to plan at length, so they must act under pressure, which makes succeeding harder and more demanding.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: When the allowed time is very short, things are available only briefly, so events appear and vanish quickly.

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Tying the clock running out to losing the game makes the deadline a clear, explicit threat that players focus on, as in racing games.

can_cause.name: Handicap Achievements
can_cause.why: Giving extra reward for finishing a goal within a time allowance rewards players who accept the pressure, such as through speedruns.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When players choose the time limit, they set a cap on session length themselves.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Play Sessions
can_cause.why: A time limit on a game instance gives everyone a known end point, which makes it easier to agree on whether to play.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Linking an expired clock to removing a player makes the deadline explicit and focuses players' attention on it.

can_cause.name: Resource Caps
can_cause.why: Because the time allowed has a fixed maximum, time becomes a resource with a ceiling on how much anyone can have.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: With a time limit, players have to treat the time left as something they spend and manage while pursuing goals.

can_cause.name: Sustenance Rewards
can_cause.why: Letting players earn extra time by completing actions, such as reaching checkpoints in racing games, rewards them by prolonging play.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Needing to finish something before time runs out, especially with a visible clock, creates pressure and unease about achieving it.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: Limiting how long each update round lasts, or how many rounds exist, turns a turn-based structure into a timed tick structure.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: A fixed time limit ends the game instance at a set point, so players may finish equal, which makes tied outcomes possible.

can_cause.name: Time Limited Game Instances
can_cause.why: A clock can serve as the end condition for a session or mode of play, bounding how long that instance lasts.

can_cause.name: Time Pressure
can_cause.why: Having to act before a deadline, shared among players, makes them feel rushed and push to finish sooner.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: With little time, players can't do everything, so they must choose between actions and weigh which is worth the limited time.

can_cause.name: Cooldown
can_cause.why: Attaching a required waiting time to an action before it can be reused is exactly what creates the cooldown.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: Letting players set a clock or a number of turns directly fixes how long the game instance will last.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: A reward that can only be collected for a limited time can serve as a skippable goal, since players may choose to go for it.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Requiring something to be completed before a deadline puts players under pressure, which is enough to make a race.

can_cause.name: Repeat Combos
can_cause.why: A deadline is a core ingredient: it forces the repetitions to happen quickly, which is what turns plain repetition into a combo.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: A countdown on how long an ability can be used directly makes that ability last only a limited time.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: Strict time limits force each session to end, which means the game stops on a clock and not because anyone achieved victory.

changes.name: Ability Losses
changes.why: A time limit can set how long a lost ability stays gone, creating a recovery period.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: A deadline adds pressure to aiming and shooting, since players must hit their targets within the time available.

changes.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
changes.why: A deadline on shared actions that happen at different times can strengthen the tension and guilt already present among collaborators.

changes.name: Continuous Goals
changes.why: The length of time a player must keep up a goal like surviving or evading can be set by a time limit.

changes.name: Decreased Abilities
changes.why: A time limit can bound how long a weakened state lasts, giving recovery periods.

changes.name: Early Elimination
changes.why: A clear time limit tells eliminated players how long the game will last, easing the downside of waiting.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: Taking harm after staying in a place for a set period ties a time limit to the game world's effects.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: A goal can be made available only for a limited span, so players must pursue it before it disappears.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Evading goals often use a duration players must keep it up to win, so time sets the winning condition.

changes.name: Experimenting
changes.why: With little time to plan, players may try something with little hope of success just to learn for the next attempt.

changes.name: Game Pauses
changes.why: Time limits can bound how long a pause may last, and pausing real-time play undoes the pressure the clock creates.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Changes in the world, like areas becoming unusable, can impose deadlines, and traces can be removed after a while to avoid clutter.

changes.name: Helplessness
changes.why: Penalties like helplessness are often made temporary with a time limit to keep the gameplay balanced and varied.

changes.name: Hotseating
changes.why: Limiting the time per turn restricts waiting for others, making it practical for players to share one device in turns.

changes.name: Hovering Closures
changes.why: A visible countdown makes the approaching ending of a goal or session feel close and about to arrive.

changes.name: Improved Abilities
changes.why: A time limit can set how long a boost lasts, making it a temporary advantage that supports balance.

changes.name: Invulnerabilities
changes.why: Time limits are often attached to invulnerability so it lasts briefly, avoiding balance problems that permanent immunity would cause.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: The winner can be whoever holds the leading position for a set length of time, which also ends the game.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Other players' impatience creates implicit deadlines, and designers may add formal ones to keep balance and shared pressure.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: A time limit can make a gained ability only temporary, helping balance between players or teams.

changes.name: Player Physical Prowess
changes.why: A fixed duration caps how much physical effort or endurance players need to provide.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Time can set how long a power-up lasts and how long before a new one appears, balancing play and adding variety.

changes.name: Preventing Goals
changes.why: Goals about stopping something can be won by holding out until the time has passed.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: In multiplayer games a clock can be used to limit how long a player may use a space alone.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: A clock caps how much play time can be spent on solving puzzles.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Adding a clock to a race makes the time pressure more noticeable than just the competition against others.

changes.name: Renewable Resources
changes.why: Delays before a power-up reappears or an action is available again set the interval at which the resource renews.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: A clock can make a resource vanish after some time, such as when other players exploit a shared one.

changes.name: Reward Widgets
changes.why: If rewards are collected automatically after a delay, collecting them manually becomes an optional goal done before time passes.

changes.name: Safe Havens
changes.why: A countdown can mark when a refuge stops being safe, forcing players to leave.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: A scene can be given a limit on its duration, so players must finish what they do in it within that span.

changes.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
changes.why: A timer before each reduction in world size produces tension and also limits how long the game instance lasts.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: A solo game has no other players creating pressure, so time limits only appear if the designer deliberately adds them.

changes.name: Switches
changes.why: Time can determine how long a switch stays active, as a modulated item in the game.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: With little time available, players cannot plan thoroughly, which restricts tactical planning.

changes.name: Tension
changes.why: Knowing time is running out while trying to reach a goal increases tension.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: Time limits can cap the number of rounds in addition to how long each round lasts.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Tiles that dissolve after a while turn the changing world into a deadline for players to move on.

changes.name: Traces
changes.why: Marks left by actions are removed after a time so the world does not become crowded with them.

changes.name: Trading
changes.why: A clock limits how long players can spend on trading, guaranteeing a maximum for that activity.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: A trap with a delay before activation gives players a limited window to move away.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Capping the length of each turn reduces the time players wait for others.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Time limits can be counted in updates to the game state, so they work even without real-time play.

changes.name: Arithmetic Progression
changes.why: Forcing a wait between similar investments stops players stacking many identical arithmetic investments at once, though it can reduce their freedom of choice.

conflicts_with.name: Downtime
conflicts_with.why: A deadline pushes players to plan and act instead of idling, since once time is up they can no longer act.

conflicts_with.name: Game Pauses
conflicts_with.why: Pausing lets players interrupt their experience of time pressure, though the limit still applies once play resumes.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Limits such as automatic collection before a deadline make the repeated tasks optional rather than required.

conflicts_with.name: Pottering
conflicts_with.why: Deadlines force players to hurry or follow the game's schedule, undermining the freedom to act whenever they wish.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: Players control the pace and can bend things, so deadlines are harder to enforce.

patterns.name: Weapons
patterns.what_it_is: Items used to cause death and destruction in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Weapons must differ in damage, range, speed, ammo or special effects so choosing one matters, and the world must offer situations where each is better. Acquisition should feel earned.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several weapons with different names and models but identical stats and handling.
patterns.knobs: damage; range; rate of fire; ammo limits; accuracy; special effects and unlock timing

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Ranged weapons are a new way to attack, so players must now aim and fire at targets rather than just closing in.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Different weapons let characters or units specialize in different roles, so each can be the one best suited to certain tasks.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: Weapons are what let characters hurt things in the game world, and different weapons can deal different amounts of harm.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Some weapons can stun a target, which forces that target to be unable to act for a short while.

can_cause.name: Equipment
can_cause.why: Weapons are items used for combat, so they count as gear a character carries, unless the game only has one kind.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: When a new weapon is handed out during play, it gives the player a more capable way to fight, which works as a reward.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: A weapon is a concrete object inside the game that players can find, carry and use.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: A weapon can make existing combat actions better, such as stronger hits, faster attacks, easier aiming, or longer reach.

can_cause.name: MacGuffins
can_cause.why: Magical or especially powerful weapons can become the object that a story revolves around, as in many traditional tales.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A weapon can give a character something they could not do before, like attacking from afar or stunning a target.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Because weapons improve what a character can do in combat, the result depends on both the player's own skill and the character's gear.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: When only some players or characters get hold of a weapon's new powers, those powers become a special advantage for them.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Firing certain weapons, such as rockets or concussion grenades, can propel the user, giving movement others lack.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Weapons can be grouped into collections, either only weapons or a mix of weapons and armor, designed to go together.

can_cause.name: Sidegrades
can_cause.why: A new weapon that gives no clear advantage over the ones already available is just a different option, not a better one.

can_cause.name: Tools
can_cause.why: Weapons are a kind of tool whose purpose is combat, so designing them follows the same thinking as designing tools.

can_cause.name: Variable Accuracy
can_cause.why: Having many weapon types gives a natural place to make each one hit with a different level of precision.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: A variety of weapons offers different ways of performing aim and shoot actions.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing which weapons exploit which enemy weaknesses is knowledge that applies across sessions and helps players choose well.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Knowing which weapons enemies are vulnerable to lets players plan their approach before combat begins.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Enemy weaknesses to particular weapons make players plan which weapon to bring to bear.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with new abilities, access to new weapons gives players different things to do.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Weapons can make aiming easier, for example through better accuracy.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Weapons change what an avatar is able to do in combat by improving or adding abilities.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Weapons change what a character is able to do in combat by improving or adding abilities.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Weapons change how fighting works by making characters more efficient at it and by offering tactical and strategic choices.

changes.name: Critical Hits
changes.why: Some weapons can be designed to make critical hits more likely.

changes.name: Critical Misses
changes.why: Some weapons can be designed so that critical misses become more or less likely.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Weapons delivered by vehicles can upset fairness between players, because vehicles also improve movement and may add armor.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of weapons among players leads to imbalances.

patterns.name: Tools
patterns.what_it_is: Elements that give actions in the world or make them easier to do.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A tool must open up a new action or clearly improve one, and players must have a reason to want it and a way to obtain and use it. Scarcity or wear makes the choice of tool matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A named item that only gives a cosmetic change or a tiny bonus nobody notices, or one that every character has from the start.
patterns.knobs: which actions it enables or boosts; how common it is; whether it wears out

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Because tools can be limited to certain groups or users in the game world, who gets to use them can trigger social reactions inside the fiction.

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Using a tool such as a ranged weapon can require the player to actually aim and hit a target, so the tool brings that skill-based action into play.

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Since tools are separate items that can be picked up, players get a goal of gathering them.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: When several tools can be used at once, designers can decide to reward particular pairings with a combined effect.

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: Tools let different characters or units be good at different things, and in team play players can specialize around who holds which tool.

can_cause.name: Crafting
can_cause.why: Some tools exist to enable or influence crafting, so having them lets players make things.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: Weapons are a common kind of tool, and they exist to cause or alter damage.

can_cause.name: Equipment
can_cause.why: Tools are items that characters carry or wield, so they change how the character works by being part of its equipment.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Tools change the results of actions, and choosing among them makes players feel their own decisions had even more effect than they did.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Receiving a tool is itself a reward that makes later actions easier or possible.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When several tools are available, players can pick which to use, giving them meaningful options.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Tools can grant new or privileged abilities, so acquiring them lets players fulfil goals of becoming more capable.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Tools are valuable items, so players want to obtain them, and unequal possession in multiplayer strengthens that desire.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Tools are a type of game item, so they are separate objects that can be picked up, dropped, destroyed or traded.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: A tool can make an avatar or unit perform an existing action better than normal, for example through bonuses to skills.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A tool can let a character do something it otherwise could not, because the ability comes from the item.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Because tools alter the outcome of what avatars or units do, success depends on both the player's skill and the character's equipment.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Tools can give abilities that others lack, especially when the tools are scarce or when only some players hold them.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Some tools enable special ways of moving, such as a grappling hook that lets the player swing.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: Where a tool can be obtained matters, so places that supply tools become valuable spots for players to seek out.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Tools, like armor, can be grouped into matching collections that players try to assemble.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: When tools have limited uses, wear out, or can be stolen or traded away, the abilities they give do not last.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Tools give extra or better abilities through believable objects, so the game world's theme isn't broken.

can_cause.name: Vision Modes
can_cause.why: Some tools such as thermal sights give the player a different way of seeing, extending sensory abilities.

can_cause.name: Weapons
can_cause.why: Weapons are a specialized kind of tool whose purpose is to allow or influence damage and combat.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: When players fight over tools in a multiplayer game, opponents become targets to remove.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Rare tools that took effort to obtain can be traded between players for real money, giving them value outside the game.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Tools stay useful to players across sessions, and with multiple players they can be exchanged.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Using a tool brings a benefit but demands resources or causes wear, so players compare these against each other.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: A tool can determine how shooting is done, so the item shapes what the player must do to hit.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: Certain tools allow alarms to be switched off or on, changing whether the player gets detected.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Tools change what avatars are able to do by giving them better or additional abilities.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Equipping tools makes characters work differently, so two characters can behave unlike each other.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Weapons and other tools affect how fights play out by changing damage and how attacks are performed.

changes.name: Conditional Passageways
changes.why: Items like keys and ID cards act as tools that decide whether a player can get through a restricted path.

changes.name: Controllers
changes.why: Some tools are what let players activate a controller in the game world.

changes.name: Crafting
changes.why: Certain tools are needed for, or alter, the process of making items.

changes.name: Critical Failures
changes.why: A tool can raise or lower how likely it is that an action goes badly wrong.

changes.name: Critical Successes
changes.why: A tool can change the odds of an action succeeding exceptionally well.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies can use tools too, so what they carry changes how they behave and how hard they are.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Tools that restore health are common, so they directly alter how much damage a character can survive.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Tools can raise skills, giving users bonuses to actions they are already trained in.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Tools change what units can do by supplying improved or new abilities.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Tools can give holders a clear edge over those without them, which creates unequal standing between players.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Uneven distribution of tools among players leads to imbalances.

patterns.name: Game Items
patterns.what_it_is: Objects inside the game world that can be carried or used.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each item should have identity and an effect or use that matters, and be carried, found or moved. Different agents may use them differently.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Items are collectable, but all do the same or nothing, so picking them up changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: types and effects of items; how scarce they are; whether they wear out or can be dropped

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Designers can name a destination for an item, and the goal is met either automatically on arrival or when the player deliberately drops it there.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: Items can carry notes, pictures or memories, so finding one lets players piece together what happened earlier in the world.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When players may drop items they hold, they decide for themselves where to leave them, which is a real choice they control.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: An item, especially a single one in a fixed spot, makes a natural thing for players to aim at and take as a goal.

can_cause.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
can_cause.why: If players aren't playing at the same time, an item changing hands means different players effectively see different owners over time.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Most kinds of items can carry story content, so they can be used to tell a story in games generally.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers can deliberately place items to drive a fixed story, and MacGuffins exist specifically for this purpose.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: If players know where an item is, they can hurry to reach it before others do, creating a race.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: When items sit in a board, world or level, the spots where they lie become places where that resource can be found.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Items are a kind of resource, differing only in that each unit has its own identity and presence in the world.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Items can be handed out after players finish achievements or quests, giving them something tangible and useful for their effort.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When valuable items might be lost, for example by theft, players worry about keeping them, which builds tension.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Having items present in the world helps the setting feel coherent, though the theme also limits how those items can look.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Because players can drop items where they choose, they can leave marks of their own passage in the world.

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Taking items that belong to others counts as stealing, which breaks norms and triggers hostile reactions from those affected.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Items that can be stolen by others give players something to protect, so they must keep watching for thieves.

can_cause.name: Character Development
can_cause.why: Giving a character better armor, tools or weapons makes it more capable, so acquiring gear is itself a way the character develops.

can_cause.name: Equipment
can_cause.why: Any item that can be equipped, rather than merely carried, becomes equipment.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Items need value beyond a single session to be worth trading, which a persistent world gives them.

can_cause.name: MacGuffins
can_cause.why: When a MacGuffin does exist in the game, it can take the form of an object the player can hold or handle.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: When players must gather a set of items but not every available one, collecting the leftovers is a goal they can skip.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Items can be given a price and sold, either by the provider or between players, so owning better ones can be bought.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Items placed in the world, like false power-ups or hidden triggers, can serve as traps of any visibility type.

changes.name: Achievements
changes.why: Items can be handed out as the prize for earning an achievement.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Items can lie on a board before anyone picks them up, changing what the board contains.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Items can be placed in a world as pick-ups waiting to be found, adding to what the world holds.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Items can be placed within a level before being collected, adding to what the level offers.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Items can be given as the reward for completing a quest.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Items a character holds or gains are part of its resources and can be rewards.

patterns.name: Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: What the player receives and experiences as pleasant.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Rewards must be tied to meaningful achievements and valued by players. Their size and timing should match the effort, so players feel they earned them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Rewards given for anything, or of no practical or emotional value, like a badge that changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: reward size; how often they are given; what triggers them and how certain they are

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: When rewards come as many small separate pieces, players are drawn into gathering them, which turns into a collecting activity.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: If players must wait before a reward becomes available, they have a reason to come back to the game later to claim it.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Events
can_cause.why: A reward that can only be obtained during a short window becomes a fleeting event players must catch or miss.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Getting a reward signals that a player has succeeded at a goal of improving their skill or ability.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: Receiving a reward can show that a player's own plan for how to develop their character or position has worked out.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Tension arises depending on when rewards are given and how sure players are that they will actually get them.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: A reward that can only be collected for a limited time can serve as a skippable goal, since players may choose to go for it.

can_cause.name: Repeat Combos
can_cause.why: Picking up a reward is often the action that starts the count, as in CityVille where collecting rewards builds toward the combo.

can_cause.name: Reward Widgets
can_cause.why: A reward widget comes into being when an ordinary reward is made to show up as a clickable object placed in the game space.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Rewards are handed out to mark that a player has finished a part of the game that was hard.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Improving an item that a player already has, rather than giving a new one, is another way rewards shape items.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Rewards are given to show that a player has demonstrated real skill at playing.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Rewards and penalties balance each other: a reward can soften a penalty, and a penalty can offset a reward.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Killing other players can be rewarding in itself, but extra rewards can make it more appealing.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Completing a quest is a typical moment when a game hands the player a reward.

changes.name: Reward Widgets
changes.why: Rewards can be placed in the game world as visible objects, requiring movement to pick them up.

conflicts_with.name: Illusionary Rewards
conflicts_with.why: Ordinary rewards change the game state in players' favor, while these don't, and a normal reward can lose its effect and become one depending on context.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A reward design may not fit the game's fiction, so it can break the theme when theme matters.

patterns.name: Cards
patterns.what_it_is: Elements used to hand out various resources without showing in advance how they are distributed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decide what is printed, which card types exist and in what numbers; use shuffling or hidden hands so the randomness and secrecy matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Cards are used only as a menu or list, never shuffled or hidden, so a table would work just as well.
patterns.knobs: deck size; number of each card type; information shown on each side

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: When a card grants a player new abilities, the card itself stands in for part of what that player's character can do.

can_cause.name: Action Programming
can_cause.why: Cards can each stand for an action, so players can pick and arrange them to plan what they will do.

can_cause.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
can_cause.why: A card can simply be a marker that records something for a player, such as an ability, spare action points, or an extra chance.

can_cause.name: Budgeted Action Points
can_cause.why: A card held or spent can represent a unit of allowance that limits how much a player may do.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Cards that carry their own special rules can be played together so their effects build on each other.

can_cause.name: Decks
can_cause.why: Cards are often gathered into a pack of chosen types and amounts, which is exactly what a deck is.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Since cards are separate items that can be handed out, players can take turns choosing which ones they get to keep.

can_cause.name: Drawing Stacks
can_cause.why: Cards are easy to shuffle and stack, so a pile from which players draw unseen cards comes naturally.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: A card kept by a player can be spent later to get another attempt or second try.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Cards that give players abilities or stand for actions become the thing players pay attention to and act through.

can_cause.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
can_cause.why: Physical cards can belong to individual players, who bring or collect different ones, so each player's set of elements differs.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: When players can work out which cards are still unplayed, remembering what has already appeared helps them predict what comes next.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A card can give its holder a power they lacked before, so gaining the card means gaining the ability.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Shuffling and drawing from a stack of cards gives unpredictable results, while the designer still controls which cards are in it.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Cards can be made to stand for different kinds of resources and handed out in a chosen mix.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Individual cards can be parts of a larger collection, so players gather several cards to complete a set.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Adding new cards to what a player holds gives the player new or better abilities, an easy way to develop.

can_cause.name: Anonymous Actions
can_cause.why: When players put cards down together, observers can't tell whose card is whose, so each individual contribution stays hidden.

can_cause.name: Collectible Card Games
can_cause.why: The game is built from cards, and these provide the collectible pieces that players own and bring to matches.

can_cause.name: Cycle Deck Engines
can_cause.why: The engine runs on cards whose effects let you draw further cards, so each card played pulls in the next ones.

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: Cards can be dealt face-down to each player, so a goal stays hidden from everyone else.

can_cause.name: Tile-Laying
can_cause.why: The page says the pattern is not limited to tiles; cards can also be laid out so that their positions relative to one another matter.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Gaining or arranging cards is one way to develop a construct and change its capabilities.

patterns.name: Abstract Player Constructs
patterns.what_it_is: An unseen part of the game that stores the player's parameters and possible actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The construct must hold information that actually drives what players can do in the world (resources, abilities, units), and must be under player control. It needs a clear link to the game world to matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A player sheet or panel exists, but it only displays information and has no effect on what happens in the game world.
patterns.knobs: what data it stores; how it connects to units and the world

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: When constructs give different players different special abilities, such as picking a leader and civilization, everyone begins the game with unequal strengths.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Since these constructs live outside the game world, hidden things like attributes need no in-world explanation, which makes the world feel more like reality, where much is unseen.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Players who must manage or interact with these abstract records may feel they are doing bookkeeping chores instead of playing the game itself.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: When no full character is used, such a construct can still carry some of the planned story, though it struggles to engage players emotionally.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: A construct's state and growth show how well a player is doing, so any threat to it makes players anxious about success or failure.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Development needs something abstract tied to the player to improve, so having such constructs makes development possible at all.

can_cause.name: Difficulty Levels
can_cause.why: Starting players with differently strong constructs like countries, based on the setting, means some positions are naturally harder to play than others.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: These give players something abstract under their control whose growth they can plan, so they are needed for this kind of planning.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Even non-person entities like countries or civilizations can hold goals players adopt, so playing them can count as roleplaying.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: Tracking which levels a player has completed in their game profile works much like a points total in other solo games.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Constructs can change what bases are able to do and which actions they allow.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Constructs hold complexity that the world cannot show itself, and so they shape what happens within it.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Constructs can change the abilities and available actions of installations, as seen in the Victoria series.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Constructs can change what units can do, such as species abilities affecting the creatures in Ursuppe.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Giving different constructs different starting strengths, as in Europa Universalis and Victoria, makes players unequal and so disrupts balance between them.

patterns.name: Health
patterns.what_it_is: A measure of how much damage a character can take before serious penalties.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Damage must reduce the value and reaching zero or thresholds must have real consequences. Sources of damage and ways to restore it need to be balanced so the number matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A health bar that never drops meaningfully or refills freely, so damage has no effect on play.
patterns.knobs: maximum health; damage amounts; healing availability

can_cause.name: Non-Localized Resources
can_cause.why: Health is usually a pool that isn't tied to a place and gets used up as play goes on, so it works as this kind of resource.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Health is a number that drops during play and can be restored by healing, so players spend and manage it like any other resource.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: A health value displayed on the HUD gives an avatar one abstract changing quality, making a very weak form of character.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: Besides lowering the target's health, a critical hit adds extra consequences, so health loss is one part of how it shows up.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Damage applied to health lowers the main value players need to stay alive, which is the most common form of this penalty.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Giving something a health value is a natural way to make it a character, and a health display alone can hint at one for an avatar.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Because hits wear health down gradually instead of ending things at once, fights have more steps and effects that build up over time.

changes.name: Crosshairs
changes.why: Enemy health may stay hidden until players aim at a target, so the crosshair becomes the way to find out how hurt it is.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Damage can exist alone, but once health is present, damage has something to reduce, and together they create energy penalties.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Objects that can be broken sometimes carry a health value, so they take several hits before being destroyed.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Health sits between full strength and losing a life, giving intermediate states instead of an immediate jump to losing a life.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units are a natural fit for a health value, which shows how much punishment each one can take before being lost.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: When few values are shown constantly, like health on a screen, it is easier to see them as belonging to the avatar.

patterns.name: Damage
patterns.what_it_is: Harmful effects from actions or events that lead to bad consequences.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Damage must be tied to clear causes players can avoid, must be measured in a visible way, and must lead to a real consequence when it piles up. The amount per hit must be small enough to allow several failures.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A health bar that drops but is refilled so easily or so cheaply that taking hits never matters.
patterns.knobs: damage per hit; how much health there is; how often damage sources occur

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: When fighting depends on player skill, damage gives that skill something to act on, so hits and dodges combine player ability with character stats.

can_cause.name: Deterioration
can_cause.why: Damage lets items wear down gradually and eventually break, instead of staying intact until some single event destroys them.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: Hazards in the surroundings can inflict damage, and often the harm they cause is exactly what makes them what they are.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Taking damage is a way of being punished for failing to avoid danger, so damage is itself a kind of penalty.

can_cause.name: Player Killing
can_cause.why: Hits add up over time, so accumulated damage can be what finally lets one player eliminate another.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: In skill-based fighting, damage is one of the system parts that ties the player's own aim and timing to the character's stats.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Damage counts down how many more failures a player can afford, so it behaves like a stock that is spent, though on a smaller scale.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: When damage comes in several forms or has different effects, players benefit from learning which is which, and that understanding becomes strategic knowledge.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because players can foresee what damage does, both the threat of being hit and actually being hit make them anxious.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Damage can leave visible marks on damaged things, giving players clues about what happened earlier.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: When an environmental effect or game item causes damage, together they can work as a trap.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: The simplest way to create a critical hit is to make an attack deal more damage than a normal one.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Damage is the usual tool for building this penalty, since it subtracts from a value the player depends on.

can_cause.name: Life Penalties
can_cause.why: Taking damage in a game that has lives can directly cost the player a life, so damage can hand out the life loss.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Damage caused by moveable tiles is often an event the player cannot influence once it is triggered.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Avatars are among the usual entities that can be harmed, so damage shapes how they fare.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters are common targets that can suffer damage.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Damage lets attacks wear opponents down gradually, so a fight is made of many hits instead of one decisive blow.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: Things players build can be destroyed by damage, which makes investing in building a risky choice.

changes.name: Consumers
changes.why: Making consumers perform actions whose required resources are expressed as health makes damage a result of their consumption.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Damage is what allows objects in the game world to be broken or destroyed.

changes.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
changes.why: Physical items in the game world can be harmed by damage when they are destructible.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Because damage accumulates, a single successful attack need not remove an enemy, so several successes are required.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Damage can make items degrade over time.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: Losing the contested position can lead to taking damage, so not holding it carries a cost.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Damage measures how many failures remain before a life is lost, and can also cause life loss directly.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Failing to steer around dangers leads to damage, so moving well is how players avoid it.

changes.name: Obstacles
changes.why: Running into obstacles one failed to avoid can cost players damage.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Damage can reduce a character's skills, which weakens what they can do.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units are common entities that take damage, and enough of it destroys them.

changes.name: Variable Accuracy
changes.why: Damage can ruin a player's aim in games where accuracy varies, which counts as a form of harm.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Damage can target resources and reduce them, for example by lowering health or energy.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: Permanent protection reduces how often damage matters, though it need not remove damage entirely if other damage types remain.

patterns.name: Budgeted Action Points
patterns.what_it_is: Points the player spends to take actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Points must be scarce enough that players have to choose, actions must cost different amounts, and replenishment must be set clearly. If everything is affordable, there is no budget.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Points are shown, but they are so many and refill so fast that no choice is ever limited by them.
patterns.knobs: points per turn or period; cost per action; refill rate; cap

can_cause.name: Action Caps
can_cause.why: Because every action spends from a small pool of points, only so many actions fit into a turn or time window.

can_cause.name: Action Programming
can_cause.why: Points can be spent to choose actions that get queued up in a sequence and carried out later.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Strong abilities can be given a higher point price, so players cannot use them as often as weaker ones.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Handling the points and weighing which actions to buy gives players more to juggle and think through.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide for themselves which of the available actions to spend their points on, and may repeat them.

can_cause.name: Helplessness
can_cause.why: Once the points are used up, a player can no longer act and may feel stuck until they come back.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: When points pay for moving, how far a unit can travel is bounded by how many points remain.

can_cause.name: Resource Caps
can_cause.why: The pool of points has a maximum, so players cannot stockpile beyond a set amount.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Players must decide how to spend and save a finite supply of points across the actions they want.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Points act as an indirect resource, since they are spent to pay for actions rather than being the goal.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Having several affordable actions to pick from pushes players to think ahead about how to use their points.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Choosing among actions with a limited budget gets players working out short-term moves and how to spend points for best effect.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Spending points on one action means they are unavailable for others, so players give something up with every choice.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Limited points make the benefit of coming back clear, because once they are spent you wait for them to refill before acting again.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: When action points refill through a regenerating resource, players must wait for refills, which creates a tick rhythm.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Each character can have its own budget of points limiting what it can do, or points can be used to build the character beforehand.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting actions such as attacking or shooting cost points, so players must decide how much to put into combat.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Before play, points can be spent to pick which gear a character starts with.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: Points can be put into longer-term choices such as developing technologies, trading present actions for future gain.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Moving costs points, so how far and how often units can move depends on the budget.

changes.name: New Abilities
changes.why: A new ability's strength is softened because using it takes points away from other actions.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: A special ability gives less advantage since using it uses up points that could have gone to other actions.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Actions cost points from a value that slowly refills, limiting how often they can be used as time passes.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Points can be used before play to pick the skills a character will have.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Turns can be shaped by points, such as refilling everyone's points each turn or taking one action in turn until all are spent.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: In turn-based play the points are usually refilled at the start of each turn, setting how much a player can do.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Each unit can hold its own pool of points that it spends on moving, turning, and fighting.

patterns.name: Regenerating Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources that accumulate by themselves as game time passes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear refill rate and usually a cap must be set, and the resource must matter enough that players spend it and wait for it. Refill speed should shape pacing of play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A resource that refills so quickly or so little that it never runs short, or one nobody needs, so the refill changes no decision.
patterns.knobs: regeneration rate; cap size; what pauses or speeds up regeneration

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Because time passing keeps adding new units of the resource into play, regeneration works as a steady way of inserting game elements without any player action.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Since the resource refills just by waiting, it never runs out for good, which turns an ordinary resource into a renewable one.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: When resources refill over time in a lasting world, you are drawn back to use them once they have recovered.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: Resources that refill at set intervals force players to wait for the next refill before acting, which produces ticks.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Ammo can be made to refill over time, so designers control how often players can shoot by tuning how fast it comes back.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Action points that return as time passes mean players must wait for more actions, so the refill pace sets how fast play moves.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Health that heals on its own over time changes how players handle damage, since they can recover instead of needing to find healing.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Lives that come back after a wait, as in some puzzle games, let players retry without a permanent limit on attempts.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: In an ongoing world players could drain every resource for good, so refilling over time keeps supplies available and play going.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Any resource can be given a self-refilling rate, and adjusting that rate lets designers tune pacing and the choices players make.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Renewable Resources
conflicts_with.why: A resource cannot sensibly be both permanently finite and one that grows back on its own, so the two ideas work against each other.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Competition
conflicts_with.why: If supplies keep refilling with time, players have less reason to fight over a scarce amount, so competition for them weakens.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Some resources refilling by themselves may not fit the game's story or setting, which can make the world feel less believable.

patterns.name: Tiles
patterns.what_it_is: Pieces used to hand out resources without showing beforehand what is where.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Tile types and counts must be chosen so they distribute resources or build the world in a way that matters. Hidden or randomised tiles need a known distribution.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tiles are all identical in effect, so which one you get changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: number of tiles; mix of types; hidden or shown

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: Like cards, tiles can be gathered by a player into a personal collection that represents what that player has built or owns, and adding more tiles lets it grow.

can_cause.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
can_cause.why: Tiles can be used like markers to record game state, such as who owns something or how strong a unit is, often by flipping or turning them.

can_cause.name: Configurable Gameplay Areas
can_cause.why: Because tiles are separate pieces, they can be arranged differently before play begins, so the play area changes between games, as in Settlers of Catan.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Adding tiles to the play area is itself a way of building something during the game, as when players place tiles to extend the world.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: When tiles fill the whole space and make up the world itself, nothing in the play area contradicts the fiction, so the game world stays believable.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Tiles are physical items that can be handed out by letting players pick them from a shared selection, which is a way of distributing them during play.

can_cause.name: Drawing Stacks
can_cause.why: Tiles can be piled face down so players take them one at a time as needed, as in Carcassonne.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: A tile can stand for a kind of terrain or surrounding condition, so placing or having it in the world carries that condition's effect on play.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Players place, remove, flip or otherwise handle tiles, so those tiles become the spots where their attention and actions gather, as with flipping in Othello.

can_cause.name: Game Boards
can_cause.why: Tiles can be the pieces that a board is made of, dividing it into clear areas that players can easily tell apart.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Tiles are commonly joined together to form the world players act in, whether built up, worn away, or laid out before play.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: Tiles can serve as the building blocks of a level, breaking it into distinct sections whose positions and options are easy to judge.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: When the set of tile types is fixed and tiles are drawn and played, players can try to remember which have already appeared and which remain.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Tiles can share an identical back so they can be shuffled or hidden, making the order in which types appear or the layout they form unpredictable.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Since each tile is a separate piece that can be added, removed or moved, the shape of the play area can change as the game goes on.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Like cards, tiles can be collected into groups that belong together, so players gather matching or related pieces.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: A tile can be given special features such as resources or abilities, which makes the place it marks more valuable to hold or reach.

can_cause.name: Territories
can_cause.why: Because each tile marks a clear area, it can be claimed by a player, and ownership can be changed by flipping or controlling the tile.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Adding tiles to a player's setup, as in Puerto Rico, gives new or improved abilities.

can_cause.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Generators work with abstract ideas but must finally output concrete building blocks, and these are usually tiles that make up the world.

can_cause.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Board pieces that can be removed make convenient units for shrinking, since taking one away cleanly cuts down the play area.

can_cause.name: Tile-Laying
can_cause.why: Tiles are the namesake and main element: players place them so their positions next to other tiles shape the game.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Placing tiles on a player's board is one way a construct is developed, as in Puerto Rico.

patterns.name: Heterogeneous Game Element Ownership
patterns.what_it_is: Each player brings their own game elements to a new game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Components must differ enough in function that choosing and combining them matters, and the sets must be balanced or limited so that having more or rarer pieces does not decide the game. Players also need time and means to build and tune their own sets.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players bring their own pieces but all pieces are functionally the same or one set is clearly best, so ownership changes nothing in play.
patterns.knobs: how much the elements differ in power; limits on set size or cost; how much players can customise

can_cause.name: Betting
can_cause.why: Since players bring their own pieces, those pieces can be wagered against each other, so owning game elements naturally leads to staking them on outcomes.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: When the elements players bring do not all work the same way, certain pairings of them will team up for special effects.

can_cause.name: Construction
can_cause.why: Players must assemble their own set of elements from what they own before a game, so building that set becomes an activity of its own.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Buying, winning or losing the pieces happens in the real world, so what occurs to them affects players beyond a single match.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because each player picks which owned elements to bring, they decide for themselves how their side of the game is put together.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Players add elements of their own choosing into the game at the start, so each person decides what they put in.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: Players who want particular elements they lack can swap with others who own them, making exchange a natural part of play.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Obtaining the elements costs real money or effort up front, and players hope that spending will pay off in better play later.

can_cause.name: Memorabilia
can_cause.why: Since any one element might not appear in a game, bringing, getting or winning a special one becomes a notable event worth remembering.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Players treat the elements they own as raw material and play a building and collecting activity around them before and between actual matches.

can_cause.name: Pay to Play
can_cause.why: Because players need to have their own pieces to take part, joining in indirectly requires spending money to obtain them.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: Owning and arranging a personal collection of elements lets players tinker with it just for fun, sometimes simply for looks.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Elements are bought with real money, so those who can afford better or more pieces may start a game with an edge.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: In the building activity around the game, the owned pieces are the stock players draw upon and manage to put together their sets.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Players belonging to a team are themselves the contributed parts of a game, so each game gets members brought by different people.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When players own more kinds of elements than they can use at once, they must pick which ones to use and which to leave.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each player needs to bring only part of what is required, which eases setup anywhere, yet it also means players must carry their pieces.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: The many possible sets of elements players might bring mean each game can begin from a very different arrangement.

can_cause.name: Collectible Card Games
can_cause.why: Players each own different sets of game pieces, which is exactly what lets everyone bring their own distinct cards to a match.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: When players own different elements, such as their own cards, knowing how those elements combine is important lasting knowledge.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: When players own different elements, they can plan how to set up their own part of the game to make strong combinations.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: Players can make their own stacks to draw from out of the elements they own, instead of sharing one common stack.

changes.name: Fixed Distributions
changes.why: When players build their own drawing stacks, they decide beforehand what the contents and proportions of those stacks will be.
