changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: The pattern only makes sense when several players each contribute their own pieces to a game.

changes.name: Tension
changes.why: If elements can change hands because of how play goes, players have more at stake, which noticeably changes how tense the game feels.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Players can be allowed to pick which units they own and how many.

conflicts_with.name: Combos
conflicts_with.why: Not all elements work alike, so some combinations of them can be much stronger, and this can upset fairness between players.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Differences in the combos players can build from their own elements can leave some players stronger, undermining even footing between them.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Players need less than a whole game to play, but they must still have their own pieces, or carry spare ones for others to borrow.

patterns.name: Hands
patterns.what_it_is: A set of game elements of a certain kind that a player currently holds.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must hold hidden elements they can pick between, with a size limit and a clear way to refill. The elements held need to matter enough that choosing among them is a real decision.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hand where the next play is forced or all cards are identical or visible, so holding them gives no choice.
patterns.knobs: hand size; refill rule; whether hands are secret or open

can_cause.name: Containers
can_cause.why: A hand is a holder that gives each player ownership of cards or tiles they've collected but haven't yet put into play.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because a hand holds several elements, players get to pick which one to use now and which to keep for later turns.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Hands are usually hidden, so working out or peeking at an opponent's hand gives a strategic edge and becomes something players aim for.

can_cause.name: Secret Resources
can_cause.why: Players normally keep their hands hidden from opponents, so the cards or tiles inside act as private resources only the holder knows about.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: A hand of items that cannot be replaced lets players deduce what remains as play goes on, so later outcomes become easier to foresee.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: Hands are most often filled with cards, and the actions those cards offer determine what a player can do from their hand.

changes.name: Collectible Card Games
changes.why: In these games the hand is what shows a player which actions are available to them at any given moment.

changes.name: Decks
changes.why: Hands are usually filled from decks, so how a hand is refilled and sized changes how a deck gets used.

changes.name: Tile-Laying
changes.why: Holding several tiles lets a player choose which one to place on their turn, which is how hands shape tile-laying play.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Tiles can fill a hand just like cards, so a player holds several to choose from and place later.

patterns.name: Drawing Stacks
patterns.what_it_is: A stack of cards or tiles in a set order, drawn from to determine an outcome.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The pile must be hidden and shuffled, and its mix of element types must be set on purpose so the odds are real. Players need reasons to care what comes next, such as hands to build or plans to make.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pile of cards that is never shuffled or whose contents are all the same, so what comes out is known and drawing changes no decision.
patterns.knobs: what goes into the stack and in what mix; number of stacks; how it is seeded or shuffled

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Players draw cards or tiles from the stack to gather resources, so pulling from it is how they build up what they own.

can_cause.name: Containers
can_cause.why: The stack holds game elements together in one pile that players take from, so it works as a place where pieces are stored.

can_cause.name: Drafting
can_cause.why: Players pick game elements from the stack, or from visible ones beside it, to choose what they keep, which is the core of drafting.

can_cause.name: Fixed Distributions
can_cause.why: Designers decide how many of each element go in the stack, so the mix is set beforehand even though the order is shuffled.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: As the stack shrinks, or when a special card shows up, players can see how far along the game is.

can_cause.name: Geometric Progression
can_cause.why: Each card not drawn becomes more likely to come up on the next draw, so odds climb in a pattern like geometric growth.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Since players can't control what comes off the top, good or bad draws feel like fortune, especially when choosing between several stacks.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Players who see the cards they or others draw can remember what has already come out and so what remains in the stack.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: Shuffling sets an unpredictable order, so what a player draws next is a matter of chance.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Because cards are held back in a shuffled pile, players don't know what they will get until they draw it.

can_cause.name: Cycle Deck Engines
can_cause.why: Players keep pulling fresh cards from their draw pile, and the engine works by letting them go through most or all of it.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because cards or resources come out one at a time, players can remember what has already appeared and use that to work out what remains and plan around it.

changes.name: Decks
changes.why: The cards or tiles that make up a deck are what get put into the stack, so the stack is a way to use a deck.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Drawing from the stack is how cards come into players' hands, so what the stack gives shapes what they hold.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Cards or tiles drawn from stacks often represent resources, so the stack controls how players gather them.

changes.name: Tile-Laying
changes.why: When the stack holds tiles, drawing them supplies the pieces players then place on the board.

changes.name: Fixed Distributions
changes.why: Drawing items from a stack without putting them back means the whole set is used up over time, so the mix is assured.

patterns.name: Pick-Ups
patterns.what_it_is: Items lying in the game world, usually picked up by touching them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Items must be placed where reaching them costs something or means a choice, and they must give a gain that players care about. They should be visibly distinct so players can find and want them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Items lie everywhere in such quantity or with such trivial value that players grab them on autopilot and nothing is decided.
patterns.knobs: how many are placed; where; how much each gives; whether they respawn and how fast

can_cause.name: Ammunition
can_cause.why: Ammo is a common thing players find lying around, so a collectible object in the world is a typical way to hand out more bullets.

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: When an item must be actively activated to be grabbed instead of touched automatically, players need to interact with it, so it becomes something to click.

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Because players tend to gather these items anyway, designers can turn that into a formal goal like taking every pill to finish a level.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Collectibles are easy to tell apart and visibly change the world when taken, so they make clear targets for goals about acquiring things.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When players need the items to reach goals, they must travel around the world to find them, which pushes them to explore.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Placing collectible items in the world is a common way to keep supplying players with things like ammo, armor or health.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: When the collectible is itself the resource, the spot where it lies marks a place players can go to get that resource.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: Some collectibles are not the resource but let players obtain it, so they act as a source without being the resource themselves.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Collectibles can be the resource itself, and after pickup they often turn into a number such as ammo, health or armor.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: If players need collected resources to finish main goals, then gathering the items by moving around becomes a smaller goal that serves the bigger one.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Since these items are noticeable and vanish when taken, a spot where one is missing hints that someone has already been there.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: After pickup, an item can stop being an object and just raise a number held in something like a player's abstract status.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor is one of the resources commonly delivered by collectibles that add to a number once picked up.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: A collected item can lose its individual identity and increase a numerical value kept on the character who took it.

changes.name: Deliver
changes.why: Needing to first pick up an item before bringing it somewhere adds a required step to delivery goals.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Taking collectibles visibly changes the board, and hunting for them encourages players to move around it.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Collectibles are usually made by taking ordinary game items and making them something players can take.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Picking items up visibly changes the world, and needing them sends players moving through it.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Health packs lying in the world are a typical collectible, and picking one up adds to the player's health value.

changes.name: Inventories
changes.why: Picked-up items are meant to be collected, so they go into an inventory, or they add to a number stored there.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Collecting items changes what a level looks like and can be required to complete it, such as taking all pills.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Some collectibles exist only to give players an extra life when they are taken.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Players steer their avatar toward items to grab them, so the desire to collect shapes how they move around.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: When collected resources are needed for goals, players have a reason to travel through the space to reach the items.

changes.name: Non-Localized Resources
changes.why: A collectible is a single spot in the world that feeds a resource which otherwise is not tied to any place.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Taking a collectible can turn it into a resource amount, so the pickup changes how much players have.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Some collectibles have no other purpose than to raise the player's score, as ordinary pills do in Pac-Man.

patterns.name: Inventories
patterns.what_it_is: A place where everything a character carries is stored.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It needs limits (space, weight) and real actions (use, drop, equip, trade) so that managing items is a choice. The limits must be tight enough to force choosing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An item list with no limit and no actions beyond viewing, so carrying anything is free and no decision arises.
patterns.knobs: capacity; what actions are available; how items are sorted and accessed

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because inventories let characters keep items out of sight yet instantly usable, the game world stays believable while play stays smooth.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Managing items by hand in an inventory takes effort that isn't the fun part of play, so it can feel like tedious chores.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: When an inventory opens as a separate screen, it brings in interface elements that don't exist inside the game world itself.

can_cause.name: Resource Caps
can_cause.why: Inventories usually have limited room, so a character can only carry so many items, which creates a ceiling on what can be held.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Carrying items fits the setting, so an inventory can support the theme, though it can also work against it.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Inventories give the basic means to hold and move items between owners, which trading depends on.

can_cause.name: Transferable Items
can_cause.why: Since inventories are where items are held and handled, they provide the groundwork that lets items be passed between characters, such as through stealing or trading.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Inventories change what characters can do by setting how many items they can carry, which restricts them.

changes.name: Deterioration
changes.why: Some games let players use their inventory to counteract wear on items, such as Fallout letting players negate the effects of deterioration.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Inventories give players a place to examine, drop, and otherwise handle items, and they limit how many can be stored.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Items carried by a group of characters can be managed through inventories, and Dragon Age II shares one inventory among the player and companions.

changes.name: Pick-Ups
changes.why: If a picked-up item keeps its identity as an item after retrieval, the inventory shapes how it is handled afterward.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Inventories can hold resources as well as items, and these often cannot be dropped, so the inventory affects what resources are available.

changes.name: Upgrades
changes.why: Some games, like Fallout 3 and Dragon Age II, let players install upgrades on items through the inventory screen.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: They help players remember things they would need to keep track of anyway, so they adjust the upkeep rather than cause it.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Inventories can show items differently from the game world or allow unrealistically large loads, and pausing screens make this worse.

patterns.name: Armor
patterns.what_it_is: Items that protect against damage.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Armor must reduce the damage taken in a measurable way, with costs or limits (weight, slots, class restrictions) so equipping choices matter. Combat needs to be dangerous enough that protection is valuable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Armor looks impressive and has a high number, but damage is so small or armor so abundant that it never changes outcomes.
patterns.knobs: damage reduction per piece; who can wear which; weight and slot limits

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: A designer can make armor cost the wearer some skill or attribute, so stronger protection comes with a penalty that keeps choices balanced.

can_cause.name: Equipment
can_cause.why: When armor is a game item, players must be able to pick which pieces to wear, so it works as equipment.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Armor can be an object in the game world that a character owns and carries, which makes it an ordinary game item.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: For the wearer, armor makes them better at surviving combat, so it feels like a boost to their abilities.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Armor can instead be a countable supply, such as a number that drops when hit and is restored by finding more.

can_cause.name: Sets
can_cause.why: Games can group several armor pieces, or armor together with weapons, into matching collections that are designed to be used together.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Damage applied to armor wears down the player's protection, a numeric loss that leaves them more exposed.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Protection comes with a drawback like reduced speed, so players must decide whether the safety is worth the loss.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Armor changes how well an avatar withstands attacks, and often changes how the avatar looks, signaling its protection to players.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Armor changes how well a character withstands attacks, and a game may restrict which characters are allowed to use particular pieces.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: By shielding the fighter's health, armor shifts how fights unfold, and to opponents it acts as a reduction in their ability to hurt.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Armor sets how much harm gets through, and in some games hits wear down the armor itself too.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Armor stands between attacks and a character's health, so health is lost more slowly, and losing armor makes losing health more likely.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Realistic games often penalize skills for characters wearing powerful armor, since heavy gear hampers them.

patterns.name: Decks
patterns.what_it_is: Sets of cards the game uses as a single whole; they can be shared or personal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The set of cards must be shaped so that what is left in the deck gives useful information and chance. Players should be able to see or learn what the deck holds.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pile of cards that is reshuffled every time, so no one can track anything and the order is irrelevant.
patterns.knobs: number and mix of cards; one shared deck or one per player

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Because tracking which cards have already left the deck gives you an edge, players are pushed to remember what has been played and what remains.

can_cause.name: Randomness
can_cause.why: A deck's order is unknown to players, so whatever card comes next is a matter of chance in any card-based game.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing what is in a deck, whether because you built it or it was pre-set, lets you plan around what you may draw.

changes.name: Collectible Card Games
changes.why: Each player brings or is given a personal deck to play with, so decks are a defining, constantly present part of this kind of game.

patterns.name: Non-Renewable Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources whose amount does not grow during the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be no generation or replenishment of the resource anywhere in the game, and there must be consumers that use it up. Without consumption, players can hoard it and the scarcity never bites.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A resource labelled as finite but with a hidden refill, or one so plentiful for the game's length that it never runs out and never changes decisions.
patterns.knobs: starting amount; consumption rate; whether the limit is global or per player

can_cause.name: Action Caps
can_cause.why: When actions need a specific resource that can never be refilled, each player can only perform that action as many times as they hold the resource.

can_cause.name: Irreversible Events
can_cause.why: Using up, capturing, or removing such a resource from the game cannot be undone, because nothing can bring the resource back.

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: If the energy needed to use an ability cannot be refilled, running out makes the loss permanent instead of temporary.

can_cause.name: Complete Resource Depletion
can_cause.why: Since these resources can't be replaced once used, any use of them moves the game toward having none left.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: With resources that cannot be replaced, less remains later, so grabbing the last ones matters more than the first.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: As limited resources get used up, what is left becomes easier to work out, so players can predict more as the game nears its end.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: When resources can't be replaced, experimenting with them costs something, so players plan more carefully.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: As non-renewable items get captured, fewer of them remain in the game, so each further capture matters more and more.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: Cards are often dealt out and then leave play once used, so they cannot be used again.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: If companions can die and cannot be replaced, the pool of possible companions shrinks, making each loss matter.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: A deck that is drawn through only once, or very few times, runs out and cannot keep supplying cards.

changes.name: Fudged Results
changes.why: Player-held fudging abilities need not be used up permanently, since they can be refilled, but making them non-renewable would limit their use.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Lives can be a resource that only goes down as play continues, with no way to get it back.

changes.name: Mules
changes.why: Because the resource cannot be gathered again and again, using helper units to repeatedly collect it becomes less effective.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Since you cannot fix uneven holdings of such resources by simply adding more, gaps between players are harder to correct.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: Limiting how many times a special ability can be used turns it into a resource that gets used up.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Once cards or similar items are used up and the pool shrinks, outcomes become more predictable, which changes how much chance is involved.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Starting players with resources that never replenish encourages planning across the whole session.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: If all units exist from the start and can be lost, they cannot be replaced, which tends to speed up the game.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: If a hand starts with a fixed set that is never refilled, its contents are used up and the hand steadily shrinks.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: A world that goes on forever has trouble with resources that run out for good, since play must still work once they are gone.

conflicts_with.name: Regenerating Resources
conflicts_with.why: A resource cannot sensibly be both permanently finite and one that grows back on its own, so the two ideas work against each other.

conflicts_with.name: Renewable Resources
conflicts_with.why: A resource cannot sensibly be both permanently finite and one that is replenished, so the two ideas work against each other.

patterns.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
patterns.what_it_is: The player improves something outside the game world, such as a rating, rank, or reputation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a player-level structure that can be improved, with improvements that really change which options are open or how strong they are. Players should be able to see progress and ideally choose its direction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Numbers on a sheet go up, but they unlock nothing and change no decisions, so it is just a counter.
patterns.knobs: what can be improved; cost and pace of improvement; how much choice players have over direction

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Growing your player's powers makes your actions feel stronger, so you feel more in control, even when the game raises difficulty to cancel out that gain.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: If improving your player's attributes demands a lot of repeated effort or resources, players may repeat tasks just to get the development.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: Developing a player's construct often opens up new abilities tied to what the player focuses on, making new options available.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Because the player's own structure visibly grows, the work spent in play feels rewarded and worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Listed as working together with Abstract Player Constructs and Freedom of Choice to create Investments, but the page gives no explanation.

can_cause.name: Player-Planned Development
can_cause.why: When something abstract the player controls can grow in chosen ways, players get richer room to plan how it should develop.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: As the player's construct gains new or better abilities, players get more options to choose from as play goes on.

changes.name: Bases
changes.why: Improving bases is one way to improve the player's construct, so development affects how bases work.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: Development is the internal growth of the things players focus on, so it changes those focal points.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: Developing the player's construct can come from more or improved territories, so development shapes their role.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Development can come from more or improved units, such as gaining promotions, so it changes how units work.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Constructs often grow stronger over a game, so this ongoing development keeps changing them.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: With several players developing at different paces, their strengths can drift apart, which upsets fairness between them.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: In worlds that keep running, differences grow over time and newcomers are measured against long-time players.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Development gives some players more power than others, and over time this gap makes it hard to keep players evenly matched.

patterns.name: Lives
patterns.what_it_is: The number of attempts a player has before the game ends.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Failure must remove a life but not end the game at once, and running out must end it. Dangers must be real enough that lives are actually lost.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players have a number of lives but gain them so easily, or are so seldom hit, that losing one never matters.
patterns.knobs: starting number of lives; how often they are lost; how they can be regained

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: Lives are a number or counter that exists as a game concept rather than a physical thing, so they almost always appear as part of such constructs.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Since each life can be lost, players constantly aim to stay alive as long as possible with the lives they have.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: Because losing one life doesn't end the session, players get further tries as long as at least one life remains.

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Once the last life is gone, that loss must end the session, otherwise it would be no different from losing any earlier life.

can_cause.name: Non-Localized Resources
can_cause.why: The count of lives belongs to the player overall and is not tied to a place or object in the game world.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Running out of lives must remove the player from play, or losing the final life would feel no different from losing others.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: The number of lives a player holds is something that can be gained, spent, and lost during play, so it works as a resource.

can_cause.name: Spawning
can_cause.why: After a life is lost the player continues, so the game must put them back in play, even if at the exact spot they died.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Each life can be lost to enemies, traps, or other players, so players try to keep staying alive for as long as they can.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players can easily grasp what is at stake, so the risk of losing a life makes moments of danger feel more tense.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: Giving players limited lives in a multiplayer game means they can be knocked out when lives run out, leaving a final survivor.

can_cause.name: Tick-Based Games
can_cause.why: When lives come back at regular intervals, players must wait for ticks before they can play again.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Lives are usually attached to avatars, tying how well the player does to how long their avatar can keep going.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: The page only says lives are sometimes used together with boss monsters, without explaining why.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Lives are usually attached to characters, linking the player's successes and failures to what happens to that character.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Losing lives is often the result of failing to dodge attacks in fights, so lives raise the stakes of combat.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: Objects that can be destroyed can be given lives through parallel lives, so several of them can be lost one after another.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Because wiping out all of an opponent's lives removes them from the game, killing other players gains a clear benefit.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A counter of lives is a system element shown to players, which shifts how they perceive other game elements.

conflicts_with.name: Permadeath
conflicts_with.why: Lives mean players have more than one, whereas permadeath means a single death is final, so the two cannot both hold.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Real characters don't have several lives, and returning after death through spawning also feels unrealistic, which can clash with the theme.

patterns.name: Loot
patterns.what_it_is: Items, usually random, that the player finds in the world as a reward.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Defeating or searching things must yield items with some randomness and enough variety that players want to check. Items must matter to later play, and distribution among players needs handling.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies drop items that are always the same or worthless, so killing them gives no reason to look.
patterns.knobs: drop rate; spread of item quality; what kinds of items can drop; how it is shared

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Hunting for one specific drop can turn into tedious grinding when players must sift through lots of items they don't want before finding it.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Loot puts new items or resources into the player's hands as a result of play, which is a straightforward way of adding game elements.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When several players want the same drop, they may stop talking it over and simply hurry to grab it before anyone else.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Defeating enemies pays out items taken from them, so the loot works as the prize players receive for completing an elimination goal.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: If players know what kinds of drops exist and how likely each is, they start working out how to get the ones they want.

can_cause.name: Bidding
can_cause.why: When players in a multiplayer game find loot, they may decide among themselves to divide it by bidding, so bidding appears spontaneously.

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Giving inhabitants valuables makes them targets, which lets players treat them as enemies worth attacking.

can_cause.name: Ninja Looting
can_cause.why: Ninja looting can only happen if there are dropped resources to take, so the existence of loot is the basic precondition for it.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: Loot is something players collect from foes or characters, which makes it one concrete way resources become available.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: Ammunition is one of the resource types a drop can contain, so loot changes how much of it players have.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor is one of the item types that can be taken from defeated foes, so loot decides what protection players end up with.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Because winning fights yields drops, loot gives players an extra reason to fight beyond whatever motives already exist.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Defeating or removing a target is what earns the drop, so loot adds a payoff to elimination goals.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Carrying valuables can be reason enough for players to treat inhabitants as enemies, and enemies are the usual source of drops.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Equipment can be part of what a defeated opponent leaves behind, so loot affects which gear players acquire.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: Drops can consist of items such as armor, tools and weapons, so loot determines which items players come to own.

changes.name: Game Masters
changes.why: A game master can shape what drops appear to keep things balanced or fit the story, and players may even give them wish lists.

changes.name: Generic Adversaries
changes.why: Ordinary, interchangeable opponents are the most common holders of drops, which they release when killed.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Non-player characters can also be a source of drops when they are targets of elimination goals.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Disagreements over how drops are split can leave a group's members unable to settle on a fair division, weakening the group's stability.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Drops can include resources like money or energy, but if the contents were fully known ahead of time it would just be an ordinary resource.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Tools can be part of a drop, and tools the owner didn't use while fighting can seem odd and clash with the setting.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons are a typical drop from defeated foes, though ones the owner could have used but didn't can look inconsistent.

patterns.name: Ammunition
patterns.what_it_is: Consumable items without which a weapon cannot be used.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Ammo must run out and be refilled by effort (pick-ups, trading, reloading), so players have to ration it. Several ammo types with different effects add meaningful choices.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Ammo is displayed but is effectively unlimited or always at hand, so shooting never involves a decision.
patterns.knobs: ammo supply and cap; reload time; number of ammo types

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Special ammunition types can give a weapon extra power or effects, so the ammo players pick shapes what their character can do.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Ammo handed out can help players keep fighting and reach their next goal, so it works as a reward that eases progress.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When several ammo types fit one weapon, players decide which suits the situation, which gives them real options.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: Ammo can be shown as a concrete object in the game world, not just an abstract number.

can_cause.name: Non-Localized Resources
can_cause.why: Once gained, ammo is simply added to a player's supply and is not tied to a place on the map.

can_cause.name: Pick-Ups
can_cause.why: Ammo can be a collectible object lying in the world that players grab, sitting between abstract counters and full items.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Ammo is something players must have and spend to fire weapons, so it acts as a resource.

can_cause.name: Sustenance Rewards
can_cause.why: Depending on the game's design, ammo can be given to keep players going so they can continue using their weapons.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: If specialized ammo is hard to obtain, the powers it grants are only available for a short time before running out.

can_cause.name: Energy Penalties
can_cause.why: Damage applied to ammunition lowers how much the player can still shoot, which is a numeric loss that limits their actions.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Limited ammo or reloading downtime means each shot has a cost, so players must plan when and how to fire.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Spending limited shots, or picking special rounds that hit harder or truer but do less damage, forces players to weigh gains against costs.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons need ammo to be used, so ammo controls how often and in what way a weapon can be fired.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Limited ammunition restricts how often players may shoot, adding tension and making them decide between firing now or waiting.

patterns.name: Extra Chances
patterns.what_it_is: You can try again if you are not happy with the result of an action.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decide which events can be retried, how many retries exist, how they are earned or refilled, and whether retries can be stacked. The game state must allow trying again, and other players' actions must not make the retry impossible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A retry that is so limited, or so late, that players never actually use it to change an outcome.
patterns.knobs: how many retries; how they are gained and which events they apply to

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: A retry gives another shot at a random outcome, so if success is possible at all, the odds of eventually succeeding go up.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because retries improve the odds of a good outcome, players tend to feel they control results more than they truly do.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players decide whether and when to spend a retry, so they get a real option about how to handle a bad result.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: A retry lets players change an outcome they dislike, though only weakly since the new result is still random and not chosen.

can_cause.name: Game Time Manipulation
can_cause.why: Retrying lets players undo a result and have the moment play out again, effectively bending what happened in the game's timeline.

can_cause.name: Misfortune Mitigation
can_cause.why: When a roll or draw goes badly, a retry softens the damage, though using it costs a limited resource.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Using retries amplifies whatever odds already exist, so likely outcomes become even more likely and players can foresee results better.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, retries can be given to particular characters as special powers, like a luck advantage, so others cannot disrupt them.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Retries are limited, so players must weigh when a result matters enough to spend one.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Retries can be earned, held and spent like other game assets, so designers must decide how players get and keep them.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Handing out new retries as play goes on works as a prize that players are glad to receive.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When a team shares a pool of retries, members may disagree over who should use them, creating tension between individual and group interests.

can_cause.name: Shared Resources
can_cause.why: A pool of retries held by a whole group is one concrete form of a supply that several players draw from.

changes.name: Dice
changes.why: Rerolling a die gives another try on the very same situation, softening the effect of a bad roll.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: Players can draw another card or tile from a stack after an unwanted draw, giving a second try.

changes.name: Game Termination Penalties
changes.why: The more retries players are given, the less final the termination feels, which changes how harsh the penalty really is.

changes.name: Permadeath
changes.why: Retries such as rerolls can coexist with permanent death, giving a chance to avoid a fatal result without making death reversible.

changes.name: Player Elimination
changes.why: Players risk being knocked out but can use retries to try to avoid it, though too many remove the threat.

conflicts_with.name: Game Termination Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Enough retries can weaken or negate the penalty for ending the game, undermining the penalty's purpose.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: With retries, a good result needs less luck, and others' bad luck is less likely to benefit you.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: Other players keep acting, so a retry may become impossible, making the pattern hard to offer without special powers.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: If retries let players avoid being knocked out too easily, the threat of elimination disappears.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Redoing events breaks the sense that the story world moves forward in one consistent order.

patterns.name: Betting
patterns.what_it_is: A player stakes resources hoping to win on an uncertain outcome.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must own resources they can stake, and the outcome must be uncertain with payoffs related to perceived odds. Decide whether the economy is closed or open.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bet is offered, but the payout is fixed and risk-free or the stake is trivial, so nobody weighs the choice.
patterns.knobs: stake sizes; payout ratio; when the result is revealed; optional or forced

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: If players can be scared or fooled into dropping their bets by what others do, wagering becomes a stage for deception.

can_cause.name: Delayed Effects
can_cause.why: When a wager isn't settled right away, players must wait to learn whether their stake pays off.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Players may wager game resources on their own initiative, which creates stakes and outcomes that reach beyond the game's own rules.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Wagering means deciding whether, what, and how much to stake, so players get real options to choose from.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Skill pays off when results aren't purely random, or when knowing the odds of a random event gives you an edge.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: An unresolved wager leaves players watching an ending that is close but not yet decided.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Placing a wager means putting something in at risk, hoping to get back more than was committed.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: When the event being wagered on is affected by chance, winning can feel like fortune smiling on you.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: Because staking something is optional, players can decide for themselves to chase winnings as a personal aim.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Choosing how much to stake, and which of several things to stake, is a decision about how to spend holdings.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Players can offer in-game resources as prizes for winning a wager, whatever the official rules say about it.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: The chance to wager leads players to organize their own side games around the game's resources, without any rule asking for it.

can_cause.name: Social Skills
can_cause.why: Wagering favors people who can read others, such as spotting who wants which resource or who is being fooled.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: A stake that hasn't been settled yet keeps players anxious and expectant about how it will turn out.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Wagering on game outcomes means players bind themselves to a result with something to win or lose, even though the rules don't back it.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Players can wager on how a game turns out, creating a self-made game that depends on the result rather than on playing it.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: Optional wagering lets players choose to set themselves goals of acquiring things, and wagers can be about things not usually seen as resources.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Wagers redistribute what players hold, and rewards can be a different kind of resource than the stake, converting one into another.

patterns.name: Power-Ups
patterns.what_it_is: Collectible items that immediately give a benefit or advantage.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Pickups must sit in places worth reaching and respawn on some schedule. Their effects have to matter for current goals and be balanced against the other players' advantages.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Shiny items lie around but give a negligible bonus or one that is never needed, so players ignore them.
patterns.knobs: spawn frequency and place; effect strength; effect duration or number of uses

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: When a pickup appears, players get a short-lived aim to go and gather it, which is exactly what collecting means.

can_cause.name: Ephemeral Goals
can_cause.why: Power-ups show up and can vanish or be taken, so they hand players a brief objective of grabbing them before the chance is gone.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Power-ups naturally make players want to become stronger or more capable, since they grant new or better abilities.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: A power-up is a weaker kind of game item: an object placed in the world, though it only exists to be picked up.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: Picking one up can make something the avatar already does stronger, such as quad damage multiplying weapon harm.

can_cause.name: Pick-Ups
can_cause.why: Power-ups are pick-ups that stop existing once taken, since touching them is their only use.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Because only one or a few players can grab a given power-up, the new ability it grants belongs to just those players.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players must decide when to grab a power-up or where to wait for one to appear, which is short-term planning.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: Power-ups often grant powers that last only a limited time or a few uses, then run out.

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: When their random effects are weighted by a player's situation, trailing players tend to get better boosts, as in Mario Kart.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: The spot where power-ups are found is valuable because of the benefit it provides.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: They can add theme-fitting content but strain belief since they obviously exist to give gameplay effects.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Power-ups can give an avatar a new ability or make an existing one stronger, changing what players can do.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: They clearly affect gameplay, which makes them look like game-system devices instead of things belonging to the world.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
conflicts_with.why: Power-ups vanish when an avatar touches them, so there's little point making them solid objects that players interact with physically.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: They reward some players without compensating others, though random, circumstance-weighted effects can help balance.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Their immaterial, vanish-on-touch nature feels out of place next to ordinary items and landmarks, which can clash with the game's theme.

patterns.name: Resource Caps
patterns.what_it_is: Limits on how many resources can be stored or spent.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The cap must be low enough that players actually reach it, so it forces them to spend or lose income. It also has to apply to a resource that matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cap set so high that nobody ever reaches it, so it never affects a decision.
patterns.knobs: cap value per resource; whether caps can be raised

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: A cap stops resources from piling up without limit, so it breaks runaway growth and keeps players closer together in strength.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Lowering a cap is a way to punish a player, since they can then hold less than before.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Raising a cap is a way to reward a player, since they gain room to hold more than before.

changes.name: Ammunition
changes.why: A cap can set the maximum number of rounds a player may carry, since ammunition is a countable resource.

changes.name: Arithmetic Progression
changes.why: Caps on investments force steady, evenly growing gains to be spread over time rather than gathered at once.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: A cap on how much can be invested at one time forces players to spread their spending out over time.

changes.name: Regenerating Resources
changes.why: Once a resource is at its cap, regeneration stops adding anything, so the cap decides when refilling has no effect.

changes.name: Renewable Resources
changes.why: When a renewable resource reaches the cap, new supply is wasted, so players must use it to benefit from renewal.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Any numerical resource can be given a maximum, which limits how much a player may collect or store.

changes.name: Save Files
changes.why: The number of save slots can be limited, even though this limit is rarely part of the game's story.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: The number of units a player may own can be limited, as with population limits in strategy games.

conflicts_with.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
conflicts_with.why: Using tokens to enforce a cap on holdings limits how much bookkeeping players must do, which works against the usual burden of upkeep.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: When tokens are used to track resources, limiting how much can be held restricts how much tracking is needed.

conflicts_with.name: Positive Feedback Loops
conflicts_with.why: A cap on resources that fuel the player's actions stops the gains from compounding, so the loop cannot keep growing.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Competition
conflicts_with.why: With each player able to hold only so much, there is less reason to fight over resources, so competition weakens.

conflicts_with.name: Save Scumming
conflicts_with.why: A cap on how many save files a player may have limits reloading, so the cap works against this behavior.

patterns.name: Resource Locations
patterns.what_it_is: Areas of the world where resources are located.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Locations must be placed so that getting there costs something, such as distance, risk or rivals. Resources must be useful enough to be worth the trip.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A resource node placed right at the start where everyone gets it with no effort or trade-off.
patterns.knobs: number, placement and richness of locations; access cost and who can take them

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: Once players know where resources are, getting the most out of those spots becomes the focus of play, which marks an exploitation phase.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Since players can reach these spots and others may contest them, taking hold of a resource spot becomes a goal in itself.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When resource spots are known or merely suspected to exist, players are motivated to roam the world to find and reach them.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: A place holding useful resources is by its nature somewhere players can draw those resources from, so it acts as a source.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because resource spots are valuable, they are often places worth fighting over or holding, which makes them strategically important.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Designers decide where resources are placed within the world, so resource locations shape how the world is laid out and used.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Putting resource spots in areas players can't yet enter lets them see rewards ahead of time and set goals to reach them.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: The choice of which resources to put in which spot determines what players can find and where, shaping how those resources are obtained.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: In games built on territories, each distinct gameplay area can hold its own resource, so resource locations give each territory its character.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Some games only put resources in certain tiles, so resource locations decide which tiles hold value and which do not.

patterns.name: Renewable Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources that are replenished in some way during the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a clear way the resource comes back (spawning, producing, timers) and a limit on speed or amount, so that using it is still a real choice. Players should be able to over-use it and suffer for it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Resources are called renewable, but they come back so fast or in such quantity that spending them has no cost.
patterns.knobs: what renews; renewal speed and conditions; maximum stock

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: When renewing a resource takes an action, being the one allowed to perform that action can be a special power only certain characters have.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: Players must work out how much of a renewable resource they can spend without wrecking its ability to refill.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When several players draw on the same renewable supply, one player overusing it hurts everyone else sharing it.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Because overspending can damage future refills, players must choose between meeting immediate needs and keeping long-term benefits.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Action points are a typical resource that can be made renewable by refilling them.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: If renewing resources takes an action, being able to do it can be a special ability that characters hold.

changes.name: Extra Chances
changes.why: Extra chances are a typical resource that can be renewed so players get them again.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: Owning the sources that renew resources can become a goal players pursue when control can change hands.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Health is a typical resource that can be renewed so it is restored during play.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Lives are a typical resource that can be renewed so players get more of them.

changes.name: Mules
changes.why: Mules only help for short stretches when resources do not renew, so renewal changes how useful they are.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Long-running worlds need renewal so resources are not used up entirely or piled up in particular places or states.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Making a resource renewable means it keeps being introduced into the game rather than running out.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units are a typical resource that can be renewed so players can get replacements.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Renewable Resources
conflicts_with.why: A resource cannot sensibly be both permanently finite and one that is replenished, so the two ideas work against each other.

patterns.name: Energy Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A punishment that reduces a numeric supply the player needs to take actions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The value must matter for actions and lead to a worse outcome at some threshold; the loss must be large enough to notice and be recoverable or not by design.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A health bar that drops but regenerates instantly or never reaches a threshold, so nothing is at risk.
patterns.knobs: amount lost per event; starting amount and maximum; recovery rate and threshold effects

can_cause.name: Game Termination Penalties
can_cause.why: When there are no lives, running a value like health down to its limit can end the game directly and knock the player out.

can_cause.name: Life Penalties
can_cause.why: When a game has lives and the reduced value is tied to them, running it down to the threshold costs the player a life.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Shrinking a number the player needs to act is simply one specific way of punishing the player, so it counts as a kind of penalty.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Losing a value that threatens worse outcomes later makes players nervous, though less so than losing a life or ending the game.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: When the reduced value is connected to the lives, losing it can cost the player a life; without lives it leads to termination.

patterns.name: Memorabilia
patterns.what_it_is: Content or items earned in the game that remain available after it ends.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a durable item, such as a kept component or a produced record, tied to a specific game instance and actually handed to the player. It must carry some value in memory, status or later use.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A generic souvenir or a stats screen that nobody keeps, shows or cares about, and that is not tied to anything that happened in play.
patterns.knobs: what is kept; how scarce or personal it is; whether it has use in later games

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: A kept souvenir, especially one won from another player, shows others what you achieved, so owning it earns you recognition from your fellow players.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Physical keepsakes must be handed to players, so needing them in hand works against letting people play anywhere and anytime.

patterns.name: Facilitating Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: Rewards that make later actions or progress through the game easier.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reward must actually change what players can do or how easily they do it, such as new abilities, better tools, stronger skills or progress toward the end. The strength should match the effort required to earn it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reward that looks like a power-up but gives a negligible bonus, so play is no easier than before.
patterns.knobs: size of the ability or power boost; how often and how hard it is to earn

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Getting stronger or more capable can make players feel their actions matter more than they truly do, since the reward itself boosts how effective they feel.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Being able to do things better can widen what players are able to do, giving them more options in how they play.

can_cause.name: Player Agency
can_cause.why: When players can act more effectively, their choices have a bigger impact on the game, which strengthens their sense of agency.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: These are a kind of reward: they give players something in return for play, specifically a gain that makes acting or finishing the game easier.

changes.name: Dynamic Goal Characteristics
changes.why: A reward can simply change what a goal demands, making it easier to meet, so it alters the goal's requirements as play goes on.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Moving players on to a new level counts as a reward that advances them spatially toward the end of the game.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: If players weren't allowed to pick what they get better at, the reward gives them power without real choice, working against their freedom.

conflicts_with.name: Player Agency
conflicts_with.why: When the improvement is handed out rather than chosen by players, being stronger doesn't give them real control over their development, undermining agency.

patterns.name: Action Caps
patterns.what_it_is: The game limits how many actions can be taken per turn or per period of time.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The cap must be tighter than what players would like to do, so that they have to choose which actions to spend. It matters most in turn-based or tick-based play where the player cannot simply act faster.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A limit exists on paper but is so generous that it is never reached, so players never need to prioritize.
patterns.knobs: number of actions per turn or period; whether the cap is per action type or total

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: A shared pool of extra actions, like Space Hulk's command points, lets any piece act more flexibly, so a cap can actually widen the options players have.

can_cause.name: Resource Caps
can_cause.why: Because actions count as a limited resource, restricting how many you may take is itself a ceiling on that resource.

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: With only so many actions available, players must decide how to spend them, which turns the action supply into something to manage.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: The number of actions you can take works like a currency that you hold and spend, so actions become a resource.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Since you cannot do everything, you must think ahead about which actions are worth using, which pushes you to plan.

changes.name: Arithmetic Progression
changes.why: When repeating an action steadily increases a reward, a cap stops players from piling up those repeats at once and spreads them over time.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: These games only become interesting for caps because players must choose which actions to do in a tick, since they cannot do them all.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Caps matter most here because players must pick which actions to use in a turn when they cannot do everything.

changes.name: Visits
changes.why: Limiting how much a visitor can do keeps the owner doing most of the work in their own space, so their effort still matters.

conflicts_with.name: Analysis Paralysis
conflicts_with.why: Caps push players to plan carefully, which can cause overthinking in multiplayer turn-based games, though a small enough cap keeps the choices few.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Unless the cap is used to grant extra actions, restricting how many things you may do reduces how free your choices are.

patterns.name: Deterioration
patterns.what_it_is: Items wear out from active use.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Wear must actually reduce an item's usefulness, and players must be able to fix, replace or manage items so that using them is a choice. The speed of wear must be noticeable but fair.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A durability bar that wears so slowly, or is repaired so cheaply, that players never think about it.
patterns.knobs: wear per use; repair cost; what happens at zero durability

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: When an item wears out completely, its owner loses whatever it let them do, like a Minecraft tool that eventually breaks.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Because strong gear wears down with use, its power can't be relied on forever, which keeps it from dominating the game.

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: As an item wears down gradually, it works less well, such as weapons in Fallout 3 dealing less damage as they degrade.

can_cause.name: Destructible Objects
can_cause.why: If worn items are removed once they stop providing anything useful, they effectively become objects that can be used up and destroyed.

can_cause.name: Temporary Abilities
can_cause.why: Since wear steadily uses up an item's usefulness, the abilities it grants last only for a limited time rather than permanently.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Each use wears the item down, so players must weigh the benefit of using it now against the wear it costs.

can_cause.name: Vulnerabilities
can_cause.why: Wearing down is a weakness of equipment, because the more it is used the less dependable it becomes.

changes.name: Abilities
changes.why: Wear reduces or removes what an item lets its user do, so abilities become weaker or disappear as the item is used.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Armor wears down mainly because it absorbs attacks, so its protection shrinks the more hits it takes.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Any gear can be made to wear down with use, which limits how long it stays useful and invites repair or replacement.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Tools are common targets for wear, so using them gradually degrades them, as with tools in Minecraft.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons commonly wear out through use, such as dealing less damage in Fallout 3 as they degrade.

patterns.name: Ephemeral Events
patterns.what_it_is: Events that exist in the game only for a limited time and then disappear.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Events must start and end by clear rules, last briefly in game time, and offer something that is not available otherwise.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An event that is announced as limited but lasts so long or repeats so often that missing it costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: duration; frequency; what triggers them; what they offer

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Events that only exist for a while give you a reason to play during that window, if you learn about them.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Short-lived events can draw players back, but only if players learn about them, for instance through announcements or seasons.

patterns.name: Steadily Decreasing Resources
patterns.what_it_is: A supply that inevitably shrinks as the game goes on.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be no way to generate or refill the resource, and players must have a reason or requirement to use it. The depletion rate sets how long the game can last.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A resource meter that goes down but is refilled by pick-ups or regeneration, so it never really runs out.
patterns.knobs: starting amount; consumption rate; whether anything can restore it

can_cause.name: Entrenching Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because options for spending a shrinking resource vanish as it runs out, players' earlier choices lock them into paths and fewer alternatives remain.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: When a resource can never be replenished, each time a player spends it becomes a weighty commitment rather than a casual, repeatable choice.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: If the depleting resource is the one needed to survive, or players' demand for it has no ceiling, it eventually runs out and winning becomes impossible.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: The pattern restricts a resource by blocking ways to add more during play and giving players reasons to use it up.

changes.name: Survive
changes.why: When the draining resource is what players need to stay alive, survival goals become something the game itself works against.

conflicts_with.name: Spawning
conflicts_with.why: Spawning brings in some kind of resource, which works against a game where resources only run down, unless spawning itself spends a resource.

patterns.name: Chargers
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the world where the player's resources change while they stay there.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The effect must be strong enough to be worth a detour, tied to a place, and must cost something (time, risk, exposure).
patterns.just_a_label_when: A glowing pad is placed on the map, but the effect is negligible or the pad is on the route anyway, so nobody chooses it.
patterns.knobs: refill speed; size of the boost; number and placement of locations; exposure to risk

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: Chargers are parts of the game world itself that act on whoever stands in them, so they work as effects of the environment.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: Chargers create natural spots to head toward, and reaching them lets players strengthen their position, which builds their ability to do well.

can_cause.name: Improved Abilities
can_cause.why: A charger can give a temporary upgrade, such as a speed boost, to anyone using it, making them more capable than before.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: The benefit only exists at the charger's spot, so players get the ability or bonus only while they are in that place.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: When a charger lets players exceed the game's normal limits, like moving faster than otherwise possible, the boost counts as a privileged ability.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: A charger refills supplies again and again for players nearby, so what they spend can be regained by returning to it.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: Chargers are fixed places where players go to obtain resources, so they serve as spots in the world where resources can be found.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Chargers can hand out resources like ammunition or health, and they can also be treated as valuable resources in their own right.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because chargers give supplies, boosts and goals to head for, the areas that contain them become important places to control or visit.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: In races, chargers give players something extra to aim for along the way, which helps them in the main goal of winning.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Since the benefit accrues the longer you stay, players must choose between remaining on the charger and doing other things.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Chargers become natural destinations in the world, so players have a reason to travel across the map to reach them.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: A charger can restore health, such as medicine cabinets that heal avatars, changing how much damage players can endure.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Players must steer or move their avatar onto the charger to benefit, so moving around the world gets shaped by where chargers are.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Chargers like speed boosters give racers a boost along the course, so they affect speed and who gets ahead.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Chargers replenish what players hold, such as ammunition, and how fast they refill changes how much players have available.

patterns.name: Secret Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources whose existence or properties at least one player does not know.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Hide resources through fog, hands, or unrevealed placement, and make finding or knowing them valuable. Players need a reason to search or infer.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hidden resource that is irrelevant to play or that players can always see anyway, so hiding changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much is hidden; how many resources; how easy it is to discover them

can_cause.name: Easter Eggs
can_cause.why: A hidden resource tucked away in the game world can work like an Easter egg, though it only feels distinct if the resource is rare or unique.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When players suspect hidden resources might exist, they get a reason to go find out what and where they are.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Players who know some resources may be hidden are motivated to roam the world and search for them.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Hidden resources placed in the world, like secret areas, add something extra to discover within the setting.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Because resources may be hidden, scouting becomes more rewarding since it can uncover them as an added payoff.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Resources can be concealed from players, requiring them to find them.

patterns.name: Shared Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources that several players can access during a game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Several players must be able to use or change the same resource, and the resource must be scarce or important enough that sharing creates tension or cooperation.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A common pool so plentiful that nobody has to negotiate or compete for it.
patterns.knobs: who has access; how much is available; rate of use or refill

can_cause.name: Resource Competition
can_cause.why: When several players can draw on the same supply, they end up contending over who gets to use it, so rivalry over that supply appears.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Sharing a supply puts players in spots where their own interest and the group's interest pull apart, and this worsens when they must also cooperate.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Because everyone's dealings revolve around the common supply, players may settle into distinct parts in how they handle or claim it.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Resource Distribution
can_cause.why: Everyone with access to the same supply holds the very same stock of it, so no one has more than another.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Contending over the common supply creates pressure, and it grows when cooperating players distrust one another about how it gets used.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Since others may use up the common supply, a player's window for using it is effectively shortened, acting like a deadline.

changes.name: Bag Building
changes.why: The items placed into a common bag are held in common, so the bag-building process turns into something players share.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: When a whole team draws from one pool of lives, the lives stop being individual and become a common supply.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: A penalty can be applied to the common supply itself, so its effect falls on everyone with access rather than a single player.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Sharing alters ordinary resources by letting other players also manipulate them, which changes how players perceive who owns them.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: A reward can be given into the common supply, so everyone with access to it benefits from that payout.

changes.name: Shared Penalties
changes.why: The common supply can be what a group-wide penalty hits, so the loss lands on all who hold it.

changes.name: Shared Rewards
changes.why: The common supply can be what a group-wide reward is paid into, so all holders gain from it.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: Handing players common resources along with the goal affects how they go about working toward it.

patterns.name: Bases
patterns.what_it_is: Stationary objects in the game world that give players actions or resources.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each base must provide something useful that is tied to its place, and be buildable, capturable or destroyable so that holding it matters. Position should create real strategic differences.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A building is shown at a spot but gives nothing different from anywhere else, so ownership changes no choices.
patterns.knobs: what each base gives; cost to build; whether it can be captured or destroyed

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: Setting up new bases is what spreading out looks like, so phases where players are founding bases mark the game's growth stage.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: Once bases exist, using them well to gain their benefits marks the phase where players cash in on what they built.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: A base that someone else already holds gives other players a clear target: take it over, which becomes a goal.

can_cause.name: Installations
can_cause.why: A base is a more elaborate version of an installation, a fixed built structure that sits in the game world.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Because a base cannot move, whatever actions or benefits it offers can only be used at that one spot.

can_cause.name: Resource Locations
can_cause.why: Bases are often placed where resources already exist, or they supply resources themselves, so they turn into resource spots.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: A newly built base usually makes its spot important to hold, unless that spot was already valuable before anything was built.

changes.name: Choke Points
changes.why: Players can use bases to influence narrow passages, since where a base stands can affect who controls movement through them.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Bases are deliberate constructions placed in the world, so having or building them changes what the game world contains and offers.

changes.name: Laning
changes.why: Whether bases exist or can be built is likely to change how the laning phase plays out.

changes.name: Strategic Locations
changes.why: Building a base can create a new important spot, so constructing bases changes which places in the world matter.

patterns.name: Pay to Play
patterns.what_it_is: To play, you must pay in one form or another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Payment must be required to start or to continue playing, and it needs to be tied to something players want enough to pay. The price and timing have to fit what players find acceptable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A payment that is optional for cosmetic extras only, so nobody actually pays to play, or one required once at purchase, which is just ownership.
patterns.knobs: price; when payment is demanded (entry, continue, extras); what each payment buys

can_cause.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
can_cause.why: Charging players to play brings in money, and that income may be needed to pay for the dedicated staff who run the game.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Since players are already paying to take part, the game can also sell them extras that give them an edge.

changes.name: Game Over
changes.why: Players can pay to keep going after a Game Over has actually happened, so the loss no longer ends their session.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Paying can buy players extra lives, letting them carry on playing after losing the ones they started with.

changes.name: Pick-Ups
changes.why: Selling pick-ups means players who get stuck can only progress by paying, which makes paying an indirect cost of playing.

changes.name: Upgrades
changes.why: Selling upgrades means players who get stuck can only progress by paying, which makes paying an indirect cost of playing.

patterns.name: Free Gift Inventories
patterns.what_it_is: A set of items given to a player to hand out to others as they see fit.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Periodically grant gift items with some randomness, and let players choose recipients, often limited to friends or neighbors. The gifts need to be useful so giving matters.
