patterns.just_a_label_when: A gift button exists, but the items are worthless or automatically sent, so nobody chooses and nothing is exchanged socially.
patterns.knobs: how often gifts are granted; how random their contents are; who can receive them

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: Handing over presents to other players costs the giver nothing in direct terms, so giving looks like a selfless act of helping others.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: By passing gifts to others, players appear to work together and help each other progress, even though no formal joint goal exists.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: A gift can carry an unspoken expectation that the receiver will return the favor later, so giving creates a debt to be repaid.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because players choose who benefits from the gifts, they feel their decisions matter more than they truly do.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Receiving a gift can make a player feel obliged to give something back, so the giving can act as social pressure.

can_cause.name: Inventories
can_cause.why: The gifts are held as a set of items a player stores and later hands out, which is exactly what an inventory is.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: The gifts are usually something the game grants to players, so they work as rewards that are then passed on.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Gifts given with the hope of getting something back later amount to an indirect exchange, even though no trade is negotiated.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Giving gifts needs no real-time interaction, so recipients can collect them whenever they next play, which suits players who are not online together.

changes.name: Casual Gameplay
changes.why: Gifting offers social contact with no direct negative consequences and little effort, which fits relaxed, low-commitment play.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Players mostly play alone, and gifting lets them interact socially without needing to be online together or risking harm to each other.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: The gifts contain resources, and since they keep being supplied to hand out, those resources seem renewable unless limited and shown by status indicators.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: An extra reward can be offered for players other than the one who earned the main reward.

patterns.name: Illusionary Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: Rewards that do not help with goals and improve nothing.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reward must still feel like a recognition to players, through look, status, information, or social value, even though it gives no gameplay benefit. Players need some reason to want it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reward that changes the game state after all, or one so dull that no one notices or wants it.
patterns.knobs: how attractive or visible the reward is; how hard it is to earn; how much social or story value it carries

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Players who are ahead may chase these non-mechanical prizes, spending effort on something that doesn't strengthen them, which gives trailing players room to catch up.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Receiving a prize makes players feel their actions mattered, even though the prize changes nothing about the game's state or outcome.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Though they give no in-game advantage, they can still pay off outside the game, such as earning standing among other players.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Because they offer something to collect or unlock, players have a reason to repeat tedious actions even when nothing in the game gets easier.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Handing one out tells players something about where they stand in the game, so the prize doubles as a signal of progress.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Such prizes can show players information about the game state, which helps them see how they're doing and build up their skill.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Where a game can't be won, these prizes can still give players something to aim for.

conflicts_with.name: Rewards
conflicts_with.why: Ordinary rewards change the game state in players' favor, while these don't, and a normal reward can lose its effect and become one depending on context.

patterns.name: Increasing Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: The further the game progresses, the bigger or better the rewards.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Rewards must really grow in value that players can use or see, paced against rising difficulty or costs so they keep up. The growth should be noticeable between stages.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Rewards that are labelled bigger but are worth the same, or are cancelled out by matching cost increases so nothing feels better.
patterns.knobs: growth rate per stage; reward type (resources or abilities); match to rising difficulty

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Because the prizes keep growing, each later stage of play ends with a bigger payoff than the one before, so finishing later stages feels more significant.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Since the prizes get bigger over time, how large or strong a player's rewards are tells them roughly how far along in the game they are.

changes.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
changes.why: Growing rewards can be set against steadily tougher challenges, so players feel the increasing effort is repaid and the difficulty stays balanced.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Many stories show heroes growing stronger, so giving players stronger rewards over time lets the gameplay's growth match the story's growth.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Giving players larger amounts of resources as rewards later in the game changes how much those resources matter and how they function.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: This pattern changes ordinary rewards by making them grow in size or quality the further players progress.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Growing rewards can keep a likely winner from being obvious, but only when it is still uncertain who will actually earn those rewards.

conflicts_with.name: Sidegrades
conflicts_with.why: Increasing rewards rely on things getting more powerful, whereas sidegrades only offer variety without more power, so the two pull in opposite directions.

patterns.name: Individual Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: A reward that goes to only one player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reward must go to a single player and matter enough that others want it for themselves. It creates competition only if players can compete for it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A reward given to one player that has no value or is quietly shared with everyone, so it makes no difference who gets it.
patterns.knobs: size of the reward; who qualifies; how contested the winning is

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Individual Rewards is simply one kind of reward, so it counts as a reward whenever a game hands something out for actions or completed challenges.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When a player sees that a group would gain more from the reward than they would alone, keeping it for themselves creates a tension between self and group.

can_cause.name: Delayed Reciprocity
can_cause.why: When a reward goes to just one player, the others who helped get nothing now and must count on being repaid afterward.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: In team games, personal rewards tempt members to rush ahead of one another in a race, setting teammates against each other.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Since only one player gets the payoff, helping each other becomes less appealing and harder to arrange, even when several players contributed.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Giving the prize to just one person can weaken the motivation to work together and make cooperating more complicated.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: When the reward goes to a single player, players have less reason to chase a common aim, and pursuing it becomes more complex.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: With only one player, whoever performs the actions and completes the challenges is necessarily the one who receives the reward, so it is always individual.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Rewards
conflicts_with.why: A given reward cannot go to everyone and to only one player at once, so the two kinds exclude each other.

patterns.name: Parallel Lives
patterns.what_it_is: Losing one element does not stop the game, but losing all or a set number does.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must control several elements at risk at once, and losing one must hurt but not stop play. The elements should matter enough that players must decide which to protect, so threats come at them concurrently.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Several units where only one really matters, or ones so easily replaced that losing them never forces a choice.
patterns.knobs: how many elements; how much each is worth; how many must be lost to end the game

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: Once a player has lost every one of their separate pieces, they can no longer keep playing, so they drop out of the game.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Parallel lives add to ordinary lives by spreading the risk over many elements, and losing them all can cost just one proper life.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Managing several lives at once means players may face several sources of penalties simultaneously.

patterns.name: Collectible Card Games
patterns.what_it_is: Each player builds their own card collection and draws on it to pick cards for a session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Cards must differ in power or function, be acquired over time, and be built into decks, with new cards released regularly.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Cards are sold in packs, but all are nearly equal or a few dominate, so collecting and deckbuilding don't matter.
patterns.knobs: rarity distribution; how cards are obtained; deck size; expansion frequency

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Individual cards carry their own rules, so when a player puts several together, their effects can stack into larger combined outcomes.

can_cause.name: Deck Building
can_cause.why: Since each player brings a personal collection, they must pick which cards to include before playing, which makes assembling a deck a task of its own.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Players must obtain cards and choose which to use before a match, so meaningful activity happens outside the actual play session.

can_cause.name: Fudged Results
can_cause.why: When new cards arrive, their unfamiliar effects can surprise players, which feels to them like the game's outcomes being bent in unexpected ways.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Better cards can cost more and a bigger collection offers more options, so spending money can translate into an edge in play.

patterns.name: Sockets
patterns.what_it_is: Slots in an item where upgrades, such as gems, are inserted.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Socket counts must be limited and the upgrades must offer meaningfully different benefits, so that choosing what goes where is a real decision. Whether upgrades can be removed changes how risky the choice feels.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Sockets that always take the same single best upgrade, or are so plentiful that nothing needs to be chosen.
patterns.knobs: sockets per item; types of sockets; whether upgrades are removable; how upgrades are obtained

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because sockets are slots the player fills on their own initiative, players decide when they want to upgrade their gear and which upgrade to use.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When upgrades can be taken back out of sockets, players can swap them around and weigh the different benefits each upgrade offers against the others.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Sockets are built into pieces of equipment, and designers choose how many each kind of item has and what types they are.

changes.name: Upgrades
changes.why: Sockets decide where upgrades can go, and different socket types can restrict which upgrades fit, shaping how upgrades are used.

patterns.name: Sustenance Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: A reward that refills something constantly used up, such as health or fuel.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Something must be constantly draining so the refill matters, and the refills must arrive at a pace that keeps players near, but not at, running out. Timing and placement of supplies is the main design work.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Pickups that top up a resource nobody ever runs short of, so collecting them is pointless.
patterns.knobs: drain rate; amount per pickup; how often and where supplies appear

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Because players keep needing more of the supply, they go out and gather it repeatedly, which turns resupplying into a gathering activity.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Players must keep getting the replenishing reward over and over to avoid penalties, so obtaining it never becomes a one-time objective.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Sustenance rewards are simply one kind of reward available in games, so they fall under the broader reward category.

changes.name: Consumers
changes.why: Anything that uses up resources creates a need for those resources, so supplying them is shaped by what those consumers burn through.

changes.name: Tension
changes.why: Resupplying eases pressure for a while, but if the needed supply keeps draining, the pressure returns and lasts longer.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Vehicles use up things like fuel, so players need refills as rewards if they are to keep driving them.

patterns.name: Non-Localized Resources
patterns.what_it_is: Resources that are at least partly not tied to a place in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have a world in which other things have locations, and the resources must be held as abstract counts that cannot be seen, stolen or carried in space. Designers choose which resources and whether all or only acquired instances are abstract.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A counter in the interface that is still tied to a physical item players must go and fetch or guard in the world, so it behaves as a located resource anyway.
patterns.knobs: which resources are abstract; whether all instances or only collected ones are non-localized

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Non-Localized Resources are a kind of Resource, one that simply has no place in the game world, so each one is a specific form of Resources.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Because these resources are fully or partly missing from the game world, they change what the world contains compared with a world where all resources are physically placed.

changes.name: Inventories
changes.why: In games with inventories, non-localized resources can be tied to certain inventory parts, so particular resources are handled separately from everything else carried.

patterns.name: Resource Sources
patterns.what_it_is: Places, abstract or real, within the world where resources can be found or obtained.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each source needs a clear way to obtain resources, with a cost, a limit or competition. Different sources should give different kinds or amounts so choosing among them matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A source that gives resources automatically with no action or limit, so it works like a number going up.
patterns.knobs: yield per source; cost or effort to use it; number of sources and their types

can_cause.name: Resource Management
can_cause.why: When players can change, defend, or create the places where resources come from, they must start deciding how to handle those supplies.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: If players need what a source offers, they start thinking ahead about how and when to go get it.

can_cause.name: Loot
can_cause.why: When enemies or characters can be robbed of useful goods, they become a place players go to gather resources, and that is where loot comes from.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Sources determine how players get hold of resources, so they shape how those resources enter play.

patterns.name: Converters
patterns.what_it_is: Elements that turn one resource into another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The exchange must have a clear ratio and cost, and the output must be worth more to the player than the input in some situations. Players need to decide when and how much to convert.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A conversion exists, but the rate is so good or bad that nobody ever uses it or everyone always does.
patterns.knobs: conversion ratio; speed; what goes in and out

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Turning one component into another builds layers of game components, so players must understand chains of relations.

can_cause.name: Spawn Points
can_cause.why: Converters produce new elements and so can be viewed as spawn points, since things come out of them.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Turning one thing into another means giving up the input, so players judge whether the output is worth the exchange.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: With many resources and ways to convert between them, players have more different things they can do.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: A converter can be one way new item instances appear at a location after the first ones are taken.

changes.name: Grinding
changes.why: Turning resources into something else through converters can limit grinding's impact, though the converting can itself become more grinding.

changes.name: Renewable Resources
changes.why: Converters let abstract resources be told apart by their state, so a closed economy can still keep renewing them.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Resources can be upgraded into more valuable resources by converters.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Converters under a player's control can turn units into upgraded versions or produce new ones.

patterns.name: No-Use Bonus
patterns.what_it_is: Unused actions are given a bonus so they get chosen more often later.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must be chosen from a shared set, and the bonus must grow enough over turns to shift the value of the neglected option. The reward type should matter to players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bonus so small or so irrelevant that unpopular actions stay ignored, or one that arrives only after the action has already become attractive for other reasons.
patterns.knobs: what resource is added; how much per unused turn; whether the bonus accumulates or resets

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Each turn, bonuses that appear on unchosen actions are a small amount of resources added to the game that all players share in, not just one.

can_cause.name: Renewable Resources
can_cause.why: Unchosen actions get fresh resources added each turn, so resources in the game keep being replenished instead of being used up for good.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When a skipped action piles up bonuses, players must weigh taking that growing reward against other options, which makes their choices harder.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Adding bonuses to actions nobody picked changes how appealing each way of spending points is, evening out how often they get used.

changes.name: Predictable Consequences
changes.why: An action with many stacked bonuses is likely to be picked, which is easy to foresee, but new trade-offs make other choices harder to predict.

changes.name: Role Selection
changes.why: Roles that nobody picks gain extra rewards, which makes them more attractive next turn and spreads players' choices more evenly across roles.

patterns.name: Consumers
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements that use up resources.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Something must really be spent or drained, at a rate that matters to what players can do. Players must have to deal with that demand, by feeding it, controlling it or competing with it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Something is described as using resources, but the amount is trivial or nothing ever runs short.
patterns.knobs: how much and how fast they consume; what they consume; whether players control them

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Capture abilities can be extended so that game elements consume what they take, which makes consuming an ability.

can_cause.name: Complete Resource Depletion
can_cause.why: Consumers keep using up resources, and if they use them faster than new ones arrive, the supply eventually runs out entirely.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Things that automatically drain a player's resources act like enemies, threatening loss without any benefit.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: Using up something to achieve an effect is a cost, which players must compare with the benefit they get.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Consumers offer one way to carry out removal, though they do not by themselves give players the needed actions.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Resource flows must be managed, so how consumers use up resources affects how supply and demand stay balanced in the world.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Things that use up resources deplete them, and together with producers they shape the flow of supply and demand.

patterns.name: Asymmetric Resource Distribution
patterns.what_it_is: Players receive different sets of resources, so each has their own possibilities.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Resource differences must change what a player can do, with trade, scarcity or access to keep it interesting, and enough balance to stay fair enough. (The source page is a stub, so this is a best reading of the name.)
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players hold different amounts of some resource that has no use or can be freely swapped, so the gap changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how big the differences in starting or ongoing resources are; who gets what

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: When the game world hands out resources unevenly, players begin with different amounts or kinds of materials to work with.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Giving some players fewer resources than others makes them less efficient, which works as a handicap.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Giving players unequal resources makes them play differently, and the page lists it twice among the asymmetry-based routes to variety.

changes.name: Mutual Goals
changes.why: Unequal resources make the incentive to reach the shared goal differ from player to player.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Giving players unequal starting resources pushes them toward different strategies, though it can harm fairness unless controlled.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Unequal resources give some players more possibilities to compete than others.

patterns.name: Containers
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements inside which other elements can be stored or hidden.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A container must limit or organise what it holds, through capacity, access or location, so that holding something changes what can be done with it. Players should have to choose what goes in and out.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bag or chest exists, but it holds anything without limit and puts nothing in the way of using the contents.
patterns.knobs: capacity; access rules; what can be put in

can_cause.name: Resource Caps
can_cause.why: A container can hold only so much, so its size gives the cap a physical form inside the game world.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Containers regulate what resources and items a character can hold.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Containers limit how much of a resource players can hold.

patterns.name: Symmetric Resource Distribution
patterns.what_it_is: All players receive resources in equal amounts and on equal terms.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each player must start with, and have access to, equal amounts and kinds of resources. Equal sharing must also hold up over time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The totals are equal on paper, but the resources are placed so some players can reach or use them more easily.
patterns.knobs: amount and kind of starting resources; placement of resource sources

can_cause.name: Player Balance
can_cause.why: Giving everyone the same resources at the start means no player begins with a built-in edge.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Giving all players equal resources pushes the game toward fairer, similar starting conditions.

conflicts_with.name: Varied Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Symmetry removes variety, so when everyone has the same resources there is less difference between players and sessions.

patterns.name: Enemies
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements that actively get in the way of the player reaching their goals.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Enemies must act against the player's goals with real consequences, and the player needs ways to face them; they also need to fit the theme to be recognised.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies drawn as threatening but too weak or passive to hurt or block anyone.
patterns.knobs: number of enemies; their strength and behaviour; how they appear

can_cause.name: Aim & Shoot
can_cause.why: Shooting at foes is the most typical way players beat enemies, as in first-person shooters, so enemies naturally create aiming-and-firing actions.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: When foes show up, players must watch and react to them, so keeping track of enemies takes up their attention.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Enemies can be trapped or taken rather than killed, so one way to overcome them is a goal of capturing them.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Foes that can act against the player, such as by moving, make winning harder and force players to work for success.

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: An overall fight against an enemy can be split into a set of smaller goals, such as several duels, that together form one collection.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Enemies can damage health or lives and be fought back, so their presence gives players a reason and means to fight.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Foes with different abilities, or patrolling guards, give players several things to weigh and respond to at once.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: When some enemies are passive or only look for players, players can choose to stay hidden rather than fight them.

can_cause.name: Consumers
can_cause.why: Enemy actions cost players resources like health or lives, so enemies behave as something that drains what players own.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Enemies are drawn with distinct shape and color, and huge bosses stand out, so players notice them in the game world.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Enemies are commonly beaten by being destroyed, and some seek to destroy the player, so elimination goals arise on both sides.

can_cause.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
can_cause.why: Adding more foes, or tougher ones, as play goes on makes the opposition steadily harder to deal with.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Players often must learn who an enemy is or find its weak spots before they can act against it.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: A foe can be turned to the player's side by winning it over, as with converting units, so beating it can mean gaining it.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: Enemies can patrol or watch over an area, giving them the job of keeping players out or noticing them.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Beating an enemy can mean making its goals permanently impossible, so enemy goals can be blocked by players.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: A permanent enemy can be the main driving force of a story, giving the narrative a clear opponent to build around.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Players are motivated to get past enemies, whether by destroying, avoiding, or converting them, so overcoming becomes a goal.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Enemies can punish players in ways other than killing them, such as taking resources, which counts as a penalty.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers can fix when and how an enemy appears, such as in a cutscene, so the story shapes how the enemy affects play.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: Enemies work against what players want, and players work against theirs, so each side's aims block the other's.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: When enemies are controlled by the game rather than by other players, players are fighting the game's own opposition.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Since enemies can remove health or lives, or stay hostile for a limited time, players get the goal of lasting through the threat.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: When players can choose how and when to meet enemies, or can use weaknesses and traps, they can plan their approach.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Having hostile elements in the world that threaten players makes them feel uneasy and under pressure.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Many game themes need opponents, so including enemies helps the game fit its setting and story.

can_cause.name: Boss Monsters
can_cause.why: A boss can start as an existing enemy type made harder with special abilities, so it still reads as a stronger version of a familiar foe.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: Foes placed at a narrow passage block movement until players defeat them, so beating them is the condition for passing.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Facing opponents makes players try various approaches to find out what hurts them, such as their weak spots.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Spotting enemies first lets players decide whether to avoid them or choose whom to attack first.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: Enemies holding choke points or strongholds deny passage to the places they guard, making those places off-limits until beaten.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled opponents can chase the same hill goal as a lone player, so they compete with that player over it.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Players must discover how a particular enemy can be beaten, which turns the fight into something to deduce.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When no human rivals exist, computer-controlled opponents can compete against the player, giving a race an opponent to beat.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: When enemies' whereabouts are uncertain to players, players must go looking for them, which creates a scouting goal.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: Defeated opponents can hand over loot, so they serve as a place where players obtain resources.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: A missing or changed enemy can signal that something happened there, so the absence itself acts as a negative trace.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: When enemy actions are partly decided by chance, players can't know what the enemies will do next.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Randomizing enemies is one way to vary play, and giving them different traits makes encounters differ.

changes.name: Camping
changes.why: Enemies bring disturbances that make staying in one safe place harder or impossible.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Making enemies stronger, more numerous, or more varied raises how hard the game feels.

changes.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
changes.why: Enemies with hidden advantages or sudden powerful actions make it harder for players to judge their odds.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Players avoid enemy penalties by dodging, but what matters is the threat of harm the enemies pose.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Enemies can be placed on a board, and their positions or hard-to-reach final foes shape how it is played.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Enemies can appear as surprises while players explore, changing what they find in the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Where enemies are placed in the world changes how the environment feels and plays.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Enemies can be placed or arrive in waves at levels, which shapes the challenge of each one.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: In games about steering movement, enemies are extra hazards players must actively steer around.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Adding enemies can create conflict in otherwise cooperative games and can bring players together against a shared foe.

changes.name: Player Balance
changes.why: Computer enemies with special abilities or extra information can feel unfair to players and upset the sense of balance.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Without other players, enemies are what supply conflict or combat in a one-person game.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Enemies disturb players' planning, though control over encounters or traps can still encourage some planning.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Players who choose when to meet enemies, or know their weaknesses and traps, can plan approaches in the moment.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Enemies can block routes or fill areas players must cross, forcing them to choose how to get through.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Enemies can be part of a character's social relations in the game world.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: NPCs given opposing goals become adversaries, which allows competitions needing many participants in single-player games.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Adding enemies to a quest makes it harder and more complex.

conflicts_with.name: Camping
conflicts_with.why: Enemies disturb players who try to stay in one place, making camping harder or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Companions
conflicts_with.why: Non-player characters can be made into enemies or companions, so players can end up choosing one over the other.

conflicts_with.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
conflicts_with.why: Enemies whose abilities or odds are hidden make it hard for players to tell how likely they are to win.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Explaining why enemies can't be met early or why they appear can strain the game world's logic.

conflicts_with.name: Helpers
conflicts_with.why: A non-player character can be turned into either a helper or an enemy, which sets up a tradeoff.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Enemies with special abilities or extra information can feel unfair and upset players' sense of balance.

conflicts_with.name: Stimulated Planning
conflicts_with.why: Enemies disturb what players are doing, making careful planning harder or impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Traverse
conflicts_with.why: Enemies that fill the route players must cross can block the way and make crossing harder.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Opponents can offset players' gains and, when more difficult than expected, work against the feeling of influence.

patterns.name: Traps
patterns.what_it_is: Elements or events that kill or wound characters.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The hazard must be able to hurt the player in a way that matters, and be fair, either learnable by observation or memory or spotted by clues. The penalty has to be real for players to change their movement.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A hazard that does so little harm, or is so telegraphed, that players walk through it without any change in behaviour.
patterns.knobs: damage or penalty; how well hidden it is; how often it triggers; whether it resets

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: A trap that springs without warning can be staged inside a story so that someone the player trusted turns out to have led them into danger.

can_cause.name: Consumers
can_cause.why: A trap that can fire repeatedly keeps draining the player's health or resources each time it is triggered, so it acts as a recurring drain.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Tangible Game Items
can_cause.why: Players can use physical objects in the world, working under the game's physics rules, to build traps themselves.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: Traps give players something to dodge, so avoiding their effects becomes a goal in itself.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: They can hurt enemies or serve as distractions, giving players additional tactical options.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: A trap placed as a barrier, or one that covers a whole region like an acid lake, makes that region unsafe or unreachable.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Traps you cannot spot beforehand kill or hurt you first, so players learn by remembering where those dangers are for next time.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: With traps close by, players cannot step freely and must restrict where and how they move nearby.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Springing a trap costs the player something, such as lost abilities, damage, or even lives and units.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Traps can be set off to force events, such as sealing an area or opening a tunnel, so the story follows its planned path.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: Traps are hazards built into the game itself, so players face the environment rather than each other, unless another player placed them.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Traps that disguise themselves as useful items or helpful effects mislead players into going for something harmful.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Players must plan routes and actions to avoid hazards in order to succeed.

can_cause.name: Surprise Attacks
can_cause.why: When the player does not know a trap is there, it strikes unexpectedly, working like an ambush.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: If players know a trap exists but not exactly where or when it fires, they feel nervous as they proceed.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: A triggered trap forces players to move away before it activates, giving them a limited window to leave.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: A trap becomes an overwhelming event when, once sprung, the player can neither stop its activation nor dodge what it does.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Traps are paired with time limits or scripted sequences so that players who are not watching get caught.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Traps give players a way to remove targets, and they invite planning ahead.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Traps made from destructible objects let players use the environment against others, which requires planning where and when.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Traps let players remove opponents without attacking directly, especially when players can place or move them.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: A trap's harmful effects can be set to affect only certain game elements, such as those representing enemies.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Traps make poking around the world riskier, since players may trigger a hazard while looking for new places.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Traps are elements added into the world that threaten players and can render parts of it dangerous or cut off.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: Traps can help defend something, since they harm those who approach it without a defender attacking.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Traps can block access to areas, either as a barrier or as an effect over the whole region, or open up new ones.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Springing a trap can cause an instant death, which uses up a life.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Nearby traps force players to move more carefully and in more complicated ways to get past them.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Traps constrain where players can safely move and can demand careful movement to avoid them.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: A trap can pretend to be a power-up, so what looks like a reward actually hurts the player.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: Traps in the way make saving someone else more dangerous for the rescuer.

changes.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
changes.why: Some traps, like crushers and flame jets, run on a fixed cycle, so players need rhythmic timing to get past them.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Triggering a trap can destroy units outright, so what it does can change how many units a player keeps.

conflicts_with.name: Safe Havens
conflicts_with.why: A place must be free of harmful effects like traps to be safe, so the two cannot coexist in the same spot.

patterns.name: Obstacles
patterns.what_it_is: Elements that block the shortest path between two places.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Obstacles must sit on routes players want to take and force a detour, a wait, or some action to bypass them. Whether they can be destroyed, moved or ignored by some players defines what they mean for play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Decoration placed off the routes that players take, or an object that can be walked through or around at no cost.
patterns.knobs: size and placement; whether they can be removed or bypassed, and by whom

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: Obstacles placed strategically narrow the available routes into tight passages, so movement is funneled through a few spots and play becomes more challenging.

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: Skilled players can slip past stationary objects or other vehicles by steering and reacting precisely, so dodging obstacles becomes a test of hand skill.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Obstacles that slow, weaken or damage players through environmental effects stand out in the game world because of what they do, and visuals can emphasize this.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Experts can get past several obstacles at once or without spending extra resources, using timing, dexterity or clever route-finding that novices lack.

can_cause.name: Hiding Places
can_cause.why: Opaque obstacles stop players and agents from seeing what is behind them, so they work as basic building blocks for spots to hide.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: When an obstacle such as a locked door blocks the way into a region, players cannot enter until they remove it or have a special ability.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Because obstacles restrict how avatars and units can move or maneuver through a world, they directly impose limits on movement.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Players can treat getting past obstacles as a puzzle, for example by finding the cheapest route or by using portals between places.

can_cause.name: Secret Areas
can_cause.why: Obstacles can hide areas by blocking them from view or making them harder to notice, intentionally or not, so players may miss them.

can_cause.name: Transport Routes
can_cause.why: Placing obstacles so that certain areas are harder to notice can create routes for travel that players must discover.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: Something physically in the way stops movement until removed, for example by a switch, so clearing it is the condition.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Obstacles blocking a narrow passage by their mere presence push players to clear them away.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: An obstacle is not a trap by default, but becomes one when players moving too fast are caught off guard by it.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Non-transparent obstacles block line of sight, which interferes with shooting at targets and changes which places are good for sniping.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Obstacles affect how avatars can move through the world, since they have to get around or past them.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Obstacles placed well in the way of movement, especially by forming choke points, make traveling through the world harder and more demanding.

changes.name: Destructible Objects
changes.why: When a destructible object is destroyed, it can leave behind debris that becomes a new obstacle, so the two can affect each other.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Blocking access to areas or forcing detours is a common reason for placing obstacles on game boards.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Large obstacles make it hard to get an overview of surroundings, which complicates exploring the world.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Big obstacles hide the surroundings from view, so finding your way around becomes more difficult.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Obstacles in game worlds block access to areas, force detours and affect how avatars and units can move.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Levels can contain obstacles that block areas or force detours, shaping the routes players can take.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: Obstacles that are not transparent stop players from seeing past them, cutting off views across the area.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Obstacles limit how avatars and units can steer through boards, worlds or levels, forcing them to find ways around.

changes.name: Moveable Tiles
changes.why: Obstacles can change the direction a tile moves in, which gives players a roundabout way of steering the tiles.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Obstacles slow or block progress and can create choke points, so they shape how movement must be done.

changes.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
changes.why: In rhythm-focused games, hitting an obstacle can serve as the in-world reason for the player's failure to keep the beat.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: Blocking line of sight can make a spot with a good view worse for sniping, while making the spots behind cover better.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Large obstacles make it difficult to survey surroundings, which makes crossing the world harder.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Obstacles affect how units can move through game worlds, as they must go around or past them.

changes.name: Vehicle Sections
changes.why: Higher speeds in vehicle sections mean obstacles are more of a challenge, as there is less time to react.

conflicts_with.name: Warp Zones
conflicts_with.why: If warp zones are available from the beginning, they let players skip past obstacles and so make them pointless as barriers to movement or sight.

patterns.name: Boss Monsters
patterns.what_it_is: Powerful enemies that must be defeated to progress toward the goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A boss must differ in how it is fought, via special abilities, weak points or phases, not just extra health. It should be placed at a point of closure and be foreshadowed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A normal enemy is renamed 'Boss' with a bigger health bar, so the same tactics work and it feels like a slog.
patterns.knobs: boss health and damage; special abilities and weak points; number of phases or lives; placement

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Bosses are tougher than ordinary enemies and call for different play, so they give specific stretches of a game a harder, more demanding feel.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Beating a boss is a goal players must achieve, and because the encounter is planned, defeating it becomes a required target.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Placed at the end of levels or instances, a boss marks a bigger finish point, so players feel a larger chunk of the game is complete.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Players must get past the boss to move on, and its special abilities make defeating it a goal that needs real effort.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Bosses can be planned as the finale of levels, quests or instances, so they act as built-in story beats.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: A boss is a stronger, more special enemy than usual, so meeting one raises the player's sense of tension more than ordinary foes do.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: When a boss is placed at a closure point or designed as a character with a defined nature and history, it fits the game's theme.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Bosses often stand out because of their sheer size, though the pattern can be applied to make them even more noticeable.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: A boss with special abilities forces players to figure out how to beat it, so the fight becomes a puzzle.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Giving bosses special abilities that ordinary enemies lack makes fighting them feel different from the rest of a level.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Bosses can serve as the finale of a game board, though this happens less often than with levels or quests.

changes.name: Instances
changes.why: A boss can act as the finale of an instance, giving that section of play a planned climactic ending.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A boss can close out a level, and a level may even center on a specific boss when it is a finale level.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: A boss can serve as the climactic end of a quest, giving it a planned finale.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: Bosses often guard the resolution of rescue goals, balancing the importance of whoever is being rescued.

conflicts_with.name: Combat
conflicts_with.why: Immunities and weak points can make fighting an ineffective way to beat a boss, so other solutions may work better than fighting.

patterns.name: Red Herrings
patterns.what_it_is: Items or information created to confuse or distract players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decoys must look as plausible as the real clues and cost players something to check. The game must also have real uncertainty so that players cannot tell them apart at once.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A fake clue that is obviously irrelevant at first glance, so it is ignored and does not distract anyone.
patterns.knobs: ratio of false to real clues; how convincing the decoys look; cost of following a false lead

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Misleading items and facts make players work harder to figure out what is true, so reaching the right action becomes more demanding.

can_cause.name: Complex Gameplay
can_cause.why: Decoys add extra outcomes and extra things to weigh, so players juggle more possibilities before deciding what to do.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because false leads sit next to the real one, players can pick among several options even if only one is actually right.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Deciding which items or information deserve attention and which are bait is itself a puzzle players must work out.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Once players know decoys may exist, they can't be sure their efforts will pay off, which raises unease.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Filling a world with irrelevant extras makes it feel fuller and more believable, which helps the setting seem coherent.

changes.name: Conceal
changes.why: Players can place decoys to help hide their real units or plans, making concealment goals easier to achieve.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Mystery stories use false leads to keep players unsure which suspect or clue is the real one.

changes.name: Gain Information
changes.why: Decoys give players wrong or useless data, so collecting accurate knowledge takes more care.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: Players hunting for a needed item can be sent after the wrong objects, making getting the right one harder.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Irrelevant content scattered around the world gives players more to check, making exploration slower and harder.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Extra misleading content in the world makes finding the right way around more difficult.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Decoy objects and information fill the world with content that doesn't serve the goal, adding extra material to the setting.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Levels get filled with useless or misleading items that players must sift through.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Misleading elements in a story make it less certain how events will unfold, and can spring plot surprises.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Fixed plots, especially mysteries, use false leads to keep players guessing about how the story will progress.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Misleading elements send players the wrong way, making the puzzle harder to study properly.

conflicts_with.name: Supporting Goals
conflicts_with.why: Something players take to be a helpful side goal may turn out to be a decoy, so the two can be confused.

patterns.name: Achilles' Heels
patterns.what_it_is: A strong enemy has a weak spot, and hitting it is the easiest way to win.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The target must be really resistant to normal attacks, with one specific weakness that is much more effective. Players must be able to discover it (clues, experimenting) and have the means to exploit it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A weak point is labeled on the enemy but normal attacks work just as well, so nobody needs to look for it.
patterns.knobs: how much more damage the weak point takes; how hidden it is; what is needed to exploit it

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing where a foe's or your own hidden weak point lies is valuable information that players can carry across encounters and use to their advantage.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Because a weak spot is the key to winning or staying safe, players plan ahead in the long run to exploit it or guard it.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Players work out the concrete moment-to-moment steps needed to reach and strike a weak point, or to shield their own.

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: When a character or unit has a weak spot others can exploit, players are pushed to hide that piece while showing or sacrificing others.

can_cause.name: Evade
can_cause.why: A weak spot on a unit gives players a reason to shield that particular spot, which creates a goal of evading attacks there.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Games with enemies push players to try different attacks until they discover the particular weakness that works against them.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Finding out an enemy's weak point is a kind of information target, so discovering it counts as a goal of gaining information.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Working out the hidden weak spot of an enemy or boss is a puzzle for the player to figure out.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Giving certain enemies a particular weakness makes players handle those enemies differently, which varies the encounters in a level.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: A player's own character can be given a hidden weak point, which then has to be protected or kept secret.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Tough bosses are the usual holders of a weak point, so beating them demands finding and hitting it rather than brute force.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Characters under a player's control may carry a special weakness, though this is less common and forces players to guard it.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fights change because the weak point is the only or easiest way to win, so players aim for it instead of fighting normally.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Harm can only be dealt, or is dealt much more easily, through the special weakness, which changes how damage is achieved.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Goals of destroying a target are reshaped because the target can only be removed by exploiting its special weakness.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies, especially tough ones, are the typical owners of a weak spot, which turns beating them into a search for the right attack.

changes.name: Invulnerabilities
changes.why: The weak spot punctures an otherwise complete immunity, making it partial instead of absolute.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: Goals of getting past an obstacle are changed because the obstacle yields only to its particular weak point.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: Exploiting a weak point may need a certain tool, which gives that tool an extra, specific purpose.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Some weak points can only be hit with a certain weapon, which gives that weapon a special role.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Combining specific strengths and weaknesses can leave a unit with one critical weakness, motivating players to hide or evade.

conflicts_with.name: Invulnerabilities
conflicts_with.why: The weak point exists to break a complete immunity, so it works against the very invulnerability that it is built on.

patterns.name: Incompatible Goals
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: two or more goals that cannot be completed together because they exclude each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The goals must truly exclude each other in play, either for one player or between players, and be known to those pursuing them. Players need to feel the cost of choosing one over another.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Goals that are described as conflicting but can all be completed in the same game, so no choice has to be made.
patterns.knobs: how many goals clash; whether they clash for one player or between players; how soon the conflict is visible

can_cause.name: Collaborative Actions
can_cause.why: When goals clash only for a single player, different players can each take one goal and act together so that all of them get completed.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: When one player holds several goals that can't all be done together, they must struggle with which to give up or postpone.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Teammates who share an overall aim but hold goals that exclude each other end up competing against their own side.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: If clashing goals can end with a player being removed from the game, the aim becomes being the one who remains.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Teammates with clashing goals must weigh helping the group against pursuing their own aim, creating a tension between personal and shared benefit.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since finishing one goal tends to play out differently than finishing another, each game session can unfold in its own way.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Clashing goals bring tension and conflict into the story, so the narrative mirrors the opposition found in the gameplay goals.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: When one player can't do all goals together, they must choose which to chase or in what order, shaping their plans.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Having to choose among goals that can't all be met affects how a player acts out their character's choices.

changes.name: Sidequests
changes.why: Because a player can't pursue every goal at once, they must decide which side goals to take on and when.

changes.name: Configuration
changes.why: If two arrangement goals need the same elements that cannot be reused, completing one rules out the other, so players must choose between them.

conflicts_with.name: Mutual Goals
conflicts_with.why: A set of goals can't both exclude each other and be shared by everyone, so the two kinds can't describe the same goals.

conflicts_with.name: Tied Results
conflicts_with.why: Tied results let several players meet the same goal together, which is exactly what incompatible goals rule out.

patterns.name: Movement Limitations
patterns.what_it_is: Changes that make moving worse than it was before.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Movement must already matter in the game, and the limitation must be felt in play, with players needing to plan around it. It should be tied to places, states or enemies.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A slowdown so small or so easily avoided that players ignore it and route exactly as before.
patterns.knobs: how much speed or range is lost; how long it lasts; terrain costs

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: If movement is hampered badly enough, players can only do well in certain places or situations, which carves out zones where they are competent.

can_cause.name: Damage
can_cause.why: Slowing or hindering movement can stand in for or accompany hit damage as a way of hurting a player's capabilities.

can_cause.name: Decreased Abilities
can_cause.why: Making movement worse, such as slower or harder to steer, is a direct way to weaken what a player can do.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a player temporarily loses all ability to move, they are stuck waiting with nothing useful to do.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Hindered movement can be used as a punishment instead of, or alongside, losing health.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Being restricted in how you can move makes situations feel more pressing and risky.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Capping top speed for those in front in a race slows leaders and keeps the field bunched.

can_cause.name: Critical Hits
can_cause.why: A critical hit can leave the target hampered in how it moves, which is an extra consequence beyond health loss.

can_cause.name: Handicap Systems
can_cause.why: Slowing or restricting some racers, or giving others a head start, handicaps them in a race.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: Since moving is harder, escaping or dodging threats becomes a tougher goal to achieve.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: With fewer movement options available, the player has fewer choices about what to do.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Hindered movement often makes getting around the game world harder.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: These limitations are negative changes applied directly to how movement works, such as lowering speed or making control harder.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Slowing racers, for example the leader, helps balance a race and can serve as a handicap so others can catch up.

patterns.name: Player Physical Prowess
patterns.what_it_is: The game's outcome depends on how well players control their own bodies.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Tasks must really test strength, endurance, precision or reflexes, and be scored so that ability decides the result. The demand must be clearly measured.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game labelled 'active' where physical skill makes no difference to the result.
patterns.knobs: how demanding the physical tasks are; time limits; how strictly performance is scored

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because players must physically perform activities, they are likely to train those abilities outside the game, so exercise spills over into real life.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: Physical abilities can be improved with practice, so players can get better at the game by developing their bodies' skills.

can_cause.name: Performance Uncertainty
can_cause.why: Outcomes depend on what players' bodies can do in the moment, which varies and cannot be fully predicted, so results stay uncertain.

can_cause.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
can_cause.why: Players have to actually carry out specific physical actions themselves, so what they do in the real world directly changes the game.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: Since players must physically act things out, their bodily skill sets how well they can perform those required actions.

changes.name: Physical Navigation
changes.why: When games involve moving through real places, players' physical ability affects who gets to the goal locations first.

changes.name: Robotic Players
changes.why: Robots must be designed around the physical demands of the game and balanced against what human players' bodies can do.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: When a game tests bodily ability, tiredness affects how well people perform, so swapping in reserves lets players or coaches change how uncertain performance is.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Needing bodily ability lets who a person physically is decide how they do, so outside traits leak into the game.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Players differ in physical ability and in willingness to improve it, which makes it harder for the game to fit varied groups.

patterns.name: Ghosts
patterns.what_it_is: Records of players' past attempts, including your own, become opponents in a new game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must record player actions and replay them in the same setup so the ghost's performance can be compared directly. Decide whether ghosts affect the player and whose runs get saved, and the setting needs a clear measure such as time or score.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A ghost that is always the same fixed, designer-made run, or one that is shown but has no way to compare or race, so there is nothing at stake against it.
patterns.knobs: whose runs are saved and how they are chosen; whether the ghost can affect the player; whether runs are shared

can_cause.name: AI Players
can_cause.why: Although a ghost cannot react to anyone, the game itself replays its recorded moves, so it acts as a very basic computer-controlled opponent.

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each person plays a whole session at a different time, and results are compared afterward through the recording, so players never need to be present together.

can_cause.name: Avatars
can_cause.why: A ghost is a recorded player's presence in the game world, so it can be treated as a character that stands in for that player.

can_cause.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
can_cause.why: Ghosts are usually displayed as a see-through figure on the track or map, showing where an earlier attempt was at each moment.

can_cause.name: High Score Lists
can_cause.why: A ghost keeps an entire past session rather than just a number, so it works like a leaderboard entry you can actually watch and play against.

can_cause.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
can_cause.why: Many people's recorded sessions fill your game, so you effectively share the world with others while each of you plays alone.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: Playing against others' recorded runs gives a solo game a feel of multiplayer competition, with full sessions finished before results are compared.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Because ghosts bring in time limits, the player ends up trying to get to the goal before the recorded run does.

can_cause.name: Replays
can_cause.why: A ghost is simply an earlier session's recorded actions played back again inside the current session.

can_cause.name: Speedruns
can_cause.why: Having a recorded run to beat adds a time limit, which pushes players to finish the same course as fast as possible.

can_cause.name: Time Limits
can_cause.why: Beating a recorded run means finishing before it does, which makes the ghost's pace act as a clock the player must beat.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Ghosts add extra entities and sequences of recorded actions to the world, so it contains more going on than it would without them.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Few game settings include see-through beings that nobody can touch or affect, so a ghost often does not fit what the story world allows.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Few game themes include immaterial agents whose actions cannot be influenced, so adding ghosts can clash with the setting a game is built around.

patterns.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
patterns.what_it_is: The more successfully the player plays, the harder the challenges become.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Success must feed back into a harder next challenge, such as stronger enemies, bigger waves or tougher levels, and the climb must be steady and outpace most players' skill. Without an end condition, or with one far away, the difficulty keeps rising instead of flattening.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies get bigger numbers or new skins, but skilled players still cruise through because nothing demands more skill.
patterns.knobs: difficulty growth rate per success; step size and ceiling of the scaling curve

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because each challenge gets harder, players keep meeting tasks that stretch them, so the game is built to give them demanding play at some point.

can_cause.name: FUBAR Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Difficulty keeps rising until players are in overwhelming situations, which sets them up to enjoy things going completely wrong.

can_cause.name: Further Player Improvement Potential
can_cause.why: Once difficulty climbs past what a player can currently do, there is always room for them to get better at the game.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Each time a player beats a tougher challenge, they complete a bigger goal, so the climb produces larger and larger finishing points.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: Since the game pushes players into overwhelming situations, they eventually fail, and that dramatic failure can itself be fun.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Rising difficulty keeps players unsure they will succeed, and this uncertainty is a main reason designers include the pattern.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: A game that can never be won can keep making challenges harder indefinitely, so this pattern fits it best and works there most reliably.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Stories usually want tension to build as they go, and steadily harder gameplay supports that same rise.

patterns.name: Generic Adversaries
patterns.what_it_is: Enemies that cannot be told apart from one another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: One template spawned in numbers, simple enough to be interchangeable, with a defined spawn timing and place. Some small random variation or loot variety helps stop them feeling flat.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Enemies that look different (new skins or names) but behave and fight exactly the same, or a single 'crowd' that never poses a threat.
patterns.knobs: how many appear and how often they spawn; how strong they are; how much variation is allowed

can_cause.name: Enemies
can_cause.why: Because every adversary of a type behaves the same, designers can fill the world with large numbers of hostile opponents from a single template.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Since these foes are plentiful and easy to spawn on demand, players can be given endless fights to work through for progress.

can_cause.name: Repetitive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Each of these foes calls for the same actions and solutions, so facing them again and again gets monotonous unless something else changes.

can_cause.name: Units
can_cause.why: A unit is one of many interchangeable pieces, so having identical adversaries is exactly what makes such units possible.

can_cause.name: Waves
can_cause.why: Because the opponents are identical and can be created as needed, a designer can send them at the player in large groups, one batch after another.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: Enemies that are all alike can serve as NPCs, though varied looks or traits help them feel less interchangeable.

patterns.name: Quizzes
patterns.what_it_is: A set of questions asked to players during the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Questions must fit the audience, be well written and have fair answer options. The number of questions and format should suit their role in the game.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Questions are shown but are so easy or guessable that knowledge makes no difference.
patterns.knobs: number of questions; difficulty; multiple choice or free answer

can_cause.name: Lucky Guess Solutions
can_cause.why: When players don't know an answer, which is likely since nobody knows everything, they can just guess and sometimes get it right by chance.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Players can remember answers they've seen before and carry that knowledge into later sessions, which makes it a way to get better at the quiz.

can_cause.name: Minigames
can_cause.why: A quiz can be a short side activity inside a bigger game, and how many questions it has depends on that role.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Because players often don't know every answer, they have to work out or deduce a response from what they do know.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: Players who already know the facts being asked about answer more easily, so what they learned outside the game gives them an edge.

can_cause.name: Trial and Error Solutions
can_cause.why: With multiple choice questions and several allowed attempts, players can try options one after another until they hit the correct one.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: Once a player has learned a question's correct answer, there is nothing left to figure out about it, so playing the same quiz again is less interesting.

patterns.name: Waves
patterns.what_it_is: Attacks at set times by a large number of identical enemies.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Groups of enemies must arrive on a schedule with pauses between, with escalating size or type, and defeat must threaten the player. Rests need to be long enough to prepare.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A steady trickle of enemies labeled as waves, with no clear groups, pauses or growth.
patterns.knobs: wave size; time between waves; growth rate; enemy mix and resistances

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Sending many foes at the player in one timed burst forces the player to handle a lot at once, which makes play demanding.

can_cause.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
can_cause.why: Because later waves usually come harder than earlier ones, the player faces steadily tougher opposition as the game goes on.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Waves change how enemies reach the player, bunching them into timed massed attacks instead of letting them appear in a steady trickle.

patterns.name: Game Worlds
patterns.what_it_is: Fictional worlds in which the game takes place.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The world must actually define where things are and how they move or interact, with boundaries and rules that tie into the actions. The fiction should explain and support the rules, not sit apart from them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A fictional setting used only as wallpaper or a title, while the rules would work the same on a plain grid.
patterns.knobs: size and boundaries; continuous vs discrete space; what elements and resources are placed in it

can_cause.name: Dedicated Game Facilitators
can_cause.why: When a world must keep its state between play sessions and nobody wants the bookkeeping, a computer or other dedicated helper has to hold that state.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Having a fictional world gives the game a setting that its elements and characters' behavior can be made to fit, so consistency becomes possible.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: Because the world is a place with laid-out objects and details, the way things are shown and positioned can tell story without any dialogue.

can_cause.name: Explicit Random Seeds
can_cause.why: When worlds are generated with randomness, letting players type in a chosen seed lets them rebuild the exact same world again.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: A world that can't be seen all at once, and may hide secrets, gives players a reason to go look around.

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: Maps and landmarks help players find their way around a world, and the world's shape and size make that finding-your-way a real task.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: If designers deliberately plan the order and layout of events in a world, the world itself carries a fixed story path.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: A fictional world gives players a place and inhabitants to act as and within, which is the basis for playing a role.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: When players must move avatars or units through a world, getting from one place to another naturally becomes a goal.

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: Information in this pattern mostly reaches players through the game world, so the world is the main carrier of what the single character learns.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Detailed worlds in games that run themselves leave players to maintain and describe the world, which is upkeep.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: In a world where the viewpoint can be moved, such as with a god or third-person view, players can survey the state.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Worlds that are randomly generated or built by the players differ between sessions, so the setting offers new challenges each time.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Randomizing game worlds, or letting players construct them, makes each instance different.

changes.name: Expansion
changes.why: How big a world is, what its terrain looks like, and where resources lie all shape how players can spread out into it.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: A world's layout and contents constrain how players can steer through it, and maneuvering in turn changes how the world is experienced.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: A world naturally limits where players can go, and how they move affects how the world feels to them.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Where resources are placed gives a world character, and how scarce or reachable they are changes how players treat them.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
