conflicts_with.why: Invisible walls used to bound an open world are not part of the fiction, so they can break the world's believability.

conflicts_with.name: Invisible Walls
conflicts_with.why: Using them to keep players inside a world's edges is practical, but they don't fit the fiction and can undercut its consistency.

patterns.name: Levels
patterns.what_it_is: A part of the game where all the action takes place until a goal or end condition is reached.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each level needs boundaries, a goal or end condition, and real differences in content or play, not only looks. The number and order of levels shape pacing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Levels differ only in colors or theme, while the play stays the same.
patterns.knobs: number of levels; how they differ; how much randomness; length of each

can_cause.name: Campaigns
can_cause.why: Chaining levels lets a designer move a story forward in controlled steps, so a series of levels naturally becomes a campaign.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Designers know exactly which challenges each level holds, so they can keep some levels simple and relaxed.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because the designer controls what each level contains, they can deliberately build levels that demand more from the player.

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Every level has an end, so finishing one gives a natural stopping point, stronger when you cannot go back.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Levels each show a different part of a larger world, which hints that the world is bigger and holds the game together.

can_cause.name: Ever Increasing Difficulty
can_cause.why: Making each successive level harder steadily raises the challenge until the game is finished, or forever if levels are generated.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: A level is only a portion of the game, so failing it is separate from losing the entire game.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When several levels are available at once, as in Super Mario, players decide which one to play.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Moving into a new level puts the player in front of new game elements, adding them to the game as a whole.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: A level assumes another one follows, so finding the way to the next level becomes a short-term exploration goal.

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: Levels shrink the world to a bounded area, limiting how much players must find their way around, though designers must still plan routes.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: A level can either be a piece of a bigger world or be the entire world, so levels define how the world is delimited.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Finishing each level serves the larger aim of finishing the game, giving players smaller goals nested inside a bigger one.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Completing a level feels like a clear ending while more levels remain, and this is stronger when saving happens only between levels.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: While play is confined to one level, the rest of the game world is closed off and cannot be reached.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Unless randomly generated, levels are authored in advance, so designers can fix the order in which the story unfolds.

can_cause.name: Quick Travel
can_cause.why: Completing a level usually sends players straight to another level, skipping the distance in between.

can_cause.name: Scenes
can_cause.why: A level is essentially a scene whose boundaries are clearly defined, so it works as a distinct unit of the game.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Levels are limited chunks of world, so reaching the exit is a natural goal, often marked by opening a door or beating a boss.

can_cause.name: Unknown Goals
can_cause.why: Each level can have different end conditions, so players may not know what they will need to accomplish in the next one.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Levels can differ in structure, goals and activities, so moving between them changes what players do.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Short levels solved as puzzles can each be viewed as a separate game, and the series of them forms the larger one.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Small levels that each work like a complete game let players stop after a short, satisfying chunk of play.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: When levels are randomly produced for each game, players meet different layouts and challenges on every playthrough.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: In games with unlimited tries, which levels a player has cleared serves like points for comparing progress.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: Different levels can carry their own rules, so progressing from one level to another swaps which rules apply.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Dividing a world into levels means players only have to find their way in a smaller area at a time, making it easier.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Levels that require different skills mean mastering the game takes more skills, or the flexibility to switch between them.

changes.name: Hotseating
changes.why: Finishing a level is a natural moment for the next player to take over the game.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: In games with movement, players are typically held within the current level until it is completed.

patterns.name: Game Boards
patterns.what_it_is: A surface where it is easy to move elements and keep track of their positions relative to each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The layout must carry spatial relations that matter to the rules, such as movement, regions and positions. It should organize components the game needs.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A board is included, but it is just a backdrop; positions on it have no rule effect.
patterns.knobs: size and layout; number and type of regions; connections between spaces

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Because boards often work as maps, a board can show the game's world and the places within it that players move through.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: A board can be built with blocked spaces inside it or around its edges, giving it areas pieces cannot enter.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: Making a board is much like making a level, especially when one game uses several different boards in turn.

can_cause.name: Score Tracks
can_cause.why: When a board records how players move tokens from place to place to win, that progress itself acts as a score track.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: In board and tabletop games, a board or map used with dice and tokens is something outside the fictional world, so it counts as non-diegetic.

conflicts_with.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: A physical board forces players to be near it to play, which works against gameplay that can happen anywhere.

patterns.name: Persistent Game Worlds
patterns.what_it_is: The world exists by itself, whether or not anyone is playing it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Servers or facilitators must keep the world running continuously, with state updated even when players are absent. Characters and items must be tracked over time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A world that exists only while players are logged in or that resets each session, called persistent in marketing only.
patterns.knobs: what state persists; how the world updates while players are away; reset schedule

can_cause.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because the world keeps running without everyone present, players can take part at different times instead of all gathering together, so play becomes partly asynchronous.

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: A world that continues over time has specifics that must be found, described, and updated, creating state-handling work.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Items, characters and invested effort stay valuable over time, so players do things outside the game such as trading for real money, and storytelling adds more.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because storytelling and trading go beyond the world's own rules, they produce outside effects like real-money sales and out-of-game narrative activity.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Since the world is always available and latecomers and drop-ins are supported, players can pick when they play instead of following a fixed schedule.

can_cause.name: Internal Rivalry
can_cause.why: Social contact accumulates over a long time in an ongoing world, which lets competition between players develop alongside guilds and status.

can_cause.name: Temporal Consistency
can_cause.why: Since the world must preserve what happened to characters and items, it can't be undone, and designers aim for events to stay consistent over time.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Resources, building, and character growth give players many things of value, so there are plenty of chances to include trading among them.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: A world that keeps going between sessions lets regenerating resources, delayed effects and timed events give you reasons to return.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: A world that continues over time gives items lasting value beyond one session, making them meaningful to trade.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: A world that lasts needs new rules or added content, otherwise players run out of anything left to explore.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Listed as combining with Player-Planned Development or Character Development to create Investments, but the page gives no explanation.

can_cause.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
can_cause.why: Because the world continues over time, purchased advantages keep their value for a long while, making buying worthwhile.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: A world that keeps its state makes the results of building or character growth last, so work is not lost.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Together with construction or creative control, the lasting worlds players make end up different from one game instance to another.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Since there is no set end point, long-term growth of a character stays valuable, so players treat it as an investment they own.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: The world has to keep track of characters even when their players are away, and attachment to them grows over time.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: The attachment players feel for long-lasting things can spread from their characters to the groups they belong to.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: The world must remember items, though short-lived ones like power-ups needn't persist, and items can be traded for real-world money.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Persistence makes a game world exist independently of sessions, which changes how players relate to it and how they behave in it.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Persistent worlds suit very large player groups best, and such games let a single character's play run for years.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: A world that continues between sessions makes the most sense when many players share it, and lets their social interaction grow over time.

changes.name: Player-Planned Development
changes.why: Because the world lasts with no fixed endpoint, players regard their long-term plans for a character as an investment they own.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Because the world endures, players may play their characters more cautiously, and roleplaying becomes the basis for the world's ongoing storytelling.

changes.name: Spawn Points
changes.why: When a world keeps updating between visits, spawn points must keep activating, with care taken not to create too many instances.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: These games need the world to keep updating at each tick whether or not players act in between.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Visiting only works without players being online together if the game world keeps existing and changing between sessions.

conflicts_with.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
conflicts_with.why: In worlds that keep running, differences grow over time and newcomers are measured against long-time players.

conflicts_with.name: Character Development
conflicts_with.why: In a world that keeps running, those who started earlier or played more have stronger characters, so latecomers are at a disadvantage.

conflicts_with.name: Crafting
conflicts_with.why: In lasting worlds, repeated or chain crafting can flood the economy with items unless the effort matches their worth.

conflicts_with.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
conflicts_with.why: Because the game never ends, it is hard to keep making closures steadily more intense, so the two rarely combine.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptibility
conflicts_with.why: The world keeps changing even when you're away, so stepping out can still bring negative consequences.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Renewable Resources
conflicts_with.why: A world that goes on forever has trouble with resources that run out for good, since play must still work once they are gone.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Crafting and character growth accumulate over time in a persistent world, which can ruin fairness between players.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: A world that continues without end cannot follow a fixed plot, so it must rely on never-ending stories or small scripted pieces.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Without a never-ending story, a world that goes on forever struggles to keep its theme consistent, especially when it has small scripted pieces.

patterns.name: Extra-Game Consequences
patterns.what_it_is: Events in the game affect something outside it, for better or worse.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game's results must really feed into something outside the game state, such as prizes, money, the next game session's rules or another game. Players must know about the link and care about it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'real-world prize' or carry-over that players find worthless or that never actually changes anything outside the match.
patterns.knobs: what outside thing results are tied to (money, rewards, future games); how large the stakes are

can_cause.name: Altruistic Actions
can_cause.why: Letting in-game purchases or play send real money or goods to a good cause gives players the experience of being generous, as in buying special seeds for charity.

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Giving feedback for basic actions that doesn't alter the game state can still make clicking feel rewarding and encourage players to keep doing it.

can_cause.name: Legacy Games
can_cause.why: Results from one play session can add, remove or change components or rules, so later sessions of the same game play out differently.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When play can affect things beyond the game, such as money or emotions, players feel more is at stake and so more tension.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Stakes set outside the rules, such as on a bet, still make players bound to an outcome, though the designer can't control them.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Quick games without lasting outside effects let players test freely, since a failed session can simply be restarted.

changes.name: Investments
changes.why: Entry fees and betting tie what players put into the game to real-world costs, and time and effort invested can also gain outside value.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: Outside consequences can be linked to in-game penalties, adding real losses or lost standing to what happens in the game.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Extra-game consequences can add real-world prizes or social standing that are often tied to corresponding in-game rewards.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Scores can be converted to real money at a set rate, which makes points in the game matter outside it and creates gambling.

changes.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
changes.why: Games played in public spaces can intentionally be set up so that the outside effects feed back into the game state.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Positive outside-the-game recognition can offset too-hard challenges.

changes.name: Tension
changes.why: Real-world rewards or penalties can add to any tension already coming from play.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Telling players about consequences outside the game brings in things that don't belong to the game's own world, which breaks its internal consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Anonymity is used to prevent harm from players oversharing with strangers, so real-world consequences of play become much less likely, which clashes with them occurring.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Consequences outside the game are not part of the game's theme, so informing players of them clashes with the setting.

patterns.name: Strategic Locations
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the world where control or access gives an advantage.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The location must give a real advantage, such as resources, safety or access, and be noticeable to players. The advantage must be balanced between sides or contested.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A prominent landmark that gives no advantage when held, so players ignore it.
patterns.knobs: size of the advantage; how many such places; how visible they are; how evenly they are distributed

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: Once a player reaches a valuable spot, staying put there to keep others from using it becomes a natural goal.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: When locations can be owned, their value makes players want to take them over through controlling the area.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: If players know valuable places exist but not where, they set out to search the world for them.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: After reaching a valuable place, players may defend it so opponents cannot get access to it.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Because some places give lasting advantages, players can remember where they are and use that knowledge later.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Knowing which places are valuable, especially when their worth comes from map layout, is knowledge players can carry between plays.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Players who know where the valuable spots are can build long-term plans around them, weighing risk against reward.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: When players know where a valuable spot is, they set a goal of travelling to it.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Identifying which places in the game matter strategically is something players want to learn, so it works as an information target.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Valuable places on a board, such as the center in Chess, change how much each position matters.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Players who remember valuable places use that knowledge to find their way around the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Valuable places in a world focus play on certain parts and change how much each area matters.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: Holding a valuable place gives an advantage, which suits goals about being the one in control.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Valuable spots in a level focus play on specific parts and change how players move through it.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Knowing valuable places helps players choose the best routes when competing to reach them.

changes.name: Spawning
changes.why: If players can pick where they appear, knowing valuable places affects which spawn point they choose.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: When places can be owned, valuable ones become the territory players most want to take.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Uneven access to key places gives some players advantages over others.

patterns.name: Inaccessible Areas
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the world that can be seen but not visited.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The areas must be visible and be blocked by a believable barrier, and the blocking must be reliable. If players are meant to get in later, a visible condition for access helps.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An area that looks blocked but can be reached by an exploit, or that is blocked with no visible reason so it feels like an arbitrary wall.
patterns.knobs: how much of the world is blocked; what blocks it; whether and how access is later unlocked

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Blocked-off areas make a small, limited play space feel like part of a bigger world, so the setting seems believable and consistent.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: When the playable space surrounds an unreachable zone, that zone acts as an environmental effect; lava, water or poison also make areas unenterable.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Visible but unreachable surroundings and entities emerging from them make a small play area look larger than it really is.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: Because players cannot enter these areas, their options for where to move are restricted, which is a limit on movement.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Opening areas only at set moments, such as after goals or quests, lets designers unfold the story in their intended order.

can_cause.name: Sniper Locations
can_cause.why: Spots that can't be entered but still allow shooting or throwing let someone attack from there without being reached.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: When some players or units can reach an area others cannot, that area gives the first group a valuable advantage.

can_cause.name: Transport Routes
can_cause.why: Blocking everything except certain paths in a large free-movement space turns those paths into the routes players must use.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Seeing a blocked area, especially one with useful things inside, gives players a goal of finding a way to reach it.

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: Blocking off parts of the space leaves only a few openings between regions, and those remaining openings act as choke points.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: When an area is sealed off and guarded by enemies, players must clear those enemies to proceed, making removal necessary.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Keeping certain characters out of an area leaves it unreachable for threats, which makes it a refuge.

changes.name: Dialogues
changes.why: Blocked areas stop movement but not other actions, so characters can still talk across them.

changes.name: Environmental Storytelling
changes.why: Controlling which places are reachable and when lets designers reveal the world's story gradually through what players can see.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Closing off places removes options, so players have less say in where they go.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Unreachable areas can ring a board or sit inside it, shaping where pieces can go.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Players must work out routes around or into blocked places, which changes how they find their way through the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Unreachable areas can surround the playable space so all action stays inside, while the world still seems bigger.

changes.name: Laning
changes.why: Unreachable areas placed between lanes force players to stay in their lane instead of crossing over.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Levels can be fenced in by unreachable areas or have blocked pockets inside them, shaping where play happens.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Blocked areas stop players and units from moving into or out of certain places, so movement must go around them.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: Small blocked pockets can lie along a route, and blocking everything else leaves just the route to travel.

changes.name: Scripted Information Sequences
changes.why: Showing the events in a place players can see but not enter keeps them from disturbing the set story without it feeling forced.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If the reason an area can't be entered doesn't fit the game's setting, such as an invisible wall, the theme feels broken.

conflicts_with.name: Vehicles
conflicts_with.why: Vehicles usually travel more easily, possibly across other terrain, so they can undercut the reasons an area was made unreachable and clash with the theme.

patterns.name: Territories
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the world that belong to one of the inhabitants of the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Ownership must be clearly marked and able to change hands, and owning a territory must bring a benefit. Players need means to take or defend them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Regions have names and colours but owning them gives nothing, so nobody fights over them.
patterns.knobs: number and size of territories; benefits of owning; cost of capturing

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: When territories are treated as player constructs, they aren't part of a player's focus loci, so land parcels can act as abstract things the player manages.

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Territories give a formal structure to area control by defining which areas are owned and what holding them means, though the two can also work separately.

can_cause.name: Expansion
can_cause.why: When adding new territories becomes the main way a player grows their abstract holdings, play turns into phases centered on expanding.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: If territories hold location-fixed abilities that are scarce, such as supply points, those abilities become privileged and worth fighting over.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: Because territories can change hands, they become something players compete for and count as assets, especially when they contain resource generators.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Since territories can be lost, players must worry about which ones to defend, and that worry creates tension.

can_cause.name: Zone of Control
can_cause.why: Territories are usually passive, but they can be set up so that the owned area also exerts influence over neighboring space, as in Civilization.

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Construct Development
can_cause.why: Gaining more territories or improving them strengthens the player's construct, as in the Civilization series.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Controlling territory can be the reason for an ownership goal when tied to area control, elimination, investments or control transfer.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Formally defined territories give control clear targets and let the game recognise who holds what.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Territories split a game world into domains held by different players, changing how the world is divided up and played over.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Territories divide a level into separate domains held by different players, changing how the space is structured.

changes.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
changes.why: Players may need to own a territory to use abilities tied to it, either through what it contains or its nature, so ownership gates those abilities.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Gaining territories is one way a construct can develop and grow.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Showing ownership usually means drawing a colored overlay on the world, which is not something that exists inside the game world's fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
conflicts_with.why: Ownership is shown by overlays placed on the world itself, and such interface elements don't belong to the game's fictional setting.

patterns.name: Safe Havens
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the game world where game elements are safe from any threat.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The place must be truly shielded from traps, enemies and other players, by access rules or disabled hostile actions. It also needs a reason to go out again, such as risk and reward outside, or it just becomes a hiding spot.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pretty calm-looking area that enemies can still walk into or that still damages you, so it protects nothing.
patterns.knobs: where havens are and how many; what they block; whether they expire or need a condition to enter

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Placing resource generators inside a haven gives a team a protected source of supplies, which helps even out the advantage between sides.

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: When players have useful things to do inside the haven, such as resupplying, they tend to stay there rather than venture out.

can_cause.name: Check Points
can_cause.why: Havens act as natural stopping points along a route, so players can treat reaching one as a milestone while crossing the world.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Some havens make it impossible for your own actions to hurt you, so players can freely try things without fear of consequences.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Because a haven stops attacks in that spot, the ability to attack is effectively tied to place and unavailable there.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: If there are meaningful small things to do inside a haven, players can relax and tinker there without pressure.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Havens act as checkpoints and strategic spots, so players think ahead about how to reach them and what to do there.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Since havens act as checkpoints on a journey, their positions become valuable places that players deliberately aim for.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Since nobody can attack in a neutral haven, players feel safe enough to meet and swap goods with each other.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Spawning avatars can be shielded by havens so they are not attacked the moment they enter the world.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: Pieces or characters inside a haven cannot be taken, which changes how capturing works.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting is impossible inside a haven, but it exists only in contrast to the rest of the world, so combat is shaped rather than ruled out.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: Elements inside a haven cannot be removed by attackers, so elimination actions work differently there.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Special protected squares on a board stop attacks on pieces standing there.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Havens carve out protected zones within a dangerous world, defining safe areas against everything else.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Havens can stop attacks within or between levels, giving players a protected break point.

changes.name: Pervasive Gameplay
changes.why: Safe areas let location-based play avoid interfering with other activities in particular places while play continues elsewhere.

changes.name: Spawn Points
changes.why: A haven around where characters appear prevents enemies from attacking them as soon as they enter.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Havens work as checkpoints along a route, giving players reachable goals while crossing the world.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units placed in havens are protected from hostile actions, and can also be made immune to dangers others face.

changes.name: Player Killing
changes.why: Marking some areas of the game world as off-limits to killing lets designers control where and how much it occurs.

conflicts_with.name: Camping
conflicts_with.why: Protected spots attract campers, yet that same protection discourages anyone from camping near them.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Safe places let players relax, which reduces stress, so they can undercut the pressure a game builds.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A safe zone may seem unexplained in the setting, so it needs an in-world reason to fit the theme.

conflicts_with.name: Traps
conflicts_with.why: A place must be free of harmful effects like traps to be safe, so the two cannot coexist in the same spot.

patterns.name: Warp Zones
patterns.what_it_is: Links between distant places in the world that make them neighbors.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Entrances and exits must connect distant places with clear activation rules, and the shortcuts must matter for travel, loops or map topology. Their effect on obstacles and exploration should be considered.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A portal between two spots that are already next to each other, or one used only for cutscenes.
patterns.knobs: number and placement; destinations; activation conditions; one-way or two-way; who can create them

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Warp zones are often set up in linked pairs, so a player who goes through one can come back through the other, which keeps the world believable.

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: A warp zone inside the world can be shown as a visible element of the surroundings, such as a portal or magical effect.

can_cause.name: Flanking Routes
can_cause.why: When players can build their own warp zones, as engineers do in Team Fortress 2, they can open unexpected paths to attack from the side.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: If a warp zone must be switched on each time, players decide for themselves when and whether to skip across the world.

can_cause.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
can_cause.why: Warp zones placed inside the world can also appear as interface-style map markers rather than as objects that belong to the fiction.

can_cause.name: Installations
can_cause.why: A point-to-point warp zone inside the world can take the form of a built structure in the setting, such as a teleporter.

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: Warp zones give players a way to travel between places where ordinary routes do not work.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Warp zones can appear or be revealed as the story unfolds, and can carry players to the spot the story needs next.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Being able to create warp zones is itself a special movement power that lets a character skip across the world.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: In Portal, players place their own warp zones to get past obstacles, so using them is itself the puzzle.

can_cause.name: Quick Travel
can_cause.why: Warp zones let players jump swiftly between separated parts of the game world instead of traveling the whole way.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Edge warp zones that are always active let a flat map behave like a round world, so the setting stays coherent.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Boards and levels more often contain warp zones because moving between them is usually done by quick travel.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Because text-game moves are really warps, going north then south may not bring you back, so players must puzzle out the layout.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Warp zones link distant or separate parts of a world, even whole distinct worlds like Minecraft's Nether, changing how the space is connected.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Levels that are not physically joined seem connected because the game moves players between them once objectives are done.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Warp zones change how players can move by letting them skip across space where normal routes would not work.

changes.name: Obstacles
changes.why: A warp zone can bypass whatever stood in the way, making obstacles pointless, especially if it is available from the start.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If a zone itself, or the areas it leads to, aren't part of the world, using it reveals the fiction as constructed.

conflicts_with.name: Obstacles
conflicts_with.why: If warp zones are available from the beginning, they let players skip past obstacles and so make them pointless as barriers to movement or sight.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Warp zones can break the theme by pointing to unreachable areas, or by skipping the time that such travel should take.

conflicts_with.name: Transport Routes
conflicts_with.why: Warping is an alternative to routes and jumps between places without a believable physical connection, which undercuts the world's consistency.

patterns.name: Conditional Passageways
patterns.what_it_is: A passage is open only if a condition is met, like a key, level, or quest.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The passage must be blocked for real until a condition is met, and the condition should require something the player does or gets. The player should be able to see the blockage and learn how to open it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A door looks locked but opens with a trivial action or no real requirement, or the player can walk around it.
patterns.knobs: what is required to open it; how visible the requirement is; whether it stays open or can close again

can_cause.name: Access Rewards
can_cause.why: Passing through the barrier means you met its requirement, so getting past it is itself the prize for what you did.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: When the requirements are known and involve learning or mastering something, players pursue that skill-building just to get through.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: When the requirement is collecting a particular item, such as a key or card, players set out to acquire it to pass.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Because gates demand finishing earlier, easier challenges first, players reach bigger completion milestones step by step as they advance.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Locking areas until conditions are met forces players to reach places in a set order, so the story unfolds as the designer intended.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Only those who satisfied the condition can go through, giving them movement options that others in the game world lack.

can_cause.name: Quick Returns
can_cause.why: Some passages open only once you reach a certain point, after which coming back is easy, so the barrier eases travel afterward.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: If only certain players or teams may pass, others are shut out, creating places where the permitted ones are protected.

can_cause.name: Secret Areas
can_cause.why: When players don't realize a blocked route exists, the area behind it stays hidden until discovered.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Blocking some players from certain areas, such as those in vehicles, or letting only some in, creates safe zones that even out advantage.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Gates can link parts of a world that can't be walked between continuously, deciding how players get from one area to another.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Meeting the passage's condition opens up places that were previously unreachable, so the gate decides when they become available.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Players typically must finish one level before moving on, so the gate controls access between levels.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: The barrier is first built on a possible route and then blocks travel, so it limits where and when players can move.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: A passage can apply only to certain players or require team coordination, so team membership decides who gets through.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: A route is first made so travel between two points is possible, then blocked until the condition is met.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Goals located behind blocked areas become challenges because reaching them requires first meeting the passage's condition, shaping who completes them and when.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Some passages allow or forbid vehicles, often because vehicles are too large for the opening, so the gate limits who can pass.

changes.name: Warp Zones
changes.why: Warp zones can be set to activate only in certain circumstances, making that shortcut a conditional passage.

patterns.name: Extra-Game Input
patterns.what_it_is: The game's state changes something outside it, and neither a player nor the rules does so.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Pick the outside source (real-world time, other games, non-players, facilitators), and give the game rules for accepting and processing that input. Players must be able to see how the source affects play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A feature that reads an outside signal but never lets it change anything meaningful in the game state.
patterns.knobs: which outside sources are allowed; how strongly their input alters the game state

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: When players can influence the outside input, they may act to trigger it, and the game thereby makes them notice certain real-world things.

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: When clock or calendar information feeds into the game from outside, game events can happen at particular real-world times.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: If players are able to shape the outside input themselves, they may be pushed to do things outside the game purely to steer that input.

can_cause.name: Handles
can_cause.why: Some outside input never changes gameplay but supplies material like profile pictures, which social games use to give players recognizable identities.

can_cause.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
can_cause.why: Combined with pervasive play, input from outside the game is the typical way of making real-life activities feed into game state.

changes.name: Encouraged Return Visits
changes.why: Input based on dates and times creates events tied to the real world, which can change how likely players are to come back.

changes.name: Pervasive Gameplay
changes.why: Outside activities coexisting with the game offer easy ways for them to influence play, either by design or because they are hard to prevent.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Dropping outside input straight into the game as content can clash with the game's story world unless that world resembles where the input came from.

patterns.name: Private Game Spaces
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the game space directly controlled by only one player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Other players' actions must truly be blocked or limited in that space. The designer decides what visitors may do and how spaces interact with the shared game.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Each player has a named area, but others can attack, alter or sabotage it freely, so it gives no safety.
patterns.knobs: who may enter or act; what visitors may do; whether the space is permanent or temporary

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since nobody else can disrupt your space, you can play relaxed without worrying about reacting to opponents.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: Other players start out unable to enter or act in your space unless you have accepted them as neighbors.

can_cause.name: Instances
can_cause.why: Each player's space works like their own separate copy of the game area, where outsiders can only do limited things.

can_cause.name: Pottering
can_cause.why: With no other players to worry about, you can wander and tinker aimlessly in your space without pressure.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Because others cannot touch your space, it becomes a protected place where your progress stays secure.

can_cause.name: Startgame
can_cause.why: Temporary private spaces, such as players being far apart, give everyone a clear early phase before they interact.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Since others cannot interfere, you can safely think ahead, and parallel planning means waiting less for opponents.

can_cause.name: Territories
can_cause.why: Players own their private spaces, which makes them a kind of claimed territory belonging to one person.

can_cause.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
can_cause.why: Each player gets a space of their own, so they can treat it as a personal game while still being lightly connected to others.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: Safety from interference gives players creative control, so building and developing things in their space works especially well.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: Others cannot be hurt by your absence or disrupted by your return, so joining and leaving whenever you like is easier.

changes.name: Early Leaving Players
changes.why: When players act in separate spaces, a departure barely affects others, though this also limits how much players can influence each other.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A game space can be an actual part of the game world, or just part of the game state.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: With separate spaces, existing players are not harmed or threatened by newcomers, so joining is easier to allow.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: In multiplayer games these spaces can be temporary or permanent, changing how much players can affect each other.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Developments in a private space accumulate over time in lasting worlds, though visits from others can partly offset this.

changes.name: Turn-Based Games
changes.why: Because players' actions affect each other less, everyone can plan their moves in parallel instead of waiting.

changes.name: Tick-Based Games
changes.why: When each player acts in their own space, ticks let them play at different times, making the game asynchronous.

conflicts_with.name: Analysis Paralysis
conflicts_with.why: With fewer causal links between players, competition is less likely to cause overthinking, so the pattern tends to reduce this problem.

conflicts_with.name: Combat
conflicts_with.why: Giving players a private space lets them stay safe from attacks unless they allow neighbors in, reducing fighting.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: Without direct interference from others, play feels less pressured, so games with private spaces are less likely to be tense.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Private spaces can clash with the story, since rivals leaving each other's holdings untouched can seem illogical in the setting.

patterns.name: Scenes
patterns.what_it_is: A part of the game tied to a specific place and time within the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define each scene's location, who is present and how it ends, whether by a time limit, a condition, or a game master's call. Scenes must differ in setting or situation to feel like separate units.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Chapter labels over one continuous stretch of play where nothing about place, cast, or situation changes between them.
patterns.knobs: scene length; how scene ends are decided; how many characters and locations per scene

can_cause.name: Adventures
can_cause.why: Scenes let designers chop a story into separate located episodes, so they can pace and structure an adventure step by step.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When scenes aren't built as fixed levels, world details can be made up only when needed, so new elements can be dropped in as play goes.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: A scene presents a slice of the game world, showing players only the part where the current action takes place.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Scenes give designers firm control over how a story is laid out, since each episode can be placed and ordered deliberately.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because designers decide which scenes occur and how long they last, the story's course is set ahead of play.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Without fixed levels, scene details are settled only when needed, so the world can be reshaped from scene to scene.

can_cause.name: Melodramatic Structures
can_cause.why: Changing scenes is the moment where the game can hand the player a different character, which gives the player a wider picture than any single character.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Scenes can guarantee that players actually meet a boss, since the boss is built into a particular episode.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: A scene can put the spotlight on one character, deciding who is present and sometimes who can act.

changes.name: Environmental Storytelling
changes.why: Placing story clues in a scene ensures players will encounter them, because the scene fixes where play happens.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Scenes restrict the area where play takes place, so moving around matters less or stops mattering.

changes.name: Storytelling
changes.why: Scenes whose details are created only when needed leave room for stories to be told and shaped during play.

conflicts_with.name: Movement
conflicts_with.why: Scenes can make the movement actions of gameplay unnecessary, which takes away the very activity that movement is about.

conflicts_with.name: Open Destiny
conflicts_with.why: Scenes let designers give players local influence over events without letting the overall story arc vary, so they serve as a way to avoid this pattern.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Scene-based structure lets designers deliberately jump between times, as when a game switches between modern and historical characters.

patterns.name: Check Points
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the game world that mark progress toward the goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Placement along a route that matches the goal, clear signalling, and a real effect when reached (progress counted, order or area control).
patterns.just_a_label_when: A marker is visible, but reaching it changes no state, so skipping it costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: number and spacing; whether order is forced; how visible they are; what happens on reaching them

can_cause.name: Backtracking Levels
can_cause.why: Placing a check point at the far end of a level makes players travel out to it and then return, creating the backtracking structure.

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Check points are scattered places to visit, so reaching them already amounts to gathering a set, especially when order or completeness is optional.

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Check points can mark the spot where something carried must be brought, as with the area where a captured flag has to be delivered to score.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Where check points are placed pulls players into wandering around the world to find and reach them while pursuing another aim.

can_cause.name: Goal Indicators
can_cause.why: A check point is a spot showing where a goal is achieved or approached, so it tells players what they are heading toward.

can_cause.name: Herd
can_cause.why: Check points can serve as the destination that creatures or objects must be guided to, turning guiding them there into the goal.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: Because check points are distinctive places in the world, players can use them to recognize where they are and navigate.

can_cause.name: Point of Interest Indicators
can_cause.why: A check point marks a location as relevant to play, drawing the player's attention to a place worth going to.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Reaching a check point shows how far a player has advanced through a level or ongoing goal, since it records a state change.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Check points can sit at places that already matter, or they can make an ordinary place matter just by being a target there.

can_cause.name: Supporting Goals
can_cause.why: Check points are not the main aim but help players work toward some larger objective by giving smaller places to reach.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Check points reached or passed can remain as marks of where players have been or how far they have gotten.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: Check points set places to move between, so a goal of crossing the world becomes reaching one point after another.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: When holding an area counts as reaching a check point, the ownership goal is fulfilled through that area control.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Reaching check points shows how control of an area is gained, since visiting them is how a player takes the area.

changes.name: Arenas
changes.why: Placing check points so that they draw many players to one spot can bring players together into an arena.

changes.name: Continuous Goals
changes.why: Check points let players see how far they have come within an ongoing goal that has no single endpoint.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Check points affect how players move around a world, and can bring them together in large worlds.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Check points show how far a player has gotten through a level and can bring players together in large levels.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Since players head toward check points, where these are put shapes the routes and paths players take through the world.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: By their placement, check points draw many players to the same places, solving the problem of getting players co-located.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Check points are typically geospatial widgets, objects that exist for game purposes rather than belonging naturally to the game world, so they clash with a consistent fiction.

patterns.name: Spawn Points
patterns.what_it_is: Places where characters, units, or enemies appear.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Placement must take safety, fairness between sides and strategic value into account, since spawn locations draw camping and attacks. Safe zones or protection are often needed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A marked point that all elements simply appear from with no influence on fighting, routes or balance, or one placed so far from anything that nobody cares about it.
patterns.knobs: where they are placed; how many there are; whether they are fixed or moving; protection around them

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: If new arrivals show up unprotected at a spawn point, other players can wait nearby to ambush them, and when spawned items are goals, players may linger there.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Where you place spawn points decides how dangerous the arrival area is, so placement helps set how hard the game feels.

can_cause.name: Flanking Routes
can_cause.why: When players can place spawn points themselves, they can set up new arrival spots that let them approach opponents from unexpected sides.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Spawn points near a world's edge can look like entrances from beyond the map, making the world seem larger than the playable area.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because new game elements appear at spawn points, controlling or watching those spots matters, which makes the locations strategically important.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: A player whose avatar appears at a spawn point under immediate threat feels pressure, since they must react right away.

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Resources appear at spawn points over time rather than always being there, so collecting them requires coming back later.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Letting certain players, like squad leaders, act as places where others appear is a special power not available to all.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: If respawning after dying is part of the penalty, where the spawn point sits affects how harsh or mild that penalty feels.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies that appear during play come out of spawn points, so those locations shape where and how foes show up.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Spawn points are among the elements a designer can place on a board to populate it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: These are places where the game keeps adding elements, and they tend to become places players care about.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Placing these in a level lets new elements appear during play, and where players appear sets their starting conditions.

changes.name: Safe Havens
changes.why: Pairing a haven with the place where characters appear keeps respawning players from being attacked immediately.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Real life has no place where things simply appear, so spawn points need an explanation like magic or teleportation to fit the setting.

patterns.name: Choke Points
patterns.what_it_is: Places on the map where the way into other areas can be blocked.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The narrow passage must be the main (or only) route, with few alternatives, and the surroundings must make blocking or holding it worthwhile.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A narrow spot exists, but there is an equally easy bypass, so nobody needs to pass it or defend it.
patterns.knobs: width and length of the passage; number of alternative routes; who controls it

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Because a choke point is the narrow gateway to other regions, players naturally try to hold it, so fighting to own that spot becomes a goal.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: When several choke points lead to a place, players pick which one to push for, and teams may even attempt multiple at once.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: A narrow passage that everyone must pass through shapes how movement works, so holding it gives a real advantage and makes it a valuable spot.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When something like an environmental hazard sits in the choke point, players can choose to risk going through it rather than being forced to.

can_cause.name: Conditional Passageways
can_cause.why: A narrow spot guarded by enemies or obstacles stops travel until the defenders or blockers are removed, making the route conditional.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: When a narrow passage is guarded by enemies or blocked by obstacles, players must remove them to get past, making removal necessary.

changes.name: Arenas
changes.why: Choke points mark where an arena ends and make its open space feel larger by contrast with the tight approaches around it.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting at a choke point gets easier or harder depending on who holds it, and it favors short-ranged powerful weapons.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies controlling a choke point can block the way, so getting through it means beating them.

changes.name: Flanking Routes
changes.why: Several choke points between the same areas act as alternative routes, but easier alternative routes can stop a spot from working as a choke point.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Narrow sections can be built into a board so that only a few passages join its different parts.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Designers can build narrow sections into a world so that only a few passages link its separate regions.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: A choke point is a small place that must be passed through, so guarding it becomes a natural goal.

changes.name: Herd
changes.why: With fewer exits at a choke point, the creatures being driven have fewer places to escape, making herding easier.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Designers can include narrow sections in a level so that just a few passages connect its other parts.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Because routes are squeezed into small areas, how players and units can travel through the world is affected.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Since everyone has to funnel through the same narrow places, players are more likely to run into each other.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Having to pass through a narrow, watched spot leaves little room to hide, so sneaking past becomes harder.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: A narrow passage, especially one held by enemies, makes crossing from one place to another more difficult.

changes.name: Vehicle Sections
changes.why: Vehicle-impassable choke points sharply set the tight passages apart from open areas, causing speed to differ greatly and changing play there.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: A choke point can be built to hinder only vehicles, and it may make players leave the vehicle to bypass it.

conflicts_with.name: Flanking Routes
conflicts_with.why: If a location always has an easier way around it, it stops working as a choke point because players will simply avoid it.

patterns.name: Purchasable Game Advantages
patterns.what_it_is: The player can spend real money to gain advantages in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goods must be tied to meaningful game effects, with prices and transfer rules defined. The designer must accept the effect on balance and on other players' sense of effort.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A shop exists, but items are cosmetic or trivially available through play, so buying gives no real edge.
patterns.knobs: what can be bought; prices; power of purchases; tradability

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Buying or selling advantages happens outside normal play with real money, so each purchase is an action that sits beyond the game's own rules.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: When money spent outside the game brings new advantages into it, the outside transaction feeds directly into what happens inside play.

can_cause.name: Game Element Trading
can_cause.why: When players sell advantages to one another, the purchase becomes an exchange of game elements between those players.

can_cause.name: Unlocking
can_cause.why: When the game provider is the seller, paying can skip a requirement and open content immediately, like paying to avoid needing neighbors in CityVille.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Players can choose to pay real money to meet goals right away.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: Action points can be sold for money, letting players pay to do more than their normal allowance permits.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Players discussing deals inside and outside the game makes buying advantages hard to avoid, though some designs accept and encourage it.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Players aren't competing directly against each other, so selling advantages doesn't upset fairness between them.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Because items and characters carry value, players or facilitators can sell them for real money, which adds to the world's economy.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Each unit of a resource can be given a real-money price, which makes resources an easy thing to sell, as in FarmVille.

conflicts_with.name: Equipment
conflicts_with.why: Games wishing to avoid buyable advantages can make equipping permanent, so used gear cannot be traded on to other players.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Buying a result lets players skip the repetitive effort of earning it, removing that grind.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Paying lets one player get the same progress that another earns through skill, which undermines the value of mastery.

conflicts_with.name: Irreversible Events
conflicts_with.why: Making equipment soulbound prevents trading it, which closes off one way of buying advantages.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Buying advantages from outside the game can easily destroy equal chances.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: When others can simply buy what you worked for, your achievements feel less worthwhile.

patterns.name: Transport Routes
patterns.what_it_is: A path that must be traveled to reach certain places in the game world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Routes must be the actual way between key places, with no free shortcut, and take meaningful time or effort. Something on or about the journey, such as hazards, choices or waiting, makes the travel matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A corridor that players can bypass or skip with instant travel, so it adds only a loading pause.
patterns.knobs: route length; number of alternative routes; whether shortcuts or fast travel exist

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: When enemies oppose the player or the route can only carry so much, the path becomes a narrow spot where movement gets held up.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because routes physically connect places that could plausibly be linked in the game's fiction, travel between them makes sense inside the world.

can_cause.name: Game World Navigation
can_cause.why: When several routes lead somewhere, players must work out which one to take, so finding their way becomes part of play.

can_cause.name: Laning
can_cause.why: If different routes join the same starting and ending areas, players end up spread across parallel paths, each one acting like a lane.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: A long route that asks little of the player's attention can produce calm stretches with little happening.

can_cause.name: Traverse
can_cause.why: A route gives players the simple goal of getting from one end to the other.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: A route makes players move between two points on a board, shaping how they cross it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A route makes players move between two points in the world, shaping how they cross it.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A route makes players move between two points in a level, shaping how they cross it.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: The basic point of a route is to make players move from one place to another, so it shapes that movement.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Travel
conflicts_with.why: Games use instant jumps so they do not need to provide routes for travelling between places, making the two alternatives to each other.

conflicts_with.name: Warp Zones
conflicts_with.why: Warping is an alternative to routes and jumps between places without a believable physical connection, which undercuts the world's consistency.

patterns.name: Flanking Routes
patterns.what_it_is: Alternative paths to the needed place that others may not know about.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Add alternative paths to key locations that are less obvious or less defended than the main route. For them to matter, defenders must be unable to guard everything and the routes must lead to something worth reaching.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Extra paths that are as obvious as the main route or all covered by the same defenders, so nobody surprises anyone.
patterns.knobs: how many alternate routes; how hidden, narrow or long they are compared with the main route

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because unguarded side routes make sneaking possible, defenders must keep watching those paths to block movement through them, which keeps their attention constantly busy.

can_cause.name: Laning
can_cause.why: Giving players several parallel paths, typically three, to reach the same place splits movement into separate lanes.

can_cause.name: Scouting
can_cause.why: Since side routes can hide enemy approaches, players need to send someone out to find where opponents are actually coming from.

can_cause.name: Selectable Set of Goals
can_cause.why: Extra ways to reach or take a location let players choose which approach to use instead of following one fixed path.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Side routes may be left unguarded, so players can slip through unseen, and the possibility encourages sneaking even more.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Because side routes add pressure on top of what the areas they lead to are worth, they become valuable spots to hold or watch.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Using or defending against side routes depends on where units are and what players know about them, so you must plan around that.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Multiple ways to reach or capture a place give players different strategies to try, so matches don't always play out the same.

can_cause.name: Combos
can_cause.why: Paths that let players hit an enemy from two directions at once make a coordinated attack, which is a combo of positions.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: With alternative routes available, one teammate can keep enemies busy while others take the route around, a classic team combo.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Alternate paths to key locations make them harder to hold and add variety to play.

changes.name: Arenas
changes.why: Alternate paths placed near an arena create a different style of play, making the arena stand out as its own kind of space.

changes.name: Camping
changes.why: Side routes make waiting in one spot riskier because enemies can come from another direction, and may make camping pointless.

changes.name: Choke Points
changes.why: Side routes bypass narrow passages, so they reduce how much those passages matter and can undermine their purpose.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Extra paths make it harder to win or hold an area in a fight, since enemies may arrive from unexpected directions.

changes.name: Combos
changes.why: If a side route is left unguarded, attackers can hit from two directions at once in a two-pronged attack.

changes.name: Galleries
changes.why: If a gallery upsets player or team balance, extra routes give those in the lower area other ways to get through.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: A flanking route is a region shaped by how a board's parts connect, and it often becomes a strategic location.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A flanking route is an abstract region of the world's space which affects how players can move around.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: Because there are more ways in, defenders must watch every access, and with too few players or units they cannot cover them all.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Additional routes change how easily players can get from place to place, and some can be one-way or limited to certain vehicles.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Hidden approaches mean you can't easily be sure where enemies are or which way they will come, so gathering information gets harder.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: If the area is too open for the sniper, extra routes let enemies approach from the side and reach the spot more easily.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Unguarded side routes make sneaking goals possible, and where they are already possible the routes make them more attractive.

changes.name: Surprise Attacks
changes.why: Since opponents may not expect or watch these routes, attackers can use them to strike from an unforeseen direction.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: A route can be made usable only by vehicles, or only by those on foot, which changes who can take it.

conflicts_with.name: Camping
conflicts_with.why: Routes around a camper's position let opponents attack from other directions, making camping pointless.

conflicts_with.name: Choke Points
conflicts_with.why: If a location always has an easier way around it, it stops working as a choke point because players will simply avoid it.

patterns.name: Self-Service Kiosks
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the game world where players make deals or get services themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Place them at chosen spots with services that players actually need, such as trading, healing, or quests, and let their stock refill or limit it. Their location should shape movement.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A kiosk whose service is never needed or is available everywhere else, so no one has to go there.
patterns.knobs: what services; where placed; stock and refill rate; prices

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: Players can walk up to a kiosk and listen to rumors from it, making hearing gossip one of the common services offered.

can_cause.name: Helpers
can_cause.why: Some kiosks appear as non-player characters who assist the player, so such a helper is one way a kiosk can look.

can_cause.name: Installations
can_cause.why: A kiosk gives players actions for reaching its services, which makes it a fixed installation in the world.

can_cause.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
can_cause.why: Because a kiosk offers its services only at its own spot, players must go there to use those abilities.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: A kiosk can be shown as a character, such as a vendor who can only trade and talk and can't be attacked.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Players can receive quests at a kiosk, which is one of the typical services it hands out.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Since a kiosk's services exist only at its spot, that spot becomes worth visiting and planning around.

can_cause.name: Tools
can_cause.why: Using a kiosk is an action players take to reach its services, so it works somewhat like a tool.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: A kiosk can act like a vending machine where players buy and sell items, one of the most usual services.

changes.name: Deterioration
changes.why: A kiosk can offer repairs, letting players fix items that have worn down or been damaged.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Kiosks are placed at chosen spots on a board, so they shape which services are available where.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Designers pick which services appear at which places in the world, so kiosks affect how the world is used.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Kiosks can be placed at chosen points inside a level, giving that level services at particular spots.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: A kiosk can provide training, letting players improve their skills by visiting it.

patterns.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
patterns.what_it_is: Worlds built by an algorithm rather than drawn by hand by an author.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The generator needs good rules, parameters and randomness that produce varied yet playable worlds. Balance checks or seeds help keep results fair and reproducible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Worlds are generated, but outputs look nearly identical or are broken, so the variety adds no new play.
patterns.knobs: generator parameters; amount of randomness; seed use; balance constraints

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Algorithm-built worlds can be far bigger than hand-made ones, so players have lots of places to choose from when deciding where to explore.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: The algorithms take some input and output whole worlds, so the world itself is produced by the generator rather than built by hand.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Generated worlds are huge, which feels open, but the truly interesting gameplay is rare and sits mostly in a few hand-placed spots.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because random input is almost always used, each new game gives players a different world to explore, which gives a reason to play again.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Since the world is expected to be vast, a generator that produces great size lets the game keep up the feeling of a big, coherent setting.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: A generator can make large worlds containing different kinds of play, or produce different worlds each time that play differently.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Generated worlds can spread strategic locations, tools or weapons unevenly across players.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Generated worlds can make prepared stories irrelevant unless story creation is built into the generation process.

patterns.name: Sniper Locations
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the game world that are good for shooting from far away.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The spot needs a long sightline over a useful area and relative safety, for instance through height, cover or hard access. Counterplay such as flanking routes or kill replays keeps it from dominating.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A high ledge with a nice view that is exposed from every side or overlooks nothing worth shooting at, so nobody gains from using it.
patterns.knobs: sightline length; amount of cover; how hard it is to reach; how many counter-routes exist

can_cause.name: Area Control
can_cause.why: Enemies holding a sniper spot can watch and threaten the ground in view, so others struggle to move through it.

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: Because snipers can set up slow, strong shots from relative safety, they are tempted to stay put in these spots.

can_cause.name: Hiding Places
can_cause.why: Sniper spots are usually also places where the shooter is hard to notice, so they commonly double as hiding spots.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Staying unnoticed is an advantage in these spots, so players try to sneak both when getting there and while staying.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: They give a natural advantage for attacking at range, which makes the spot valuable to hold within the level.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Reaching a sniper spot and using it well, or pushing out someone already there, takes forethought rather than rushing.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: Strongholds and sniper positions held by enemies deny the surrounding larger area, so players can't safely enter it.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: These spots offer vantage points for long-range shooting, changing how aiming and shooting plays out in a level.

changes.name: Arenas
