changes.why: Sniper spots can be added to an arena so that its open play area becomes watched and attacked from a safe position.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: By offering strategic places to fight from, they change how fighting unfolds across the play space.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Whoever uses them, whether players or enemies, the spots change how hard it is to defeat those enemies.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: They give boards places that offer a ranged advantage, changing how fighting is done there.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: They add positions in the world from which long-range attacks are possible, shaping how fights play out there.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: They give a natural advantage point, so they are good candidates for places players compete to hold.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Placing them in a level creates strategic spots that change how ranged combat is done there.

changes.name: Surprise Attacks
changes.why: Players can set up slow, powerful shots in relative safety, so ambushes become easier, though not every shot is a surprise.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Revealing sniper positions to only some team members keeps snipers from becoming too strong while still limiting how useful the spots stay.

patterns.name: Meta Servers
patterns.what_it_is: Servers that assign players to game servers and store shared data about them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The service must really connect players to game servers, remember their data across sessions and offer features like friend lookup. It needs enough players to make the routing worthwhile.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A server list or login screen that only lists servers and neither routes players nor stores anything across sessions.
patterns.knobs: what the server stores and offers: matchmaking, friend lists, global rankings

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: A server above individual games can store records that matter across games, letting them follow players between servers and be shared globally.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: They store and pass on information between games to the game servers, supporting play that spans many game instances in large games.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: A meta server sits above the individual game servers and helps players find the one that suits them, shaping how players get spread across servers.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: These help remote players find one another to start games.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: They let players choose and move between game servers, adding another layer of mediation on top.

patterns.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
patterns.what_it_is: The world's basic layout can change during a session or between sessions.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The world must be made of parts that can be rearranged, and either the rules or the players must actually rearrange them. Changes have to alter what choices are good, not just how things look.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A world that is re-skinned or has cosmetic changes, but the layout and routes play out the same every time.
patterns.knobs: what can change; when it changes (between games or during play); who triggers the change and how often

can_cause.name: Asymmetric Starting Conditions
can_cause.why: When the world's layout changes from one game to the next, players may begin in positions that are not equally good, so starts end up uneven.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: A layout that differs each time you play gives players something new to discover, so they have reason to explore it again.

can_cause.name: Persistent Game World Changes
can_cause.why: If a reconfiguration is not automatically undone after a while, the altered world stays that way and players keep playing in the new form.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Because the world can be rearranged between sessions or by players' actions, each new playthrough feels different, which gives players reason to return.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Changing the world's structure changes what situations players face, so play differs from one session to another, especially when players do the rearranging.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: When the world changes each session, players have to memorize the new layout anew, especially if they can't see all of it.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Reconfigurability is a property applied to a game world, determining whether and when its fundamental structure can be altered.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Changing the world during play without a sensible in-story reason can make the world feel illogical and break its internal consistency.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Changing the world can spread tools, weapons or locations unevenly, though it can also be used to balance.

patterns.name: Quick Travel
patterns.what_it_is: Ways to reach another place in the world, skipping intermediate points.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Travel points must be reachable, with rules for when it works and what it costs. The world should have enough distance that the shortcut matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A map teleport exists, but the world is so small or the travel so restricted that nobody needs it.
patterns.knobs: where it is available; cost; unlock conditions; one-way or two-way

can_cause.name: Abilities
can_cause.why: Since moving is tied to what game elements can do, jumping across the world works as something a player or character is able to perform.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When jumping ahead is an action in players' hands, they decide whether to skip the journey or walk it themselves.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: A forced jump can be one of the scripted events in a story's fixed sequence, moving players to where the plot needs them.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Instant travel is usually stronger than ordinary movement, so it can be a special power that sets its holder apart.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: Because skipping the places in between is typically more powerful than regular moving, it can serve as the basis for a special form of movement.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Granting a jump, for example after finishing a level, can act as a prize that recognizes good player performance.

can_cause.name: Setback Penalties
can_cause.why: A jump can also be handed out as a negative consequence, relocating players in response to how poorly they performed.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: When a jump is imposed as a reward or penalty, players cannot refuse it, so it becomes an event they have no say over.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Choosing destinations on a map implies more world exists than players actually visit, though a limited destination list can give away the limits.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Quick travel can be built into the world itself, changing it so that distant places connect without a continuous series of locations between them.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: It changes how players get around by letting them reach faraway spots without passing through the spaces between, and may even alter line of sight.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: Jumping is commonly used to carry players from one scene to the next when the story changes location.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Skipping across the map removes the need to cross uneventful ground by hand, reducing movement chores.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Skipping repeated trips through already known areas removes a repetitive chore, so jumping counters the grind of long, linear travel.

conflicts_with.name: Transport Routes
conflicts_with.why: Games use instant jumps so they do not need to provide routes for travelling between places, making the two alternatives to each other.

patterns.name: Time Limited Game Instances
patterns.what_it_is: The game's rules themselves limit how long a single game can last.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clock or a turn/action count must be built in so the session truly ends at a known point, with end and scoring rules that work when time runs out. The cap should be clear to players before they start.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A timer shown on screen that never ends the session or changes who wins, so players can ignore it.
patterns.knobs: length of the session cap; whether players can choose it

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Because every session has a fixed maximum length, each one is certain to reach an ending point, so players will always eventually hit game over.

can_cause.name: Time Pressure
can_cause.why: When the cap is based on a running clock, players see time draining away and feel pushed to act faster before it runs out.

can_cause.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
can_cause.why: Short rounds with fixed endings give players regular chances to start or stop without disturbing anyone.

can_cause.name: Game System Player
can_cause.why: A turn limit acts as a passive opponent: when time runs out the players lose, so the clock itself plays against them.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: Combined with a self-run meta game, games that have a time limit give players a way to pick how long play lasts.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: Together with ending play to win, a game that stops at a set time can leave players evaluated as equal when it stops.

changes.name: Meta Games
changes.why: Bounded inner games make it easier to line up and synchronize the larger structure that strings many games together.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: With only so much time to play, players have a limited window to earn points, which changes what skills help them score highly.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Capping each match's length lets organizers guarantee when the whole event finishes, since every individual game has a known upper bound.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: With saves, a time limit loses its point from a planning view, since you can restore the state and try again.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: A game with no real end cannot sit with a rule that forces each session to stop after a limited time.

patterns.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
patterns.what_it_is: Features of the real physical place where the game is played affect the play itself.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Actions must be bound to specific physical places or distances, so that moving the body matters for what you can do. Distances, boundaries and the space's features must actually be used by the rules.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game played in a room or park where the place is only a backdrop and any spot would work equally well.
patterns.knobs: size and shape of the space; which actions are allowed only inside it or at certain spots

can_cause.name: Events Timed to the Real World
can_cause.why: When play happens in actual physical places, outside happenings affect the game and become game events, whether the designer planned them or not.

can_cause.name: Hybrid Gameplay Spaces
can_cause.why: A game must first have a real physical play area before that area can be combined with a virtual one into a hybrid space.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: If players can't see everything about the physical space at once, those who know the place better gain an edge.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Real-world gameplay spaces, combined with self-run play and adjustable areas, let players set boundaries that shape how long a session lasts.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Playing in real places is a main way to put players where other activities happen, especially in games needing little interaction.

can_cause.name: Physical Navigation
can_cause.why: Play happens in actual physical surroundings, so finding your way through the game means finding your way through the real place.

changes.name: AI Players
changes.why: If computer-controlled players are to take full part in a game played in physical space, they need robotic bodies that can move there.

changes.name: Live Action Roleplaying
changes.why: Live action roleplay can be staged in a tiny room where space is irrelevant; adding real space makes movement and distance matter to play.

patterns.name: Secret Areas
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the game world that are hard to notice.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Hide areas behind obstacles or hidden triggers, give subtle clues, and put something worth finding inside. Players must be able to find them with effort.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An 'area' that is empty or trivially visible, or one that cannot actually be found, so searching earns nothing.
patterns.knobs: how well hidden; clue strength; reward inside; how many

can_cause.name: Easter Eggs
can_cause.why: A secret area can be a deliberately planted hidden bonus, such as a concealed room that shows its creator's name.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When players know or suspect hidden spots exist, they are motivated to search the world more carefully instead of just following the main path.

can_cause.name: Hiding Places
can_cause.why: Because a secret area may be unknown to other players and to enemies, it can serve as a safe spot to hide.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Designers often include hidden areas not required for progress, giving players an extra thing they can choose to hunt for.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Secret areas are commonly stocked with resources, so players who find them are paid off for their searching.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: Knowing where a secret area is gives a player an advantage, which makes that location valuable to know about.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Secret areas let a designer conceal some portion of a board from players.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Secret areas let a designer conceal some portion of the world from players.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Secret areas let a designer conceal some portion of a level from players.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: A quest may require players to find a secret area, making the hidden space part of the task.

patterns.name: Landmarks
patterns.what_it_is: Noticeable objects in the game world that make it easier to find your way.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Objects must stand out and be visible from many places so players can use them to orient. They must be spread across the space and be distinguishable from each other.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Many similar tall objects or decorations that look alike, so players still get lost.
patterns.knobs: how many; how large and distinctive; where placed; how often visible

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A distinctive object can be set up so players follow it or read it as a hint about where to go.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Landmarks may be needed to make a world feel coherent, since their look can be what establishes the theme.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Standout objects can be placed so they form a trail players follow.

changes.name: Environmental Storytelling
changes.why: They cannot carry much information, but they can still contribute a meaningful part of a story told through the world.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Distinct elements help players find their way around the board.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Players who are less likely to get lost feel safer venturing out, so exploring is encouraged.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Recognizable objects let players work out where they are by their position relative to them.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Distinct elements help players find their way around the world.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Distinct elements help players find their way around a level.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: They can be placed to show the route racers must follow, such as glowing pillars of light.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: Placing them along a route makes it more significant and gives players a sense of how far they have traveled.

patterns.name: Hiding Places
patterns.what_it_is: Places in the game where a person or thing can be hidden.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Seekers must truly be less able to notice things in them, and there must be enough, well-placed spots to make concealment a real option without making it trivial. Players should be able to judge how good a spot is.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Decorative crates or bushes that do not block sight or detection, so hiding in them is no safer than standing in the open.
patterns.knobs: number, size and placement of hiding spots; how well they hide; how clearly players can tell they are hidden

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Hiding spots give players somewhere to put themselves or objects where others can't see them, which is exactly what trying to conceal something requires.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
can_cause.why: When hiding depends on how well others perceive you, players may not know how good their spot really is, so a gap between player and character knowledge appears.

can_cause.name: Safe Havens
can_cause.why: Anyone inside a hiding spot is hard for others to find or attack, so the spot ends up working as a place of safety.

can_cause.name: Stealth
can_cause.why: Places that avoid detection let players move and act unseen, so sneaking becomes possible in the first place.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Hiding spots make gathering information about others harder, since what you are looking for may be tucked away unseen.

changes.name: Safe Havens
changes.why: An existing safe haven can be turned into an explicit hiding spot, adding concealment to its protection.

changes.name: Scouting
changes.why: Hiding spots make scouting harder because the things a scout looks for can be out of sight.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: How many hiding spots exist and where they sit changes how easy or hard it is to stay unseen.

patterns.name: Instances
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the world are created for a particular group of players when they are needed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The system must create isolated copies on demand with a set group size, and the content must be worth entering as a group. Access conditions (group size, timing) should be clear.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A zone called an instance that everyone still shares, so crowding and interference are the same as before.
patterns.knobs: group size required; how often and when instances open; content and difficulty inside

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: When entry to an instance is limited to certain times or conditions, players tend to wait near its entrance until they can get in.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: If a player may go into the same instance more than once, each visit gives another attempt at it.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: An instance is a separate space that players choose to try entering, so it stays closed off until they do.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: An instance works like a level: a self-contained area with its own content, which players decide to enter.

can_cause.name: Non-Consistent Narration
can_cause.why: Because several groups can enter the same instance repeatedly, the story events inside it happen again and again, so the narration contradicts itself.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: Splitting players into limited-size instances means servers carry less traffic and are used more efficiently.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Instances let games with huge player populations keep small groups apart, avoiding overcrowding and ensuring players actually meet each other.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Instances are mainly used within persistent worlds, giving groups their own sub-areas that are created when needed and discarded afterward.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Quests are often placed inside instances so a limited number of players take part, letting designers balance them for that group size.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game World Changes
conflicts_with.why: Instances get created, discarded and recreated, so what happens inside them has little lasting effect on the wider game world.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Since instances can be re-entered by the same or different groups, the same events replay, which clashes with a believable flow of time.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: When an instance is recreated many times, players notice its enemies and rewards are just game mechanics, which breaks the fiction.

patterns.name: Invisible Walls
patterns.what_it_is: Barriers that stop you from passing but do not stop you from looking.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Collision must reliably stop movement at the edge while the view carries beyond it, and placement should be where players do not expect to go. The more natural the edge looks, the less it breaks immersion.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A boundary players can walk through, or one that is obvious and unexplained so it simply looks like a bug.
patterns.knobs: where the walls are placed; how much is visible beyond; how they are disguised

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because players can see terrain beyond the barrier, the world feels like a bigger, believable place rather than a small box, even though only part is playable.

can_cause.name: Framed Freedom
can_cause.why: Players seem free to roam, but the barrier quietly sets the real limits, and whether they know it depends on whether they bump into it.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Seeing a wide world makes players feel they can go anywhere, which gives a sense of choice until they run into the barrier.

can_cause.name: Illusion of Open Space
can_cause.why: Showing scenery past the playable edge makes the world look larger than it is, and this costs little to build.

can_cause.name: Inaccessible Areas
can_cause.why: The barrier blocks movement into regions players can still see, which turns those regions into places they cannot enter.

can_cause.name: Memorizing
can_cause.why: Hidden barriers in a maze mean players cannot see the walls and must remember where they are to find a path.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: The barrier stops players from moving into certain places, so it works as a blocker even though it does not hide the view.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Showing a larger world supports the setting, and explaining the barrier as a force field or hex keeps it fitting the theme.

can_cause.name: Transport Routes
can_cause.why: When some directions are blocked, the paths still open become the main ways players travel through the world.

changes.name: Conditional Passageways
changes.why: A barrier can sit at or around a gateway, such as a force field, tempting players to meet the requirements needed to pass.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: It keeps play inside a designed part of the world while the rest is shown only as backdrop.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: It limits how players can move through a level, keeping them in the intended area.

changes.name: Scripted Information Sequences
changes.why: Since players can see world parts they cannot affect, it gives a story reason why a scripted scene cannot be interfered with.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Players can see where the goal is yet cannot walk straight to it, so they must find a route around the barriers.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: They can expose that players lack the freedom of movement they first assumed.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Hitting a barrier that cannot be seen or explained breaks the believability of the world, unless it is given an in-world reason.

conflicts_with.name: Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Using them to keep players inside a world's edges is practical, but they don't fit the fiction and can undercut its consistency.

patterns.name: Shrinking Game Worlds
patterns.what_it_is: The game world gets smaller and smaller as the game goes on.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Parts of the world must be permanently removed on a schedule or by player action, forcing players closer together. Shrinkage needs to be irreversible and fast enough to matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A map whose edges close only cosmetically or so slowly that the game ends before anyone feels it.
patterns.knobs: how fast and in what order the world shrinks; what triggers it

can_cause.name: Environmental Effects
can_cause.why: The world getting smaller acts like a force of nature in the game space, changing conditions for everyone playing in it.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: As the space tightens, players are pushed together, so each clash matters more and the outcome of the whole game gets decided step by step.

can_cause.name: Movement Limitations
can_cause.why: When parts of the world vanish, players have less ground to move on, so where they can go is restricted.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: A world that shrinks must be changeable by its nature, and each shrinking step is a change to the world's layout.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: With less room to move and opponents closing in, players feel growing pressure about what will happen next.

can_cause.name: Time Limited Game Instances
can_cause.why: Since the world only gets smaller and cannot regrow, play cannot go on forever and the match is guaranteed to end.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: Disappearing parts of the world can leave players stuck or cut off, especially when opponents choose which parts are removed.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Shrinking changes the whole play area for everyone at once, which makes it a drastic event that affects all players.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The pattern changes the size of a game world over time, so the space players start in is not the space they end in.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: The playable space gets smaller as play proceeds, which limits what players can do.

patterns.name: Illusion of Open Space
patterns.what_it_is: The world looks more spacious than it really is: there are fewer playable zones than it seems.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The unreachable scenery must look credible, be consistent with the setting, and be blocked in ways players do not easily notice. It breaks down if the blocks are obvious or conflict with the theme.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A flat backdrop or map edge that obviously ends, so players see the limit at once and the world does not feel bigger.
patterns.knobs: how much unreachable scenery is shown; how the blocks are disguised; level of detail of distant areas

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: When the world seems to continue past where you can walk, its presentation doesn't abruptly stop at the edge of the playable area, so the fiction stays believable.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: A world that looks bigger makes players feel they could go many places, giving them a sense of choosing where to travel.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Many themes suggest wide open spaces, so making the world feel bigger helps the game match what its theme implies.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The pattern makes a world appear bigger than the area where play really happens, without needing to build all of that space.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: It is often applied here because it makes sense that players can see more of the world than the route lets them pass through.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If players discover the illusion, such as hitting a barrier, the theme's promise of open space is broken, even though the in-world fiction may hold up.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: It may reveal that the freedom players assumed they had is not real.

patterns.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
patterns.what_it_is: Ordinary life activities unrelated to the game change its state.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design must pick which everyday activities count, measure them reliably, and map them to clear state changes. Players need to see the link between what they did and what the game did in response.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that only shows your steps or activity as a decorative number, while nothing in play depends on it.
patterns.knobs: which activities count; how they are measured and converted into game state changes

can_cause.name: Changes in Perception of Real World Phenomena due to Gameplay
can_cause.why: Doing everyday activities with an added game purpose can lead players to view those activities differently than before.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: Using ordinary real-life activities to change the game means the game takes in input from outside the game itself, so this is a kind of it.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Letting real-world activities drive game state spreads play into everyday life, making pervasive play possible.

can_cause.name: Real World Knowledge Advantages
can_cause.why: Since good performance at certain real-world activities pays off in the game, knowing how to do those activities well helps players.

can_cause.name: Ubiquitous Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because ordinary activities count as game input, play can happen wherever and whenever players are doing them, making ubiquitous play possible.

changes.name: Robotic Players
changes.why: Because the game uses what real players do in life, robotic players become harder to design, though this is rarely a practical issue.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: When things done outside the game change its outcome, players' real-life circumstances shape play instead of only in-game actions.

conflicts_with.name: Mimetic Interfaces
conflicts_with.why: One feeds ordinary non-game activities into the game, while the other builds in-game activities that merely resemble real ones, so the two approaches don't fit together.

patterns.name: Persistent Game World Changes
patterns.what_it_is: Changes in the game world that do not revert on their own.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Player actions must alter the world state and that state must be kept, not reverted by resets or temporary instances. There must be ways to change the world, such as building, destroying or moving things.
patterns.just_a_label_when: World changes that vanish on reload or after a short time, or that are only visual and do not affect later gameplay.
patterns.knobs: which changes persist; for how long; whether and when the world resets

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because changes to the world stay put, they can lock the story onto a fixed path, since earlier events keep shaping what comes next.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: When player actions leave lasting marks on the world instead of vanishing, players feel their work mattered beyond a brief moment.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The pattern affects the external world players act in, making it something that keeps changing rather than staying the same, unlike players' own attributes.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Lasting changes strengthen the feeling that effort matters in a world that already continues to exist, though the word persistent is used differently in each.

conflicts_with.name: Instances
conflicts_with.why: Instances get created, discarded and recreated, so what happens inside them has little lasting effect on the wider game world.

patterns.name: Quick Returns
patterns.what_it_is: World design where returning to a point is much easier than getting there.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It should open only after the outward journey, so return is cheaper than getting there. It must link to places players actually revisit.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A shortcut exists but is as long as the original route or opens before the journey, so nothing is saved.
patterns.knobs: when it unlocks; how fast; which places it connects

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: A quick return is itself a special way of getting around, so it adds a distinct form of travel through the world.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: A return method can be given to players as a newly gained power, such as a skill they unlock that carries them back.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Return methods can be limited to the player, who can use them while others or enemies cannot, making the shortcut a special power.

can_cause.name: Privileged Movement
can_cause.why: The fast way back can be something only the player's character is allowed to do, setting their travel apart from normal movement.

can_cause.name: Quick Travel
can_cause.why: When a return works by instantly jumping between two points, it is a narrower, often one-way or limited version of fast travel.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Being sent instantly back after finishing a goal serves as a prize, sparing the player a tedious walk home.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Instant transport back after a goal is a dramatic, overwhelming moment that happens to the player rather than being earned step by step.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Adding fast ways back changes how the world is traversed, since previously visited areas become easy to get to again.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A level can include a shortcut out so players need not walk the whole way back after reaching its end.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: Routes between places can be made shorter on the return trip, so coming back is much easier than going out.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Once players have met a goal of reaching somewhere, a quick return spares them from having to cross the same ground again.

conflicts_with.name: Backtracking Levels
conflicts_with.why: A quick return would skip the walk back, but this pattern depends on players actually traveling the whole level again, so the two cannot coexist.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: Fast ways back cut down the dull effort of traveling, easing movement chores.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Repeated trips over known ground feel like grinding, and a fast way back removes that repetition, so the two pull in opposite directions.

patterns.name: Vehicle Sections
patterns.what_it_is: Game areas designed for driving or flying a vehicle.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The terrain scale, obstacles and routes must suit vehicle speed and abilities, and vehicles must be available there. Walking through should be clearly worse than driving.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A big open area with a car parked in it where walking is just as fast and the layout is the same.
patterns.knobs: size of area; vehicle availability; density of obstacles and choke points; speed difference versus walking

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Walking through a vehicle area, or entering it by accident without a vehicle, makes the player's trip tedious and pointless, which is the excise.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: In a continuous world mixing vehicle and other areas, knowing where one type ends and the other begins helps players plan, which counts as strategic knowledge.

can_cause.name: Transport Routes
can_cause.why: These areas are stretches of a world set aside for traveling in vehicles, so they function as transport routes.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Whole boards can be made into vehicle areas and mixed among other boards, changing how those boards are played.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Parts of a continuous world can be designated for vehicle travel, so the world mixes vehicle and non-vehicle regions.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A whole level can be a vehicle area, or most of a level can be, with a few places requiring travel on foot.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Such areas often let players make use of what their vehicle can do, which shapes how they steer and position themselves.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Because players travel using vehicle capabilities, and vehicle travel is faster than ordinary travel, how movement works in that area changes.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: Parts of the game built around vehicle use shape when and where players ride them.

patterns.name: Laning
patterns.what_it_is: All movement follows a few set routes, which makes the game more predictable.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The map must offer a small fixed set of routes between areas, such as bases, and make leaving them hard or pointless. The lanes must lead to real choices and meetings between opponents.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Paths are drawn but players can walk anywhere, so the lanes are ignored.
patterns.knobs: number of lanes; their width and length; how blocked the space between lanes is

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: Because movement is funneled into a few set routes, crowding tends to occur inside those lanes or where they finish, forming narrow spots.

can_cause.name: Scouting
can_cause.why: Opposing forces approach along the same lanes from both sides, so you must think about what enemies are doing and may want to look ahead.

can_cause.name: Startgame
can_cause.why: The way players respond to the available lanes makes up the opening phase of a match.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Having several lanes to pick from forces players to make choices, which pushes them to think about longer-term plans.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Choosing among lanes creates immediate decisions about how to handle each route, which encourages players to plan their moves in the short term.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Lanes are a way of shaping level layout, since designers lay out the map as a small set of routes.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Lanes limit where agents can go, narrowing free movement into a few predictable paths.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Lanes often serve as the paths for units, whether player-controlled or not, while avatars may use slower or riskier alternatives.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Fixed lanes make enemy arrival predictable, while players still choose different tactics.

patterns.name: Visits
patterns.what_it_is: A temporary stay in a part of the world controlled by another player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be private player spaces, a way to be allowed in (friends or neighbors), and a small set of allowed actions, preferably helpful ones. The visit should also leave the owner something to see or gain.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A view-only gallery of another player's space where the visitor can do nothing and nobody notices the visit.
patterns.knobs: who can visit; which actions visitors have; daily action caps; benefits to host and visitor

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: A visit is just a player traveling into an area owned by someone else, so going there is a kind of movement, though with fewer things to do.

can_cause.name: Public Player Statistics
can_cause.why: Walking through another player's space lets you see what they have built or achieved, which gives a small, informal way of seeing their progress.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Visits make parts of the world a guest can enter but with fewer actions available there than in other areas of the world.

changes.name: Massively Single-Player Online Games
changes.why: Visits let games where everyone mostly plays alone gain some social contact while keeping the relaxed, low-conflict feel of casual play.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: Visits need an area owned by another player, and they open that otherwise solitary space to restricted guests so it feels less lonely.

patterns.name: Configurable Gameplay Areas
patterns.what_it_is: A physical play space that can be assembled differently from session to session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The area must be built from rearrangeable pieces or markers, and the changes must alter distances, routes or length of play. Someone must be responsible for setting it up each time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The board can technically be rearranged, but players always use the same standard layout, or every layout plays the same.
patterns.knobs: how many layout variants; who sets it up; how much the layout can vary

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
can_cause.why: Since changing the play area changes how long a game takes, players or facilitators can bargain over how long a given round will last.

can_cause.name: Negotiable Game Sessions
can_cause.why: Because the size or layout of the area affects play time, those in charge can discuss and agree on what a session will look like.

can_cause.name: Reconfigurable Game Worlds
can_cause.why: This is the special case where the world is arranged before play starts, which is one direct way of making a world reconfigurable.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: When players can set the play area themselves, in a self-run game, the game can be fitted to wherever they are.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Fictional game spaces can be altered from one game to the next, for example by rearranging how the world is laid out before play starts.

changes.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
changes.why: When play happens in physical locations, the area can be changed between games, for instance by moving markers or by installing the supporting technology differently.

patterns.name: Galleries
patterns.what_it_is: Raised platforms from which narrow passages are easy to keep in view.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Build elevated positions overlooking a narrow route that enemies must follow for some distance, with height giving a real advantage. Alternate routes can offset the advantage.
patterns.just_a_label_when: There is a raised ledge, but the enemy can bypass it or it gives no combat edge, so the height means nothing.
patterns.knobs: height and length of the overlook; availability of flanking routes; cover

can_cause.name: Camping
can_cause.why: Because the high ground gives a strong, hard-to-reach advantage, players are tempted to stay put there and wait for opponents to walk by.

can_cause.name: Choke Points
can_cause.why: Overlooking the narrow passage turns that passage into a spot where anyone passing through is exposed and forced to funnel along under fire.

can_cause.name: Sniper Locations
can_cause.why: Raised areas give a good view over the lower passage, so they can also work as places to shoot at others from a distance.

can_cause.name: Strategic Locations
can_cause.why: The advantages of holding the high ground make these areas worth fighting over and valuable to control.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting changes because those above can attack those below for a long stretch while enjoying the benefit of height.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Since the high ground favors whoever holds it, opponents become easier or harder to deal with depending on which side is elevated.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Height differences built into a board are the main way a gallery is created, shaping how the board plays.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Elevated areas that overlook passages can be built into a world's terrain, changing how fighting and travel work there.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: Holding the elevated spot makes defending a location easier, since attackers must pass through the overlooked area below.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: A gallery can be used to give extra advantage to the places players are trying to hold in this kind of goal.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Designers can use height differences within a level to create overlooked passages that change how the level plays.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Players in the lower area must travel along the elevated area for some distance, so their routes are constrained and exposed.

patterns.name: Fake Game Cancellations
patterns.what_it_is: The game pretends to be shut down so it can later surprise players with a continuation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a believable cancellation message through some channel, and contact details collected beforehand so players can be reached again. It only fits games meant to blur the line between game and real life.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cancellation notice so unconvincing, or with no way to contact players again, that nobody is surprised or it simply ends the game.
patterns.knobs: how convincing and through which channel the cancellation is announced; how long before players are re-contacted

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: Pretending the game is off leaves players unsure what is part of the game, which is the blurred line between game and reality that this style of play wants.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: Shutting down the game's servers is a simple way to make the cancellation look real to anyone checking whether the game is still running.

patterns.name: Hybrid Gameplay Spaces
patterns.what_it_is: The game is played at once in a real place and in a virtual or abstract one.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a real link between physical places and virtual ones (sensors, overlays, or rules), so that where the player physically is changes what happens in the game. Both parts of the space need to matter for play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game set in a real location that only uses it as a backdrop, where the virtual part ignores where players actually are.
patterns.knobs: how strongly physical position affects the virtual state; the sensing or overlay method; size of the real area

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Input
can_cause.why: Because the game depends on a real-world space, things happening in the physical setting, on purpose or by accident, can end up affecting play from outside the game's rules.

can_cause.name: Pervasive Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since part of the play happens in real places, play may spill into everyday life, though whether that works depends on which actions the game actually asks of players.

patterns.name: Backtracking Levels
patterns.what_it_is: The player must finish a level and then return along the same path.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must detect reaching the far end and then require a trip back, ideally with something changed or earned so the return is not just repeated walking. No shortcuts back.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are told to 'go back', but a teleport or instant exit takes them there, so the return trip has no content.
patterns.knobs: level length; what changes on the return; whether shortcuts exist

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because the return trip passes through the same space again, the surroundings can make the second pass feel different from the first, giving players new kinds of play.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: This is a kind of level where players pass through it and then must come back through it again.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: A board can be set up so players must cross all of it and then cross it again in reverse.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A level is changed from a one-way path into one players must cover to the end and then retrace fully.

changes.name: Transport Routes
changes.why: The route through the space is designed so players walk it out and then return along it, getting more use from it.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Players end up with two travel goals, reaching the far point and then coming back, instead of just one, which changes the traversal aim.

conflicts_with.name: Quick Returns
conflicts_with.why: A quick return would skip the walk back, but this pattern depends on players actually traveling the whole level again, so the two cannot coexist.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Without an extra reward at the far point, walking all the way back feels like effort that earns nothing, weakening the sense that effort pays off.

patterns.name: Scores
patterns.what_it_is: Numbers used in the game to decide who wins.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define what raises or lowers the number, by how much, and what values trigger events or end the game. Players must see the score as tied to the actual goal for it to drive play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A score shown on screen that does not determine winning, ranking, or any decision, so players ignore it.
patterns.knobs: points per action; end threshold; public versus hidden; penalties

can_cause.name: Abstract Player Constructs
can_cause.why: Scores are a basic number that the game tracks for each player, so they are one of the most common kinds of player-held game data.

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Because points keep piling up, players are always working to gather more of them, which makes accumulating points an ongoing activity.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Raising your number never finishes, so the game always gives players something to keep working toward.

can_cause.name: Exploitation
can_cause.why: In games with distinct phases, the stretch where players focus on squeezing out as many points as possible is the cashing-in phase.

can_cause.name: Facilitating Rewards
can_cause.why: Points help players reach the end or a win, so earning them acts as a reward that moves them toward finishing.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: When everyone can see the totals, one glance shows how each player or team is doing overall.

can_cause.name: High Score Lists
can_cause.why: Ranked numbers from past plays can be stored and shown, letting single players measure themselves against others or their own earlier tries.

can_cause.name: Investments
can_cause.why: Players may have to choose between taking points now or building up abilities that pay off later, so points compete with future advantage.

can_cause.name: Non-Localized Resources
can_cause.why: When points can be spent, they belong to the player in general rather than sitting at a specific place on the board.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: In tournaments, low point totals can be the reason a player gets knocked out of continued competition.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: A visible total shows how far players have come, and in games that cannot be won it is the way to see advancement.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Games can end when someone hits a target number or has the most at the end, so players hurry to get ahead.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Players want to beat their own earlier totals, or opponents, which gives them a reason to start another round.

can_cause.name: Resources
can_cause.why: If players are allowed to deliberately lower their points to pay for other actions, the points work as something to spend.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Points are generally added when players succeed at goals, so gaining them is itself a payoff for good play.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Seeing the totals openly lets players think ahead about what they need to do to catch up or stay in front.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When totals are visible or hidden until the end, players stay unsure who is winning, keeping excitement up.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: Two players can end with identical numbers, so using points for outcomes means equal results may happen.

can_cause.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
can_cause.why: Reaching a set point total can stop the game, so the number that triggers the end decides who wins.

can_cause.name: Construction/Scoring Phase Shift
can_cause.why: Where points decide the game, players eventually stop improving their position and turn their efforts to collecting points, creating the shift.

can_cause.name: Predictable Winner
can_cause.why: Visible scores show everyone how players compare, so people start judging who is likely to win, even if the numbers mislead.

can_cause.name: Tiebreakers
can_cause.why: When a game ends as soon as someone finishes, several players can finish together, and their scores can then separate them.

changes.name: Back-to-Back Game Sessions
changes.why: When games are played one after another, points from each round can be compared or used to break ties between the sessions.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Finalizing totals can happen when a character dies, and dying may also lower the points, so the two affect each other.

changes.name: King of the Hill
changes.why: Racing to reach a target number is the usual result of points, while King of the Hill offers a different way to compete.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Hitting certain point totals can grant extra lives, as a shared jackpot does in Pinball Dreams.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: Setting a point value that triggers events like ending the game is a way of defining what players are trying to achieve.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Points give players an obvious way to compete against one another by comparing numbers.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Points let solo players compare themselves with earlier plays or other people, for example through high score lists.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: A point total is usually attached to a team as a whole, so the group is compared rather than individuals.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Points work as information carried between games, so results from many games can be compared and used for rankings.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: With no way to win, a points total still shows players how well they are doing.

changes.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
changes.why: Points are normally the main method for deciding the winner once play is over.

changes.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
changes.why: Points can trigger the game's end when reached, or break ties if several players could end it simultaneously.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Showing scores makes players see the game as a system, which can change how they perceive everything else.

conflicts_with.name: Save Points
conflicts_with.why: Players can return to earlier states and retry to push their score higher, so the score no longer reflects a single uninterrupted run.

conflicts_with.name: Save-Load Cycles
conflicts_with.why: A score no longer shows how well you played in one continuous run if you can rewind and retry parts of it.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Points are difficult to justify within a game's theme, so they easily clash with it.

patterns.name: Player Elimination
patterns.what_it_is: A player is forcibly removed from the game before it ends for everyone.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Clear elimination conditions are needed, together with a plan for what eliminated players do, such as spectating, and for how long the others keep playing. Game length must keep waiting time acceptable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are 'out' in name but are respawned at once or keep playing, so being eliminated costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: how easily and how early players can be eliminated; what eliminated players can still do

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Once a player is knocked out, their own session is finished, so that player experiences a game-over moment even while others keep playing.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: In games with closed economies, removing players pushes their resources into the hands of fewer and fewer remaining players as the game goes on.

can_cause.name: Individual Penalties
can_cause.why: Being eliminated hits one particular player rather than everyone, so it works as a punishment aimed at a single person.

can_cause.name: Last Man Standing
can_cause.why: Because players drop out one by one, the game can be won by whoever is still alive after everyone else is gone.

can_cause.name: Spectacular Failure Enjoyment
can_cause.why: In some situations, the player who is knocked out can still find the dramatic way they lost entertaining.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Players who are out can keep watching the rest of the game, which partly makes up for no longer playing.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Since losing means everything invested is wasted if the session ends against your will, the threat of it makes players more nervous.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: When the first player is knocked out well before the others finish, their sessions end at noticeably different times.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Games
can_cause.why: If a game cannot be won, the player is bound to be removed eventually, since endless waiting or impossible goals would frustrate then bore them.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, an eliminated player is out of play and must wait for others to finish.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Dropping out may be acceptable in the final phase of a game, where players are more willing to accept being knocked out.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Where several people play, one can be removed while the others carry on, which changes how the shared game works.

changes.name: Synchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Elimination breaks everyone playing together, so synchrony only holds among those who have not yet been knocked out.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Teams can be wiped out when their members are eliminated, and the team structure affects how elimination plays out.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Players with lower scores than others can be removed from a tournament, so it shapes who stays in contention.

changes.name: Value of Effort
changes.why: Being knocked out wastes all the work a player put in, while survivors and the one who eliminated them feel their effort mattered more.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players know a game does not promise they will keep playing to the finish, which undermines feeling overly powerful.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Chances
conflicts_with.why: If retries let players avoid being knocked out too easily, the threat of elimination disappears.

conflicts_with.name: Fudged Results
conflicts_with.why: Frequent rescues from elimination mean being eliminated no longer reliably happens.

conflicts_with.name: Game Masters
conflicts_with.why: A game master can prevent eliminations by fudging results, but can also kick players out whenever they please.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Removing a player completely is the most definite misfortune and ends their chance of success.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Players' characters usually have major roles in a planned story, so killing them off breaks the plot.

conflicts_with.name: Team Balance
conflicts_with.why: When teams exist, losing members unevenly can leave one team much weaker than another.

conflicts_with.name: Togetherness
conflicts_with.why: Players who are removed have to sit out, so the group does not finish the session together.

conflicts_with.name: Value of Effort
conflicts_with.why: Players lose all value of what they invested when forced out before finishing, which damages their feeling that effort pays off.

patterns.name: Unwinnable Games
patterns.what_it_is: Games that have no winning conditions at all.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The system needs no reachable winning state, plus something that guarantees play ends, such as rising difficulty, a survive goal or a time limit, and some way to compare results like scores. Otherwise players have no reason to continue.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that calls itself endless but actually has a final boss, a victory screen or a reachable completion state.
patterns.knobs: how fast difficulty rises; length of time limit or resource drain; presence of score tables

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Since the game can never be completely beaten, players come back to improve on earlier results, which keeps them replaying.

can_cause.name: Surrendering
can_cause.why: With no win to reach, the only way players stop is by giving up on the game design itself.

can_cause.name: Unwinnable Game States
can_cause.why: Because the game has no winning state at all, every moment of play is necessarily a state from which winning is impossible.

can_cause.name: Early Leaving Players
can_cause.why: If a game offers no real chance of winning, players are more likely to quit before it ends.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: A game with several players can still have no winning condition, so the unwinnable design applies to group play as well.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: A game played alone can also be built without any winning state, so the unwinnable design applies to solo play too.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: In games that never end, players grow more skilled and more powerful, which can make the challenge too easy unless difficulty rises too.

conflicts_with.name: Endgame
conflicts_with.why: A game that can never be won has no end, so it normally cannot have a final phase.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Since players cannot truly win, a global sense of influence is hard to keep, so designers rely on local influence.

conflicts_with.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
conflicts_with.why: With no way to win, there is no building toward ever-larger closures, so the two generally can't be combined.

conflicts_with.name: Main Goals
conflicts_with.why: A main goal normally lets the game be completed, while an unwinnable game by definition cannot be completed, so the two pull against each other.

conflicts_with.name: Main Quests
conflicts_with.why: Finishing the main quest is a way to win, so a game designed so that nobody can win clashes with having one.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: They end only in failure and may run indefinitely, which limits possible stories and clashes with non-repetitive narration.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: If nobody can win in the first place, there is no one to predict as winner, unless players compare scores against each other.

conflicts_with.name: Time Limited Game Instances
conflicts_with.why: A game with no real end cannot sit with a rule that forces each session to stop after a limited time.

conflicts_with.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
conflicts_with.why: This needs a winner to be named at the end, but an unwinnable game has no winner to name.

conflicts_with.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: This needs ending play to count as a win, but an unwinnable game has no winning state to reach by stopping.

patterns.name: Progress Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: Show how close the player is to finishing, beyond the arrangement of the elements themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must show measurements tied to real goals, at the right moment and in a readable way. The information has to help players decide what to do next.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A bar is on screen but is cosmetic, misleading or unrelated to actual goals, so it does not guide anything.
patterns.knobs: what is measured; how precisely; when it is shown; to whom

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Seeing how your actions move you toward a closure lets you judge whether you are likely to reach it.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When the displayed progress matches the game's main goals exactly, players may feel their actions matter more than they truly do.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: When the indicator shows values that largely decide how a game session ends, such as scores, it becomes an indicator of the overall game state.

can_cause.name: Goal Indicators
can_cause.why: Closures usually relate to goals, so showing how close you are to a closure also shows how close you are to a goal.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: Progress displays can keep a closure visibly near but unreached, especially when paired with combos or development time.

can_cause.name: Illusionary Rewards
can_cause.why: If the displayed progress lines up perfectly with the game's overarching goals, moving it can feel like a reward without real value.

can_cause.name: Near Miss Indicators
can_cause.why: If the display only appears right after you narrowly failed to reach a goal, it shows how close you came.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: These displays show measurements to the player rather than the game world, so they sit outside the fiction unless given an in-world form.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When players can see their own and other players' progress displays, they naturally compare and compete over who gets there first.

can_cause.name: Scores
can_cause.why: Scores are a typical value central to a game's outcome, so showing them acts as a progress display of the game state.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing how close or far a closure is keeps players anxious or excited about whether they will reach it.

changes.name: Combos
changes.why: A progress display can show how far through a combo you have gotten, helping with extended actions of this kind.

changes.name: Delayed Effects
changes.why: Displays can tell players how long remains until a postponed effect occurs.

changes.name: Development Time
changes.why: Displays can show how long remains before something finishes developing, and can create hovering closures with it.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: Displays help players see how far along they are in actions that take a long time to complete.

changes.name: Grind Achievements
changes.why: A display shows how much of a repetitive effort has been done toward the achievement.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Visible measures of advancement help players perceive how close they are in the race, even for abstract goals.

changes.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
changes.why: A display can tell players which action in a required series comes next.

changes.name: Time Limits
changes.why: Displays can show how much time remains before the limit ends, informing players about it.

changes.name: Time Pressure
changes.why: By revealing how much time is left, displays change how urgent the time constraint feels.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: A display shows how far players have travelled toward a traverse goal, such as on a map.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Since such games cannot be won, a display can instead let players compare their game instance with others.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Displays give players more information about the game state, which reduces the uncertainty that pattern depends on.

patterns.name: Tied Results
patterns.what_it_is: Two or more results are counted as equal and have the same consequences.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Results must be coarse enough that equal values can happen, and the rules must say that equal means equal. The game needs several competitors to compare.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Scores are so fine-grained that ties essentially never happen, so tie rules are never used.
patterns.knobs: scoring granularity; whether ties share rewards or are broken

can_cause.name: Shared Penalties
can_cause.why: When players are judged equal they get the same outcome, so a bad result is split among them without any formal team.

can_cause.name: Shared Rewards
can_cause.why: Players judged equal receive the same reward, so a prize is shared among them without needing teams or other formal groups.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: A player can let others share a reward with them, but doing so lowers their own benefit, creating a conflict between self-interest and generosity.

changes.name: Tournaments
changes.why: Allowing ties adds more kinds of outcomes that can be carried over into the larger meta game that the tournament represents, adding granularity.

conflicts_with.name: Excluding Goals
conflicts_with.why: Since completing one goal voids the others, a shared or equal outcome cannot occur, making ties impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Incompatible Goals
conflicts_with.why: Tied results let several players meet the same goal together, which is exactly what incompatible goals rule out.

conflicts_with.name: Tiebreakers
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker exists to remove ties, so it works against them, although it can still occasionally end in one.

patterns.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
patterns.what_it_is: The winners are decided only after the gameplay has finished.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a clear end trigger and a scoring or comparison step afterward, and the standings must stay hard to calculate during play, through hidden scores or complexity. Otherwise the result is known early.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A final tally that merely confirms a leader who was obvious and uncatchable long before the end.
patterns.knobs: end trigger; how visible scores are; scoring formula; hidden versus open information

can_cause.name: Construction/Scoring Phase Shift
can_cause.why: When players sense the game is about to end, they can switch from building up resources to cashing in points, since the winner is only decided afterward.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: A player who thinks they lead but fears others will overtake them may rush the game to its end, since the result only counts then.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because nobody knows for sure who has won until play stops, players stay uneasy about their chances, and the strength of that feeling depends on how well they think they are doing.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Since the winner is not known until after play, every closure can stay meaningful to the very end when paired with hidden scoring.

can_cause.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
can_cause.why: Where players may end the game quickly, someone who correctly judges they are ahead can stop play and win, combining the two patterns.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: Not knowing who will win until play is over changes how the final phase feels and how players act in it.

changes.name: Game Over
changes.why: Declaring a winner only after play ends depends on the game reaching its end state, so the ending becomes the moment results are revealed.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: One way to choose a winner is to judge results only once play is over.

changes.name: Time Limited Game Instances
changes.why: When a game round has a time limit, the winner is worked out once that limit stops play, rather than during the round.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: If everyone can already see who will win, the winner is clearly not being decided after play finishes.

conflicts_with.name: Single-Player Games
conflicts_with.why: Deciding a winner afterwards only makes sense when several players could win, so it doesn't fit a game with one player.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Game States
conflicts_with.why: Since the winner is only decided once play is over, players can't be sure they've lost beforehand, so the hopeless feeling is avoided.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: This needs a winner to be named at the end, but an unwinnable game has no winner to name.

conflicts_with.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: The two conflict because here the winner is decided after play ends, though a successful rush to end the game can still produce this kind of win.

patterns.name: Last Man Standing
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: knock out rivals until you are the only surviving player or team.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players must be able to eliminate each other (lives, health, or removal) with goals that conflict. The game ends or moves on when only one remains, and it should handle what eliminated players do.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Players are called survivors but cannot really remove each other, so the winner is decided by something else.
patterns.knobs: how easily players are eliminated; how many lives; whether alliances or surrender are allowed

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: Because everyone is trying to knock out rivals, players may gang up on whoever is strongest, and they sometimes form short alliances to do it.

can_cause.name: Collections
can_cause.why: Each opponent a player knocks out can be counted as a trophy, so beating rivals builds up a set of defeated opponents.

can_cause.name: Early Elimination
can_cause.why: Players drop out one by one during the struggle, so some are knocked out well before the final survivor is decided.

can_cause.name: Endgame
can_cause.why: Since players are removed step by step and a sole survivor ends play, phases using this goal naturally feel like a game's closing stretch.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Every player removed is a small finished step, and it makes the next removal matter more, so the stakes rise as play goes on.

can_cause.name: Interferable Goals
can_cause.why: Every player wants to eliminate the others, so pursuing your own goal directly hurts or blocks everyone else's goal.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: To be the last one left, you have to beat the other players, so defeating opponents becomes part of the challenge.

can_cause.name: Survive
can_cause.why: Everyone is being targeted for elimination, so staying in the game while others are trying to remove you is central to play.

can_cause.name: Symmetric Goals
can_cause.why: All players have the same aim of eliminating each other, so each side wants exactly what every other side wants.

can_cause.name: Tournaments
can_cause.why: Eliminating losers until one remains gives a simple structure for running a tournament.

can_cause.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
can_cause.why: Once only one player remains, actions that remove others no longer matter, so winning comes with the competition ending.

can_cause.name: TvT
can_cause.why: Applying the last-one-survives contest to whole teams instead of single players gives you teams competing against each other.

patterns.name: Tiebreakers
patterns.what_it_is: Rules for separating results that would otherwise be equal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The secondary rule must be clear in advance and rarely tie itself. It should feel fair to players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A tiebreaker rule exists but ties on it are just as common, so ties remain.
patterns.knobs: which secondary criteria are used and in what order

can_cause.name: Excluding Goals
can_cause.why: Because a tie can't stand, only one player or team can come out on top, so one side reaching the goal shuts the others out.

can_cause.name: Incompatible Goals
can_cause.why: With ties ruled out, players can't both succeed, so their aims clash and one side's success means the other's failure.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Since a tie is never allowed, players cannot split a prize or a loss even if they would like to, which creates awkward choices.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Forcing a single outcome makes every close contest matter more, since players know a dead heat won't save them from losing.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: A tiebreaker rule can itself leave players equal, so a further tie may appear and some games stack several tiebreaking levels.

can_cause.name: Varying Rule Sets
can_cause.why: A sudden-death extension continues play only when a tie occurs, so some games run longer than others under a different rule.

changes.name: Bidding
changes.why: Ties make it unclear who gets the reward, so a tiebreaker is used to produce a clear order among bids.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: They make sure a contest cannot stay undecided, so every attempt to defeat an opponent ends as a success or failure.

changes.name: PvP
changes.why: When players compete for a goal and ties are not wanted, an extra rule is needed to decide a single winner.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Extra rules make sure that only one competitor is declared winner when several finish together.

changes.name: Score Tracks
changes.why: Reaching a certain spot on a track first can decide ties, and having tiebreakers also changes how the track gets used.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: When points end up equal, extra rules are added to separate players and give a single winner.

changes.name: Tiebreakers
changes.why: A tiebreaker can itself end in a tie, so designers may add another tiebreaker after it.

changes.name: Tied Results
changes.why: A tiebreaker is applied exactly when the main rule gives equal outcomes, so ties become rarer or disappear.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Team contests can end level, so a method for deciding a winner may be needed, just as with individual contests.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Penalties
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker splits tied players apart, which removes the equal outcome that would otherwise have given them a shared penalty.

conflicts_with.name: Shared Rewards
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker picks a single winner from tied players, so the tie that would have led to a shared reward no longer occurs.

conflicts_with.name: Tied Results
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker exists to remove ties, so it works against them, although it can still occasionally end in one.

patterns.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: The player who reaches a state that itself ends the game wins.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a specific achievable end condition that declares a winner at once, plus rules for simultaneous achievement or ties. The goal must be within reach of competing players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A goal that exists on paper but the game ends by timer anyway, or the winner is decided by a later count.
patterns.knobs: threshold needed (score, targets, survivors); tiebreaker rules; time cap

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Because reaching the winning state stops play, the game ends for everyone involved at that moment, so players hit game over as soon as someone wins.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: The winner is usually the biggest outcome of a game session, and this pattern settles it right at the end of play, completing the largest closure.
