can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: When a player is close to reaching the ending goal, everyone knows play may stop soon, which makes the moments before it feel tense.

can_cause.name: Game System Player
can_cause.why: When the game ending counts as a win for the system, the passing of the limit works like a quiet opponent that beats the players.

can_cause.name: Tiebreakers
can_cause.why: If several players can end the game simultaneously, a tie arises, so another measure like score is used to pick the winner.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: Combined with time-limited game instances, ending play to win becomes a specific case of a timeout leaving players equal.

changes.name: Endgame
changes.why: The exact condition chosen for ending play strongly shapes how the final phase of the game unfolds, if the game has one.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: A goal that ends play and crowns its achiever works when several players compete, unlike the alternative of deciding the winner afterwards.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: A lone player can also win by reaching an ending goal, such as finishing a story's last challenges, so the pattern is not limited to competition.

changes.name: Time Limited Game Instances
changes.why: Players can end a timed game early by winning, and if nobody has won when time runs out, a tie or the game system can win.

conflicts_with.name: Game Termination Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Ending play this way is a reward while this pattern's ending is a penalty, so the two are hard to combine.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: This needs ending play to count as a win, but an unwinnable game has no winning state to reach by stopping.

conflicts_with.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
conflicts_with.why: The two conflict because here the winner is decided after play ends, though a successful rush to end the game can still produce this kind of win.

patterns.name: Game Over
patterns.what_it_is: An event after which the player can no longer take part in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Define clear triggers such as losing lives or elimination, with real exclusion from play. The risk must be credible.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A Game Over screen appears, but the player instantly resumes with no loss, so there is no exclusion.
patterns.knobs: what triggers it; how easily it can be reached; whether and how play can resume

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: When a player is knocked out but a new game instance starts soon, the knocked-out player just waits, so the lockout becomes idle waiting time.

can_cause.name: Extermination
can_cause.why: Once players can be locked out, everyone starts trying to eliminate others, and rising risk of being locked out marks the start of a phase focused on eliminating opponents.

can_cause.name: Unsynchronized Game Sessions
can_cause.why: In a multiplayer game, one player hitting a loss state stops their play while the others carry on, splitting the endings.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Even when a game cannot be won, being locked out can still happen as a penalty, so it works as the way the game ends.

changes.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
changes.why: Play can stop before the winner is known, so the lockout comes first and the result is settled afterwards.

conflicts_with.name: Fake Game Overs
conflicts_with.why: A fake game over only pretends the game ended while real play continues, so it cannot coexist with an actual game over event.

patterns.name: Shared Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A goal to meet a requirement, or else the penalty falls on several players at once.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A failure must hit a group or common pool, so that everyone has a stake in avoiding it. Decide how it is divided or whether players can negotiate it.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A penalty labelled as shared but hitting each player individually, or so mild that nobody cares to coordinate.
patterns.knobs: who shares it; its size; how it is split or negotiated

can_cause.name: Mutual Goals
can_cause.why: Since everyone suffers the same loss on failure, players share the aim of avoiding it, or the penalty makes an existing shared aim matter more.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: A shared penalty is simply a penalty, just one that lands on several players together instead of on one person.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: When one failure hurts everyone, players must weigh their own interests against the group's, which is the tension behind many social dilemmas.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Deciding how to handle, spread out, or accept the group's penalty can lead a player to take on a recognizable role in the group.

can_cause.name: Teams
can_cause.why: Teams form when players both suffer the same penalties and enjoy the same rewards, so shared penalties are one of the two required parts.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Going through a loss alongside other players gives them a feeling of being in it together.

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: When a group suffers together if a shared goal fails, each member is committed to making it succeed.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: When punishments apply to every member of a faction, the group's rules affect everyone together.

conflicts_with.name: Altruistic Actions
conflicts_with.why: When teammates suffer together, helping a teammate also helps yourself, so the action stops being truly unselfish.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Players may suffer penalties they did not cause and could not avoid, which clearly shows how little control they have.

conflicts_with.name: Individual Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Individual penalties are designed to avoid hurting other players directly, whereas shared penalties deliberately hit several players, so the two pull in opposite directions.

conflicts_with.name: Tiebreakers
conflicts_with.why: A tiebreaker splits tied players apart, which removes the equal outcome that would otherwise have given them a shared penalty.

patterns.name: High Score Lists
patterns.what_it_is: Results are saved after a game so they can be compared.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Results must be saved and shown where players will see them, be comparable across attempts, and be ordered fairly with ties handled. Someone must care about the comparison, whether themselves, friends, or the world.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A list that resets on exit, is hidden in a menu, or is full of unreachable or fake entries so no one tries to beat it.
patterns.knobs: how many entries are kept; who can see them (local, friends, global); time-limited versus all-time lists

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Landing a spot on the list is an outcome that lasts beyond the match, so what happens in one play session carries into the world outside it.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: The list keeps results from finished sessions, such as scores, times or percentages, which makes it a stored record of how people played.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Because the saved results can be seen later, players can build a bigger game on top of the original, like trying to climb the rankings.

can_cause.name: Player-Defined Goals
can_cause.why: Seeing past results gives players their own targets to chase, such as topping their earlier run or passing a friend, though the game never asks for this.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Players want to do slightly better than their last attempt, so they keep coming back for more sessions even after finishing the main play.

can_cause.name: Social Rewards
can_cause.why: When friends and others can see your ranking, you get recognition from them for doing well, which feels like a reward.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Since results stay visible after a session ends, other people can look at them and notice how well someone played, even without watching live.

can_cause.name: Tied Results
can_cause.why: Because lists are ordered, two players can land on the same value, so the designer must either break the tie or show both as equal.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: Sharing scores lets solo players compare themselves with others, which turns a single-player game into a form of multiplayer.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Beating earlier results is a simple, visible target that pushes players to keep improving their skill at the game.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: A shared or global list turns a solo game into a contest, because players can compare their results with other people's.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: In games with no way to win, the list still gives players something to aim for, namely a better result than before.

patterns.name: End State Scoring
patterns.what_it_is: Points are added up only after the game has ended.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A large share of points must be hidden or uncounted until the end and depend on the final state, so players cannot easily calculate standings.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A final tally that merely repeats a score everyone already knows, so the end changes nothing.
patterns.knobs: how many points are held until the end; how hidden the scoring is; what final conditions give points

can_cause.name: Analysis Paralysis
can_cause.why: Players may burn lots of time trying to work out everyone's standings and possible final points, and open information makes this nearly certain unless standings are easy to see.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: When players can't work out who is ahead before the final count, they tend to feel their own moves matter more than they really do.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because nobody can be sure of the standings until the final tally, everyone stays anxious about how the last count will turn out.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Outcome
can_cause.why: With points revealed only at the end and standings hard to calculate, nobody knows who will win until the final count.

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: When scores are only revealed at the end and are partly hidden, players can conceal their standing, which makes bluffing about it easier.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Final scoring can happen when a player's elimination ends play, though that ending may only be temporary rather than permanent.

changes.name: Game Over
changes.why: Final scoring takes place once gameplay ends, so it shapes how a permanent ending of the game is resolved and who wins.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Some or all points are held back and only handed out after play stops, changing when players actually receive their score.

conflicts_with.name: Beat the Leader
conflicts_with.why: If points are only counted at the end, players cannot tell who is ahead during play, so they have no clear target.

conflicts_with.name: Surrendering
conflicts_with.why: When it is hard to tell who is winning, players are less likely to decide they are beaten and quit.

patterns.name: Game Termination Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A player is removed from the game early as a punishment while the others' game continues.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Elimination must really remove the player from play, with no cheap way back (no free continues, easy rejoin or endless extra chances). The trigger, such as losing the last life or health hitting zero, must be clear and plausibly threatening.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'Game Over' screen that drops you back a few seconds earlier with everything kept, so nothing is actually lost.
patterns.knobs: what triggers elimination; how easy it is to rejoin or continue

can_cause.name: Game Over
can_cause.why: Being removed from play as a penalty ends the game for that player, so the affected player experiences a game over.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Losing your session is a cost imposed for failing or being targeted, which makes it one particular kind of penalty.

can_cause.name: Player Elimination
can_cause.why: The penalty takes a player out of the game while it continues for others, which is exactly what eliminating a player means.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because a player might get thrown out, they feel anxious about it, and the more likely it seems, the stronger that feeling.

changes.name: Unwinnable Games
changes.why: Unwinnable games can still punish players for ending play, since failing or quitting can have consequences even without any victory.

changes.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
changes.why: Penalties for ending the game can take players out of influencing the game for a while before the winner is decided, changing how the result comes about.

conflicts_with.name: Extra Chances
conflicts_with.why: Enough retries can weaken or negate the penalty for ending the game, undermining the penalty's purpose.

conflicts_with.name: Fake Game Overs
conflicts_with.why: Penalties for ending a game make no sense when the game hasn't truly ended, so a fake ending and such penalties clash.

conflicts_with.name: Fudged Results
conflicts_with.why: Fudging exists to dodge game-ending outcomes, so used often it cancels the penalty's effect.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Easy rejoining turns the removal into a temporary penalty, so it no longer ends the player's participation.

conflicts_with.name: Winning by Ending Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Ending play this way is a reward while this pattern's ending is a penalty, so the two are hard to combine.

patterns.name: Grind Achievements
patterns.what_it_is: Rewards for repeating the same action many times.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A counter requires many repetitions of an action, set high enough to reflect real dedication but still reachable by persevering. Repeated tasks should vary or be meaningful or they are only chores.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A threshold so low it's reached by accident, or one that counts something players already do constantly, so it marks no extra effort.
patterns.knobs: required count; whether tasks must differ or be the same; how visible the progress is

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: A grind achievement is simply a kind of achievement: a named recognition players earn once they've done some activity enough times.

can_cause.name: Collecting
can_cause.why: Because the award needs the same sort of goal reached many times, players end up gathering up those repeated successes, which makes collecting a part of play.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: When the achievement asks for different tasks rather than one repeated task, players must visit and try varied places, such as discovering many locations or whole regions.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: Offering the same achievement at several counts means that once players reach one level, the next, larger one becomes their new target.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Reaching these achievements requires doing the same action over and over, so players naturally end up grinding.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Like achievements in general, they give players an extra layer of goals outside the core game to chase and compare.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: They hand players a prize for persevering, so they work as a reward like other achievements do.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: They show how much time and dedication a player has put in to a game or its community, so the effort feels recognized, though less strongly than goal achievements.

conflicts_with.name: Predetermined Story Structures
conflicts_with.why: Repeating events and encounters many times, or filling play with menial tasks, can break story consistency and slow the unfolding of a fixed story.

conflicts_with.name: Testing Achievements
conflicts_with.why: A grind achievement needs a high number of repeats; if the count is too low, it turns into a testing achievement instead.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Achievements built on collecting spawned items are problematic when the items appear from nowhere.

patterns.name: Goal Achievements
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: complete a game task in order to earn an achievement reward.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Goals must be real, challenging and require skill, and the achievements must be recorded persistently and, ideally, be visible to others. Difficulty must be high enough that getting one reflects mastery rather than luck or routine play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A badge for something trivial or automatic, such as finishing the tutorial, which changes nothing about how people play.
patterns.knobs: which goals have achievements; how hard they are; who can see them

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: A goal achievement is simply one kind of achievement: a lasting record, kept outside any single play session, that the player reached a particular objective.

can_cause.name: Grind Achievements
can_cause.why: Requiring a simple goal to be completed many times, once players have gotten skilled enough that it feels routine, turns a goal achievement into a grind achievement.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Like achievements generally, goal achievements give players something to collect and compare, which creates a game of pursuing them layered on top of the main game.

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Each goal achievement shows a goal was reached, and a series spread across levels or challenges shows players how far along they are.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Earning a goal achievement works as a reward, though if the goal is too easy it feels like a prize merely for trying something.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Because these achievements usually demand beating a real challenge, they make the effort feel worthwhile, especially when others can see the proof of skill.

can_cause.name: Handicap Achievements
can_cause.why: Giving a separate goal-based achievement for each difficulty setting is an easy way to make the player's chosen harder condition earn its own award.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Goal achievements that need to be distinguishable from easy or grind awards are often paired with hard-to-reach goals or difficult action sequences, raising the challenge.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: These achievements can require players to show real skill, so earning them documents how well someone has mastered the game.

conflicts_with.name: Luck
conflicts_with.why: If chance can stand in for skill, such as a random enemy attack being hit by accident, the achievement stops proving mastery and drifts toward grinding.

patterns.name: Secret Scoring Mechanisms
patterns.what_it_is: Ways to earn points that are revealed only when used or in the final count.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Offer hidden ways to score that are revealed only when used or at final count, and make them large enough to change who wins. It needs a multiplayer game with a visible leader to disturb.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Hidden points that are tiny or that everyone can already deduce, so the leader is still obvious.
patterns.knobs: size of hidden points; how many hidden scoring routes; when they are revealed

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: When a hidden point source only pays out if a player quietly meets a private requirement, it works like a secret goal that player is pursuing.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Because nobody knows how many hidden points rivals hold, everyone stays unsure about who is ahead, which keeps players on edge until the reveal.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Hidden scoring keeps the final result uncertain, so every closure stays important right up until play ends.

changes.name: End State Scoring
changes.why: Hidden points are often tallied automatically when final scoring begins, so the end count includes scores nobody saw coming and the final tally changes more.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Hiding how points are earned leaves players uncertain about who is leading.

changes.name: Score Tracks
changes.why: Since some points never appear on the public track, the track shows only part of each player's real total and so matters less.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Hidden point sources make players uncertain about each other's totals, so the scores in a multiplayer game are only partly known during play.

changes.name: Winner determined after Gameplay Ends
changes.why: Hidden points keep the final result open until the end, so what happens along the way can still seem to affect who wins.

conflicts_with.name: Beat the Leader
conflicts_with.why: When scoring is hidden, players cannot judge who is in front, so they lack the basis for ganging up on anyone.

conflicts_with.name: Predictable Winner
conflicts_with.why: Hiding how points are counted stops players from working out who is leading, so a winner can't be foreseen.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Game States
conflicts_with.why: Players trailing on visible scores can still hope that hidden points or others' unknown totals will let them catch up, so they feel less beaten.

patterns.name: Closure Points
patterns.what_it_is: Moments when part of the game state is removed or becomes unavailable.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Reaching them must actually remove or lock part of the game state, and players must see what is ending.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'level complete' screen appears, but everything carries over and can be revisited, so nothing really closes.
patterns.knobs: how often they occur; reversibility; how clearly they are signalled

can_cause.name: Goal Indicators
can_cause.why: If a game always shows its closure moments in the same recognizable way, players learn to read them as signs of what the game's larger aims are.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Because closure points drop old parts of the game state and bring in new ones, they are how bigger stages of completion get built up as play moves on.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Closure points give players a clear moment where earlier work visibly pays off, letting them feel that their effort counted.

patterns.name: Handicap Achievements
patterns.what_it_is: A reward for a goal completed while voluntarily making the game harder.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The restriction must really raise difficulty, such as limited weapons or time limits, and be optional, with the achievement recorded and visible. It needs a base game strong enough to support the harder play.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A 'challenge' whose handicap is trivial or cosmetic and makes no difference to how you play.
patterns.knobs: kind and severity of the restriction; which goals it applies to

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: Handicap achievements are a subcategory of achievements, so they work as lasting recognition of what a player has done, just with a harder condition attached.

can_cause.name: Challenging Gameplay
can_cause.why: Because the player must finish a goal under a self-imposed limitation, the play becomes harder, and this can open up challenge players might otherwise never try.

can_cause.name: Goal Achievements
can_cause.why: They are built on an ordinary goal and just add a limitation to it, so they count as a kind of achievement for reaching a goal.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Collecting these achievements creates an extra layer of play on top of the game, where players pursue the awards as a separate activity.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: Players can always finish the underlying goal without the handicap, so taking on the handicap is a choice, making it more optional than other achievements.

can_cause.name: Optional Rules
can_cause.why: The handicap can be seen as extra rules players choose to adopt, such as limiting weapons, and then must follow themselves.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Getting the achievement pays players back for finishing something in a harder way than required, so it works as a reward.

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: Players must make sure they obey the handicap rules themselves while pursuing the achievement, so they are running that extra game on their own.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Players get recognition for extra effort even though that effort was entirely their own choice, which makes the effort feel worth something.

changes.name: Gameplay Mastery
changes.why: Since the achievements require harder play, earning them lets players show off how skilled they are, perhaps more clearly than ordinary goal achievements do.

conflicts_with.name: Casual Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Such achievements usually push players into harder play, which clashes with the easygoing nature of casual games.

patterns.name: Social Rewards
patterns.what_it_is: Rewards that raise a player's standing among people rather than giving an in-game benefit.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The reward must be visible to other players, through lists, titles or shown achievements, and must be something that others actually respect. It should not change the in-game balance.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A badge that only the owner ever sees, or one handed out for trivial actions so that it earns no recognition from anyone.
patterns.knobs: how visible rewards are to others; how hard they are to earn; how many kinds exist

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Because the reward is about how other players see you rather than helping you in the game, its effects land outside play itself.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Since this reward doesn't change game balance, designers can hand it out for repetitive effort without making one player stronger than another.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: It is a kind of reward, but what it gives is appreciation from other players instead of an advantage in the game.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Rewards that others can see give exhibitionists something to brag about.

patterns.name: Testing Achievements
patterns.what_it_is: A reward for the player simply trying out some action.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The tested activities should be optional ones players might otherwise skip, and trying should be cheap. The reward should be noticeable enough to nudge behavior.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The achievement is for something every player does anyway, so it never changes what anyone tries.
patterns.knobs: which activities are included; how easy the trigger is; how visible the reward is

can_cause.name: Achievements
can_cause.why: Testing Achievements are simply one kind of achievement, awarded just for having tried an activity, so using them automatically creates achievements.

can_cause.name: Experimenting
can_cause.why: Because the reward comes from merely trying something new, players are nudged to poke at unfamiliar features while they are still learning them.

can_cause.name: Meta Games
can_cause.why: Every achievement type can feed collection goals, and these easy ones add cheap items to collect without much extra effort for players.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: In games with different ways to play, rewarding a short try of each style gives players a reason to come back and play another way.

can_cause.name: Rewards
can_cause.why: Getting an achievement for trying something works as a reward, giving players a payoff for stepping into an activity.

can_cause.name: Grind Achievements
can_cause.why: The goals of a testing achievement can be counted further, so the first success gives the testing award and a set number of successes gives the grind one.

can_cause.name: Grinding
can_cause.why: Collections paired with testing achievements can push players to repeat actions to complete sets, producing grinding and grind achievements.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Fallout: New Vegas gives an achievement for recruiting any companion, which pushes players to try using one instead of ignoring the option.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Achievements can be given just for attempting a particular quest, which makes players try quests they might otherwise skip while following a single path.

changes.name: Varied Gameplay
changes.why: When players choose between different ways of playing, an award for trying each one gets them to sample styles they would otherwise not pick.

conflicts_with.name: Grind Achievements
conflicts_with.why: A grind achievement needs a high number of repeats; if the count is too low, it turns into a testing achievement instead.

conflicts_with.name: Grinding
conflicts_with.why: Encouraging players to try other parts of the game gives them a break from grinding.

patterns.name: Life Penalties
patterns.what_it_is: A punishment the player receives upon losing a life.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs Lives and a clear trigger for losing one, either a direct hit or full damage. Losing a life must move the player closer to game end, with respawn in between.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A life counter drops but players can regain lives freely or ignore it, so failure costs nothing.
patterns.knobs: what triggers a life loss; how many lives exist; whether lives can be regained

can_cause.name: Game Termination Penalties
can_cause.why: When a player loses a life and has none left, the game must apply an ending penalty, otherwise lives wouldn't mean what they normally do.

can_cause.name: Penalties
can_cause.why: Losing a life is itself a cost imposed on the player for failing, so it counts as a kind of penalty.

can_cause.name: Spawning
can_cause.why: While the player still has lives left after losing one, they need to be put back into the game world, which requires respawning.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Knowing a mistake could cost a life makes players nervous, and the feeling grows sharper when only one life remains.

changes.name: Death Consequences
changes.why: Losing a life is one specific form of what happens to a player on dying, so it shapes and narrows that consequence.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Losing a life is itself a penalty, and it can bring further effects because losing every life ends the session.

conflicts_with.name: Fudged Results
conflicts_with.why: If fudges frequently prevent life loss, the penalty stops meaning anything.

patterns.name: Fake Game Overs
patterns.what_it_is: The game announces that everything is over when in fact it is not.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a believable game over presentation, then a clear resumption of play. It fits only games where a real game over exists and carries weight, so the fake can shock players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game over screen that is obviously fake or comes with no loss, so players feel no sense of failure.
patterns.knobs: how convincing the fake ending is; how and when play resumes

can_cause.name: Fake Game Cancellations
can_cause.why: Because the game pretends play has ended when it hasn't, players briefly think the session was cancelled, and that false ending is what produces the fake cancellation.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The false game-over screen is an interface element sitting outside the game's story world, so showing it brings a non-diegetic feature into play.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players who believe they've suddenly failed feel a jolt of worry until play resumes, so the trick generates tension.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: The fake ending bends what players take to be real about the game's state, which makes it a case of play that blurs or alters reality.

conflicts_with.name: Game Over
conflicts_with.why: A fake game over only pretends the game ended while real play continues, so it cannot coexist with an actual game over event.

conflicts_with.name: Game Termination Penalties
conflicts_with.why: Penalties for ending a game make no sense when the game hasn't truly ended, so a fake ending and such penalties clash.

patterns.name: Predetermined Story Structures
patterns.what_it_is: The order in which the story is presented is fixed before the session begins.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Story beats need triggers tied to player progress, and the narrative must connect to goals, characters and clues. The designer must decide how much player choice may bend the order.
patterns.just_a_label_when: There are cutscenes and text, but they are skippable decoration that neither guide goals nor react to what the player does.
patterns.knobs: how linear the story is; how many branches; how story events are triggered

can_cause.name: Companions
can_cause.why: Companions are characters that designers plan into the narration, and they work as focal points through which the planned story reaches players.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: A cutscene is a pre-made story event, and a whole story structure can be assembled from them, so each can count as a story structure itself.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Designed story structures limit what players can do, yet they can also make the choices players do get feel more consequential than they really are.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: Most story narration only describes what happened and doesn't change the game state, so its effects stay outside the game's rules.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: Planned events can be placed so players feel fortunate, but this only works if the fortunate event comes as an unexpected surprise.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Revealing a story set in advance through gameplay is the main way narrations get told in a game.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Because the story is fixed in advance, earlier events and foreshadowing let players guess what comes next, especially when the story is replayed.

can_cause.name: PvE
can_cause.why: Players often face characters the designers created as part of the story, so the story's cast becomes the opposition in play.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Players think about how the story may unfold, and combined with goals and clues this encourages them to plan ahead.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Having story parts authored before play gives the game a way to tell a story to its players.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Events can be designed to foreshadow what may happen later, which builds anticipation and tension in players.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: A scripted story can set up moments that radically change a character or make different choices lead to very different outcomes.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: With a fixed story and clues scattered in it, players try to deduce what comes next, which creates information-seeking goals.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Story progress can depend on obtaining clues, which turns obtaining them into an ownership goal.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: In such games a prepared story can help set the game apart from the real world.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Games lacking an overarching story can add small local stories to give bosses more substance.

changes.name: Character Development
changes.why: Stories focus on player characters, so the story events are a way of affecting how those characters develop.

changes.name: Gain Competence
changes.why: Goals of improving one's position can be combined with narrative goals, and finishing them can lead to character development.

changes.name: Instances
changes.why: An instance can hold a self-contained story that different groups experience independently without affecting each other.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: In a world that persists, a story can only be used once or only as a local story without world-wide effect.

changes.name: Player Characters
changes.why: Stories tend to center on player characters, shaping what happens to them.

changes.name: Player-Created Characters
changes.why: Such characters are not designed by the designers, but prepared stories can influence them or become part of them to support certain narratives.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Because the story focuses on the player character and its development, it can motivate players to roleplay.

conflicts_with.name: Characters
conflicts_with.why: If important characters die through death consequences, the planned story can be broken.

conflicts_with.name: Coupled Games
conflicts_with.why: A fixed story in both games forces one to pause until the other catches up, or lets players learn upcoming events by playing the other game.

conflicts_with.name: Death Consequences
conflicts_with.why: If a key character in a scripted story can die, the planned plot can be broken.

conflicts_with.name: Early Leaving Players
conflicts_with.why: A planned story can break when a participant disappears, since the facilitator or system counted on that player's role.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: A set story limits possible actions and event order, which restricts how much influence players feel they have.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: Once a story branch is explored, the outcome is known, so choices there become meaningless.

conflicts_with.name: Grind Achievements
conflicts_with.why: Repeating events and encounters many times, or filling play with menial tasks, can break story consistency and slow the unfolding of a fixed story.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Extra characters brought by newcomers strain a fixed story unless a game master can work them in.

conflicts_with.name: Multiplayer Games
conflicts_with.why: With more players, it gets harder to let everyone affect a fixed story, and some players' effort matters less.

conflicts_with.name: Negotiable Game Instance Duration
conflicts_with.why: A story with fixed events assumes a certain length of play, so if players shorten or stretch the game, the story may not fit unless it can scale.

conflicts_with.name: Persistent Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: A world that continues without end cannot follow a fixed plot, so it must rely on never-ending stories or small scripted pieces.

conflicts_with.name: Player Elimination
conflicts_with.why: Players' characters usually have major roles in a planned story, so killing them off breaks the plot.

conflicts_with.name: Player-Created Characters
conflicts_with.why: Stories written in advance by designers may not have roles that fit characters players invented, making the two hard to combine.

conflicts_with.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
conflicts_with.why: Generated worlds can make prepared stories irrelevant unless story creation is built into the generation process.

conflicts_with.name: Randomness
conflicts_with.why: If much of the design depends on chance, planned story elements can become irrelevant.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: When a game is replayed and the story reused, players can predict it and lose surprises.

conflicts_with.name: Self-Facilitated Games
conflicts_with.why: Players hold the power to ignore or change the story, which undermines its being fixed beforehand.

conflicts_with.name: Speedruns
conflicts_with.why: These ask players to ignore everything except the most efficient play, so the story is disregarded.

conflicts_with.name: Unwinnable Games
conflicts_with.why: They end only in failure and may run indefinitely, which limits possible stories and clashes with non-repetitive narration.

patterns.name: Narration Structures
patterns.what_it_is: The structure of stories that the game contains or can generate.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Events and goals must be linked to the story so that progress moves it forward. The structure needs points of tension and closure that gameplay actually reaches.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A story told in intro text and cutscenes that has no link to the goals or actions, so play would be identical without it.
patterns.knobs: how tightly the story is tied to goals; how linear or branching it is

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: A story's structure naturally has moments where parts of the plot wrap up, so a narration gives players those checkpoints along the way.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: The story context helps players make sense of where things stand in the game, giving them a picture of the current situation.

can_cause.name: Goal Indicators
can_cause.why: Closure points in a story can show players what they are heading toward, so the narrative ends up signalling goals.

can_cause.name: Hovering Closures
can_cause.why: A narration keeps players wondering how it will end, leaving the outcome pending while they keep playing.

can_cause.name: Secret Goals
can_cause.why: The story can supply a reason why individual players have hidden gameplay aims, which makes those private objectives feel believable.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Players want to find out what happens next or how the story ends, and that curiosity creates tension.

can_cause.name: Goal Hierarchies
can_cause.why: A story's hierarchical or sequential structure can be filled in with goals, turning it into a goal hierarchy.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: A story helps players understand intricate evolving gameplay from a narrative angle as well as from the rules angle.

changes.name: Deliver
changes.why: The narration can support the design of delivery goals by giving them story context.

changes.name: Evade
changes.why: The narration can support evading goals by giving them story context.

changes.name: Gain Ownership
changes.why: The narration can support goals of acquiring things by giving them story context.

changes.name: Main Goals
changes.why: The story gives players reasons to pursue main goals and links the game's narration to their main motivation.

changes.name: Mandatory Goals
changes.why: The story gives reasons within the game world for completing required goals and tells players how to achieve them.

changes.name: Overcome
changes.why: The narration can support overcoming goals by giving them story context.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: The narration can support rescue goals by giving them story context.

conflicts_with.name: Player-Planned Development
conflicts_with.why: A story fixed before play works against letting players plan how things develop.

conflicts_with.name: Pottering
conflicts_with.why: Idle tinkering by design produces nothing noteworthy, so it gives the story no events to build on.

conflicts_with.name: Tension
conflicts_with.why: A story can lack tension itself, or block players who want to interact with the game system, which reduces tension.

patterns.name: Non-Player Characters
patterns.what_it_is: Characters in the game world that players do not control.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a world for NPCs to live in, and each NPC needs a clear role and recognizable look. Whether they act as agents with goals or only as scenery or story devices decides how much they matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Figures standing in the world that do nothing, say nothing and affect nothing, so they are scenery with a name tag.
patterns.knobs: how many NPCs; what role each has; whether they have agency and goals

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Characters without agency can still act as the sender or receiver of a delivery, giving the player someone in the world to bring something to or from.

can_cause.name: Dialogues
can_cause.why: Talking with NPCs is a common function, ranging from a canned line saying they have nothing to say to conversation being the main way of playing.

can_cause.name: Factions
can_cause.why: NPCs can be grouped into social blocs that players deal with or join, so how you treat one NPC can affect a whole group.

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: NPCs in conversation can pass along rumors that point toward optional goals or show that the world remembers past events.

can_cause.name: Guard
can_cause.why: An NPC can be the thing the player must protect, which turns a person in the world into the objective of a goal.

can_cause.name: Helpers
can_cause.why: NPCs without agency can only offer services to players, like a kiosk, so they act as simple helpers.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: An NPC companion can be tied to the player's story so that choices about them pull the player in opposing directions.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: NPCs carry information and emotion through people and social relations, so they form the core of how stories are told, even if only seen in cutscenes.

can_cause.name: Predefined Goals
can_cause.why: Through conversation, NPCs can hand out, back up or close out goals that the designers set ahead of time.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers can build NPCs and events around them in advance, then let the story unfold through dialogue with them.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: NPCs commonly hand out and judge quests, giving players tasks and deciding when they have been completed.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: A world that should have inhabitants feels wrong without individual people in it, so NPCs help the world fit its theme.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: NPCs can handle buying and selling of transferable items even when they have no agency of their own.

can_cause.name: Boss Monsters
can_cause.why: Unique bosses are usually built as characters with their own nature, history and appearance, rather than as copies of normal enemies.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled characters with helpful goals can guide and assist players, pushing play toward being easy and supported.

can_cause.name: Combat
can_cause.why: Computer characters whose goal is to stop the player supply the opposing side that makes a fight happen.

can_cause.name: Cooperation
can_cause.why: Computer characters given the purpose of supporting the player will assist rather than betray, giving the player a cooperative partner.

can_cause.name: King of the Hill
can_cause.why: Game-controlled characters can pursue the same hill goal as a player, standing in for rival players and competing with them.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Dealing with rivalries among game characters in a group gives players social situations to figure out.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: System-controlled characters can serve as nonviolent rivals so a lone player still has someone to beat.

can_cause.name: Resource Sources
can_cause.why: Non-player characters can give out loot, so they act as a place where players can obtain resources.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Non-player characters give players diegetic figures to interact with, and game masters roleplaying them makes the exchange flexible.

can_cause.name: Team Combos
can_cause.why: Computer-controlled characters can coordinate with the player to produce what is effectively a team combo.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Making NPCs into enemies lets quests be tuned to be harder, since opponents with opposing goals raise the challenge.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Having any NPC implies a world they live in, so adding them calls for a fuller world or leaves it feeling inconsistent.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: NPCs can be given helpful or hostile goals, which lets designers shift quests toward casual, complex or challenging play.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: An NPC can be the person the player must save, making a character in the world the objective of the goal.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Opposing NPCs let a single player practice things like racing in a meta game, and NPCs can also teach skills through conversation.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Other characters in the world can tell or show the player things, giving another route for information in a world-centered pattern.

conflicts_with.name: Units
conflicts_with.why: NPCs are individual people with variation that players don't control, whereas units treat inhabitants as an undifferentiated group, so the two clash.

patterns.name: Cutscenes
patterns.what_it_is: Story clips during which the player can do nothing.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must carry information the player needs and be placed at points where a pause fits, such as before a challenge or at a change of place. Their length and the ability to skip them decide whether they help or annoy.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A long cinematic that adds no new information and changes no state, which players simply skip.
patterns.knobs: length; frequency; whether they can be skipped

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: A cutscene can set up a situation or stress an upcoming choice, making players notice which actions define their character.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can reveal information about future challenges, such as enemy weaknesses, letting players judge how likely they are to win.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: Cutscenes stop gameplay, so players have nothing to do while the scene runs, which is a break in activity.

can_cause.name: Enforced Agent Behavior
can_cause.why: During a cutscene, players or other agents are made to act as the scene dictates, with no say in what happens.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: When a cutscene only moves the story forward and leaves the game state unchanged, its effects stay outside the game's mechanics.

can_cause.name: Game Pauses
can_cause.why: Cutscenes halt play, and the game clock too in real-time games, so they work as a pause in the game.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: A cutscene can show players the layout or situation of a new level, giving them a summary of where things stand.

can_cause.name: Goal Indicators
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can give players hints about future challenges, which point toward what they should aim for.

can_cause.name: Lull Periods
can_cause.why: If players find a cutscene dull, the stopped gameplay becomes a stretch where little of interest happens.

can_cause.name: MacGuffins
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can show details of key story objects, and such objects may exist only within cutscenes yet still belong to the game world.

can_cause.name: No-Ops
can_cause.why: To make sure players cannot miss the information, cutscenes remove their ability to act, so any input they give does nothing.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can give details about non-player characters that normal play cannot, and these characters may exist only in cutscenes.

can_cause.name: Point of Interest Indicators
can_cause.why: Cutscenes shown when players meet new enemies, bosses or traces can mark those things as worth attention.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Cutscenes are the most common way to unfold a fixed story, and a fixed story can in turn be partly built from cutscenes.

can_cause.name: Props
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can show props that the ordinary gameplay could not, and props may exist only within them while still being part of the game world.

can_cause.name: Scenes
can_cause.why: A cutscene is a scene whose content is localized and fixed, presented as a sequence players watch rather than act in.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can give knowledge about coming challenges and show goals and odds, which gives players something to plan around.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Cutscenes are one of the most controlled ways to tell a story, presenting the game world's alternative reality or its set plot.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: A cutscene can tell players how to handle future challenges, for example by showing an enemy's weak point.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because a cutscene takes complete control of the game state, the designer can guarantee the presentation fits the game's theme.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: A cutscene may use a third-person camera for dramatic effect, regardless of the view the game normally uses.

can_cause.name: Transport Routes
can_cause.why: When a cutscene carries players from one location to another, it functions as the means of travel between those places.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: A cutscene takes over the game state completely, overriding whatever players or the game were doing.

can_cause.name: Unpredictable Behavior
can_cause.why: The first time players see a particular cutscene it can contain surprises, which make agents seem to act unpredictably.

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A cutscene plays automatically, so it can deliver the clue without the player missing it, or point them to where the clue is.

can_cause.name: First-Person Views
can_cause.why: Cutscenes can show the action through a character's eyes at a given moment, even when the rest of the game presents the world another way.

can_cause.name: God Views
can_cause.why: A cutscene can show the world from above without a player-controlled camera, since its viewpoint movement can be fully scripted in advance.

can_cause.name: Helpers
can_cause.why: A scripted cutscene can bring in a helper at a given moment, usually as part of a fixed story, like the tow in Mario Kart.

changes.name: Achilles' Heels
changes.why: Cutscenes can reveal an enemy's weak point to players, giving them knowledge for meeting future challenges.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Cutscenes can change how players see their avatars, since the scenes make the avatars act in ways players do not control.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Cutscenes are commonly placed when players first meet a boss, announcing its presence and marking it as important.

changes.name: Character Defining Actions
changes.why: Cutscenes can present defining actions as part of the story, or can break them by showing the character acting against how the player sees them.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Cutscenes are commonly placed when players first meet new enemies, showing their presence and marking them as noteworthy.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: A cutscene may use a first-person camera for dramatic effect, even if the game normally uses another view.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Cutscenes give the designer complete control over how players perceive the world, including details gameplay could not show.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: A cutscene may use a god's-eye camera for dramatic effect, regardless of the view the game normally uses.

changes.name: Inaccessible Areas
changes.why: Cutscenes can give players a look into places they cannot reach, and can make them aware such places exist.

changes.name: MacGuffins
changes.why: Cutscenes can show details of key story objects, and such objects may exist only within cutscenes yet still belong to the game world.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Cutscenes can give details about non-player characters that normal play cannot, and these characters may exist only in cutscenes.

changes.name: Open Destiny
changes.why: A cutscene shown after the game ends can tell what happened afterward, which helps players realize the future was left open.

changes.name: Quick Returns
changes.why: Cutscenes can depict a fast trip back to an earlier place, covering the movement instead of having players play it.

changes.name: Quick Travel
changes.why: Cutscenes can show the fast trip between places, covering the movement instead of having players play it.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Cutscenes stop gameplay and, in real-time games, also stop the running game time.

changes.name: Traces
changes.why: Cutscenes are commonly placed when players come across traces, so that these can be marked as points of interest.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Cutscenes usually present a character's traits in the world, which restricts what players can choose.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: Automatically played scenes reduce the risk that players miss a clue, or point them to the elements that hold it.

changes.name: Penalties
changes.why: In single-player games, a cutscene can emphasize a penalty's effects without interrupting other players.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Quests are often opened and closed with cutscenes, which mark their start and finish dramatically.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Short story scenes can draw attention to a reward or tie the story to when it is handed out.

conflicts_with.name: Character Defining Actions
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes take control away from players and may show the character acting against how players see them, undermining the sense that their own actions define the character.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes remove player agency, which makes it hard to also make players feel their influence is larger than it is.

conflicts_with.name: Freedom of Choice
conflicts_with.why: In cutscenes, players or other agents are made to act as scripted, which limits what players can choose to do.

conflicts_with.name: Minimalized Social Weight
conflicts_with.why: Cutscenes are made to draw attention to the story presentation, which runs against keeping social aspects of play small.

patterns.name: Player Characters
patterns.what_it_is: Characters the player directly controls and through whom they take part in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The character needs its own traits, abilities and a role in the story that give the player something to act through and care about. The link between player knowledge and character knowledge needs to be handled.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A named figure on screen with no traits, history or effect on play, which is really just a cursor.
patterns.knobs: how detailed the character is; its power compared with others; how much the player can shape it

can_cause.name: Agents
can_cause.why: When players steer a single character, that character feels like an acting being with its own will rather than a mere piece being moved around.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: A player character gives players one specific place in the game world through which they act and interact with it.

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: Because players control a character, they get a natural way to talk about events and other characters, including in-world rumor-sharing.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Players' characters can help build up the story as it unfolds during play.

can_cause.name: Parties
can_cause.why: A party can be made up entirely of player characters, as is typical in multiplayer games.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Player characters matter to prewritten stories, mainly through the events they take part in and some set traits, though not necessarily every detail.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: A player character gives players a natural starting point for playing a role, and the freedom to decide how to act it out.

can_cause.name: Storytelling
can_cause.why: Having a character of their own lets players tell stories about what it does and experiences, using the creative control they have.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: A character stands between a player and others, so people interact with the character and not the person controlling it.

conflicts_with.name: Character Defining Actions
conflicts_with.why: If defining actions shape a player character in ways the player dislikes, it can break their emotional engrossment, since players feel they own that character's interpretation.

conflicts_with.name: Game Element Insertion
conflicts_with.why: Putting new player characters in because someone arrives late can cause balance problems among the players.

conflicts_with.name: Late Arriving Players
conflicts_with.why: Bringing in a newcomer's character mid-game is hard to do fairly, since the character holds the game values players care most about.

conflicts_with.name: Player Balance
conflicts_with.why: Characters of late-arriving players can be inserted into the game, giving them different conditions from the others.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Since players control how their characters behave, they may act in ways that don't fit the game's theme unless someone supervises or their actions are limited.

patterns.name: Storytelling
patterns.what_it_is: Stories that are told inside the game itself.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs agents, places and conflicts that carry a story, and a way to deliver it that does not break the game's own world. Choose between a fixed story and one that follows what players do.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A story told only in a manual or intro that has no connection to actions in play, so it could be removed without changing anything.
patterns.knobs: fixed vs. adaptive story; how it is delivered (cutscenes, environment, facilitator); how often it appears

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Telling stories can count as acting outside the game proper when the telling doesn't affect the game state or only partly involves decisions that matter to it.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Letting players narrate gives them room to decide what happens or what is said, which widens the choices open to them.

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: Stories often bring in new objects, places or events, so telling a story naturally adds elements to the game.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: A story can describe and thereby bring a game world into being, including showing what its history looks like.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Mastery
can_cause.why: In games like Once Upon a Time and roleplaying games, being good at telling stories counts as a skill that makes someone better at playing.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: Telling stories either supplies a game with an existing narrative frame or builds and extends one as play goes on.

can_cause.name: Player Created Game Elements
can_cause.why: When players or human game masters narrate, the things they invent and add to the world are elements created by the players.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: Being the storyteller is a role a player can take, and doing it well gives a feeling of having fulfilled that role.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Stories can wrap every action and event in the game in the feel of its fictional reality, keeping everything fitting together.

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: When someone tells a story without interruption, whether a game master or a player, the telling works as a cutscene.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: Narrative can be used as a channel to express the emotions agents feel about what happens in the game world.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Telling what specific characters do counts as roleplaying when they act in line with their personality and context.

changes.name: Fudged Results
changes.why: A story can offer an in-world explanation for why a result was bent, making the adjustment feel natural.

changes.name: Game Element Insertion
changes.why: Narration can justify newly added elements in the fiction so they fit the world rather than feeling arbitrary.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Storytelling can shape how a world is presented, its history and how its events are framed.

changes.name: Persistent Game Worlds
changes.why: Stories told in a lasting world can influence how it develops and feed ongoing, never-ending narratives.

changes.name: Player Created Game Elements
changes.why: Narration can explain player-made additions in story terms, keeping them consistent with the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players' freedom to tell their own story can introduce non-diegetic elements that break the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Storytellers with creative control may add unfitting objects or events, or make characters act out of character, spoiling the fiction's coherence.

patterns.name: Props
patterns.what_it_is: World objects that exist only for appearance and play no part in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They need to fit the setting and be visually distinct from usable items. They work best when they also provide mood, landmarks or clues.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Objects are scattered randomly with no theme, or look like usable items so players waste time on them.
patterns.knobs: how many; where placed; how distinct from usable items

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A prop can be shaped or placed so it hints at where to go or what happened, giving players direction without any interaction.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Filling the world with objects that merely exist makes it feel like a believable place, so props help the world stay consistent with itself.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: Props placed around a scene let the setting hint at events and add story flavor without characters or text telling it.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Props can be things players want to acquire, such as objects needed to satisfy goals like decorating a farm or pleasing zoo animals.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Varied props make wandering the world more interesting, and decoys that look like sought-after things force players to search around.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: A prop made large or distinctive stands out in the scenery, so players can recognize it and use it to orient themselves.

can_cause.name: MacGuffins
can_cause.why: Since a prop needs no function and little needs to be revealed about it, it can serve as an objective that matters only in the story.

can_cause.name: Obstacles
can_cause.why: Large props like buildings or trees can physically block movement, offering a natural-looking alternative to invisible barriers.

can_cause.name: Player Aids
can_cause.why: Physical props such as maps can be used at the table to help players understand the game, without being part of the rules.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: A prop can look like a hint or marker while leading nowhere, misleading players who expect it to mean something.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Adding more detailed objects to a world makes it fit its setting and mood better, strengthening the theme.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Props can be arranged to look like evidence left behind by someone or something, guiding players about what has passed through.

can_cause.name: Feelies
can_cause.why: A feelie is simply a kind of prop that lives outside the game's main medium, so props are the broader category it belongs to.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Props add decorative detail to a board, making it richer without changing what players can do on it.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Props make exploring more interesting through variety, and decoy props can make searching necessary because players must sort real finds from fake ones.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Props designed as clues, traces or landmarks help players find their way, while decoy props can make finding the way harder.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Props fill a world with details that define it, adding richness without adding anything players can actively do.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Props add detail to a level, filling out the scenery so it feels like a place rather than an empty layout.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Props can't drive a fixed story alone, but they add flavor and can carry parts of it through the setting.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Props supply details that make it easier for players to imagine and act out being in the fictional world.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A prop that looks like a usable object but does nothing, or draws interest and then can't be used, exposes an inconsistency in the world.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: When a prop looks the same as or very similar to other game items, it blurs what is functional and breaks the theme.

patterns.name: Replays
patterns.what_it_is: Recordings of a past game that can be watched again.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must record enough state or input to replay faithfully, and players must be able to find and watch the result. Playback is only useful if there is something worth reviewing or sharing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A replay button that records poorly, drifts from what happened, or cannot be viewed, shared or used for anything.
patterns.knobs: what is recorded; who controls recording; how long recordings are kept and how they are shared

can_cause.name: AI Players
can_cause.why: When the system keeps recorded sessions, it can feed the saved actions to computer-controlled entities, so they behave like earlier human players.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Starting and stopping a recording is something done outside the game's own rules, so letting players make replays gives them such out-of-game actions.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Consequences
can_cause.why: A replay is something gameplay leaves behind outside the game itself, which makes it a consequence that lives beyond the session.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: When players decide whether and when to record, they gain an extra option about what to do with their play.

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Players who choose to record can later turn those saved sessions into stories about what happened in that specific playthrough.

can_cause.name: Gameplay Statistics
can_cause.why: A replay shows what happened in one particular session, so it works as a way of presenting data about that session.

can_cause.name: Ghosts
can_cause.why: Saved system-made recordings can drive see-through opponents that repeat the earlier run's actions, so players race against past performances.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Because a session is saved, other people can watch it afterwards, even though they were not present or playing at the time.

can_cause.name: Speedruns
can_cause.why: Recordings let runs be shown, compared and used as opponents, supporting the contest of finishing a game as fast as possible.

changes.name: Enactment
changes.why: Replays let players store what they enacted during play, so their performance can be kept and viewed later.

changes.name: Extra-Game Broadcasting
changes.why: Saved recordings can be sent out to audiences outside the game, giving broadcasting something to show.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Where it is unsure how well players will perform, replays capture their actions so the outcome can be stored and reviewed.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: Replays are said to make particular sense when players physically act things out, since that performance can then be preserved.

changes.name: Single-Player Games
changes.why: Replays can give solo games a social side, since recordings may be shared and bragged about even when no one plays together.

changes.name: Speedruns
changes.why: Recording a run allows others to watch it at their convenience, as long as there is some way of sharing the recording.

patterns.name: Loyalty
patterns.what_it_is: The drive to keep your word and support a person, group or cause within the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a character, faction or cause to be loyal to, with a cost for breaking it and tempting reasons to do so. Without that choice it is only background story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The story says you serve a faction but nothing in play rewards or punishes staying with it.
patterns.knobs: what penalties follow betrayal; how many competing loyalties; how tempting the alternatives are

can_cause.name: Committed Goals
can_cause.why: Breaking a loyalty usually brings penalties, so the player is bound to the commitment and must keep honoring it rather than drop it freely.

can_cause.name: Continuous Goals
can_cause.why: Loyalty to a person, faction or party is a relationship that has to be kept up over time instead of being finished once.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Players may feel bad about letting down those they are loyal to, or try to make up for a past lapse in showing it.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: When a player holds goals that clash with a loyalty, or several loyalties that cannot all be satisfied, they are torn between choices.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: When players can choose whether to take on a loyalty at all, that commitment becomes a goal they may accept or decline.

can_cause.name: Overcome
can_cause.why: Giving other agents goals that oppose a loyalty creates conflicts, so the player must get past those obstacles to stay faithful.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Loyalty can be set up or ended by scripted story events, and stating it as a promise or ritual ties goals into the plot.

can_cause.name: Preventing Goals
can_cause.why: When something opposes whatever the player is loyal to, staying faithful can mean stopping those opponents from succeeding.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: A loyalty can be imposed on a player by a dramatic game event, so it exists without the player choosing it.

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Declaring loyalty to a cause, character or faction, or breaking it, is an action that clearly defines who the character is.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Where players feel loyal to a group, adding rivalry within it creates the tension between group and self.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Adding loyalty to an avatar gives the player's figure a commitment that shapes what it should or should not do.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Loyalty adds a commitment to a character, and choosing to keep or break it can define who that character is.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Companions can leave if they feel their loyalty has been misused by how the player acts, so loyalty affects how they behave toward the player.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Loyalty to a faction adds rules and expectations about how members must act, shaping what a faction means to the player.

patterns.name: Helpers
patterns.what_it_is: Characters not controlled by players who help the player.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decide what each helper can do and where or when it appears, so the help matches a real moment of need, such as a puzzle, a shortage, or a lack of information. The help must be useful enough to rely on but limited enough that players still have to make their own choices.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character stands in the world with a friendly name and model but only repeats flavor lines, so players gain nothing and never need to consult it.
patterns.knobs: how much and what kind of help they give; how often, where and when they are available; what it costs the player to use them

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Helpers often hand players hints, such as gossip, that nudge them toward what to do next without stating it outright.

can_cause.name: Gain Competence
can_cause.why: A helper that withholds aid until the player makes amends gives the player a goal of becoming capable enough to earn that help.

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: When a helper won't share help automatically or has withdrawn it, players must pursue the knowledge it holds, creating an information-seeking goal.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Helpers can push a scripted story forward and add extra detail to it, so they serve as a vehicle for the plot.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Helpers can perform special services players can't do themselves, such as healing damage or crafting.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: Helpers can assign tasks or assist with them, so talking to them can hand players missions to carry out.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Because helpers speak indirectly rather than stating the true game state, what they say can mislead players.

can_cause.name: Trading
can_cause.why: Some helpers act as merchants or service providers, letting players exchange goods with them.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Helpers appear within boards and assist players there, changing how play on that board goes.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Helpers live in the game world and give players help while they explore it, shaping the experience there.

changes.name: Helplessness
changes.why: A helper can rescue players from a stuck or hopeless situation, such as being towed out of the ocean in Mario Kart or revived by companions.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Helpers placed within a level give players aid in that specific place, affecting how the level is played.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Helpers can move a fixed story along and supply extra details to it, altering how the plot unfolds for players.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Helpers give aid in completing quests, and gaining a helper's aid may itself require a quest, changing how those quests play.

conflicts_with.name: Enemies
conflicts_with.why: A non-player character can be turned into either a helper or an enemy, which sets up a tradeoff.

patterns.name: Detective Structures
patterns.what_it_is: The player knows exactly as much as one particular hero does.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must truly limit what the player knows to what their one character perceives, and give clues through the world. It works best with a single player.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The player controls one character but the interface shows information the character could not know.
patterns.knobs: how much the character knows; how clues are spread over the game

can_cause.name: Gain Information
can_cause.why: Because players only learn what their one character can learn, they naturally set goals to find out more, whether about the story or the world.

can_cause.name: Game World Exploration
can_cause.why: Since information mostly comes through the game world itself, players explore it to find what they need to know, and this exploring can be done just by moving around.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Limited, incomplete information plus the chance of surprises keeps players unsure what comes next, especially when clues hint that something may happen.
