can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: Restricting players to one character's viewpoint means they begin without the full picture, and unseen events happening elsewhere in the world can keep that gap open.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Limiting knowledge to one protagonist is one specific way of deciding how a game's story is presented to players.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Controlling what the player learns, and in what order, helps make sure fixed story events are revealed in the intended sequence.

conflicts_with.name: God Fingers
conflicts_with.why: In open worlds, a pointer-style control lets players explore away from any particular character, breaking the single-character limit on information.

conflicts_with.name: Melodramatic Structures
conflicts_with.why: The two start out incompatible, and since the page says this clash must be kept up through the whole game, they cannot easily coexist.

conflicts_with.name: Split-Screen Views
conflicts_with.why: Players can see the other players' screens, so each can see what others' characters see, which undermines restricting information to one character.

conflicts_with.name: Units
conflicts_with.why: Controlling several units gives players multiple viewpoints at once, which goes against restricting information to a single character's perspective.

patterns.name: MacGuffins
patterns.what_it_is: Game elements the story revolves around and that drive the narrative forward.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A chosen object or character must be what goals such as capture, deliver or protect point to, so story and play both depend on it. It need not be detailed, only important to the goals.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The story mentions a special object but no goal or action in the game involves it.
patterns.knobs: which goals refer to it; how present it is in the world; how its importance is shown

can_cause.name: Alien Space Bats
can_cause.why: A MacGuffin that clashes with the game's world and its theme would turn into an out-of-place element, so it must fit the setting to avoid that.

can_cause.name: Capture
can_cause.why: Capturing needs something to grab, and a MacGuffin can be that object without needing any special traits beyond being the thing everyone wants.

can_cause.name: Deliver
can_cause.why: Delivering needs something to carry to a destination, and a MacGuffin can fill that role since only its being transported matters, not what it is.

can_cause.name: Eliminate
can_cause.why: Eliminating needs a target to be destroyed, and a MacGuffin can be that target without needing any particular characteristics.

can_cause.name: Gain Ownership
can_cause.why: Simply getting hold of something is a goal that needs a game element but no specific traits, so a MacGuffin can serve as the prize.

can_cause.name: Game Items
can_cause.why: When MacGuffins are present as concrete objects, they can be items; this is especially common when the goal is capturing, delivering, or eliminating.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: MacGuffins give players something to rally their goals around, which lets a story take shape in the game.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: By supplying the thing characters strive for, a MacGuffin sets up a story framework that is planned ahead of play.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A MacGuffin can define the aim of a smaller, local task, not just the game's overall goal.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Having a MacGuffin may be necessary to keep the game's theme coherent, even though how it looks is rarely constrained by the theme.

changes.name: Eliminate
changes.why: If enemies carry important objects, players are more driven to remove them, and this also marks them as enemies.

patterns.name: Gossip
patterns.what_it_is: Game characters pass information to each other by word of mouth.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Information in the world must be uncertain, so statements can be true, false or partial and players can't instantly check them. Someone must actually pass messages along, and acting on them must matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Idle chatter lines that repeat facts already known or never affect any decision, so it is flavour text only.
patterns.knobs: who talks to whom; how reliable the information is; what topics it covers

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: Gossip can tell players how they or others behaved in the game world, so what a character did spreads and brings good or bad social results.

can_cause.name: Betrayal
can_cause.why: When players trade talk in negotiation, they can pass on false or damaging tales about others, which lets them break someone's trust.

can_cause.name: Information Passing
can_cause.why: Gossip is a spoken exchange between characters, so whenever it happens, facts or rumors move from one character to another.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Gossip most often concerns characters, so what is said about them shapes what others know or believe of them.

changes.name: Delayed Reciprocity
changes.why: Gossip helps sustain players' belief that favors will be repaid later, because information about who did what keeps circulating.

changes.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
changes.why: Game-provided gossip can point players toward notable places or things in the world that are worth noticing.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Rumors told by characters in the game can hint at possible quests, informing players about tasks they might take on.

changes.name: Dialogues
changes.why: Rumors heard earlier can change what is available to say later, and they also act as a source of hints.

patterns.name: Alien Space Bats
patterns.what_it_is: A silly or supernatural explanation for why the game world differs from ours.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The fantastic element must have visible consequences in the world and its gameplay (new items, abilities, enemies), kept consistent with the theme. Introduced mid-game, it should be explained by the story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A mention of magic or aliens is in the backstory, but the world and rules play exactly like the real-world version.
patterns.knobs: how big a departure from reality; when it appears; how many new elements it brings

can_cause.name: Game Element Insertion
can_cause.why: When a fantastical agent appears mid-game, it gives a reason to bring in new enemies, items, or units that fit that agent's nature.

can_cause.name: Narration Structures
can_cause.why: A mid-game fantastical event is usually a surprise, so it changes how the story unfolds and shifts the way the narrative develops.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Giving the altered world a fantastical cause lets its odd features feel like they belong together, so the setting hangs together as one theme.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: When such an agent shows up during play, it usually arrives as a huge, world-changing event that goes far beyond ordinary happenings.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: New fantastical elements can unlock fresh element insertions and make levels differ from each other, so play stays varied across the game.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: They are a physical story element in the world, often explained at the start by a summary update.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: A fantastical cause arriving during play can justify adding new kinds of enemies that suit what was introduced.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: A fantastical event can justify new environmental effects, since the strange agent's nature explains why the surroundings behave differently.

changes.name: Game Items
changes.why: A fantastical event can justify new items appearing, since the agent's nature explains why such objects now exist.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: These implausible causes change aspects of the real world, so the resulting game world is a twisted version of ours rather than invented from nothing.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: New abilities and game elements introduced by the fantastical cause can be used to make one level feel different from another.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Such explanations are usually planned in advance as part of a fixed story, because improvising them live would be hard to pull off convincingly.

changes.name: Privileged Abilities
changes.why: When a fantastical agent appears during play, it can give a reason to hand the player new special abilities.

changes.name: Summary Updates
changes.why: These explanations are best given early, often through summaries or marketing material, so players aren't caught off guard and their expectations of the theme stay intact.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: A fantastical event during play can justify adding new units, since the agent's nature explains why they now exist.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: If the effects of the fantastical element aren't carried through to the story, world, and gameplay, the setting stops feeling coherent and the theme breaks.

patterns.name: Campaigns
patterns.what_it_is: A chain of pre-designed game episodes played in order.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The parts must be linked by shared story, carried-over progress and connecting material, so they feel like one arc. Decide what state carries over between parts.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Levels are grouped under a 'campaign' title but nothing carries over and nothing links them, so they are just a list.
patterns.knobs: number and length of parts; what carries over; amount of story between parts

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: A campaign fixes in advance a sequence of parts that players go through in order, so the story's overall shape is already laid out before play begins.

patterns.name: Adventures
patterns.what_it_is: Pre-designed events and challenges used to build the content of a play session.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs ready settings, events, characters and goals that can be used with little preparation, and ideally structure (quests, scenes) plus room for a game master to adapt when players go off-script.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pile of lore and locations is labeled an adventure, but it has no goals or events for players to run into, so a group can't actually play it.
patterns.knobs: how scripted or open the content is; length; how many are linked into a sequence

can_cause.name: Campaigns
can_cause.why: When several adventures are written to be played one after another, the linked sequence becomes a campaign, like the chain of Dungeons & Dragons modules from G1 through Q1.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: An adventure is itself a ready-made set of settings, events and characters prepared before play, so it is a case of a story whose shape is fixed in advance.

patterns.name: Finale Levels
patterns.what_it_is: Levels built to feel like the conclusion of a storyline.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Build the last area to resolve the narrative arc, with harder play and a boss or climax, positioned so it feels like the end. The difficulty and story should peak together.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The last level is just another ordinary level with a credits screen, with no rise in challenge or sense of closure.
patterns.knobs: difficulty spike of the final level; how much story resolution it carries

can_cause.name: Closure Points
can_cause.why: Because a finale wraps up the story arc, it becomes a clear spot where an adventure or campaign visibly reaches its end.

can_cause.name: Higher-Level Closures as Gameplay Progresses
can_cause.why: Finishing a finale ends the narrative arc and usually comes with harder play, so completing it feels like a bigger payoff than earlier stages.

can_cause.name: Levels
can_cause.why: A finale is built as an enclosed play area, so it can be designed with the same tools as any ordinary level.

can_cause.name: Scenes
can_cause.why: The page says finales can produce scenes as well as levels, but does not explain what in play makes that so.

changes.name: Adventures
changes.why: A finale sits at the end of an adventure and sets its overall shape by acting as the explicit point where it concludes.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: Final bosses can show up elsewhere, but the finale is often the sealed-off place where they can actually be beaten.

changes.name: Campaigns
changes.why: Some adventures serve as a campaign's last stretch, so a finale shapes how the whole campaign is structured and where it ends.

patterns.name: Summary Updates
patterns.what_it_is: A recap of events before or after the game itself to bring the player up to speed.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The summary must give players what they need to know about the setting or the consequences, at the right time and in short enough form to be read. It fits games with a planned story.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A recap screen that repeats what the player already knows, or one so long that it is skipped without being read.
patterns.knobs: when it appears; how long it is; how much information it contains

can_cause.name: Cutscenes
can_cause.why: A summary update is a kind of cutscene: it pauses active play to tell players what happened before or after, so each summary is a cutscene.

can_cause.name: Downtime
can_cause.why: In multiplayer games, an out-of-play player is given only a recap while waiting for the others to continue.

changes.name: Adventures
changes.why: Summary updates are usually written alongside an adventure, giving players the background before it starts and the outcome once it ends.

changes.name: Campaigns
changes.why: Because they are attached to scenes and adventures, summaries also shape the wider campaign, and can be written specifically to open or close one.

changes.name: Melodramatic Structures
changes.why: In games built around melodrama, a summary can explain the new situation players find themselves in, helping them make sense of changing circumstances.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: When a game's story is planned in advance, designers can write summaries to fit its fixed parts, delivering needed background at planned points.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: Summaries are written together with scenes, so players are told what they need to know when moving into or out of each one.

patterns.name: Feelies
patterns.what_it_is: Real physical items packaged with the game that strengthen the impression it makes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Props must fit the game's world and tone and ideally carry clues, backstory or help, so that using them deepens immersion. They must be made to match the theme of the game.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Generic box extras, such as stickers or a poster, with no link to the story or play, so they add nothing to the experience.
patterns.knobs: how many props; how themed they are and whether they carry clues or helpful information

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A prop can carry hints about the game, so a designer can use a feelie to nudge players toward solving something, like a map with hints.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because feelies are extras made to deepen the experience, they should fit the game world's internal logic, so this consistency matters even more for them.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Being physical objects that sit outside the game medium, feelies stand out from the rest of the game's in-world elements.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Broadcasting
can_cause.why: When a feelie shows events that already happened in the game world, such as a diary, it conveys that world's story outside the game itself.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Since feelies are extras, a designer can fill them with misleading details, giving players false leads along with or instead of real hints.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Feelies exist to enrich the experience, so they are usually made to match the game's theme in look and feel.

can_cause.name: Props
can_cause.why: Physical extras packaged with a game, like a map or booklet, are props that exist outside the game itself and carry no gameplay.

patterns.name: Phasing
patterns.what_it_is: In one session, world elements are removed or changed for some players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design must define the phases, the triggers for entering and leaving them, and whether players share a phase. Gameplay must also be tied to what each phase shows, so the difference actually matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Different players see slightly different scenery, but nothing in their goals, options or story differs, so nobody notices or cares.
patterns.knobs: how many phases exist; what triggers entering and leaving; whether players share a phase

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because the world changes to match each player's own progress, players feel their actions reshape it more than they really do, since the change is only shown to them.

can_cause.name: Instances
can_cause.why: When a group of players shares a phase and everyone else is phased out, only that group can interact with the same things, which works just like an instance.

can_cause.name: Non-Consistent Narration
can_cause.why: Different players are shown different versions of the world or story, so the accounts of what happened no longer match across players.

can_cause.name: Private Game Spaces
can_cause.why: Phasing gives players different available actions depending on which part of the game space they are in, producing private areas.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Phasing changes what elements of the world are shown, so the world itself, or at least how players perceive it, differs depending on the player.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Phasing works by having each player's interface show different things, which only makes sense when play is experienced through a mediating presentation.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: In a game shared by many players, phasing lets subgroups or individuals see different game elements, such as teams seeing themselves as friendly and others as enemies.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Players can be shown world changes tied to their place in a fixed story without designers having to make those changes permanent for everyone.

changes.name: Private Game Spaces
changes.why: When phasing is applied to a single player, that player gets their own version of the world that others cannot interact with, like a private space.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Taking on a quest can move a player into a temporary phase, so the world updates or removes elements, like completed quest givers, to reflect their progress.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players see different versions of the world, so those comparing their experiences find the world doesn't add up.

patterns.name: Scripted Information Sequences
patterns.what_it_is: A preset chain of events plays out while the player can still act.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Place scripted events at particular points so players can still act, give reasons for them to watch, such as clues or threats, and decide how interruptible they are.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cutscene in disguise, where the player is locked in place or the world is frozen, so there is no gameplay during the sequence.
patterns.knobs: how interruptible; trigger location; whether they threaten the player; clue content

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: The scripted events happen at fixed spots in the game world, so the story is told through the place itself while players move around.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Unlike a cutscene, players can wander elsewhere or keep playing while the events run, so they still decide what to do.

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: A scripted sequence can show non-player characters acting on their own goals, making them seem to have purposes beyond the player.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: The sequence plays out the same fixed way each time, so designers can deliver a set story without stopping gameplay.

can_cause.name: Traps
can_cause.why: If the sequence endangers players' health or lives unless they get out of its way, it works as a trap and pushes them to notice it.

can_cause.name: Ultra-Powerful Events
can_cause.why: Once a sequence starts, players typically cannot stop or change it, so it runs its course regardless of what they do.

can_cause.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
can_cause.why: Scripted scenes naturally pull players' eyes, and paired with traps or required continuing events they punish those who stop watching.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: If players notice that information follows a script, they realize events are predetermined and feel less influential.

conflicts_with.name: Own Agenda
conflicts_with.why: In games meant for replay, scripted sequences get seen repeatedly and become noticeable patterns, which undermines the impression that agents act from their own goals.

conflicts_with.name: Replayability
conflicts_with.why: Seeing the same sequence repeat across playthroughs reveals its artificial nature, weakening the illusion that characters act independently.

patterns.name: Character Alignments
patterns.what_it_is: A system classing heroes as good, evil, or neutral by their moral stance.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Alignments must be linked to what characters can do or how others treat them, and breaking one's alignment must have an effect.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A moral label appears on the character sheet but never affects rules, NPC reactions or penalties.
patterns.knobs: number and axes of alignments; penalties for acting against them; whether alignment can be changed

can_cause.name: Ability Losses
can_cause.why: When a character acts against their alignment, the game can punish them by weakening their abilities, for instance because a god disapproves or because of psychological fallout.

can_cause.name: Characteristics
can_cause.why: An alignment is a trait attached to a character that limits which actions that character may take and how others can act toward them, such as revealing it with a spell.

can_cause.name: Social Dilemmas
can_cause.why: Because alignments are stated openly, designers can build tough choices that belong to the characters themselves rather than only to the players.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Alignments steer how characters are expected to behave, and breaking those expectations can bring penalties or push a character to switch alignment.

changes.name: Factions
changes.why: Alignments can describe the shared norms of a group, so a faction's members and actions are shaped by the alignment it holds.

changes.name: Player-Created Characters
changes.why: Players choose an alignment when making their character, which pushes them to think about how that character will act and be played.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Alignments tie moral stances to kinds of actions, giving players a guide for how their character would behave in the story.

patterns.name: Companion Quests
patterns.what_it_is: Goal: complete a quest built around the player's companion.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Triggers that players can notice, goals that matter to the companion's story, and rewards that change the companion or the relationship.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A companion has a quest on the list, but it is generic, has no story link to them, and changes nothing about them.
patterns.knobs: number of quests per companion; triggers; rewards and effect on the companion

can_cause.name: Actions Have Diegetically Social Consequences
can_cause.why: How a companion's quest turns out can decide which ending the player gets, so choices made for a follower visibly change the story's result.

can_cause.name: Open Destiny
can_cause.why: Because the quest centers on a follower, how it resolves can leave that companion's fate undecided and dependent on what the player does.

can_cause.name: Optional Goals
can_cause.why: A companion quest is a kind of sidequest, so players can choose to skip it and still carry on with the main game.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Designers write companion quests to give followers a prepared story arc that players can explore, rather than letting it emerge from play.

can_cause.name: Quests
can_cause.why: A companion quest is simply a quest, a goal given as an in-world mission, whose focus happens to be a follower instead of the player.

can_cause.name: Sidequests
can_cause.why: Companion quests are a specific type of sidequest, since they are extra missions centered on followers and not part of the main objective.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: The quests give followers their own story to play through, changing them from simple helpers into characters with goals and arcs players can explore.

patterns.name: Non-Consistent Narration
patterns.what_it_is: Narration in the game whose parts do not agree with each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Story elements must be repeated or contradict the game world's history, with instances or phasing isolating the inconsistency so that only the players inside it see it. It must be a deliberate trade-off for the sake of reuse or scale.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A story that is just sloppy and contradictory by accident, with no reuse or purpose behind it, which only breaks immersion without giving anything back.
patterns.knobs: how much story content is reused; how isolated each player's copy is (instancing or phasing)

changes.name: Adventures
changes.why: Adventures can be replayed or reused for different groups, so the narration about them gets repeated and ignores earlier playthroughs.

changes.name: Campaigns
changes.why: Campaign stories can be reused for groups who join later, so the same narration is told again despite what already happened elsewhere.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Improvised storytelling can include repeated or contradictory elements, and this often goes unnoticed or is not treated as a problem.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Designers can alter a fixed story by deliberately reusing some of its parts, choosing which pieces repeat and how players may notice.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Quests are handed to every player who meets the requirements, even repeatedly, so the story ignores that others already completed them.

conflicts_with.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
conflicts_with.why: When separate game instances do not affect the larger story, players' sense of power over the narrative is limited.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Replaying story events that already happened makes the narration contradict the timeline of the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Repeating story content makes characters act as if earlier events never occurred, which clashes with the theme the world is supposed to hold.

patterns.name: Player Aids
patterns.what_it_is: Handouts with extra information about the game world or the current situation.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The aid must hold information players can use or react to, and be given at a well-chosen moment. Its look and material should fit the fiction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A handout that only repeats what the players already know and is thrown away unread.
patterns.knobs: what information it holds; when it is handed out; its material and visual design

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A handout such as a letter or map can carry information that helps players work out what is going on or what to do next.

can_cause.name: Feelies
can_cause.why: A player aid can serve as a feelie when it fits the game's world and theme, though feelies that only add flavor and give no information are not aids.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Handouts are given to players as the prepared story unfolds, either at set events or from the start, so they help deliver that fixed plot.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Because a handout can hold information relevant to a puzzle, players can use what it reveals when they try to solve it.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Holding items that could exist in the game world can inspire players to act in character.

patterns.name: Melodramatic Structures
patterns.what_it_is: The story is built so the player or viewer knows more than any character.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must show events from several viewpoints or add commentary, and this extra knowledge must change how the player reads what the character does. The perspective shifts have to be large enough to matter.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with several playable characters or a wide camera that shows the player nothing beyond what the current character already knows.
patterns.knobs: how often the viewpoint switches; how much the player is told beyond the character

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: The pattern shapes how a game tells its story by letting the player hold knowledge that the in-game people do not have.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: It can be layered onto a fixed story, giving players extra knowledge about it, while characters' available gameplay actions stay the same.

conflicts_with.name: Detective Structures
conflicts_with.why: The two start out incompatible, and since the page says this clash must be kept up through the whole game, they cannot easily coexist.

patterns.name: Contextualized Conversational Responses
patterns.what_it_is: A character replies in conversation taking into account everything currently happening in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Replies must be chosen from relevant game state, such as who is speaking, where, and what has happened, using rules or authored dialogue per character or place. Players should notice that the replies fit.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A character has many lines, but they are picked at random or ignore what just happened.
patterns.knobs: how many state variables affect replies; how much dialogue is written; per-character or per-location variants

can_cause.name: Own Agenda
can_cause.why: When a computer-controlled character voices fitting emotions about the specific situation it is in, players read it as having its own goals and concerns.

can_cause.name: Dialogues
can_cause.why: Replies that adapt to the situation supply the conversation content, which makes the exchange work as a dialogue and stay true to the setting.

changes.name: Algorithmic Agents
changes.why: Designers can build the context-sensitivity into an agent's own rules, so what it says changes according to the game state it checks.

changes.name: Dialogues
changes.why: Instead of rules, designers can write dialogue lines tied to a particular character or place, so what is said fits the current circumstances.

patterns.name: Contextualization
patterns.what_it_is: A scene interrupts the current one to show important information, like a memory or a look ahead.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be a clear signal for starting and ending such scenes and someone with authority to call them. They must give information that changes how the current scene is understood.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A scene break is announced, but it just repeats what players already know and changes nothing about the main scene.
patterns.knobs: who may trigger it; how often; flashback or flash-forward; which characters take part

can_cause.name: Meta-Techniques
can_cause.why: The pattern is itself a game-stepping-out technique, so using it means players apply a rule-level device that works on the story rather than inside it.

can_cause.name: Scenes
can_cause.why: Each use produces a whole new short scene, such as a remembered or anticipated moment, that is played out and cuts into the ongoing action.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: During these inserted scenes players can portray their character at another time, or play other figures who matter to the story, changing who is on stage.

changes.name: Enactment
changes.why: Players get to act out events from other moments rather than only the present one, so the range of what they can portray widens.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: Dropping into an already running scene, the inserted material interrupts it and adds context, so the original scene is altered while it continues.

conflicts_with.name: Temporal Consistency
conflicts_with.why: In live-action roleplay, staging scenes from the future or past steps outside the single running timeline, so the order of events is broken.

patterns.name: Game State Overviews
patterns.what_it_is: Information that gives more than you can see just by looking at the game elements.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Collect scattered information into views such as maps or panels that support planning, and make them accurate and easy to read. They should show things players can't see directly.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An overview screen exists, but it shows only what is visible anyway or is too cluttered to use.
patterns.knobs: what information is included; level of detail; how accessible it is during play

can_cause.name: Progress Indicators
can_cause.why: Because an overview shows where you and others stand, it works as a way to tell how far along everyone is.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Seeing your own and others' positions side by side makes players feel they are racing each other.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: When people outside the game can also see the overview, they can follow what is happening and watch along.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: When an overview shows a player is ahead, they may try to finish the game quickly before others catch up.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Information about your own and others' situations gives players material to think through and plan around.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: Overviews reveal your own and other players' situations, which helps players understand the bigger picture and choose strategies.

can_cause.name: Balancing Effects
can_cause.why: Public information such as scores lets players see who is ahead, which they need in order to gang up on the leader.

changes.name: Area Control
changes.why: Overviews present who holds which areas, changing how players follow and judge control.

changes.name: Camping
changes.why: An overview can help players know where camping spots are located, informing combat planning.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Shared knowledge of the state in multiplayer games affects how players coordinate with each other.

changes.name: Extra-Game Actions
changes.why: The overview is part of the interface, which already sits outside the game world, so it can also show information about these actions.

changes.name: Fog of War
changes.why: Overviews affect how hidden or revealed parts of the world are perceived and how much the fog matters.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Overviews give information that supports moving around and discovering the world.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Overviews help players find their way by showing where things are.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Overviews change how players perceive the structure and layout of a level.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: Having state information shown can change how much a player needs to remember during puzzle-like play.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Overviews give information that helps players decide how to move, directly or through race positions.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Seeing the shared state affects how players interact with each other.

changes.name: Preventing Goals
changes.why: Overviews can show the state relevant to blocking goals, helping players know what to stop.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Overviews can alter how puzzle information is held and recalled by the player.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: Showing positions on a track or board lets players see where everyone stands in a race.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Overviews give players information about the world that scouting would otherwise gather.

changes.name: Sniper Locations
changes.why: Overviews can reveal where sniping spots are, helping players plan for combat.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Overviews help players plan fights by showing where threats and advantageous positions are.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Overviews give information that helps players cross the game world toward a destination.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Overviews let players keep track of all the units they command.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Summaries of the game's state encourage players to view elements through the lens of the system rather than the setting.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Navigation
conflicts_with.why: Overviews can reveal too much, lessening the challenge of finding your own way.

conflicts_with.name: Memorizing
conflicts_with.why: When the state is shown to players, there is less need to remember it themselves.

conflicts_with.name: Reconnaissance
conflicts_with.why: Overviews can reveal too much information, making scouting for it less necessary.

patterns.name: Game State Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: An indicator, not the game world itself, tells about the game or other players.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Show information players really need, in a form they can read quickly and tied to decisions. Choose what is shown beyond what the avatar could sense.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An indicator is on screen, but it shows something irrelevant or duplicates what is already obvious.
patterns.knobs: what is displayed; update speed and prominence; diegetic versus non-diegetic

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Indicators that show things the avatar couldn't sense, or things outside the player's current focus, give players a wider picture of what is happening.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: Many indicators, such as map icons or floating markers, don't fit the fiction of the game world, so they end up being features outside it.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: When indicators reveal how far other players have progressed, players can see who is ahead and begin competing to get there first.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Indicators change quickly and grab attention, so players become more aware of things like a ticking clock and feel pressure.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Indicators can add to how avatars look, such as highlighting the selected one or showing owner names, helping when avatars alone are too complex to read.

changes.name: Budgeted Action Points
changes.why: The number of action points left is a typical thing players need to see, so indicators display it.

changes.name: Capture
changes.why: Indicators help players weigh risk against reward when they're going after a capture goal.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: When characters are complex, their depiction alone may not convey enough, so indicators supplement it.

changes.name: Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Indicators can show how far other players have got in a shared action so teammates know what stage it is at.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: When many rules and states are in play, indicators help players stay informed about the state in ways the world alone can't.

changes.name: Cooldown
changes.why: Showing how long until an ability is usable again is a common use, so players know when they can act.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Indicators can display how much harm has been taken, giving players a readout rather than leaving them to guess.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: Markers show whether an avatar is controlled by a human or not, which matters when players can join and leave.

changes.name: Ephemeral Events
changes.why: Indicators can draw attention to fleeting events the game detects, so players don't miss them.

changes.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
changes.why: More information helps players plan their moves, which supports the feeling that their tactical choices matter.

changes.name: Extended Actions
changes.why: Indicators can show how much time has been spent on a long action, so players can see its progress.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: Indicators can mark where or who the important focus points are in the world, or in a race.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Indicators let players perceive more of the world than they otherwise could, adding information beyond what is directly observable.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Remaining health is among the most common things shown, letting players see how close they are to defeat.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Indicators show how many lives are left so players know how many failures they can still afford.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: Having the state displayed can make players' need to remember session details smaller or remove it altogether.

changes.name: No-Ops
changes.why: Indicators show when a player is forced to wait and cannot act, so the lockout is visible.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Score values are a typical piece of state displayed, often via a score track.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Showing how near the player is to being spotted makes sneaking easier, as with a visibility gauge.

changes.name: Temporary Abilities
changes.why: Because these run out through time or uses, an indicator is needed to show what is left.

changes.name: Time Limited Game Instances
changes.why: Indicators show the time remaining in sessions that end on a clock.

changes.name: Time Limits
changes.why: A display of the time left makes the limit visible to players as it runs down.

changes.name: Time Pressure
changes.why: Because time displays draw attention, they make players more conscious of how little time remains.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Indicators can mark which units are selected, since that fact isn't part of the game world itself.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Showing numbers like lives or scores in any form can push players to see other elements as game systems instead of in-world things.

conflicts_with.name: Memorizing
conflicts_with.why: If the game displays the details, players needn't remember them, which reduces or removes the memory challenge.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Giving players extra information about the state removes some of what they would otherwise be unsure about.

patterns.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
patterns.what_it_is: Interface elements tied to a place in the world but not part of it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Information must be attached to a location or object in the world, positioned so it is seen when needed, and it should actually help players decide something. Accept that it breaks the fiction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A marker or label that repeats what is already obvious on screen, or one placed in a HUD corner far from the thing it describes.
patterns.knobs: what information is shown; where and when it appears; whether it shows through walls or only in view

can_cause.name: Chat Channels
can_cause.why: Messages from chat can be shown near the characters who spoke them, so the chat text is placed at spots in the game world.

can_cause.name: Check Points
can_cause.why: Route points, such as racing way points, are hard to fit into the story world, so they are shown as widgets placed at those locations.

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Clues can be shown as widgets at their locations so players are unlikely to overlook them, as in detective-style games.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Every widget is information about the game state, shown at a place in the world, so each one acts as an indicator of that state.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: When many widgets are shown at once, together they give players a broad picture of what is going on in the game.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: Widgets work as markers fixed on places or on things like enemies and units, helping players find and refer to them.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The widgets are not really part of the game world, so placing them in it brings in elements that the story world cannot explain.

can_cause.name: Power-Ups
can_cause.why: Power-ups are only loosely present in the world and may not fit its story, so widgets can stand in as the power-up itself.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Widgets such as racing checkpoints can lay out a visible trail through the world that players follow.

can_cause.name: Auto-Aim
can_cause.why: Lock-on aiming often shows enemies with clear markers placed in the game space, and these marker widgets are one way the aiming help is delivered.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Showing a handle through map-style on-screen widgets gives the avatar a name-like trait, which is a light form of character.

can_cause.name: Reward Widgets
can_cause.why: A reward widget comes into being when a reward is shown as a clickable object placed in the game space, which is what these widgets are.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Widgets attach to avatars, such as hovering names or glowing outlines that let teammates see each other through walls.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Widgets near avatars can show abstract character details, and showing a handle can start giving avatars or units a character identity.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Clues shown as widgets are hard to miss, which changes how games built around investigation play out.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: Markers such as selection circles or the god finger show where the player's attention or control currently sits.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Widgets give players information at specific places in the world, adding an information layer on top of it.

changes.name: Handles
changes.why: Player names can float above avatars as widgets, so the name is shown right where the avatar is.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: Health bars float above units or characters, so their condition can be read at their location.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Widgets deliver information at specific places in a level, such as route points or markers, shaping how players read it.

changes.name: Mini-maps
changes.why: A weaker form puts widgets on mini-maps, which still pins them to world locations, as pings do in strategy games.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Shared markers visible through objects and placed by members help a party cooperate on the same targets.

changes.name: Pick-Ups
changes.why: Widgets are added to pick-ups so players are less likely to miss where they are.

changes.name: Power-Ups
changes.why: Widgets make power-up locations noticeable so players don't overlook them.

changes.name: Props
changes.why: When a prop does offer a bit of information through a click, interface markers placed at its location show players that it can be used.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Markers and pings on targets let team members point things out to each other and act together.

changes.name: Territories
changes.why: Territories are hard to explain within the story world, so widgets are a common way to show their extent.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Widgets on units show health or which unit is currently selected, so the status is visible right at the unit.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Linking such widgets to installations makes sure they stand out in the game world.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Map-like interface elements can show goals and the state of the world, supporting planning.

conflicts_with.name: Challenging Gameplay
conflicts_with.why: Taking away map aids or outlines, as in realism mode, makes finding things harder, so the aids work against challenge.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Widgets are not actually part of the game world yet appear in it, so the world can't stay fully consistent.

conflicts_with.name: Experimenting
conflicts_with.why: Widgets that highlight important objects take away the need for players to explore and look around on their own.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Widgets are non-diegetic additions in the world, so the game's theme can't be fully kept intact.

conflicts_with.name: Territories
conflicts_with.why: Ownership is shown by overlays placed on the world itself, and such interface elements don't belong to the game's fictional setting.

patterns.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the world stand out by shape, color, or texture and hint at what can be done with them.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The feature must stand out from its surroundings and mean something consistent, so that players learn what it signals. It should still fit the world.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Something is shiny or colored differently but the look has no link to what it is or does.
patterns.knobs: how strongly it stands out; how reliably it signals the same thing

can_cause.name: Clickability
can_cause.why: Making an activatable item look different from its surroundings signals that it can be interacted with, which supports players knowing what to click.

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Marking pickups, chargers, resource generators or traps with a striking look hints at what is there, and vulnerable spots on entities can be flagged the same way.

can_cause.name: Environmental Storytelling
can_cause.why: A feature can be placed or styled purely to narrate something, such as luring players toward a spot, so the world itself tells part of a story.

can_cause.name: Illusionary Rewards
can_cause.why: Spotting a marked item feels like a win, yet the item may not actually help the player, so the reward is only apparent.

can_cause.name: Landmarks
can_cause.why: Distinctive, easily seen features give players fixed reference points they can use to orient themselves in boards, worlds, or levels.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Characters
can_cause.why: A character can exist entirely as a striking feature of the world, without taking part in gameplay.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: A feature can draw players to a spot where nothing useful is, misleading them on purpose.

can_cause.name: Stimulated Planning
can_cause.why: Because a standout feature gives players a reason to head toward or steer clear of it, they start planning their route.

can_cause.name: Strategic Knowledge
can_cause.why: If a feature's meaning can be understood before its effects show, players can recall and reuse that knowledge when the same feature reappears.

can_cause.name: Traces
can_cause.why: Positioning noticeable features in particular ways can imply that something happened there earlier, leaving a trail players can read.

changes.name: Achilles' Heels
changes.why: Marking an entity's weak spot with a distinctive look gives players a hint about where to strike.

changes.name: Alarms
changes.why: A distinctive look on a fixed-location element can tell players where an alarm sits in the world.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Agency-bearing elements like the player's character can be given a distinctive look, which is a common use of the pattern.

changes.name: Boss Monsters
changes.why: A boss that is already large can be made to look even more noticeable through added distinguishing features.

changes.name: Chargers
changes.why: Giving a charging spot a distinctive look tells players where it is, though it may not help them.

changes.name: Check Points
changes.why: Locations that do not rely on physical game elements, like race checkpoints, are marked by distinctive surroundings so players recognise them.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: A change in how an entity looks can show that it has been hurt, reflecting what happened in play.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Narrative-related features can be planted to support games built around investigating, offering things to find and interpret.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Enemies are among the agent-like elements that can be given a distinctive appearance, which is a common use of the pattern.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: A distinctive look can indicate where an environmental effect is located in the game world.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Variations in how a board looks can create standout spots that draw players' attention.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Landmarks created by standout features make it easier for players to complete exploration goals.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Distinctive features serve as landmarks that help players find their way around the world.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Differences in the appearance of parts of a world make certain places more noticeable than their surroundings.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: A big installation can be made even more visible by adding distinguishing features to it.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Variations in how a level looks can mark interesting spots and help players pick them out.

changes.name: Location-Fixed Abilities
changes.why: A typical use is telling players where in the world a location-bound ability can be found.

changes.name: MacGuffins
changes.why: Narrative-related objects can be made to stand out through distinctive features, tying them into the story.

changes.name: Narration Structures
changes.why: Standout features can be used to shape story-related elements of a game, like plot objects.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Agent-like characters can be given a distinctive appearance, or even be made entirely of such features.

changes.name: Pick-Ups
changes.why: A distinctive look shows players where collectible items are, acting as a clue even if the item is not helpful.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Most games need these features designed before play begins, since the story is fixed in advance.

changes.name: Resource Locations
changes.why: A distinctive look can tell players where to find resources in the game world.

changes.name: Safe Havens
changes.why: A distinctive look can tell players where safe places are located in the world.

changes.name: Strategic Locations
changes.why: Locations not tied to physical elements are usually marked by distinctive things nearby so players recognise their importance.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Distinctive features can lure players near a trap or let them guess one is there, which can reduce surprise.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Landmarks created by standout features can make it easier to reach goals involving crossing the world.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units, as agent-like elements, can be given a distinctive appearance so players can pick them out.

changes.name: Vehicles
changes.why: A vehicle that is already big can be made even more noticeable with added distinguishing features.

changes.name: Warp Zones
changes.why: A distinctive look can tell players where a warp zone is located in the game world.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Elements that stand out strongly may be perceived as not belonging to the world, even if they technically do.

patterns.name: Mediated Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: Players act in the game and communicate with each other through a technical system.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The design needs a game system or server that takes player input, decides what it means, and decides what each player gets to see. The designer must choose what the system shows, hides and delays.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game that runs on a computer or network but lets players see and change everything directly, so the system filters or interprets nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much the system filters and delays what players see and do

can_cause.name: Actor Detachment
can_cause.why: When the system limits how players can talk to each other, they feel distanced from one another, which can produce detachment from the people behind the characters.

can_cause.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
can_cause.why: When a system deliberately restricts communication, it can go further and force players to stay unidentified to one another.

can_cause.name: Game Worlds
can_cause.why: Since the system builds what players see and hear, it takes on the job of presenting the state of the game world to them.

can_cause.name: Player Anonymity
can_cause.why: If the system limits how players can communicate and this is done on purpose, players can end up not knowing who the others are.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Because the system controls what players experience of the world, a designer can steer them along a fixed story.

can_cause.name: Split-Screen Views
can_cause.why: This kind of view is hard to offer unless a system builds the presentation shown to players, so mediation makes it possible.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: Showing the action from outside a character needs a system constructing the picture, so these views are hard to support without mediation.

can_cause.name: Tiered Participation
can_cause.why: When only some of the gameplay can be reached through the system, some players join through it while others take part physically, with different expectations.

can_cause.name: Tooltips
can_cause.why: Hints shown on request need a system producing the presentation, so they are hard to offer without mediation.

can_cause.name: Vision Modes
can_cause.why: Switching how the game state is displayed needs a system generating the display, so these modes are hard without mediation.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Combined with phasing in multiplayer games, it lets each player feel like the protagonist of the story despite sharing the world.

can_cause.name: Private Game Spaces
can_cause.why: Where the system mediates play, phasing can limit what players can do in each area, creating spaces others cannot affect.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: Because a system mediates, the game state can be held still until a player is ready to act, which allows turns at different times.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: When talk between players passes through a system, face-to-face social interaction disappears, making working together harder.

changes.name: Enactment
changes.why: Acting through a system limits how expressive a performance can be, so nuance is hard, but slipping out of character is less noticeable.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: When players' communication is also routed through the system, they lose direct social contact, changing how multiplayer play works.

changes.name: Meta Games
changes.why: When the game is run by a system, that system must handle the time between games, which lobbies commonly help with.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: When a medium such as a computer controls what players see and do, the designer can control how the prewritten story is delivered, making it easier to use.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Where a system mediates play, phasing can partly let quests affect a world that many players share.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: When play runs through technology, lobbies and invitations can be used to set up teams ahead of play.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: When a system runs the game, it can provide lobbies where players coordinate joining and leaving before the match begins.

conflicts_with.name: Interruptibility
conflicts_with.why: When play happens through a medium, other players may not see why someone stopped, making the interruption confusing.

conflicts_with.name: Social Adaptability
conflicts_with.why: Since mediation makes interruptions harder to support, it works against letting a game fit players' varying social situations.

patterns.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
patterns.what_it_is: Tokens don't represent world objects but simply store data about the game state.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Tokens must correspond to values the game really tracks and be easy to read and update, with a choice of public or hidden. Too many cause extra chores for players.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Tokens are on the table but players track values in their heads or on paper anyway, so the tokens are only decoration.
patterns.knobs: what values are tracked; how many tokens; public or hidden

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: Tokens that hold game state force players to spend effort updating and handling them, which is upkeep work with no real decision in it.

can_cause.name: Extra Chances
can_cause.why: Tokens can stand for spare tries or lives, so holding one literally shows a player still has another attempt.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Moving, counting and updating tokens are things players do outside the game's fiction, purely to keep the state accurate.

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: Even though tokens are not part of the world, players can aim actions at them, for example to show an action is done or to gain a power.

can_cause.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
can_cause.why: A token that is not part of the fiction but sits on the game board becomes an out-of-world interface piece located within the world.

can_cause.name: New Abilities
can_cause.why: Receiving a token can mark that a player has gained a power to affect the game world, so the token itself represents the new ability.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: When tokens are visible to everyone, they record the state openly so players can survey it.

can_cause.name: Token Placement
can_cause.why: The pieces players put down to mark chosen actions are bookkeeping tokens, even when a game calls them workers.

changes.name: Action Programming
changes.why: Players can lay down cards as tokens to fix in advance what their characters or robots will do later.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: Tokens keep the game state on the table, so players don't need to hold it in their heads.

changes.name: Resources
changes.why: Tokens can stand for money, spare tries or points, so they record how much of each resource a player has.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: Because tokens uphold the state, players can run the game without a computer or referee keeping track.

changes.name: Skills
changes.why: Tokens record which skills or attributes a player has and when they are newly gained or improved.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Visible tokens show the current state, which makes it easier and more tempting for players to think ahead.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Tokens such as first-player or current-player markers show whose turn it is, even when seating order doesn't decide it.

conflicts_with.name: Excise
conflicts_with.why: When tokens are used to cap how much of a resource can be held, the limit reduces the upkeep work of handling them.

conflicts_with.name: Resource Caps
conflicts_with.why: Using tokens to enforce a cap on holdings limits how much bookkeeping players must do, which works against the usual burden of upkeep.

patterns.name: Third-Person Views
patterns.what_it_is: The camera follows a chosen object and moves with it, rather than seeing through the hero's eyes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The camera must follow a chosen entity smoothly and show enough surroundings to play. Controls must fit the camera angle.
patterns.just_a_label_when: The camera sits behind the character but is so fixed or so cramped that it gives no extra view of surroundings.
patterns.knobs: camera distance and angle; follow smoothness; which entity is followed

can_cause.name: Character Defining Actions
can_cause.why: Watching your own avatar on screen can remind you it is a character with its own personality and goals, slightly nudging how you act.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Because the view shows everything around the followed entity, including what is behind it, players get a broad picture of the surrounding situation.

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: A camera following a specific avatar still ties what players see to one character, so it can carry the pattern in open worlds.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Offering this view along with first-person lets players pick how they see the world.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Seeing both shooter and target makes aiming harder, so some third-person games switch to first-person for aiming, or add auto-aim to help.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Third-person views usually lock onto the player's avatar, centering the visuals on it and letting the player see it.

changes.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
changes.why: Turning is not centered on the player's focus point, so movement feedback feels less natural and precise physical actions can get harder.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: The two views can't be used at once, but games can let players switch between them or show third-person moments through mirrors and killcams.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: A third-person view can lock onto a chosen focus point, keeping the player positioned on it, so the two need to be designed together.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The view is a way of presenting the game world, centered on a followed entity and showing its surroundings.

changes.name: God Fingers
changes.why: A god-finger selection can pick the focus point, after which the view switches from the overview to following that selected thing.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: A game can use an overview as its basic presentation and drop into a followed view once something has been chosen.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: Seeing how your controlled entity sits relative to other things makes steering and positioning easier than from a first-person view.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Third-person views can follow a unit, or a small group of units, so players need not keep manually re-centering the view.

changes.name: Character Defining Actions
changes.why: Seeing the character from outside encourages players to interpret it, which helps them notice what its actions say about it.

conflicts_with.name: Live Action Roleplaying
conflicts_with.why: Showing the world from a position no in-world observer occupies can't be provided even by facilitators when everyone physically acts out their characters.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players see more than their avatar can, and the avatar may sense things players can't, so what each knows no longer matches.

patterns.name: Communication Channels
patterns.what_it_is: The game provides ways for players to send messages to each other.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Channels must reach the right people at the right time and fit the pace of the game, with ways to filter noise.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A channel is offered but is too slow, too noisy or unavailable when coordination is needed.
patterns.knobs: channel types; audience scope; delay; filtering and moderation

can_cause.name: Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Channels let players talk to each other, and that talk can stay in the game world's voice, so in-fiction communication becomes possible.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because a channel permits in-fiction talk, the game world's fiction can be kept coherent if players choose to speak in character.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: A channel may be the only way players can act out characters through speech or messages, so it gives them a stage for enactment.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: Players can use channels to chat about things unrelated to the current play, such as sharing strategies, which counts as activity outside the game itself.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Players can use the same channels to step out of the fiction and talk as themselves, so out-of-character conversation becomes possible.

can_cause.name: Possibility of Anonymity
can_cause.why: A channel is the basic requirement for hiding behind a pseudonym while talking, because there must be some way to speak before identity can be concealed.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Letting players interact through messages shapes how groups form and how members settle into or keep particular roles.

can_cause.name: Togetherness
can_cause.why: Talking, bragging, and negotiating with others through the game gives players the feeling of being part of a shared experience.

can_cause.name: Uncertainty of Information
can_cause.why: The game can intercept or alter messages, or invent fake ones, so players cannot be sure what they receive is true.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: A helpless player can use a way of talking to others to ask for aid, and that request makes others feel they should respond.

changes.name: Asynchronous Collaborative Actions
changes.why: Players can talk about joint actions that are not done at the same moment, which makes them easier to arrange.

changes.name: Asynchronous Gameplay
changes.why: The pattern is just as useful when players take turns at different times, so channels shape such play too.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Discussing plans through channels makes working together easier, more interesting, and better grounded.

changes.name: Diegetic Communication
changes.why: With several channels available, different ones can be set aside for in-fiction talk so it stays separate from other talk.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: Special channels can be given to players grouped in a lobby, tailoring who talks with whom.

changes.name: Helplessness
changes.why: Channels let others in a multiplayer game voice guilt or negotiate over a helpless player, changing how helplessness plays out.

changes.name: Massively Multiplayer Online Games
changes.why: Such games with huge player populations nearly always provide many kinds of channels, from chat to preset gestures.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: When play happens through a system, channels are what allow any deeper social interaction between players to take place.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Channels only make sense where several players exist, and they change how those players relate to each other.

changes.name: Mutual FUBAR Enjoyment
changes.why: Being able to talk while things go wrong together strengthens the shared fun of the experience.

changes.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
changes.why: Offering separate channels lets designers give out-of-character talk its own space apart from in-fiction messages.

changes.name: Player Kicking
changes.why: Removing a player is easier and better justified when the group can discuss it through a channel first.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Channels help players coordinate and time their actions while the game keeps running.

changes.name: Reflective Communication
changes.why: Players can think and talk about their play through channels, which makes such reflection easier.

changes.name: Roleplaying
changes.why: Channels extend what players can do when acting in character, giving more ways to engage in roleplay.

changes.name: Social Dilemmas
changes.why: Players can debate a dilemma through channels, making negotiation and social interaction more likely.

changes.name: Spectators
changes.why: Designers can give onlookers their own dedicated channels, separate from those used by the active players.

changes.name: Synchronous Gameplay
changes.why: The pattern works equally well when players act at the same time, helping them talk during play.

changes.name: Team Combos
changes.why: Combined team actions become easier to arrange when teammates can discuss them as they happen.

changes.name: Trading
changes.why: Players can haggle and arrange exchanges more easily when they can talk to each other about them.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Talking to each other lets players share, on purpose or by accident, more about themselves than the game itself requires.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players can use the open channel to speak out of character, which breaks the believability of the game's fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Players tend to reveal personal details in conversation, and can also set up outside channels, which makes forced anonymity hard to maintain.

conflicts_with.name: Ragequitting
conflicts_with.why: The sense of togetherness that talking creates can work against players angrily leaving, so the two pull in opposite directions.

patterns.name: First-Person Views
patterns.what_it_is: The world is shown as a creature inside that world would see it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Needs an avatar in the game world and a camera or presentation that shows only what that avatar could perceive, including line of sight. For immersion, movement and aiming should respond naturally.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A camera placed at the character's head height that still shows the player things the avatar could not perceive, such as through walls.
patterns.knobs: field of view and what the avatar can see; whether players can switch viewpoints

can_cause.name: Detective Structures
can_cause.why: Because players only know what their avatar can perceive, what information they hold is controlled, which lets mystery-style games hide clues and reveal them gradually.

can_cause.name: Line of Sight
can_cause.why: Seeing the world from the avatar's position means players can only perceive things the avatar could actually see, so obstacles block what is visible.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
can_cause.why: The view is tied to what the avatar senses, so the player knows exactly as much as the character does, with no gap between them.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Seeing through the character's eyes, together with indicators or special vision, expresses what the character can perceive even when there is no other character definition.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Offering this view alongside a third-person one lets players choose how they look at the game world.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: When paired with indicators or special vision, what the player can see depends on both their own attention and the character's abilities.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: Seeing from the avatar's own position gives feedback like real movement, which helps with precise aiming and shooting, and some games switch to it for aiming.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: A first-person view limits what players see and can make them imagine an avatar from tools or weapons shown as held.

changes.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
changes.why: Because the view feels like moving through the real world, it makes skill-heavy physical actions feel more immersive and easier to judge.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: It lets players experience the world from inside it rather than from outside, changing how the space is presented to them.

changes.name: Maneuvering
changes.why: The view gives movement-like feedback, so steering or moving through space feels immersive and engaging for players.

changes.name: Third-Person Views
changes.why: The two views mostly can't coexist, except when mirrors, cameras or portals let avatars see themselves, or when players can choose between them.

conflicts_with.name: God Fingers
conflicts_with.why: The choice of where the player's attention and control sit limits which views are possible, and an avatar's-eye view doesn't fit well with that kind of control.

patterns.name: Traces
patterns.what_it_is: World elements that lead the player to places that matter in the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The marks must be noticeable but not obvious, and reliably (or deliberately unreliably) connect to something in play such as enemies, loot or traps. Players must be able to read them and act on them.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Decorative marks that sit in the world but correspond to nothing, so following them gets players nowhere.
patterns.knobs: how visible they are; how reliable they are; how long they last; whether players can alter them

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Spotting a trace tells players something about where to go or what happened, so each trace works as a hint toward interesting gameplay.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: Traces get noticed because they stand out from their surroundings, so the attention they draw makes them this kind of feature.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Traces left before play, especially as part of environmental storytelling, reveal the designer's planned events and so help the fixed story unfold.

can_cause.name: Reconnaissance
can_cause.why: Finding traces can be either the main aim of scouting or a supporting hint, so looking for them is itself scouting.

can_cause.name: Red Herrings
can_cause.why: Players can move trace elements to fake a trail, so a trace can point toward something other than what it appears to show.

can_cause.name: Tactical Planning
can_cause.why: Traces made during play show what happened and where, so players can use them to decide their next moves.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Traces point players toward spots where danger or rewards wait, and heading toward them without knowing what is there builds unease.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Traces can be shown as leftovers of earlier events in the world, so they fit the setting instead of feeling pasted on.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When players can alter traces, they must choose between spending time hiding their own trail and doing something else, such as hiding guards.

changes.name: Challenging Gameplay
changes.why: Traces can give players accurate or misleading information about what lies ahead, letting designers tune how hard play feels.

changes.name: Damage
changes.why: Harm done in play can leave visible marks behind, so damage is one way traces appear as consequences of events.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Traces suit stories where players piece together events gradually from a single viewpoint, as detective stories do.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Traces commonly show where enemies are or have been, so players can find or track them.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: Traces can lead players to specific points on a board and can change how the board looks.
