changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Traces give hints about where to look, which shapes where players choose to search when exploring.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Traces affect where players want to go, and dropped items can mark a route they have taken.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Traces send players to particular places in a world and can alter how parts of it appear.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Traces lead players to particular spots in a level and can change how its parts look.

changes.name: Movement
changes.why: Because traces affect where players want to go, they shape and support the movement needed to reach goals.

changes.name: Puzzle Solving
changes.why: Traces serve as hints that players can use to work out the answer to a puzzle.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Detecting traces can be the main aim of scouting or a hint that supports it.

changes.name: Resource Locations
changes.why: Traces can show where supplies are, as with signs of earlier survivors that lead players to restock.

changes.name: Traps
changes.why: Traces can warn of traps, or players can fake a trail to lure others into one.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: When a goal is getting somewhere, traces can mark the route, steering the player's way there.

patterns.name: Chat Channels
patterns.what_it_is: Channels where players exchange messages directly inside the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Useful channel types (local, team, global), a way to find the right audience, and rules about who may speak and what.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A chat box exists, but it is empty, hidden, or so noisy and mixed that nobody uses it for coordinating.
patterns.knobs: types and scope of channels; moderation or filtering; friend lists

can_cause.name: Ambiguous Responses
can_cause.why: Because players type whatever they like, their wording can be vague or open to several readings, so a reply may not clearly say what the sender means.

can_cause.name: Communication Channels
can_cause.why: A chat channel is simply a communication channel carried by written text, so having one automatically gives players a way to talk.

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Free-form typing lets players act out their character's feelings and story beats that the game's own actions might not let them express.

can_cause.name: Guilting
can_cause.why: Since players can write anything, they can use messages to make others feel bad or obligated, which the page lists as a consequence of free expression.

can_cause.name: Information Passing
can_cause.why: When characters receive what is typed in a channel, knowledge travels from one character to another through those messages.

can_cause.name: Mediated Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players interact through typed text rather than directly, so at least part of the game is experienced through that medium.

can_cause.name: Social Roles
can_cause.why: Being able to talk freely makes it easier for players to take on and play out particular roles among other players.

can_cause.name: Dialogues
can_cause.why: Free chat becomes a true dialogue system when paired with computer-controlled characters or with utterances that alter the game state.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Where players chat, emotes let them express their characters' feelings in text, which supports roleplaying.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: Free chat lets players talk with characters in the most nuanced way, which can strengthen the sense of theme, though it also invites abuse.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Free-form messages let players coordinate and plan together, which supports working toward shared goals.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: The same channels usually carry over into lobbies, so players can chat there before play begins.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: Servers normally handle the receiving, storing and delivering of messages, so chat shapes what they do and who can reach whom.

changes.name: Meta Servers
changes.why: When chat runs over a meta server, players can reach everyone playing the game, not just those on one server.

changes.name: Parties
changes.why: Channels can be limited to party members, letting them talk privately among themselves.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Channels can be restricted to teammates so they can communicate secretly, away from other players.

conflicts_with.name: Actor Detachment
conflicts_with.why: Chatting lets players reveal personal details beyond gameplay, undoing the hiding of identities that mediated play would otherwise give.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Text boxes or overlays sit outside the game world, and mixing player and character channels can also break the fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Enforced Player Anonymity
conflicts_with.why: Because free text can reveal outside-the-game details about players, it is hard to keep them truly anonymous.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players control what they write, so they can say things that clash with the game's theme and designers cannot guarantee a fitting tone.

patterns.name: Dialogues
patterns.what_it_is: Conversations inside the game world that the game system controls.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Replies must lead somewhere, giving information or changing the game state, and the system must handle what players can say. The choices should fit the characters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A conversation tree where every option leads to the same answer and nothing changes.
patterns.knobs: number of branches; how choices affect the game state

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Gossip is a kind of information passed in conversation, and that same information can serve as hints, so dialogue can end up delivering clues.

can_cause.name: Communication Channels
can_cause.why: A dialogue is itself one form of communication channel, so having one means the game provides a way for parties to exchange messages.

can_cause.name: Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Because the game controls what can be said inside a dialogue, messages can be delivered in the game world's own terms.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Replies from characters can appear inside the game world, such as speech bubbles, showing the player something about what is going on.

can_cause.name: Gossip
can_cause.why: Gossip is one specific sort of information passing, and dialogue is made of information passing, so conversations are where gossip gets shared.

can_cause.name: Information Passing
can_cause.why: Every statement made in a dialogue conveys something to the listener, so each utterance is an act of passing information.

can_cause.name: Internal Conflicts
can_cause.why: A dialogue offers several possible next lines, each with its own aim, so players must weigh competing goals against each other.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Dialogues are written ahead of play and their lines follow a cause-and-effect order, so they fix the story's course in advance.

changes.name: Companions
changes.why: Companions matter greatly to the player's character, so they tend to get richer and more elaborate conversation systems.

changes.name: Detective Structures
changes.why: Conversation lets players ask around and gather facts, even from places they cannot reach, which suits investigating a mystery.

changes.name: Ephemeral Goals
changes.why: Characters can give out, move forward and report on short-term objectives through what they say.

changes.name: Helpers
changes.why: Helpers have important relations with the player's character, so they are given more developed conversation options.

changes.name: Non-Player Characters
changes.why: Computer-controlled characters can be made to start talks themselves or reply in various ways, changing how talking with them feels.

changes.name: Quests
changes.why: Talking is a common way for a game to hand out a quest, track how it is going and report its completion.

patterns.name: God Views
patterns.what_it_is: The world is shown without being tied to any object inside it.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A camera players can move freely over the world, independent of units, with enough detail to be useful. Decide what stays hidden (fog of war) so there is still uncertainty.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A zoomed-out camera that is actually locked to a character or a fixed spot, so the player still sees only what that character sees.
patterns.knobs: camera freedom and zoom range; how much is hidden by fog of war; number of display modes

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Because the view isn't tied to any one game element, players can see the whole world and shift that view quickly, which gives them an overview of what's going on.

changes.name: Freedom of Choice
changes.why: Players can vary how they look at play and more easily see which actions are actually available, which affects how many choices they feel they have.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The view lets the world be presented and shifted independently of its contents, changing how players take in the world as a whole.

conflicts_with.name: Aim & Shoot
conflicts_with.why: From a high overview it is too hard to line up the shooter and target accurately, so precise aiming does not work well.

conflicts_with.name: Avatars
conflicts_with.why: When an avatar limits what a player perceives, an all-seeing overview becomes impossible.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Navigation
conflicts_with.why: A view that lets players look around the world freely, ignoring in-game objects, makes finding the way trivial.

conflicts_with.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Players can see far more than any character in the world could, so it's hard to limit their awareness to what the character knows.

conflicts_with.name: Reconnaissance
conflicts_with.why: With an unrestricted view, scouting becomes trivial because players can simply look wherever they like, unless information is hidden from them.

patterns.name: Split-Screen Views
patterns.what_it_is: The screen is divided into parts, each constantly showing its own view of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must run on a shared screen with real-time play, with a layout that gives each view enough space to be readable. It should adapt when the number of players changes.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A divided screen where the views are so small or the same that players cannot play independently, or one view is only a static picture.
patterns.knobs: number of views; layout; size of each view; whether it changes with joining players

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: When a spare view is left over, such as the fourth quadrant in a three-view layout, it can show an overview of the game's overall situation.

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: Giving each player their own section of one screen lets several people play together on one display, each looking at their own part of the world.

changes.name: Cooperation
changes.why: Seeing what teammates are doing, even when their characters are in different places or on separate screens, makes coordinating with them easier.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Splitting the screen lets players be in different places and face different ways, and gives players with several screens a better view of each other's actions.

changes.name: Real-Time Games
changes.why: Since everyone acts at once, each player needs a constantly visible view of their own; splitting one screen makes simultaneous real-time play possible on one display.

conflicts_with.name: Detective Structures
conflicts_with.why: Players can see the other players' screens, so each can see what others' characters see, which undermines restricting information to one character.

conflicts_with.name: Hotseating
conflicts_with.why: Both solve the same problem of several players sharing one screen, so using them together is redundant and one makes the other unnecessary.

patterns.name: Extra-Game Broadcasting
patterns.what_it_is: Game events are sent out through channels other than the one where the game is played.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Decide which events get sent, when and through what channel, and put players in control of sharing so it does not feel like spam. Events like achievements, rewards and uncertain moments are worth sending.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A share button or notification stream that sends trivial events nobody wants to see, so no one outside the game ever reacts.
patterns.knobs: which events are broadcast; how often and through which channel

can_cause.name: Encouraged Return Visits
can_cause.why: Messages sent outside the game can remind absent players about chores, recent happenings, or coming events, pulling them back to play.

can_cause.name: Fake Game Cancellations
can_cause.why: Announcements through outside media can be staged to pretend a game has been shut down, which fits games that hide that they are games.

can_cause.name: Game Instance Stories
can_cause.why: Whatever gets announced outside the game retells what happened in a particular play session, so each broadcast is a small story of that session.

can_cause.name: Invites
can_cause.why: Letting players decide to push game news outward means they can use that channel to ask friends to join, without the game spamming everyone.

can_cause.name: Non-Player Help
can_cause.why: Players can choose to post their game situation outside the game, which lets people who aren't playing step in and assist them.

can_cause.name: Public Player Statistics
can_cause.why: Sending out what players are doing makes their performance visible to anyone, which works as openly available information about how players are doing.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Because game events appear in another medium, people not playing can follow along and watch, so watching becomes easy to arrange.

can_cause.name: Value of Effort
can_cause.why: Showing one's feats, like speedruns or builds, to an outside audience gives the effort extra worth through others seeing it.

changes.name: Achievements
changes.why: Earned achievements make good good-news items to announce outside the game, so broadcasting often focuses on them.

changes.name: Construction
changes.why: When players can trigger broadcasts, things they built become worth showing off, so the effort of building feels more worthwhile.

changes.name: Encouraged Return Visits
changes.why: Outside messages can remind you of tasks you need to do, strengthening the pull to return.

changes.name: Ephemeral Events
changes.why: Outside messages can warn players that a short-lived event is coming, so they know to come back and catch it.

changes.name: Events Timed to the Real World
changes.why: Ads for upcoming events can work well here, since things seen in the real world can remind people of the game event.

changes.name: Performance Uncertainty
changes.why: Moments where the outcome of a player's skill is in doubt make interesting news, so they are good candidates for being announced outside.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Handing out rewards is positive news, so it is a fitting event to announce through outside channels.

changes.name: Public Player Statistics
changes.why: Sending stats out to people who aren't even playing, such as on Facebook, widens who gets to see them.

patterns.name: Crosshairs
patterns.what_it_is: An on-screen mark that helps aim a weapon or choose a target more precisely.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The marker must show where an action will land, with fixed or movable placement, and match how aiming really works. It can also carry accuracy or target information.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A crosshair is drawn on screen, but it is not where shots actually go, so it does not help aiming.
patterns.knobs: fixed or movable; auto-aim strength; how much accuracy or target information it shows

can_cause.name: God Fingers
can_cause.why: When the aim point can move freely, the reticle acts as a pointer that triggers actions directly on whatever it targets, instead of picking items from a list.

can_cause.name: HUD Interfaces
can_cause.why: Because the reticle is a graphic laid over the game view, it can become part of the heads-up display or cause one to be added.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The reticle is an overlay that the characters in the game world couldn't see, so adding it brings in an element existing only for the player.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: The reticle shows players where a shot will go, which makes aiming and firing at targets easier to do.

changes.name: Combat
changes.why: Fighting often depends on aiming at foes, and the reticle supports this by helping players target them accurately.

changes.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
changes.why: The reticle gives visual help for actions needing precise hand control, since players can see exactly what their aim is pointing at.

changes.name: Friendly Fire
changes.why: The reticle can change when it points at allies, or vanish entirely, which warns players and helps prevent them from hitting teammates.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: The reticle's look is often changed to match whichever weapon is currently equipped, so it reflects that weapon's behavior.

patterns.name: Equipment Slots
patterns.what_it_is: Spaces where the player puts the items they want to use.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Slots must be limited and specialised so that choosing for one means giving up another, and items must differ enough to make that a real trade-off.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Slots that can always be filled with the same best items so there is never a choice.
patterns.knobs: number and types of slots; whether they replace or add to an inventory; how much items differ

can_cause.name: Competence Areas
can_cause.why: When slots are the only way to carry gear, the particular mix of items a player places in them can amount to choosing what they are good at.

can_cause.name: Inventories
can_cause.why: Slots can work as a strictly limited inventory, so a player holds only what fits in the slots and must leave or drop other items.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: With only a few slots and no general inventory, putting one item in a slot means giving up another, so players weigh each option's pros and cons.

changes.name: Armor
changes.why: Each slot is dedicated to one kind of gear, so armor pieces get their own slots that show which armor the player is wearing.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Slots by themselves, without an inventory, simplify equipment handling, which suits avatars where players focus on a single mode of interaction.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Used with an inventory, slots let players change how a character performs by choosing which carried items are equipped, including companions as well as player characters.

changes.name: Equipment
changes.why: Slots let players show which of the many items they found they want to use, and each slot is limited to a certain type of equipment.

changes.name: Inventories
changes.why: Slots can sit on top of an inventory as the place where players pick what to use, or replace it by tightly limiting what can be carried.

changes.name: Tools
changes.why: A slot can be reserved for tools, so tools have their own dedicated place instead of being mixed into a generic carrying list.

changes.name: Weapons
changes.why: Weapons get dedicated slots, often one per hand, with two-handed weapons filling both, and sometimes extra weapon slots to give players more choice.

patterns.name: Score Tracks
patterns.what_it_is: A strip on which the players' points are marked.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Provide a track with enough spaces, a rule for overflow or shared spots, and public visibility. It gains meaning when it also affects turn order or tiebreaks.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A track that only mirrors a number kept elsewhere, is hidden or rarely consulted, so no one reacts to what it shows.
patterns.knobs: track length; what happens at the end or on shared spots; whether position affects turn order or ties

can_cause.name: Beat the Leader
can_cause.why: Because everyone can see who is ahead on the track, players may team up against the front-runner to pull them back.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: The track's markers show each player's current standing, so the board itself reports the state of the game.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Seeing all players' markers on one track gives a quick summary of how everyone is doing in scoring.

can_cause.name: Movement
can_cause.why: Whenever points are gained, a player's marker is moved along the track, so updating a score is itself a kind of moving.

can_cause.name: Races
can_cause.why: Since markers advance as points are earned, players are effectively racing each other along the track.

can_cause.name: Speedending
can_cause.why: A player who leads but sees rivals about to overtake them can try to finish the game early.

can_cause.name: Varying Turn Orders
can_cause.why: The positions of markers on the track can decide who goes first each round, so order changes as standings change.

changes.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
changes.why: A track lets one marker per player stand in for many point tokens, so fewer tokens are needed, though not none.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: Moving a marker on a track makes recording points less tedious than handling piles of tokens, which cuts some of the administrative effort.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: A board that isn't already a score track can have one added to it, so tracking progress adds to the board.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: The track gives a way to store and display points, which changes how scores are handled in play.

changes.name: Tiebreakers
changes.why: Players sharing or reaching the same spot on the track can have ties settled by how the track's positions are arranged or ordered.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: Players' places on the track can fix who acts when, as in games where track position sets turn order.

patterns.name: Gameplay Statistics
patterns.what_it_is: Records of values and events that can be viewed during or after the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must track meaningful events or values and make them reachable by players during or after play, and players must care about them, for example to compare or review. Presentation should be readable and persistent.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A stats screen full of numbers that nobody looks at or can use, or records that are lost as soon as the session ends.
patterns.knobs: what is recorded; how long it is kept and who can see it

can_cause.name: Excise
can_cause.why: When players must update their own character sheets by hand, that bookkeeping chore is itself the work of keeping gameplay records.

can_cause.name: Memorabilia
can_cause.why: Saved records of what happened in play give players a keepsake of their games that they can look back on later.

can_cause.name: Spectators
can_cause.why: Because the records exist as artifacts outside the moment of play, other people can follow and watch what players have done.

can_cause.name: Meta Servers
can_cause.why: Meta servers gather results like stats from each individual game server, so those per-match numbers are the material that lets a meta server keep player records across games.

changes.name: Abstract Player Constructs
changes.why: Records about a player's progress are often held inside constructs that stand in for the player, so the statistics shape what those hold.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Many statistics are stored in the characters themselves, so the recorded values change how a character is described.

changes.name: Game Lobbies
changes.why: Records can be shown in systems outside actual play such as lobbies, which alters what players see there.

changes.name: Scores
changes.why: Player scores are one of the main things worth recording, so tracking them turns plain points into lasting records.

changes.name: Public Player Statistics
changes.why: Public stats are simply the player's own recorded gameplay data opened up so others can see it, not just the player.

patterns.name: Vision Modes
patterns.what_it_is: The same view of the world is shown in different ways, such as thermal vision.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each mode must reveal information the normal view hides, such as hidden objects or clues, and have a cost, limit or tradeoff so switching is a real decision. Otherwise one mode wins permanently.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A colored filter that shows exactly the same information as the normal view.
patterns.knobs: what each mode reveals; energy or duration limits; how many modes exist; how they are unlocked

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Switching views can uncover hints in the world that are invisible in the normal view, so players learn things by looking differently.

can_cause.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
can_cause.why: A special view can make certain objects stand out from their surroundings, so players can spot the things that matter.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Because the views often act as special abilities, players feel more powerful and influential than the game's actual demands warrant.

can_cause.name: Secret Areas
can_cause.why: A different view can reveal hidden routes or places that the ordinary view never shows, leading players to concealed spaces.

can_cause.name: Varied Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players must keep changing how they look at the world, so the way they play shifts between different viewing styles.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Special ways of seeing give the avatar a perceptual capacity, which counts as an abstract character trait.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: Special sight options in a first-person view make what the player perceives a mix of their own attention and the character's abilities.

can_cause.name: Privileged Abilities
can_cause.why: Switching how the world is seen does not add actions but changes what a player perceives and can do, setting them apart.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: Seeing through a character's eyes suits sight-altering abilities, so the same first-person camera can show different information depending on the active mode.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: The same game world can be presented in several ways, so the mode changes what players perceive of it without changing the world.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: Overview perspectives have no story reason to hide information, but with huge amounts of data, separate views can reduce overload.

changes.name: Line of Sight
changes.why: A mode can make some things visible that were hidden, or let sight pass through objects that normally block it.

changes.name: Picture-in-Picture Views
changes.why: The mode can be applied to a small inset window only, changing what is shown there while the main picture stays unchanged.

changes.name: Third-Person Views
changes.why: Watching a character from behind or above fits sight-altering abilities, so the same camera can show different information depending on the active mode.

changes.name: Secret Areas
changes.why: Special ways of seeing can help players notice a hidden area or sense that something is unusual.

conflicts_with.name: Experimenting
conflicts_with.why: Modes that reveal important objects spare players from exploring to find them.

conflicts_with.name: Gameplay Mastery
conflicts_with.why: Game-provided help with seeing makes challenges easier, so players need less of their own skill.

patterns.name: Discard Piles
patterns.what_it_is: A place where cards or tiles are put after they have been played.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The pile must have a rule for whether it is open or closed and whether cards come back. Its contents must matter, for example by refilling the deck or being searchable.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A pile where used cards just sit, nobody looks at it and it never affects play.
patterns.knobs: open or closed; whether cards can be retrieved; whether it refills the deck

can_cause.name: Drafting Spreads
can_cause.why: When players may take from the pile of used cards, as in Rummy's last played card or the whole pile, it becomes a source for refilling hands.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: If a game ends after cards or tiles are used up, a growing pile of used ones shows players how far along the game is.

can_cause.name: Cooldown
can_cause.why: Cards placed in the discard pile are unlikely to return to the hand right away, creating a waiting period before reuse.

can_cause.name: Replays
can_cause.why: Keeping a separate discard pile for each trick lets players rebuild what was played afterwards, acting as a replay of a card game.

changes.name: Analysis Paralysis
changes.why: Piles anyone can look through give players a fuller picture of the game, which gives them more to think over and can stall decisions.

changes.name: Cards
changes.why: Cards that have been played get a set place to go, and in some games can later be taken back out of it.

changes.name: Collectible Card Games
changes.why: Used cards wait in the pile so a player's whole set gets played before any card is used again.

changes.name: Decks
changes.why: Used cards wait in the pile so every card gets played before reuse, so the pile shapes how a deck cycles.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: When the drawing stack runs out, the used cards can be shuffled to form a new one, so they return to play.

changes.name: Hands
changes.why: Where players may pick cards back out of the pile, what they end up holding is partly decided by what has been thrown away.

changes.name: Memorizing
changes.why: Hidden piles that can't be looked through reward players who remember which cards were already played, as with Blackjack.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Piles whose contents are visible let players work out what remains and what may come, which gives them material to plan with.

changes.name: Tiles
changes.why: Tiles that have been played get a set place to go, just like used cards, and may be reused later.

patterns.name: God Fingers
patterns.what_it_is: An interface element showing where the player is currently acting on the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A pointer that works anywhere in the world and is unaffected by it, with actions tied to what it selects or points at. The input handling must be responsive and the available actions clear.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A cursor that appears but can only click menus, or one that merely shows position without letting players act on the world.
patterns.knobs: which actions the pointer allows; selection modes; its range and precision

can_cause.name: Focus Loci
can_cause.why: A pointer lets players pick any spot in the world to act on or look at, so it works as a point of focus.

can_cause.name: Geospatial Game Widgets
can_cause.why: The pointer is an interface element tied to locations in the game world, which lets players navigate and interact with places regardless of where their characters are.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The pointer is not affected by world events and usually exists outside the game's fiction, so it counts as an element the characters can't perceive.

changes.name: Attention Demanding Gameplay
changes.why: Because the pointer lets players select and command characters or units from anywhere, they can handle many simultaneous demands more easily.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: Players use the pointer to choose an avatar, direct where it goes, or pick what it interacts with, shaping how the avatar is controlled.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: A pointer fits an overhead view naturally, because players can pan and scroll with it to bring new parts of the world into sight.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Players click on units to select them, then point to show where they should move or what they should attack.

conflicts_with.name: Detective Structures
conflicts_with.why: In open worlds, a pointer-style control lets players explore away from any particular character, breaking the single-character limit on information.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A free, world-external pointer to manipulate things isn't part of the fiction, unlike a figure the player controls inside it.

conflicts_with.name: First-Person Views
conflicts_with.why: The choice of where the player's attention and control sit limits which views are possible, and an avatar's-eye view doesn't fit well with that kind of control.

patterns.name: HUD Interfaces
patterns.what_it_is: Information and action buttons are shown over the picture of the world, as if on glass before the eyes.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: It must show the information players need at the moments they need it without cluttering the view, and update reliably with the game state. What it includes should match what the design wants players to track.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A screen overlay with decorative or redundant elements that tell the player nothing useful for decisions.
patterns.knobs: what information is shown; how large and prominent; whether it fits the game world

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A HUD can be the only place a player gets certain hints, so by showing them it creates those clues in the first place.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: An overlay layer is a clear, always-visible spot for showing the current condition of the game, so it naturally supplies these indicators.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Because the overlay sits in front of the world view, it gives players a clear place to see the overall situation at a glance.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: HUDs often display things like attributes that characters in the game world wouldn't see or know about, which brings in elements outside the fiction.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: When the overlay doesn't clash with the game world's fiction, the information shown feels like it belongs, which helps keep the theme coherent.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Showing a handle or health value on screen gives an avatar abstract qualities, which is a minimal form of character.

changes.name: Aim & Shoot
changes.why: A crosshair on the overlay directly shapes how players aim and fire, since it shows them where their shots will go.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: A HUD can remind players of clues available elsewhere, changing how easily they recall or find them.

changes.name: Equipment Slots
changes.why: When slots replace an inventory they offer little functionality, so they are simple enough to fit directly into the heads-up display.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: The view gives no overview of the whole game state, so extra on-screen information such as health, weapons or maps is added to make up for it.

changes.name: Health
changes.why: When the player's own avatar isn't visible, a heads-up display is how its health value gets shown to them.

changes.name: Lives
changes.why: Lives are typically shown continuously on the HUD because they are central to how a session is progressing.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: On-screen displays of handles or health give an avatar abstract qualities.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Information overlaid on the display isn't part of the world, and may clash with some themes.

patterns.name: Non-Diegetic Features
patterns.what_it_is: Parts of the game's presentation that do not fit into its fictional world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game needs a world with a fiction and then must show information that does not belong to it, such as indicators, markers or notifications. Placement and prominence decide how much they break consistency.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A HUD element dressed up as an in-world object so it looks diegetic, or an indicator that duplicates what the world already shows and adds nothing.
patterns.knobs: how much non-diegetic information is shown; how prominent it is and whether it can be hidden

can_cause.name: Multiplayer Games
can_cause.why: When several people play together, they can all see the out-of-world elements on screen, which gives them something shared to notice and talk about.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
can_cause.why: Because players notice the out-of-world elements, they chat about them with each other, and that talk itself happens outside the game world.

changes.name: Drop-In/Drop-Out
changes.why: Out-of-world notices can tell players when others join or leave a game that allows this, keeping everyone informed.

changes.name: Game State Indicators
changes.why: Since information about the game's status is usually presented outside the fiction, these features often take the form of state indicators.

changes.name: Player/Character Awareness Consistency
changes.why: Showing players extra information can bring what they know closer to what their character would plausibly know.

conflicts_with.name: Clues
conflicts_with.why: Clues delivered through interface elements from outside the game world break the consistency of its setting.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Having elements that aren't part of the world directly contradicts a world made only of its own elements.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Out-of-world elements don't match the game's theme or setting, which challenges how well everything fits together thematically.

patterns.name: Cameras
patterns.what_it_is: Abstract objects that define the point from which the game world is seen.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The camera type (follow or fixed, over-shoulder or overhead) must be chosen to match what players need to see, and control must not burden them. It affects surprise and tension through what is hidden.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A camera is present but it is fixed to show everything or is so awkward that it gets in the way, and view makes no difference to play.
patterns.knobs: camera type and angle; player control or automatic; field of view

can_cause.name: Dexterity-Based Actions
can_cause.why: When steering the camera is not easy during play, the player must also manage fiddly controls, which adds a skill demand to the game.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Actions
can_cause.why: If players can control the camera, they need extra actions such as panning, rotating or zooming that exist only to adjust the view.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Letting players adjust or switch the camera means they decide for themselves which part of the world they look at.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: A camera can show the world from a better spot than any single game element, so players can take in the overall situation.

can_cause.name: God Views
can_cause.why: A camera that stays fixed relative to the environment, rather than following an entity, gives the player a view over the world from above.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: A camera that moves along with a game entity shows that entity from outside, giving the player a view of it.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When the camera moves freely between units, players cannot watch everywhere, so they must pick which parts of the world deserve their attention.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Cameras determine what part of the game world players see and from where, so they shape how the world is presented.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Because the camera decides how play is shown to the player, changing it changes how gameplay is mediated.

changes.name: Picture-in-Picture Views
changes.why: A camera can supply a third-person view inside a first-person game by showing it in a small inset.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: A camera is an incorporeal thing that gives views no character in the game world has or could have, which clashes with in-world consistency.

patterns.name: Game Lobbies
patterns.what_it_is: A place where players gather before a game starts.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Provide a place to find players and games, choose settings, and communicate before starting. It needs server infrastructure and communication tools.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A lobby screen exists, but it only auto-assigns players with no choice or talk, so it is just a loading screen.
patterns.knobs: lobby scope; communication tools; filters and matchmaking options

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Because a lobby lets players pick which game to join or who to team up with, they get real control over their playing partners.

changes.name: Back-to-Back Game Sessions
changes.why: In games made of repeated matches, the lobby is where players hang out between rounds and talk over the match they just finished.

changes.name: Difficulty Levels
changes.why: When players set the rules together, lobby chat gives them a place to negotiate which difficulty setting the group will use.

changes.name: Early Elimination
changes.why: Players knocked out before a match ends can wait in the lobby and stay busy until the next game starts.

changes.name: Game Servers
changes.why: Once a player connects to a particular server, a lobby on that server lets everyone there gather before play starts.

changes.name: Instances
changes.why: Lobbies used during play let players find partners first and then enter an instance together instead of alone.

changes.name: Interruptibility
changes.why: When pausing is allowed, the lobby shows who has stepped away and lets players agree how to deal with it.

changes.name: Late Arriving Players
changes.why: Players already in the lobby can chat and decide whether to wait for others to show up or begin immediately.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Lobbies let players in computer-run multiplayer games choose what kind of game to play and with whom.

changes.name: Meta Games
changes.why: When a game is really a series of matches, the lobby is the shared space that ties those matches together.

changes.name: Meta Servers
changes.why: At the top level, a lobby on a meta server helps players browse and choose which game server to join.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: Lobbies help players who are far apart find each other and pick roles.

changes.name: Player Elimination
changes.why: Players who are out of the current match can use the lobby to occupy themselves until the match is over.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Lobbies give players a place to gather and form teams before play starts.

changes.name: TvT
changes.why: Lobbies let players sort out who joins and leaves before play, which helps when games are run through a mediating system.

patterns.name: Mini-maps
patterns.what_it_is: A small map showing the game world in broad outline.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The map must show the player's position and relevant things in the world in a readable way, and the world must be big enough that overview is needed. What it shows or hides should be chosen deliberately.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A small map that is too vague or too cluttered to read, or a world so small that nobody ever looks at it.
patterns.knobs: how much it shows: zoom, markers, hidden areas

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: A mini-map can carry hints that exist only on it, telling players roughly where something interesting is so they must still find the exact spot in the world.

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Besides showing where the player's focus is, a mini-map often displays other information about the current situation, so it works as a status display.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: By showing the whole world area separately from the main view, it lets players see how their position relates to the world at a glance.

can_cause.name: Picture-in-Picture Views
can_cause.why: A mini-map is a small extra display placed inside the main screen that shows a different view of the world than the main one.

can_cause.name: Split-Screen Views
can_cause.why: A mini-map is a small, continuously updated alternate view of the game world, so it counts as a weak form of split-screen.

can_cause.name: Team Strategy Identification
can_cause.why: In team games, a mini-map shows where teammates are, so players can base a joint approach on knowing everyone's positions.

changes.name: Check Points
changes.why: Where checkpoints are located in the world can be marked on the mini-map, making them visible to players.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: Clues can be placed only on the mini-map to point to a general area while the player must look in the world to pinpoint it.

changes.name: Environmental Effects
changes.why: The mini-map can show where environmental effects are and the main environment features such as land and sea, so players know what lies around.

changes.name: Focus Loci
changes.why: The mini-map shows where players' points of attention are, including other players' locations, relating them to the larger world.

changes.name: Game World Exploration
changes.why: Seeing the layout ahead of time or recording it afterward helps players explore, sometimes making exploration so easy it stops being a challenge.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Showing where players are and where to go helps them find their way, and can make navigating trivial.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A mini-map presents the world or level in a small, compact form, and may let players zoom or pan to see different parts.

changes.name: Installations
changes.why: Installations are world elements that can be interesting to mark on the mini-map so players know where they are.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Levels can be shown in compact form on a mini-map just as larger game worlds can.

changes.name: Multiplayer Games
changes.why: In games with many players, the mini-map lets them see teammates and others, which supports working together.

changes.name: Races
changes.why: In races, the mini-map gives players awareness of the course and surroundings, which is one main reason for adding it.

changes.name: Strategic Locations
changes.why: Important places in the world are worth displaying on the mini-map so players can quickly spot them.

changes.name: Teams
changes.why: Team members can see each other's positions on the mini-map, which helps them coordinate and combine their actions.

changes.name: Traverse
changes.why: Because players can see the world layout and their position, moving from place to place becomes easier.

changes.name: Team Combos
changes.why: A mini-map shows teammates' and enemies' positions, giving players the information they need to coordinate their combined actions.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Exploration
conflicts_with.why: If a mini-map shows places the player hasn't been to, it hands over what they were supposed to discover.

conflicts_with.name: Game World Navigation
conflicts_with.why: Showing position and direction on a small map takes away the uncertainty that navigation depends on, so the challenge can vanish.

patterns.name: Point of Interest Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: Hints that guide the player to important places and objects in the world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The indicator must be clear and well timed, pointing at things that really matter. The game has to decide how much help it gives so it doesn't ruin exploration.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A marker is always on screen but is ignored, or points at things that don't matter.
patterns.knobs: how many things are marked; how obvious the marker is; when it appears

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: When the game tells players where to go or look, they need less effort to find their way, so play becomes easier and more relaxed.

can_cause.name: Characters
can_cause.why: Pointing out notable things adds a perceptual capability to the avatar, which counts as an abstract trait of a character.

can_cause.name: Player/Character Skill Composites
can_cause.why: When added to a first-person view, they let what is noticed in the world depend on both the player and the character's abilities.

changes.name: Cameras
changes.why: Indicators often work by moving or turning the camera toward the interesting spot, so the camera's behavior changes.

changes.name: Clues
changes.why: By drawing attention to certain places, indicators make it more likely that players notice clues placed there.

changes.name: Diegetically Outstanding Features
changes.why: Pointing players at a spot makes them aware of features in the world that stand out, which they might otherwise miss.

changes.name: First-Person Views
changes.why: Indicators can be used in first-person play, where they can stand in for what the character perceives.

changes.name: Game World Navigation
changes.why: Showing which way to move or look makes it easier for players to find their way through complicated game worlds.

changes.name: God Views
changes.why: Indicators work with overhead perspectives too, guiding attention to important spots in the world.

changes.name: Mini-maps
changes.why: A mini-map or compass is one interface element that can carry the pointer toward an interesting location.

changes.name: Third-Person Views
changes.why: Indicators can be used when players see their avatar from behind, for example turning it toward the exit.

conflicts_with.name: Experimenting
conflicts_with.why: Pointing out important entities for the player removes the need to search and explore for them.

patterns.name: Alarms
patterns.what_it_is: Warnings about an important change in the game, like fuel running low or guards spotting the hero.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: A clear trigger and a perceivable signal, plus a real consequence (enemies converge, a timer starts) so players must react. Players should know what raised the alarm and whether it can be stopped.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A siren sounds but nothing in play changes, so players ignore it.
patterns.knobs: what triggers it; how loud or visible; what penalty follows; whether it can be reset

can_cause.name: Bluffing
can_cause.why: When players can trigger alarms themselves, they can set off a false one to mislead others, so the alarm becomes a tool for deception.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: Since alarms are triggered at set moments, a designer can use them to make a planned story beat happen reliably, though player-controlled alarms make this harder.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Alarms can be used against enemies or as distractions, adding tactical options beyond just being a hazard.

can_cause.name: Thematic Consistency
can_cause.why: The theme can call for alarms and limit how they look and work, so alarms that fit the setting help keep the world consistent.

changes.name: Enemies
changes.why: Raising an alarm can bring in new enemies or send existing ones to the spot, and it explains why their behavior changes.

changes.name: Game Boards
changes.why: A raised alarm changes how players have to relate to the board, since the situation on it is now different.

changes.name: Game State Overviews
changes.why: Alarms pass along information about what is happening in the game, so they work as a quick summary of important changes.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: Once an alarm is raised, players must treat the world differently than before, because its state has changed.

changes.name: Guard
changes.why: Alarms tell guarding players about threats or detection, which makes the job of protecting something easier.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: A raised alarm changes how players must approach the level they are in, because conditions there have changed.

changes.name: Reconnaissance
changes.why: Setting off an alarm can mean the scouting goal has failed, or make finishing it harder by adding a penalty.

changes.name: Rescue
changes.why: Alarms can make the rescue longer or harder, since being detected can bring trouble down on the players.

changes.name: Stealth
changes.why: Setting off an alarm shows the player was spotted, so it can mean failing a sneaking goal or make it harder to finish.

changes.name: Thematic Consistency
changes.why: Alarms can help build a game's theme, but the theme in turn limits what kinds of alarms fit.

changes.name: Units
changes.why: Units controlled by the system may switch from passive to active behavior when an alarm goes off.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Letting only special avatars or units raise alarms keeps the story on track but may make no sense within the game world.

patterns.name: Auxiliary Game Screens
patterns.what_it_is: The game uses several separate screens, such as a TV and a phone at once.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each screen must show information that differs from, or adds to, the main screen, such as private data or overviews, so that looking at it affects decisions. Decide whether it shows shared overviews or private facts.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A second screen only mirrors the main one or shows decoration, so no one needs to look at it.
patterns.knobs: what information goes on the screens; shared or private; number of screens

can_cause.name: Conceal
can_cause.why: Because each player's extra screen can show private views, one player can know things others don't, which lets designers build goals about hiding information from opponents.

can_cause.name: Crossmedia Gameplay
can_cause.why: Since play can stretch across different kinds of displays, such as a console and a handheld, the game already spans media, though only in a mild way.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: A secondary screen can hold a summary of the game's situation, like health or scores, so players needn't leave the main view to check it.

patterns.name: Crossmedia Gameplay
patterns.what_it_is: One session is played across several different kinds of media at once.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Each medium must be given a distinct job that the others cannot do, and the media must be linked by shared game state or goals. Players need clear ways to move between media without friction.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with a companion website or app that only shows ads or duplicates information, so dropping it changes nothing in play.
patterns.knobs: how many media are used; how much each one contributes to the game state

can_cause.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
can_cause.why: When a game spreads across many media, those media can be blended among everyday non-game media, so players may not be sure what belongs to the game.

can_cause.name: Rabbit Hole Invitations
can_cause.why: Non-interactive media like TV shows and commercials can be used to invite people into the game, which is easier before the main play begins.

can_cause.name: Real World Gameplay Spaces
can_cause.why: If the media a game needs are in different places, or some use location as input, play spreads into the physical world.

can_cause.name: Functional Roles
can_cause.why: When players use different devices or media, each can only do certain things, which pushes them toward different roles.

can_cause.name: Predetermined Story Structures
can_cause.why: The story parts can be spread over several different media, so that crossmedia play carries the prepared story.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Using several media lets a fixed story be revealed in pieces from different viewpoints, or lets clues arrive from varied sources.

patterns.name: Drafting Spreads
patterns.what_it_is: The options players take turns choosing from are laid out in view of everyone.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The display must show several different elements that are refilled in a clear way. Their values must differ so that choosing and watching others matters.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A display where all cards are alike or the order is fixed, so picking is not a decision.
patterns.knobs: number of cards shown; how it is refilled; extra cost to pick deeper ones

can_cause.name: First Player Advantages
can_cause.why: Whoever picks first sees the whole spread untouched and can grab the best item, so later players face weaker leftovers.

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Showing several items at once lets players pick among them, and showing more items gives them more options to choose from.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Because the available items are visible, players can foresee what they might get, and a bigger display makes outcomes easier to anticipate.

can_cause.name: Trade-Offs
can_cause.why: When reaching items further down the spread costs something extra, players must weigh a better item against paying that price.

changes.name: Deck Building
changes.why: The page only says spreads can be used in games with deck building; it gives no reason for how they change it.

changes.name: Decks
changes.why: The spread is a way to draft items out of a deck, so players pick from visible cards rather than only taking unknown ones.

changes.name: Drafting
changes.why: An open display gives drafting a visible set of options, letting players see alternatives and guess what others may take later.

changes.name: Drawing Stacks
changes.why: Spreads are often built from part of a drawing stack, which also supplies replacements when items are taken.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Since the displayed options often come from random sources, players choosing among them reduces how much chance decides what they get.

patterns.name: Mimetic Interfaces
patterns.what_it_is: Sensors judge how accurately the player copies movements, and this is part of the game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The sensors must measure real physical movement and the game must score how well it is done. Tolerance should be tuned so players can learn gradually.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A game with a themed controller, such as a plastic guitar, where pressing buttons gives the same result and the physical action is not really measured.
patterns.knobs: how strictly the performance is judged; how tolerant the early levels are

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Because the game reads the player's real bodily movements as input, the player has to act out the in-game action rather than just trigger it.

can_cause.name: Exaggerated Perception of Influence
can_cause.why: Games can let players keep going, judge leniently, or play the real sounds, so players feel they are performing better than they actually are.

can_cause.name: Player Physical Prowess
can_cause.why: When the required movements resemble real-world skills, how well players do depends on their own physical ability.

can_cause.name: Role Fulfillment
can_cause.why: The movements copy what athletes or musicians do, so performing them lets players feel they are taking on that role.

changes.name: Minigames
changes.why: Such interfaces usually support only a narrow set of detectable actions, so short minigames suit them and add variety through changing themes.

changes.name: Rhythm-Based Actions
changes.why: Rhythms are simple to present and simple to check against what the player does, so measuring physical performance fits them well.

conflicts_with.name: AI Players
conflicts_with.why: A computer player doesn't use the physical interface, so when people must act with their bodies, the AI clearly isn't competing under the same conditions.

conflicts_with.name: Minimalized Social Weight
conflicts_with.why: These interfaces draw attention to the player because they involve visible physical performance, which works against keeping social pressure low.

conflicts_with.name: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
conflicts_with.why: One feeds ordinary non-game activities into the game, while the other builds in-game activities that merely resemble real ones, so the two approaches don't fit together.

patterns.name: Near Miss Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: After a failure, the player sees how close they or others came to the goal.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must measure closeness to success and show it clearly after a failure. It needs to be informative enough that players use it for their next attempt.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A generic failure message, or a near-miss display that shows the same thing whether the miss was narrow or wide.
patterns.knobs: how precisely the near-miss is measured and shown; how often it is displayed

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Seeing how close a failed try came tells the player what to change, so the near-miss information works as a hint for the next attempt.

can_cause.name: Determinable Chance to Succeed
can_cause.why: Knowing how narrowly they missed lets players estimate how likely the next try is to work, so the odds become something they can judge.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: They are basic indicators that show how close something came, contributing information about the state.

can_cause.name: Luck
can_cause.why: When a later attempt with poor odds succeeds, players feel lucky, and knowing how near earlier misses were sharpens that feeling.

can_cause.name: Replayability
can_cause.why: Learning how close they came makes players want to try again, since the near miss suggests success is within reach next time.

can_cause.name: Tension
can_cause.why: Being told they almost succeeded makes players more aware of how near the goal was, which raises the strain before the next attempt.

can_cause.name: Outcome Indicators
can_cause.why: A near miss indicator is a special case that reports the result of an action that almost succeeded, so it counts as an outcome indicator.

changes.name: Outcome Indicators
changes.why: A near-miss indicator is itself a kind of outcome indicator, reporting how a failed attempt turned out rather than just that it failed.

changes.name: Save-Load Cycles
changes.why: When players can reload saved states, seeing how nearly they succeeded tempts them to reload and retry the attempt.

changes.name: Stimulated Planning
changes.why: Near-miss feedback gives players fresh information that pushes them to think through and adjust their plans as part of play.

changes.name: Tactical Planning
changes.why: Learning how close an attempt came gives players information they can use to revise their short-term tactics.

changes.name: Variable Accuracy
changes.why: In games where aim quality varies, a player who was nearly hit can be given lower accuracy to offset the near-miss warning.

conflicts_with.name: Auto-Aim
conflicts_with.why: Assisted aim bends shots toward targets, so it can become impossible to notice a shot that nearly missed, leaving nothing for such indicators to show.

patterns.name: Picture-in-Picture Views
patterns.what_it_is: One image or view is shown inside another.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The inset must show information players really need during play that the main view cannot, in a place and size that does not hide the main action. Its content should change what players decide.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A small window duplicates what the main view already shows, or is too tiny or cluttered to read, so nobody uses it.
patterns.knobs: what it shows; its size and position; whether players can move, resize or switch it

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: When the small inset shows abstract information, it works as a readout of how the game currently stands, even though it is a view.

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: An inset can show either a local or global view of the game world, giving players a summary they otherwise couldn't see.

can_cause.name: Point of Interest Indicators
can_cause.why: Insets can be shown on the fly during play to draw attention to something important, without replacing the whole screen.

can_cause.name: Split-Screen Views
can_cause.why: The inset divides the display into separate presentations at once, so it is a kind of split screen where one part sits inside the other.

can_cause.name: Third-Person Views
can_cause.why: The inset typically shows something from outside the player's own viewpoint, so it creates an external perspective, unless it shows what a diegetic entity sees.

changes.name: Killcams
changes.why: A killcam shown in only a small part of the screen, instead of taking over the whole presentation, is an inset view used to highlight an event.

patterns.name: Emotes
patterns.what_it_is: Commands with which a player shows their hero's feelings without affecting the game's course.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need a simple way to trigger the actions, visible to nearby others, and a reason to use them such as social play or role-playing.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A few emote buttons that nobody sees, or whose output is the same canned animation that carries no personal expression.
patterns.knobs: freeform or fixed list; how many emotes; who sees them and how they are labelled

can_cause.name: Enactment
can_cause.why: Free-typed emotes let players decide how their character acts and feels, so they get to play out the character's behavior in their own words.

can_cause.name: Roleplaying
can_cause.why: Because players can write what their character does and feels, emotes let them visibly act in character, which shows they are roleplaying.

can_cause.name: Emotional Attachment
can_cause.why: In games where play happens through an avatar, visual emotes give the avatar a way to express feelings inside the game world.

changes.name: Avatars
changes.why: When avatars are graphical, emotes can be paired with set actions like dances that the avatar performs, adding expression to the avatar's behavior.

changes.name: Characters
changes.why: Emotes give players a way to show their character's feelings through actions that change nothing in the game state.

changes.name: Chat Channels
changes.why: Emotes are typed in the chat and shown to nearby players, so they add a different kind of message to the chat channel.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Truly freeform emotes let players put anything they like into the game world, which can break what fits inside the game's fiction.

conflicts_with.name: Thematic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Since players can write anything into a freeform emote, they may add content that clashes with the game's intended theme.

patterns.name: First Player Tokens
patterns.what_it_is: A token shows who goes first in the turn order.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have a changing turn order across rounds and the token must be passed according to clear rules. For orders with more than two positions, more markers or an order track may be needed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A token that stays with one player or is ignored because the order never changes.
patterns.knobs: how the token is passed; how many positions in the order need markers

can_cause.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
can_cause.why: A first player token is a physical piece players use to record a piece of game state, namely who goes first, so it counts as a bookkeeping token.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: When turn order changes, players must spend effort remembering who goes first; the token takes over that remembering and reduces this upkeep burden.

changes.name: First Player Advantages
changes.why: Holding or showing the token makes it obvious to everyone who goes first, which slightly emphasizes the benefit that position gives.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: Without a computer or referee, players must manage the order themselves, and a physical token gives them an easy way to do that.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: The token shows whose turn comes first in each round, helping players keep track of who acts when.

changes.name: Varying Turn Orders
changes.why: When the starting player changes between rounds, the token (or a set of position tokens) marks the current order so nobody forgets or disputes it.

patterns.name: Goal Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: Information that shows the player what their current goals are.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: They must give accurate, timely information about goals and progress toward them, in a form players can read at a glance. The information must connect to something players can act on.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A quest log or marker that is vague, outdated or hidden, so players still don't know what to do or how close they are.
patterns.knobs: how much detail is shown; how precise (exact vs vague); how often it is updated

can_cause.name: Game State Overviews
can_cause.why: Because goal indicators show where players stand relative to their objectives, they naturally help players grasp the overall situation of the game.

changes.name: Time Limits
changes.why: When a time limit is part of how a goal is defined, showing the goal to players changes how that limit is presented and perceived.

changes.name: Time Pressure
changes.why: When a goal includes a deadline, displaying the goal changes how strongly players feel rushed, since the information about it is now visible.

conflicts_with.name: Player-Defined Goals
conflicts_with.why: Showing designer-made goals pulls players' attention toward them, which competes with players inventing and following objectives of their own.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Goal indicators give players information about their objectives, and that openness removes the not-knowing that uncertainty of information depends on.

patterns.name: Tooltips
patterns.what_it_is: An explanation shown when the player pays attention to a game element.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The text must contain information that actually helps decisions, appear at the right moment and with the right delay, and not flood the player. It should cover the elements players are likely to be unsure about.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A popup that merely repeats the item's name or flavour text and teaches nothing about how it works.
patterns.knobs: which elements get tips; how much detail; hover delay before showing

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: Hovering over something reveals text about what it is or does, which hands players hints they can use to decide what to do.

can_cause.name: Non-Diegetic Features
can_cause.why: The text boxes that pop up exist only for the player, not for the game world, and they vanish again shortly afterward.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Tooltips deliver strategic knowledge without cluttering the screen, so players can use it when planning.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: Quick explanations on demand help players keep track of many elements and rules, so intricate games feel easier to handle.

changes.name: Crosshairs
changes.why: Whatever the aiming mark points at can show extra text, so the aim tool also becomes a way to ask the game for details.

changes.name: God Fingers
changes.why: Resting the pointer on an element brings up details about it, so the pointer now also works as a tool for requesting information.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Tooltips give designers a concrete way to pass on knowledge about how the game works, which players can then use to plan.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Pop-up text is not part of the game world, so showing it can break the feeling that everything seen belongs inside that world.

patterns.name: Outcome Indicators
patterns.what_it_is: Extra signals about how an action ended, beyond its effect in the world.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be an outcome that players cannot easily read from the world itself, and the indicator must report it clearly and at the right time. The detail level can be varied to keep some uncertainty.
patterns.just_a_label_when: An indicator that repeats what is already obvious on screen, or one that appears too late or too vaguely to help players understand what happened.
patterns.knobs: what outcomes are indicated; how precise the information is; how long and when it is shown

can_cause.name: Game State Indicators
can_cause.why: Outcome indicators are a kind of game state indicator, since they show players that something changed in the game as a result of what happened.

can_cause.name: Predictable Consequences
can_cause.why: Because players are told what an action achieved, they can learn what their actions lead to and anticipate results of similar actions later.

changes.name: Game State Overviews
changes.why: Outcome indicators can be included as one part of an overview, adding information about what recently happened to the picture of the game's current situation.

changes.name: Rewards
changes.why: Showing the result of an action makes any reward the player earned from it visible and clear, so they notice they succeeded.

conflicts_with.name: Uncertainty of Information
conflicts_with.why: Indicators exist to tell players what an outcome was, so the more clearly they do that, the less is left unknown to the player.

patterns.name: Explicit Random Seeds
patterns.what_it_is: The player can enter the number from which the game builds its randomness.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The game must have a seeded random generator and show a clear way for players to enter and share the seed. The same seed then has to give the same results every time.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A seed field exists, but the game mixes in the clock or other randomness, so identical seeds give different worlds.
patterns.knobs: what the seed controls (whole world, level layout, just a setup); how visible the seed input is

can_cause.name: Freedom of Choice
can_cause.why: Letting players type in their own starting number means they, not the game, decide which random outcome the session is built from.

changes.name: Game Worlds
changes.why: A chosen seed can shape how a world's starting setup is arranged, so the same number brings back the same arrangement.

changes.name: Levels
changes.why: Entering a seed can steer the random setup of a single level, so players can get the same layout again.

changes.name: Luck
changes.why: Players who land a fortunate start can reuse its seed to get that same good start again, reducing how much chance decides things.

changes.name: Procedurally Generated Game Worlds
changes.why: Players supply the number the generator works from, so they control how the automatically built world turns out and can recreate it.

changes.name: Randomness
changes.why: Instead of the game picking a number on its own, the player's number drives the random sequence, changing where the unpredictability comes from.

patterns.name: Loading Hints
patterns.what_it_is: Game tips that are shown while the game is loading.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: There must be waiting moments, and the hints must be useful, correct and varied enough to be read. They should connect to what the player will do next.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Vague or repeated tips, or generic lore lines, that teach nothing about play.
patterns.knobs: how many hints; how they are chosen; how long they display

can_cause.name: Clues
can_cause.why: While players are stuck waiting, the hints shown on screen hand them useful pointers about how to play, so the idle moment becomes a source of guidance.

can_cause.name: Strategic Planning
can_cause.why: Strategic knowledge is too large to show during play, so hints on loading screens give players what they need to plan.

changes.name: Complex Gameplay
changes.why: Tips shown during waits give players a little extra explanation of the game's many parts, making an intricate game easier to grasp and understand.

changes.name: Downtime
changes.why: Loading pauses are forced waits that would otherwise be dull; showing hints in them gives that empty time some value for the player.

changes.name: Predetermined Story Structures
changes.why: Because the hints can touch on the plot, the waiting screens can carry pieces of the authored story forward, not just gameplay advice.

changes.name: Strategic Knowledge
changes.why: Designers gather strategy facts and choose which ones to display, so the hints become a channel that passes this knowledge to players.

patterns.name: Rabbit Hole Invitations
patterns.what_it_is: A vague invitation that draws a person into a particular game.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The cryptic messages must be placed where target players will find them and be intriguing enough to follow. Several are spread over media and time since individual ones may be missed.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A clue is posted, but it is too obscure or in the wrong place, so nobody finds or follows it.
patterns.knobs: how many; where posted; how cryptic; timing

can_cause.name: Crossmedia Gameplay
can_cause.why: The cryptic invitations are placed in media other than the game itself, such as trailers and posters, so play stretches across different media before it begins.

can_cause.name: Extra-Game Broadcasting
can_cause.why: The invitations are messages sent out through channels outside the game proper to reach people and pull them toward playing, which is what this broadcasting means.

can_cause.name: Puzzle Solving
can_cause.why: Because the invitations are cryptic, people must first work out and decode them before they can actually enter the game.

changes.name: Alternate Reality Gameplay
changes.why: Games that hide their existence need a way to recruit players, so cryptic invitations are a fitting way to draw people into such gameplay.

patterns.name: Current Player Tokens
patterns.what_it_is: A token showing whose turn it is.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The token must be clearly visible and the rules must say exactly when it passes. It is most useful when turns are long or players act out of turn.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A token that sits on the table but is passed late or ignored, while players still ask whose turn it is.
patterns.knobs: token size and visibility; the exact moment it is handed over

can_cause.name: Bookkeeping Tokens
can_cause.why: A current player token is a physical marker that records game state, namely whose turn it is, so it counts as a specific kind of bookkeeping token.

changes.name: Excise
changes.why: Knowing clearly who is up makes the chore of closing one turn and starting the next smoother, so less effort is spent on administration.

changes.name: Self-Facilitated Games
changes.why: In games where players run the rules themselves with no automation, the token gives them a simple way to track whose turn it is.

changes.name: Turn Taking
changes.why: In games where players act in turns, the token passes from player to player to show whose turn it is, even after breaks or long turns.

patterns.name: Meta-Postures
patterns.what_it_is: Agreed poses and gestures convey information about the game without breaking character.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The gestures must be few, easy to learn, clearly different from each other and visible without breaking the fiction. Everyone must know the meanings.
