patterns.just_a_label_when: A list of gestures on paper that players forget or ignore, so they keep speaking out of character anyway.
patterns.knobs: how many gestures; how distinct and how visible they are

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Because gestures let players pass on game information silently, they can keep the fiction unbroken instead of forcing everyone to speak out-of-character.

can_cause.name: Meta-Techniques
can_cause.why: Gesture-based signals are one specific kind of out-of-fiction aid, so using them means you are applying a broader meta-technique family.

changes.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
changes.why: Pre-agreed postures turn some out-of-game messages into quiet signals, changing how much plain out-of-character talking players need to do.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: Players must hold or perform the special gesture, so their body movement while acting a character is somewhat restricted.

conflicts_with.name: Diegetic Consistency
conflicts_with.why: Gestures used to signal out-of-game messages are not part of the fiction, though they are less noticeable than speech.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: Having gestures available can lead players to exchange more out-of-game information overall, which undermines the aim of keeping that communication low.

conflicts_with.name: Substitute Actions
conflicts_with.why: Both address the same design problem in different ways, so choosing one approach works against using the other.

patterns.name: Self-Reported Positioning
patterns.what_it_is: The player's physical location matters in the game, but the player reports it to the game themselves.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: Players need a way to report their location, and the game should use that location for something. Trust or checks decide whether reports can be false.
patterns.just_a_label_when: A check-in button whose reported place has no effect on anything in the game.
patterns.knobs: how location is reported; how often; whether reports are checked

can_cause.name: Self-Facilitated Games
can_cause.why: Because players themselves announce where they are, they act as the ones running the location side of the game, giving a limited form of players facilitating play.

can_cause.name: Social Adaptability
can_cause.why: Since players only report a position, they can skip actually traveling when short on time or unwilling, or avoid bothering people at those places.

can_cause.name: Casual Gameplay
can_cause.why: Players can claim a location they aren't at, so they only move as much as they want to.

changes.name: Mediated Gameplay
changes.why: Players send their positions to a game system, so the system relays and holds location information, changing how play is carried through that intermediary.

changes.name: Player-Location Proximity
changes.why: Proximity still matters, but players state their locations instead of being sensed, so they need not truly be there, which relaxes the physical requirement.

patterns.name: Prompting Techniques
patterns.what_it_is: In role-playing: lines that hint how to change the scene without leaving character.
patterns.needs_to_really_work: The group needs shared, easily noticed signals that fit the fiction, learned before play. Different scenes may need different prompts.
patterns.just_a_label_when: Signals are listed in the rulebook, but nobody notices or uses them, so players still break character to change scenes.
patterns.knobs: which signals exist; how subtle they are; who may use them

can_cause.name: Diegetic Consistency
can_cause.why: Prompts are chosen so they fit the game world, so players can signal scene changes without saying anything that feels out of place in the fiction.

can_cause.name: Meta-Techniques
can_cause.why: Prompting is one particular kind of meta-technique, a method players use to support their acting by coordinating without leaving the fiction.

changes.name: Enactment
changes.why: Prompts can be used alongside any kind of acting, letting players signal preferences about where the play goes without interrupting their performance.

changes.name: Physical Enactment
changes.why: Physical, live action play benefits most because prompts let it continue without out-of-character interruptions, so it is where they are used most.

changes.name: Scenes
changes.why: Prompts can be set up to signal that a certain kind of scene should begin or that a current one should end.

conflicts_with.name: Non-Diegetic Communication
conflicts_with.why: Prompting gives players other ways to pass information, so they have less need to step outside the fiction to speak.
